rewritten_text: I wonder how long you would have waited if left to yourself, or if you would have spoken at all without my prompting. My decision to thank you for helping Lydia had a strong effect—perhaps too much. If our happiness comes from breaking a promise, what happens to the moral of the story? I should not have brought it up. This is not right. You need not worry. The moral remains sound. Lady Catherine’s attempts to keep us apart actually cleared away my doubts. My current happiness does not depend on your gratitude; I was already determined to know the truth after hearing from my aunt. Lady Catherine has been useful, which should please her. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it just to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward, or did you have a more serious goal? My true purpose was to see you and decide if I could hope for your love. My stated goal was to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and if so, to tell him what I have since confessed. Will you have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is happening? I am more likely to need time than courage, Elizabeth. It must be done, and if you give me paper, I will do it now. If I did not have my own letter to write, I might sit and admire your handwriting, as someone else once did. But I have an aunt I have neglected for too long. Because she did not want to admit how much her closeness to Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner. Now, having news she knew would be welcome, she felt guilty that her aunt and uncle had missed out on three days of happiness and wrote immediately: My dear aunt, I should have thanked you sooner for your kind letter, but I was too annoyed to write. You assumed more than was true. Now, however, you may imagine whatever you like. Let your fancy run wild; unless you believe I am already married, you cannot be far from the truth.

We spent a few miserable hours waiting for the trial to begin at eleven. My father and the rest of the family had to attend as witnesses, so I went with them. Throughout this pathetic excuse for a trial, I endured absolute torture. It was being decided whether my reckless curiosity would lead to the deaths of two people: one an innocent, joyful baby, and the other a victim of a horrific, infamous murder. Justine was a talented, promising young woman, yet now she faced a shameful death because of me. I would have gladly confessed to the crime myself, but I was away when it happened, and such a claim would have been dismissed as the ramblings of a madman without saving her. Justine looked calm. Dressed in mourning, her naturally engaging face was made even more beautiful by her solemnity. She seemed confident in her innocence and did not tremble, despite being stared at and cursed by thousands. The crowd’s sympathy had been replaced by horror at the crime she was accused of. Though her composure was clearly forced, she summoned the courage to appear brave. Upon entering the court, she spotted us and briefly teared up, but she quickly regained her composure, her sad, affectionate look proving her innocence. The trial started, and after the prosecutor presented the charges, witnesses were called. Several strange facts were used against her that might have convinced anyone who did not know the truth as I did. She had been out all night when the murder occurred and was seen by a market woman near the spot where the child’s body was later found. When asked what she was doing there, she gave a strange, confused answer. She returned home at eight o’clock, and when asked where she had been, she claimed she had been searching for the child and anxiously asked if there was any news.

Every normal boy eventually feels a burning urge to hunt for buried treasure. This impulse struck Tom one day. He looked for Joe Harper but couldn't find him, and Ben Rogers had gone fishing. Finally, he found Huck Finn. Tom pulled him aside to share his secret plan. Huck was interested, as he was always ready for any activity that was fun and cost nothing, since he had plenty of time and no money. Where should we dig, Huck asked. Oh, almost anywhere, Tom replied. Is it hidden everywhere, Huck wondered. No, Tom explained, it is hidden in specific spots like islands, in rotting chests beneath dead trees where shadows fall at midnight, or under the floorboards of haunted houses. Who hides it, Huck asked. Robbers, of course, Tom said. Who else would it be? I would just spend it, Huck noted. Robbers do not do that, Tom insisted. They hide it and leave it. Do they ever come back, Huck asked. No, they usually forget the markers or die. Eventually, someone finds a cryptic map covered in symbols and hieroglyphics that takes a week to decode. What are those, Huck asked. Pictures that do not seem to mean anything, Tom explained. Do you have one, Huck asked. No, Tom admitted. Then how will you find it, Huck pressed. I do not need a map, Tom said. We can check Jackson’s Island, the old haunted house, and all the dead trees. Is it under all of them, Huck asked. Of course not, Tom replied. Then how will you know which one, Huck asked. We will try them all, Tom declared. That will take all summer, Huck argued. But imagine finding a brass pot with a hundred dollars or a chest full of diamonds, Tom countered. Huck’s eyes lit up. That sounds great, he said. Just give me the hundred dollars; I do not need the diamonds.

“I must point out, Sir Walter,” Mr. Shepherd said one morning at Kellynch Hall as he set down his newspaper, “that the current situation works in our favor. The peace will bring many wealthy naval officers home, and they will all need a place to live. There could not be a better time to find reliable tenants. Many have made fortunes during the war. If a rich admiral were to come our way—” “He would be a very lucky man,” Sir Walter interrupted. “Kellynch Hall would be a prize for him, the greatest prize he has ever taken, wouldn’t it, Shepherd?” Mr. Shepherd laughed as expected, then continued, “I believe naval officers are excellent to deal with. They have generous ideas and make ideal tenants. I suggest that if rumors of your plans get out—and it is hard to keep such things secret when you are a man of your status—we should prioritize applications from wealthy naval commanders. I can come over at any time to handle the details so you do not have to worry.” Sir Walter simply nodded. Soon after, he stood and paced the room, remarking sarcastically, “I imagine few naval officers would not be surprised to find themselves in a house like this.” “They would look around and bless their good fortune,” added Mrs. Clay, who was visiting. “But I agree with my father that a sailor would be a very desirable tenant.”

I know she would! The Widow Douglas’ generous invitation was hard to resist. Between that and Tom’s convincing, they decided to keep their plans secret. Tom worried that Huck might show up tonight to give the signal, which dampened his excitement. Still, he couldn't bear to miss the fun at the Widow’s house. He reasoned that since the signal hadn't come the night before, it was unlikely to happen tonight. The certain fun of the evening outweighed the uncertain treasure, so he decided to follow his desires and stop thinking about the money. Three miles downstream, the ferryboat stopped at a wooded hollow. The crowd rushed ashore, filling the forest with shouts and laughter. After exhausting themselves with games, they returned to camp hungry and devoured the food. Following the feast, they rested in the shade of oak trees. Soon, someone shouted, Who is ready for the cave? Everyone was. They grabbed candles and raced up the hill to the cave entrance, which was shaped like the letter A. The heavy oak door was unlocked. Inside, the small chamber felt like an icebox, with limestone walls covered in cold moisture. It felt mysterious to stand in the gloom and look out at the sunny green valley, but the novelty soon faded, and the play resumed. Whenever someone lit a candle, the others would rush them. After a brief struggle, the candle would be knocked over or blown out, leading to more laughter and chasing. Eventually, the group moved down the main path, their flickering lights revealing rock walls that rose sixty feet high. This main tunnel was only eight to ten feet wide. Every few steps, narrow crevices branched off in both directions, as McDougal’s cave was a vast maze of winding paths that led nowhere.

It is quite remarkable that she always hears Jane better than she hears me, though Jane speaks so clearly. Still, she will find her grandmother no deafer than she was two years ago, which is impressive at her age. It has been two full years since she was last here. We have never gone so long without seeing her, and as I told Mrs. Cole, we will hardly know how to make enough of her now. Are you expecting Miss Fairfax soon? Oh yes, next week. Indeed, that must be a great pleasure. Thank you, you are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is surprised and says such nice things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends in Highbury as they are to see her. She will arrive Friday or Saturday, though she cannot say which because Colonel Campbell needs the carriage himself. It is so kind of them to send her the whole way, but they always do. She wrote early to tell us, as we would not have heard from her until next Tuesday or Wednesday otherwise. I imagined as much; I feared there was little chance of hearing about Miss Fairfax today. How kind of you to say so. We would not have heard if not for her upcoming visit. My mother is delighted, as she will stay with us for at least three months. She says so clearly in the letter I am about to read to you. The Campbells are going to Ireland because Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to visit her immediately. They had not planned to go until summer, but she is impatient to see them. Until she married last October, she had never been away from them for more than a week, so being in different countries is very strange for her. She wrote an urgent letter, perhaps in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, to press them to come over. They plan to meet in Dublin and then travel to their country estate, Bally-craig, which I imagine is a beautiful place.

I question how long you might have persisted had you been left alone, or when you would have spoken had I not prompted you. My decision to thank you for your assistance with Lydia clearly had a significant impact. Perhaps too much, for what becomes of the moral if our comfort arises from a broken promise? I should not have broached the topic. This is quite improper. You need not worry, for the moral remains sound. Lady Catherine’s unwarranted attempts to divide us actually resolved my uncertainties. My current happiness does not stem from your desire to express gratitude; I was not inclined to wait for your lead. My aunt’s news gave me hope, and I was resolved to learn the truth immediately. Lady Catherine has been immensely useful, which should please her, as she enjoys being helpful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it simply to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward, or did you intend something more significant? My true goal was to see you and determine if I might ever hope for your affection. My stated purpose, or at least what I told myself, was to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and if so, to make the confession to him that I have since made. Will you ever have the nerve to tell Lady Catherine what is to happen? I am more likely to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. Still, it must be done, and if you provide paper, I shall do it at once. If I did not have a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire your steady penmanship, as another lady once did. However, I have an aunt who must not be ignored any longer. Because she was reluctant to admit how much her closeness with Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s lengthy letter. Now, however, having news she knew would be most welcome, she felt ashamed that her aunt and uncle had already missed three days of joy and immediately began to write: I should have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, for your long and kind account, but I was too annoyed to write. You assumed more than was true. But now, you may assume whatever you wish; let your imagination run wild, and unless you believe me already married, you cannot be far from the truth.

Lacking standard resources, the analyst adopts his opponent's perspective, identifying with them to instantly perceive the simple methods required to lead them into error or miscalculation. Whist has long been recognized for its impact on analytical power, attracting brilliant minds who dismiss chess as trivial. Nothing else so rigorously tests the analytical faculty. While a master chess player may excel only at that game, whist proficiency suggests a capacity for success in any intellectual conflict. By proficiency, I mean a mastery that understands every source of legitimate advantage, many of which remain hidden from the average mind. While attentive observation and a good memory are useful, and following standard rules is common, true analytical skill emerges beyond these limits. The analyst silently draws inferences from a vast array of observations. The difference between players lies not in the logic of their deductions, but in the quality of their observations. The key is knowing what to observe. The skilled player does not limit himself to the game itself; he draws conclusions from external factors. He studies his partner's face and those of his opponents. He observes how they sort their cards, counting trumps and honors based on their glances. He notes every shift in expression—certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment—as the game unfolds. From the way a player collects a trick, he determines if they can win another in that suit. He identifies bluffs by the way cards are played. A stray word, a fumbled card, the anxiety or indifference shown when concealing a hand, the way tricks are counted and arranged, or any sign of hesitation or eagerness—all provide his intuitive perception with clear evidence of the true situation.

It is just a tick. Where did you find it? In the forest. What will you trade for it? I am not sure, as I do not care to sell. Very well, it is a tiny tick regardless. Anyone can catch a tick that is not their own, but I am content. It is sufficient for me. Nonsense, there are ticks everywhere. I could gather a thousand if I chose. Then why do you not? Because you know you cannot. This is an early specimen, I believe. It is the first I have spotted this season. Listen, Huck, I will trade you my tooth for it. Let me see it. Tom unwrapped a piece of paper, and Huckleberry examined it with longing. The urge was powerful. Finally, he asked if it was authentic. Tom pulled back his lip to reveal the gap. Very well, it is a deal. Tom placed the tick inside the percussion-cap box that had recently held the pinchbug, and the boys parted, both feeling richer. Upon arriving at the small, detached schoolhouse, Tom marched inside with the air of someone who had hurried. He hung his hat and sat down with purposeful speed. The teacher, perched in his large chair, was napping to the sound of the students studying. The noise woke him. Thomas Sawyer! Tom knew that his full name meant impending trouble. Sir! Come here. Why are you late again? Tom prepared to lie, but then he noticed two yellow braids hanging down a back he recognized with a jolt of affection. Beside that figure was the only empty seat on the girls' side. He immediately replied that he had stopped to speak with Huckleberry Finn. The master froze in disbelief. The room went silent as the students wondered if Tom had lost his senses. The teacher asked him to repeat himself, and Tom did so clearly. Thomas Sawyer, this is a shocking admission. A simple punishment will not suffice. Remove your jacket. The master struck him until his arm grew weary and the switches were nearly gone. Then he ordered Tom to sit with the girls as a warning. The laughter that spread through the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth, he was overwhelmed by his adoration for his idol and the thrilling fortune of his new seat.

I walked beside a large, friendly-looking man, hoping to chat and learn more, but he immediately started telling the same old story Sir Dinadan had told me when I first angered Sir Sagramor. I excused myself and fell to the back of the group, feeling deeply depressed. I felt ready to leave this difficult life of struggle and defeat, yet I feared the unknown of eternity, especially knowing how many people there already were who knew that same story. Early that afternoon, we caught up to another group of pilgrims. Unlike the first, there was no laughter or joy here. People of all ages were present, from the elderly to infants, but everyone looked miserable. Their faces showed the deep hopelessness of those who have suffered for a long time. They were slaves. Chains connected their hands and feet to belts around their waists, and everyone but the children was linked together by a long chain running from collar to collar. They had walked three hundred miles in eighteen days on very little food, sleeping huddled together like animals. They wore only rags and were barely clothed. Their heavy irons had caused infected, worm-filled sores on their ankles, and their bare feet were cut and bleeding. Originally a group of one hundred, half had been sold along the way. The man in charge rode a horse and carried a long, knotted whip. He used it to strike anyone who stumbled from exhaustion, forcing them to keep moving without saying a word.

He had been entirely unaware of his own influence. He followed her into the garden without any plan to test it. Anxious to see how she handled Frank Churchill’s engagement, he arrived with no selfish motive, hoping only to comfort or advise her if she allowed it. Everything else happened in the moment, driven by his reaction to her words. The wonderful news that she felt nothing for Frank Churchill and was completely free gave him hope that he might eventually win her love. He had not expected immediate success; he only hoped she would let him try to win her heart. The greater hope that followed was even more enchanting: the affection he had hoped to earn was already his. In half an hour, he had moved from deep distress to near-perfect happiness. Her transformation was just as profound. This short time gave them both the precious certainty of being loved, clearing away their mutual ignorance, jealousy, and doubt. He had been jealous of Frank Churchill since the man first arrived. Loving Emma and resenting his rival had happened at the same time, each feeling revealing the other. His jealousy had driven him to leave the country, and the trip to Box Hill convinced him to go. He wanted to avoid watching those attentions again and hoped to learn indifference. However, he chose the wrong place. His brother’s home was filled with domestic happiness, and his sister Isabella reminded him too much of Emma, only highlighting Emma’s superior brilliance. He stayed as long as he could, until the morning mail brought news of Jane Fairfax. Feeling relieved—and not ashamed to be glad, as he never thought Frank Churchill deserved Emma—he felt such intense concern for her that he could not stay away. He rode home through the rain and walked over immediately after dinner to see how this wonderful woman, perfect despite her flaws, was handling the news.

The painter appeared at the studio door, gesturing for them to enter. They smiled at one another. He called out for them to hurry, noting the perfect light and inviting them to bring their drinks. They walked down the path together as butterflies flew by and a thrush sang in the pear tree. Lord Henry asked if Dorian was glad they had met. Dorian replied that he was, though he wondered if he always would be. Lord Henry shuddered at the word always, calling it a meaningless term used by women to ruin romance. He claimed the only difference between a whim and a lifelong passion is that the whim lasts a bit longer. Dorian touched Lord Henry’s arm and suggested their friendship be a whim, then returned to his pose. Lord Henry watched from a wicker chair as the only sound was the brush against the canvas. Dust motes danced in the light, and the scent of roses filled the room. After fifteen minutes, Hallward stopped, studied his subject and the painting, and frowned. He declared it finished and signed his name in red in the corner. Lord Henry examined the portrait, praising it as a masterpiece and a perfect likeness. He invited Dorian to look at himself. Dorian seemed to wake from a dream and stepped down. The painter thanked him for sitting so well. Lord Henry claimed credit for the success, but Dorian did not respond, walking slowly toward the painting to see it for the first time.

Tom managed to scratch the cupboard and was planning to work on the bureau when he was summoned to prepare for Sunday school. Mary provided a tin basin and soap, which he placed on a bench outside. He dipped the soap, poured the water onto the ground, and returned to the kitchen to dry his face on the towel. Mary took the towel away, chiding him for his behavior and insisting he use the water. Tom felt flustered but eventually steeled himself to wash properly. He returned to the kitchen with eyes closed, dripping with soap and water. However, his cleaning was incomplete, leaving a mask-like line of dirt around his chin and neck. Mary scrubbed him until he was thoroughly clean, brushing his damp hair into neat curls. Tom later flattened these curls, as he despised them as effeminate. Mary then produced his Sunday best, the only alternative to his everyday attire. She finished dressing him, buttoning his jacket, adjusting his collar, and placing his straw hat on his head. Tom appeared much improved but felt deeply uneasy, as the restriction of clean, formal clothing irritated him. He hoped she would overlook his shoes, but she greased them with tallow as expected. Frustrated, Tom complained that he was constantly forced to do things against his will.

He bowed and left. He saw no one in the street, which was a quiet, deserted side road. William Bird, a tailor, testified that he was among those who entered the house. An Englishman living in Paris for two years, he was one of the first to climb the stairs. He heard voices arguing. The gruff voice was French, and he clearly heard the words sacre and mon Dieu. He also heard sounds of a struggle, like scraping and scuffling. The shrill voice was louder than the gruff one and did not sound English; he thought it might be German or perhaps a woman's voice, though he does not speak German. Four witnesses confirmed that the door to Mademoiselle L.'s room was locked from the inside when they arrived. Everything was silent, with no groans or other noises. When they forced the door, the room was empty. The windows in both rooms were shut and locked from the inside. The door between the rooms was closed but unlocked, while the door to the hallway was locked with the key inside. A small, cluttered storage room at the end of the hall was searched thoroughly, as was every other part of the house. Chimneys were checked, and the roof trapdoor was found nailed shut and undisturbed for years. Witnesses estimated that between three and five minutes passed between hearing the argument and breaking down the door. Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker living on the Rue Morgue, testified that he was part of the group but stayed downstairs due to his nervous disposition. He heard the argument and confirmed the gruff voice was French, but he was certain the shrill voice belonged to an Englishman.

It was impossible to determine if the voice belonged to a man or a woman. The words were unintelligible, though they sounded like Spanish. The witness described the state of the room and the bodies just as we did yesterday. Henri Duval, a silversmith and neighbor, testified that he was among the first to enter the house. He largely confirmed Musèt’s account. After forcing the door, they immediately shut it to block the rapidly gathering crowd. Duval believed the shrill voice was Italian, definitely not French. He could not confirm the speaker's gender, nor did he know Italian, but the intonation convinced him of the speaker's nationality. Having known Madame L. and her daughter well, he was certain the shrill voice did not belong to either of them. Odenheimer, a restaurateur, offered his testimony voluntarily. Speaking no French, he required an interpreter. A native of Amsterdam, he was passing by when the screams began. They lasted about ten minutes, sounding long, loud, and terrifying. He entered the building and corroborated the previous evidence, with one exception: he was certain the shrill voice belonged to a Frenchman. He could not make out the words, which were loud, rapid, and uneven, suggesting both fear and anger. He described the voice as harsh rather than shrill. The gruff voice repeatedly shouted 'sacré,' 'diable,' and once 'mon Dieu.' Jules Mignaud, a banker, stated that Madame L’Espanaye had been a client for eight years, making frequent small deposits. She made no withdrawals until three days before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs in gold. A clerk accompanied her home with the money. Adolphe Le Bon, a clerk at the bank, testified that he walked Madame L’Espanaye home around noon that day, carrying the 4000 francs in two bags. When the door opened, her daughter took one bag, and the older woman took the other.

My father was gone, and his memory remained the center of my existence. While I could feel gratitude toward others, I could no longer love or hope as I once had. Everything was suffering; even my moments of pleasure were merely endured rather than enjoyed. I felt like a lonely valley surrounded by steep, black cliffs, where no sunlight could reach and no path led to brighter lands. Although friendship offered temporary comfort, it could not heal me. It arrived like a gentle visitor, and when it left, I barely noticed the loss. My inner spirit was dead, so it should not surprise you that I did not welcome the gift of a friend with joy, nor did I mourn deeply when that friendship faded. My friend was named Woodville. I will briefly share his story so you can understand how cold my heart must have been to remain unmoved by his eloquence and sympathy, and how we might have comforted each other had my misery not turned me to stone. Woodville’s troubles were not as deep as mine; his grief was a natural sorrow that purified rather than destroyed, and he would eventually emerge from its shadow brighter than before. Woodville was the son of a poor clergyman and was well-educated. He was one of the rare people favored by fortune, gifted with intellect and charm, and seemingly protected from even the smallest disappointment. His mind was pure, and his understanding was flawless. He was a brilliant poet, though that title hardly does him justice. He resembled the poets of antiquity, blessed from birth with divine inspiration. As he moved among others, he seemed surrounded by a heavenly light that set him apart. His striking beauty, the intensity of his gaze, and his captivating words left everyone around him in silent wonder, making them seem like mere attendants to his greatness.

Do you play? I think, sir, the spy said, turning to Mr. Lorry with a servile air, that I might appeal to a man of your age and kindness to ask this younger gentleman if he can justify playing the Ace he mentioned. I admit I am a spy, a disreputable job that someone must perform, but this man is not; why should he lower himself to act like one? I will play my Ace, Mr. Barsad, Carton replied, checking his watch, without hesitation in a few minutes. I had hoped, gentlemen, the spy said, trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the argument, that your respect for my sister— I could not better show my respect for your sister than by finally removing her brother from her life, Sydney Carton interrupted. You think not, sir? I have fully decided. The spy’s smooth tone, which clashed with his rough clothes, faltered against Carton’s inscrutable nature. As the spy hesitated, Carton continued, as if studying his cards: And now that I think of it, I have another strong card. That fellow-informant who claimed to be working in the country prisons; who was he? He was French. You do not know him, the spy said quickly. French, eh? Carton mused, echoing him. Well, perhaps. He is, I assure you, though it is not important, the spy insisted. Though it is not important, Carton repeated mechanically. Yet I recognize the face. I think not. I am certain not. It cannot be, the spy said. It cannot be, Carton muttered, swirling his glass. He spoke good French, yet like a foreigner, I thought? Provincial, the spy suggested. No, foreign! Carton cried, striking the table as realization dawned. Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had him before us at the Old Bailey. Now, you are being hasty, sir, Barsad said, with a smile that twisted his nose; you are really giving me an advantage over you.

I consider it one of the primary refinements of civilized society. Certainly, sir; and it has the benefit of being popular among the less civilized as well, for every savage can dance. Sir William merely smiled. Your friend performs beautifully, he continued after a pause, watching Bingley join the group; and I have no doubt you are an expert yourself, Mr. Darcy. You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir. Yes, indeed, and I took great pleasure in it. Do you often dance at St. James’s? Never, sir. Do you not think it would be a fitting tribute to the location? It is a tribute I never pay to any place if I can avoid it. You have a home in the city, I assume? Mr. Darcy bowed. I once considered settling in town myself, as I enjoy high society, but I was not certain the London air would suit Lady Lucas. He paused, hoping for a reply, but his companion remained silent. As Elizabeth moved toward them, Sir William decided on a gallant gesture and called out, My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to introduce this young lady as a wonderful partner. You cannot refuse to dance when such beauty stands before you. He reached for her hand to offer it to Mr. Darcy, who was surprised but not unwilling to accept. Elizabeth immediately pulled back, telling Sir William with some agitation, Truly, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please do not think I came this way to solicit a partner. Mr. Darcy formally requested the honor of her hand, but to no avail. Elizabeth remained firm, and Sir William’s attempts at persuasion failed. You excel so much at dancing, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you. Even if this gentleman dislikes the activity, he surely cannot object to obliging us for half an hour. Mr. Darcy is very polite, Elizabeth said with a smile. He is indeed, but given the incentive, we cannot be surprised by his willingness; who would object to such a partner? Elizabeth gave a playful look and turned away. Her refusal had not lowered her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley approached him.

The two ladies expressed great joy at reuniting with their friend, remarking on how long it had been and inquiring about her recent activities. They largely ignored the rest of the family, steering clear of Mrs. Bennet, speaking little to Elizabeth, and saying nothing to the others. They departed quickly, rising with a suddenness that startled their brother and rushing away as if desperate to avoid Mrs. Bennet’s hospitality. The upcoming Netherfield ball delighted every woman in the house. Mrs. Bennet viewed it as a tribute to her eldest daughter, feeling honored that Mr. Bingley had extended the invitation personally. Jane looked forward to a pleasant evening with her friends and their brother, while Elizabeth anticipated dancing with Mr. Wickham and observing Mr. Darcy’s conduct. Catherine and Lydia were excited simply by the prospect of a ball, intending to dance with Mr. Wickham but remaining open to other partners. Even Mary expressed her approval, noting that she found occasional social engagements acceptable as long as her mornings remained private. Elizabeth, in high spirits, asked Mr. Collins if he planned to attend and dance. She was surprised to learn he had no moral objections and feared no disapproval from his patrons. He assured her that a ball hosted by a respectable gentleman was perfectly appropriate, adding that he intended to dance with all his cousins and specifically requested the first two dances with Elizabeth, hoping Jane would understand his choice.

Numerous American women abroad affect a state of perpetual frailty, mistakenly viewing it as European sophistication, yet Mrs. Otis avoided this mistake. Possessing a robust constitution and immense vitality, she remained remarkably English, illustrating how little separates the two nations, language aside. Her eldest son, Washington—a name he perpetually lamented—was a handsome, blond youth who prepared for diplomacy by leading dances at Newport for three years and gaining fame in London as a skilled dancer. Beyond his fondness for gardenias and the aristocracy, he was quite pragmatic. Virginia E. Otis, a lithe, beautiful fifteen-year-old with expressive blue eyes, was an expert rider. She once defeated Lord Bilton in a pony race around the park, delighting the young Duke of Cheshire, who promptly proposed, only to be sent back to Eton by his guardians in tears. The twins, nicknamed 'The Stars and Stripes' for their frequent punishments, were charming boys and, aside from the Minister, the family's only genuine republicans. Since Canterville Chase lay seven miles from the Ascot station, Mr. Otis arranged for a carriage, and they departed in high spirits. It was a beautiful July evening, the air fragrant with pine. They listened to wood pigeons, observed pheasants in the ferns, and watched squirrels and rabbits darting through the brush. Upon entering the Canterville Chase avenue, however, the sky darkened, a strange silence descended, rooks flew overhead in total quiet, and rain began to fall before they arrived. An elderly woman in black silk, wearing a white cap and apron, stood on the steps to greet them.

It is truly nothing, a mere pleasure. I do not labor for profit; my existence is devoted solely to my craft. Lord Arthur placed four pounds, two shillings, and sixpence upon the table, expressed his gratitude to the German, and after politely refusing an invitation to join Anarchists for a Saturday meal, departed for the Park. Over the following two days, he remained in a fever of anticipation, arriving at the Buckingham by noon on Friday to await word. Throughout the afternoon, the porter displayed telegrams regarding horse races, divorce rulings, and weather reports, while the ticker tape provided tedious updates on parliamentary sessions and market fluctuations. At four, the evening editions arrived, and Lord Arthur retreated to the library with several papers, much to the annoyance of Colonel Goodchild, who sought to read his own Mansion House address on South African Missions and the merits of black Bishops. None of the journals mentioned Chichester, leading Lord Arthur to conclude his attempt had failed. Devastated, he found his nerves shattered. When he visited Herr Winckelkopf the next day, the man offered profuse apologies and proposed a replacement clock or discounted nitro-glycerine bombs. Having lost confidence in explosives, Lord Arthur listened as the German lamented the modern adulteration of even pure dynamite. The artisan remained optimistic that the clock might yet detonate, citing a barometer he once sent to an Odessa Governor that failed to explode for three months. While that device eventually killed only a housemaid because the Governor had departed weeks prior, it served as proof that dynamite, when mechanized, remained a potent, if tardy, instrument of destruction.

The studio smelled of roses, and as a light summer breeze moved through the garden, the scent of lilacs and flowering thorns drifted in through the open door. From his spot on the Persian divan, where he lay smoking his usual endless cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could see the golden blossoms of a laburnum tree, its branches heavy with vibrant beauty. Occasionally, the shadows of birds flew across the silk curtains over the large window, creating a fleeting, artistic effect that reminded him of Japanese painters who capture motion in still art. The steady buzzing of bees in the tall grass made the quiet feel even heavier, while the distant hum of London sounded like a far-off organ. In the center of the room, a full-length portrait of an exceptionally handsome young man stood on an easel. The artist, Basil Hallward—whose sudden disappearance years ago had caused such a stir—sat nearby. As Basil looked at the beautiful figure he had captured on canvas, he smiled with satisfaction. Suddenly, he stood up and covered his eyes, as if trying to hold onto a dream he was afraid of losing. It is your best work, Basil, the best thing you have ever done, Lord Henry said lazily. You must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too big and common. I either cannot see the paintings because of the crowds, or I cannot see the people because of the paintings. The Grosvenor is the only place. I do not think I will send it anywhere, Basil replied, tossing his head back in the peculiar way that used to amuse his friends at Oxford.

He does not comprehend English, yet evaluates based on tone. Alberto Montani, a confectioner, states he was among those who first climbed the stairs. He heard the voices in question, noting the gruff one belonged to a Frenchman who seemed to be arguing. He could not decipher the shrill voice, which sounded rapid and irregular; he suspects it was Russian, though he has never spoken with a Russian native. This aligns with the general testimony. Several witnesses confirmed that the fourth-floor chimneys were too narrow for a person to enter. The term sweeps refers to the cylindrical brushes used for cleaning flues, which were passed through every chimney in the building. No rear exit existed for anyone to escape while the group ascended. Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was wedged so tightly in the chimney that it required the combined effort of four or five men to extract it. Paul Dumas, a physician, testified that he examined the bodies at dawn. They lay on the bed frame where the young woman was discovered. Her corpse was bruised and scraped, likely from being forced up the chimney. Her throat was chafed, showing deep scratches beneath the chin and livid finger marks. Her face was discolored, her eyes bulged, and her tongue was bitten. A bruise on her stomach suggested pressure from a knee. Dr. Dumas concluded she had been strangled by unknown parties. The mother’s corpse was severely mutilated; the bones of her right arm and leg were shattered, her left tibia and ribs were splintered, and her entire body was bruised. The cause of these injuries is uncertain, though a heavy club, iron bar, or chair wielded by a powerful man could have caused them; no woman could have inflicted such damage. The victim’s head was severed and crushed, and her throat had clearly been cut with a sharp blade, likely a razor.

When we arrived at the base, he asked, "Jupiter, come here! Was the skull fastened to the branch facing outward, or toward the wood?" "The face was out, master, so the crows could easily reach the eyes," Jupiter replied. "Very well, and was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle?" Legrand asked, touching each of Jupiter's eyes. "It was this one, master—the left eye—just as you instructed," Jupiter said, pointing to his own right eye. "That suffices; we must attempt it once more." I began to perceive a certain logic in my friend's apparent madness as he shifted the peg three inches westward. Measuring fifty feet from the trunk in a straight line, he marked a new spot several yards from our previous excavation. We drew a larger circle and resumed digging. Despite my exhaustion, I felt a strange, growing interest and excitement, perhaps stirred by Legrand's air of deliberate purpose. I shoveled eagerly, finding myself half-expecting the treasure that had obsessed my companion. After ninety minutes, the dog began to howl violently. Unlike his earlier playfulness, his distress was now intense. When Jupiter tried to restrain him, the dog resisted, jumped into the pit, and clawed at the earth. He quickly unearthed human remains—two complete skeletons mixed with metal buttons and remnants of rotted wool. A few spade strikes revealed a large Spanish knife blade, followed by several scattered gold and silver coins.

Mr. Elliot looked up with great respect. How delightful! Mrs. Clay cried, though she dared not look at Anne. It is just like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not call them father and son? Oh, I do not forbid anyone from speaking their mind, but I hardly think his attentions are any different from those of other men. My dear Miss Elliot! Mrs. Clay exclaimed, raising her hands and eyes before falling into a convenient silence. Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so concerned. I invited him, after all. When I learned he was going to visit friends at Thornberry Park tomorrow, I felt sorry for him. Anne admired how well her friend acted, showing such pleasure at the arrival of a man who clearly hindered her own goals. Mrs. Clay must have hated the sight of Mr. Elliot, yet she maintained a pleasant, calm expression, appearing satisfied despite having only half the time to devote to Sir Walter. For Anne, seeing Mr. Elliot enter the room was distressing, and his approach was painful. She had previously suspected he was not always sincere, but now she saw dishonesty in everything he did. His respectful behavior toward her father, which contradicted his earlier words, was repulsive. Knowing his cruel treatment of Mrs. Smith, she could barely stand his smiles or his artificial kindness. She intended to remain cool toward him without causing a scene, hoping to quietly distance herself from the unnecessary intimacy that had developed. She was more guarded and distant than she had been the night before. He tried to spark her curiosity again about where he had heard her praised, hoping for more questions, but the spell was broken. He realized that the excitement of a public room was needed to stir his cousin’s vanity, and he could not achieve that now while surrounded by the others.

By eight o'clock, I had reached seventeen miles above the ground. It was clear my ascent was accelerating, even without the ballast I had released. Though I suffered intermittent, sharp pains in my head and ears and occasional nosebleeds, my condition was better than anticipated. Breathing grew increasingly labored, however, with each breath causing a painful spasm in my chest. I prepared my condensing equipment for use. The earth below looked magnificent. To the west, north, and south stretched an endless, calm ocean, deepening in blue and showing signs of curvature. Far to the east, I could clearly see Great Britain, the Atlantic coasts of France and Spain, and a sliver of Africa. Human structures were invisible; the world's great cities had vanished. Gibraltar was a mere speck, and the Mediterranean, speckled with islands like a starry sky, reached eastward until it seemed to spill over the horizon's edge, making me strain to hear the roar of a waterfall. Above, the sky was pitch black, filled with bright stars. Seeing the pigeons in distress, I decided to release them. I placed a gray-mottled bird on the wicker rim. It looked around nervously, fluttering and cooing, but refused to leave the car. When I tossed it a few yards away, it did not descend as I had hoped. Instead, it fought desperately to return, crying out shrilly. It managed to land back on the rim, but its head immediately slumped, and it died inside the basket.

Reviewing the terrible list of my transgressions, I struggle to accept that I am the same being who once harbored lofty dreams of virtue and grace. Yet it is true; the fallen angel transforms into a spiteful demon. Even that adversary of the divine had companions in his exile, whereas I remain solitary. You, who claim friendship with Frankenstein, seem aware of my offenses and his tragedies. However, his account could not capture the endless months of agony I suffered while consumed by futile rage. In ruining his prospects, I found no fulfillment for my own longings. I perpetually craved affection and companionship, only to be rejected. Was this not unfair? Am I the sole villain when humanity wronged me? Why is Felix not condemned for casting his friend away with disdain? Why is the peasant not reviled for attacking the one who saved his child? They are considered righteous, while I, abandoned and wretched, am viewed as a monstrosity fit only for abuse. The memory of such inequity still inflames my blood. It is true that I am a villain. I have slaughtered the beautiful and the defenseless; I have strangled the innocent in their sleep and ended the life of one who never harmed a soul. I have condemned my creator, the finest of men, to despair, pursuing him until his final ruin. He lies there, pale and lifeless. Your hatred for me cannot match the loathing I feel for myself. I gaze upon the hands that committed these acts and contemplate the mind that devised them, yearning for the moment when I am no longer haunted by these memories. Do not fear further harm from me. My task is nearly finished. No more lives are required to conclude my existence; only my own death is necessary. I will not hesitate to make this sacrifice. I shall depart your ship on the ice raft that carried me here and travel to the furthest north. There, I will build my funeral pyre and burn this wretched body to ashes, ensuring that no curious soul can ever study my remains to replicate such a creature as I have been.

No, the girl insisted. Tell me why. For one reason, she replied firmly, which the lady knows and will support, as she promised. Also, despite his wicked life, I have lived a bad one too. Many of us have shared the same path, and I will not betray those who could have turned on me but chose not to. Then, the gentleman said, hand Monks over to me and let me handle him. What if he betrays the others? I promise that if the truth is forced from him, the matter ends there. Oliver’s history contains painful details that should not be public; if the truth is revealed, the others will go free. And if it is not? Then, the gentleman continued, Fagin will not be prosecuted without your consent. I believe I could then convince you to agree. Do I have the lady’s word? You do, Rose replied. My sincere pledge. Monks will never know how you learned this? the girl asked. Never, the gentleman answered. The information will be used in a way he could never guess. I have been a liar since childhood, the girl said after a silence, but I will trust your word. After receiving their assurances, she spoke in a voice so quiet it was hard to follow, identifying the pub she had been followed from. She paused frequently, as if the gentleman were taking notes. Once she had detailed the location, the best vantage point, and the times Monks usually visited, she paused to recall his appearance. He is tall and well-built, but not stout, she said. He walks with a furtive gait, constantly glancing over his shoulders.

Meanwhile, gravity would steadily weaken in proportion to the square of the distance, and I would eventually reach those distant regions where the moon's pull overcomes the earth's, accelerating rapidly. Given this, I saw no reason to pack more than forty days of supplies. Another concern troubled me. Balloonists at high altitudes often suffer from respiratory distress, physical pain, and nosebleeds, which worsen as they climb. I wondered if these symptoms would prove fatal. I concluded they would not. These issues stem from the loss of atmospheric pressure causing blood vessels to swell, rather than a fundamental biological failure like oxygen deprivation. Since breathing is a muscular action, I believed life could persist even in a vacuum. I assumed my body would adapt to the lack of pressure and that my physical resilience would see me through the initial discomfort. Your Excellencies, these are some of the factors that inspired my lunar voyage. I will now describe the outcome of this unprecedented endeavor. After reaching an altitude of three and three-quarters miles, I tossed out some feathers and continued to rise quickly, so I kept my ballast. I wanted to retain as much weight as possible for reasons I will explain later.

Well, Jupiter, what is the matter? How is your master? To tell the truth, sir, he is not as well as he could be. Not well? I am sorry to hear that. What are his symptoms? That is the problem. He never complains of anything, yet he is very sick. Very sick, Jupiter? Why didn't you say so? Is he bedridden? No, he is not confined at all, and that is where the trouble lies. I am very worried about poor Master Will. Jupiter, I need to understand you. You say he is sick, but has he told you what is wrong? Sir, please do not get angry. Master Will says nothing is wrong, but he walks around with his head down, his shoulders hunched, and he is as pale as a ghost. He also keeps scribbling on a slate. Keeps what? He keeps scribbling figures on a slate, the strangest figures I have ever seen. I am getting scared. I have to keep a close eye on his movements. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and was gone all day. I had a big stick ready to give him a good beating when he returned, but I am such a fool that I did not have the heart to do it because he looked so poorly. I see. I think it is best you do not be too severe with him. Do not hit him, Jupiter; he cannot handle it. Do you have any idea what caused this change in behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I last saw you? No, sir, nothing has happened since then. I fear it was before that, the very day you were there. What do you mean? I mean the bug, sir. The what? The bug. I am certain Master Will was bitten on the head by that gold bug. What makes you think that? It had plenty of claws and a mouth, sir. I have never seen such a bug. It kicked and bit everything near it. Master Will caught it first but had to let it go quickly. That must be when he was bitten. I did not like the look of the bug's mouth, so I would not touch it with my fingers, but I caught it with a piece of paper I found.

Elizabeth felt despondent and melancholy, finding no joy in her usual tasks. She believed any happiness was a betrayal of the deceased, feeling that perpetual grief was the only proper homage to such ruined innocence. She was no longer the joyful girl who once strolled with me by the lake, speaking with delight of our future. The first of those life-altering sorrows meant to detach us from the world had arrived, extinguishing her brightest smiles. When I consider the tragic end of Justine Moritz, she remarked, the world looks entirely different to me. Previously, reports of vice and injustice seemed like distant legends or abstract concepts, but now that misery has struck close to home, humanity appears like monsters craving blood. I am likely being unfair, as everyone thought her guilty; had she truly committed such a crime, she would have been the most wicked of beings. To kill the child of her benefactor for mere jewels, a boy she raised and loved as her own, would be monstrous. While I could never support an execution, I would have deemed such a person unfit for society. Yet she was innocent. I feel it, and your agreement confirms it. Victor, when lies appear so much like truth, who can be certain of happiness? I feel as though I am walking along a cliff edge, with crowds pushing me toward the void. William and Justine were murdered, yet the killer remains free and perhaps even honored. Even if I were to face the scaffold for those crimes, I would never trade places with such a wretch. I heard these words in absolute agony, knowing that while I did not commit the act, I was effectively the murderer. Elizabeth noticed my distress and, gently taking my hand, urged me to find calm, noting that while she was deeply affected, she was not as miserable as I appeared.

The shock I felt at this sudden change was hard to explain, even though the shift was natural and expected. I knew that once my balloon reached the point where the moon’s gravity became stronger than the Earth’s, this reversal would happen. I had simply woken from a deep sleep to find it had already occurred. The transition must have been smooth, as I felt no physical discomfort or disruption to my equipment during the process. Once I overcame my initial terror, I focused entirely on the moon below. It looked like a map, and despite the distance, its features were incredibly sharp. I was struck by the complete lack of oceans, lakes, or rivers. Instead, I saw vast, flat plains and countless cone-shaped volcanic mountains that looked almost man-made. While the tallest peaks were under four miles high, they resembled the volcanic regions of the Campi Phlegraei. Most were actively erupting, and I watched with growing dread as volcanic rocks shot past my balloon with alarming frequency.

He kept one secret from his close friends, a secret he had held since childhood. Although he loved his peers, he could not trust them with his feelings. He was deeply in love and feared they would mock him, treating his profound passion as something trivial. A man of modest means lived near his family home and had three beautiful daughters. The eldest was the most striking, possessing both a sharp mind and a gentle spirit. She and my father had been childhood playmates, and his mother had always favored her. During his school breaks, they were inseparable. Influenced by novels and his own sensitive nature, he began speaking of love to her when he was only eleven. Though she was two years older, her upbringing left her more naive. She accepted his declarations innocently, not fully grasping their meaning. By the time she understood the nature of their bond, she was already devoted to him, fearing only that he might eventually lose interest. Their love grew more intense and tender over time, becoming an inseparable part of his life. They kept their relationship private, and despite his fear that his friends might judge him for loving someone of lower social standing, he remained determined to marry her as soon as he could overcome the necessary obstacles. Diana was truly worthy of his devotion.

Those who were once our finest patrons now lacked any time to consider us. They claimed they were fully occupied reading about revolutions and tracking the progress of modern thought. If a fire needed stoking, a newspaper sufficed, and as the government faltered, leather and iron seemed to grow more resilient; soon, no bellows in Rotterdam required repair. This situation was unbearable. I became destitute, and with a family to support, my struggles grew overwhelming, leading me to contemplate how best to end my existence. Meanwhile, creditors left me no peace. My home was constantly besieged, making me pace like a caged tiger. Three men in particular harassed me incessantly, threatening legal action. I silently swore the harshest vengeance against them should I ever gain the upper hand; only the anticipation of this retribution kept me from using a blunderbuss to end my life. I decided to hide my anger, offering them empty promises until fate might grant me a chance for revenge. One day, having evaded my creditors and feeling deeply despondent, I wandered aimlessly through quiet streets until I bumped into a bookseller’s stall. Finding a chair, I sat down and aimlessly opened the nearest volume. It was a pamphlet on Speculative Astronomy by Professor Encke or a Frenchman with a similar name. Possessing some slight knowledge of the subject, I became completely engrossed, reading the entire text twice before realizing where I was.

Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay, was finally brought to trial. The judges wore feathered hats, yet the red cap and tricolour cockade were the common attire. Observing the jury and the rowdy crowd, he felt as though the roles were inverted, with criminals judging the righteous. The city’s most vicious elements dominated the proceedings, shouting their opinions and dictating the outcome unchecked. Many men carried weapons, while women brandished knives or daggers, and some knitted while they watched. One woman, knitting intently, sat near a man Darnay recognized as Defarge. She whispered to him occasionally, appearing to be his wife, yet neither ever glanced at the prisoner, focusing instead on the jury with grim resolve. Doctor Manette sat beneath the President, dressed plainly, appearing alongside Mr. Lorry as the only observers not wearing the rough clothing of the revolution. The prosecutor charged Evrémonde as an emigrant, subject to the death penalty under a decree that ignored the timing of his return. The crowd clamored for his execution, branding him an enemy of the Republic. When the President silenced the room to question him, Darnay admitted to living in England for many years. Challenged on his status as an emigrant, Darnay argued that he did not fall under the law’s intent. He explained that he had abandoned his title and status long before the term was defined by the Tribunal, choosing instead to support himself through his own labor in England rather than exploiting the burdened people of France.

The narrow streets eventually opened into a large, empty area filled with animal pens, signaling a cattle market. Sikes slowed down because the girl could no longer keep up with their fast pace. He turned to Oliver and harshly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand. When Oliver hesitated and looked around, Sikes growled, "Do you hear me?" They stood in a dark corner, far from any passersby. Realizing that fighting back was useless, Oliver held out his hand, which Nancy gripped tightly. Sikes grabbed Oliver’s other hand and called, "Here, Bull’s-Eye!" The dog looked up and growled. Sikes placed his hand on Oliver’s throat and warned, "Listen, boy. If he makes a sound, grab him. Do you understand?" The dog growled again, licking his lips and staring at Oliver as if ready to attack. Sikes looked at the animal with grim approval and told Oliver that the dog would stop any attempt to call for help. He then ordered the boy to move on. Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail and led the way, letting out another warning growl at Oliver. They were crossing Smithfield, though Oliver had no idea where he was. The night was dark and foggy, and the shop lights barely cut through the thick mist that shrouded the streets in gloom, making the unfamiliar area feel even more depressing. After walking a short distance, a church bell struck the hour. Sikes and Nancy stopped to listen. When the bell finished, Nancy noted it was eight o’clock. Sikes snapped at her, saying he could hear it himself. Nancy wondered if others could hear it too. Sikes replied that they certainly could, recalling how clearly he could hear the noise of a fair even from inside a jail cell, where the silence of his confinement had once been nearly unbearable.

It is quite notable that she consistently understands Jane more clearly than she does me. Jane articulates so plainly! Still, she will find her grandmother no harder of hearing than she was two years ago, which is quite an achievement at my mother’s age. It has been a full two years since her last visit. We have never gone so long without seeing her, and as I mentioned to Mrs. Cole, we shall struggle to show her enough attention now. Are you anticipating Miss Fairfax’s arrival soon? Oh yes, next week. Indeed, that must be a wonderful delight. Thank you, you are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised and offers such gracious remarks. I am certain she will be just as pleased to see her Highbury friends as they are to see her. She will arrive Friday or Saturday; she cannot specify because Colonel Campbell requires the carriage himself on one of those days. It is so generous of them to provide her transportation the entire way, but they always do. Yes, next Friday or Saturday is what she mentions in her letter. That is why she wrote out of turn; normally, we would not have heard from her until next Tuesday or Wednesday. Yes, I assumed as much. I feared there was little chance of hearing news of Miss Fairfax today. How kind of you! No, we would not have received word if not for this specific reason of her visiting so soon. My mother is thrilled, as she will stay with us for at least three months. She states that duration quite firmly, as I shall soon have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is that the Campbells are traveling to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has convinced her parents to visit her immediately. They had not planned to go until summer, but she is so eager to see them again. Until her marriage last October, she had never been separated from them for more than a week, making it quite unusual to be in different countries. She sent an urgent letter to her parents—or perhaps her father, I cannot recall, but we shall see in Jane’s note—writing on behalf of herself and Mr. Dixon to insist they come over at once. They plan to meet in Dublin and then travel to their estate, Baly-craig, which I imagine is a lovely residence.

The instruments indicated an altitude of 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles, allowing me to view about one three-hundred-twentieth of the Earth's total surface. By nine o'clock, I had lost sight of land to the east, noting the balloon was drifting rapidly north-northwest. The ocean's curvature was clearly visible, though often obscured by drifting clouds. I noticed that even the lightest vapors never rose beyond ten miles above sea level. At nine-thirty, I tested the air by dropping a handful of feathers through the valve. Instead of floating, they fell straight down like bullets, disappearing in seconds. I was initially baffled, unable to believe my ascent had accelerated so drastically. I soon realized the atmosphere was too thin to support the feathers, and their rapid descent combined with my own upward velocity created the illusion. By ten o'clock, I had little to do. The flight proceeded smoothly, and I felt the balloon rising faster every moment, though I lacked the means to measure it. I felt no discomfort and was in better spirits than at any time since leaving Rotterdam, alternating between checking my equipment and refreshing the cabin's air. I performed this air renewal every forty minutes, primarily for my health. Meanwhile, I let my mind wander to the moon. Unshackled, my imagination roamed through a dreamlike landscape. I envisioned ancient forests, jagged cliffs, and waterfalls crashing into bottomless abysses. Then, I drifted into silent, sunlit solitudes where no wind blew, and vast fields of poppies and lilies stretched out, forever still and motionless.

It is just a tick. Where did you find him? Out in the woods. What will you take for him? I do not know. I do not want to sell him. Fine. It is a very small tick anyway. Anyone can run down a tick that is not theirs. I am satisfied. It is a good enough tick for me. There are plenty of ticks. I could have a thousand if I wanted. Well, why do you not? Because you know you cannot. This is an early tick, I think. It is the first one I have seen this year. Hey, Huck, I will give you my tooth for him. Let me see it. Tom unwrapped a piece of paper. Huckleberry looked at it longingly. The temptation was strong. Finally, he asked if it was real. Tom lifted his lip to show the gap. All right, Huckleberry said, it is a trade. Tom put the tick in the small box that had held his beetle, and the boys parted, both feeling richer. When Tom reached the isolated schoolhouse, he walked in briskly, acting as if he had hurried. He hung up his hat and sat down quickly. The teacher, sitting in his large chair, was dozing to the sound of the students studying. The noise woke him. Thomas Sawyer! Tom knew that using his full name meant trouble. Sir! Come here. Why are you late again? Tom was about to lie when he saw two long yellow braids hanging down a back he recognized with a jolt of affection. Beside that girl was the only empty seat on the girls' side. He immediately said, I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn! The teacher froze and stared in shock. The room went silent. The students wondered if the boy had lost his mind. The teacher asked what he had done. I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn. There was no mistaking his words. Thomas Sawyer, this is the most shocking confession I have ever heard. A simple punishment will not suffice. Take off your jacket. The teacher struck him until his arm grew tired and his switches were worn down. Then he ordered, Now, go sit with the girls! Let this be a warning. The laughter that rippled through the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth, he was overwhelmed by his awe for the girl and the thrilling fortune of sitting beside her.

Mr. Elliot looked up with such profound respect. Quite delightful! Mrs. Clay cried, though she dared not look at Anne. It is just like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not call them father and son? Oh, I do not restrict anyone’s speech. If you insist on such ideas! But honestly, I hardly notice his attentions being any different from other men’s. My dear Miss Elliot! Mrs. Clay exclaimed, raising her hands and eyes before falling into a convenient, astonished silence. Well, Penelope, you need not be so alarmed. I did invite him, after all. I sent him away with a smile. When I realized he was heading to Thornberry Park for the entire day tomorrow, I felt sorry for him. Anne admired her friend’s performance, managing to show such pleasure at the arrival of the very man who hindered her own goals. Mrs. Clay must have loathed the sight of Mr. Elliot, yet she maintained a pleasant, obliging expression, appearing satisfied despite having only half the time to devote to Sir Walter. For Anne, seeing Mr. Elliot enter was distressing, and his approach was painful. She had previously suspected his sincerity, but now she saw through everything. His deferential behavior toward her father, compared to his past remarks, was repulsive. Knowing his cruel treatment of Mrs. Smith, she could barely endure his smiles or his artificial sentiments. She intended to remain cool without provoking a confrontation. Her goal was to avoid any scene or inquiry, while quietly distancing herself from the unnecessary intimacy that had developed. She was more guarded and reserved than the night before. He tried to pique her curiosity again about where he had heard her praised, hoping for more engagement, but the spell was broken. He realized that the energy of a public room was required to stir his cousin’s vanity, and he could not achieve it now amidst the competing demands of the others.

Tom joined the Cadets of Temperance, drawn by their flashy uniforms. He pledged to quit smoking, chewing tobacco, and swearing while a member. He soon discovered that promising not to do something only made him crave it more. His urge to drink and curse became so strong that only the prospect of wearing his red sash kept him in the group. He hoped to show off at the upcoming Fourth of July parade, but he quit the order after only two days. Instead, he pinned his hopes on Judge Frazer, a local official who was dying. Tom expected a grand public funeral and spent three days anxiously checking on the Judge’s health. He even practiced wearing his uniform in front of the mirror. However, the Judge kept recovering, which annoyed Tom. He finally quit the group, only for the Judge to die that very night. Tom felt betrayed and vowed never to trust the man again. The funeral was impressive, and the Cadets marched in a way that would have made Tom jealous. Still, he was free again. Surprisingly, once he was allowed to drink and swear, he no longer wanted to. The thrill was gone. Soon, Tom found his newfound freedom boring. He tried keeping a diary, but gave up after three days of nothing to report. When a minstrel show arrived, Tom and Joe Harper formed their own troupe and enjoyed two days of fun. Even the Fourth of July was a letdown; it rained, canceling the parade, and the guest of honor, a United States Senator, was a disappointment because he was not the giant Tom had imagined. Then, a circus came to town.

When I review my terrible sins, I struggle to believe I am the same being who once dreamed of the beauty and majesty of goodness. Yet it is true; a fallen angel becomes a cruel devil. Even that enemy of God and man had companions in his misery, but I am entirely alone. You, who call Frankenstein a friend, seem to know of my crimes and his suffering. However, his account could not capture the months of agony I endured while trapped in useless rage. While I destroyed his hopes, I never satisfied my own desires. I constantly craved love and friendship, yet I was always rejected. Was there no injustice in this? Am I the only criminal when all of humanity sinned against me? Why do you not hate Felix, who drove his friend away with insults? Why do you not despise the villager who tried to kill the man who saved his child? Apparently, they are considered virtuous, while I, the abandoned wretch, am a monster to be kicked and trampled. Even now, my blood boils at the memory of this unfairness. It is true that I am a wretch. I have murdered the lovely and the helpless; I have strangled the innocent in their sleep and killed a man who never harmed anyone. I have brought misery to my creator, the finest of men, and pursued him to his ruin. There he lies, cold in death. You hate me, but your disgust cannot match my own self-loathing. I look at the hands that committed these deeds and the heart that imagined them, longing for the moment when I no longer exist. Do not fear that I will cause more harm. My work is nearly finished. I do not need to kill anyone else to complete my existence; I only need to end my own life. I will not hesitate to make this sacrifice. I will leave your ship on the ice raft that brought me here and head to the furthest north. I will build my funeral pyre and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that no curious person can ever study my remains to create another like me.

Daylight arrived as I finished the manuscript. The rain had nearly stopped, leaving the world gray and somber as the storm faded away. I went to the stranger's room and listened at his door, which stood slightly open. Hearing him speak, I knocked, but received no reply. I peeked inside to see him lying on his back, talking feverishly and waving his arms in the restless manner of the delirious. I entered quietly and leaned over him. When I spoke his name, his glassy eyes and pale face lit up with sudden joy and relief. Oh, Sandy, you have finally come. I have missed you so much. Sit by me and never leave again. Give me your hand; let me hold it. Now everything is peaceful and I am happy once more. You look like a faint mist, but you are here, and that is enough. Don't pull away; I won't need you for long. Was that the child? Hello, Central? She doesn't answer. Perhaps she is asleep. Bring her when she wakes so I can say goodbye. Sandy, are you still there? I drifted off for a moment. Have I been sick for a long time? It feels like months. I have had such strange, terrifying dreams that felt completely real. I dreamt the king was dead, that you were trapped in Gaul, and that a revolution had broken out. In my delirium, I imagined that Clarence and I fought and destroyed all the knights of England. Even stranger, I felt like a man from a distant, future age. I seemed to have traveled back and forth through time, feeling like a lonely stranger separated from you and my home by thirteen centuries of history.

I would gladly share much more, but I must be brief to secure my reward. I long to return to my family and home. In exchange for the valuable scientific insights I can provide, I ask your honorable body to grant me a pardon for the death of my creditors when I left Rotterdam. This is the purpose of my letter. The messenger, a lunar inhabitant I have instructed to act on my behalf, will wait for your decision and bring the pardon to me if it is granted. I remain your humble servant, Hans Pfaall. Upon reading this extraordinary letter, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe in shock. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his glasses, wiped them, and was so stunned that he forgot his dignity, spinning around three times in amazement. They agreed the pardon must be granted. The professor swore it, and Von Underduk concurred as they walked home to discuss the next steps. At the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor noted that the messenger had vanished, likely frightened by the local citizens. Since only a lunar inhabitant could travel such a distance, the pardon would be useless. The burgomaster agreed, and the matter ended. Rumors, however, persisted. Once published, the letter sparked endless gossip. Some skeptics made fools of themselves by dismissing the entire story as a hoax. To such people, anything they cannot understand is simply a lie. I fail to see the evidence for their accusations. Let us examine their claims.

One day, while I was studying with Mr. Pocket, I received a letter that made me incredibly nervous. Although I had never seen the handwriting before, I immediately knew who it was from. It had no formal greeting, simply stating: I am coming to London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you would meet me. Miss Havisham expects it, and I am writing to follow her instructions. She sends her regards. Yours, Estella. If I had more time, I would have bought new clothes, but I had to make do with what I owned. I lost my appetite and could not find any peace until the day arrived. Even then, I was restless and began waiting at the coach office in Wood Street long before the coach could have possibly arrived from my hometown. Despite knowing it was irrational, I felt I could not leave the office for more than five minutes. I had been waiting for about half an hour when Wemmick bumped into me. Hello, Mr. Pip, he said. How are you? I would not have expected to see you here. I explained that I was meeting someone arriving by coach and asked about his home and his father. Both are doing well, thank you, Wemmick replied, especially the old man. He is in great spirits and will be eighty-two soon. I am thinking of firing my cannon eighty-two times, provided the neighbors do not complain and the cannon holds up. But this is not business talk. Where do you think I am going? To the office? I asked. Almost, Wemmick said. I am going to Newgate Prison. We are handling a bank robbery case, and after visiting the scene, I need to speak with our client. Did your client commit the robbery? I asked. Goodness no, Wemmick answered dryly. But he is accused of it. You or I could just as easily be accused of the same thing.

April 19th. At nine this morning, I was terrified by how close the moon appeared, but my condenser pump finally showed signs of a change in the air. By ten, the air density had clearly increased. By eleven, the equipment required little effort, and at noon, I cautiously opened the rubber chamber. Although I immediately suffered from painful spasms and a headache, I decided to endure them, knowing I was descending into thicker air. However, my descent remained dangerously fast. I had assumed the moon’s atmosphere would be dense enough to support my balloon’s weight, but I was wrong. My rapid fall proved that the air was not thick enough, likely due to the geological issues I mentioned before. I was plummeting toward the surface at a terrifying speed. I quickly threw out my ballast, water barrels, equipment, and everything else in the basket, but it did not slow me down. With only half a mile to go, I removed my coat, hat, and boots, then cut the heavy basket loose. Clinging to the netting, I saw that the landscape was covered in tiny houses before I crashed into the center of a strange city. I landed in a crowd of ugly little people who stood there like idiots, grinning and staring at me and my balloon with their hands on their hips, offering no help at all.

These thoughts calmed me, and I fell into a deep sleep that afternoon, though my feverish blood prevented any peaceful dreams. The horror of the previous day played constantly in my mind: the women fleeing and Felix pulling me away from his father. I woke exhausted, and once night fell, I crept from my hiding spot to find food. After eating, I headed toward the cottage. Everything was quiet. I returned to my hovel and waited for the family to wake, but the morning passed and they never appeared. I trembled, fearing some disaster. The cottage remained dark and silent, and the suspense was agonizing. Soon, two men walked by and stopped to talk, gesturing wildly. I could not understand them, as they spoke the local language rather than the one my protectors used. Shortly after, Felix arrived with another man. I was surprised, as I thought he had been inside all morning, and I listened closely to understand what was happening. His companion asked if he realized he would lose three months of rent and his garden harvest, suggesting he take time to reconsider. Felix replied that it was useless, as they could never live there again. He explained that his father’s life was in danger because of what had happened, and his wife and sister were too traumatized to stay. He begged the man to stop arguing and just take back the property so they could leave. Felix was shaking as he spoke. They went inside for a few minutes and then left. I never saw the De Lacey family again. I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, paralyzed by despair. My protectors were gone, severing my only connection to the world. For the first time, I felt consumed by hatred and a desire for revenge. I made no effort to control these feelings, letting them carry me toward thoughts of destruction and death.

Her complexion shifted, and she fell silent. Mrs. Gardiner stood slightly behind, and as she paused, he requested the honor of an introduction to her companions. This unexpected display of courtesy made her struggle to hide a smile, knowing he sought the acquaintance of those very individuals his pride had previously rejected. She wondered at his reaction once he discovered their true identity, assuming he mistook them for fashionable society. The introduction proceeded, and as she identified their kinship, she glanced at him, anticipating a swift retreat from such embarrassing company. Though clearly startled by the connection, he maintained his composure and, far from departing, joined them in conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth felt a sense of triumph and relief that her relatives were beyond reproach. She listened intently, taking pride in her uncle’s intelligence and refined manners.
