Their talk shifted to fishing, and Mr. Darcy politely invited him to fish on the estate during his stay, offering equipment and advice on the best spots. Mrs. Gardiner exchanged a look of amazement with Elizabeth, who remained silent but felt deeply gratified, sensing the gesture was intended for her. She was bewildered by his transformation, questioning if her past rebukes could have truly softened his demeanor or if his feelings for her persisted. After walking together, the group paused by the river to examine a water plant. When they resumed their path, Mrs. Gardiner, feeling weary, relinquished Elizabeth’s arm in favor of her husband’s.

I consider it one of the first refinements of civilized society. Certainly, sir, and it has the advantage of being popular among less polished societies as well; every savage can dance. Sir William smiled. Your friend performs delightfully, he said after a pause, watching Bingley join the group. I have no doubt you are an expert yourself, Mr. Darcy. You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir. Yes, and I enjoyed it. Do you often dance at St. James’s? Never, sir. Do you not think it would be a proper compliment to the place? It is a compliment I avoid paying whenever I can. You have a house in town, I assume? Mr. Darcy bowed. I once thought of settling in London myself, as I enjoy high society, but I was not sure the air would suit Lady Lucas. He paused, hoping for a reply, but his companion remained silent. Just then, Elizabeth walked toward them. Sir William had a sudden idea and called out, My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to introduce this young lady as a wonderful partner. You cannot refuse to dance when such beauty is before you. He took her hand to give it to Mr. Darcy, who was surprised but not unwilling. Elizabeth immediately pulled back and said to Sir William, I have no intention of dancing. Please do not think I walked over here to find a partner. Mr. Darcy politely asked for the honor of her hand, but she refused. Elizabeth remained firm, and Sir William’s attempts to persuade her failed. You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you. Even if this gentleman dislikes dancing, he surely would not mind obliging us for half an hour. Mr. Darcy is very polite, Elizabeth said with a smile. He is indeed, but given the incentive, his willingness is no surprise; who would object to such a partner? Elizabeth gave a playful look and turned away. Her refusal had not lowered her in Mr. Darcy’s estimation, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley approached him.

Certainly not, Duff replied. And, to clarify for the ladies, I assume you mean this attempt was not made by a local, Mr. Losberne said with a smile. That is it, sir, Blathers answered. This is all about the robbery, then? All of it, the doctor replied. Now, what is this about the boy the servants are discussing? Blathers asked. Nothing at all, the doctor said. One of the panicked servants decided he had something to do with the break-in, but it is complete nonsense. That is easily dismissed, if so, Duff remarked. He is right, Blathers agreed, nodding while fiddling with his handcuffs like castanets. Who is the boy? What is his story? Where is he from? He did not just fall from the sky, did he? Of course not, the doctor replied, glancing nervously at the ladies. I know his entire history, but we can discuss that later. I assume you would like to see where the thieves made their attempt first? Certainly, Blathers said. We should inspect the premises before questioning the servants. That is standard procedure. Lights were brought, and Blathers and Duff, followed by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and everyone else, went to the small room at the end of the hall to examine the window. They circled the lawn to look in, inspected the shutter with a candle, traced footprints with a lantern, and poked the bushes with a pitchfork. Afterward, Giles and Brittles reenacted their roles in the previous night’s events six times, contradicting each other more frequently with every repetition. Once finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room for a private consultation, which was far more solemn and secretive than any medical board meeting. Meanwhile, the doctor paced the next room in distress, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious expressions. Honestly, he said, stopping after several rapid turns, I hardly know what to do.

But when I saw you loved by another, or imagined you might love someone else more deeply than you loved me, a monster awoke inside me. I sent your suitor away, and since then, I have known no peace. I could not sleep, and my blood felt constantly agitated. I woke to a new life, like someone dying in hope only to wake in Hell. I will not stain your mind by describing my inner battles, my self-hatred, and my despair. Let the feelings of a guilty father remain hidden; such agony should not be exposed. My mind was a storm of crime, remorse, and hate, yet beneath it all, I still felt the deepest love. Seeing your bitter, sympathetic sorrow is what finally pushed me to resolve to overcome my passion and return to being a proper father. I came here thinking that if I could relive the grief I felt when your mother died—memories I had suppressed for seventeen years—my love for her child would vanish. In a moment of false heroism, I decided to leave you, the light of my life, and never see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it failed; I overestimated my strength and underestimated my love. I would have died if you had not come to me. I wish I had died. Now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was wrong to think I could conquer my love for you; I never can. Seeing this house and these woods where my first love lived has only made it stronger. In my madness, I told myself that your mother’s spirit lived on in you, and that you should be to me what she was. Every attempt to cast this off only makes this unnatural, guilty love cling tighter, destroying both your hopes and my life. No time or distance can remove from my soul what has become a part of it. Since arriving here, I have lived in the hell of a passion that will burn until I am cold and dead.

They know how sharp he is; he will get a life sentence. They will make sure the Artful Dodger gets nothing less than life. What do you mean by lagging and a lifer? Mr. Bolter demanded. Why talk to me like that? Why not speak so I can understand you? Fagin was about to explain that these terms meant transportation for life, but the conversation was interrupted by Master Bates, who entered with his hands in his pockets and a look of mock misery on his face. It is all over, Fagin, Charley said, once he and his new companion were introduced. What do you mean? They found the man who owns the snuffbox; others are coming to identify him, and the Artful is booked for a trip overseas, Master Bates replied. I need a full mourning suit and a hatband to visit him before he leaves. To think of Jack Dawkins—the great Dodger—going away for a cheap, worthless snuffbox! I never thought he would go down for anything less than a gold watch and chain. Why didn't he rob some wealthy man of all his valuables and go out like a gentleman, rather than a common thief with no honor or glory? With this lament for his friend, Master Bates sat down, looking dejected. Why do you say he has no honor or glory? Fagin snapped, glaring at his pupil. Was he not always the best among you? Is there one of you who could match him? Not one, Master Bates replied, his voice thick with regret. Then why are you complaining? Fagin demanded. Why are you crying? Because it will not be on the record, will it? Charley retorted, his grief turning to defiance. It cannot be in the indictment; nobody will ever know how talented he was. How will he be remembered in the criminal records? Maybe he will not be mentioned at all. It is such a blow! Ha! ha! Fagin laughed, gesturing to Mr. Bolter while shaking with a fit of mirth. See what pride they take in their profession, my dear.

“Surely you don’t mean—” my sister started. “Indeed I do, Mum,” Pumblechook interrupted, “but hold on. Continue, Joseph. Well done! Proceed!” “What would everyone here say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?” “I would call it generous,” my sister replied. “Well then,” Joe said, “it is more than twenty pounds.” That wretched hypocrite Pumblechook nodded, adding with a condescending chuckle, “It is more than that, Mum. Excellent! Keep going, Joseph!” “To finish it,” Joe said, happily handing the bag to my sister, “it is twenty-five pounds.” “It is twenty-five pounds, Mum,” that deceitful swindler Pumblechook repeated, standing to shake her hand, “and it is no more than you deserve, as I stated when consulted, and I congratulate you on the funds!” Had the villain stopped there, his conduct would have been bad enough, but he worsened his offense by seizing me with a sense of ownership that eclipsed his previous behavior. “Now, Joseph and wife,” Pumblechook declared, gripping my arm, “I am a man who finishes what he starts. This boy must be apprenticed immediately. That is my way. Bound at once.” “Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, clutching the cash, “we are very grateful.” “Think nothing of it, Mum,” the wicked corn-merchant replied. “A pleasure is a pleasure everywhere. But this boy, you see; he must be bound. I promised to arrange it, to be honest.” The magistrates were holding court nearby, so we went immediately to have me apprenticed to Joe before them. I say we went, but Pumblechook shoved me along as if I had just committed a crime. The crowd clearly assumed I was guilty; as he pushed me through, people whispered, “What did he do?” and “He is young, but looks like trouble, doesn't he?” One kind-looking person even handed me a pamphlet featuring a drawing of a wicked youth in heavy chains, titled To Be Read In My Cell. The hall seemed strange, with pews taller than those in church, onlookers leaning over the railings, and powerful magistrates—one with a powdered wig—lounging in chairs, taking snuff, dozing, or reading papers, while dark portraits hung on the walls that appeared to my untrained eyes like a mix of candy and adhesive.

He did not try again. The boys lay there, counting the agonizing seconds until it felt as if time itself had stalled and eternity was fading; they were relieved when the sun finally began to set. One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, and smiled grimly at his companion, whose head rested on his knees. He nudged him with his foot and said, "Hey! You're supposed to be keeping watch, aren't you? It's fine, though—nothing happened." "Wow, did I fall asleep?" "Partly, I suppose. It's almost time to move, partner. What should we do with the rest of our loot?" "I don't know—leave it here like we always have, I guess. No point in carrying it until we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is a lot to haul around." "Fair enough. It won't hurt to come back one more time." "True, but I'd suggest coming at night as usual; it's safer." "Maybe, but listen; it might be a while before I get the right opening for that job. Accidents happen, and this isn't the best spot. We should just bury it properly—deep." "Good idea," his partner agreed. He walked over, knelt, lifted a hearthstone, and pulled out a jingling bag. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to Joe, who was already on his knees in the corner, digging with his knife. The boys instantly forgot their fear and misery. They watched every move with wide, greedy eyes. Luck! The sheer brilliance of it was unimaginable. Six hundred dollars was enough to make half a dozen boys rich. This was treasure hunting under perfect conditions—no guessing where to dig. They nudged each other constantly, a silent communication that meant, "Aren't you glad we're here now?" Joe’s knife hit something. "Hello!" he said. "What is it?" his partner asked. "A rotting plank—no, I think it's a box. Here, give me a hand and we'll see what's inside. Never mind, I've broken through." He reached in and pulled out a handful of gold coins. The boys above were just as thrilled and delighted as the men. Joe’s partner said, "Let's make quick work of this. There's a rusty pick in the weeds by the corner near the fireplace—I saw it a moment ago."

I am dining out, so I will not need you. Thank you, sir, the man replied, exiting the room. Now, Alan, we must hurry. This chest is quite heavy; I will carry it, and you can bring the rest. He spoke with urgent authority, and Campbell felt compelled to obey. They departed together. Upon reaching the landing, Dorian unlocked the door, then paused, his expression darkening with unease. He shuddered, whispering that he could not enter. It makes no difference to me, Campbell replied coldly. Dorian opened the door slightly, catching sight of his portrait leering in the sun. The torn curtain lay on the floor. He recalled failing to conceal the canvas the previous night and nearly rushed forward, but recoiled in horror. A loathsome, wet red dew glistened on one of the hands, as if the painting were sweating blood. It seemed more repulsive than the silent, still form on the table, whose distorted shadow remained fixed on the carpet. Taking a breath, he stepped inside with averted eyes, determined not to look at the corpse. He grabbed the gold-and-purple fabric and threw it over the painting. He stood there, afraid to turn, staring at the pattern of the cloth. He heard Campbell bring in the chest and tools. He wondered if Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever known one another. Leave me, a stern voice commanded. He hurried out, noting the dead man was back in the chair and Campbell was staring at a yellow face. As he descended the stairs, he heard the lock turn. Long after seven, Campbell entered the library, pale but composed. I have finished what you requested, he muttered.

Elizabeth was despondent, finding no joy in her daily life. To her, happiness felt like a betrayal of the dead, and she believed only endless mourning could honor such a tragic loss of innocence. She was no longer the cheerful girl who once walked by the lake with me, dreaming of our future. The first of life's great sorrows had arrived, extinguishing her light. Reflecting on Justine Moritz’s miserable death, she told me, "The world looks different now. I used to view accounts of injustice as distant, fictional tales, but now that misery has struck close to home, people seem like monsters hungry for blood. I know I am being unfair; everyone believed her guilty, and if she had truly murdered the child she raised for mere jewels, she would have been a monster. But she was innocent. I feel it, and your agreement confirms it. Victor, when lies can mimic the truth so perfectly, how can anyone be sure of happiness? I feel as though I am walking on a cliff’s edge, surrounded by people trying to push me into the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, yet the killer remains free, perhaps even respected. I would rather face the scaffold myself than trade places with such a wretch." I listened in agony, knowing that while I did not commit the act, I was the true cause. Elizabeth saw my pain and took my hand, saying, "My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have devastated me, but I am not as miserable as you."

By eight o’clock, I had reached an altitude of seventeen miles. My ascent was clearly accelerating, a trend that would have persisted even without my releasing ballast. Though I suffered intermittent, violent headaches and occasional nosebleeds, my condition was better than anticipated. Breathing, however, became increasingly labored, with each breath causing painful chest spasms. I prepared my condensing equipment for immediate use. The view of the earth was stunning. To the west, north, and south, a vast, calm ocean stretched out, deepening in color and showing a slight curve. Far to the east, the British Isles, the Atlantic coasts of France and Spain, and a sliver of North Africa were visible. Human structures had vanished; the world’s greatest cities were gone. Gibraltar appeared as a mere speck, while the Mediterranean, scattered with islands like stars in the sky, stretched eastward until it seemed to pour over the horizon’s edge, leaving me straining to hear the roar of a great waterfall. Above, the sky was pitch black, filled with brilliant stars. The pigeons were clearly suffering, so I decided to release them. I placed a gray-mottled bird on the wicker rim. It looked around anxiously, fluttering and cooing, but refused to leave. When I tossed it a few yards away, it did not descend as I expected; instead, it struggled frantically to return, crying out in a shrill, piercing voice. It managed to reach the rim, but its head immediately slumped, and it fell dead into the car.

The young people were desperate to visit Lyme. Captain Wentworth mentioned returning, as it was only seventeen miles from Uppercross. Despite it being November, the weather was mild. Louisa, the most enthusiastic of the group, decided they would go. Pleased to have her own way, she overruled her parents' desire to wait until summer. The party would consist of Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth. The initial plan to go and return in one day was rejected by Mr. Musgrove to spare his horses. Furthermore, a November day would not allow enough time for sightseeing once the seven-hour travel time was subtracted. They decided to stay overnight and return the following day. Although they met early at the Great House and departed promptly, it was well past noon by the time the two carriages descended the steep hill into Lyme. It was clear they would have little daylight left to explore. After checking into an inn and ordering dinner, they immediately walked to the sea. Lyme was quiet, as the tourist season had ended and most visitors had left. Since the town's architecture is unremarkable, visitors focus on its unique geography: the main street leading toward the water, the walk to the Cobb along the bay, and the beautiful cliffs stretching to the east. Anyone visiting Lyme would surely find the area charming and worth exploring.

For a moment, I was too stunned to think clearly. I knew my own drawing was quite different in detail, even if the general shape was similar. I took a candle to the other side of the room to examine the parchment more closely. When I flipped it over, I saw my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had drawn it. At first, I was simply amazed by the strange coincidence that a skull, matching my beetle in size and shape, happened to be on the other side of the paper without my knowledge. Such coincidences often leave the mind paralyzed as it struggles to find a logical connection. However, as I recovered, a far more startling realization dawned on me. I clearly remembered that the parchment had been blank when I drew the beetle. I was certain of this because I had checked both sides to find a clean spot. If the skull had been there, I would have noticed it. This mystery felt impossible to explain, yet a faint idea began to form in my mind—a glimmer of the truth that last night’s events would eventually prove. I stood up, put the parchment away, and stopped thinking about it until I could be alone. After you left and Jupiter was asleep, I began a more organized investigation. First, I considered how I had found the parchment. We discovered the beetle on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island, just above the high-tide mark. When I picked it up, it bit me, causing me to drop it. Jupiter, always cautious, looked for a leaf to grab the insect after it flew toward him.

Unless you call Miss Havisham a man. And I doubt you would go that far. Miss Havisham, in town? Joe asked. Is there any other Miss Havisham? my sister replied. She wants this boy to go play there. He is going, and he had better play, she said, shaking her head at me to encourage me to act cheerful, or I will punish him. I had heard of Miss Havisham; everyone for miles around knew of the wealthy, grim woman who lived in a large, gloomy house, barricaded against thieves and hidden from the world. Well, I am surprised, Joe said, amazed. I wonder how she knows Pip! Fool! my sister cried. Who said she knew him? Joe politely suggested that someone must have mentioned he should go play there. Could she not ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew a boy? Is it not possible that Pumblechook is her tenant and visits to pay his rent? Could she not ask him then? And could Pumblechook, always thoughtful of us—though you might not think so, Joseph—then suggest this boy, who stands here prancing—I was certainly not prancing—whom I have always served so faithfully? Well said! Uncle Pumblechook cheered. Very well put! Now, Joseph, you understand the situation. No, Joseph, my sister said reproachfully, while Joe wiped his nose apologetically, you still do not understand. You may think you do, but you do not. You do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing this boy’s fortune might be made by visiting Miss Havisham, has offered to take him to town tonight, keep him, and bring him to her tomorrow morning. Good heavens! my sister cried, throwing off her bonnet in frustration, here I am talking to idiots while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the horse catches a cold outside, and the boy is covered in dirt from head to toe!

This marriage is the right choice. I doubted it initially, but I concede the point now. Sibyl Vane was created for you; without her, you would remain incomplete. Dorian Gray squeezed his friend's hand in gratitude. I knew you would understand. Harry is so cynical he frightens me. But the orchestra is starting. It is terrible, but it only lasts five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you will see the girl to whom I have dedicated my life and all the goodness within me. Fifteen minutes later, amidst thunderous applause, Sibyl Vane appeared. She was undeniably beautiful, perhaps the most lovely creature Lord Henry had ever seen. Her shy grace and startled expression gave her the air of a fawn. A faint blush touched her cheeks as she looked out at the enthusiastic crowd, and her lips trembled. Basil Hallward stood to applaud, while Dorian Gray remained motionless, staring at her as if in a trance. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, whispering that she was charming. The scene was the Capulet hall, and Romeo had entered with his friends. As the music played, Sibyl moved through the group of poorly dressed actors like a being from a higher realm. Her movements were fluid, her throat curved like a lily, and her hands appeared to be carved from cool ivory. Yet, she seemed strangely detached. She showed no joy when she looked at Romeo. Her lines were delivered with a hollow, artificial tone. While her voice was exquisite, the delivery was completely false, draining the life from the verse and rendering the passion unreal. Dorian Gray turned pale, watching her with growing confusion and anxiety. His friends remained silent, both realizing she was utterly incompetent.

From the moment we embarked, I had watched anxiously for signs that we were being watched. I saw none. We were certainly not being followed by any boat. Had we been, I would have steered for shore to force them to reveal their intentions. Instead, we traveled without interference. He wore his boat-cloak and seemed a natural part of the surroundings. Remarkably, he was the least anxious among us. He was not indifferent, as he spoke of hoping to see his gentleman thrive abroad, nor was he resigned, but he refused to worry about danger until it arrived. If you knew what it was to sit here with my dear boy and smoke after years behind four walls, you would envy me, he told me. You do not know what it is. I think I understand the joy of freedom, I replied. He shook his head. You do not know it as I do. You must have been locked away to truly understand, but I will not be gloomy. It seemed contradictory that he would risk his life for an ideal, yet I realized that freedom without danger was foreign to his experience. He soon added, When I was on the other side of the world, I always looked toward this side. It felt hollow there, even as I grew rich. Everyone knew Magwitch, and no one cared where he went. They are not so indifferent here, at least not if they knew where I was. If all goes well, I said, you will be safe and free in a few hours. He took a long breath. I hope so. And do you think so?

At the top of the stairs, he composed himself to unleash his famous, terrifying laugh. It had proven effective before, turning Lord Raker’s hair white overnight and causing three of Lady Canterville’s governesses to quit early. He let out a chilling shriek that echoed through the vaulted ceiling, but as the sound faded, Mrs. Otis stepped out in a blue robe. She offered him a bottle of medicine, suggesting it would cure his indigestion. Furious, the ghost prepared to transform into a large black dog—a feat that had once caused a man to lose his sanity—but the sound of approaching footsteps made him pause. Instead, he simply glowed with a faint light and vanished with a mournful groan just as the twins arrived. Back in his room, he collapsed in distress. The rudeness of the twins and the practical nature of Mrs. Otis were irritating, but he was most upset that he could not wear his suit of armor. He had hoped the Americans would appreciate a ghost in armor, perhaps out of respect for the poet Longfellow, whose work he enjoyed. It was his own suit, which he had worn to great acclaim at the Kenilworth tournament before Queen Elizabeth I. However, the heavy steel breastplate and helmet had been too much for him; he had fallen hard on the stone floor, bruising his knees and hand. He remained ill for several days, leaving his room only to touch up the bloodstain. Once he recovered, he decided to try once more to frighten the American family.

A chaotic mix of farmers, butchers, traders, thieves, and idlers crowded the market. The air was filled with the whistling of drovers, barking dogs, the noise of livestock, and the shouting and swearing of the mob. Bells rang from taverns, adding to the overwhelming roar of voices and the constant pushing and shoving. The scene was filthy and deafening, leaving the senses completely overwhelmed. Mr. Sikes pulled Oliver through the thickest part of the crowd, ignoring the sights that shocked the boy. He nodded to a few acquaintances and refused several offers for a drink, pushing forward until they reached Holborn. Looking at the clock on St. Andrew’s Church, Sikes told Oliver it was nearly seven and urged him to walk faster. He jerked the boy’s wrist, forcing Oliver to trot to keep up with his long strides. They continued at this pace past Hyde Park Corner toward Kensington. When Sikes saw an empty cart labeled Hounslow, he politely asked the driver for a ride to Isleworth. The driver agreed and asked if Oliver was his son. Sikes confirmed it, his hand resting on his pocket where he kept a pistol. The driver noticed Oliver was breathless and remarked that his father walked quite fast. Sikes quickly interrupted, claiming the boy was used to it, and helped him into the cart. He told Oliver to rest on a pile of sacks. As they passed various milestones, Oliver wondered where they were going. They traveled through Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, continuing their journey without stopping.

The connection between body and soul was profound. The soul possessed animal instincts, while the body experienced moments of spirituality. Senses could refine, yet intellect could corrupt. It was impossible to distinguish where physical impulses ended and mental ones began, rendering standard psychological definitions superficial. Whether the soul was a prisoner of sin or the body existed within the soul remained an enigma. He questioned if psychology could ever become an exact science capable of revealing the hidden mechanisms of life. Currently, we misunderstand ourselves and others. Experience holds no ethical value; it is merely a label for our past mistakes. While moralists claim experience builds character, it lacks true motive power. It only proves that our future mirrors our past, and that sins once committed with regret are eventually repeated with pleasure. He believed the experimental method was the only way to analyze human passion, and Dorian Gray was the perfect subject. Dorian's sudden obsession with Sibyl Vane was a fascinating psychological study. Driven by curiosity and a desire for novelty, it was a complex emotion. The raw instincts of youth had been reshaped by his imagination into something that felt detached from the physical, making it far more dangerous. We are most enslaved by the passions we fail to understand. Often, when we believe we are experimenting on others, we are actually testing ourselves. As Lord Henry pondered these thoughts, his valet knocked to remind him it was time to dress for dinner.

Mrs. Clay’s feelings had outweighed her ambition, leading her to abandon her long-term plans for Sir Walter for the sake of the young man. Yet, she possesses both heart and intellect; it remains uncertain whose guile will ultimately prevail, or if the man who stopped her from marrying Sir Walter might eventually be charmed into making her Lady William. Sir Walter and Elizabeth were undoubtedly dismayed and humiliated by her departure and the realization of her duplicity. While they sought solace with their prominent cousins, they could not help but feel that a life of flattering others without receiving similar admiration in return was a hollow existence. Anne, confident that Lady Russell had come to appreciate Captain Wentworth, found her only regret in the lack of family connections to offer him. She felt this inadequacy deeply. The gap in their wealth meant nothing to her, but having no respectable, harmonious family to welcome him—unlike the warmth she received from his own siblings—caused her genuine distress amidst her otherwise perfect happiness. She had only Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith to introduce to him, though he was happy to embrace both. He came to sincerely value Lady Russell, despite her past errors, and he was eager to praise her in every other regard. Mrs. Smith, meanwhile, quickly earned his lasting regard. Her past kindness to Anne was sufficient, and their marriage gained them two friends rather than losing one. She was their first guest once they settled, and Captain Wentworth fully repaid her earlier support by helping her recover her husband’s West Indian assets, acting as a tireless and resolute advocate through every obstacle.

We could certainly build a thrilling superstition around this. I suppose you will name the bug scarabaeus caput hominis, or something similar, as there are many such names in natural history books. But where are the antennae you mentioned? The antennae! Legrand replied, sounding strangely agitated. I am certain you must see them. I drew them as clearly as they appear on the actual insect, which should be enough. Well, perhaps so, I said, but I still do not see them. I handed him the paper without further comment, not wanting to upset him. I was surprised by his reaction; his bad mood puzzled me, and the drawing truly lacked any visible antennae, looking much like a standard picture of a death's-head moth. He took the paper irritably and was about to crumple it into the fire when a quick look at the design caught his attention. His face turned bright red, then deathly pale. He studied the drawing closely for several minutes. Finally, he stood up, took a candle, and sat on a chest in the corner to examine the paper from every angle. He remained silent, and his behavior shocked me, but I decided not to provoke him further. He soon placed the paper in his wallet and locked it in his desk. He calmed down, but his earlier excitement had vanished. He seemed less angry than distracted, lost in deep thought for the rest of the evening. I had planned to stay the night, but given his mood, I decided to leave. He did not ask me to stay, but he shook my hand with extra warmth as I left. About a month later, while I was in Charleston, his servant Jupiter visited me. I had never seen the old man look so discouraged, and I feared something terrible had happened to my friend.

Well, you rascal, the old lady exclaimed as he entered, why have you stayed away so long? My dear Lady Clem, I never have a moment to myself, Lord Arthur replied with a smile. I suppose you mean you spend your days with Miss Sybil Merton, shopping and talking nonsense? I cannot understand why people make such a fuss about marriage. In my day, we never acted so affectionate in public or private. I assure you I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her dressmakers. Of course; that is the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I wonder you men do not take warning. People once did foolish things for me, and now I am just a poor, grumpy woman with aches and pains. If it were not for Lady Jansen, who sends me the latest French novels, I do not think I could get through the day. Doctors are useless, except for taking one's money. They cannot even cure my heartburn. I have brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem, Lord Arthur said seriously. It is a wonderful thing, invented by an American. I do not think I like American inventions, Arthur. I am quite sure I do not. I read some American novels lately, and they were nonsense. Oh, but there is no nonsense about this, Lady Clem! I assure you it is a perfect cure. You must promise to try it. Lord Arthur took a small box from his pocket and handed it to her. Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a gift? That is very sweet of you. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a candy. I will take it at once. Good heavens, Lady Clem! Lord Arthur cried, grabbing her hand. You must not do that. It is a homeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it could do you great harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You will be amazed at the result. I would like to take it now, Lady Clementina said, holding the small transparent capsule up to the light. I am sure it is delicious. The truth is, although I hate doctors, I love medicine. However, I will keep it until my next attack. And when will that be? Lord Arthur asked eagerly.

Tom enlisted in the Cadets of Temperance, drawn by the flashy appearance of their uniforms. He vowed to avoid tobacco and swearing while a member, only to discover that pledging to abstain merely intensified his urge to indulge. Only the prospect of wearing his red sash during a public event kept him from quitting. He pinned his hopes on the impending funeral of Judge Frazer, a local official nearing death. For days, Tom anxiously monitored the Judge’s health, even practicing in his regalia, but the man’s recovery frustrated him. Tom resigned in annoyance, only for the Judge to die that very night, leaving Tom feeling betrayed. The funeral procession was impressive, and the Cadets looked enviable, but Tom felt liberated. Surprisingly, once he was free to drink and swear, the temptation vanished. Soon, his newfound freedom grew dull. He tried keeping a diary but quit after three days of inactivity. When a minstrel show arrived, he and Joe Harper formed a troupe, enjoying two days of excitement. Even the Fourth of July disappointed; rain canceled the parade, and the visiting United States Senator, Mr. Benton, failed to live up to Tom’s exaggerated expectations of his stature. Then, a circus came to town.

We grew up together, separated by less than a year. We never knew conflict; our bond thrived on the harmony of our contrasting natures. Elizabeth possessed a serene, focused temperament, whereas I combined my natural fervor with a capacity for intense study and a profound hunger for wisdom. She occupied herself with the ethereal visions of poets, finding endless wonder in the majestic Swiss landscape—the towering mountains, the shifting seasons, and the dramatic Alpine weather. While she observed the beauty of the world with quiet contentment, I sought to uncover its underlying causes. The world was a mystery I longed to solve, and my earliest memories are filled with the thrill of discovering nature's hidden laws. When my brother was born seven years later, my parents settled permanently in their homeland. We split our time between a house in Geneva and a country estate on the eastern shore of the lake, living in relative seclusion. Preferring a small circle to a crowd, I remained distant from most schoolmates, forming only one deep friendship with Henry Clerval. The son of a local merchant, Henry was a boy of remarkable imagination. He embraced adventure and danger, immersing himself in tales of chivalry. He wrote heroic ballads and stories of enchantment, often organizing plays and masquerades based on the legends of King Arthur and the crusaders. My childhood was exceptionally joyful, defined by the boundless kindness of my parents, who acted not as arbitrary masters but as the devoted architects of our happiness.

We declared ourselves free men so loudly that a patriotic orator and his crowd gathered around us, looking quite aggressive. The orator announced that if we were truly free, Britain's liberties would protect us, and demanded we provide proof. When I hesitated, the king shouted that the man accusing us should be the one to prove we were not free. The king understood the law only in theory, not in practice. The crowd grew bored, and the orator explained that since we were strangers, the law required us to prove our own freedom. I asked for time to send for help, but the orator refused, claiming it would be too inconvenient for our master. When the king began to shout that he had no master, I silenced him before he could reveal his identity and appear insane. There is no need to detail the rest; the earl auctioned us off. This same cruel law existed in the American South centuries later, but it only felt truly hellish once I was the one on the auction block. We were sold like livestock. Because the town was so quiet, we fetched a price that still embarrasses me today.

What is wrong? I replied, Pap, and mam, and sis, and— Then I faltered. He said, Oh, hang it, do not carry on so; we all face hardships, and this will resolve itself. What is wrong with them? They are—are you the boat's watchman? Yes, he said, sounding quite pleased. I am the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and head deck-hand; sometimes I am the freight and passengers too. I am not as wealthy as old Jim Hornback, nor can I be as generous to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, throwing money around as he does; but I have told him many times I would not trade places with him. A sailor's life is for me, and I would not live two miles outside of town, where nothing ever happens, not for all his riches and more. I interrupted, saying, They are in terrible trouble, and— Who is? Why, pap, mam, sis, and Miss Hooker; if you would take your ferry-boat up there— Up where? Where are they? On the wreck. What wreck? Why, there is only one. You do not mean the Walter Scott? Yes. Good heavens! What are they doing there, for mercy's sake? Well, they did not go there on purpose. I bet they did not! Great goodness, there is no hope for them if they do not get off quickly! How on earth did they get into such a mess? It was easy. Miss Hooker was visiting up at the town— Yes, Booth's Landing—go on. She was visiting Booth's Landing, and just at dusk she started across with her servant in the horse-ferry to stay the night at a friend's house—I forget the name—and they lost their steering-oar. They drifted downstream, stern first, for two miles and became wedged on the wreck. The ferryman, the servant, and the horses were lost, but Miss Hooker managed to grab hold and climb onto the wreck. About an hour after dark, we arrived in our trading-scow, and it was so dark we did not see the wreck until we were right upon it; so we became wedged too. Everyone was saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best creature! I almost wish it had been me, I truly do. My word! It is the most astonishing thing I have ever encountered.

Watching him in such states, I frequently pondered the ancient theory of the dual soul, entertaining the notion of a twofold Dupin—the imaginative and the analytical. Do not mistake my account for a mystery or a work of fiction. What I observed in the Frenchman was simply the product of an intense, perhaps even unhealthy, intellect. A specific instance of his commentary will best illustrate this. One evening, we were walking along a grimy street near the Palais Royal. Both lost in thought, we had remained silent for at least a quarter of an hour. Suddenly, Dupin remarked, "He is quite small, it is true, and would be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés." "Undoubtedly," I answered instinctively, failing at first to realize—so deep was my contemplation—how perfectly he had aligned with my own thoughts. A moment later, I regained my composure, feeling utterly stunned. "Dupin," I said seriously, "this is beyond me. I am truly amazed and can hardly believe my ears. How could you possibly know I was thinking of—?" I stopped, wanting to confirm if he truly knew my subject. "Of Chantilly," he finished. "Why do you hesitate? You were telling yourself that his small stature made him unsuitable for tragedy." This was exactly what I had been considering. Chantilly was a former cobbler from the Rue St. Denis who, obsessed with the stage, had tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy, only to be widely mocked for his efforts. "For heaven's sake, tell me," I cried, "the method—if there is one—by which you read my mind." I was more shaken than I cared to admit. "It was the fruit seller," my friend replied, "who led you to conclude that the cobbler lacked the height for Xerxes and his like." "The fruit seller! You surprise me; I do not know any fruit seller." "The man who bumped into you as we turned onto this street—perhaps fifteen minutes ago." I recalled then that a fruit seller, balancing a large basket of apples, had nearly knocked me over as we moved from the Rue C— into this thoroughfare, though I could not fathom how that connected to Chantilly.

My father stayed by my side to comfort me, replacing bitter memories with hopeful prospects; I found a strange sweetness in my grief, knowing he was there to dry my tears. He further distracted me by comparing my sorrow to his own despair after losing my mother. I shuddered at his vivid descriptions; he possessed a poet’s imagination, and his account of that emotional whirlwind was so lifelike that I trembled as I listened. I marveled that he could ever return to ordinary life after such intense experiences, which seemed to transcend human capacity. His emotions felt better suited to a spirit dwelling in earthquakes and volcanoes than to a mortal man. Yet, he had changed; he was now entirely gentle and loving, his smile revealing a heart filled with kindness. Two months after my aunt died, we moved to London, where my father encouraged me to pursue more rigorous studies. He delighted in my progress, assisting me with every lesson. We socialized often, and he worked to make every day enjoyable. Our mutual love and respect made every moment charming. We lived so fully that a single week felt like months, with every new experience adding zest to our lives. We frequently traveled together to see beautiful scenery or art, or simply to find amusement. I was always happiest when near him. I regretted when others joined us, but a single tender look from my father would instantly restore my joy. Those hours of intense delight were brief, yet in retrospect, they feel like a lifetime, now obscured by the mist of grief that soon followed to hide them from my sight.

I will now share my own story. My early life holds little of note, so I will be brief. However, I must reflect on my childhood to show how, when my only hope vanished and the one affection I was allowed to hold was destroyed, my life effectively ended. My aunt was nothing like my father. While she was not a bad person, she possessed the coldest heart imaginable, entirely incapable of love. She took me in out of a sense of duty, but having lived alone for years, she refused to let a child disturb her peace. She was unmarried and had spent five years living in solitude on her inherited estate by Loch Lomond in Scotland. My father had wanted her to live with me at our family mansion near Richmond, but she refused. Instead, once she settled my father’s affairs, she took me with her to Scotland. Until I was eight, I was raised by my mother’s former servant. I lived in a distant part of the house and only saw my aunt twice a day: once at noon in my nursery, and once after her dinner. She never showed me affection and seemed constantly worried that I might annoy her. My nurse always coached me carefully before these visits, and because I was so intimidated by my aunt’s cold demeanor, I remained perfectly still and quiet during our brief meetings. Under my nurse’s care, I spent my time roaming the park and fields. Born of deep love, I was a sensitive child, and I felt a passionate attachment to everything around me, even the inanimate objects.

My father had been the center of my existence, and his memory remained the essence of my life. While I could feel thankful to others, I could never again love or hope as I once had; everything was agony, and even my joys were merely tolerated rather than savored. I existed like a lonely valley surrounded by sheer, dark cliffs, where no warmth could reach and no path led to brighter pastures. Consequently, while the presence of friendship offered temporary relief, it could not heal me. It arrived like a soft breeze, then vanished, leaving me barely aware of its absence. My inner vitality had withered, so do not wonder that I greeted the arrival of a friend—that greatest of blessings—without joy, and mourned his departure without deep sorrow. My friend was named Woodville. I shall recount his story briefly so you might understand how frozen my heart must have been to remain unmoved by his moving words and gentle compassion, and how, as he was also deeply troubled, we were suited to comfort one another, had I not been turned to stone by the Gorgon of Misery. Woodville’s sorrows were not as profound as mine; his was a natural grief, meant to refine rather than ruin the spirit, from which he might eventually emerge even more radiant. Woodville, the son of an impoverished minister, possessed a classical education. He was among the rare few favored by fortune from birth, gifted with boundless intellect and charm, and shielded by her from even the slightest flaw or fleeting disappointment. She appeared to have crafted his mind with a purity that no corruption could stain, and his judgment was beyond error. His genius was extraordinary, rising like a brilliant star that drew every gaze in admiration. He was a poet, though that title has been so cheapened it fails to capture his true nature. He resembled the poets of antiquity, blessed by the Muses at birth. Moving among men, he seemed surrounded by a divine aura that set him apart and elevated him above them. His exceptional beauty, the intense light in his eyes, and his eloquent speech, which left listeners in silent, rapturous awe, made him so superior that others seemed created merely to serve his greatness.

Emma did not regret her decision to attend the Coles' party. The visit left her with pleasant memories, and she felt the boost to her popularity more than compensated for any loss of social exclusivity. She had certainly delighted the Coles, who were good people, and she was sure her presence would be remembered for some time. Yet, perfect satisfaction is rare, and two things troubled her. She wondered if she had acted improperly by sharing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings with Frank Churchill. It was a lapse, but the idea had been so compelling that she could not help but speak, and Frank’s agreement with her assessment was such a flattering validation of her insight that she struggled to regret it entirely. Her second regret was clearer: she genuinely felt inferior to Jane in musical ability. She lamented her own lack of childhood discipline and immediately sat down to practice for ninety minutes. Harriet then arrived, and if her praise could have sufficed, Emma would have been comforted. Oh, if I could play like you and Miss Fairfax, Harriet sighed. Do not compare us, Emma replied. My playing is like a lamp compared to her sunshine. Oh, I think you are just as good, Harriet insisted. Everyone last night said how well you played. Those who understood music knew the difference, Emma said. My playing is merely good enough to earn praise, but Jane’s is far superior. Harriet persisted, arguing that Mr. Cole and Frank Churchill had both praised Emma’s taste, which Frank valued more than technical skill. But Jane has both, Emma countered. Harriet remained unconvinced, noting that Jane’s skill was expected since she would eventually have to teach for a living.

So you won't, won't you? Oh, you precious fool! It's naughty, isn't it, Oliver? asked Charley Bates. He'll end up hanged, won't he? I don't know what that means, Oliver replied. Something like this, old fellow, said Charley. He grabbed the end of his neckerchief, held it up, dropped his head to his shoulder, and made a sharp sound through his teeth, clearly pantomiming a hanging. That's what it means, Charley said. Look how he stares, Jack! I've never seen such great company; he'll be the death of me. Charley laughed heartily and returned to his pipe, eyes watering. You've been raised poorly, the Dodger said, admiring his polished boots. Fagin will make something of you, or you'll be his first failure. You should start now; you'll be in the trade sooner than you think, and you're just wasting time. Master Bates added his own moral advice, and then he and the Dodger described the many pleasures of their life, hinting that Oliver should win Fagin's favor immediately. And remember this, Nolly, the Dodger said as the Jew unlocked the door above, if you don't take handkerchiefs and watches— What's the point of talking like that? Charley interrupted. He doesn't know what you mean. If you don't take them, the Dodger explained, someone else will. The people who lose them will be worse off, you'll be worse off, and nobody gains anything except the thieves—and you have just as much right to them as they do. Exactly! said the Jew, who had entered unnoticed. It's all very simple, my dear; take the Dodger's word for it. He understands his trade perfectly. The old man rubbed his hands together, chuckling at his pupil's skill. The conversation ended as the Jew returned with Miss Betsy and a man Oliver had never seen, whom the Dodger called Tom Chitling, who had lingered on the stairs to flirt with the lady before entering.

As summer progressed, the sun’s intense heat accompanied a plague that struck the world with lethal precision. Nations succumbed and perished. Abundant crops rotted in the fields during autumn, while the desperate souls seeking sustenance for their families collapsed, dead from the pestilence, in the furrows. The forests swayed grandly above the dying, whose discordant cries mingled with the trees' solemn rustling. Birds flew through the branches and deer rested undisturbed, while livestock wandered from open stables to graze in the wheat, for the contagion claimed only humanity. Our dread intensified alongside the rising death toll. My dear Idris and I gazed at each other and our children. I promised her we would protect them, imagining a future where we would share these memories as distant, bygone terrors. I vowed they would survive, their health and voices preserved. Our eldest son sensed the surrounding tragedy and occasionally asked about the widespread ruin, yet his youthful spirit quickly dismissed such heavy thoughts. Evelyn, our joyful, innocent infant, filled the halls with laughter and playful antics, oblivious to the surrounding sorrow. Clara, our sweet and gentle daughter, remained our comfort and joy. She dedicated herself to nursing the ill, consoling the grieving, and aiding the elderly, while also engaging the young. She moved through our home like a celestial being, brightening our gloom with her presence. Though she was praised for her deeds, seeing her simple, unassuming nature as she played with the children or helped Idris made it difficult to fathom how such profound courage and wisdom existed within her. The summer dragged on, as we clung to the hope that winter might at least curb the sickness. The possibility of the disease vanishing entirely felt too precious to voice; whenever someone dared to suggest it, the listeners would break into tears and sobs, revealing the depth of their terror and the fragility of their optimism.

After dinner, the group headed to the sandbar to hunt for turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and upon finding soft spots, knelt to dig with their hands. Sometimes they retrieved fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole; the eggs were perfectly round, white, and slightly smaller than walnuts. They enjoyed a grand feast of fried eggs that night and again on Friday morning. After breakfast, they ran out onto the bar, shouting and chasing each other. They shed their clothes until they were naked, continuing their game in the shallow water against a strong current that frequently knocked them over, adding to the excitement. Occasionally, they gathered to splash water at one another, shielding their faces from the spray until they grappled and wrestled. The strongest would dunk his opponent, leaving them all in a tangled heap of limbs, surfacing to gasp and laugh. Once exhausted, they sprawled on the hot, dry sand, covering themselves with it before returning to the water to repeat the cycle. Eventually, they decided their bare skin resembled flesh-colored tights, so they drew a ring in the sand and held a circus, with three boys insisting on being clowns. Next, they played marbles until the game lost its appeal. Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom refused, having realized he had lost his string of rattlesnake rattles while undressing. Fearing he might suffer a cramp without his charm, he searched until he found it. By then, the others were tired and restless. They drifted apart, feeling melancholy as they gazed across the river at the sleepy village. Tom found himself tracing the name BECKY in the sand with his toe. He angrily erased it, ashamed of his sentimentality, yet he wrote it again, unable to resist. Finally, he cleared the sand and rejoined the other boys to distract himself.

She was right about the rats. Every so often, one would poke its nose out of a corner hole. She explained that she kept objects nearby to throw at them when she was alone, or they would never leave her in peace. She showed me a twisted bar of lead, claiming she was usually a good shot, but she had hurt her arm recently and was unsure of her aim. She waited for an opportunity and threw it at a rat, but she missed badly and winced in pain. She then asked me to try for the next one. I wanted to leave before her husband returned, but I did not show it. I took the lead, and when the next rat appeared, I threw it; if the rat had stayed put, it would have been badly hurt. She praised my aim and fetched the lead, then brought a bundle of yarn for me to help her with. As I held the yarn, she talked about her marriage, but suddenly interrupted herself. Keep your eye on the rats, she said. You should keep the lead in your lap. She dropped the lead into my lap, and I clamped my legs together to hold it. After a moment, she took the yarn away, looked me directly in the face, and asked pleasantly, Come now, what is your real name? Is it Bill, Tom, Bob, or what? I shook like a leaf, unsure of what to do. Please do not make fun of a poor girl like me, I said. If I am in the way, I will leave. No, you will not, she replied. Sit down. I will not hurt you or tell on you. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I will keep it, and I will help you. My husband will too. You are just a runaway apprentice, that is all. There is no harm in it. You were treated badly and decided to leave. Bless you, child, I would never tell on you.

Nearly a year had passed since my father returned, and it was now late May. The woods were lush and green, and the scent of fresh grass filled the air. I hoped the beauty of nature would soften his heart and help me gain his trust. I chose one of these evenings for my attempt. I invited him for a walk, leading him to a nearby beech grove where the trees shielded us from the setting sun. After walking in silence, we sat on a mossy mound. I can still see that spot clearly: the smooth, slender trunks wrapped in dark ivy, the white bark, and the young leaves. The ground was covered in moss and scattered autumn leaves, with a few old stumps nearby. The breeze stirred the canopy, revealing the blue sky, and as evening approached, the sun turned the distant trees a deep red. The wind died down, and birds flew past toward their nests. We sat together in this peaceful place, which could have been a paradise if not for our inner turmoil. I remember it vividly, hoping its stillness would give me the courage and the right words to speak. My heart raced as I prepared to address him, determined not to be turned away, yet trembling at how he might react. Finally, I began with hesitation: Your kindness and the deep affection you showed me when you first returned give me the courage to speak to you now, not just as a daughter, but with the openness of a friend.

The group was split across two adjacent benches; Anne sat on the front one, where Mr. Elliot, aided by Colonel Wallis, had secured a place beside her. Miss Elliot, encircled by cousins and receiving the Colonel’s devoted attention, appeared perfectly satisfied. Anne felt perfectly prepared to enjoy the evening’s performance. She possessed the right temperament for every mood—tender, lively, intellectual, or tedious—and had never enjoyed a concert more, at least throughout the opening act. As it concluded, following an Italian aria, she interpreted the lyrics for Mr. Elliot using their shared program. She admitted that her translation was merely an approximation, as she was a poor student of the language. Mr. Elliot countered that her ability to instantly render those complex lines into elegant English proved her expertise, regardless of her claims. Anne playfully declined his excessive praise, hoping to avoid a rigorous test of her skills. He insisted that his time in Camden Place had revealed her to be a woman of rare, understated talent. When Anne dismissed his flattery, he lowered his voice to suggest he had understood her character far longer than she realized. Surprised, she questioned how he could know her before her arrival in Bath. He explained that he had long been familiar with her reputation, personality, and manners through mutual acquaintances. Mr. Elliot successfully piqued her curiosity, for few can resist the allure of such an enigma.

Oh, that is nothing! It is a pleasure. I do not work for money; I live entirely for my art. Lord Arthur placed four pounds, two shillings, and sixpence on the table, thanked the little German for his help, and after declining an invitation to meet some anarchists for tea on Saturday, left the house for the park. For the next two days, he was incredibly excited. On Friday at noon, he drove to the Buckingham to wait for news. All afternoon, the hall porter posted telegrams about horse races, divorce cases, and the weather, while the ticker tape reported on a long session in the House of Commons and a minor stock market panic. At four o’clock, the evening papers arrived. Lord Arthur took them into the library, much to the annoyance of Colonel Goodchild, who wanted to read his own speech about South African missions and the appointment of black bishops. None of the papers mentioned Chichester, so Lord Arthur assumed his attempt had failed. He was devastated and shaken. When he visited Herr Winckelkopf the next day, the man apologized profusely and offered a free replacement clock or a case of nitro-glycerine bombs at cost. Lord Arthur had lost faith in explosives, and Winckelkopf admitted that even dynamite was often poor quality these days. The German insisted that while the mechanism had likely failed, the clock might still explode. He cited a barometer he once sent to a governor in Odessa that took three months to detonate instead of the planned ten days. Although it only killed a housemaid because the governor had left town weeks earlier, it proved that dynamite, when controlled by machinery, was a powerful if unreliable tool.

The nephew glanced at him, then turned toward the door. Good night, the uncle said. I look forward to seeing you in the morning. Sleep well. Light my nephew to his room. And burn him in his bed if you like, he muttered to himself before ringing for his valet. Once the valet left, the Marquis paced his room in a silk robe, preparing for sleep on that stifling night. Moving silently in his slippers, he paced like a refined tiger, appearing like a wicked nobleman from a fairy tale caught between human and beast. He paced his luxurious bedroom, replaying the day’s journey: the climb at sunset, the mill, the cliffside prison, the village, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender pointing at the carriage chain. The fountain brought to mind the scene in Paris, the bundle on the step, and the tall man crying out that the child was dead. I am calm now, the Marquis said, and can sleep. Leaving one light on the hearth, he drew his thin curtains and listened as the night sighed while he settled into bed. For three hours, the stone faces on the exterior walls stared blindly into the darkness. The horses rattled their stalls, the dogs barked, and an owl made a sound that bore little resemblance to the poetic ideal, as creatures rarely follow the scripts written for them. For those three hours, the stone lions and human faces watched the night. Total darkness blanketed the landscape and the dusty roads. The graveyard became a blur of indistinguishable mounds, and the figure on the Cross vanished into the gloom. In the village, the tax collectors and the taxed slept soundly. Perhaps dreaming of feasts and rest, the starving and the oppressed found temporary freedom in their slumber.

What is it? Ten o'clock, sir. What do you mean? Ten at night? Yes, sir. You asked me to wake you. Right, I remember. After failing to fall back asleep while his servant noisily stirred the fire, he rose, grabbed his hat, and left. He walked to the Temple, paced the pavement twice to clear his head, and headed for Stryver’s chambers. Stryver’s clerk had already left, so the man himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose robe, his collar open for comfort. He had the strained, bloodshot eyes typical of men who live as hard as he did, a look common to his type throughout history. You are a bit late, Memory, Stryver said. About the usual time, maybe fifteen minutes past. They entered a dim, book-lined room cluttered with papers and warmed by a roaring fire. A kettle steamed on the hearth, and a table was set with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons. I see you have finished your bottle, Sydney. Two tonight, I think. I was dining with today’s client, or watching him dine—it makes no difference. That was a brilliant point you made regarding the identification. How did you think of it? I just thought he was a handsome guy and that I would have been just like him if I had any luck. Stryver laughed, his belly shaking. You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work. Looking sullen, the jackal loosened his clothes, fetched a jug of cold water, a basin, and some towels from the next room. He soaked the towels, wrung them out, wrapped them around his head, and sat down. Now I am ready. Not much to finish tonight, Memory, Stryver said cheerfully, sorting through his papers. How much? Only two cases. Give me the hardest one first. There you go, Sydney. Get started. Stryver reclined on a sofa by the table, while Sydney sat at his own desk, surrounded by papers, bottles, and glasses.

I thanked him and apologized. He replied, "Not at all," and continued. "Miss Havisham was an heiress, and naturally considered a great catch. Her half-brother had regained his wealth, only to squander it again through debt and reckless behavior. Their relationship was far more strained than his had been with their father, and it is believed he held a lethal grudge against her for influencing their father's resentment. Now, I reach the cruel part of the story—pausing only to note, my dear Handel, that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a glass." I have no idea why I was trying to force mine into the tumbler, only that I was working with absurd persistence to cram it inside. I thanked him and apologized again, to which he cheerfully replied, "Not at all!" and resumed. "A man appeared—perhaps at the races or a public ball—and began courting Miss Havisham. I never met him, as this occurred twenty-five years ago, before you or I were around, but my father described him as a flashy individual, perfectly suited for his scheme. My father insisted he was no gentleman, maintaining that one who lacks a gentleman's heart can never truly possess a gentleman's manners. He argued that no amount of polish can hide the wood's grain; in fact, the more you apply, the more the grain shows. Regardless, this man pursued Miss Havisham relentlessly, claiming to be devoted to her. She had not been particularly romantic before, but she fell deeply and passionately in love. She idolized him. He manipulated her affections so systematically that he extracted large sums of money from her and convinced her to buy out her brother's share of the brewery at an exorbitant price, claiming that as her husband, he needed full control. Your guardian was not involved in Miss Havisham's affairs at the time, and she was far too proud and infatuated to accept advice from anyone."

I cannot say how long I remained in that state, but it must have been a significant duration. When I regained consciousness, dawn was breaking, and the balloon drifted at a tremendous altitude over an endless ocean, with no land visible on the horizon. Surprisingly, I felt little agony. A sense of budding madness colored my calm assessment of the situation. I studied my hands, wondering why the veins were swollen and the fingernails blackened. I examined my head, shaking and feeling it carefully to ensure it had not, as I feared, grown larger than the balloon itself. I checked my pockets, and finding my notebook and toothpick case missing, I felt inexplicably annoyed. I noticed pain in my left ankle, and the reality of my predicament began to dawn on me. Yet, I felt no horror. Instead, I experienced a smug satisfaction at the ingenuity I would soon display to escape. I never doubted my survival. I sat in deep thought, making the gestures of a man contemplating a complex problem from the comfort of an armchair. Finally, I reached behind me to unfasten the large iron buckle on my waistband. The three rusty teeth were difficult to move, but I managed to set them at a right angle. Holding this makeshift tool in my teeth, I began the exhausting process of untying my cravat, resting frequently until the task was finished.

The thought that once encouraged me at the start of my journey now only drags me deeper into despair. My hopes have vanished, and like the fallen angel who sought godlike power, I am trapped in a permanent hell. I possessed a vivid imagination and a sharp analytical mind; by combining these, I conceived and created a man. Even now, I cannot recall my daydreams during that process without intense emotion. I felt as if I were in heaven, proud of my abilities and excited by their potential. Since childhood, I held great ambitions, but how far I have fallen. My friend, if you had known me before, you would not recognize me in this ruined state. I rarely felt hopeless, believing a grand destiny awaited me, until I fell, never to rise again. Must I lose this remarkable man? I have always longed for a friend who would understand and love me. Here, on these desolate seas, I have found one, yet I fear I have only discovered his worth to lose him. I try to convince him to live, but he refuses. I thank you, Walton, he said, for your kindness toward such a miserable soul. But when you speak of new connections, do you think anyone can replace those I have lost? Can anyone ever be to me what Clerval was, or what Elizabeth meant to me? Even when people are not exceptionally close, childhood companions hold a power over our minds that new friends rarely achieve. They understand our early nature, which, though it changes, is never truly gone. They can judge our actions with a better understanding of our true motives. A sibling rarely suspects the other of dishonesty, while a newer friend might always be viewed with some doubt. I had friends who were dear to me not just through habit, but because of their own virtues. Wherever I go, the gentle voice of my Elizabeth and the conversation of Clerval will echo in my mind. They are dead, and only one thing could convince me to keep living in this solitude. If I were committed to a noble goal that would truly benefit humanity, I could live to see it through.

Mr. Jaggers was seated at his desk but rose at once to stand by the hearth upon my arrival. Now, Pip, be cautious, he warned. I will, sir, I replied, having prepared my words. Do not implicate yourself, he continued, or anyone else. Understand me—anyone. Tell me nothing; I have no desire to know, nor am I curious. It was clear he was aware the man had arrived. I only wish, Mr. Jaggers, to confirm what I have been told. I do not expect it to be false, but I must verify it. Mr. Jaggers nodded. Did you say told or informed? he inquired, tilting his head to listen to the floor. Told implies speech, and you cannot speak with a man in New South Wales. I will say informed, Mr. Jaggers. Good. I have been informed by Abel Magwitch that he is my long-unknown benefactor. That is the man, Mr. Jaggers confirmed, in New South Wales. And only he? I asked. Only he, he replied. I am not so unreasonable as to hold you accountable for my errors, sir, but I always assumed it was Miss Havisham. As you say, Pip, he answered, eyeing me coolly while biting his finger, I am not responsible for that. Yet it appeared so likely, I pleaded, feeling disheartened. Not a shred of evidence, Pip, he said, shaking his head and adjusting his coat. Never judge by appearances; rely only on evidence. It is the best rule. I have nothing more to say, I sighed after a pause. I have verified the facts, and that is all. Since Magwitch has revealed himself, he continued, you understand how strictly I have always kept to the facts in our dealings. There has never been any deviation. You are aware of that? Quite, sir. I warned Magwitch when he first wrote from New South Wales that he must never expect me to stray from the truth.

He stayed inside the next day, mostly hiding in his room, paralyzed by a frantic fear of death yet feeling indifferent toward life. The feeling of being hunted and trapped consumed him. A gust of wind moving the tapestry made him tremble, and dead leaves hitting the window felt like his own failed promises and regrets. Closing his eyes, he saw the sailor’s face through the glass again, and terror gripped his heart. Perhaps he had only imagined this vengeance. Real life was chaotic, but his imagination was terrifyingly logical, turning remorse into a shadow that followed his sins. In reality, the wicked were not always punished, nor the good rewarded; success simply went to the strong. Surely, if a stranger had been lurking, the servants or gardeners would have noticed. Sibyl Vane’s brother had not come for him; he had likely perished at sea. He was safe, especially since the man could not possibly know his identity. His youthful appearance had protected him. Yet, if it were only an illusion, it was terrifying that his conscience could create such vivid, haunting figures. What kind of life would he lead if shadows of his crimes mocked him from every corner or whispered in his ear? As this thought took hold, he turned pale, and the room seemed to grow cold. He had killed his friend in a moment of madness, and the memory was unbearable. Every gruesome detail returned, and the image of his sin rose before him, vivid and horrifying.

April 12th. A distinct shift occurred in the balloon’s trajectory, which, while expected, brought me immense satisfaction. After reaching the twentieth parallel south, it veered sharply eastward, maintaining that heading all day along the lunar ellipse. Notably, this maneuver caused a persistent, unsettling swaying of the car that lasted for several hours. April 13th. The loud, crackling sound from the tenth returned, causing me great alarm. I pondered its cause to no avail. The earth’s apparent size has shrunk significantly, now spanning an angle of barely twenty-five degrees. The moon remains hidden directly above me. My eastward movement has slowed, though I remain on the elliptical path. April 14th. The earth’s diameter is diminishing rapidly. I am convinced the balloon is ascending the line of apsides toward perigee, following a direct route to the moon’s closest point to earth. The moon is still obscured overhead. I have spent considerable effort condensing the air. April 15th. Earth’s continents and oceans are no longer discernible. Around noon, that terrifying noise returned, growing louder and more intense. As I stood paralyzed by dread, the car shook violently, and a massive, flaming object roared past with a thunderous boom. Once my shock faded, I concluded it was a volcanic fragment ejected from the world I am approaching—likely a meteoric stone. April 16th. Gazing through the side windows, I was thrilled to see the moon’s edge peeking out from behind the balloon’s vast frame.

The mental traits we call analytical are difficult to analyze themselves; we only recognize them through their results. We know that for those who possess them in abundance, they provide immense satisfaction. Just as a strong person takes pride in physical feats, the analyst delights in the mental activity of unraveling problems. They find joy in even minor tasks that engage this talent. They love puzzles, riddles, and codes, solving them with a sharpness that seems supernatural to others. Their conclusions, reached through rigorous method, often appear to be mere intuition. While mathematical study, particularly the branch often called analysis, strengthens this faculty, calculation is not the same as analysis. A chess player, for instance, calculates without necessarily analyzing. Consequently, the impact of chess on the mind is often misunderstood. I am not writing a formal essay, but merely introducing a unique story with these observations. I contend that the reflective intellect is better and more usefully challenged by the simple game of checkers than by the elaborate frivolity of chess. In chess, where pieces move in strange, varied ways, complexity is often mistaken for depth. The game demands intense focus; a momentary lapse leads to defeat. Because the possible moves are so numerous and tangled, errors are frequent, and victory usually goes to the player who is more focused rather than more acute. In checkers, where moves are uniform and limited, the chance for error is low. With attention less taxed, victory depends entirely on superior insight. Consider a game of checkers reduced to four kings, where mistakes are unlikely. Clearly, victory between equal players can only be secured through a brilliant, calculated maneuver born of intense intellectual effort.

Tom managed to scratch the cupboard and was planning to work on the bureau when he was called to get ready for Sunday school. Mary gave him a tin basin and soap, but Tom merely poured the water out and pretended to wash. Mary took the towel away, scolding him for his laziness. Flustered, Tom tried again, though he emerged with soap dripping from his face and a clear line where the clean skin ended and the dirt began. Mary took over, scrubbing him until he was clean, brushing his hair, and styling his curls. Tom secretly flattened his hair afterward, as he hated the curls. She then produced his Sunday suit, the only other clothes he owned. After she buttoned his jacket, adjusted his collar, and placed his straw hat on his head, Tom looked much better but felt miserable. The restriction of clean, formal clothing irritated him. He hoped she would overlook his shoes, but she polished them with tallow anyway. Frustrated, Tom complained that he was always forced to do things he disliked.

Those who were once well-off and paid taxes are the first to fail when they enter the workhouse. Losing a few inches of wood beyond his estimates hurts his profits, especially with a family to support. Sensing that Sowerberry’s complaints reflected poorly on the parish, Mr. Bumble changed the subject to Oliver Twist. He asked if the undertaker knew anyone looking for a parish apprentice, describing the boy as a burden on the parish. He pointed his cane at the sign advertising five pounds for an apprentice. Sowerberry grabbed Bumble’s coat lapel, saying that was exactly what he wanted to discuss, while complimenting the beadle’s elegant button. Bumble looked down proudly at his brass buttons, which featured the parish seal of the Good Samaritan.
