When I saw you become the object of another’s affection, imagining you loved as something other than a sacred symbol of excellence, or that you might love someone else more deeply than me, a monster awoke inside. I dismissed your suitor, and since then, I have known no peace. Sleep eluded me; my blood was in constant turmoil. I woke to a new life, like someone dying in hope only to wake in Hell. I will not stain your mind by detailing my inner battles, my self-loathing, or my despair. Let a veil cover the unimaginable sensations of a guilty father; the secrets of such an agonized heart should not be cheapened. Everything was chaos, crime, remorse, and hate, yet beneath it all remained the tenderest love. What first drove me to resolve to conquer my passion and restore a father to my child was the sight of your bitter, sympathetic sorrow. That brought me here. I thought if I could reawaken the grief I felt at your mother’s death—memories dormant for seventeen years—my love for her child would vanish. In a fit of heroism, I decided to leave you, the life of my life, and never see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it failed; I overestimated my strength or underestimated my love. I would have died had you not come to me. I wish I had truly perished. Now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was miserably mistaken to think I could conquer my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love lived, seems to have intensified it. In my madness, I dared tell myself that Diana died to give you birth, that her spirit transferred into your frame, and you should be Diana to me. Every effort to cast it off only makes this guilty, unnatural love cling closer, withering your hopes and destroying me forever. It would have been better to love despair and kiss her instead. No time or distance can tear from my soul what has become a part of it. Since arriving here, I have not for a moment ceased to feel the hell of this passion, which will burn until I am cold, stiff, and dead.

Mr. Otis was troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the peer remained firm. He did, however, convince the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her. In the spring of 1890, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s drawing-room following her wedding, her jewels were widely admired. Virginia had received the coronet, the traditional reward for good American girls, and married her young suitor once he came of age. They were a charming couple, and everyone was happy for them, except for the Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her own daughters, and, surprisingly, Mr. Otis. While Mr. Otis liked the young Duke, he held strong republican views and worried that his daughter might lose her simple values among the aristocracy. Nevertheless, his concerns were set aside, and as he walked his daughter down the aisle at St. George’s, Hanover Square, he was surely the proudest man in England. After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess visited Canterville Chase. The day after arriving, they walked to the quiet churchyard near the pine woods. After some debate, they had decided to mark Sir Simon’s grave with only his initials and the verse from the library window. Virginia scattered roses over the grave before they wandered into the ruined abbey. As she sat on a fallen pillar and her husband rested at her feet, he asked her to share the secret of what happened when she was locked away with the ghost. Virginia replied solemnly that she had never told anyone.

His primary concern was selecting a target, as he understood that murder, much like ancient pagan rites, demanded both a priest and a sacrifice. Lacking the imagination to have enemies, and recognizing that his solemn task left no room for petty grudges, he drafted a list of acquaintances and kin. After deliberation, he chose Lady Clementina Beauchamp, a beloved second cousin residing in Curzon Street. He held her in high regard, and since his inheritance of Lord Rugby’s estate rendered him independently wealthy, her passing offered no financial gain. Convinced she was the ideal candidate and unwilling to keep Sybil waiting, he resolved to act immediately. First, he addressed the palmist by writing a cheque for 105 pounds to Mr. Septimus Podgers, dispatching his valet to deliver it to West Moon Street. He then summoned his hansom and prepared to depart. Before exiting, he glanced at Sybil Merton’s portrait, vowing to guard the secret of his sacrifice and shield her from the truth. En route to the Buckingham, he purchased a basket of narcissi for Sybil. Upon reaching the club, he retreated to the library and requested a lemon-and-soda along with a volume on toxicology. He concluded that poison was the most suitable method; he found physical violence repulsive and wished to avoid the notoriety that would surely follow a more conspicuous crime, as he had no desire to become a spectacle in society columns or at Lady Windermere’s gatherings.

The cycle of suffering that dictates my life must have been interrupted, yet the cruel fate governing it would not allow such a violation of her laws. Why should I complain? Misery is my natural state; only the wretched could ever reach me. Had Woodville been happy, we would never have met. Can I, who have lived for years on tears and sorrow, hesitate to tell this story of death? Woodville had to travel to the country, kept away from his lovely bride for days. He received a letter from her mentioning a minor illness, urging him to return quickly, as his presence would be her best medicine. Delayed for three more days, he finally rushed to her. An inexplicable dread filled his heart; having heard nothing further, he feared she had worsened. He grew restless, desperate to see her healthy again, despite a dark voice whispering that he would never see her as she once was. Arriving at her home, he found it silent. Passing through the rooms, he saw a servant weeping and, trembling with fear, managed to ask if she was dead. The reply, "Not yet," hit him with less force than he had anticipated. Knowing she still lived offered him a sliver of hope. Recalling her letter, he clung to the desperate belief that his love could revive her, that she could not die while he was near. He hurried to her room, where she lay feverish and unconscious. He wrapped her in his arms, kissing her burning lips and calling her name in hushed agony. "Come back, Elinor; I am here. You promised me you would recover. Let your spirit return; you cannot die while I am with you. What is death? To lose you is to lose a part of myself, leaving me without a past or a future."

If you seek my patience and the grace of those you have wronged, sit in that chair without speaking. It has been ready for two days. Monks mumbled something but remained indecisive. You must be quick, Mr. Brownlow insisted. One word from me and the other option vanishes. The man still wavered. I have no desire to negotiate, Mr. Brownlow continued, and representing the vital interests of others, I lack the authority to do so. Is there no compromise? Monks asked, his voice trembling. None. Monks studied the old man, but finding only stern resolve in his expression, he entered the room and sat down with a shrug. Lock the door from the outside, Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, and return when I ring. The men complied, leaving the two alone. This is fine treatment from my father's oldest friend, Monks remarked, tossing aside his hat and cloak. It is precisely because I was his oldest friend, Mr. Brownlow replied, that I am moved to treat you with gentleness, Edward Leeford, despite the shame your conduct brings to that name. My hopes and memories are tied to him and the woman who died young, who would have been my wife. My heart clung to him through all his struggles until his death, and seeing you stirs those old associations. What does the name matter? Monks asked, watching his companion's distress with sullen confusion. Nothing to you, Mr. Brownlow answered, but it was hers, and even now, hearing it spoken brings back the warmth I once felt. I am truly glad you have changed it. This is all very impressive, Monks said after a long silence, during which he shifted in defiant agitation while Mr. Brownlow shielded his face with his hand.

Jane admitted she was surprised by the engagement, yet she spoke less of her shock than of her sincere hope for their happiness, refusing to let Elizabeth convince her it was unlikely. Kitty and Lydia felt no envy toward Miss Lucas, as Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman; to them, it was simply gossip to share in Meryton. Lady Lucas could not hide her triumph in finally being able to boast to Mrs. Bennet about a daughter well-married. She visited Longbourn more frequently than usual to express her joy, despite Mrs. Bennet’s bitter glares and spiteful comments. A new reserve grew between Elizabeth and Charlotte, leaving them silent on the matter, and Elizabeth felt certain their friendship could never regain its former intimacy. Disappointed in Charlotte, she turned with deeper affection toward her sister, whose integrity she trusted completely, though she grew increasingly anxious for Jane’s happiness, as Bingley had been gone a week with no word of his return. Jane had replied promptly to Caroline’s letter and was counting the days until she might hear back. On Tuesday, Mr. Collins sent a letter of thanks to their father, written with the heavy formality of someone who had lived with them for a year. Having fulfilled that duty, he wrote rapturously of his joy in winning the affection of their neighbor, Miss Lucas. He explained that he had accepted their invitation to return to Longbourn on Monday fortnight specifically to enjoy her company. He added that Lady Catherine heartily approved of the marriage and wished it to happen quickly, which he hoped would convince his dear Charlotte to set an early wedding date. Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire no longer pleased Mrs. Bennet; she was as eager to complain about it as her husband. She found it bizarre and highly inconvenient that he would visit Longbourn rather than Lucas Lodge. She detested having guests while her health was poor, and she found lovers to be the most tiresome people of all.

The row of gas-lamps stretched far into the distance, and a lone hansom cab waited by a small walled house, its driver dozing within. He hurried toward Portland Place, glancing back occasionally as if dreading pursuit. At the corner of Rich Street, two men examined a notice on a hoarding. Driven by sudden curiosity, he crossed the road. The word 'Murder' in bold black type caught his gaze. He recoiled, his face flushing deeply. The bill offered a reward for a man of medium height, aged thirty to forty, dressed in a billy-cock hat, black coat, and check trousers, bearing a scar on his right cheek. He studied the text repeatedly, pondering the fugitive's fate and the origin of his mark. He wondered if his own name might one day appear on London's walls, with a price placed upon his head. The notion filled him with sickening dread. He turned abruptly and vanished into the darkness. He wandered aimlessly, retaining only vague recollections of traversing a maze of squalid dwellings and gloomy streets. By the time he reached Piccadilly Circus, the sun was rising. Walking toward Belgrave Square, he encountered heavy wagons bound for Covent Garden. White-smocked carters with sun-weathered faces and curly hair strode along, snapping whips and calling out. A young boy sat atop a massive grey horse, clutching its mane and laughing, a cluster of primroses tucked into his worn hat. The heaps of vegetables appeared like jade against the morning sky, contrasting with the pink hues of dawn. Lord Arthur felt an inexplicable emotion. The delicate beauty of the morning struck him as profoundly sad, reminding him of days that begin in splendor only to end in turmoil. He contemplated these rustics and their casual demeanor, wondering what version of London they perceived—a city stripped of nocturnal vice and daytime smog, a ghostly, desolate place. He questioned whether they grasped the city's extremes of glory and disgrace, its intense passions, its desperate poverty, and all it creates or destroys from dawn until dusk.

I am almost certain it was you. Mr. Lorry took her small, hesitant hand and kissed it formally. He led her back to her chair, and while holding the back of it, he rubbed his chin, adjusted his wig, and gestured as he spoke, looking down at her. Miss Manette, it was I. You will see how true my claim about having no feelings is when you realize I have not seen you since. You have been a ward of Tellson’s, and I have been occupied with the bank’s other affairs. Feelings! I have no time or opportunity for them. I spend my entire life, miss, operating a massive financial machine.

It was the best of times and the worst of times, an age of wisdom and foolishness, of belief and skepticism, of light and darkness, of hope and despair. We had everything and nothing, heading straight to heaven or the opposite. In short, that era was so much like our own that some of its loudest voices insisted it be described only in the most extreme terms. A king with a heavy jaw and a plain-faced queen sat on England's throne, while a similarly jawed king and a beautiful queen ruled France. In both nations, the ruling elite were certain that their power was permanent. It was 1775. England experienced spiritual revelations just as we do now. Mrs. Southcott had recently turned twenty-five, and a prophetic soldier had announced that London and Westminster were destined to be swallowed up. The Cock-lane ghost had been silenced only twelve years prior, after tapping out messages much like the unoriginal spirits of our own time. Meanwhile, messages of far greater consequence had reached the English Crown from British subjects in America, proving more significant to humanity than any ghostly communications. France, less spiritually blessed, slid smoothly toward ruin, printing and wasting paper money. Guided by their clergy, the French amused themselves with brutal acts, such as sentencing a youth to have his hands severed, his tongue torn out, and his body burned alive for failing to kneel in the rain before a passing procession of monks. It is likely that in the forests of France and Norway, trees were already marked by Fate to be felled and fashioned into the terrifying guillotine that would soon make history.

I had not yet fully drained the cup of sorrow; the reality of my bereavement remained ungrasped. I did not yet feel in every heartbeat and thought that I stood solitary, the final survivor of my kind. As the sky grew overcast and a fine rain began at dusk, I mused that if the heavens could weep, surely a man might also. I recalled myths of people turning into fountains through their grief and wished for such a fate, hoping to join Adrian and Clara in their watery end. Sorrow is a strange force; it projects its own narrative onto the world, coloring all of nature with its own hue. Having wandered far from the shore where I landed, I discovered a coastal watchtower. I welcomed this sign of human construction amidst the desolate landscape and climbed the stairs to the guardroom. Fortunately, the space held no grim reminders of those who once stayed there. A makeshift bed of planks covered in dried corn husks and a chest containing stale biscuits provided for my hunger, which I had not previously noticed. A parching thirst, brought on by the seawater I had swallowed and my physical collapse, also plagued me. I found relief in the simple meal and a small amount of sour wine left in a flask. Lying down on the bed, the scent of the dry leaves proved soothing after the stench of seaweed. My isolation faded from my mind. I ceased to dwell on the past or future, and as my senses quieted, I drifted into dreams of my youth—of haymakers, shepherds calling to their dogs, and the familiar sights and sounds of my mountain home.

It is strange, but everyone who vanishes is supposedly spotted in San Francisco. It must be a charming city, possessing all the allure of the afterlife. What do you think happened to Basil? Dorian asked, holding his wine to the light and wondering how he could speak of it so calmly. I have no idea. If Basil wants to hide, that is his business. If he is dead, I prefer not to dwell on it. Death is the only thing that truly terrifies me. I despise it. Why? the younger man asked wearily. Because, Lord Henry said, sniffing his scented vinaigrette, one can survive anything these days except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts of this century that cannot be explained away. Let us have coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran off with played it beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was fond of her. The house is lonely without her. Marriage is just a habit, a bad one, but one misses even the worst habits. Perhaps one misses them most, as they are such a core part of one's personality. Dorian said nothing, but rose and went to the piano, letting his fingers drift over the keys. Once the coffee arrived, he looked at Lord Henry and asked, Harry, did it ever occur to you that Basil was murdered? Lord Henry yawned. Basil was popular and carried a cheap watch. Why would he be murdered? He was not clever enough to have enemies. He had a genius for painting, but one can paint like Velasquez and still be dull. Basil was dull. He only interested me once, when he confessed his obsession with you and that you were the inspiration for his art. I was fond of Basil, Dorian said sadly. But don't people say he was murdered? Some newspapers do, but it seems unlikely. I know Paris has dangerous spots, but Basil was not the type to go there. He lacked curiosity; it was his greatest flaw. What would you say, Harry, if I told you I murdered Basil? the younger man asked.

Biddy wept, and the dim garden, the lane, and the emerging stars grew hazy before my own eyes. "Has nothing ever been found, Biddy?" "Nothing." "Do you know what has become of Orlick?" "Judging by his dusty clothes, I suspect he labors in the quarries." "You have seen him, then? Why do you stare at that dark tree in the lane?" "I saw him there the night she passed away." "That was not the final time, was it, Biddy?" "No; I have spotted him there since we began walking here. It is futile," Biddy said, touching my arm as I prepared to rush out, "you know I would not mislead you; he was only there for a moment and has already departed." My fury reignited upon learning she was still haunted by that man, and I felt a deep resentment toward him. I expressed my resolve to spend any amount or exert any effort to banish him from the region. Gradually, she guided me toward a calmer conversation, describing how Joe cherished me and never uttered a complaint—she did not explicitly mention me, but I understood—always fulfilling his duties with a steady hand, a reserved tongue, and a kind heart. "Truly, one could hardly praise him enough," I remarked. "And Biddy, we must discuss these matters frequently, as I intend to visit here often now. I will not abandon poor Joe." Biddy remained silent. "Biddy, do you not hear me?" "Yes, Mr. Pip." "Aside from your calling me Mr. Pip—which strikes me as poor taste—what do you mean?" "What do I mean?" Biddy asked timidly. "Biddy," I said with self-righteous insistence, "I must ask what you mean by this?" "By this?" Biddy repeated. "Do not echo me," I snapped. "You never used to echo, Biddy." "Used not!" Biddy exclaimed. "Oh, Mr. Pip! Used!" I decided to drop that subject. After another quiet stroll through the garden, I returned to my primary point. "Biddy, I mentioned that I would visit Joe often, a statement you met with pointed silence. Please, tell me why." "Are you truly certain that you will visit him often?" Biddy asked, pausing on the narrow path to look at me under the starlight with clear, honest eyes.

We shared a mutual affection for Adrian, though she, still a child, could not fully grasp his virtues or align with his views as I did. I spent all my time with him. His gentle, sensitive nature lent a delicate, ethereal quality to our talks. He was as joyful as a singing lark, as intellectually soaring as an eagle, and as pure as a dove. He could lighten Perdita’s gravity and soothe my own restless, agonizing intensity. I viewed my past struggles and desires as a fading nightmare, feeling as transformed as if I had entered a new body with a fresh perspective on the world. Yet, I remained fundamentally the same in my strength and longing for connection. My masculine vigor persisted, softened and refined by his influence. Adrian did more than teach me history and philosophy; while helping me tame my wild spirit, he revealed his own heart, allowing me to grasp its remarkable depth. The former queen of England had tried since his infancy to instill ambition in her son. Recognizing his genius, she nurtured his talents to serve her own ends. She fostered his thirst for knowledge and his bold courage, hoping his love of liberty would eventually turn into a hunger for power. She sought to cultivate his resentment toward those who caused his father’s downfall, but failed. Instead, the stories of a nation claiming its right to self-governance earned his admiration, and he became a republican by conviction. Undeterred, his mother combined his pride of birth with patience and ambition. She studied his character intently, using praise and criticism to influence him. Though the results often disappointed her, she relied on his immense talent, confident she would eventually prevail.

Mr. Bennet remained silent during dinner, but once the servants left, he engaged his guest by noting how fortunate he was in his patroness. He remarked that Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attentiveness to his comfort was truly remarkable. Mr. Collins responded with eloquent praise, his manner becoming exceptionally solemn as he insisted he had never encountered such affability from a person of rank. He boasted that she had approved his sermons, invited him to dine at Rosings twice, and even requested his presence for cards. Though some considered her proud, he had only experienced kindness. She treated him like any other gentleman, allowed him to socialize, and permitted him to visit his relatives. She had even advised him to marry discreetly and visited his parsonage, where she offered suggestions for his upstairs closets. Mrs. Bennet agreed that she sounded like a very agreeable woman and asked if she lived nearby. Mr. Collins explained that his home was separated from Rosings Park only by a lane. When Mrs. Bennet asked about her family, he mentioned her only daughter, the heiress to a vast estate. Mrs. Bennet wondered if the girl was handsome, to which Mr. Collins replied that she was charming. He added that Lady Catherine considered her superior to all other women, as her features clearly displayed her distinguished birth.

Indeed, burglar tools. That seems to ease your mind significantly. But what startled you so? What were you anticipating we had discovered? Huck found himself in a tight spot under that searching gaze. He desperately needed a believable excuse, but his mind was blank. As the scrutiny intensified, he blurted out a nonsensical response: Sunday-school books, perhaps. Though Huck was too anxious to find humor in it, the old man erupted in hearty laughter that shook his entire frame, remarking that such mirth was as good as money for saving on medical expenses. He then told the pale, exhausted boy that he was clearly unwell and flighty, but that rest would surely restore him. Huck felt foolish for his display of nerves. He had suspected the parcel from the tavern was not the treasure after overhearing the conversation at the widow’s gate, but he had not been certain. Now, he was relieved to know for sure that the bundle was not the one he sought. Everything seemed to be falling into place; the gold remained in room number two, the criminals would soon be imprisoned, and he and Tom could claim the fortune that night without interference. As they finished breakfast, a knock sounded at the door. Huck scrambled to hide, wanting no part in the unfolding situation. The Welshman let in several guests, including the Widow Douglas, and observed crowds gathering on the hill to look at the gate. News had traveled fast. As the Welshman recounted the night’s events, the widow expressed her deep gratitude. He humbly deflected her praise, insisting she owed her safety to another person whose identity he was sworn to keep secret, noting that they only arrived because of that individual.

The intensifying intensity of Mr. Wopsle’s gaze and his evident mental turmoil were so puzzling that I remained baffled long after he had vanished into the clouds within a giant watch-case. I was still pondering the matter an hour later when I exited the theater and discovered him waiting by the entrance. We shook hands and walked down the street together. I remarked that I had noticed him observing me. He replied that he had indeed seen me, but asked who else was present. When I pressed him, he appeared dazed, insisting he could swear to the identity of a man he had seen. Alarmed, I urged him to clarify. He mused that he might have noticed the man even without my presence. I instinctively scanned my surroundings, feeling a sudden chill. He assured me the man had departed before he did. Given my own suspicions, I grew wary of the actor, fearing he might be trying to trick me into a confession, so I remained silent. He then mentioned a strange notion that the man had been with me, sitting behind me like a phantom, until he realized I was unaware of him. This renewed my unease, yet I stayed quiet, suspecting he might be attempting to link these comments to Provis, though I was certain Provis had not been there. He noted my confusion and remarked on the strangeness of the situation. When I prompted him, he asked if I recalled that Christmas Day from my childhood when he dined at Gargery’s and soldiers arrived to have handcuffs repaired. I confirmed I remembered it clearly. He asked if I also recalled the pursuit of the two convicts, during which we joined the hunt, Gargery carried me, and I struggled to keep pace with him as he led the way.

The powerful, unearthly voice—which seemed to come from no instrument—suddenly fell silent. The girl turned to help her elderly companion and finally noticed us. She was the guide for her blind father, a musician from Saxony who had settled in the village years ago. A young German student had joined them shortly before the plague began. It was clear that the nobleman had fallen in love with the musician’s daughter and fled his family to be with her, only to die early in the epidemic. The girl had kept her father alive by hiding the truth of the world’s collapse, letting him believe they were still surrounded by a living audience. On the day we arrived, she fell ill. Terrified of leaving her father alone, she found the strength to lead him to the chapel one last time. Despite her grief, she played a beautiful hymn perfectly, unaware that the earth would soon be her grave. When we appeared, her desperate courage broke. She rushed to Adrian, crying out for him to save her father before collapsing in tears. Sadly, both are now buried beneath the walnut tree where her lover rests, just as she requested. Her father held her hand until she died, refusing to let go, and passed away himself twelve hours later. They rest together under the trees, surrounded by the mountains. Though they are gone, I often imagine the music they loved still drifting through the air, bringing peace to their spirits.

He also had to consider Sybil’s parents, who were traditional and might oppose the marriage if a scandal arose, though he felt certain they would understand his motives if he explained everything. He therefore decided that poison was the best option. It was safe, certain, and discreet, avoiding the painful confrontations he, like most men of his background, deeply disliked. Knowing nothing of toxicology, he searched the library himself after the waiter failed to help. He eventually found a Pharmacopoeia and a copy of Erskine’s Toxicology. The technical language initially confused him, but he soon found a clear, detailed account of aconitine in the second volume. It was the perfect choice: swift, painless, and easy to ingest in a gelatin capsule. He noted the lethal dosage on his shirt cuff, returned the books, and walked to a prominent chemist. The proprietor, Mr. Pestle, was surprised by the request and mentioned the need for a medical certificate. However, once Lord Arthur explained it was for a Norwegian mastiff showing signs of rabies that had already bitten his coachman, the chemist was satisfied, praised his knowledge of toxicology, and filled the order. Lord Arthur placed the capsule into a silver candy box he bought on Bond Street, discarded the chemist’s container, and left for Lady Clementina’s.

Are you talking about Mr. Knightley? Of course I am. I never meant anyone else, and I assumed you knew. When we discussed him, it seemed perfectly clear. Not quite, Emma replied, forcing herself to remain calm, because everything you said then seemed to refer to someone else. I could have sworn you named Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain we spoke of the help he gave you by protecting you from the gypsies. Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how you forget! My dear Harriet, I remember our conversation perfectly. I told you I understood your feelings, given the service he provided, and you agreed, speaking warmly of your gratitude and how you felt when he rescued you. It is vivid in my memory. Oh, I see what you mean now, Harriet exclaimed, but I was thinking of something entirely different. It was not the gypsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. I was thinking of a much more precious moment: when Mr. Knightley asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused, and no one else would. That was the act of kindness and generosity that made me realize how superior he is to everyone else on earth. Good God, Emma cried, this has been a most unfortunate and deplorable mistake. What can be done? You would not have encouraged me if you had understood? At least I am no worse off than I would have been otherwise, and now, it is possible. She paused. Emma could not speak. I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse, Harriet continued, that you see a vast difference between the two men. You must think one is infinitely above me compared to the other. But I hope, even if it seems strange, that you will remember your own words about how even more unlikely matches have occurred. If I were so incredibly fortunate that Mr. Knightley did not mind the disparity, I hope you will not oppose it or create difficulties.

Her circumstances were truly difficult. While she desperately wanted to uncover the mystery of Oliver’s past, she felt bound to honor the trust the wretched woman had placed in her. The woman’s demeanor had moved Rose Maylie, and she felt a sincere desire to guide the outcast toward redemption, alongside her devotion to Oliver. They planned to stay in London for only three days before leaving for the coast. It was already midnight on the first day. How could she act within forty-eight hours, or delay their departure without raising suspicion? Mr. Losberne was with them, but Rose knew his impulsive nature too well; she feared his immediate anger toward the woman who had helped capture Oliver, and she could not risk telling him without support. These same concerns made her cautious about approaching Mrs. Maylie, who would surely consult the doctor. Legal counsel was out of the question for similar reasons. She considered asking Harry for help, but remembered their last parting. It felt wrong to summon him when he might have finally moved on and found happiness elsewhere. Troubled by these thoughts, Rose spent a sleepless night. By the next day, she reached the desperate decision to contact Harry. If his return is painful for him, it will be just as hard for me, she thought. Perhaps he will simply write, or visit without seeking me out, as he did before. She set down her pen, turning away so the paper would not witness her tears.

If he asked why I wanted it or what right I had to it, I would tell him—even if he cared little for such dreams—that I had loved Estella for a long time. Though I had lost her and faced a lonely life, everything regarding her remained more precious to me than anything else. Seeing Mr. Jaggers stand silent and unmoved, I turned to Wemmick. I told him I knew he had a kind heart, having seen his pleasant home and the gentle way he cared for his father. I begged him to speak for me and convince Mr. Jaggers to be more open. The two men exchanged a strange look. I feared Wemmick might be fired, but Mr. Jaggers softened into a smile, and Wemmick grew bolder. Mr. Jaggers teased him about his home and his father, to which Wemmick replied that his private life did not affect his work. Mr. Jaggers laughed, calling Wemmick a cunning impostor, and Wemmick playfully accused him of being one too. They looked at each other with lingering suspicion. Mr. Jaggers sighed, admitting that I knew more about dreams than he did. He then offered to present a hypothetical case, insisting he admitted nothing. He waited for my confirmation before continuing. He asked me to imagine a woman who hid her child and was forced to reveal this to her lawyer, who needed the truth to build her defense.

His only real dilemma was choosing a victim, as he understood that murder, much like ancient religious rituals, required both a killer and a sacrifice. Lacking any enemies and viewing his task as a solemn duty rather than a personal vendetta, he listed his friends and relatives. After careful thought, he selected Lady Clementina Beauchamp, his elderly second cousin living in Curzon Street. He was fond of her, and since he had inherited Lord Rugby’s vast fortune, he had no financial motive for her death. Convinced she was the perfect choice and eager to avoid delaying his plans for Sybil, he decided to act immediately. First, he wrote a check for 105 pounds to the palm reader, Mr. Septimus Podgers, and sent it to his address. After calling for his carriage, he paused to look at a photograph of Sybil Merton, vowing to keep his self-sacrificing secret hidden forever. On his way to his club, he stopped to send Sybil a basket of narcissus flowers. Once at the club, he ordered a drink and requested a book on toxicology. He had decided that poison was the most discreet method. He found physical violence repulsive and wanted to avoid any public scandal that might turn him into a celebrity or subject him to unwanted gossip in the society papers.

Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the fortress, clashed with Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, the four warriors meeting with such force that their lances shattered to the hilt. Next, Sir Pertolope emerged from the castle to face Sir Lionel, whom the green knight promptly unhorsed, an event duly recorded by the heralds. Sir Bleobaris then splintered his spear against Sir Gareth, only to be thrown to the ground himself. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin challenged Gareth, but he too was struck down, as was his brother Sir Galihud, along with Sir Dinadan, La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore, and Sir Dodinas, all of whom Gareth unseated with a single lance. King Agwisance of Ireland watched in wonder, noting how the knight shifted his colors from green to blue with each pass, making his identity impossible to discern. Gareth proceeded to unhorse King Agwisance, King Carados of Scotland, King Uriens of Gore, and Sir Bagdemagus, all with their mounts. When Bagdemagus’s son, Meliganus, struck Gareth with a valiant blow, the noble Prince Galahault challenged the multicolored knight to a joust. They collided, and while the prince’s spear broke, Gareth struck his helm so forcefully that he nearly fell before his men steadied him. King Arthur, impressed, asked Sir Launcelot to challenge the stranger. Launcelot declined, stating that the knight had already endured enough toil. He argued that it would be dishonorable to hinder a warrior who had performed so valiantly, suggesting that the knight might be fighting for a lady’s favor. Launcelot concluded that he would not deprive the man of his hard-won glory, even if he could.

Since we first boarded the boat, I had been watching carefully for any sign that we were being followed. I saw nothing suspicious. We were definitely not being trailed by another vessel; had we been, I would have steered toward the shore to force them to reveal their intentions. We traveled without any interference. He wore his boat-cloak and looked like a natural part of the surroundings. Surprisingly, he was the least anxious among us, perhaps due to the difficult life he had led. He was not indifferent, as he expressed a hope that his gentleman would thrive abroad, but he refused to worry about danger until it was directly in front of him. If you knew what it was like to sit here with me and smoke after being locked between four walls for so long, you would envy me, he told me. I replied that I understood the value of freedom. He shook his head, insisting that I could not truly appreciate it without having been imprisoned myself, though he refused to let his mood darken. It seemed strange that he would risk his life for his goals, but I realized that for a man like him, a life without danger might feel unnatural. He confirmed this, explaining that while he had grown wealthy on the other side of the world, he had always looked toward England. There, he was just Magwitch, ignored by everyone, whereas here, his presence would cause alarm if he were discovered. I told him that if all went well, he would be safe and free within a few hours. He took a long breath and said he hoped so, and I asked if he truly believed it.

Enough of this. I will begin my story; it is my final task, and I hope I have the strength to finish it. I have committed no crimes; my mistakes are easily forgiven, as they stemmed from poor judgment rather than malice. I believe few could claim they would have avoided these misfortunes through better wisdom. My fate was dictated by a cruel necessity—a force stronger than any human power, which shattered the unbreakable chains that once bound me to joy and goodness, dragging me into a misery that will only end in death. But I digress. I will pause, wipe my eyes, and try to trade my current, heavy unhappiness for the sharper emotions of the past. I was born in England to a man of high rank. Having lost his own father early, he was raised by an indulgent mother who granted him every luxury. He attended Eton and university, enjoying the independence that comes with wealth and privilege from a young age. These circumstances allowed his character to take root, growing into either virtues or vices. Because he was always free to act on his own, his personality became distinct, revealing both potential for greatness and for ruin. His reckless spending, which he justified as passion, often manifested as boundless generosity. Yet, while he focused on the needs of others, he never denied his own desires. He gave away money and time he did not value, and offered affections that he was glad to express. I cannot say if he would have been selfish had his needs conflicted with others, but he was never tested. He was raised in prosperity, surrounded by people who loved him and sought only to please him.

Following a shared mourning over the grim outcome of this affair—which Elizabeth deemed nearly inevitable and Miss Bennet could not claim was entirely impossible—the former pressed for more details. "Tell me everything I have not yet heard. What did Colonel Forster say? Did they have no suspicions before the elopement? They must have been seen together constantly." "Colonel Forster admitted he had often noticed a mutual fondness, particularly from Lydia, but nothing that caused him alarm. I feel so sorry for him; his conduct was remarkably kind. He was already traveling to see us to express his regret before he realized they were not headed for Scotland; the rumor of their flight only accelerated his arrival." "Was Denny certain Wickham would not marry? Did he know of their plans? Did the Colonel speak to him directly?" "Yes, but when questioned, Denny claimed ignorance and refused to share his true thoughts. He did not reiterate his belief that they would not wed, which gives me some hope he was previously misunderstood." "And until the Colonel arrived, none of you doubted they were actually married?" "How could such a thought occur to us? I felt some unease regarding my sister’s future happiness, knowing his past behavior was questionable. My parents were unaware of that; they simply viewed it as an imprudent match. Kitty then revealed, with a touch of pride, that Lydia’s final letter had hinted at this, as she had known of their affection for weeks." "But not before they left for Brighton?" "No, I believe not." "Did Colonel Forster seem to think poorly of Wickham? Is he aware of his true character?" "I must admit he spoke less favorably of him than before. He considered him reckless and spendthrift; since this tragedy, rumors suggest he departed Meryton with significant debts, though I hope that is untrue." "Oh, Jane, had we been less discreet and shared what we knew, this might have been avoided!" "Perhaps it would have been better," her sister answered. "But exposing someone's past faults without knowing their current state of mind felt wrong."

Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, clashed with Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, shattering their spears upon impact. Then, Sir Pertolope emerged from the castle to face Sir Lionel, whom the Green Knight promptly unhorsed. Heralds carefully recorded the performance of every knight. Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth but was himself knocked to the ground. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin challenged Gareth, only to be struck down as well. Sir Galihud then sought to avenge his brother, but Gareth defeated him just as he had the others. Gareth continued his streak, unhorsing Sir Dinadan, La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore, and Sir Dodinas with a single spear each. King Agwisance of Ireland watched in wonder, noting that the knight seemed to change his colors from green to blue with every pass, making him impossible to identify. Gareth then unhorsed King Agwisance, King Carados of Scotland, King Uriens of Gore, and Sir Bagdemagus. When Bagdemagus’s son, Meliganus, broke a spear against him, Prince Galahault shouted for the multicolored knight to prepare for a duel. They collided, and while the prince’s spear shattered, Gareth struck him so hard that he nearly fell from his horse. King Arthur praised the mysterious knight, asking Sir Launcelot to challenge him. Launcelot refused, arguing that the knight had already endured enough for one day. He insisted that a true knight should not hinder another’s glory, especially after such a display of skill. Launcelot suggested the man might be fighting for a lady’s favor and deserved to keep his hard-earned honor, declaring that he would not interfere.

I view it as a primary refinement of civilized cultures. Certainly, sir; and it possesses the merit of being popular among the world's less refined societies as well: every savage dances. Sir William merely smiled. Your friend performs beautifully, he remarked after a silence, watching Bingley enter the group; and I have no doubt you are quite skilled in the art yourself, Mr. Darcy. You witnessed my dancing at Meryton, I believe, sir. Indeed I did, and I found it quite enjoyable. Do you dance often at St. James’s? Never, sir. Do you not consider it a fitting tribute to the location? It is a tribute I avoid paying to any location whenever possible. You own a residence in the city, I presume? Mr. Darcy inclined his head. I once considered settling in town myself, as I enjoy refined company; however, I was uncertain if the London climate would suit Lady Lucas. He waited for a reply, but his companion remained silent. As Elizabeth approached, Sir William decided on a gallant gesture and called out: My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must permit me to introduce this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot decline when such beauty stands before you. He reached for her hand to offer it to Mr. Darcy, who, though startled, seemed not entirely opposed. Elizabeth pulled away, telling Sir William with some agitation: Truly, sir, I have no desire to dance. Please do not imagine I approached with the intent of seeking a partner. Mr. Darcy formally requested the honor of her hand, but to no avail. Elizabeth remained resolute, and Sir William’s efforts to persuade her failed. You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it is unkind to deprive me of the pleasure of watching you; and while this gentleman generally dislikes the pastime, I am certain he would not object to obliging us for a short while. Mr. Darcy is the soul of politeness, Elizabeth replied with a smile. He is indeed; yet given the incentive, my dear Miss Eliza, his compliance is hardly surprising; for who could refuse such a partner? Elizabeth gave a playful look and walked away. Her refusal had not diminished her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was contemplating her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley approached him.

We endured several dismal hours until the eleven o’clock start of the trial. Since my father and family were required to testify, I went with them to the courtroom. Throughout this pathetic charade of justice, I underwent agonizing torment. It was to be determined if my own reckless curiosity and forbidden experiments would lead to the deaths of two people: one an innocent, joyful infant, the other a victim of a murder made uniquely horrific by its circumstances. Justine was a virtuous young woman whose life held great promise; now, all of that was to be erased by a shameful execution, and I was the culprit! I would have gladly confessed to the crime myself, but my absence at the time meant such a claim would be dismissed as insanity, failing to save the woman who suffered because of me. Justine looked composed. Clad in mourning, her naturally charming face held a profound, striking beauty. She seemed secure in her innocence and remained steady, despite the thousands who stared and cursed her, their sympathy replaced by the perceived enormity of her alleged crime. Her calm was clearly forced; having previously been accused of guilt due to her confusion, she now summoned a display of bravery. Upon entering the court, she scanned the room and spotted us. A tear clouded her vision, but she regained her composure, her sorrowful gaze affirming her total innocence. The trial commenced, and after the prosecutor outlined the charges, witnesses were summoned. A series of bizarre facts emerged that might have shaken anyone lacking my absolute certainty of her innocence. She had been out all night when the murder occurred, and a market-woman had spotted her near the location where the child’s body was later discovered. When questioned about her presence there, she had appeared odd and provided only a muddled, incoherent reply. She arrived home around eight o’clock, and when asked about her whereabouts, she claimed to have been searching for the boy, anxiously inquiring if there was any news of him.

If he asked why I wanted it or what right I had to it, I would tell him—though he cared little for such dreams—that I had loved Estella long and deeply. Even though I had lost her and faced a lonely life, everything concerning her remained more precious to me than anything else. Seeing Mr. Jaggers stand silent and unmoved, I turned to Wemmick. I know you have a kind heart, I said. I have seen your pleasant home, your father, and the cheerful ways you balance your professional life. Please speak for me to Mr. Jaggers and explain that, given the circumstances, he should be more open. The two men exchanged a strange look. I feared Wemmick might be fired, but Mr. Jaggers relaxed into a smile, and Wemmick grew bolder. What is this? Mr. Jaggers asked. You have a father and playful habits? If I keep them separate from work, what does it matter? Wemmick replied. Pip, Mr. Jaggers said, touching my arm with a smile, this man must be the most cunning impostor in London. Not at all, Wemmick countered, I think you are another. They looked at each other again, both seemingly suspicious. You have a pleasant home? Mr. Jaggers asked. Since it does not interfere with business, let it be, Wemmick said. Looking at you, sir, I wonder if you might plan to have a home of your own one day, when you tire of this work. Mr. Jaggers nodded and sighed. Pip, he said, we will not discuss poor dreams; you have fresher experience with such things than I. But regarding this other matter, I will propose a scenario. Remember, I admit nothing. He waited for me to confirm I understood he admitted nothing. Now, Pip, he continued, consider this case. Suppose a woman in such circumstances kept her child hidden and was forced to tell her lawyer, after he insisted he needed to know the facts to prepare her defense.

Mr. Merton felt quite distressed by the second delay of the wedding, and Lady Julia, having already purchased her gown, urged Sybil to end the engagement. Despite her deep love for her mother, Sybil had committed her life to Lord Arthur and remained steadfast. Lord Arthur struggled for days with his disappointment, his nerves frayed, but his practical nature soon prevailed. Since poison had failed, he concluded that an explosive was the logical next step. He reviewed his list of relatives and decided to target his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a cultured man with a vast collection of antique clocks, which Lord Arthur realized provided the perfect opportunity for his plan. Finding an explosive device proved difficult; the directory offered no help, and he doubted the police would be useful, as they rarely anticipated such events. He then recalled his acquaintance, Count Rouvaloff, a young Russian with revolutionary leanings he had met at a party. While the Count claimed to be researching Peter the Great, many suspected he was a Nihilist agent. Lord Arthur visited his Bloomsbury lodgings to seek his help. When asked if he was becoming involved in politics, Lord Arthur, disliking pretense, admitted he had no interest in social issues and only required the device for a private family matter.

His sun-darkened face was mostly obscured by a thick beard and mustache. He carried a heavy oak club but otherwise seemed unarmed. He gave an awkward bow and greeted us in French, which, despite a regional accent, clearly marked him as a Parisian. Sit down, my friend, Dupin said. I assume you are here about the orangutan. I almost envy you owning such a fine, valuable creature. How old do you think he is? The sailor exhaled deeply, as if a heavy weight had been lifted, and answered confidently: I cannot say for sure, but he is likely no more than four or five. Do you have him here? Oh no, we lack the space. He is at a nearby stable on Rue Dubourg. You can collect him tomorrow. I assume you are prepared to prove ownership? Certainly, sir. I will be sorry to lose him, Dupin remarked. I do not expect you to go to this trouble for nothing, the man replied. I am happy to pay a reasonable reward for his recovery. That is fair, Dupin said. Let me think. My reward shall be this: you will tell me everything you know about the murders on Rue Morgue. Dupin spoke softly. He walked to the door, locked it, and pocketed the key. He then calmly placed a pistol on the table. The sailor turned red, gasping as if suffocating. He jumped up and grabbed his club, but immediately collapsed back into his chair, trembling and pale as a corpse. He remained silent. I felt deeply sorry for him. My friend, Dupin said kindly, you are unnecessarily alarmed. We mean you no harm. I give you my word as a gentleman and a Frenchman that we intend no injury. I know you are innocent of the crimes on Rue Morgue, but you cannot deny that you are involved in some way.

She was an incredible talker. It felt rude to mention that it was late and I was exhausted, so I had to stay and listen. She kept chatting in the quiet, eerie castle until a distant, muffled scream rose from deep below, sounding so agonizing that it made my skin crawl. The queen paused, her eyes brightening with delight as she tilted her head like a bird. The sound echoed again. I asked what it was. She explained it was a stubborn soul enduring the rack for hours. When I asked what he was enduring, she invited me to watch him be torn apart if he refused to confess. She was a calm, cruel woman, while I felt sick with sympathy for the prisoner. Guards with torches led us through damp, moldy stone corridors and stairways. The queen chatted about the man’s crime: he was accused of killing a stag in the royal forest. I argued that anonymous accusations were unfair and that the accused should face his accuser. She dismissed this, claiming the accuser had arrived masked at night and vanished, leaving the forester unaware of his identity. I asked if anyone actually saw the killing, and she admitted no one did, only that this stranger saw the prisoner near the scene. I suggested the accuser might be the real killer, as his masked zeal seemed suspicious. I asked why she insisted on the rack, and she replied that he must confess to save his soul. She insisted that while he would be executed for his crime, she had to ensure he confessed and received absolution to protect her own soul.

He emerged silently from the paneling, a malicious grin twisting his withered lips, while the moon obscured itself behind a cloud as he crept past the expansive bay window, which displayed his family crest alongside that of his slain wife in blue and gold. He drifted forward like a malevolent specter, the shadows themselves appearing to recoil from his presence. Pausing briefly at a distant sound, he realized it was merely a dog barking at the Red Farm, so he continued, whispering archaic oaths and waving his corroded blade through the night. Upon reaching the hallway leading to Washington’s chamber, he halted, his grey hair whipping in the wind and his burial shroud swirling into eerie shapes. As the clock chimed the quarter-hour, he sensed his moment had arrived. He let out a soft laugh and rounded the corner, only to recoil instantly with a cry of alarm, burying his pale face in his skeletal hands. Before him stood a terrifying apparition, still as stone and grotesque as a fever dream. Its skull was polished and hairless, its face bloated and pallid, frozen in a permanent, mocking sneer. Crimson light poured from its eyes, its mouth resembled a fiery abyss, and a shroud similar to his own draped its massive frame. A placard hung upon its chest, covered in ancient, cryptic script—perhaps a list of transgressions or a ledger of sins—while its right hand brandished a shining blade. Having never encountered a spirit before, he was understandably terrified. After one frantic look, he retreated, stumbling over his own winding-sheet and accidentally dropping his dagger into the Minister’s boots, where the butler discovered it the next day. Safely back in his room, he collapsed onto his bed and pulled the covers over his head. Eventually, his courageous spirit returned, and he resolved to confront the other ghost at daybreak. As dawn painted the hills in silver, he ventured back to the site of the encounter, reasoning that two ghosts were superior to one and that, with this new ally, he might finally overcome the twins.

I mistook your meaning, thinking anybody meant everyone. It applies to those of noble birth, preferably royal. The abbot intervened to ease the tension, suggesting such a gift was surely meant for the high-born. When he asked about King Arthur, the enchanter offered to reveal his status. The crowd watched with renewed fascination as the magician claimed the king was resting in his palace. The abbot offered a blessing, but I countered that the king was actually riding. This created a dilemma for the onlookers. The magician mocked my lack of incantations, but I retorted that I reserve my magic for significant moments. Stung by my sarcasm, the magician claimed the queen and court were also asleep. I dismissed this as another falsehood, noting they were active. I challenged him to predict their destination, and he claimed they would travel toward the sea by morning. When he predicted they would be far north of Camelot by the following evening, I declared his statement a lie by a hundred and fifty miles.

My once-loyal customers no longer spared me a thought. They claimed they were too busy reading about revolutions and keeping pace with the spirit of the age. If a fire needed stoking, a newspaper sufficed, and as the government faltered, my leather and iron goods seemed to grow indestructible; soon, not a single pair of bellows in Rotterdam required repair. This situation was unbearable. I became destitute, and with a family to support, my burdens grew so heavy that I spent hours contemplating suicide. Meanwhile, creditors gave me no peace. My home was besieged from dawn until dusk, leaving me pacing like a caged tiger. Three men in particular harassed me constantly, threatening legal action. I vowed to take bitter revenge if I ever caught them, and only the anticipation of that retribution kept me from ending my life with a blunderbuss. I decided to hide my rage, offering them empty promises until fate provided a chance for vengeance. One day, after slipping past my creditors, I wandered the backstreets in despair until I stumbled upon a bookseller’s stall. I collapsed into a customer’s chair and aimlessly opened the first book I found. It was a pamphlet on speculative astronomy by a professor from Berlin or a Frenchman with a similar name. Having some background in the subject, I became completely absorbed, reading the entire text twice before finally noticing my surroundings.

He could not help it. It infuriated him to believe that Becky Thatcher did not even realize he was alive. In truth, she saw him perfectly well; she knew she was winning and felt satisfied to see him suffer as she had. Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom made excuses about urgent tasks, but the girl kept talking. He thought, "I wish she would leave." Finally, he had to go, and she innocently mentioned she would be around after school, which made him despise her. "Anyone but that arrogant boy from Saint Louis!" Tom thought, grinding his teeth. "I beat you once, and I will do it again! Just wait until I catch you." He punched and kicked the air, finishing his imaginary fight with satisfaction. Tom rushed home at noon, unable to stand Amy’s happiness or his own jealousy. Becky continued looking at pictures with Alfred, but as Tom failed to appear, her triumph faded into sadness. She listened for his footsteps, but he never came. Eventually, she felt miserable for pushing things too far. When Alfred tried to show her another picture, she snapped, "Leave me alone! I don't care about them!" and walked away crying. Alfred tried to follow, but she shouted, "Go away! I hate you!" He stopped, confused, while she walked off in tears. Alfred entered the empty schoolhouse, feeling humiliated and angry. He realized the truth: she had only used him to get back at Tom Sawyer.

Three or four months passed, and winter had arrived. I had attended school consistently, learning to read, write, and spell a bit, though my multiplication skills stalled at six times seven equals thirty-five, a limit I felt I would never surpass. I never cared much for mathematics. Initially, I despised school, but eventually, I grew accustomed to it. When I felt overwhelmed, I would skip class, and the subsequent punishment actually improved my mood. Over time, school became easier, and I grew used to the widow’s habits, which no longer irritated me as much. While living indoors and sleeping in a bed felt restrictive, I occasionally slipped out to sleep in the woods before the weather turned cold. I still preferred my old life, but I was beginning to appreciate the new one. The widow noted my slow but steady progress, expressing satisfaction and pride in my development. One morning at breakfast, I accidentally knocked over the salt cellar. I reached to toss some over my left shoulder to ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson intervened, scolding me for the mess. Although the widow defended me, I knew the bad luck was inevitable. I left the house feeling anxious, wondering what misfortune awaited me. Since there was no way to prevent this specific omen, I walked along feeling dejected and vigilant. I headed to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the high board fence. A fresh inch of snow covered the ground, revealing footprints. Someone had come from the quarry, lingered by the stile, and then circled the garden fence. It was strange they had not entered. I could not understand it, and it seemed quite peculiar. Before following the tracks, I knelt to examine them more closely.

Good heavens, the Duchess mused, he is a foot doctor after all. How appalling. I hope he is at least a foreigner, as that would be slightly more acceptable. I must introduce him to you. Introduce him, the Duchess exclaimed, you cannot mean he is present? She began searching for her tortoise-shell fan and worn lace shawl, prepared to depart instantly. Naturally he is here; I would never host a gathering without him. He claims I possess a purely psychic hand and that had my thumb been shorter, I would have become a confirmed pessimist and entered a convent. Oh, I understand, the Duchess replied, feeling relieved, he predicts fortunes, I presume? And misfortunes as well, Lady Windermere responded, quite a few. Next year, for example, I face great danger by land and sea, so I plan to reside in a balloon and hoist my dinner up in a basket nightly. It is all inscribed on my little finger or palm, I cannot recall which. But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys. My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I believe everyone should have their palms read monthly to know what to avoid. One does it anyway, but the warning is pleasant. If someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself. Allow me, Lady Windermere, offered a tall, handsome young man who had been listening with an amused smile. Thanks, Lord Arthur, but I fear you would not recognize him. If he is as remarkable as you claim, I could hardly miss him. Describe him, and I will bring him to you at once. He does not resemble a palmist at all. He is not mysterious, esoteric, or romantic. He is a short, stout man with a comical bald head and large gold-rimmed spectacles, appearing like a cross between a family physician and a country lawyer. I apologize, but it is not my fault. People are so vexing. My pianists resemble poets, and my poets resemble pianists. I recall inviting a terrible conspirator to dinner last season, a man who had bombed many people and wore chain mail with a dagger in his sleeve; yet when he arrived, he looked like a pleasant clergyman and spent the evening telling jokes.

He explained that while traveling from his home through Datchet, he noticed smoke rising from the inn's chimney. Expecting to find fellow travelers, he knocked and was let in. Only Lucy and her mother were there; the mother was paralyzed by rheumatism, and as the other local residents had all departed, they were left behind. Lucy begged the man to stay until her mother recovered enough to travel, warning that they would surely die if abandoned. The man refused, insisting he had to rejoin his wife and children who had already left. As a final hope, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris. He delivered it, and Idris read the following with great distress: Honoured Lady, I hope you will remember and pity me. I am writing in a state of confusion. A month ago, my mother lost the use of her limbs. She is improving, and I am certain she could travel within a month if you could help us as you promised. However, everyone else has left. I tried to ask Samuel Woods to wait for us, but his home was already empty. I have seen no one until this man arrived. What will become of us? My mother is too ill to know our true situation. Please send someone to help. If I move her now, she will die, and even if she recovers, I do not know how we could travel so many miles to the sea. By then, you will all be in France, separated from us by the terrifying ocean.

Men wed out of weariness, women out of curiosity; both end in disappointment. I doubt I shall marry, Harry, for I am too deeply in love. I am simply applying one of your own maxims. Who is the object of your affection? Lord Henry inquired. Dorian Gray flushed as he replied, An actress. Lord Henry shrugged, calling it a trite beginning. You would feel differently if you saw her, Dorian insisted. Who is she? Sibyl Vane. I have never heard of her. No one has yet, but they will; she is a genius. My dear boy, women are merely decorative; they possess no genius, only a charming way of saying nothing. They are the victory of matter over mind, just as men are the victory of mind over morals. Harry, how can you say that? It is the truth, Dorian. I am currently studying women and find them simple: there are only the plain, who are useful for appearances, and the painted, who try to look young rather than speak brilliantly. Nowadays, a woman is content if she looks younger than her daughter. Tell me, how long have you known this genius? Your perspectives frighten me, Harry. Never mind that; how long? About three weeks. Where did you meet her? I will tell you, but do not be unkind. It is your fault, really; you sparked a frantic desire in me to understand life. After we met, I felt a pulse in my veins. While walking through the park or Piccadilly, I watched passersby with a wild curiosity, wondering about their lives. Some fascinated me, others terrified me. The air felt poisoned, and I developed a craving for sensation.

Are you referring to Mr. Knightley? Certainly. I never imagined anyone else, and I assumed you understood. Our previous conversation seemed perfectly clear. Not entirely, Emma replied with strained composure, as your comments appeared to concern someone else. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill, particularly regarding his assistance when the gypsies accosted you. Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how your memory fails you! My dear Harriet, I recall our discussion vividly. I remarked that your affection was understandable given his help, and you agreed, speaking fervently of your gratitude and your feelings when he arrived to save you. I remember it distinctly. Oh dear, Harriet exclaimed, I recall your meaning now, but I was focused on something entirely different. It was not the gypsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. I was thinking of a far more significant moment: when Mr. Knightley asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused, leaving me without a partner. That act of kindness and noble generosity made me realize his superiority over everyone else. Good heavens, Emma cried, this has been a truly disastrous misunderstanding! What can be done? You would not have encouraged me had you known? At least I am no worse off than I would have been otherwise, and now it is possible. She hesitated. Emma remained silent. I do not wonder, Miss Woodhouse, Harriet continued, that you perceive a vast difference between the two men regarding me. You must consider one vastly superior to the other. Yet, I hope, even if it seems strange, that you might recall your own words about how even greater disparities have resulted in marriage. If I were so incredibly fortunate that Mr. Knightley did not mind the difference in our stations, I hope you will not oppose it or create obstacles.

When the morning arrived for Admiral and Mrs. Croft to inspect Kellynch Hall, Anne felt it best to walk to Lady Russell’s to avoid the encounter, though she later regretted missing the chance to meet them. The meeting went perfectly, settling the matter immediately. Both ladies were eager to agree, and the Admiral’s genuine, open-hearted nature impressed Sir Walter, who had been further softened by Mr. Shepherd’s flattery regarding his reputation for refinement. The property, the tenants, and the terms were all accepted without dispute, and the legal documents were prepared immediately. Sir Walter even complimented the Admiral’s appearance, suggesting he would be presentable with a better haircut, while the Admiral remarked to his wife that the Baronet, though unremarkable, seemed harmless. The Crofts were scheduled to move in at Michaelmas, and with Sir Walter planning to relocate to Bath the month prior, preparations began at once. Lady Russell, knowing Anne would have no say in their new home, hoped to keep her at Kellynch until after Christmas. However, due to her own upcoming travel, she could not extend a formal invitation. Anne, despite dreading the heat of Bath and mourning the loss of the autumn season in the country, ultimately felt it was best to depart.

I would wake up eventually to investigate the cause of a sound, perhaps spotting a steamboat chugging upstream so far away that I could only distinguish if it had a stern or side wheel. Then, for an hour, there was nothing to see or hear—just pure solitude. Later, a raft would drift by in the distance, and I might see a man chopping wood; the axe would flash, and only after it rose again would the dull thud finally reach us across the water. We spent our days idling in the silence. Once, a dense fog rolled in, and the passing rafts beat tin pans to warn off steamboats. A vessel passed so close we could clearly hear the crew talking, swearing, and laughing, yet we saw nothing. It felt eerie, like ghosts haunting the air. Jim thought they were spirits, but I argued that ghosts wouldn't curse the fog. Once night fell, we pushed off, letting the current carry us while we smoked and dangled our legs in the water. We stayed naked day and night whenever the mosquitoes allowed, as I never cared for clothes and the ones Buck’s family gave me were too restrictive. Sometimes the river was entirely ours. We watched the distant banks and islands, occasionally spotting a candle flickering in a cabin window or a light on a passing raft, sometimes accompanied by the faint sound of a fiddle or a song. Life on a raft is beautiful. We would lie on our backs, gazing at the star-speckled sky, debating whether the stars were created or simply happened. Jim insisted they were made, but I argued they just happened, as it would have taken too long to create so many.

Yet there was something even more flamboyant. He would become a pirate! That was the path! Now his future appeared clear and radiant with incredible brilliance. How his reputation would spread, striking terror into hearts! He envisioned himself sailing the lively waves aboard his sleek, dark-hulled vessel, the Spirit of the Storm, his grim flag hoisted high. At the height of his notoriety, he would return to his village, marching into church tanned and rugged, dressed in a velvet doublet, jack-boots, and a crimson sash, armed with pistols and a weathered cutlass, his plumed hat and skull-and-crossbones flag signaling his arrival. He imagined the thrill of hearing the congregation whisper, "It is Tom Sawyer the Pirate, the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!" It was decided; his life’s work was chosen. He would depart home the following morning to begin. He needed to gather his supplies, so he approached a decaying log and dug beneath it with his knife. Hearing a hollow sound, he performed a solemn ritual: "What has not arrived, come! What is here, remain!" He cleared the soil to reveal a small wooden box. Inside sat a single marble. Tom was stunned, scratching his head in confusion. "Well, that is truly bizarre!" he muttered. He threw the marble aside, deep in thought. His belief in a childhood superstition had crumbled; he and his friends had always considered this ritual foolproof. The legend claimed that burying a marble with the proper words would cause every lost marble to return to that spot after a fortnight. Since it had failed, his confidence was shattered. He had never known it to fail, conveniently forgetting that he had previously lost the locations of his own buried treasures. After pondering the mystery, he concluded that a witch must have meddled and ruined the spell.

He jumped up and grabbed her arm. "Show him to me. Which one is he? Point him out. I must see him!" he shouted, but the Duke of Berwick’s carriage blocked their view, and by the time it passed, the other carriage had vanished. "He is gone," Sibyl whispered sadly. "I wish you had seen him." "I wish I had, because I swear to God, if he ever hurts you, I will kill him." She looked at him in horror. He repeated the threat, his words sharp as a blade. Bystanders stared, and a nearby woman giggled. "Come away, Jim," she whispered. He followed her through the crowd, feeling satisfied with his outburst. At the Achilles Statue, she turned to him with pity in her eyes, though she soon laughed. "You are foolish, Jim; just a bad-tempered boy. How can you say such horrible things? You are just jealous. I wish you would fall in love; it makes people good, and what you said was wicked." "I am sixteen," he replied, "and I know what I am doing. Mother cannot help you. I wish I were not going to Australia. I would quit if my contract were not already signed." "Don't be so serious. You sound like a character from one of Mother’s silly plays. I won't argue with you. Seeing him is perfect happiness. You would never harm someone I love, would you?" "Not as long as you love him, I suppose," he muttered. "I shall love him forever!" she cried. "And he?" "Forever, too!" "He had better." She pulled away, then laughed and touched his arm, dismissing him as just a boy. At Marble Arch, they caught a bus to their shabby home on Euston Road. It was after five, and Sibyl needed to rest before her performance. Jim insisted she lie down, preferring to say goodbye without their mother present, as he hated the scenes she was prone to making.

She was right about the rats. Every so often, one would poke its nose out from a corner hole. She explained that she kept objects nearby to throw at them when alone, or they would never leave her in peace. She showed me a knotted bar of lead, claiming she was usually a good shot, but a recent arm injury made her aim uncertain. She waited for an opening and threw it at a rat, missing widely and crying out in pain. She then asked me to try for the next one. I wanted to leave before her husband returned, but I kept that to myself. I took the lead, and when the next rat appeared, I threw it; had the rat stayed put, it would have been badly hurt. She praised my aim and fetched the lead, along with a hank of yarn for me to hold. As I held the yarn, she spoke of her marriage, though she paused to warn me to keep an eye on the rats and keep the lead in my lap. She dropped the metal into my lap, and I clamped my legs together over it. Moments later, she removed the yarn, looked me in the eye, and asked for my real name. I trembled, unsure how to respond. I asked her not to tease a poor girl, offering to leave if I were a burden. She insisted I stay, promising she would not hurt or betray me. She urged me to trust her with my secret, assuming I was merely a runaway apprentice who had been treated poorly. She assured me there was no harm in it and that she would help me.

The following day was set for the confrontation to avoid any cooling of our honor, and Drummle arrived bearing a polite note from Estella confirming she had danced with him repeatedly. I had no choice but to express regret for my previous outburst and dismiss the notion that I was anywhere to be found. Drummle and I sat glaring at each other for an hour while the rest of the group argued, eventually concluding that our mutual goodwill had progressed remarkably. I recount this casually, yet it weighed heavily upon me. It caused me immense distress to imagine Estella favoring such a wretched, awkward, and sullen fool, who was so clearly beneath her. I still believe it was a spark of genuine, selfless love that made the idea of her stooping to such a man unbearable. While I would have been miserable regardless of her choice, a more suitable partner would have caused me a different sort of pain. I quickly discovered that Drummle was shadowing her and that she permitted it. Soon, he was constantly in pursuit, and we crossed paths daily. He persisted in his dull, stubborn way, while Estella kept him tethered, alternating between encouragement and disdain, sometimes flattering him and other times acting as if he were a stranger. The Spider, as Jaggers dubbed him, possessed the patient, predatory nature of his kind. Furthermore, he held a foolish confidence in his wealth and lineage that served him well, often mimicking the effect of true focus. Thus, by doggedly tracking Estella, he outlasted more capable rivals, ready to strike at the opportune moment. At an Assembly Ball in Richmond, where Estella eclipsed every other woman, Drummle hovered near her with her apparent consent. I decided to confront her about him, finding my chance when she sat alone among the flowers, waiting for Mrs. Blandley to escort her home.

You have not been in Bath long enough, he remarked, to appreciate the local evening gatherings. Oh no, she replied, they hold no appeal for me. I do not play cards. I know you did not used to, he said, but time brings many changes. I have not changed that much, Anne insisted, then paused, worried she might be misunderstood. After a moment, he added as if moved by sudden emotion, It has been a long time. Eight and a half years is a significant period. Anne wondered if he would have continued, but Henrietta interrupted, eager to leave before other guests arrived. They had to move. Anne claimed she was ready, though she felt a deep reluctance to leave her seat. Had Henrietta known her regret, she might have pitied her. Their departure was halted by the arrival of Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose presence chilled the room. The atmosphere of comfort and freedom vanished, replaced by forced politeness and cold silence. Anne was mortified by the change. She noted that Captain Wentworth was acknowledged by both, with Elizabeth even speaking to him and glancing his way repeatedly. Elizabeth had a plan. After some small talk, she invited the Musgroves to a small gathering the following evening. She extended the invitation gracefully, placing her cards on the table with a smile for everyone, and a more deliberate one for Captain Wentworth. Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to recognize the value of a man with his presence and appearance.

My father’s last name was Pirrip and my first name was Philip, but as a baby I could only manage to say Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and that is what everyone called me. I know my father’s name from his tombstone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the local blacksmith.
