Since I never met my parents or saw pictures of them—as they lived before photography—I imagined what they looked like based on their graves. The square letters on my father’s stone made me think he was a stout, dark man with curly hair. From the inscription about my mother, Georgiana, I childishly decided she was sickly and freckled. Beside their grave were five small stones for my brothers who died in infancy. I grew up believing they were born lying on their backs with their hands in their pockets, never taking them out. We lived in the marsh country near the river, about twenty miles from the sea. My first clear memory of the world comes from a cold, raw afternoon. That day, I realized this overgrown, bleak place was the churchyard where my parents and brothers were buried. I saw the dark, flat marshes filled with dikes and cattle, the grey river, and the distant, wild sea where the wind originated. I realized the small, shivering boy crying in fear was me. Suddenly, a terrifying voice shouted, "Be quiet!" A man jumped up from behind the gravestones. "Stay still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!" He was a frightening man dressed in coarse grey clothes, with a heavy iron shackle on his leg.

Once I had submitted the petitions, I found myself drawn to the locations where they were held, feeling as though my presence offered them some small measure of hope. Driven by this anxious agitation, I would pace the streets at night, passing the offices and homes where I had left my appeals. To this day, the bleak western districts of London on a chilly, dusty spring evening, with their imposing, closed residences and endless lines of streetlamps, evoke a profound sadness in me due to those memories. My daily visits were now curtailed, and he was under tighter guard. Suspecting that I might be accused of smuggling poison to him, I requested to be searched before sitting by his bed, assuring the ever-present officer of my honest intentions. No one treated us with cruelty; they simply performed their duties without malice. The officer and the other prisoners acting as nurses—criminals, yet capable of compassion—consistently informed me that his condition was worsening. As time passed, I observed him gazing quietly at the ceiling, his expression dull until my voice briefly animated his features. Often unable to speak, he would communicate through gentle squeezes of my hand, which I learned to interpret clearly. By the tenth day, a significant shift occurred. His eyes brightened as I walked in, fixed upon the entrance. Dear boy, he greeted me, I feared you were late, though I knew that was impossible. It is exactly the right time, I replied, as I waited at the gate. You always wait at the gate, don't you? Yes, so I would not miss a single moment. Thank you, dear boy, God bless you, you have never abandoned me. I squeezed his hand, unable to forget that I had once intended to do just that. And the best part, he added, is that you have been more at ease with me since I fell into this misfortune than when things were bright.

You will be glad to hear that no disaster has marked the start of this venture you viewed with such dread. I arrived yesterday, and my first duty is to assure my dear sister of my safety and my growing confidence in the project's success. I am already far north of London. Walking the streets of St. Petersburg, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks that invigorates me and fills me with joy. Do you understand this feeling? This wind, blowing from the regions I am heading toward, gives me a taste of those icy lands. Inspired by this promising breeze, my daydreams grow more intense. I try in vain to believe the pole is a place of frost and desolation; in my imagination, it is always a region of beauty and delight. There, Margaret, the sun is always visible, its broad disk skimming the horizon and casting a perpetual glow. There—if I may trust the explorers who came before me—snow and frost are banished. Sailing over a calm sea, we may reach a land more wonderful and beautiful than any yet discovered. Its features may be unique, just as the celestial phenomena in those uncharted solitudes surely are. What might we find in a land of eternal light? I may discover the mysterious force that attracts the compass needle and clarify celestial observations that only this voyage can explain. I will satisfy my intense curiosity by seeing a part of the world never before visited and walking on land no human has ever touched. These are my motivations, and they are enough to overcome any fear of danger or death, filling me with the joy of a child setting off on an expedition. Even if my theories are wrong, you cannot deny the immense benefit I will provide to all future generations by finding a polar passage to distant lands, or by uncovering the secret of the magnet, which can only be achieved through a journey like mine. These thoughts have calmed the nerves I felt when I began this letter. My heart glows with an enthusiasm that lifts my spirit, for nothing settles the mind like a steady purpose—a goal upon which the soul can fix its focus.

Do not misunderstand; I was never truly insane. I remained aware of my condition even when wild thoughts pushed me toward madness, keeping those struggles hidden in silence. To others, I appeared only as a broken-spirited girl who spoke softly, shed hidden tears, avoided company, and never smiled. That was all they saw. Eventually, I escaped my guardian’s home and vanished. Based on the letters I left behind, people assumed I had taken my own life, so they stopped searching for me. I left London on a small ship bound for northern England. Once I was truly alone, peace finally returned. As the ship sailed across the calm sea, I sat on deck feeling like a changed person. I was no longer the miserable Mathilda, but a young hermit dedicated to solitude, determined to keep my heart free from despair. My simple, nun-like clothing, the secret of my survival, and the promise of a lonely future brought comfort to my wounded heart. The breeze refreshed me as I watched sunlight dance on the waves and birds skim the water. I slept without dreams and woke to enjoy my quiet freedom. After four days, we reached our destination. I left the coast immediately, heading inland to find the isolated home I had imagined. I wanted a house on a vast, empty plain where I could see the horizon and wander without meeting anyone. I did not hate people, but I knew my peace of mind required solitude. I settled in a desolate, stony heath covered in short grass, marked only by a few rushes near a small pool.

Listen closely; I have mastered the tongue of misery, for I am misery itself—a bizarre, triumphant spirit. Yet that is a lie, for the tide may be murky but lacks bitterness. We rest, closing our eyes in peace, and upon waking, we find liberation. Delay no longer, you laggard! Observe this inviting draught. Understand that I am a benevolent spirit, not a mortal woman, beckoning you to drink with persuasive words. As I spoke, I watched his face. His profound beauty and the divine empathy radiating from his gaze, combined with his earnest, questioning expression, dissolved my rigid despair, replacing it with tender sorrow. Seeing his own eyes grow moist, he took my hands and sat beside me. This is a tragic path you propose, my dear friend, and your suffering must be immense to harbor such dark notions. You crave death, yet fear it, desiring my company. I lack your courage; even with you, I dare not perish. Hear me out, and consider if you should truly sway me, even if your desperate eloquence could make death seem brighter than heaven. I have harbored such dark desires myself, yet I have conquered that phantom. Just as you played the role of Despair, I shall act as Una to lead you safely from this gloom. Listen and let your heart soften. We do not grasp the meaning of this world, with its blend of light and shadow. We are placed here to exist and to hope. I cannot define that hope, but we must pursue some greater good; that is our duty. If adversity strikes, we must resist it, cast it aside, and continue our search for what we are meant to seek. Whether this pursuit prepares us for another life or simply serves to pave the way for those who follow, I cannot say.

When the wedding occurred three weeks later, St. Peter’s overflowed with a fashionable crowd. The Dean of Chichester conducted the ceremony impressively, and observers noted the couple’s striking appearance. Beyond their looks, they were genuinely happy. Lord Arthur never regretted his sacrifices for Sybil, and she offered him her deepest devotion and affection. Reality did not diminish their romance; they remained forever youthful. Years later, after two children arrived, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, the Duke’s gift to his son. While sitting under a lime-tree watching the children play, she asked Sybil if she was happy. Sybil confirmed her joy and asked the same of her guest. Lady Windermere claimed she lacked time for happiness, noting she grew bored with people once she knew them. When asked about her social favorites, she dismissed them as dull once their novelty faded, specifically recalling the fraudulent Mr. Podgers, whose romantic advances had soured her on palmistry in favor of telepathy. Sybil warned her not to mock palmistry, as Arthur took it quite seriously. When Lady Windermere questioned this, Sybil directed her to Arthur, who approached with yellow roses and his children. Upon being asked if he truly believed in palmistry, Arthur smiled and replied that he owed his entire life’s happiness to it.

Saturday nights in our village brought a pleasant feeling of tidying up and pausing before starting fresh, which emboldened Joe to stay out thirty minutes past his usual time. As his rum and water finished, Joe stood to leave, taking my hand. Wait a moment, Mr. Gargery, the stranger said. I believe I have a shiny new shilling, and if I do, the boy shall have it. He found it among his change, wrapped it in crumpled paper, and handed it to me, insisting it was mine. I thanked him, staring rudely while clutching Joe. He bid Joe and Mr. Wopsle goodnight, then gave me a strange look with his one good eye, or rather, he winked it in a way that felt significant. On the walk home, Mr. Wopsle left us, and Joe walked with his mouth open to air out the taste of rum. I was too stunned by this encounter with a ghost from my past to speak. My sister was in a decent mood, so Joe told her about the shilling. She immediately suspected it was counterfeit, but when I unwrapped it, it was genuine. Then she noticed two one-pound notes inside the paper, damp and smelling of livestock. Joe grabbed his hat and rushed back to the pub to return them. I sat on my stool, certain the man would be gone. Joe soon returned, confirming the man had vanished, though he had left word about the money.

You have not stayed in Bath long enough, he remarked, to appreciate the evening social gatherings. Oh no, she replied, those events hold no appeal for me, as I do not play cards. I recall you did not care for them previously, but time brings many shifts. I have not altered that much, Anne exclaimed, then paused, worried about being misunderstood. After a brief silence, he spoke as if moved by sudden emotion, noting that eight and a half years is indeed a significant span. Anne was left to wonder if he might have continued, but Henrietta interrupted, eager to depart before more guests arrived. They had to leave, and though Anne claimed readiness, she felt a deep reluctance to abandon her seat and the room, knowing Henrietta would pity her if she understood the depth of her feelings. Their departure was halted by the arrival of Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose presence instantly dampened the atmosphere. The room’s previous ease and cheer vanished, replaced by a stiff, hollow formality to match her father and sister’s cold elegance. Anne noted with satisfaction that Captain Wentworth was acknowledged by both, with Elizabeth even addressing him and offering a more gracious reception than before. Elizabeth had been contemplating a strategy, which soon became clear. After exchanging trivialities, she extended an invitation to the Musgroves for a small gathering the following evening. She spoke with grace, placing her cards on the table with a polite smile for everyone, and a more deliberate one for Captain Wentworth, having realized during her time in Bath the value of a man with his distinguished appearance.

Should I ask them? Or perhaps Miss Bates? She lives closer, and she likely understands everyone's preferences as well as anyone. We need more input. Shall I invite Miss Bates to join us? Mrs. Weston hesitated, asking if she would be helpful. Emma disagreed, noting that Miss Bates would be grateful but too distracted to provide any real information. Still, Mrs. Weston insisted she found Miss Bates amusing and did not need to invite the whole family. Mr. Weston then joined them and enthusiastically agreed. He urged Frank to fetch Miss Bates, suggesting she would enjoy the plan and help them overcome their hesitation. He insisted that Frank bring both the aunt and her niece. Frank initially misunderstood, but after being corrected, he hurried off to invite them both. While he was gone, Mrs. Weston reconsidered the venue and decided the problems were actually quite minor. The remaining details regarding furniture, lighting, and refreshments seemed easy to manage. Everyone invited was expected to attend, and Frank had already requested to extend his stay. It was destined to be a wonderful dance. When Miss Bates arrived, she was thrilled by the plan. While she offered no practical advice, her constant, enthusiastic approval was very welcome. For the next half hour, the group walked between the rooms, happily planning and anticipating the event.

“Now,” Mr. Lorry said, placing his hand softly on the Doctor’s arm after a brief pause, “what do you attribute this episode to?” “I suspect,” Doctor Manette replied, “that there was a powerful and unusual resurgence of the memories that originally triggered his illness. I believe some deeply painful associations were suddenly brought to mind. It is likely he had long feared these associations might resurface under specific conditions. He attempted to brace himself, but perhaps that very effort left him less capable of enduring the shock.” “Would he recall what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry inquired, hesitating slightly. The Doctor glanced sadly around the room, shook his head, and replied quietly, “Not in the least.” “And regarding the future?” Mr. Lorry suggested. “Regarding the future,” the Doctor said, regaining his composure, “I am very hopeful. Since Heaven mercifully restored him so quickly, I have great hope. Having succumbed to a complex pressure he long dreaded and fought, and having recovered once the storm passed, I trust the worst is behind him.” “Well, that is a great comfort. I am grateful!” Mr. Lorry exclaimed. “I am grateful!” the Doctor echoed, bowing his head reverently. “There are two other matters,” Mr. Lorry continued, “on which I seek guidance. May I proceed?” “You could do your friend no greater service.” The Doctor offered his hand. “First, he is studious and remarkably energetic; he pursues professional knowledge and experiments with great fervor. Is he doing too much?” “I believe not. It may be the nature of his mind to require constant occupation. This could be partly innate and partly a result of his suffering. If his mind were not engaged in constructive pursuits, it would be more prone to drift toward unhealthy thoughts. He may have recognized this himself.” “You are certain he is not under excessive strain?” “I am quite certain.” “My dear Manette, if he were currently overworked—” “My dear Lorry, I doubt that is possible. He has endured such intense pressure in one area that he requires a counterweight.” “Forgive my persistence as a businessman. Assuming he were overworked, would it manifest as a recurrence of this disorder?”

Do you visit here often? I have never returned since. Neither have I. As the moon rose, I remembered the peaceful look on his face before he died and the pressure of his hand when I spoke his final words. Estella broke the silence. I have often intended to return, but circumstances prevented me. Poor old place. Moonlight touched the mist and the tears falling from her eyes. Trying to compose herself, she asked if I wondered why the property was left in such ruins. Yes, Estella. The land is mine. It is the only thing I have kept. Everything else is gone, but I held onto this through all those miserable years. Is it going to be developed? Finally, yes. I came to say goodbye before it changes. And you, she asked with genuine interest, do you still live abroad? Still. And you are doing well, I hope? I work hard for a living, so yes, I am doing well. I have often thought of you, Estella said. Have you? Lately, very often. For a long time, I avoided remembering what I had thrown away when I was too young to understand its value. But now that I am free to remember, I have let those thoughts back into my heart. You have always held a place in mine, I replied. We were silent until she spoke again. I never thought I would say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place, Estella said. I am glad to do so. Glad to part again? Parting is painful for me. The memory of our last goodbye has always been sad. But you told me then, God bless you, God forgive you, she said earnestly. If you could say that then, you will say it now, now that suffering has taught me to understand your heart. I have been bent and broken, but I hope I have been reshaped into something better.

Looking at him, one might think he had been struck by a curse. He stood frozen, his face pale and sorrowful. Having lived a life of wealth and carefree ease, he was now suddenly confronted by the crushing weight of fate. It felt monstrous. Was his future already written in the lines of his hand, a secret record of sin he could not decipher? Was he merely a pawn moved by unseen forces, or a vessel shaped by a potter for either glory or disgrace? His mind rebelled against the thought, yet he felt a dark tragedy looming, forcing him to carry an unbearable burden. Unlike actors, who choose their roles, people in real life are often cast in parts they are ill-suited for. The world is a stage, but the casting is poor. Suddenly, Mr. Podgers entered. Seeing Lord Arthur, he recoiled, his face turning a sickly, greenish-yellow. They locked eyes in a tense silence. Podgers spoke first, claiming he had come to retrieve a glove for the Duchess. Lord Arthur stopped him, demanding a direct answer to a question. Podgers tried to excuse himself, citing the Duchess's impatience, but Lord Arthur refused to let him leave. Dismissing the Duchess as unimportant, Lord Arthur approached him and held out his hand. He demanded the truth, insisting he was no longer a child.

On the hearth lay several thick, blood-stained locks of grey hair, seemingly torn out by the roots. The floor held four gold coins, a topaz earring, various silver spoons, and two bags containing nearly four thousand francs. A corner bureau had been ransacked, though many items remained. A small iron safe found under the bed was open, its key still in the lock, containing only unimportant papers. No trace of Madame L’Espanaye appeared, but soot in the fireplace led to the discovery of her daughter’s corpse, shoved head-first up the chimney. The body was still warm, showing abrasions from the struggle, facial scratches, and deep bruises on the throat suggesting strangulation. A search of the rear courtyard revealed the old lady’s body, her throat so severely slashed that her head detached when moved. The remains were hideously mutilated, barely recognizable as human. No leads exist for this horrific mystery. The following day, the paper added that while many had been questioned regarding the Rue Morgue tragedy, no light had been shed on the case. Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, testified that she had known the victims for three years. She described them as affectionate and reliable with payments, though she could only speculate on their finances, noting rumors that the mother earned money by fortune-telling and had savings.

If you want one for home use, I can provide an excellent item and guarantee your satisfaction. May I ask who it is for? If it is for the police or anyone at Scotland Yard, I cannot help. English detectives are our best friends, and their stupidity allows us to do as we please. I would hate to lose them. Lord Arthur assured him it had nothing to do with the police, explaining the clock was for the Dean of Chichester. Herr Winckelkopf remarked that he was surprised by such religious devotion in a young man. Lord Arthur blushed and admitted he knew nothing of theology. After confirming it was a private matter, Winckelkopf left and returned with a small piece of dynamite and a French clock topped with a gold figure of Liberty. Lord Arthur was pleased and asked how it worked. Winckelkopf explained that he would set the timer for the exact moment of the explosion. Lord Arthur requested it be set for Friday at noon, when the Dean would be home. Winckelkopf noted this in his ledger. When Lord Arthur asked for the bill, Winckelkopf replied that the dynamite cost seven shillings and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and shipping five shillings. He added that he was happy to help a friend of Count Rouvaloff. Lord Arthur asked about the cost of his labor.

I cannot say how long I remained in that state, but it must have been quite a while. When I finally regained consciousness, dawn was breaking. The balloon was at a massive height over a vast ocean, with no land in sight anywhere. Surprisingly, I did not feel the agony one might expect. Instead, a sense of calm bordering on madness took over as I surveyed my situation. I examined my hands, wondering why the veins were swollen and my fingernails were black. I checked my head repeatedly, relieved to confirm it had not grown larger than the balloon itself. I then checked my pockets and felt strangely annoyed to find my notebook and toothpick case missing. I noticed pain in my left ankle, and a vague awareness of my predicament began to dawn on me. Oddly, I felt no horror. If anything, I felt a smug satisfaction at how cleverly I would escape this mess, never doubting my survival. I sat in deep thought for a few minutes, making the thoughtful gestures of a man pondering a complex problem in his armchair. Once I had gathered my thoughts, I carefully reached behind my back to unfasten the large iron buckle on my trousers. The three teeth of the buckle were rusty and stiff, but I managed to set them at a right angle. Holding the buckle in my teeth, I slowly untied my necktie, resting several times before finally succeeding.

Many American women abroad affect a sickly appearance, mistaking it for European sophistication, but Mrs. Otis avoided this mistake. She possessed a robust constitution and immense vitality. In many ways, she was quite English, proving that America and England share everything today, except perhaps language. Her eldest son, named Washington in a moment of parental patriotism he later regretted, was a handsome, fair-haired man. He prepared for American diplomacy by leading dances at the Newport Casino for three seasons and was a celebrated dancer in London. His only weaknesses were gardenias and the aristocracy; otherwise, he was quite sensible. Virginia E. Otis, a fifteen-year-old girl, was as graceful as a fawn, with large, expressive blue eyes. A skilled rider, she once beat Lord Bilton in a pony race around the park, finishing near the Achilles statue. This delighted the young Duke of Cheshire, who proposed to her immediately, only to be sent back to Eton by his guardians in tears. Next were the twins, nicknamed The Stars and Stripes because they were constantly being punished. They were charming boys and, aside from their father, the only true republicans in the family. Since Canterville Chase is seven miles from the Ascot station, Mr. Otis arranged for a carriage to meet them, and they began their journey in high spirits. It was a beautiful July evening, the air fragrant with pine. They heard wood pigeons, spotted pheasants in the ferns, and watched squirrels and rabbits darting through the brush. As they entered the avenue of Canterville Chase, however, the sky darkened, a strange silence fell, a flock of rooks flew overhead, and rain began to drop before they reached the house. An elderly woman in a black silk dress, white cap, and apron stood on the steps to greet them.

For years, Dorian Gray remained under the spell of that book, or perhaps he simply never wanted to escape it. He ordered nine large-paper copies from Paris, binding them in various colors to match his shifting moods and the impulses of a nature he often struggled to control. The protagonist, a fascinating Parisian who blended romanticism with science, felt like a mirror of his own future. The novel seemed to tell the story of his life before he had even lived it. In one respect, he was luckier than that fictional hero. He never suffered the strange fear of mirrors, polished metal, or still water that plagued the Parisian after his once-remarkable beauty began to fade. Dorian read the tragic conclusion with a sense of cruel delight, finding a dark satisfaction in the despair of a man who had lost what he valued most. Yet, the beauty that had captivated Basil Hallward and so many others never abandoned Dorian. Even those who heard scandalous rumors about his lifestyle in London clubs found it impossible to believe them when they saw him. He always appeared untouched by the world. Crude men fell silent in his presence, rebuked by the purity of his face, which reminded them of the innocence they had lost. They marveled at how someone so graceful could remain untainted by such a sordid, sensual age. Often, after returning from mysterious, long absences that fueled gossip among his supposed friends, he would sneak upstairs to his locked room. Using the key he kept constantly with him, he would stand before Basil’s portrait with a mirror, comparing the aging, wicked face on the canvas to the fair, laughing youth reflected in the glass.

What is the trouble? I said, Dad, and Mom, and my sister, and— Then I broke down. He said, Oh, don't carry on so; we all have our troubles, and this one will turn out fine. What is the matter with them? They are—are you the watchman of the boat? Yes, he said, sounding quite pleased with himself. I am the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and head deckhand; sometimes I am the freight and passengers too. I am not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I cannot be as generous to everyone as he is, throwing money around, but I have told him many times I would not trade places with him. A sailor's life is the life for me, and I would not live two miles out of town where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and more. I interrupted and said, They are in a terrible amount of trouble, and— Who is? Why, Dad, Mom, my sister, and Miss Hooker; if you would take your ferryboat and go up there— Up where? Where are they? On the wreck. What wreck? Why, there is only one. You do not mean the Walter Scott? Yes. Good heavens! What are they doing there? Well, they did not go there on purpose. I bet they did not! Goodness, there is no chance for them if they do not get off quickly! How on earth did they get into such a mess? It was easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting up at Booth's Landing. She was visiting there, and just at dusk she started across with her maid in the horse-ferry to stay the night at a friend's house, but they lost their steering oar, drifted downstream, and crashed onto the wreck. The ferryman, the maid, and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker managed to grab hold and get onto the wreck. About an hour after dark, we came along in our trading scow, and it was so dark we did not notice the wreck until we were right on top of it. We crashed too, but all of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and he was such a good person! I almost wish it had been me. My word! That is the most incredible thing I have ever encountered.

When we returned to the raft and tallied our earnings, the king had collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also swiped a three-gallon jug of whiskey from beneath a wagon while walking through the woods. The king remarked that, all things considered, this surpassed any day he had spent in missionary work. He insisted that heathens simply could not compete with pirates when it came to exploiting a camp meeting. The duke had felt proud of his own efforts until the king revealed his haul. He had printed two horse-sale flyers for local farmers, earning four dollars. He also secured ten dollars in newspaper advertisements, offering a discount to four dollars if paid upfront, which the clients accepted. Although the paper cost two dollars annually, he sold three subscriptions for fifty cents each by demanding cash instead of the usual payment in firewood and onions, claiming he had just purchased the business. He also composed a sentimental three-verse poem titled, "Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart," and set it for publication for free. In total, he brought in nine dollars and fifty cents, which he considered a fair day's work. He then showed us a flyer he had printed for our own use, free of charge. It featured an illustration of a runaway slave carrying a bundle on a stick, with a two-hundred-dollar reward listed below. The text described Jim perfectly, claiming he had escaped from a plantation near New Orleans and was heading north. The duke explained that we could now travel during the day. If approached, we could tie Jim up, hide him in the shelter, and present the flyer to claim we had captured him upriver and were transporting him to collect the reward.

We could certainly build a chilling superstition around this. I suppose you will name the beetle scarabaeus caput hominis, or something similar, as those titles appear often in natural histories. But where are the antennae you mentioned? The antennae! Legrand replied, appearing strangely agitated. I am certain you must see them. I drew them as clearly as they appear on the actual insect, which should suffice. Very well, I said, perhaps you did, but I still cannot see them. I handed him the paper silently, not wanting to provoke him. I was surprised by his reaction; his irritability baffled me, as the drawing clearly lacked antennae and looked remarkably like a standard death’s-head moth. He took the paper crossly and nearly crumpled it for the fire, but a sudden look at the sketch froze him. His face flushed crimson, then turned deathly pale. He studied the drawing intently for several minutes before rising to take a candle to a sea-chest in the corner. There, he examined the paper from every angle with intense focus. He remained silent, and though his behavior stunned me, I chose not to aggravate his mood. Eventually, he placed the paper in his wallet and locked it inside a desk. He calmed down, though his earlier enthusiasm had vanished, replaced by a deep, distracted reverie that my attempts at conversation could not break. I had planned to stay the night, but given his state, I decided to leave. He did not ask me to stay, though he shook my hand with unusual warmth as I departed. About a month later, during which time I had not seen Legrand, his servant Jupiter visited me in Charleston. The old man looked so dejected that I feared some terrible misfortune had struck my friend.

He bowed and left. The street was empty; it is a quiet, isolated lane. William Bird, a tailor, testified that he was among those who entered the house. An Englishman living in Paris for two years, he was among the first to climb the stairs. He heard voices arguing. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman; he recalled hearing 'sacré' and 'mon Dieu.' He also heard sounds of a struggle—scraping and scuffling. The shrill voice was louder than the gruff one and did not sound English; it seemed German, or perhaps a woman's. He does not speak German. Four witnesses confirmed that the door to Mademoiselle L.'s room was locked from the inside when they arrived. Everything was silent. Upon forcing the door, they found no one. The windows in both rooms were shut and locked from within. The connecting door was closed but unlocked. The door to the hallway was locked with the key inside. A small, cluttered room at the top of the stairs was found with its door ajar. They searched every inch of the house, including the chimneys. The four-story building had a roof trapdoor that had been nailed shut for years. Witnesses estimated the time between hearing the voices and breaking down the door at three to five minutes. The door was difficult to open. Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker living on the Rue Morgue, testified that he was part of the group but stayed downstairs due to his nervous disposition. He heard the argument and confirmed the gruff voice was French, but he insisted the shrill voice belonged to an Englishman.

The gauge showed I had reached an altitude of 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles, allowing me to see about one three-hundred-twentieth of the Earth's total surface. By nine o'clock, the land to the east had vanished, and I noticed the balloon drifting quickly to the north-northwest. The curve of the ocean below was clearly visible, though clouds often blocked my view. I noted that even the thinnest vapors never rose more than ten miles above sea level. At nine-thirty, I dropped a handful of feathers through the valve to test the air. Instead of floating, they fell straight down like bullets, disappearing in seconds. I was confused at first, unable to believe my ascent had suddenly accelerated so much. I soon realized the air was too thin to support the feathers, and their rapid fall combined with my own upward speed made them vanish instantly. By ten o'clock, I had little to do. Everything was going well, and I felt the balloon rising faster every moment, though I could no longer measure the exact speed. I felt no pain or discomfort and was in better spirits than at any time since leaving Rotterdam. I spent my time checking my equipment and refreshing the air inside the chamber every forty minutes, mostly as a health precaution. Meanwhile, my mind wandered to the moon. Unshackled by reality, my imagination roamed through a dreamlike landscape. I pictured ancient forests, jagged cliffs, and waterfalls crashing into bottomless pits. Then, I imagined silent, midday solitudes where no wind blew, and vast fields of poppies and lilies stretched out, perfectly still and quiet forever.

Raymond paced the room in a fury while I waited to hear his complaints. Adrian leaned against the wall and remarked that our behavior was as ridiculous as that of schoolboys. Raymond insisted that this was part of a tyrannical system he would no longer tolerate. He demanded to know why he, as Protector of England, should be treated like a slave, his privacy violated and his friends insulted. He declared he was finished with it all, removed the star of his office from his chest, and threw it onto the table, announcing his resignation. Adrian challenged him to find anyone else in England capable of taking his place, urging him to recognize his own worth. He reminded Raymond that only months ago, the country viewed his life and the Protectorate as inseparable. He recounted how Raymond had improved their cities, established useful institutions, and protected the weak from the powerful. Adrian pleaded with him to overcome this bad mood and resume his duties, promising that the people would support him if he could only master himself. Raymond replied gloomily that Adrian’s advice would be better suited to himself, as he possessed the wisdom and justice to rule. Raymond admitted that he had taken on a task he was unfit for, as he could not even control his own passions. He swore by God that his resignation was not a temporary outburst but a permanent decision to abandon the burden of power.

Jane admitted she was surprised by the engagement, though she focused more on wishing the couple happiness than on her own shock. Elizabeth could not convince her that the match was unlikely. Kitty and Lydia did not envy Miss Lucas, as Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman; to them, it was simply gossip to share in Meryton. Lady Lucas felt triumphant that she could now boast of a well-married daughter to Mrs. Bennet. She visited Longbourn frequently to share her joy, despite Mrs. Bennet’s bitter reactions. A sense of awkwardness grew between Elizabeth and Charlotte, leaving them unable to discuss the matter. Elizabeth realized their friendship had lost its former intimacy. Disappointed in Charlotte, she turned to her sister Jane with renewed affection, worrying about her future as Bingley had been gone a week with no word of his return. Jane had replied to Caroline’s letter and was anxiously awaiting a response. On Tuesday, Mr. Collins sent a formal letter of thanks to Mr. Bennet, expressing deep gratitude. He then excitedly announced his engagement to Miss Lucas, explaining that he planned to return to Longbourn in two weeks to see her. He noted that Lady Catherine fully supported the marriage and hoped for a quick wedding, which he expected would convince Charlotte to set an early date. Mrs. Bennet was no longer pleased by Mr. Collins’s return. She complained that his visit to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge was inconvenient and annoying. She disliked having guests while she felt unwell, and she found lovers to be the most irritating company of all.

She watched me closely for a moment before asking quietly, "What do you want for them?" I replied, "Only that you do not group them with the others. They may share the same blood, but they are not the same in nature." Miss Havisham repeated her question, still studying me. I felt myself blush as I answered, "I am not clever enough to hide that I do want something. If you would provide the money to help my friend Herbert in a way he will never know, I could show you how." She rested her hands on her cane to focus on me. "Why must he not know?" she asked. "Because I began this help two years ago without his knowledge, and I do not want to be exposed. I cannot explain why I cannot finish it myself; it is someone else's secret." She turned her gaze to the fire. After a long silence, the coals shifted, and she looked back at me with renewed focus. Estella continued knitting throughout. When Miss Havisham looked at me again, she asked, "What else?" I turned to Estella, my voice shaking. "Estella, you know I love you. I have loved you for a long time." Estella looked up, her expression unchanged as her fingers kept moving. Miss Havisham glanced between us. "I should have said this sooner, but I was mistaken. I hoped Miss Havisham intended us for each other. I stayed silent while I thought you had no choice in the matter, but I must speak now." Estella shook her head without stopping her work. "I know," I said. "I have no hope that you will ever be mine, Estella."

I fail to grasp why she desired my company, yet I would surely be misled again under identical conditions. Caroline delayed her return visit until yesterday, offering no message in the interim. Her arrival was clearly joyless; she offered a brief, stiff excuse for the delay, said nothing of future meetings, and appeared so transformed that I decided to end our acquaintance upon her departure. I blame her, yet I pity her. She was mistaken to target me, as she initiated every step toward closeness. I pity her because she must realize her error, driven by concern for her brother. I need not elaborate; while we know her worry is groundless, it explains her conduct, and her devotion to him is natural. Still, I wonder at her fears, for if he cared for me, we would have met long ago. She inadvertently confirmed he knows I am in town, yet she seems to convince herself he prefers Miss Darcy. It is baffling. Were I not wary of harsh judgment, I might suspect duplicity. I shall strive to discard these troubling thoughts and focus on your affection and the kindness of our aunt and uncle. Write soon. Miss Bingley hinted he might abandon Netherfield, though she was uncertain. Let us not speak of it. I am delighted by the good news from Hunsford. Do visit them with Sir William and Maria; you will find it pleasant. Yours, etc. This letter troubled Elizabeth, though she felt relieved that Jane would no longer be deceived by the sister. Any hope regarding the brother had vanished.

I must depart, unsure of my destiny, yet I shall return here or join your group as quickly as I can. A single word or glance will suffice to determine if I visit your father’s home tonight or never again. Such a note was not easily overcome. Half an hour of quiet contemplation might have calmed her, but the mere ten minutes she had before being interrupted offered no relief. Each passing moment only increased her turmoil. It was an overwhelming joy. Before she had even begun to process her emotions, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta arrived. The urgent need to appear composed triggered an immediate internal battle, but eventually, she could maintain the facade no longer. Unable to grasp their conversation, she was forced to claim she felt unwell. Seeing her pale, they were alarmed and insisted on staying by her side, which she found unbearable. Had they simply left her alone in the room, she might have recovered, but their presence was maddening, and in her desperation, she declared she would return home. By all means, dear, Mrs. Musgrove urged, go home at once and rest so you are ready for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no physician. Charles, call for a sedan chair; she must not walk. Yet a chair was out of the question. It would destroy her chance of encountering Captain Wentworth during her walk through town, which she felt certain would happen. She vehemently refused the chair, and Mrs. Musgrove, concerned only that Anne might have suffered a physical injury, was satisfied once assured there had been no fall, allowing her to leave with the hope of seeing her recovered by evening. Desperate to ensure no detail was missed, Anne insisted, I fear it is not entirely clear. Please be so kind as to tell the other gentlemen that we expect your entire party tonight. I worry there has been some confusion, and I particularly want you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both. Oh, my dear, it is perfectly understood, I assure you.

She now wished the encounter had not occurred. Assuming he had consumed too much of Mr. Weston’s wine, she expected him to talk nonsense. Hoping to keep him composed, she prepared to discuss the weather with calm gravity. However, as soon as they passed the gate and joined the other carriage, he interrupted her, grabbed her hand, and began declaring his love. He spoke of his adoration, his fear of rejection, and his intense passion, clearly expecting her to accept him immediately. Mr. Elton, who she thought loved Harriet, was now professing his love for her. She tried to stop him, but he persisted. Though angry, she decided to remain restrained, hoping his behavior was merely the result of intoxication. She replied with a mix of seriousness and humor, hoping to address his state: "I am astonished, Mr. Elton. You forget yourself. You must mistake me for my friend. I will gladly deliver any message to Miss Smith, but please, no more of this to me." He repeated her words with a feigned, boastful amazement that forced her to respond sharply: "Mr. Elton, this is extraordinary. I can only assume you are not yourself, or you would not speak this way to me or about Harriet. Please stop, and I will try to forget this." But Mr. Elton was not too drunk to understand his own actions. He denied her accusations, dismissed his interest in Miss Smith, and continued to press her urgently for a favorable answer.

May I ask you two questions? Monks looked surprised. You may ask, but whether I answer is another matter. That makes three, Mr. Bumble joked. Is that what you expected from me? the matron asked. It is, Monks replied. What is your other question? What will you do with it? Can it be used against me? Never, Monks said. It will not be used against me either. Stay back, or your life is in danger. He pushed the table aside, pulled an iron ring, and opened a trap-door at Mr. Bumble’s feet, causing him to jump back. Look down, Monks said, lowering his lantern. Do not fear me. I could have dropped you in earlier if I wanted. The matron approached the edge, and Mr. Bumble followed out of curiosity. Below, the muddy water rushed rapidly, its sound drowning out everything else as it swirled against the rotting wooden supports of an old water-mill. If you threw a body down there, where would it be by morning? Monks asked, swinging the lantern. Twelve miles downstream and torn to pieces, Bumble replied, pulling away. Monks took the small packet from his coat, tied it to a heavy lead weight, and dropped it into the water. It sank instantly without a sound. The three looked at each other, breathing more easily. There, Monks said, closing the trap-door. If the sea ever gives up its dead, it will keep its gold and silver, along with that trash. Our meeting is over. By all means, Mr. Bumble agreed quickly. You will keep quiet about this, won't you? Monks asked with a threatening look.

In reality, as one ascends to any given altitude, the weight of the air surpassed in further climbing does not increase proportionally to the added height; rather, it decreases at a constant ratio. It is clear that no matter how high we travel, we cannot reach a point where the atmosphere ceases to exist. I maintained that it must persist, even if in a state of extreme rarefaction. Conversely, I knew that many argued for a definitive limit to the atmosphere. However, a factor often overlooked by these proponents seemed worthy of serious study. When comparing the intervals of Encke’s comet at its perihelion—while accounting for all planetary gravitational disturbances—the periods are clearly shortening. The major axis of the comet’s orbit is shrinking in a slow, steady decline. This is exactly what one would expect if the comet encountered resistance from an incredibly thin ethereal medium throughout its orbit. Such a medium would retard the comet’s velocity, weakening its centrifugal force and allowing the sun’s gravity to pull it closer with each revolution. There is no other explanation for this variation. Furthermore, the comet’s nebulosity contracts rapidly as it nears the sun and expands as it moves away. Was I not reasonable to assume, like M. Valz, that this condensation results from the compression of that same ethereal medium, which grows denser near the sun? The zodiacal light also demanded attention. This radiance, visible in the tropics and distinct from any meteoric glow, extends obliquely from the horizon, generally following the sun’s equator. It appeared to be a thin atmosphere stretching from the sun outward, at least past the orbit of Venus, and likely much further. I could not believe this medium was restricted to the comet’s path or the sun’s immediate vicinity.

Spirits of the storm, take me! Powers of destruction, open your arms and hold me forever, unless a kinder fate has decreed that after long suffering I might find my reward and feel my heart beat against another’s once more. The Tiber, nature’s own path across the continent, lay at my feet, lined with tethered boats. I planned to take a few books, supplies, and my dog, then drift down the current into the sea. I would hug the coast, sailing past the beautiful shores of the Mediterranean, Naples, and Calabria, braving Scylla and Charybdis. With nothing to lose, I would head toward Malta and the Cyclades. I would avoid Constantinople, a place belonging to a past life, and sail along Asia Minor and Syria. Passing the Nile, I would head north, leaving Carthage and Libya behind to reach the Pillars of Hercules. Eventually, I might find a watery grave, succumb to illness, or perhaps find the companion I seek. If not, I will wander forever, an old man mourning his lost youth, sailing from one bay to the next, crossing the ocean, leaving Europe for Africa, and finally mooring my boat in the fragrant islands of the Indian Ocean. These are wild dreams, yet they have dominated my thoughts since I stood atop St. Peter’s a week ago. I have chosen my boat and packed my meager supplies. I have selected a few books, primarily Homer and Shakespeare, though I can restock at any port. I do not expect things to improve, but the monotony of my current life is unbearable.

Mr. Otis felt troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to rethink, but the kindly peer remained resolute. He eventually persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the ghost’s gift. When the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s drawing-room in the spring of 1890 following her wedding, her jewels were widely admired. Virginia had earned the coronet that rewards virtuous American girls and wed her youthful suitor once he reached his majority. Their mutual affection was so delightful that everyone approved of the union, save for the Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had unsuccessfully sought the Duke for one of her seven daughters, and, oddly, Mr. Otis himself. While fond of the young Duke, Mr. Otis held theoretical objections to titles, fearing that the decadent influence of a pleasure-seeking aristocracy might erode republican values. These concerns were ultimately dismissed, and as he escorted his daughter down the aisle at St. George’s, Hanover Square, he was surely the proudest man in England. Following their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess visited Canterville Chase, walking the next afternoon to the secluded churchyard near the pines. After much debate regarding Sir Simon’s tombstone, they had settled on his initials and the library window verse. Virginia scattered roses over the grave before they wandered into the abbey’s ruined chancel. The Duchess rested on a collapsed pillar while her husband reclined at her feet, smoking and gazing at her. He soon discarded his cigarette, grasped her hand, and remarked that a wife should keep no secrets from her husband. Virginia replied that she had none, but he smiled and insisted she had never revealed what occurred while she was trapped with the ghost. She answered solemnly that she had never told anyone.

“Darn it, Tom,” I remarked, “you could at least explain. What is a bar sinister?” “I haven't a clue. But he requires one. Every nobleman has them.” That was his typical manner. If he chose not to clarify something, he simply wouldn't. You could question him for days to no avail. With the coat of arms settled, he began drafting a melancholy epitaph, insisting Jim needed one just like the others. He composed several, reading them aloud: 1. Here a captive heart burst. 2. Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and his friends, fretted away his sorrowful life. 3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit found rest after thirty-seven years of solitary confinement. 4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, the natural son of Louis XIV. Tom’s voice shook as he read, nearly overcome with emotion. Unable to choose, he decided Jim should carve them all. Jim protested that carving such a volume of text into logs with a nail would take a year, and he lacked the skill to form letters. Tom promised to outline them so Jim only had to trace the lines. Then he added, “Actually, logs won't suffice; dungeons don't have log walls. We must carve these into stone. We will bring in a rock.” Jim argued that stone was even worse, fearing the labor would keep him trapped indefinitely. Tom offered to let me assist. He then inspected our progress with the pens. The work was incredibly tedious and slow, preventing my hand sores from healing while showing little progress, so Tom declared, “I have a solution. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the inscriptions, so we can accomplish both tasks with a single stone.”

The following day, the ghost felt exhausted. The intense stress of the past month had taken its toll, leaving his nerves frayed and his reactions jumpy. After five days of seclusion, he decided to abandon the bloodstain in the library; if the Otis family did not want it, they clearly did not deserve it. They were materialistic people, incapable of appreciating symbolic phenomena. While he could not control his astral manifestations, he felt a solemn duty to haunt the corridor weekly and moan from the oriel window twice a month. Despite his wicked past, he remained conscientious regarding his supernatural obligations. For the next three Saturdays, he patrolled the hallway between midnight and three, taking care to remain undetected. He removed his boots, stepped lightly on the creaky floorboards, wore a velvet cloak, and used the Rising Sun Lubricator to silence his chains. Though initially humiliated by the need for oil, he eventually recognized its utility. Nevertheless, the family continued to harass him. They stretched strings across the hall to trip him, and once, while dressed as Black Isaac, he slipped on a butter-slide the twins had built, suffering a painful fall. Enraged by this final insult, he decided to reclaim his dignity by confronting the boys the following night as Reckless Rupert, the Headless Earl. He had not used this disguise in seventy years, not since he had terrified Lady Barbara Modish so thoroughly that she broke her engagement to the current Lord Canterville’s grandfather and eloped with Jack Castleton, swearing she would never marry into a family that tolerated such a ghastly phantom.

I don't rush him, risking a clumsy failure. Instead, I approach from the side, moving gradually so he never suspects my intent. Then, in a flash, he is on his back, completely bewildered by how it happened. That is how I handled brother Dowley. I began speaking in a relaxed, casual tone, as if merely passing time. No one could have predicted where my argument would lead. "Friends, there are many strange things about law, custom, and the evolution of human opinion. Written laws fade, but unwritten ones are eternal. Consider the unwritten law of wages: they must rise gradually over the centuries. We know current wages, and we know what they were one or two hundred years ago. That history reveals the law of progress, allowing us to estimate wages from centuries past. We do not stop there; we apply this law to the future. I can predict wages for hundreds of years to come." "What do you mean?" "In seven hundred years, wages here will be six times higher. Farmhands will earn three cents a day, and mechanics six." "I wish I could live then!" interrupted Smug the wheelwright, his eyes gleaming with greed. "And that is not all; they will receive board as well, though it will be meager. Two hundred and fifty years later, mark my words, a mechanic's wages will be twenty cents a day. This is law, not guesswork." The group gasped in awe, and Dickon the mason murmured, his eyes and hands raised in disbelief.

I recall the conditions during our nineteenth-century civil war. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars a day in gold, while in the South, he received fifty in nearly worthless Confederate currency. Since a pair of overalls cost three dollars in the North and seventy-five in the South, Northern wages held twice the purchasing power. I enjoyed seeing our new coins circulating among the local workers, including milrays, mills, cents, nickels, and some silver. Gold was only found at the goldsmith’s bank. While Marco was arguing with a shopkeeper over salt, I asked the goldsmith to change a twenty-dollar gold piece. After testing the coin and questioning me extensively about my identity and history, the banker seemed stumped. I continued to volunteer absurd details about my life—my dog, my wife’s religion, and an acquaintance with extra thumbs—until the curious man was satisfied, if slightly annoyed. He respected my wealth and refrained from being rude, though he took his frustration out on his staff. Changing the twenty clearly strained the bank’s resources, much like asking a small-town shopkeeper to break a two-thousand-dollar bill. The goldsmith likely wondered how a traveler could carry such a fortune, as he followed me to the door and watched me leave with a look of reverent admiration.

The beetle was remarkably heavy, and I could hardly blame Jupiter for his assessment of it. However, I could not fathom why Legrand agreed with him. When I finished examining the insect, Legrand spoke grandly, saying he had summoned me for my counsel and assistance in furthering the designs of Fate and the bug. I interrupted, insisting he was unwell and needed rest, suggesting I stay with him until he recovered from his fever. He told me to check his pulse, but I found no sign of fever. I urged him to go to bed, but he insisted he was as well as he could be given his current excitement, which I could relieve by helping him. He explained that he and Jupiter were heading into the mainland hills and needed a trusted companion. I asked if the beetle was connected to this expedition. When he confirmed it was, I refused to participate in such an absurd plan. He expressed regret, saying they would have to go alone. Fearing he had lost his mind, I asked how long they would be gone. He said they would leave immediately and return by sunrise. I made him promise that once this obsession was settled, he would follow my medical advice. He agreed, and we set off. With a heavy heart, I joined Legrand, Jupiter, and the dog. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, seemingly more to keep the tools away from his master than out of any desire to work.

It was after two when a sudden turn brought me to the lake, near a cove where a small skiff lay anchored. Near our home, I spotted my father and aunt strolling on the grass. I climbed into the boat, and being practiced in such things, shoved off and rowed with all my might. Clad in white with only my tartan rachan draped over me, my hair flowing loose, I propelled the craft with such surprising speed that my father later remarked I resembled a spirit rather than a girl. As I neared the bank, he caught the boat, and I sprang out into his embrace. My life truly began then. Everything shifted from monotonous gloom to vibrant joy. The happiness of being with my father surpassed my wildest hopes. We were inseparable, our conversations endless. Having spent sixteen years away in lands largely unknown to Europe—wandering through Persia, Arabia, and northern India—he had moved among the locals with rare freedom. His tales of their customs, his stories, and his vivid descriptions filled our hours when we were not discussing our own future. The sound of affection was so novel that I listened raptly as he spoke of his feelings during those long years of seeming neglect. He explained that while he initially could not bear to think of me, his grief eventually gave way to hope. Amidst deserts and cities, he imagined my small, fairy-like form. The northern breeze felt sweeter, as if it carried my spirit. He had often dreamed of returning to take me to some peaceful, fertile island. As he finally traveled home, his fervent hopes were plagued by agonizing fears; he dreaded that the sun and moon might shine upon my grave rather than my living self. Yet, he concluded, he had found his Mathilda, his comfort and his hope.

Upon returning to the raft, the king tallied his earnings at eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He also brought back a three-gallon jug of whisky discovered beneath a wagon while walking through the woods. The king remarked that, all things considered, this surpassed any day he had spent in missionary work, noting that heathens were no match for pirates when it came to exploiting a camp meeting. The duke had felt satisfied with his own efforts until the king revealed his haul. He had earned four dollars printing horse bills for farmers and collected ten dollars for newspaper advertisements by offering a discount for advance payment. He also secured three subscriptions at half a dollar each, insisting on cash instead of the usual payment of wood and onions, claiming he had slashed prices after taking over the business. He even composed a melancholy three-verse poem titled "Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart" to include in the paper for free. In total, he had collected nine dollars and a half, which he considered a fair day's labor. He then presented a handbill he had printed for our benefit, featuring an illustration of a runaway slave with a bundle on a stick and a two-hundred-dollar reward notice. The text described Jim perfectly, stating he had fled a plantation near New Orleans and was likely heading north. The duke explained that this would allow us to travel by day. If approached, we could bind Jim, hide him in the wigwam, and claim we had captured him upriver, using the handbill to explain that we were taking him back to collect the reward because we lacked the funds for steamboat passage.

Rising early and once more evading my creditors, I hurried to the bookstore to spend my remaining cash on texts regarding mechanics and practical astronomy. Back home, I studied them constantly, quickly gaining the expertise needed for my plan. Meanwhile, I worked to appease my three persistent creditors. I finally succeeded by selling half my furniture to pay part of the debt and promising the rest upon the completion of a project for which I requested their help. Being simple men, they were easily persuaded. Once settled, I secretly sold my remaining property with my wife's help and borrowed significant sums under various pretenses, ignoring how I would ever repay them. With these funds, I bought fine cambric muslin, twine, rubber varnish, a custom wicker basket, and other materials for a massive balloon. I instructed my wife on how to assemble it while I wove the netting and prepared the rigging. I also purchased a quadrant, compass, telescope, modified barometer, and two obscure astronomical tools. Under cover of night, I transported five fifty-gallon iron-bound casks, a larger one, six ten-foot tin tubes, a specific semi-metal, and twelve jugs of common acid to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam. The gas produced from these materials is unique to my work, or at least never used this way before. I would gladly reveal the secret, but it rightfully belongs to a man in Nantes, France, who shared it with me under specific conditions.

“I must remark, Sir Walter,” Mr. Shepherd stated one morning at Kellynch Hall while setting aside his paper, “that current circumstances favor us. This peace will bring many wealthy naval officers back to land, all seeking residences. It is an ideal moment to secure reliable tenants. Many have amassed great fortunes during the war. If a wealthy admiral were to present himself, Sir Walter—” “He would be a fortunate man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter answered. “Kellynch Hall would be his greatest prize, regardless of what he captured at sea; eh, Shepherd?” Mr. Shepherd laughed as expected, then continued, “I find naval gentlemen are excellent to deal with. They possess liberal views and make desirable tenants. I suggest that if rumors of your intentions spread—which is likely, as your actions are always under scrutiny, unlike my own—we should prioritize applications from wealthy naval commanders. I can arrive within two hours to handle any inquiries, sparing you the effort.” Sir Walter merely nodded. Soon, he stood and paced, remarking dryly, “I imagine few naval officers would not be astonished to inhabit a house of this caliber.” “They would certainly look about and count their blessings,” added Mrs. Clay, who was present, as a drive to Kellynch always benefited her health. “Yet I agree with my father that a sailor could prove a very suitable tenant.”

I do not understand why she wanted to be close to me, but I would likely be fooled again if the situation repeated itself. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday, and I received no word from her in the interim. When she finally arrived, it was clear she took no pleasure in the visit. She offered a brief, formal apology for the delay, said nothing about seeing me again, and acted so differently that I decided to end our acquaintance. I pity her, even if I must blame her. She was wrong to single me out, as she initiated every step toward intimacy. However, I pity her because she must realize her behavior was improper, and I am certain her anxiety regarding her brother is the cause. I need not elaborate; while we know her worry is unnecessary, it explains her actions. Given how dear he is to her, her concern is natural. Still, I wonder why she harbors such fears, as he would have sought me out long ago if he cared for me. She let slip that he knows I am in town, yet she speaks as if she wants to convince herself he prefers Miss Darcy. It is baffling. If I were not afraid of being judgmental, I would suspect her of duplicity. I will try to dismiss these painful thoughts and focus on my happiness, your affection, and the kindness of our aunt and uncle. Please write soon. Miss Bingley mentioned he might never return to Netherfield and might give up the house, though she was uncertain. We should not discuss it. I am glad you have such good news from our friends at Hunsford. Please visit them with Sir William and Maria; I am sure you will be comfortable. This letter pained Elizabeth, but she felt relieved that Jane would no longer be deceived by the sister. Any hope regarding the brother was now entirely gone.

Suddenly, Mr. Podgers dropped Lord Arthur’s right hand and grabbed his left, leaning so close that his glasses nearly touched the palm. His face turned deathly pale for a moment, but he quickly regained his composure. Looking up at Lady Windermere, he forced a smile and said, "He has the hand of a charming young man." "Of course he does," Lady Windermere replied, "but will he be a charming husband? That is what I need to know." "All charming young men are," Mr. Podgers said. "I don't think a husband should be too fascinating," Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully. "It is quite dangerous." "My dear, they are never too fascinating," Lady Windermere insisted. "But I want details. Details are the only things that matter. What will happen to Lord Arthur?" "Well, within the next few months, Lord Arthur will take a voyage—" "His honeymoon, of course!" "And he will lose a relative." "Not his sister, I hope?" Lady Jedburgh asked anxiously. "Certainly not his sister," Mr. Podgers replied with a dismissive wave. "Merely a distant relative." "I am terribly disappointed," Lady Windermere said. "I have nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives anymore; they went out of style years ago. Still, she should probably keep a black silk dress on hand; it is always appropriate for church. Now, let us go to supper. They have likely eaten everything, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so distracted by politics lately that I am never certain of his work. I wish General Boulanger would stay quiet. Duchess, you must be tired?" "Not at all, dear Gladys," the Duchess replied, waddling toward the door. "I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the palm reader is fascinating. Flora, where is my fan? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas. And my lace shawl? Thank you, Sir Thomas, you are very kind." The woman finally managed to reach the stairs, dropping her perfume bottle only twice. Throughout this, Lord Arthur Savile stood by the fireplace, gripped by a sickening sense of impending doom. He smiled sadly at his sister as she passed on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking beautiful in pink brocade and pearls, and he barely heard Lady Windermere calling him to follow. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the fear that anything could come between them filled his eyes with tears.

However, I must caution you that I intend to inform Sybil of everything. She joins me for lunch tomorrow to discuss millinery, and should Mr. Podgers discover you possess a volatile temper, a predisposition to gout, or a spouse residing in Bayswater, I shall surely disclose it all to her. Lord Arthur offered a smile and a shake of his head. I have no fear, he replied. Sybil understands me as thoroughly as I understand her. Oh, I regret hearing that. A successful marriage relies on mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical, merely experienced, which amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is eager for a palm reading. Do not mention his engagement to one of London's loveliest women, as that was reported in the Morning Post a month back. Dear Lady Windermere, the Marchioness of Jedburgh exclaimed, please let Mr. Podgers remain. He just suggested I pursue acting, and I am quite intrigued. If he told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly whisk him away. Come here at once, Mr. Podgers, and examine Lord Arthur’s hand. Well, Lady Jedburgh said, pouting as she stood, if I am forbidden from the stage, I must at least be permitted to join the audience. Certainly, we shall all be spectators, Lady Windermere agreed; now, Mr. Podgers, do tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is a particular favorite of mine. Yet, upon viewing Lord Arthur’s palm, Mr. Podgers turned noticeably pale and remained silent. A tremor appeared to seize him, and his thick, bushy brows twitched in that peculiar, vexing manner they adopted when he was perplexed. Large beads of sweat emerged on his sallow forehead like a toxic dew, and his plump fingers turned cold and damp. Lord Arthur observed these odd displays of distress, and for the first time, he felt a sense of dread. His instinct was to flee the room, but he held his ground. It was preferable to face the worst than to endure this agonizing uncertainty. I am waiting, Mr. Podgers, he stated. We are all waiting, Lady Windermere added in her brisk, impatient style, but the palmist offered no response. I suspect Arthur intends to take up acting, Lady Jedburgh remarked, and after your reprimand, Mr. Podgers is hesitant to confirm it.

So, what is the result? What impression have I made on your imagination? I felt a chill as Dupin asked me this. A madman, I said, must have committed this crime—some raving lunatic escaped from a nearby asylum. In some ways, he replied, your idea is not irrelevant. But the voices of madmen, even in their worst fits, never match the strange voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to a nation, and their language, however incoherent, always retains the structure of speech. Besides, the hair I now hold is not human. I pulled this tuft from Madame L’Espanaye’s clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it. Dupin, I said, completely unnerved, this hair is most unusual; it is not human. I have not claimed it is, he said, but before we decide, look at this sketch. It is a copy of what witnesses described as bruises and deep nail indentations on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat. You will see, my friend continued, spreading the paper, that this drawing shows a firm, fixed hold. There is no slipping. Each finger kept its grip until the victim died. Try to place your fingers into these impressions. I tried and failed. We are not giving this a fair trial, he said. The paper is flat, but a throat is cylindrical. Here is a piece of wood the size of a throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again. I did, but the difficulty was even more obvious. This, I said, is not the mark of a human hand. Read this passage from Cuvier, Dupin replied. It was a detailed anatomical account of the large, tawny orangutan of the East Indian islands. The giant size, immense strength, agility, ferocity, and imitative nature of these animals are well known. I immediately understood the horror of the murder. The description of the fingers, I said after reading, matches this drawing perfectly.

I visited several shops to buy the clothes needed for his transformation. Once finished, I headed to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but he stood up as soon as I entered and moved to the fireplace. "Now, Pip," he warned, "be careful." "I will, sir," I replied, having prepared my words. "Don't compromise yourself or anyone else," he said. "Don't tell me anything. I have no curiosity." I realized he already knew the man had arrived. "I only want to confirm what I have been told is true," I explained. Mr. Jaggers nodded. "Did you say 'told' or 'informed'?" he asked, staring at the floor. "'Told' implies a conversation, and you cannot speak to a man in New South Wales." "I will say 'informed,' Mr. Jaggers." "Good." "I have been informed by Abel Magwitch that he is my long-term benefactor." "That is the man," Jaggers confirmed. "And only he?" I asked. "Only he." "I know you are not responsible for my mistakes, but I always assumed it was Miss Havisham." "As you say, Pip," Jaggers replied coolly, biting his finger. "I am not responsible for that." "It certainly looked like it, sir," I said sadly. "There was no evidence, Pip," he replied, shaking his head. "Never judge by appearances; rely only on evidence. That is the best rule." I sighed, standing in silence for a moment. "I have verified the information, and that is all." "Since Magwitch has revealed himself," Jaggers continued, "you understand how strictly I have always stuck to the facts. You are aware of that?" "Quite, sir." "I warned Magwitch when he first wrote to me from New South Wales that he must never expect me to stray from the truth."

The area seemed a cluster of alleys, trenches, and small garden patches, suggesting a rather unexciting retreat. Wemmick’s home was a modest wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, its roof carved and painted to resemble a battery equipped with cannons. My own work, Wemmick remarked, asking if I found it attractive. I praised it warmly, noting it was perhaps the tiniest dwelling I had ever encountered, featuring odd gothic windows—mostly decorative—and a gothic entrance barely large enough for entry. That is a genuine flagpole, Wemmick explained, and I raise a real flag on Sundays. Furthermore, once I cross this bridge, I lift it—like this—to sever all access. The bridge was merely a plank spanning a four-foot-wide, two-foot-deep ditch. Yet, it was delightful to witness the genuine pride and enjoyment with which he raised and secured it. Every night at nine, Greenwich time, the cannon fires, he noted. You will see it there, and when it goes off, I believe you will call it a Stinger. The weapon sat within its own lattice-work fortress, shielded from the elements by a clever umbrella-like tarpaulin. In the back, hidden to maintain the fortification theme—since I believe in fully committing to an idea—there is a pig, along with chickens and rabbits. I build my own frames to grow cucumbers, and you can judge my salad at supper. So, if this place were ever under siege, it could hold out for quite a while regarding supplies, he added with a serious smile. He then led me to a nearby arbor, reached by such winding paths that it took some time to arrive. Our glasses were prepared there, and our punch chilled in an ornamental pond beside the bower. This circular pool, featuring a central island that might serve as our salad, included a fountain that, once a small mill was activated and a pipe uncorked, sprayed with enough force to dampen the back of one's hand.

One final word, Rose. Dearest Rose, just one! Harry pleaded, blocking her path. If my circumstances had been less fortunate—if a quiet, obscure life had been my lot, or if I were poor, ill, or weak—would you have rejected me? Or does my potential for wealth and status inspire this hesitation? Please do not force me to answer, Rose replied. The situation is hypothetical and will never occur; it is unfair to press me. If your answer matches my hopes, Harry insisted, it would brighten my solitary journey. It is no small thing to offer such comfort to one who loves you above all. In the name of my deep devotion and all I have endured for you, answer me. If your life had been different, Rose conceded, if you were only slightly above my station, and I could have been a source of comfort in a humble life rather than a hindrance in high society, I would have been spared this pain. I am happy now, but I admit I would have been happier then. Memories of girlhood dreams flooded her mind, bringing tears that offered a strange relief. I cannot help this vulnerability, but it strengthens my resolve, Rose said, offering her hand. I must go. I ask for one promise, Harry said. Within a year, I may speak to you on this matter one final time. Not to pressure me into changing my mind, for that would be futile, Rose replied with a sad smile. No, Harry said, only to hear you confirm your decision. I will offer you whatever status I have attained, and if you still refuse, I will never again attempt to sway you. Then let it be so, Rose agreed. It is merely one more moment of pain, and by then, I may be better prepared to endure it. She reached out her hand once more.

She felt a sudden urge to go to the door to check if it was raining. Why doubt her own intentions? Captain Wentworth had to be gone by now. She stood up, determined to go; she was tired of her mind constantly second-guessing itself. She would simply see if it was raining. However, she was immediately forced back by the arrival of Captain Wentworth himself, accompanied by a group of friends he must have met nearby. He seemed more surprised and flustered by the sight of her than she had ever seen; his face turned quite red. For the first time since they had met again, she felt she was the more composed of the two. She had been prepared by the last few moments, so the initial shock had passed. Still, she felt a mix of agitation, pain, and pleasure—a confusing blend of delight and misery. He spoke to her briefly, then turned away, clearly embarrassed. It was neither cold nor friendly; it was simply awkward. After a short time, he approached her again to exchange polite, meaningless questions. Anne noticed he was far less at ease than usual. They had grown accustomed to speaking with a calm indifference, but he could not manage that now. Whether time or Louisa had changed him, he was clearly unsettled. He looked healthy and spoke of Uppercross and the Musgroves, even mentioning Louisa with a brief, familiar spark in his eye, yet he remained visibly uncomfortable. It saddened, though did not surprise, Anne to see Elizabeth refuse to acknowledge him. She knew they both recognized each other and that he expected a greeting, making it painful to watch her sister turn away with cold indifference. Finally, the servant arrived to announce that Lady Dalrymple’s carriage had pulled up, much to Elizabeth’s relief.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire read only one book for pleasure: the Baronetage. It occupied his idle hours and comforted him in times of trouble.
