He admired the oldest entries and looked down upon the newer ones with pity. Most of all, he loved reading his own family history. The book always opened to the same page: ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL. Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married Elizabeth Stevenson of Gloucester in 1784. She died in 1800, leaving behind their children: Elizabeth, born 1785; Anne, born 1787; a still-born son in 1789; and Mary, born 1791. Sir Walter had personally updated this entry to include Mary’s marriage to Charles Musgrove of Uppercross in 1810 and the exact date of his wife’s death. The book then detailed the family’s history, noting their origins in Cheshire, their service as high sheriffs, their time in Parliament, and their baronetcy granted by Charles II. It concluded with the family crest and motto, followed by Sir Walter’s handwritten note naming his heir, William Walter Elliot. Vanity defined Sir Walter’s character. He had been a handsome youth and remained a striking man at fifty-four. He obsessed over his appearance and his social standing more than anyone else. He believed beauty was second only to his title, and he worshipped himself for possessing both. His looks and rank were his greatest assets, as they had helped him secure a wife far better than he deserved.

The ringmaster gave a brief address, expressing his hope for no further disruptions and offering the man a chance to ride if he could manage to stay mounted. The crowd chuckled in agreement, and the man climbed aboard. Immediately, the horse began bucking and thrashing while two circus hands struggled to restrain it. The intoxicated man clung to the animal's neck, his legs flailing wildly as the audience roared with laughter. Eventually, the horse broke free and galloped around the ring with the man swaying precariously, his limbs dangling as the spectators grew ecstatic. I felt only terror for his safety. Soon, however, he pulled himself upright, grabbed the reins, and stood tall upon the racing horse. He shed seventeen layers of clothing, tossing them into the air until he stood revealed as a slim, handsome performer in a brilliant costume. He whipped the horse into a frenzy before leaping off, bowing, and exiting to thunderous applause. The ringmaster, realizing he had been duped by his own employee’s secret prank, looked utterly miserable. I felt foolish for being deceived, yet I would not have traded places with that ringmaster for any amount of money. While there might be superior circuses elsewhere, this one satisfied me completely, and I would gladly attend it again.

P.S.—Do tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are the fashion. Lord Arthur looked so serious and unhappy over the letter that the Duchess laughed uncontrollably. My dear Arthur, she cried, I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what shall I say about the clock? I think it is a great invention, and I would like one myself. I do not think much of them, Lord Arthur said with a sad smile, and after kissing his mother, he left the room. Upstairs, he threw himself on a sofa, his eyes filling with tears. He had tried his best to commit the murder, but he had failed twice, through no fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, but it seemed as if fate itself had betrayed him. He felt overwhelmed by the uselessness of good intentions and the futility of trying to be noble. Perhaps it would be better to end the engagement. Sybil would suffer, but suffering could not ruin a nature as fine as hers. As for himself, it did not matter. There is always a war where a man can die or a cause to which he can give his life, and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no terror. He would let fate decide his future; he would no longer interfere. At seven-thirty, he dressed and went to his club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he had to dine with them. Their trivial talk and idle jokes did not interest him, and as soon as coffee arrived, he left, making up an excuse to get away. As he exited, the porter handed him a letter from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to visit the next evening to see an explosive umbrella that went off when opened. It was a new invention from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces. He had decided to stop his experiments. He wandered to the Thames Embankment and sat by the river for hours. The moon peeked through tawny clouds like a lion’s eye, and countless stars sparkled in the sky like gold dust on a purple dome. Occasionally, a barge drifted into the murky water, and railway signals shifted from green to red as trains shrieked across the bridge.

We both loved Adrian, though Perdita, still a child, could not fully appreciate his virtues or share his interests as I did. I was always by his side. His gentle, sensitive nature gave our conversations a tender, ethereal quality. He was as joyful as a singing lark, as ambitious in thought as an eagle, and as innocent as a dove. He could lighten Perdita’s seriousness and soothe my own restless, troubled spirit. I looked back on my past struggles as if they were a fading nightmare, feeling as though I had been reborn into a new body with a different way of perceiving the world. Yet, I remained the same in my strength and my deep need for connection. My masculine drive did not vanish, but it became softened and more human. Adrian taught me more than just history and philosophy; while he helped me tame my reckless spirit, he also revealed his own heart, allowing me to understand his remarkable character. The former queen of England had tried to instill ambition in her son from infancy. Recognizing his genius, she nurtured his talents to serve her own goals. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his bold courage, hoping his love of freedom would eventually turn into a desire for power. She wanted him to resent those who had forced his father to abdicate, but she failed. Instead, the stories he heard about a nation claiming its right to self-governance inspired him, and he became a republican by principle. Still, his mother did not give up. She combined his pride of birth with patience and ambition, carefully studying his personality. She used praise and criticism to influence him, and though his reactions never matched her expectations, she relied on his talents and remained confident that she would eventually win him over.

If Lydia had known her sister wanted to stop her from such a bright future, she would have been devastated. Only her mother could have truly understood her feelings. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was the only thing comforting her mother, who was saddened that her husband refused to go. The family remained unaware of the truth, and their excitement continued until the day Lydia left. Elizabeth was about to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Having spent time with him since returning home, her nerves had settled, and her old feelings for him were gone. She now found his gentle manner artificial and tiresome. Furthermore, she was annoyed that he tried to renew his flirtatious behavior toward her. She felt insulted that he assumed she would be flattered by his attention after he had ignored her for so long. On the regiment's final day in Meryton, Wickham dined at Longbourn. Elizabeth, feeling no desire to be kind, mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had spent three weeks at Rosings, then asked if he knew the Colonel. Wickham looked surprised and uneasy, but quickly recovered and smiled. He admitted he had known him well and called him a gentleman. When Elizabeth praised the Colonel, Wickham asked how long he had stayed at Rosings. After she confirmed it was nearly three weeks and that they had met daily, he noted that the Colonel’s manners differed from his cousin’s. Elizabeth replied that Mr. Darcy improved the more one knew him. Wickham looked suspicious and asked, with a forced smile, if it was his social skills that improved.

I went to the plantation and questioned the older residents. Eventually, an elderly woman mentioned she knew of Bessop’s Castle, though she insisted it was merely a tall rock rather than a building. I offered her payment, and she reluctantly agreed to lead me there. After we arrived, I dismissed her and began my inspection. The site was a cluster of cliffs, one of which was strikingly tall and appeared almost man-made. I climbed to the top, uncertain of my next move. While pondering, I noticed a narrow ledge on the eastern face, about a yard below me. It was small and projected from a niche that resembled an antique chair. I was certain this was the devil’s seat mentioned in the manuscript, and the solution to the riddle began to take shape. I realized the good glass referred to a telescope, a common term among sailors. The specific coordinates and compass heading were clearly instructions for aiming it. Excited, I rushed home to retrieve a telescope and returned to the rock. I lowered myself onto the ledge, finding I could only sit in one specific position, which confirmed my theory. I used the telescope, interpreting the degrees as an elevation above the horizon and the compass heading as the horizontal direction. After setting my compass, I aimed the glass at roughly forty-one degrees of elevation and scanned the area until I spotted a circular opening in the foliage of a distant, towering tree.

I am certain she would! The Widow Douglas’ generous welcome was an alluring prospect. Between that and Tom’s arguments, the matter was settled. They agreed to keep their plans for the evening secret. It soon struck Tom that Huck might arrive that very night to signal him, which dampened his excitement. Yet, he could not bring himself to abandon the Widow’s party. He reasoned that since no signal had appeared the previous night, it was unlikely to occur now. The guaranteed enjoyment of the evening surpassed the vague promise of treasure, so, with a boy’s typical resolve, he chose to follow his immediate desire and dismiss thoughts of the money for the rest of the day. Three miles downriver, the ferry docked at a wooded hollow. The group hurried ashore, filling the craggy woods with their shouts and laughter. After exhausting themselves with various games, the wanderers returned to camp with hearty appetites to consume their provisions. Following the meal, they rested and conversed under the shade of large oaks. Eventually, someone called out to ask who was prepared to explore the cave. Everyone agreed. They gathered bundles of candles and raced up the hill toward the A-shaped entrance. The heavy oak door stood open. Inside, the chamber was as cold as an icehouse, its limestone walls damp with moisture. Standing in the shadows, looking out at the sunlit valley, felt romantic and mysterious. However, the novelty faded quickly, and the play resumed. Whenever a candle was lit, a scuffle ensued until it was extinguished, sparking more laughter and chasing. Eventually, the group moved down the main passage, their dim lights illuminating the towering rock walls sixty feet above. This main path was narrow, and every few paces, even tighter crevices branched off, as McDougal’s cave was a sprawling maze of winding, interconnected tunnels that led to nowhere.

April 19th. This morning, to my immense relief, the moon’s surface appeared alarmingly close by nine o’clock, and my condenser pump finally signaled a shift in the air. By ten, I sensed the density rising. By eleven, the equipment required minimal effort, and at noon, I cautiously loosened the tourniquet. Feeling no ill effects, I opened the gum-elastic chamber and detached it from the car. Predictably, this hasty, risky experiment brought on spasms and a severe headache. Yet, since these breathing troubles were not life-threatening, I resolved to endure them, knowing I was rapidly descending into the moon’s thicker atmospheric layers. My descent remained dangerously swift, and it became clear that while the moon possessed an atmosphere, its density was insufficient to support the balloon’s weight, contrary to my expectations based on terrestrial gravity. My rapid fall confirmed this, likely due to the geological anomalies I previously mentioned. As I plummeted toward the surface, I frantically jettisoned my ballast, water casks, condenser, chamber, and every other item in the car. It was futile; I continued to drop at a terrifying speed. With only half a mile remaining, I discarded my coat, hat, and boots, then cut the heavy car loose. Clinging to the netting, I barely glimpsed a landscape filled with tiny dwellings before crashing into the center of a bizarre city. I landed amidst a crowd of grotesque little beings who stood like simpletons, arms akimbo, grinning foolishly and staring at me and my balloon without offering any help or speaking a word.

While these events unfolded at the workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in his old hideout—the same place Oliver had been taken from—staring into a dim, smoky fire. He held a pair of bellows on his lap, having tried to stir the flames, but he had drifted into deep thought, resting his chin on his hands while staring blankly at the rusty grate. Behind him, the Artful Dodger, Charley Bates, and Mr. Chitling played a game of whist, with the Dodger playing against the other two. The Dodger, always sharp, watched the game closely, frequently sneaking glances at Mr. Chitling’s cards to adjust his own strategy. Because it was cold, the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe in his teeth, removing it only to take sips of gin-and-water from a large pot on the table. Charley Bates was also focused, but being more excitable, he drank more of the gin and made constant jokes that were inappropriate for a serious game. The Dodger tried to lecture him on his behavior, but Charley just brushed him off with witty insults, which Mr. Chitling found hilarious. Interestingly, Chitling and his partner always lost, yet Charley found this incredibly funny, laughing loudly after every hand and claiming he had never had so much fun. That is two doubles and the rubber, Mr. Chitling said with a long face, pulling half a crown from his pocket. I have never seen anyone like you, Jack; you win everything.

What is wrong? Oliver asked. Hush, the Dodger replied. Do you see that old man at the book stall? The gentleman across the street? Oliver asked. Yes, I see him. He will do, the Dodger said. A perfect target, Charley Bates added. Oliver looked at them in surprise, but they did not let him ask questions. The two boys crept across the road and slipped behind the man. Oliver followed a few steps, then stopped in silent amazement, unsure whether to move forward or turn back. The gentleman looked very respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a green coat with a velvet collar, white trousers, and carried a bamboo cane. He had picked up a book and was reading it as intently as if he were in his own study. He seemed completely lost in the text, unaware of the street or the boys nearby. Oliver watched in horror as the Dodger reached into the man's pocket, pulled out a handkerchief, and handed it to Charley Bates. Then, both boys sprinted around the corner. Suddenly, the truth about the handkerchiefs, watches, and jewels became clear to Oliver. Terrified, he felt as though he were burning up. Confused and scared, he turned and ran as fast as he could. This all happened in a minute. As Oliver started running, the old man reached for his pocket, realized his handkerchief was gone, and turned around. Seeing the boy sprinting away, he assumed Oliver was the thief. He shouted Stop thief! at the top of his lungs and chased after him, still holding his book.

She was correct regarding the rats. Occasionally, one would poke its snout from a corner crevice. She explained that she kept objects nearby to throw at them while alone, or they would pester her incessantly. She displayed a knotted bar of lead, claiming she was usually an accurate thrower, though a recent arm injury made her uncertain of her aim. She waited for an opportunity and fired at a rat, missing significantly and crying out in pain. She then instructed me to target the next one. I was anxious to depart before the man returned, but I concealed my intent. I took the lead, and when the next rat appeared, I threw it; had the creature remained stationary, it would have been quite injured. She praised my effort, predicting I would catch the next one. She retrieved the lead and brought a skein of yarn, asking for my assistance. I held my hands up for the yarn, and she resumed discussing her domestic affairs. Suddenly, she interrupted herself to warn me to watch for rats and keep the lead in my lap. She dropped the weight, and I clamped my legs around it while she continued speaking. Moments later, she removed the yarn, stared directly at me, and asked for my true name. I stammered, confused. She pressed for my identity, asking if I were Bill, Tom, or Bob. I trembled, unsure how to respond. I begged her not to mock a poor girl, offering to leave if I were a burden. She insisted I remain, promising she would not harm or betray me. She urged me to trust her with my secret, suggesting I was merely a runaway apprentice. She assured me there was no shame in fleeing poor treatment and that she and her husband would offer their support.

What is the trouble? I said, Pap, and mam, and sis, and— Then I broke down. He said, Oh, don't take on so; we all have our troubles, and this will turn out fine. What is wrong with them? They are—are you the watchman of the boat? Yes, he said, sounding quite pleased. I am the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and head deck-hand; sometimes I am the freight and passengers too. I am not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I cannot be as generous as he is with his money, but I have told him many times that I would not trade places with him. A sailor's life is for me, and I would not live two miles out of town where nothing ever happens, not for all his money. I interrupted and said, They are in a terrible mess, and— Who is? Why, pap and mam and sis and Miss Hooker; if you would take your ferry-boat and go up there— Up where? Where are they? On the wreck. What wreck? Why, there is only one. You do not mean the Walter Scott? Yes. Good heavens! What are they doing there? Well, they did not go there on purpose. I bet they did not! There is no chance for them if they do not get off quickly! How on earth did they get into such a scrape? It was easy. Miss Hooker was visiting up at Booth's Landing. In the early evening, she started across with her servant in the horse-ferry to stay the night at a friend's house. They lost their steering-oar, drifted down about two miles, and got stuck on the wreck. The ferryman, the servant, and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker managed to grab onto the wreck. About an hour after dark, we came along in our trading boat. It was so dark we did not see the wreck until we were right on top of it, and we got stuck too. Everyone was saved except Bill Whipple—and he was such a good person! I almost wish it had been me. My goodness! That is the most incredible thing I have ever heard.

Catching sight of the creature, the Ourang-Outang bolted through the chamber door, descended the stairs, and escaped into the street via an open window. The Frenchman pursued in desperation, while the ape, clutching the razor, paused periodically to mock its chaser before darting away again. This pursuit persisted through the silent, early morning hours. While traversing an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the beast noticed a light shining from Madame L’Espanaye’s fourth-story window. It sprinted to the structure, scaled the lightning rod with startling speed, grabbed the open shutter, and swung onto the bed’s headboard in under a minute, kicking the shutter wide as it entered. The sailor felt a mix of relief and dread; he hoped to trap the animal, yet feared its potential actions inside. Driven by concern, he followed, climbing the rod with ease. Upon reaching the window level, he could only lean over to peer inside, where the sight nearly caused him to lose his grip in terror. This moment triggered the blood-curdling screams that awakened the neighborhood. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed for bed, had been organizing papers from an open iron chest in the center of the room. With their backs to the window, they likely failed to notice the intruder initially, perhaps mistaking the shutter’s movement for a gust of wind. As the sailor watched, the massive beast grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by her loose hair and brandished the razor near her face, mimicking a barber’s movements.

“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said 'anybody,' and I assumed that meant everyone.” “It does—anybody of noble birth, preferably royal.” “That seems reasonable,” the abbot said, hoping to keep the peace. “It is unlikely such a gift would be used for anyone less than those born to greatness. Our King Arthur—” “Would you like to know about him?” the enchanter interrupted. “Most gladly,” the abbot replied. Everyone was immediately filled with awe again, the foolish people. They watched the magic spells with interest and looked at me with a smug expression when the announcement came: “The king is tired from the hunt and has been sleeping soundly in his palace for two hours.” “God bless him,” the abbot said, crossing himself. “May that sleep refresh his body and soul.” “That would be nice if he were actually sleeping,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping; he is riding.” This caused trouble, as it created a conflict of authority. No one knew who to believe, though I still had some credibility. The magician, feeling insulted, said, “I have seen many prophets and magicians, but never one who could see the truth without using spells.” “You have lived in the woods too long. I use spells myself, as these brothers know, but only when it is truly necessary.” I knew how to hold my own when it came to sarcasm, and that comment made him squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and the magician replied, “They are all asleep, overcome by fatigue, just like the king.” I countered, “That is another lie. Half of them are busy with their own affairs, and the queen and the others are not sleeping; they are riding. Perhaps you can show off a bit more and tell us where the king, the queen, and their companions are going?” “They are sleeping now, as I said, but tomorrow they will ride toward the sea.” “And where will they be the day after tomorrow at sunset?” “Far to the north of Camelot, with half their journey complete.” “That is another lie, by at least a hundred and fifty miles.”

Few people would have been so persistent as she was, refusing to accept Jane’s initial refusal. She insisted on waiting rather than writing a denial, and by yesterday evening, it was decided that Jane would go. It was a complete surprise to me, as I had no inkling of it until Jane pulled Mrs. Elton aside to announce she had decided to accept Mrs. Smallridge’s offer. We all spent the evening with Mrs. Elton, as she had insisted we join them while we were walking on the hill with Mr. Knightley. Although she tried to persuade him, Mr. Knightley declined from the start and did not attend. My mother, Jane, and I went, and it was a pleasant evening, despite everyone appearing somewhat exhausted from the earlier party. Even enjoyment can be tiring, and I am not sure the others truly relished it, but I remain grateful to our hosts. I suspect Miss Fairfax had been contemplating the decision throughout the day. While the departure will be difficult for her and her friends, I hope the family she joins will be kind. Indeed, there is everything to ensure her happiness. Aside from the Sucklings and Bragges, Mrs. Elton knows of no finer or more elegant establishment. Mrs. Smallridge is delightful, the lifestyle rivals Maple Grove, and the children are charming. Jane will be treated with great kindness, and her salary is truly remarkable.

The next morning, the Otis family discussed the ghost over breakfast. The American Minister felt annoyed that his gift had been rejected. He stated that while he meant the ghost no harm, throwing pillows at him was rude, given how long the spirit had lived there. The twins laughed at this, but their father insisted that if the ghost refused the lubricant, they would have to confiscate his chains to ensure a quiet night. The rest of the week remained peaceful, save for the recurring bloodstain in the library. It was baffling, as Mr. Otis kept the room locked and the windows barred. The stain’s shifting colors—ranging from dull red to vermilion, purple, and even emerald-green—became a source of amusement and betting for the family. Only young Virginia felt distressed by the sight, nearly crying when the stain turned green. The ghost reappeared Sunday night. A loud crash in the hall drew the family downstairs, where they found a suit of armor collapsed on the floor and the ghost sitting in a chair, clutching his knees in pain. The twins fired their pea-shooters with practiced precision, while the Minister leveled his revolver and ordered the spirit to raise his hands. With a furious shriek, the ghost vanished through them like mist, blowing out Washington’s candle and plunging the hall into darkness.

The surrounding oaks housed a colony of nightingales. I am there now, with Idris by my side in the prime of youth. Remember, I am twenty-two, and she has seen barely seventeen summers. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian was busy in his boat, dangerously plucking a branch from a submerged oak. I wondered if he was tired of life to risk such a stunt. He secured his prize and navigated the flood, but the current carried him away. He had to land far downstream and walk back to us. Idris watched him land and waved, relieved, suggesting we wait for him. We were alone as the sun set and the nightingales began to sing. The evening star shone brightly in the fading western light. Idris gazed at it, remarking on its flickering glow, which she felt mirrored the wavering, fearful, and loving nature of our own lives. I begged her not to look at distant stars but to listen to me. I had been silent for so long, desperate to offer her my entire soul. I told her that my love for her was as constant as the star’s light, and it would last until my end. The joy of that moment is mine alone to keep. I still feel her against me and recall the intensity of that first kiss. We walked in silence to meet Adrian. Later, after he took his sister home, I asked him to return. Walking along the moonlit paths, I confessed my feelings and hopes to him. He looked troubled for a moment and said he should have seen this coming, noting the conflict that would surely follow.

I bored a hole into the keg above the pitcher and inserted a tapered wooden plug. After some testing, I adjusted the fit so that water would drip into the pitcher, filling it exactly in one hour. This was easily verified by checking the water level over time. My bed was positioned so that my head lay directly beneath the pitcher’s spout. Once the pitcher filled, the overflow would spill from the spout, falling four feet onto my face and waking me from even the deepest sleep. By eleven, everything was ready, and I went to bed confident in my device. It worked perfectly; every hour, my reliable alarm woke me. I would empty the pitcher back into the keg and return to sleep. These interruptions were less bothersome than expected, and when I finally woke for the day at seven, the sun was already high. April 3rd. The balloon had reached a massive altitude, and the earth’s curve was clearly visible. Below, a cluster of black specks in the ocean appeared to be islands. To the north, a brilliant white line on the horizon suggested the ice of the Polar Sea. I was eager to travel further north, perhaps even directly over the Pole, though I regretted that my extreme height would hinder a detailed survey.

It is strange, yet everyone who vanishes is supposedly spotted in San Francisco. It must be a charming city, offering all the allure of the afterlife. What do you suppose became of Basil? Dorian asked, lifting his Burgundy to the light, surprised at his own calm. I have no clue. If Basil prefers to vanish, that is his affair. If he is dead, I prefer not to dwell on it. Death is the sole thing that frightens me. I loathe it. Why? the younger man asked tiredly. Because, Lord Henry replied, sniffing his vinaigrette box, one can endure anything today except that. Death and vulgarity are the only nineteenth-century realities one cannot rationalize. Let us take coffee in the music-room. You must play Chopin. The man my wife eloped with played it beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was quite fond of her. The house feels empty. Marriage is merely a habit, a poor one, yet one misses even the worst habits. Perhaps one misses them most, as they are integral to one's character. Dorian rose silently, moved to the next room, and let his fingers wander over the piano keys. Once coffee arrived, he paused and asked, Harry, have you considered that Basil might have been murdered? Lord Henry yawned. Basil was well-liked and carried a Waterbury watch. Why murder him? He lacked the wit to make enemies. He possessed artistic genius, certainly, but one can paint like Velasquez and remain utterly tedious. Basil was dull. He only intrigued me once, when he confessed his intense adoration for you and that you were the driving force of his art. I was quite fond of Basil, Dorian said, his voice tinged with sorrow. But do people not claim he was murdered? Some newspapers suggest it, though it seems unlikely. I know Paris has its dark corners, but Basil lacked the curiosity to frequent them. That was his primary flaw. What would you say, Harry, if I confessed to murdering Basil? the younger man asked.

Emma did not regret her decision to visit the Coles. The next day, she enjoyed reflecting on the event, feeling that the popularity she gained was well worth the loss of her usual privacy. She had certainly delighted the Coles, who were good people, and she was sure her presence would be remembered for some time. Perfect happiness is rare, however, and two things troubled her. She worried that she had acted wrongly by sharing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings with Frank Churchill. It was a lapse in judgment, yet his willingness to listen to her theories was so flattering that she found it hard to regret speaking. Her second regret was clearer: she was genuinely unhappy that her own musical skills were inferior to Jane’s. She felt ashamed of her lack of practice as a child, so she sat down and played for an hour and a half. Harriet interrupted her, and if praise could have helped, Harriet would have comforted her. Oh, if I could play like you and Miss Fairfax, Harriet said. Do not compare us, Emma replied. My playing is like a lamp, while hers is like sunshine. Oh, I think you play just as well as she does, Harriet insisted. Everyone last night said how well you played. Those who truly understand music know the difference, Emma said. My playing is merely good enough to be praised, but Jane’s is far superior. Harriet disagreed, noting that Mr. Cole and Frank Churchill had both praised Emma’s taste, and that Frank valued taste over technical skill. Emma reminded her that Jane possessed both. Harriet remained unconvinced, arguing that Jane’s skill was only expected since she would eventually have to teach for a living.

Spirits of the tempest, take me! Forces of ruin, embrace me eternally, unless a gentler fate has ordained that after long suffering I might find my recompense and once more feel my pulse quicken beside a kindred soul. The Tiber, nature’s own path across the continent, lay before me, lined with moored vessels. I resolved to board one with my books, supplies, and dog, drifting down the river to the sea. I would sail the Mediterranean, skirting the lovely coasts of Naples and Calabria, braving Scylla and Charybdis, and venturing toward Malta and the Cyclades. I would bypass Constantinople, a place belonging to a past life, and navigate past Asia Minor, Syria, and the Nile, eventually reaching the pillars of Hercules. Whether I perish in the ocean depths, succumb to illness, or find the companion I seek, I will continue. If I remain alone, I will sail on, aged and weary, forever navigating new bays and promontories, leaving Europe behind to traverse the African coast and the Cape, until I finally anchor in some remote, fragrant island of the Indian Ocean. These are frantic visions, yet they have dominated my thoughts since I stood atop St. Peter’s a week ago. I have secured my boat, gathered my provisions, and chosen my books—Homer and Shakespeare—though I can replenish my library at any port. I do not anticipate improvement, but I can no longer endure the monotony of my current existence.

Not everyone would have been so persistent as she was, refusing to accept Jane’s initial refusal. She flatly declared she would not write a rejection yesterday as Jane requested, insisting on waiting. Sure enough, by last night, it was decided that Jane would go. It was a complete surprise to me; I had no idea. Jane pulled Mrs. Elton aside and announced that, after considering the benefits of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had decided to accept. I knew nothing of it until it was finalized. You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton? Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton insisted we come. It was arranged on the hill while we were walking with Mr. Knightley. She told us we all had to join her. Mr. Knightley was there too? No, he declined from the start. Even though Mrs. Elton claimed she wouldn't let him off the hook, he didn't show. My mother, Jane, and I were there, and we had a pleasant evening. Kind friends are always agreeable, Miss Woodhouse, though everyone seemed exhausted after the morning outing. Even pleasure is tiring, and I cannot say anyone seemed to enjoy it much. Still, I will always consider it a pleasant party and feel grateful to the friends who included me. I suppose Miss Fairfax had been making up her mind throughout the day? I expect so. Whenever the time comes, it will be difficult for her and her friends, but I hope her position has every possible advantage regarding the family's character and manners. Thank you, Miss Woodhouse. Indeed, everything is in place to make her happy. Aside from the Sucklings and Bragges, there is no nursery establishment as liberal or elegant in all of Mrs. Elton’s circle. Mrs. Smallridge is a delightful woman, and their lifestyle is nearly equal to Maple Grove. As for the children, they are the most elegant, sweet children anywhere, aside from the little Sucklings and Bragges. Jane will be treated with such regard and kindness; it will be a life of pure pleasure. And her salary! I really cannot venture to mention her salary to you, Miss Woodhouse.

In that harsh attack on Chantilly published in yesterday’s Musée, the writer made shameful comments about the cobbler changing his name when he became an actor. He also quoted a Latin line we have discussed before: Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum. I had explained that this line refers to Orion, once spelled Urion, and I knew you remembered it. It was obvious you would connect Orion with Chantilly. I saw by your smile that you did, and that you were thinking of the poor cobbler’s death. You had been walking with a stoop, but then you stood up straight, and I knew you were considering Chantilly’s small stature. I interrupted your thoughts to say that since he was such a tiny man, he would be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés. Shortly after, we were reading the evening Gazette des Tribunaux when a report caught our attention. Extraordinary Murders. At three this morning, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were woken by terrifying screams from the fourth floor of a house on the Rue Morgue, where Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Camille, lived. After failing to enter normally, neighbors and two police officers broke down the door with a crowbar. The screaming had stopped, but as they climbed the stairs, they heard two rough voices arguing loudly. By the second landing, those sounds also ceased, and the house went silent. The group searched the rooms and forced open a locked back bedroom on the fourth floor. The scene inside shocked everyone. The room was in total chaos, with furniture smashed and scattered. The bed had been stripped and thrown into the middle of the floor, and a blood-stained razor lay on a chair.

Dorian, these matters must concern you. Every gentleman cares for his reputation. You surely do not wish to be branded as base or corrupt. While you possess status and fortune, those things are not absolute. I do not credit these rumors, especially when I look at you. Sin inevitably marks a man’s countenance; it is impossible to hide. There is no such thing as a secret vice. If a man is corrupt, it manifests in his mouth, his eyelids, or even his hands. Last year, a man I will not name sought a portrait. I refused him despite his generous offer because I detested the shape of his fingers. I later learned my instincts were correct; his life is truly wretched. Yet, looking at your innocent, youthful face, I cannot believe these accusations. Still, I see you rarely, and you avoid my studio. When I am apart from you and hear these vile whispers, I am at a loss. Why does the Duke of Berwick exit a club room upon your arrival? Why do so many London gentlemen shun you? You were once close with Lord Staveley. When your name arose at dinner last week regarding your miniatures, he sneered, claiming that while you possess artistic taste, you are unfit for the company of virtuous women. When I demanded an explanation, he spoke plainly before everyone. It was appalling. Why is your companionship so ruinous to young men? Consider the poor boy in the Guards who took his own life, or Sir Henry Ashton, who fled England in disgrace.

I went to the plantation and questioned the older workers. Finally, an elderly woman mentioned she knew of Bessop’s Castle, though she insisted it was actually a tall rock rather than a building. I offered to pay her to lead me there, and she eventually agreed. We found the site easily, and after she left, I examined the area. The 'castle' was a collection of cliffs, one of which stood out for its height and unnatural shape. I climbed to the top, unsure of my next move. While thinking, I noticed a narrow ledge on the eastern side, just below where I stood. It was small and shaped like an old-fashioned chair. I was certain this was the 'devil’s seat' mentioned in the manuscript, and I felt I had finally solved the mystery. I realized the 'good glass' referred to a telescope, a common term among sailors. The specific coordinates and directions were clearly instructions for aiming it. Excited, I hurried home to get my telescope and returned to the rock. I lowered myself onto the ledge and found I could only sit in one specific position, which confirmed my theory. I used my pocket compass to face northeast by north and adjusted the telescope to an elevation of forty-one degrees. As I scanned the area, my gaze was caught by a circular opening in the leaves of a distant, towering tree.

Unless you refer to Miss Havisham as a man. And I expect even you would hesitate to claim that. Miss Havisham, in town? Joe asked. Is there any Miss Havisham elsewhere? my sister replied. She desires this boy to visit and play there. Naturally he is going. And he had best play there, my sister added, gesturing for me to appear cheerful and lively, or I shall punish him. I had heard of Miss Havisham in town—everyone for miles around knew of her—as a wealthy, stern woman residing in a vast, gloomy house fortified against thieves, living in total isolation. Well, I never! Joe exclaimed, amazed. I wonder how she came to know Pip! Fool! my sister shouted. Who claimed she knew him? Some person, Joe suggested mildly, mentioned she wanted him to go and play there. Could she not ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to play there? Is it not possible that Uncle Pumblechook is her tenant, and occasionally visits to pay his rent? Could she not then inquire if he knew of a boy? And could Uncle Pumblechook, always thoughtful of us—though you might not realize it, Joseph, she said with deep reproach, as if he were a heartless nephew—then suggest this boy, who stands here prancing—which I certainly was not—that I have always been a devoted slave to? Excellent! Uncle Pumblechook cried. Well stated! Cleverly put! Now Joseph, you understand the situation. No, Joseph, my sister continued reproachfully, while Joe wiped his nose apologetically, you do not yet understand the situation. You may think you do, but you do not, Joseph. You are unaware that Uncle Pumblechook, sensing that this boy’s fortune might be made by visiting Miss Havisham, has offered to drive him to town tonight in his cart, keep him overnight, and escort him to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. Good heavens! my sister cried, tossing aside her bonnet in frustration, here I am speaking to simpletons, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the horse catches a chill outside, and the boy is covered in soot from head to toe!

Seeing the creature, the orangutan bolted through the chamber door, down the stairs, and out an open window into the street. The Frenchman followed in despair, while the ape, razor still gripped in its hand, paused occasionally to gesture at its pursuer before darting away again. The chase continued through the silent, early morning streets. Passing an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the beast noticed a light shining from an open fourth-story window in Madame L’Espanaye’s home. It rushed to the building, scaled the lightning rod with incredible speed, grabbed the open shutter, and swung itself onto the bed’s headboard in less than a minute, kicking the shutter further open as it entered. The sailor felt both relief and dread. He hoped to trap the animal, as it could only escape by descending the rod, yet he feared what it might do inside. Driven by this anxiety, he followed. Though a sailor could easily climb the rod, he could only reach far enough to peer into the room once he neared the window. What he saw nearly caused him to fall in terror, triggering the horrific screams that woke the neighborhood. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed for bed, had been organizing papers from an open iron chest in the center of the room. With their backs to the window, they likely did not notice the beast at first, assuming the shutter had been blown by the wind. As the sailor watched, the massive animal grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by her loose hair and brandished the razor near her face, mimicking the motions of a barber.

Three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with fashionable guests for the wedding. The Dean of Chichester performed an impressive ceremony, and everyone remarked that the bride and groom were a stunning couple. More importantly, they were truly happy. Lord Arthur never regretted his sacrifices for Sybil, and she offered him her complete devotion and love. Reality did not destroy their romance; they remained forever young at heart. Years later, with two children, they hosted Lady Windermere at Alton Priory, the Duke’s wedding gift. While sitting under a lime tree watching the children play, Lady Windermere asked Sybil if she was happy. Sybil confirmed she was and asked if Lady Windermere felt the same. Lady Windermere admitted she lacked time for happiness, noting that she grew bored with people once she knew them well. When asked if her famous guests satisfied her, she complained that they were only interesting for a short time and often behaved poorly. She mentioned the fraud Mr. Podgers, noting that while she forgave his financial requests, his romantic advances ruined palmistry for her; she now preferred telepathy. Sybil warned her not to criticize palmistry, as Arthur took it very seriously. When Lady Windermere questioned if he truly believed in it, Sybil directed her to Arthur, who was approaching with their children and a bouquet of roses. Lady Windermere asked him directly if he believed in palmistry. Arthur smiled and confirmed he did, explaining that he owed all his happiness to it.

When Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, purchased Canterville Chase, everyone warned him he was making a mistake, as the property was undoubtedly haunted. Lord Canterville, a man of strict integrity, felt obligated to mention this when they discussed the sale. We have not lived there ourselves, Lord Canterville explained, since my grandaunt, the Duchess of Bolton, suffered a permanent shock when two skeleton hands appeared on her shoulders while she dressed for dinner. I must inform you that the ghost has been seen by my relatives and the local rector. After the Duchess's incident, our younger servants refused to stay, and my wife often lost sleep due to strange noises in the halls and library. Mr. Otis replied that he would take the furniture and the ghost as they were. I come from a modern country where money buys everything, he said. If ghosts existed in Europe, we would have brought one home for a museum or a traveling show by now. Lord Canterville smiled and noted that the ghost had been seen since 1584 and always appeared before a family death. The family doctor does the same, Mr. Otis countered. Ghosts do not exist, and I doubt the laws of nature change for the British aristocracy. You are certainly very direct in America, Lord Canterville said, not fully grasping the remark. If you do not mind a ghost, that is fine, but remember I warned you. Weeks later, the sale was finalized, and the Otis family moved to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, formerly a famous New York beauty, was now a handsome, middle-aged woman with striking features.

The Attorney-General told the jury that the defendant, despite his youth, was a veteran of treasonous activities punishable by death. He argued that this collaboration with the enemy was not a recent development, but part of a long-standing pattern of suspicious travel between France and England. Had these crimes been successful, they might have remained hidden, but Providence led an irreproachable patriot to uncover the plot and report it to the government. This witness, once the defendant’s friend, had courageously chosen to sacrifice their bond for the sake of the nation. While Britain did not erect statues to such heroes as the ancients did, the witness remained a shining example of virtue. This patriotism had even inspired the defendant’s own servant to search his master’s belongings and seize incriminating documents. The Attorney-General anticipated criticism of this servant, yet he personally held the man in higher regard than his own family, urging the jury to do the same. He concluded that the testimony of these two witnesses, supported by the recovered documents, would prove the defendant had systematically provided the enemy with sensitive intelligence regarding British military forces.

With no work to occupy him, he rhythmically cupped his knuckles into his palms, alternating hands and stroking his beard in a continuous, mechanical cycle. Pulling him from the mental drift that followed his speech felt like reviving someone from a faint or trying to extract a final confession from a dying man. "Did you ask for my name?" "I certainly did." "One Hundred and Five, North Tower." "Is that all?" "One Hundred and Five, North Tower." With a sound that was neither a sigh nor a groan, he returned to his labor until the silence was broken again. "You are not a shoemaker by trade?" Mr. Lorry asked, watching him closely. The man’s hollow eyes darted to Defarge for help, but finding none, they returned to Lorry. "I am not a shoemaker by trade? No. I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to--" He drifted off again, his hands continuing their repetitive motion. Eventually, his gaze returned to Lorry, and he started, speaking as if waking from a dream. "I asked permission to teach myself, and after a long time, I finally got it. I have made shoes ever since." As he reached for his work, Lorry persisted. "Monsieur Manette, do you remember me?" The shoe fell, and he stared intently at Lorry. "Monsieur Manette," Lorry said, touching Defarge’s arm, "do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does no memory of an old banker, a past business, or a former servant stir in your mind?" As the long-time prisoner stared between them, faint traces of a once-sharp intellect flickered across his forehead, struggling through the fog of his mind. They clouded over, faded, and vanished, but for a moment, they had been there.

Spirits of the storm, take me! Powers of destruction, open your arms and hold me forever, unless a kinder fate has planned a different end where I might eventually find peace and feel my heart beat alongside another. The Tiber River, nature’s own path across the land, lay at my feet, lined with tethered boats. I planned to take a few books, some supplies, and my dog, then float down the river to the sea. From there, I would sail along the beautiful Mediterranean coast, passing Naples and Calabria, and braving the dangers of Scylla and Charybdis. With nothing left to lose, I would head toward Malta and the Cyclades. I would avoid Constantinople, as its familiar sights belong to a life I have left behind. I would sail past Asia Minor, Syria, and the Nile, eventually reaching the Pillars of Hercules. Before this long journey ends, I might find the peace of the ocean depths, or perhaps succumb to illness while drifting alone. I might even find the companion I seek. If not, I will wander forever, growing old and grey while my youth remains buried with those I loved. I will keep sailing, following the wind from one bay to the next, leaving Europe behind to travel along the African coast and eventually moor my boat in the fragrant islands of the Indian Ocean. These are wild dreams, but they have consumed my imagination since I stood on St. Peter’s a week ago. I have chosen my boat, packed my supplies, and selected a few books, primarily Homer and Shakespeare. The world’s libraries are open to me, so I can always restock. I do not expect things to improve, but I can no longer endure the monotony of my current life.

Emma found no reason to change her negative opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her initial assessment proved accurate; every subsequent meeting confirmed that the woman was self-important, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and rude. While Mrs. Elton possessed some beauty and minor talents, she lacked the judgment to realize she was not the sophisticated expert she imagined herself to be. She arrived in the country convinced she was there to enlighten the locals, believing her own social standing far surpassed that of any woman in Highbury. Mr. Elton appeared not only happy with his wife but genuinely proud of her. He acted as though he had brought a woman to Highbury who eclipsed even Emma Woodhouse. Most of their new acquaintances, influenced by Miss Bates’s enthusiasm or simply inclined to be agreeable, accepted Mrs. Elton at her own valuation. Consequently, her reputation for excellence spread, while Emma maintained a polite facade, describing her only as pleasant and well-dressed. Over time, Mrs. Elton’s attitude toward Emma soured. Offended by Emma’s lack of interest in a close friendship, she grew cold and distant. While this distance was a relief, the underlying malice only deepened Emma’s dislike. Furthermore, the Eltons treated Harriet with open sneering and neglect. Emma hoped this would help Harriet move on, but the behavior reflected poorly on the couple. It was clear they had discussed Harriet’s past feelings for Mr. Elton, likely painting Emma in the worst possible light to soothe his ego. As a result, they shared a mutual dislike for Emma, often bonding over their criticism of her. Unable to show their hostility toward Emma directly, they directed their contempt at Harriet. Meanwhile, Mrs. Elton took an immediate, intense interest in Jane Fairfax. She was not content with mere admiration; she insisted on inserting herself into Jane’s life as a patroness. Long before Emma lost favor with her, she had already been subjected to Mrs. Elton’s unsolicited plans to befriend and assist Jane.

With no labor to occupy him, he rested his right knuckles in his left palm, then swapped them, then stroked his beard, repeating these motions rhythmically without pause. Bringing him back from the aimless wandering that followed his speech felt like rousing someone from a faint or trying to catch the final words of a dying soul. Did you inquire about my name? I certainly did. One Hundred and Five, North Tower. Is that everything? One Hundred and Five, North Tower. With a sound that was neither sigh nor groan, he returned to his work until the quiet was interrupted once more. You are not a shoemaker by profession? Mr. Lorry asked, watching him closely. His hollow eyes shifted to Defarge for assistance, but finding none, they returned to the questioner after glancing at the floor. I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not. I learned it here. I taught myself. I requested permission to... He drifted off, continuing his repetitive hand motions for several minutes. Eventually, his gaze returned to the face before him, and he started, speaking like someone just roused from sleep about a topic from the previous night. I asked for permission to teach myself, which I finally obtained after much struggle, and I have produced shoes ever since. As he reached for the shoe that had been removed, Mr. Lorry asked, while maintaining steady eye contact: Monsieur Manette, do you recall anything of me? The shoe fell, and he stared intently at the man. Monsieur Manette, Mr. Lorry said, touching Defarge’s arm, do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does no memory of an old banker, a past business, a former servant, or a bygone time stir within you, Monsieur Manette? As the long-term prisoner stared alternately at Mr. Lorry and Defarge, faint traces of a once-sharp intellect emerged briefly on his forehead through the dark haze that clouded him. They were obscured again, fading away, but for a moment, they had been visible.

I considered feigning death; my satisfied heirs would claim my fortune, granting me my liberty. Yet, the scheme required careful planning; I needed to ensure I was not left penniless. Alas, what wretched measures I was forced to adopt! Otherwise, a lifetime of deceit awaited me. Whenever remorse for my planned deception made me hesitate, the arrival of an aunt or cousin would solidify my resolve by reminding me that death is inevitable. They would claim my father had lost his senses since my mother passed, calling him insane and suggesting I was lucky he had not killed me during one of his episodes. They spoke with delicate hints, whispering in dark, soft tones with sympathetic expressions, while I listened calmly, my nerves fraying, unable to challenge their blasphemy. What a delightful life, entirely devoid of honesty! I wore a dove’s expression while harboring a fox’s heart, feeling only the shame of my lies rather than any sense of righteous innocence. Having once worn the bright cloak of sincerity, I now had to adopt a multicolored one; it felt awkward initially, but practice allowed me to drape it elegantly. I might stain my soul with falsehood until its true nature was hidden. Oh, beloved father, accept your daughter’s pure heart; let me join you untainted, or you will not recognize me. Just as grief transformed Constance, deceit would alter me until, in heaven, you would fail to know me. To remain happy now and in our future reunion, I must escape this mocking existence. Only in solitude can I be myself and belong to you. Even now, I look back with loathing upon the schemes and struggles I endured to effect my departure. I could detail the methods I employed to secure a modest living and convince others of my death, but I choose not to.

I met the strange man I am about to describe at Warwick Castle. He drew me in with his genuine simplicity, his incredible knowledge of antique armor, and the ease of his company, as he did all the talking. We drifted to the back of the tour group, and he immediately began sharing fascinating observations. As he spoke in a soft, flowing manner, he seemed to slip out of the present and into a distant, forgotten age. He cast such a spell that I felt as if I were walking among the ghosts and dust of antiquity, conversing with a relic of that time. He spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors, Sir Launcelot, Sir Galahad, and the other knights of the Round Table as if they were his own neighbors or rivals. As he continued, he appeared to grow impossibly old, faded, and musty. He turned to me and asked, as casually as if discussing the weather, if I knew about the transposition of epochs and bodies. I admitted I had not, but he was so indifferent that he did not even notice my reply. A moment of silence followed, broken by the tour guide’s droning voice: "Sixth-century hauberk, from the time of King Arthur and the Round Table; once belonging to Sir Sagramor le Desirous. Note the hole in the left breast, which cannot be explained; it is thought to have been made by a bullet, perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers." My acquaintance offered a smile—not a modern one, but something from centuries past—and muttered to himself, "I know it well, I saw it happen." After a pause, he added, "I did it myself." By the time I recovered from the shock of his remark, he had vanished. That evening, I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, lost in dreams of the past while rain lashed the windows and wind howled outside. I occasionally read from Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, savoring its tales of wonder and adventure, breathing in the scent of its ancient names, and dreaming once more.

Eventually, the Westminster tower clock struck twelve, the deep resonance making the night seem to shudder. The railway lights extinguished, leaving only one lamp glowing like a ruby on a mast, while the city's roar faded. At two, he rose and walked toward Blackfriars. Everything appeared surreal, like a strange dream. The houses across the river seemed constructed of darkness, as if silver and shadow had remade the world. St. Paul’s dome loomed like a bubble in the dusky air. Near Cleopatra’s Needle, he spotted a man leaning over the parapet. As he approached, the man looked up, the gaslight illuminating his face. It was Mr. Podgers, the palmist. His flabby face, gold-rimmed glasses, weak smile, and sensual mouth were unmistakable. Lord Arthur paused, a sudden idea striking him, and crept up behind. He grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and threw him into the Thames. A coarse oath and a heavy splash followed, then silence. Lord Arthur peered over, seeing only a top hat spinning in the moonlit water before it sank. He briefly imagined he saw the bulky figure swimming toward the bridge stairs, feeling a sickening sense of failure, but it was merely a reflection. When the moon emerged from the clouds, the vision vanished. Believing he had fulfilled his destiny, he sighed with relief, whispering Sybil’s name. A voice suddenly asked if he had dropped something. He turned to see a policeman with a lantern. He smiled, replied that it was nothing important, hailed a passing cab, and headed to Belgrave Square. For the next few days, he fluctuated between hope and fear. Sometimes he expected Mr. Podgers to walk in; other times, he felt Fate could not be so cruel. He visited the palmist’s West Moon Street address twice but could not bring himself to ring the bell, torn between a longing for certainty and a fear of it. Finally, the news arrived. He was in the club smoking room, listening wearily to Surbiton discuss a song from the Gaiety, when a waiter entered with the evening papers.

Rose faced a difficult dilemma. She desperately wanted to uncover the mystery of Oliver’s past, yet she felt bound to protect the secret shared by the troubled woman she had met. That woman’s plea had moved Rose deeply, and she genuinely wanted to help the outcast find redemption. They planned to stay in London for only three more days before leaving for the coast. It was already midnight of the first day, leaving her little time to act without raising suspicion. Mr. Losberne was staying with them, but Rose knew his impulsive temper. She feared he would react with such fury that he would ruin any chance of helping the girl. For the same reason, she could not tell Mrs. Maylie, who would immediately consult the doctor. Legal help seemed equally impossible. She briefly considered asking Harry for advice, but the memory of their last goodbye stopped her. She worried that calling him back would be unfair, especially if he had finally moved on and found happiness without her. Troubled by these thoughts, Rose spent a restless night. By the next day, she reached a desperate decision: she would contact Harry. She worried about the pain of seeing him again, but hoped he might simply write back or visit without forcing a personal encounter. As she began to write, she set down her pen and turned away, unable to let even the paper witness her tears.

Well, you rascal, the old lady exclaimed as he entered, why have you stayed away so long? My dear Lady Clem, I am never free, Lord Arthur replied with a smile. I suppose you mean you spend your days with Miss Sybil Merton, shopping and flirting? I cannot fathom why people make such a spectacle of marriage. In my time, we never acted so affectionate in public or private. I assure you I have not seen Sybil in twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she is entirely occupied by her dressmakers. Naturally; that is the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I am surprised you men do not take warning. People once did foolish things for me, and now I am just a rheumatic creature with a wig and a foul temper. If not for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me the most scandalous French novels, I could not endure the day. Doctors are useless, except for collecting fees; they cannot even cure my heartburn. I have brought you a remedy for that, Lady Clem, Lord Arthur said seriously. It is a remarkable invention from America. I do not think I like American inventions, Arthur. I am certain I do not. I read some American novels recently, and they were utter nonsense. Oh, but there is no nonsense in this, Lady Clem! It is a perfect cure. You must promise to try it. Lord Arthur pulled a small box from his pocket and handed it to her. The box is charming, Arthur. Is it truly a gift? That is very sweet. And is this the wonderful medicine? It looks like a candy. I will take it immediately. Good heavens, Lady Clem! Lord Arthur cried, grabbing her hand, you must not do that. It is a homeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it could cause you great harm. Wait until you have an attack, then take it. You will be amazed by the result. I would like to take it now, Lady Clementina said, holding the transparent capsule with its floating bubble of liquid aconitine up to the light. I am sure it is delicious. The truth is, although I despise doctors, I love medicine. However, I will save it for my next attack. And when will that be? Lord Arthur asked eagerly.

You should adopt my philosophy. Only think of the past when it brings you joy. I cannot credit you with such a philosophy. Your memories must be so free of regret that your contentment comes from ignorance, not wisdom. It is not so for me. Painful memories intrude, and they should. I have been selfish my entire life. As a child, I knew what was right, but I was never taught to control my temper. I was raised with good principles but allowed to follow them with pride and arrogance. As an only son, I was spoiled by my parents. They encouraged me to be selfish, to care only for my own family, and to look down on everyone else. I remained that way until I was twenty-eight. I would still be that man if not for you, dearest Elizabeth. You taught me a difficult but necessary lesson. You humbled me. I approached you expecting to be welcomed, but you showed me that I was not worthy of a woman like you. Had you convinced yourself that I would accept you? I had. What must you think of my vanity? I truly believed you were waiting for my proposal. My behavior must have been at fault, though I never meant to mislead you. My high spirits often led me astray. You must have hated me after that evening. Hate you? I was angry at first, but my anger soon turned toward myself. I am afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming? No, I felt only surprise. Your surprise could not be greater than mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special treatment, and I expected nothing more than what I was owed. My goal then, Darcy replied, was to show you through my kindness that I was not petty enough to hold a grudge. I hoped to earn your forgiveness and improve your opinion of me by showing that I had taken your criticisms to heart.

When we reached the tree, he asked, Jupiter, come here. Was the skull nailed to the branch facing out or toward the wood? The face was out, master, so the crows could easily reach the eyes. Legrand touched Jupiter’s eyes and asked, Was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle? It was this eye, master, the left one, just as you told me, Jupiter said, pointing to his own right eye. That will do, we must try again. I began to see a method in my friend’s madness as he moved the peg three inches to the west. He measured fifty feet from the trunk in a straight line, marking a spot several yards from our previous excavation. We drew a larger circle and began digging again. Despite my exhaustion, I felt a strange, growing excitement. Legrand’s deliberate, thoughtful manner had affected me. I dug eagerly, finding myself genuinely expecting to uncover the treasure that had obsessed my companion. After an hour and a half, the dog began to howl violently. This time his distress was serious. When Jupiter tried to restrain him, the dog resisted, leaped into the hole, and frantically clawed at the dirt. Within seconds, he unearthed two human skeletons mixed with metal buttons and remnants of decayed wool. A few more spade strokes revealed a large Spanish knife, followed by several loose gold and silver coins.

Four days following these strange events, a funeral procession departed Canterville Chase around eleven at night. Eight black horses, adorned with nodding ostrich plumes, pulled the hearse, while the leaden casket rested beneath a purple pall embroidered with the golden Canterville crest. Servants carrying torches flanked the carriages, creating a striking scene. Lord Canterville, having traveled from Wales, served as chief mourner, riding in the lead carriage with young Virginia. The American Minister and his wife followed, then Washington and the boys, with Mrs. Umney in the final carriage; it seemed fitting that she, having endured the ghost’s presence for over fifty years, should witness his final departure. The Reverend Augustus Dampier conducted the solemn service at a grave prepared beneath an ancient yew tree. As the coffin descended, the servants doused their torches, and Virginia placed a cross of almond blossoms upon it. Moonlight suddenly illuminated the churchyard, and a nightingale sang from a nearby thicket. Recalling the ghost’s vision of the Garden of Death, Virginia wept silently throughout the return journey. The following morning, Mr. Otis met with Lord Canterville to discuss the jewels the spirit had bestowed upon Virginia. These items, particularly a sixteenth-century Venetian ruby necklace, were so valuable that Mr. Otis hesitated to let his daughter keep them. He insisted that, under the laws of mortmain, the gems were rightfully family heirlooms. He urged Lord Canterville to reclaim them as recovered property, noting that his daughter was merely a child with no desire for such extravagant luxuries.

Were our proud dreams meant to fade like this? We once considered ourselves just below the angels, yet we proved no better than fleeting insects. We called ourselves the finest of creatures, only to find we were merely dust. We complained that the pyramids outlasted their builders, yet even a simple straw hut lasts longer than the entire human race. How can we reconcile this decline with our past ambitions and perceived power? Suddenly, an internal voice spoke clearly: This was decreed from eternity. The forces of time were bound to this outcome since the beginning. Do you wish to reverse the unchangeable laws of necessity? Eternal, unchanging necessity, you who weave the unbreakable chain of events, I will not complain. If my human mind cannot accept that everything is right, I will sit among the ruins and smile, knowing that we were born not to enjoy, but to submit and hope. Would the reader grow tired if I described our long journey from Paris to Geneva in detail? Could I even find the words to express our endless miseries? Patience, reader. Whether you are a spiritual being or a human living on earth, you will read of our extinct race and wonder if we were as fragile as you. We were, so weep for us. Shed tears of compassion, but pay attention to the story of your predecessors. The final events of our journey through France were so horrific that I dare not dwell on them. Every moment holds a painful story that would chill your blood. It is right that I build this record for your instruction, but I will not force you to witness every gruesome detail.

“Drat my hat! I need Virginia!” the young Duke exclaimed with a laugh, and they raced toward the train station. There, Mr. Otis asked the station-master if anyone matching Virginia’s description had been spotted, but he learned nothing. The official promised to send inquiries along the tracks and keep a sharp lookout. After purchasing a hat for the Duke from a shopkeeper closing for the night, Mr. Otis rode to Bexley, a nearby village known for gypsy encampments on the adjacent common. They woke the local constable, but he offered no leads. After scouring the common, they returned to the Chase by eleven, exhausted and devastated. Washington and the twins met them at the gate-house with lanterns, as the path was pitch black. No sign of Virginia had surfaced. The gypsies had been located in Brockley meadows, but she was not among them; they claimed they had simply miscalculated the date of Chorton Fair and departed in haste. They were genuinely upset by the news, as they appreciated Mr. Otis letting them camp on his land, and four of them remained to assist in the search. The carp-pond had been searched and the entire estate combed, yet nothing was found. It was clear that Virginia was gone for the night, and Mr. Otis and the boys returned to the house in profound despair, followed by the groom with the horses. Inside, they found the staff terrified, and Mrs. Otis lay on the library sofa, nearly hysterical with worry, while the housekeeper tended to her. Mr. Otis insisted she eat and ordered supper for everyone. It was a somber affair; few words were spoken, and even the twins were uncharacteristically quiet, as they adored their sister. Once finished, Mr. Otis ignored the Duke’s pleas and sent everyone to bed, declaring that nothing more could be achieved until morning, when he would summon detectives from Scotland Yard.

With that finished, I unfastened a few more loops from the rim, fed in more fabric, and reattached the loops to their corresponding buttons. This allowed me to slide the entire upper section of the bag between the netting and the hoop. The hoop now rested inside the car, while the weight of the car and its contents hung entirely from the buttons. While this seemed precarious, it was perfectly secure; the buttons were robust and spaced closely enough that each bore only a fraction of the load. Even if the car had been three times heavier, I would have felt no concern. I raised the hoop back inside the rubberized covering, propping it near its original height with three light poles to keep the bag distended and the netting properly positioned. Finally, I sealed the enclosure by gathering the fabric folds and twisting them tightly from the inside with a stationary tourniquet. Three circular panes of thick, clear glass were set into the sides of the covering, providing a full horizontal view. A fourth window in the bottom, aligned with a small hole in the floor, allowed me to look straight down. I could not install a window overhead due to the way the fabric bunched at the closure, but this was irrelevant, as the balloon itself would have blocked any upward view. About a foot below one side window, I placed an eight-inch circular opening with a threaded brass rim, into which I screwed the condenser tube, keeping the machine itself inside the rubberized chamber.

Furthermore, this knot is a specialty of Maltese sailors. I found the ribbon near the lightning rod, and it could not have belonged to the victims. If my deduction that the Frenchman is a sailor from a Maltese ship is wrong, the advertisement does no harm; he will simply assume I was misled. However, if I am correct, I have gained a significant advantage. Even if innocent of the murder, the Frenchman will hesitate to claim his orangutan. He will reason that he is poor and the animal is a fortune, so why lose it to fear? He will tell himself the beast was found far from the crime scene, and it is impossible to prove he is implicated. He will conclude that since the advertiser knows he owns the animal, avoiding it might draw more suspicion. He will decide to claim the creature and keep it hidden until the investigation ends. Just then, we heard footsteps on the stairs. Be ready with your pistols, Dupin whispered, but do not show them until I signal. The visitor had entered the open front door and started up the stairs, then hesitated and began to descend. As Dupin moved toward the door, the man turned and climbed back up, finally knocking on our chamber door. Come in, Dupin said cheerfully. A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—tall, muscular, and possessing a daring, not entirely unpleasant, expression.

“Never!” the girl replied. “Why?” “For one reason,” she answered resolutely, “which the lady understands and will support—I have her word. Furthermore, despite his wicked life, I have lived poorly too. Many of us have shared the same path, and I will not betray those who could have turned on me but chose not to, however corrupt they may be.” “Then,” the gentleman said, as if reaching his goal, “hand Monks over to me and let me handle him.” “What if he betrays the others?” “I promise that if the truth is extracted, the matter ends there. Oliver’s history contains painful details that should not be public; if the truth emerges, the others will go free.” “And if it does not?” she asked. “Then,” the gentleman continued, “Fagin shall not face justice without your consent. I believe I could then provide reasons to persuade you.” “Do I have the lady’s word?” she inquired. “You do,” Rose answered. “My sincere pledge.” “Monks will never discover how you learned this?” the girl asked after a pause. “Never,” the gentleman replied. “The information will be used in a way he could never suspect.” “I have been a liar among liars since childhood,” she said after another silence, “but I will trust your word.” After receiving their assurances, she spoke in a voice so hushed it was hard to follow, describing the tavern she had left that night. She paused frequently, seemingly while the gentleman took notes. Once she had detailed the location, the best vantage point for surveillance, and the times Monks usually visited, she paused to recall his appearance. “He is tall,” she said, “and well-built but not heavy. He has a furtive gait, constantly glancing over his shoulders as he walks.”

The tempest howled throughout the night, yet nothing unusual happened. By morning, however, the gruesome bloodstain had returned to the floor. Washington, having exhausted his Paragon Detergent, concluded it must be the ghost. He scrubbed it away, but it reappeared the following day, and again the third, despite Mr. Otis locking the library and keeping the key. The family grew intrigued; Mr. Otis reconsidered his skepticism, Mrs. Otis planned to join the Psychical Society, and Washington drafted a treatise on the persistence of bloodstains linked to crimes. That night, all skepticism regarding ghosts vanished. After a sunny day, the family enjoyed an evening drive, returning at nine for a light supper. They avoided any talk of spirits, focusing instead on typical topics for refined Americans: the acting prowess of Fanny Davenport, the scarcity of American staples like hominy in England, the cultural significance of Boston, the efficiency of baggage checks, and the merits of the New York accent. No one mentioned the supernatural or Sir Simon de Canterville. By eleven-thirty, the house was dark. Later, Mr. Otis was roused by a metallic clanking in the hallway. He rose, lit a match, and noted it was one o’clock. Remaining composed, he checked his steady pulse. As the clanking and footsteps persisted, he donned his slippers, grabbed a small phial from his kit, and stepped into the corridor.

Goodbye, Uncle George. I will be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thanks for the information. I prefer to learn everything about my new friends and nothing about my old ones. Where are you eating, Harry? At Aunt Agatha’s. I invited myself and Mr. Gray, who is her latest favorite. Tell your aunt to stop bothering me with her charity requests. I am tired of them. She thinks I exist only to write checks for her silly causes. I will tell her, but it won’t matter. Philanthropic people lose all sense of humanity; it is their defining trait. The old man grunted in agreement and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked toward Berkeley Square. So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s parents. Even told crudely, it was a strange, modern romance. A beautiful woman risked everything for a passionate affair, followed by a few weeks of happiness cut short by a treacherous crime. After months of agony, a child was born, the mother died, and the boy was left to the care of a cold, loveless man. It was an interesting background that made the boy seem more perfect. Every beautiful thing has a tragic history; the world must suffer for the smallest flower to bloom. How charming he had been at dinner, sitting across from him with wide, wonder-filled eyes. Talking to him was like playing a violin; he responded to every touch. There was something thrilling about influencing others. To project one’s soul into another person, to hear one’s own ideas echoed back with the passion of youth, and to share one’s temperament like a perfume—that was a true joy in this vulgar, common age. Dorian was a marvelous subject, or at least, he could be molded into one.

Once my tears subsided, reason and memory returned, allowing me to reflect calmly on my situation. Though only hours had passed, my world had undergone a profound transformation; it felt as if years had elapsed since morning. My father was dead to me, and I felt as though I were mourning his actual passing. Yet, he was not dead to the world, only to me.
