I had to flee from him more urgently than from any enemy, never to see or speak to him again. The agony of this realization left me breathless, unable to think clearly. I resolved to live in total seclusion, perhaps moving to the Continent to join a convent—not for religious reasons, but to escape the world entirely and find a place to weep in silence. But what of my father? Would he ever overcome the fierce passion that now consumed him? Perhaps, years from now, when age had cooled his intensity, he might be a father to me again. This thought brought a melancholy smile to my lips and allowed me to hope. Time would pass, and though it might be difficult, I had not lost him forever. Let him wander in desolation for another sixteen years; let him cry out to the forests and waterfalls of distant lands; let him endure hardship and the elements. I consign you to this life, my miserable father. Go, live among savages, sleep beneath the open sky, let your body wither and your heart grow cold, until all your youth has vanished.

Upon my return, I found this letter from my father: My dear Victor, you have likely been waiting for me to set a date for your homecoming. I considered writing only a brief note, but that would be a cruel kindness. I cannot bear to imagine your shock if you arrived expecting a joyful welcome only to find us in tears. How can I tell you of our tragedy? I know you still care for our family, and I cannot spare you this pain. I wish I could prepare you, but I know it is impossible; even now, your eyes are racing across the page to find the terrible news. William is dead. That sweet, gentle, happy child has been murdered. I will not try to comfort you, but will simply explain what happened. Last Thursday, May 7th, I went for a walk in Plainpalais with my niece and your brothers. The evening was warm, so we stayed out longer than usual. By dusk, we realized William and Ernest were missing. We waited on a bench until Ernest returned alone, asking if we had seen his brother. He explained that they had been playing hide-and-seek, but William had vanished and never returned. We were alarmed and searched until dark, when Elizabeth suggested he might have gone home. He was not there. We went back out with torches, as I could not bear the thought of my boy lost in the cold night. Elizabeth was in agony. At five in the morning, I found my beautiful boy, who had been so full of life the day before, lying dead on the grass. The marks of a killer’s fingers were on his neck. We brought him home, and my expression revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She insisted on seeing the body. I tried to stop her, but she pushed into the room, examined the victim’s neck, and cried out, O God!

Despite her efforts, the boy grew paler and more miserable. She tried hot baths, showers, and plunges, but he remained as gloomy as ever. She then added a bland oatmeal diet and medicinal plasters, treating him like a vessel to be filled with various quack remedies. Tom had grown indifferent to her constant interference, which deeply worried his aunt. She felt she had to break through his apathy, so when she heard of a new medicine called Pain-killer, she bought some immediately. After tasting the fiery liquid, she abandoned her other treatments and pinned all her hopes on it. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched anxiously. Her worries vanished when he reacted with intense, wild energy, as if she had set him on fire. Tom decided he needed a change. He realized that while his suffering might seem romantic, the constant medical attention was becoming too much. He hatched a plan and began pretending to love the medicine. He asked for it so frequently that he became a nuisance, eventually leading his aunt to tell him to help himself. While she would have trusted Sid, she secretly monitored the bottle because it was Tom. She noticed the liquid level dropping, never suspecting that he was actually using it to fill a crack in the floorboards. One day, as Tom was pouring the medicine into the floor, the aunt’s yellow cat approached, begging for a taste. Tom warned the cat, Peter, that he should be sure he wanted it, but the animal insisted. Tom pried the cat’s mouth open and poured the medicine in. Peter leaped into the air, let out a loud yowl, and raced around the room, crashing into furniture and knocking over flowerpots in a chaotic frenzy.

A few days later, Virginia and her friend were riding near Brockley meadows when she tore her riding habit on a hedge. Returning home, she tried to sneak in through the back stairs to avoid being seen. Passing the open door of the Tapestry Chamber, she thought she saw her mother’s maid and looked in to ask for help with her dress. To her shock, the Canterville Ghost was sitting by the window, watching the autumn leaves blow past. He looked so sad and worn out that Virginia, instead of running away, felt sorry for him and decided to offer comfort. She walked in so quietly that he did not notice her until she spoke. She told him she felt sorry for him and promised that if he behaved, her brothers would leave him alone once they returned to school. The ghost looked at her in surprise and insisted that he had to rattle his chains and haunt the halls, as that was his only purpose. Virginia reminded him that he had been wicked and killed his wife. The ghost admitted it but argued it was a private family matter. Virginia insisted that killing was wrong. The ghost complained about his wife’s poor cooking and lack of style, noting that while he had killed her, he felt it was unfair that her brothers had starved him to death in retaliation.

I was disappointed to hear Jim say that; it lowered my opinion of him. My conscience bothered me more than ever, until I finally told myself, "Stop it—it isn't too late—I will paddle to shore at dawn and report him." I felt light and happy immediately, as if my troubles had vanished. I began watching for a light, humming to myself. Soon, one appeared. Jim shouted, "We are safe, Huck! We are safe! Jump up and celebrate! That is Cairo at last, I know it!" I replied, "I will take the canoe and check, Jim. It might not be the right place." He quickly prepared the canoe, placing his coat inside for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle. As I pushed off, he said, "Soon I will be shouting for joy, and I will say it is all because of Huck. I am a free man, and I never could have been free if it weren't for you. Jim will never forget you, Huck; you are the best friend I have ever had, and the only friend I have left." I was paddling away, eager to turn him in, but his words drained all my resolve. I slowed down, unsure if I was glad I had left. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called out, "There you go, the true Huck; the only white gentleman who ever kept his promise to old Jim." I felt sick. Still, I told myself I had to do it. Just then, a skiff with two armed men approached. They stopped, and I did too. One asked, "What is that over there?" "A piece of a raft," I said. "Are you on it?" "Yes, sir." "Is there anyone else?" "Only one man, sir." "Well, five enslaved men ran away tonight up the river. Is your man white or black?" I hesitated. I tried to speak, but the words would not come. I tried to find the courage, but I lacked the nerve. Realizing I was failing, I finally said, "He is white." "We will go see for ourselves," the man said. "I wish you would," I replied, "because it is my father on the raft, and maybe you could help me tow it to the shore where the light is."

Everyone compares the voice to a language they do not know. The Frenchman thinks it sounds Spanish, though he admits he would only recognize words if he knew the language. The Dutchman claims it was French, yet he required an interpreter to testify. The Englishman believes it was German, a language he does not speak. The Spaniard is certain it was English, relying solely on the tone since he knows no English. The Italian thinks it was Russian, despite never having spoken to a Russian. A second Frenchman disagrees with the first, insisting it was Italian, though he also relies only on the intonation because he does not know that language. How incredibly strange that voice must have been for people from across Europe to find nothing familiar in its sound. You might suggest it was the voice of an Asian or African, though such people are rare in Paris. Regardless, consider three points: one witness calls it harsh rather than shrill, two others describe it as quick and uneven, and no one could identify any actual words. Dupin continued, I do not know what you make of this, but I believe the logical conclusions drawn from these descriptions of the voices are enough to form a suspicion that should guide our investigation. I mean that these are the only logical conclusions, and the suspicion follows inevitably. I will not reveal my suspicion yet, but keep in mind that it gave a clear direction to my search of the room. Let us imagine ourselves in that room now. What should we look for first? The means the murderers used to escape. It is safe to say that neither of us believes in the supernatural.

Were our grand visions destined to vanish? We claimed a status just below the angels, yet we proved as fleeting as insects. We styled ourselves the pinnacle of creation, only to reveal our essence as mere dust. We lamented that pyramids survived their creators, yet even a humble straw hut possesses more permanence than all of humanity. How can we reconcile this decline with our former ambitions and perceived potential? Suddenly, a distinct inner voice spoke: This was ordained from eternity; the horses of Time have carried this outcome since the dawn of existence. Would you attempt to reverse the immutable laws of Necessity? Eternal, unyielding Necessity, weaver of the unbreakable chain of events, I shall not complain of your decrees. Though my mind struggles to accept that all which exists is right, I will sit among the wreckage and smile, knowing we were born not for pleasure, but for submission and hope. Will the reader grow weary if I detail our arduous trek from Paris to Geneva? Could I possibly document the relentless succession of our miseries? Patience, reader; whether you are a spiritual entity or a human descendant, you will read of this extinct race and wonder if they were as fragile as you. They were indeed, so weep for them; yet attend to this chronicle of your predecessors. The final events of our journey through France were so horrific that I dare not linger. To analyze every moment would be to recount tales so harrowing they would chill your blood. It is my duty to build this monument to the lost race for your instruction, without forcing you to endure the gruesome details of our suffering.

Colonel Grangerford was a true gentleman, as was his entire household. He came from a fine lineage, a trait Widow Douglas—a woman of unquestioned social standing—likened to the breeding of a horse, a sentiment my father echoed despite his own lack of refinement. The Colonel was remarkably tall and slender, possessing a pale, dark complexion devoid of any color. He shaved his gaunt face daily, revealing thin lips, narrow nostrils, a prominent nose, and thick brows over deep-set, jet-black eyes that peered out like they were emerging from caves. His forehead was broad, and his straight black hair reached his shoulders. With his long, thin hands, he dressed daily in pristine white linen, donning a blue tail-coat with brass buttons on Sundays and carrying a silver-topped mahogany cane. He was a man of serious demeanor, never boisterous, yet possessed a kindness that inspired immediate trust. While his rare smile was pleasant, his sudden, rigid posture and the sharp glint beneath his brows made one instinctively seek safety before questioning the cause. He never needed to demand respect; his presence alone ensured decorum. He brought a sense of warmth to any room, and though his rare moments of displeasure were brief, they were enough to keep everyone in line for days. When he and his wife appeared each morning, the family rose and remained standing until they were seated. Tom and Bob would then prepare bitters at the sideboard, waiting to toast the Colonel and his wife with a polite, "Our duty to you, sir, and madam." The couple would acknowledge them with a slight bow and a word of thanks before they all drank. Finally, Tom and Bob would prepare a diluted mixture for Buck and me, allowing us to join in the toast to the elders.

I would gladly share much more, but I must be concise to secure my compensation. I long to return home to my family. In exchange for the insights I can provide regarding various physical and metaphysical sciences, I request that your honorable assembly grant me a pardon for the deaths of my creditors during my flight from Rotterdam. This is the purpose of my letter. Its bearer, a lunar inhabitant I have trained to act as my messenger, will await your decision and return with the pardon if it can be secured. I remain your humble servant, Hans Pfaall. Upon reading this remarkable letter, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe in shock, while Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and spun around three times in sheer amazement, momentarily forgetting his dignity. They agreed the pardon must be granted. Rub-a-dub swore it would be done, and Von Underduk concurred, taking his colleague's arm to head home and discuss the necessary steps. At the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor noted that since the messenger had vanished—likely terrified by the locals—the pardon would be useless, as only a moon-dweller could manage such a journey. The burgomaster agreed, and the matter concluded. Yet, rumors persisted. Once published, the letter sparked endless speculation. Some self-important critics dismissed the entire affair as a hoax, a term they apply to anything beyond their limited understanding. I fail to see the basis for such claims. Let us examine their arguments.

He was incredibly stubborn, muttering only "that cursed bug" throughout our journey. I carried two lanterns, while Legrand swung the scarab on a piece of cord like a magician. Seeing this clear sign of his mental decline, I nearly wept. I decided to humor him for now, hoping to intervene more effectively later. My attempts to learn our destination failed; he refused to discuss anything, answering every question with "we shall see!" We crossed the island creek by skiff and climbed the mainland hills, heading northwest through wild, untracked country. Legrand led with purpose, pausing only to check landmarks he had set previously. After two hours, as the sun set, we reached a desolate plateau near the top of a steep, densely wooded hill. Huge boulders lay scattered, held back from the valleys only by the trees they leaned against. Deep ravines added to the grim atmosphere. The plateau was choked with brambles, requiring a scythe to clear a path. Jupiter followed Legrand’s orders to cut through to a massive tulip tree. It stood among several oaks, dwarfing them all with its majestic form, wide branches, and beautiful foliage.

Were our grand ambitions destined to vanish? We once considered ourselves just below the angels, yet we proved as fleeting as insects. We claimed to be the pinnacle of creation, only to reveal ourselves as mere dust. We lamented that pyramids outlived their creators, yet even a simple shepherd’s hut possesses more permanence than all of humanity. How can we reconcile this decline with our former potential? Suddenly, a clear inner voice spoke: This was decreed from eternity; the forces of time were bound to this outcome since the beginning. Do you seek to reverse the unchangeable laws of necessity? Eternal, unchanging Necessity, weaver of the unbreakable chain of events, I will not complain. If my mind cannot grasp that all is right, I will accept that what must be, is, and sit among the ruins with a smile. We were born not to enjoy, but to submit and hope. Will the reader grow weary if I detail our long journey from Paris to Geneva? Could I possibly record the endless miseries we endured? Patience, reader. Whether you are a spiritual being or a human descendant, you will read of this extinct race and wonder if they were as fragile as you. They were, so weep for them, but listen to their story. The final events in France were so horrific that I dare not dwell on them. Every second held a nightmare that would chill your blood. I must build this monument to our history for your instruction, but I will not force you to witness every gruesome detail of our suffering.

Please consider, ma’am, Oliver pleaded, tears welling despite his resistance. Think of how young and kind she is, and the joy she brings to everyone. I am certain that for your sake, for her own, and for those she makes happy, she will not perish. Heaven would never allow her to die so young. Hush, Mrs. Maylie replied, resting a hand on his head. You speak like a child, yet you remind me of my duty. I had momentarily forgotten it, but I hope for forgiveness; I am old and have witnessed enough suffering to understand the pain of losing those we love. I also know that the youngest and best are not always spared. This should comfort us, for Heaven is just, and such trials remind us that a brighter world exists, reached quickly. God’s will be done; He knows how deeply I love her. Oliver was surprised to see Mrs. Maylie suppress her grief with a single effort, standing tall and composed. He was even more astonished that this resolve held throughout the following days of care, as she performed her duties steadily and seemingly cheerfully. He was young and did not yet understand the strength of a resolute mind under pressure, a strength often unknown even to its possessor. A restless night followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie’s fears were confirmed; Rose had fallen into a dangerous fever. We must act, Oliver, and avoid useless sorrow, Mrs. Maylie said, looking firmly at him. This letter must be sent immediately to Mr. Losberne. Take it to the market town four miles away by the footpath, and have it dispatched by horseback to Chertsey. The innkeepers will handle it, and I know I can trust you to ensure it is done. Oliver could not speak, but his expression showed his eagerness to depart.

Regarding that matter, I shall remain silent, and you may rest assured that no unkind words will escape me once we are wed. Elizabeth felt compelled to interject. You are moving too quickly, sir, she exclaimed. You overlook the fact that I have not yet responded. Let me do so immediately. I thank you for your flattering offer, but I must decline. Mr. Collins waved his hand formally and replied that he was well aware young women often reject suitors they intend to accept, sometimes doing so repeatedly. Consequently, he remained undeterred and expected to marry her soon. Elizabeth insisted that his hope was strange given her clear refusal. She assured him she was not the type of woman to gamble her happiness on a second proposal. She was entirely serious; he could not make her happy, and she was certain she would be a poor match for him. Furthermore, she believed Lady Catherine would find her unsuitable. Mr. Collins solemnly disagreed, stating he doubted Lady Catherine would disapprove and promised to praise Elizabeth's modesty and virtues when he next saw her. Elizabeth urged him to cease such praise and trust her word. She wished him wealth and happiness, noting that by declining his hand, she was ensuring he would not be miserable. She added that he had fulfilled his duty to her family and could inherit Longbourn without guilt, considering the matter closed. As she rose to leave, Mr. Collins spoke again, stating he expected a more favorable response when he next addressed the subject. He claimed he did not view her refusal as cruelty, as he understood it was customary for women to decline an initial proposal, and he believed she had already offered as much encouragement as propriety allowed.

April 12th. The balloon changed direction as I had hoped, turning sharply east at the twentieth parallel south to follow the moon’s path. This shift caused the car to sway noticeably for several hours. April 13th. The loud, crackling noise returned, leaving me baffled. The earth appeared much smaller, covering only twenty-five degrees of my view. The moon was directly overhead and hidden, and I made little eastward progress. April 14th. The earth shrank rapidly. I realized the balloon was traveling directly toward the moon’s closest point to earth. I spent much time condensing the air to breathe. April 15th. The earth’s features were no longer visible. Around noon, that terrifying sound returned, growing louder and more intense. As I braced for disaster, the car shook violently while a massive, flaming object roared past like thunder. I eventually concluded it was a volcanic rock ejected from the moon, similar to the meteoric stones found on earth. April 16th. Looking through the side windows, I was thrilled to see the edge of the moon’s disk peeking out from behind the balloon.

Emma Woodhouse, beautiful, intelligent, and wealthy, with a comfortable home and a cheerful personality, seemed to possess the best of life’s blessings. She had lived nearly twenty-one years with very little to trouble her. As the younger of two daughters to an affectionate, doting father, she had managed his household since her sister’s marriage. Her mother had passed away when she was too young to remember much, and an excellent governess had filled that role with motherly love. Miss Taylor had been with the family for sixteen years, acting more as a friend than a teacher, especially toward Emma. Their relationship was like that of sisters. Miss Taylor’s gentle nature meant she rarely imposed restrictions, and for a long time, they had lived as equals, with Emma doing as she pleased, valuing Miss Taylor’s advice but ultimately following her own. The true downsides of Emma’s life were her tendency to have her own way and an inclination toward vanity; these were the only threats to her happiness. However, she was currently unaware of these dangers, so she did not consider them problems. Sorrow arrived—a mild sorrow, but not one born of self-reproach. Miss Taylor married, and her absence brought Emma her first real grief. On the wedding day, after the guests had departed, Emma and her father sat down to dinner, facing a long, lonely evening. Her father fell asleep as usual, leaving Emma to reflect on her loss. While the marriage promised happiness for her friend—Mr. Weston was a man of excellent character, wealth, and charm—and Emma took pride in having encouraged the match, it was a devastating day for her. She would miss Miss Taylor every hour. She remembered sixteen years of kindness, from her early childhood lessons and games to the devoted care she received during every illness.

I hail from a small, mist-covered island, a place that seems a mere dot when compared to the vastness of the world, yet it holds a weight of intellectual influence that surpasses much larger and more populous nations. It is certain that human intellect is the true architect of all greatness, with Nature serving merely as its initial servant. England, nestled in the northern, turbulent waters, often appears in my dreams as a grand, well-crewed vessel conquering the seas. In my youth, this land was my entire world. Gazing from my native hills across the cultivated plains and mountains dotted with homes, I felt that this spot was the heart of the earth, while the remainder of the globe felt like a distant myth, easily ignored. My life has always illustrated the profound influence of change on human existence. This instability was almost a family legacy. My father was gifted by nature with abundant wit and imagination, yet he lacked the reason to steer or the judgment to navigate his life. Though of humble origins, he rose to public prominence, quickly squandering his modest inheritance amidst a life of luxury. In his youth, he was celebrated by the elite and even the young monarch, who sought his company to escape the burdens of state. My father’s lack of self-restraint constantly drew him into crises that only his cleverness could resolve. He carried the burden of mounting debts with a carefree spirit, his presence so prized at elite gatherings that his failings were overlooked and met with excessive praise. Such popularity, however, is fleeting, and the troubles he faced grew far more rapidly than his ability to overcome them.

We eventually decided to live together during my time in the city. Since my finances were more stable than his, I paid to rent and furnish a decaying, strange old mansion in a quiet, lonely part of the Faubourg St. Germain. The house had been abandoned for years due to local superstitions we chose not to investigate. If people knew how we lived, they would have thought us mad, though harmlessly so. We lived in total isolation, admitting no visitors. I kept our location secret from my old friends, and Dupin had long since cut ties with everyone in Paris. We lived entirely within our own private world. Dupin had a strange obsession with the night, and I easily adopted his eccentric habits. Since we could not have darkness all the time, we faked it. At dawn, we closed the heavy shutters and lit scented candles that cast only a faint, ghostly light. We spent our days reading, writing, or talking until the clock signaled the arrival of true night. Then, we would walk the streets arm in arm, discussing our earlier topics or wandering the city to find the mental stimulation that comes from observing the crowds. During these walks, I admired Dupin’s remarkable analytical skills. He clearly enjoyed using them and admitted as much. He would chuckle and claim he could see right through people, often proving it by revealing intimate details about my own thoughts. At these moments, his manner became cold and detached, his eyes looked vacant, and his voice shifted from a rich tenor to a high, sharp pitch that remained precise and deliberate.

These events haunted Felix, making him the most wretched of his family when I first met him. He could have handled poverty with pride, but the Turk’s betrayal and the loss of his beloved Safie were far more painful. Her arrival, however, revived his spirit. When news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his fortune and status, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return home. Safie, outraged, tried to argue, but her father angrily repeated his demand. Days later, the Turk told her he feared his location had been exposed and he would be turned over to the French. He had hired a ship to Constantinople, leaving her behind with a servant to follow later with his remaining assets. Alone, Safie decided her course. She despised the idea of living in Turkey, as it conflicted with her faith and values. Discovering her father’s papers, she learned of her lover’s exile and his location. After much hesitation, she took her jewels and money, leaving Italy for Germany with a local attendant who spoke Turkish. They reached a town near the De Lacey cottage when her attendant fell fatally ill. Safie cared for her devotedly, but the girl died, leaving the Arabian alone in a foreign land. Fortunately, the innkeeper, having learned their destination from the attendant, ensured Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely.

He was certainly entertaining, but I felt let down. When I asked about the chainmail, he just laughed and claimed it was too cold for England. Oh, look, Mr. Podgers is here! Mr. Podgers, please read the Duchess of Paisley’s palm. Duchess, take off your glove—the right one, not the left. The Duchess reluctantly unbuttoned her slightly dirty glove, protesting that it did not seem proper. Lady Windermere replied that nothing interesting ever was, then introduced them, warning Mr. Podgers not to suggest the Duchess had a larger mountain of the moon than she did. The Duchess insisted she had no such thing. Mr. Podgers examined her short, square fingers and agreed, noting her mountain of the moon was undeveloped. He praised her life line and predicted she would live to a great age and be very happy. He noted her moderate ambition and strong sense of duty. When the Duchess seemed pleased, he added that she was thrifty, which made Lady Windermere laugh. The Duchess defended her thrift, explaining that when she married, her husband had eleven castles but no livable homes. Lady Windermere quipped that he now had twelve houses and no castles. Mr. Podgers stepped in, praising the Duchess for valuing comfort and modern conveniences. Lady Windermere then asked him to read Lady Flora’s palm. A tall girl with sandy hair and sharp shoulders stepped forward, offering a bony hand. Mr. Podgers immediately identified her as a pianist, though perhaps not a true musician.

I walked quickly to my college, suddenly shivering at the thought that the creature I had left in my apartment might still be there. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might encounter him. I asked Henry to wait at the bottom of the stairs while I rushed up to my room. My hand was on the lock before I paused, trembling. I threw the door open, expecting a ghost, but the room was empty. Relieved that my enemy had fled, I clapped my hands and ran back down to Clerval. We went up to my room, but I could not control my excitement. My skin tingled, my pulse raced, and I could not sit still; I jumped over chairs and laughed loudly. Clerval initially thought I was just happy to see him, but my wild eyes and strange, heartless laughter soon frightened him. My dear Victor, he cried, what is wrong? Do not laugh like that. You look ill. What is the cause of this? Do not ask me, I shouted, covering my eyes as I imagined the monster entering the room. He can tell. Save me! I felt the creature grab me, struggled violently, and collapsed. Poor Clerval. He had looked forward to our meeting, only for it to turn into a nightmare. I did not see his distress, as I lost consciousness for a long time. This began a nervous fever that kept me bedridden for months. Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that he had kept the severity of my illness a secret to spare my elderly father and Elizabeth from unnecessary grief.

He does not understand English, but judges by the tone of voice. Alberto Montani, a confectioner, testified that he was among the first to climb the stairs. He heard two voices. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman and seemed to be arguing. He could not understand the shrill voice, which spoke quickly and unevenly; he guessed it was Russian, though he had never spoken to a Russian before. He agreed with the other witnesses. Several witnesses confirmed that the fourth-floor chimneys were too narrow for a person to fit through. The brushes used by chimney sweeps were passed through every flue, and there was no back exit for anyone to escape while the group climbed the stairs. Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was wedged so tightly in the chimney that it took four or five men to pull it down. Paul Dumas, a physician, testified that he examined the bodies at daybreak. They were lying on the bed where the young woman was found. Her body was bruised and scraped, likely from being forced up the chimney. Her throat was chafed, with deep scratches under her chin and dark spots that looked like fingerprints. Her face was discolored, her eyes bulged, and she had bitten her tongue. A large bruise on her stomach appeared to be from a knee. Dr. Dumas concluded she had been strangled. The mother’s body was horribly mutilated. Her right arm and leg bones were shattered, her left shin and ribs were broken, and her entire body was bruised. He could not determine the exact weapon, but a heavy club, iron bar, or chair wielded by a very strong man could have caused such injuries; no woman could have inflicted them. The mother’s head was severed and shattered, and her throat had been cut with a sharp instrument, likely a razor.

He abandoned the effort entirely. The boys remained motionless, tracking the agonizingly slow passage of time until the sun finally began to dip below the horizon. One snore stopped abruptly. Injun Joe rose, surveyed the room, and gave his companion a sharp nudge with his boot. He chided the man for his lapse in vigilance, though he conceded that nothing had occurred. The comrade expressed surprise at having dozed off. Joe suggested it was nearly time to depart and inquired about their remaining loot. They decided to leave the six hundred and fifty dollars in silver hidden there until they headed south, though Joe insisted they bury it deeper to ensure its safety. The comrade retrieved the jingling bag from beneath a hearthstone, distributed some cash to both of them, and handed the rest to Joe, who began excavating a corner with his knife. The hidden boys watched with intense fascination, thrilled by the prospect of such a fortune. Suddenly, Joe’s blade hit an obstruction. He discovered a box buried in the dirt and pried it open. Reaching inside, he pulled out a handful of gold coins. The boys above were just as ecstatic as the men below. Joe’s partner suggested they retrieve a rusty pick from the weeds near the fireplace to finish the job quickly.

During his brief visit, Emma had seen him rarely, yet enough to sense that their initial encounter had passed, leaving her with the impression that his manner had grown increasingly pretentious and irritable. She truly marveled that she had ever found him agreeable; his presence now evoked such unpleasantness that, unless viewed as a necessary moral penance, she would have preferred never to encounter him again. She wished him well, but his proximity caused her distress, and she would have been far happier knowing he was settled twenty miles away. His marriage would surely mitigate the discomfort of his remaining in Highbury, as a Mrs. Elton would provide a convenient pretext for altering their social interactions and allowing their former intimacy to fade unnoticed. Emma gave little thought to the woman herself. She was likely suitable for Mr. Elton and sufficient for Highbury, though she would probably appear plain compared to Harriet. Regarding social standing, Emma felt entirely secure, convinced that despite his arrogance and rejection of Harriet, he had made no significant match. While her character remained unknown, her background was discoverable, and aside from her ten thousand pounds, she seemed no better than Harriet. She possessed no notable lineage or connections. Miss Hawkins was the daughter of a Bristol merchant, though given his modest earnings, his trade was likely equally unremarkable. She spent winters in Bath, but her home was in Bristol, where she had lived with an uncle in the legal profession—presumably a dull clerk. The family's only claim to prestige rested on an elder sister who had married a man near Bristol wealthy enough to maintain two carriages, which served as the pinnacle of Miss Hawkins's social history.

I woke early, managed to slip past my creditors, and hurried to a bookstore. I spent my remaining cash on books about mechanics and astronomy. Once home, I studied them constantly until I felt ready to carry out my plan. Meanwhile, I worked to appease the three creditors who had been bothering me. I finally succeeded by selling some furniture to pay half their debt and promising the rest once I finished a project I invited them to help with. Since they were simple men, they easily agreed. Once things were settled, I secretly sold my remaining property with my wife's help. I also borrowed small amounts of money under various excuses, never worrying about how I would pay it back. With this cash, I bought fine cambric muslin, twine, rubber varnish, a custom wicker basket, and other supplies for a massive balloon. I instructed my wife on how to sew the balloon while I wove the twine into a net and attached the hoop and cords. I also purchased a quadrant, compass, telescope, a modified barometer, and two rare astronomical tools. At night, I transported several large casks, long metal tubes, a specific semi-metal, and a dozen jugs of acid to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam. I planned to create a unique gas that no one else had ever used for this purpose. I would gladly reveal the secret, but it belongs to a man in Nantz, France, who shared it with me under strict conditions.

What is the result? What impression have I made on your mind? I felt a chill as Dupin asked me this. A madman did this, I said, some raving lunatic escaped from a nearby asylum. In some ways, he replied, your idea is not off base. But the voices of madmen, even in their worst fits, never match that strange voice heard on the stairs. Madmen belong to a nation, and their language, however confused, always has the structure of speech. Besides, the hair of a madman is not like this. I pulled this tuft from the tight grip of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you make of it. Dupin, I said, completely shaken, this hair is very strange; it is not human. I did not say it was, he replied, but before we decide, look at this sketch I have drawn. It is a copy of what was described in the testimony as dark bruises and deep nail marks on the throat of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and as a series of purple spots from fingers. You will see, my friend continued, spreading the paper on the table, that this drawing shows a firm, fixed hold. There is no slipping. Each finger kept its grip until the victim died. Try to place your fingers into these marks. I tried and failed. We are not giving this a fair test, he said. The paper is flat, but a human throat is round. Here is a piece of wood about the size of a throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again. I did, but the difficulty was even clearer. This is not the mark of a human hand, I said. Read this passage from Cuvier, Dupin replied. It was a detailed anatomical description of the large orangutan from the East Indian Islands. The giant size, incredible strength, speed, wild ferocity, and tendency to imitate are well known. I understood the horror of the murder at once. The description of the fingers, I said after reading, matches this drawing perfectly.

I am quite unlearned, and it worries me, if only slightly. Tell me your trouble. I have a cousin, my only kin and an orphan like me, whom I cherish deeply. She is five years my junior, residing on a southern farm. Financial hardship separated us, and she remains unaware of my situation, as I cannot write, and even if I could, how would I explain it? It is best this way. Indeed, it is better so. As we traveled, and as I gaze upon your kind, resolute face that offers me such strength, I have been wondering: if the Republic truly aids the impoverished, reducing their hunger and suffering, she might live a long life, perhaps even to old age. What then, my gentle sister? Do you think, she asks, her enduring eyes filling with tears and her lips trembling, that the wait will feel long for me in that better land where I hope we shall both find mercy? It cannot be, my child; there is no time or sorrow there. You bring me such comfort. I am so ignorant. Should I kiss you now? Is the time at hand? Yes. She kisses him, he kisses her, and they offer solemn blessings. His thin hand remains steady as he lets her go; her patient face shows only a sweet, bright resolve. She precedes him and is gone; the knitters count twenty-two. I am the Resurrection and the Life, says the Lord; he who believes in me, though he die, shall live, and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die. The murmuring voices, the upturned faces, and the pressing crowd, surging like a great wave, all vanish. Twenty-three. That night, people in the city remarked that his face was the most peaceful they had ever seen, with many calling it sublime and prophetic. Another notable victim of the same blade, a woman, had recently asked at the scaffold to record her final thoughts. Had he spoken his own, and were they prophetic, they would have been these: I see Barsad, Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the juror, the judge, and the long lines of new oppressors who rose from the ruins of the old, all meeting their end by this same retributive machine before it finally falls into disuse.

Weeks passed, and I became increasingly obsessed with you. I had painted you as Paris in armor, as Adonis with a spear, and as a figure on an ancient barge. Those works were what art should be: ideal and detached. One day, I decided to paint a portrait of you as you truly are, in your own clothes and time. I am not sure if it was the realism or your own striking personality, but as I worked, every brushstroke seemed to expose my secret. I feared others would discover my devotion. I felt I had revealed too much of myself, so I decided never to show the painting. You were annoyed, but you did not understand. Harry laughed at my concerns, but I ignored him. Once the painting was finished, I felt justified in my decision. However, after the portrait left my studio, I felt foolish for thinking it contained anything more than a handsome subject and my own technical skill. I now believe that the passion an artist feels is rarely visible in the final work. Art is more abstract than we imagine; it often hides the artist rather than revealing them. When I received an offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the centerpiece of my exhibition. I never expected you to refuse, but I see now that you were right. The picture must not be shown. Please do not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have confessed.

Her complexion shifted, and she fell silent. Mrs. Gardiner stood slightly behind her, and when she paused, he asked for the honor of an introduction to her companions. This gesture of courtesy caught her off guard, and she barely suppressed a smile, noting his eagerness to meet the very people his pride had once rejected. She wondered at his reaction once he realized their true identity, assuming he mistook them for high society. The introduction proceeded, and as she identified them as her relatives, she glanced at him, expecting him to flee from such embarrassing company. He was clearly surprised, yet he maintained his composure. Instead of leaving, he turned to walk with them and began speaking with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth felt a sense of triumph; it was satisfying to know she had family members who required no apology. She listened intently, taking pride in her uncle’s intelligence and refined manners. The discussion shifted to fishing, and Darcy politely invited him to fish on the estate whenever he liked, offering his own equipment and advice on the best spots. Mrs. Gardiner exchanged a look of amazement with Elizabeth. Though Elizabeth remained silent, she was deeply gratified, sensing the gesture was meant for her. She was bewildered by his transformation, questioning how his behavior could have softened so significantly. She doubted her past criticisms could have caused such a shift, refusing to believe he still harbored feelings for her. After walking for some time, the group paused by the river to examine a water plant. When they resumed, Mrs. Gardiner, tired from the morning’s walk, found Elizabeth’s support insufficient and switched to walking with her husband.

The stars remained brilliant when I roused, and the position of Taurus indicated it was midnight. My sleep had been plagued by restless visions. I dreamt I attended Timon’s final banquet, arriving hungry only to find the dishes filled with nothing but steam. My host, taking the form of Raymond, chased me away, hurling vessels that emitted foul vapors. His figure warped into a towering specter marked by the plague, growing until it threatened to shatter the very sky. This nightmare became unbearable, forcing me to wake and regain my composure. My immediate concern was Perdita; I needed to return to her, offering support to her broken spirit by balancing the demands of duty with the gentleness of shared sorrow. Guided by the stars, I departed the ruins of the Golden City with great effort. Outside the walls, I secured a horse from a group of soldiers and hurried toward my sister. The landscape had shifted; the army’s camp was dismantled, and the scattered, demoralized remnants of the troops wandered about in shock. With a heavy heart, I entered the palace, hesitating to approach. Perdita sat upon the marble floor, her head bowed, hair untidy, and hands wringing in distress. She was deathly pale, her face etched with pain. When she looked up, the brief flicker of hope in her eyes was heartbreaking. I could not speak, my face twisting into a grimace. She grasped the meaning of my silence, bowing her head once more. When I finally found my voice, the sound startled her; she dreaded hearing the confirmation of her tragedy spoken aloud. Instead, she stood and whispered, urging me to be quiet because Clara had finally fallen asleep after much weeping.

P.S. Do tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are in fashion. Lord Arthur looked so solemn and miserable over the note that the Duchess burst into laughter. My dear Arthur, she exclaimed, I will never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what should I say about the clock? I think it is a brilliant invention and would like one myself. I don’t think much of them, Lord Arthur replied with a sad smile, and after kissing his mother, he left the room. Upstairs, he collapsed onto a sofa, his eyes welling with tears. He had tried his best to commit this murder, yet failed twice through no fault of his own. He had attempted to fulfill his duty, but it seemed as if Destiny had betrayed him. He felt crushed by the pointlessness of good intentions and the futility of trying to be virtuous. Perhaps it would be better to end the engagement. Sybil would suffer, certainly, but such pain could not truly damage a nature as noble as hers. As for himself, what did it matter? There is always a war in which a man can die or a cause to which he can sacrifice his life; since existence held no joy for him, death held no terror. He would let Destiny decide his fate and would no longer intervene. At seven-thirty, he dressed and went to his club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he was forced to dine with them. Their trivial chatter and idle jokes failed to interest him, and he left as soon as coffee was served, inventing an excuse to escape. As he exited, the porter handed him a letter from Herr Winckelkopf, inviting him to inspect an explosive umbrella that detonated upon opening. It was the latest invention from Geneva. He tore the letter into pieces, having decided to abandon his experiments. He wandered to the Thames Embankment and sat by the river for hours. The moon peered through tawny clouds like a lion’s eye, while countless stars glittered across the sky like gold dust on a purple dome. Occasionally, a barge drifted into the murky current, and railway signals shifted from green to red as trains shrieked across the bridge.

Reviewing my terrible list of sins, I struggle to believe I am the same being who once cherished noble visions of goodness. Yet it is true; the fallen angel turns into a malicious devil. Even that enemy of God and man had companions in his isolation; I am entirely alone. You, who call Frankenstein a friend, seem to know of my crimes and his suffering. However, his account could not capture the months of misery I endured, trapped in helpless rage. While I destroyed his hopes, I never satisfied my own cravings. I constantly sought love and companionship, only to be rejected. Was there no injustice in that? Am I the only criminal, when all humanity sinned against me? Why do you not hate Felix, who drove me away with insults? Why not despise the villager who tried to kill the one who saved his child? No, they are considered virtuous, while I, the abandoned wretch, am a monster to be kicked and trampled. My blood still boils at the memory of this unfairness. It is true that I am a monster. I have murdered the lovely and the helpless; I have strangled the innocent in their sleep and killed a man who never harmed anyone. I have condemned my creator, the finest of men, to misery, pursuing him to his final ruin. He lies there, cold and dead. You hate me, but your disgust cannot match my own self-loathing. I look at the hands that committed these deeds and the heart that conceived them, longing for the moment when they will haunt me no more. Do not fear further harm from me. My work is nearly finished. No more deaths are required to complete my existence; only my own. I will not hesitate to make this sacrifice. I will leave your ship on the ice raft that brought me here and head to the northernmost point of the globe. I will build my funeral pyre and burn this miserable body to ashes, ensuring that no curious, wicked person can ever study my remains to create another like me.

I turn now to my own history. My early life holds little of note, yet I must reflect on my childhood to show how the loss of one hope rendered my future hollow, and how the destruction of my only cherished affection extinguished my spirit. My aunt was nothing like my father. While not malicious, she possessed the coldest heart imaginable, entirely incapable of love. She took me in out of a sense of duty, yet having lived undisturbed for years, she refused to let a child disrupt her peace. Unmarried, she had spent five years alone on her inherited estate by Loch Lomond in Scotland. Though my father requested she live with me at our family home near Richmond, she refused. Once she settled my father’s affairs, she left England, taking me to her Scottish estate. Until I was eight, my mother’s former servant cared for me. I lived in a secluded wing, seeing my aunt only twice daily: once at noon in my nursery, and once after her dinner in the parlor. She never showed affection, seemingly fearing I might disturb her. My nurse coached me carefully, and my aunt’s cold demeanor instilled such awe that I remained perfectly still during our brief, strained visits. Under my nurse’s guidance, I roamed the park and fields freely. Born of deep love, I was a sensitive child, passionately attached to everything around me, even inanimate objects.

Keep in mind the points I have highlighted: the strange voice, the unusual agility, and the lack of motive in such a brutal murder. Let us examine the crime itself. A woman was strangled by hand and shoved headfirst up a chimney. Ordinary killers do not commit murder this way, nor do they dispose of bodies like that. You must admit that forcing a corpse into a chimney is bizarre and defies any normal human behavior, even among the most depraved. Consider the strength required to shove the body into that space so tightly that it took several men to pull it back down. Consider the evidence of incredible physical power. On the hearth lay thick clumps of grey hair torn out by the roots. You know how much force is needed to pull out even a few hairs. We both saw the locks, and their roots were still attached to bits of scalp—proof of the immense strength used to rip out so much hair at once. The old lady’s throat was not just cut; her head was completely severed using only a razor. Notice the brutal ferocity of these acts. Regarding the bruises on Madame L’Espanaye’s body, the doctors correctly identified they were caused by a blunt object. That object was simply the stone pavement in the yard, where she landed after falling from the bedroom window. This seems obvious now, but the police missed it because they were so focused on the locked windows that they could not imagine them ever being opened. If you combine these facts with the strange disorder of the room, we have a clear picture: astounding agility, superhuman strength, brutal ferocity, a motiveless crime, a grotesque horror unlike anything human, and a voice that sounded foreign to everyone who heard it, lacking any clear or understandable language.

The cramped alleys and courtyards eventually opened into a wide expanse containing animal pens and other signs of a livestock market. Sikes slowed down here, as the girl could no longer maintain their previous brisk pace. He turned to Oliver and harshly ordered him to grasp Nancy’s hand. When the boy hesitated and glanced around, Sikes growled at him to obey. They stood in a shadowed corner, hidden from any passersby. Realizing that fighting back was useless, Oliver extended his hand, which Nancy gripped firmly. Sikes grabbed Oliver’s other hand and called for his dog. Bull’s-Eye looked up and snarled. Sikes pressed his hand against Oliver’s throat, warning him that if he uttered even a whisper, the dog would attack. The animal growled and stared at Oliver, clearly eager to strike. Sikes praised the dog’s readiness with grim satisfaction, telling Oliver that he knew the consequences if he tried to call for help. The dog wagged its tail and led the way forward. They were crossing Smithfield, though it was indistinguishable to Oliver in the dark, foggy night. The shop lights barely pierced the dense mist, which cloaked the surroundings in gloom and deepened Oliver’s sense of confusion and despair. After they had walked a short distance, a deep church bell tolled. His captors paused, listening to the sound. Nancy noted it was eight o’clock, to which Sikes retorted that he was perfectly capable of hearing it himself. Nancy wondered aloud if others could hear it, and Sikes confirmed they could, recalling how the noise from a fair had been audible even from inside his jail cell, making the silence of his confinement feel unbearable.

If you are asking for my patience and the mercy of those you have hurt, sit in that chair without another word. It has been waiting for you for two days. Monks muttered something unclear, still hesitating. You must be quick, Mr. Brownlow said. One word from me, and your chance is gone forever. The man still wavered. I have no desire to argue, Mr. Brownlow continued, and since I am protecting the interests of others, I do not have the right to. Is there no other way? Monks asked, his voice shaking. None. Monks looked at the old man, but seeing only stern resolve, he walked into the room and sat down with a shrug. Lock the door from the outside, Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, and return when I ring. The men obeyed, leaving the two alone. This is fine treatment from my father’s oldest friend, Monks said, throwing down his hat and cloak. It is precisely because I was your father’s oldest friend, Mr. Brownlow replied. It is because my hopes were tied to him and to the woman he loved, who died young and left me alone. It is because he stood with me at his sister’s deathbed when we were boys—a woman who would have been my wife had heaven willed it. My heart stayed loyal to him through all his mistakes until he died. Because of these memories, and because even seeing you brings him to mind, I am moved to treat you gently, Edward Leeford, even though I am ashamed of how you carry that name. What does the name matter? Monks asked, watching the older man’s distress with stubborn confusion. What is the name to me? Nothing to you, Mr. Brownlow replied. But it was hers, and even now, it brings back the joy I once felt just hearing it. I am very glad you changed it. This is all very dramatic, Monks said after a long silence, during which he shifted in sullen defiance while Mr. Brownlow covered his face with his hand.

You should adopt some of my philosophy. Only think of the past when remembering it brings you joy. I cannot credit you with such a philosophy. Your memories must be so free of regret that your contentment comes not from wisdom, but from ignorance. It is not so for me. Painful memories intrude, and they should not be pushed away. I have been selfish my entire life, in practice if not in principle. As a child, I knew what was right, but I was never taught to control my temper. I was given good values but left to pursue them with arrogance. As an only son, I was spoiled by parents who, though good people, encouraged me to be overbearing and to value no one outside my own circle. I looked down on the rest of the world, believing them inferior to me. I was that way from age eight until twenty-eight, and I would remain so if not for you, my dearest, loveliest Elizabeth. I owe you everything. You taught me a difficult but vital lesson. You humbled me. I approached you certain of acceptance, but you showed me how inadequate I was to please a woman like you. Had you convinced yourself I would accept you? I had. What must you think of my vanity? I believed you were hoping for my proposal. My behavior must have been at fault, though I never meant to deceive you. My high spirits often led me astray. You must have hated me after that evening. Hate you? I was angry at first, but my anger soon shifted toward myself. I am almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming? No, I felt only surprise. Your surprise could not exceed mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special treatment, and I expected nothing more than what I was owed. My goal then, Darcy replied, was to show you through every civility that I was not petty enough to resent the past. I hoped to earn your forgiveness and improve your opinion of me by showing that I had taken your criticisms to heart.

You do not know me unless you have read the book The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that does not matter. Mr. Mark Twain wrote it, and he mostly told the truth, though he exaggerated a few things. Everyone lies sometimes, except perhaps Aunt Polly, the widow, or Mary, who are all featured in that book. At the end of that story, Tom and I found the robbers' hidden money in a cave, making us both rich. We each received six thousand dollars in gold. Judge Thatcher invested it for us, earning us a dollar a day, which was more money than we knew how to spend. The Widow Douglas adopted me and tried to civilize me, but living in her house was difficult because she was so strict and proper. Eventually, I could not stand it anymore, so I ran away, put on my old rags, and lived in my sugar barrel, feeling free and happy. However, Tom Sawyer found me and promised that if I returned to the widow and acted respectable, I could join his new band of robbers. So, I went back. The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, though she meant no harm. She forced me back into those new clothes, which made me sweat and feel restricted. The old routine started again. She rang a bell for supper, and I had to be on time. Before eating, I had to wait for her to say grace over the food, even though there was nothing wrong with it, other than everything being cooked separately. I prefer when food is mixed together so the flavors blend. After dinner, she read to me from the Bible about Moses. I was interested at first, but when she mentioned that Moses had been dead for a long time, I lost interest because I do not care about dead people.

After settling our friend into his new office, we turned our attention toward Windsor. Its proximity to London made our departure from Raymond and Perdita feel less like a painful separation. We said our goodbyes at the Protectoral Palace, where it was charming to watch my sister embrace her new role with appropriate dignity. Her internal pride and humble demeanor were in constant conflict. Her shyness was genuine, stemming from a fear of being misunderstood and a sensitivity to public neglect, traits she shared with Raymond. Yet, Perdita was more considerate of others; her bashfulness often arose from a desire to ensure those around her did not feel inferior—a thought that never occurred to her. While Idris’s upbringing might have better suited her for formal ceremonies, she found such routines tedious. Conversely, despite the challenges, Perdita clearly enjoyed her position. She was so preoccupied with new ideas that she felt little pain at our departure; she said an affectionate goodbye and promised to visit, showing no regret over our separation. Raymond was in high spirits, overwhelmed by his new authority. His mind was filled with grand plans, and he vowed to his friends and the world that his time as Protector would be marked by some act of extraordinary glory. We discussed them and reflected on these changes as we returned to Windsor Castle with a smaller group. We felt immense relief to escape political turmoil and embraced our solitude with renewed enthusiasm. We remained busy, and I channeled my energy into intellectual pursuits; rigorous study proved an excellent remedy for the restlessness that idleness would have surely invited. Perdita allowed us to take Clara back to Windsor, and she, along with my two lovely children, provided constant joy. The only shadow over our peace was Adrian’s health. He was clearly declining, though without clear symptoms, unless his bright eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks signaled consumption. He remained free of pain or fear, dedicating himself to his books and finding rest in the company of his sister and me.

These occurrences weighed heavily upon Felix, making him the unhappiest of his kin when I first encountered him. He might have borne destitution with pride had it been the consequence of his integrity, but the Turk’s betrayal and the absence of his dear Safie were far more agonizing and permanent wounds. The Arabian’s appearance, however, revitalized his spirit. Once word arrived in Leghorn that Felix had lost his fortune and status, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her suitor and prepare for a return to her homeland. Safie’s noble spirit rebelled against this decree; she tried to argue, but her father departed in a rage, repeating his harsh command. Soon after, the Turk rushed into her room, claiming his presence in Leghorn had been exposed and he would soon be surrendered to the French. He had secured a ship for Constantinople, departing within hours, and intended to leave Safie with a trusted servant to follow later with his remaining assets. Left to herself, Safie contemplated her options. Living in Turkey was repulsive to her, conflicting with both her faith and her heart. Discovering documents detailing her lover’s exile and location, she eventually resolved to act. Carrying her jewels and some currency, she fled Italy with a local servant who spoke Turkish, heading for Germany. She reached a town near the De Lacey cottage, but her companion fell gravely ill and passed away. Left solitary, unable to speak the local tongue and naive to the world, Safie was fortunate. The innkeeper, having learned their intended destination from the deceased servant, ensured Safie reached her lover’s home safely.

With their agreement settled, they toasted the contract with another cup of peppermint tea, which helped calm the lady’s nerves. As she drank, she informed Mr. Bumble that the old woman had passed away. Very good, he said, sipping his drink. I will stop by Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to collect the body tomorrow. Was that what upset you, my dear? It was nothing in particular, she replied evasively. It must have been something, Mr. Bumble insisted. Won’t you tell your own B.? Not now, she said. One of these days, after we are married. After we are married! Mr. Bumble exclaimed. It was not some rude pauper, was it? No, no, my love, she quickly interrupted. If I thought any of them had dared to look at your lovely face, he continued, clenching his fist. They would not have dared, she replied. They had better not, he said. Let any man, local or otherwise, try it, and he will not do it twice. Though his words were not exactly romantic, his aggressive gestures convinced her of his devotion, and she admiringly called him a dove. The dove then turned up his collar, put on his hat, and after an affectionate embrace, stepped out into the cold night. He paused briefly in the men’s ward to insult the paupers, just to ensure he still had the necessary harshness to be a workhouse master. Satisfied with his temperament, he walked toward the undertaker’s shop, dreaming of his future promotion. Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry were out, and Noah Claypole was too lazy to close the shop, even though it was late. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane on the counter, but received no answer. Seeing a light in the back parlor, he peeked inside and was quite surprised by what he saw.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire was a man who read only the Baronetage for his own entertainment. It provided him with distraction during idle moments and comfort when troubled. His mind was stirred to admiration by the oldest titles, while domestic worries shifted to pity and disdain as he scanned the numerous creations of the previous century. If all else failed, he could always find his own history, which held his unwavering interest. The book naturally fell open to this entry: ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL. Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, Gloucestershire. By this lady, who passed away in 1800, he had issue: Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; and Mary, born November 20, 1791. This was the original printed text, but Sir Walter had updated it for his family’s benefit by adding Mary’s marriage to Charles Musgrove of Uppercross on December 16, 1810, and precisely noting the date of his wife’s death. The text continued with the standard account of the family’s origins and rise: their early settlement in Cheshire, mentions in Dugdale, service as high sheriffs, parliamentary representation, loyalty, and the baronetcy granted in the first year of Charles II, along with the names of all the women they had married. This spanned two elegant pages, ending with the family arms and motto, the location of Kellynch Hall, and Sir Walter’s own handwritten addition: Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter. Vanity defined Sir Walter Elliot’s entire character, both regarding his appearance and his social standing. He had been strikingly handsome in his youth and remained a very fine-looking man at fifty-four. Few women were as preoccupied with their looks as he was, and no valet to a newly minted lord could be more pleased with his social position. He viewed beauty as a blessing second only to his baronetcy, and as the man who possessed both, he was the constant subject of his own deepest devotion. His handsome features and high rank were well worth his affection, as they had surely secured him a wife far superior to anyone he deserved.

These representatives were sent to Adrian, the chosen mediator, traveling from Paris to Calais across empty towns and ruined landscapes while harboring intense mutual animosity, and they now argued their respective positions with fierce partisanship. Through separate interviews and thorough inquiry, we discovered the actual situation in Paris. Since parliament named him Ryland’s deputy, the remaining English had deferred to Adrian as their leader, legislator, and protector for their journey to foreign lands. Initially, our emigration plan assumed no prolonged separation, with the Earl of Windsor holding ultimate authority. However, unexpected events forced our groups to remain apart from the supreme leader for nearly two months, leading to conflict upon their arrival in Paris. They discovered Paris to be a wasteland. While early plague reports reached us, communication eventually ceased as mortality rates climbed. Even within England, travel became infrequent. Few vessels crossed the channel, and those who attempted the journey often perished at sea or succumbed to the infection before sharing news of France’s ruin. We had hoped to find many survivors abroad, but the plague had devastated France even more thoroughly than England. The road from Calais to Paris was entirely devoid of life. In Paris, only about a hundred people remained, wandering the streets or gathering to discuss the past with their characteristic, persistent spirit. The English occupied the lifeless city without resistance. A few pale residents lingered at the Tuileries, questioning why the islanders had come to their doomed city, as those suffering in misery often believe their own agony is the most severe, wishing only to trade their specific torment for any other.

Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to put you at ease. But what startled you? What were you expecting us to find? Huck was in a tight spot. The man’s gaze was fixed on him, and he would have given anything for a believable excuse. Nothing came to mind, and as the man’s eyes bored into him, he blurted out a nonsensical reply: Sunday-school books, maybe. Huck was too anxious to smile, but the old man laughed heartily, shaking with mirth, and remarked that such a laugh was worth a fortune for the health benefits. He added, Poor boy, you look pale and exhausted. You aren’t well at all, which explains why you seem a bit rattled. You will recover soon. Rest and sleep will set you right. Huck felt foolish for showing such suspicious nerves. He had stopped believing the parcel from the tavern was the treasure after hearing the conversation at the widow’s gate, but he hadn’t been certain. The mention of the bundle had caught him off guard. Still, he was relieved to know for sure that the package was not the treasure, which put his mind at ease. Everything seemed to be falling into place; the gold must still be in room number two, the men would be arrested that day, and he and Tom could claim the treasure that night without fear. Just as breakfast ended, there was a knock at the door. Huck scrambled to hide, wanting no part in the recent events. The Welshman let in several guests, including the Widow Douglas, and saw crowds of people climbing the hill to look at the gate. The news had spread. The Welshman recounted the night’s events to the visitors. The widow expressed her deep gratitude for being saved. Don’t mention it, madam, he replied. There is someone else you owe more to than me and my boys, but he doesn’t want his name revealed. We wouldn’t have been there if not for him.

Are you starving, Sir Simon? I have a sandwich in my case if you would like it. No, thank you, I do not eat, but you are much kinder than your rude, dishonest family. Stop, Virginia cried, stamping her foot. You are the rude one. You stole my paints to touch up that silly bloodstain in the library. You took my reds, my emerald green, and my yellow, leaving me only with indigo and white. I could only paint depressing moonlight scenes. I never told on you, even though emerald green blood is ridiculous. The ghost replied meekly, what else could I do? Real blood is hard to find, and since your brother started this with his detergent, I felt justified in taking your paints. As for the color, that is a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, though I know you Americans do not care for such things. You know nothing about it, Virginia countered. You should move to America to improve your mind. My father would gladly pay for your trip, and there would be no trouble at customs. You would be a huge success in New York. Many people there would pay a fortune to have a family ghost. I do not think I would like America, the ghost said. I suppose because we have no ruins or history, Virginia remarked sarcastically. No ruins? The ghost retorted. You have your navy and your manners. Good evening, Virginia said. I am going to ask my father to give the twins an extra week of holiday. Please do not go, he pleaded. I am lonely and unhappy. I want to sleep, but I cannot. That is absurd, she replied. You simply need to go to bed and blow out the candle.

He was brought to you. You understand that I am aware of the situation? That is true, Defarge replied. A subtle nudge from his wife, who continued her knitting and humming, signaled him to keep his responses brief. The spy continued, noting that the daughter had come to him and departed under his supervision, accompanied by a man named Lorry from Tellson and Company, to England. Defarge confirmed this again. The spy remarked on his acquaintance with the Doctor and his daughter in England. When asked if they heard from them, Defarge answered negatively. Madame Defarge looked up from her work, stating they had received word of their arrival and perhaps a few letters, but their paths had since diverged. The spy mentioned the daughter was to be married. Madame questioned the delay, suggesting the English were cold. The spy laughed off her comment about his nationality. He then revealed that Miss Manette was marrying a Frenchman, the nephew of the late Marquis, now known as Charles Darnay in England. Madame continued knitting, but the news clearly unsettled her husband, whose hands trembled as he lit his pipe. The spy noted this reaction carefully. Having achieved his goal, the spy paid for his drink and departed, expressing his hope to see the couple again.

He said nothing about the matter until their visitor left for the night. Once he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said, “Jane, I congratulate you. You will be a very happy woman.” Jane immediately went to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness. “You are a good girl,” he replied, “and I am pleased to think you will be so well settled. I have no doubt you will do well together. Your personalities are quite similar. You are both so agreeable that you will never make a firm decision, so easygoing that your servants will cheat you, and so generous that you will always spend more than you earn.” “I hope not,” Jane replied. “Being reckless with money would be inexcusable for me.” “Spend more than they earn? My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife cried, “what are you talking about? He has four or five thousand a year, and likely more.” Turning to her daughter, she added, “Oh, my dear Jane, I am so happy! I know I won’t sleep a wink tonight. I knew this would happen. I always said it would. I knew you couldn’t be that beautiful for nothing! I remember thinking you would end up together the moment I saw him arrive in Hertfordshire last year. He is the handsomest young man ever seen!” Wickham and Lydia were forgotten. Jane was clearly her favorite child, and for the moment, she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters soon began asking her for favors she might be able to grant in the future. Mary asked to use the library at Netherfield, and Kitty begged for a few balls there every winter. From that point on, Bingley visited Longbourn daily, often arriving before breakfast and staying until after supper, unless a neighbor forced him to attend a dinner he felt obligated to accept. Elizabeth had little time to talk with her sister, as Jane focused entirely on Bingley when he was present. However, Elizabeth proved useful to both during their brief times apart. When Jane was away, Bingley would talk to Elizabeth about her, and when Bingley left, Jane would seek out Elizabeth to talk about him. “He has made me so happy,” Jane said one evening, “by telling me he had no idea I was in town last spring!”

Well, you rascal, the elderly woman exclaimed as he walked in, why have you stayed away so long? My dear Lady Clem, I am constantly occupied, Lord Arthur replied with a smile. I assume you mean you spend your days with Miss Sybil Merton, shopping for clothes and whispering sweet nothings? I fail to see why everyone makes such a spectacle of marriage. In my youth, we never engaged in public displays of affection. I promise I have not seen Sybil in a full day, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she is entirely devoted to her dressmakers. Naturally; that is why you visit a plain old woman like me. I am surprised you men do not learn from experience. Men once acted foolishly for my sake, and now I am merely a rheumatic invalid with a wig and a sour disposition. If not for Lady Jansen sending me scandalous French novels, I would be bored to tears. Physicians are useless, save for collecting fees; they cannot even remedy my indigestion. I have brought you a remedy for that, Lady Clem, Lord Arthur said seriously. It is a remarkable invention from America. I doubt I would care for American gadgets, Arthur. I recently read some American fiction, and it was utter nonsense. This is quite practical, I assure you! You must promise to use it, Lord Arthur insisted, producing a small box from his pocket. The box is lovely, Arthur. Is it truly a gift? How kind. And this is the medicine? It resembles a candy. I shall try it immediately. Good heavens, Lady Clem! Lord Arthur exclaimed, seizing her hand. You must not. It is a homeopathic remedy, and taking it without symptoms could be dangerous. Wait for an attack, and then use it. You will be amazed by the effect. I would prefer to take it now, Lady Clementina said, examining the transparent capsule containing a bubble of liquid aconitine. I am certain it is delightful. Though I despise doctors, I adore medicine. Very well, I shall save it for my next episode. And when might that occur? Lord Arthur inquired anxiously.

Though Perdita’s name went unspoken, I knew his indecision stemmed from his love for her. Who was more worthy of his affection than my noble sister? She possessed the regal grace of a queen and loved him deeply, even as disappointment dampened her feelings and ambition conflicted with his own. We arrived at the House that evening. Raymond seemed lighthearted and carefree, despite knowing his future would be decided during the upcoming debate. A roar like a thousand swarms of bees greeted us as we entered the coffee-room. Politicians gathered in groups, their faces anxious and their voices intense. The aristocratic party, representing England’s wealthiest and most influential men, seemed calm, as the debate would proceed without their direct interference. Near the fireplace stood Ryland and his followers. Ryland, a man of humble origins who had amassed a fortune from his father’s manufacturing business, had spent his life strengthening the power of the people. Initially, he had not minded Lord Raymond’s influence, as it weakened his political rivals. Now, however, things had gone too far. The lesser nobility welcomed the return of a monarchy, hoping to regain their lost status. The spirit of royalty was reviving, and many people were eager to submit to it once more. While some stood firm as pillars of the republic, the term itself had lost its appeal to the masses, many of whom craved the glitter of a crown. Ryland was ready to fight back, declaring that he would no longer tolerate this movement and intended to sweep away the influence Raymond had gained. When Raymond entered the room, his supporters cheered. They crowded around him, calculating their strength and discussing the new members who had yet to declare their allegiance.

She would be surrounded by those who loved her and possessed better judgment than she did; sufficiently secluded for safety and busy enough to remain cheerful. She would never be tempted, nor would temptation find her. She would be respectable and happy, and Emma conceded that she was the luckiest person alive to have inspired such steady, enduring devotion in such a man—or, if not the luckiest, second only to herself. Harriet, increasingly occupied by her commitments to the Martins, spent less time at Hartfield, which was for the best.
