Their intimacy was bound to fade, shifting into a more tempered goodwill, and this natural transition was already occurring. By late September, Emma accompanied Harriet to church, watching her marry Robert Martin with a satisfaction that no memory of Mr. Elton could diminish. Indeed, she barely noticed Mr. Elton, viewing him only as the clergyman whose blessing might soon be bestowed upon her. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith were the first of the three engaged couples to wed. Jane Fairfax had left Highbury to return to the comfort of the Campbells, and the Churchills were in town, awaiting November. Emma and Mr. Knightley tentatively chose the intervening month for their own wedding, hoping to marry while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield so they could enjoy a two-week seaside trip. Everyone approved, but how could they convince Mr. Woodhouse, who still spoke of the marriage as a distant prospect? When first approached, he was so distressed that they nearly lost hope. A second mention caused less pain; he began to accept the inevitable, a promising sign of resignation. Yet he remained unhappy, and his visible misery sapped his daughter’s resolve. She could not bear to see him suffer or feel neglected. Although she largely believed the Knightleys' assurances that his distress would vanish once the wedding was over, she hesitated, unable to move forward.

Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by ghosts. The perpetrators were physical beings who made a physical escape. How, then? Fortunately, there is only one logical path to follow, and it leads to a certain conclusion. Let us consider every possible exit. It is certain the killers were in the room where the daughter was discovered, or the adjacent one, when the group climbed the stairs. We need only search those two spaces. The police inspected the floors, ceilings, and walls thoroughly; no hidden passages could have eluded them. Still, I verified this myself. There were no secret exits. Both doors opening into the hallway were locked from the inside. As for the chimneys, while wide at the base, they narrow too much to allow even a large cat to pass. Since these routes are impossible, we must look to the windows. The front windows were observed by the street crowd, so the killers must have used the back ones. Having reached this conclusion, we must not discard it due to perceived impossibilities; instead, we must demonstrate that these obstacles are not truly impossible. There are two windows in the room. One is clear and fully visible. The other is partially blocked by the head of a heavy bed. The first was locked from within and resisted all attempts to open it. A stout nail had been driven through a gimlet-hole in the frame. The second window had an identical nail, and it also refused to budge. The police, satisfied that no one had escaped that way, saw no reason to remove the nails. My own inspection was more thorough, precisely because I knew that any apparent impossibility had to be proven false.

I am going, Master Will, I really am, the man replied promptly, almost to the end now. Out to the end! Legrand shouted, are you at the end of that branch? I am almost there, master. Oh my! Goodness! What is this on the tree? Well, Legrand cried, delighted, what is it? It is nothing but a skull. Someone left their head in the tree, and the crows have eaten all the meat off it. A skull, you say? How is it attached to the branch? What is holding it there? Let me look, master. This is very strange. There is a large nail in the skull that fastens it to the tree. Now, Jupiter, listen carefully to me. Do you hear? Yes, master. Pay attention. Find the left eye of the skull. Hmm, that is difficult. There is no eye left at all. Curse your stupidity! Do you know your right hand from your left? Yes, I know that. It is my left hand that I use to chop wood. Exactly. You are left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now, can you find the left eye of the skull, or where it used to be? Have you found it? There was a long pause. Finally, the man asked, Is the left eye of the skull on the same side as the skull's left hand? Because the skull does not have any hands at all. Never mind, I have the left eye now. What should I do with it? Drop the beetle through it as far as the string will reach, but be careful not to let go of the string. That is done, Master Will. It was easy to put the bug through the hole. Look out for it down there! During this conversation, Jupiter was hidden, but the beetle soon appeared at the end of the string. It glistened like polished gold in the final rays of the setting sun. The beetle hung clear of the branches and would have landed at our feet if dropped. Legrand immediately used his scythe to clear a circular space three or four yards wide directly beneath the insect. Once finished, he ordered Jupiter to release the string and climb down.

At one point, the lieutenant inquired why he had traveled so far across the ice in such an unusual craft. His face darkened with profound sorrow as he answered, "I am searching for someone who escaped me." When asked if the man he chased used the same method of travel, he confirmed it. I mentioned that we had spotted a man on a dog-drawn sledge crossing the ice just before rescuing him. This caught his interest, and he began asking many questions about the path taken by the creature he called a dæmon. Later, when we were alone, he remarked that he had surely piqued my curiosity, yet I was too polite to pry. I agreed that it would be rude and cruel to bother him with questions, though he noted that I had saved his life. He then asked if the ice breaking might have destroyed the other sledge. I told him I could not be sure, as the ice did not fracture until late, and the traveler might have reached safety by then. Since then, a renewed vitality has stirred within the stranger. He is desperate to watch the deck for the sledge, but I have insisted he stay in the cabin, as he is too frail for the cold. I have assured him that we will alert him if anything appears. This concludes my record of these events. The stranger is recovering but remains quiet and anxious when others visit. Still, his gentle demeanor has won over the crew. I have grown to care for him like a brother, moved by his deep, persistent sadness. He must have been a remarkable man in his prime, for even in his current state, he is captivating. I once wrote to you, Margaret, that I would find no friend at sea, yet I have discovered a man whom I would have cherished as a brother had he not been so shattered by misfortune.

A few days later, Virginia and her companion were riding through Brockley meadows when she tore her riding habit on a hedge. Returning home, she attempted to sneak in through the back stairs to avoid being seen. Passing the open door of the Tapestry Chamber, she thought she saw her mother’s maid and looked in to request a repair. To her shock, the Canterville Ghost sat by the window, watching the autumn leaves drift by. He leaned his head on his hand, appearing so profoundly miserable that Virginia, despite her initial urge to flee, felt a surge of pity and decided to offer comfort. Her footsteps were so quiet and his sorrow so deep that he did not notice her until she spoke. I am sorry for you, she said, but my brothers return to school tomorrow, and if you behave, no one will bother you. It is ridiculous to ask me to behave, he replied, turning in surprise toward the girl. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and wander at night; that is my purpose. That is no reason to exist, and you know you have been wicked, she countered. Mrs. Umney told us you killed your wife. I admit it, the ghost said petulantly, but it was a private family matter. It is wrong to kill anyone, Virginia insisted with a touch of stern morality. I despise such abstract judgment, he snapped. My wife was plain, could not starch my ruffs, and was a terrible cook. She even ruined a magnificent deer I had hunted. It is all over now, though I still think it was unfair of her brothers to starve me to death in retaliation.

No imagination could capture the majesty of such a sight occurring in the dead of night; it would have resembled hell itself. Even in daylight, my hair stood on end as I peered into the yawning abyss, picturing myself wandering through those strange, vaulted halls and ghastly, glowing chasms of fire. I had narrowly escaped disaster. Had the balloon remained in the cloud a moment longer—or had I not decided to drop ballast to avoid the damp—I would have been doomed. Such dangers are often overlooked, yet they are the most severe risks of ballooning. By now, however, I had reached an altitude where I no longer feared them. By seven o'clock, my barometer showed I had climbed nine and a half miles. Breathing became difficult, and my head throbbed with intense pain. Feeling moisture on my cheeks, I realized it was blood streaming from my ears. My eyes also caused me distress; they felt as though they were bulging from their sockets, and everything I saw appeared distorted. Alarmed by these unexpected symptoms, I foolishly threw out fifteen pounds of ballast. This sudden, rapid ascent into the thin atmosphere nearly killed me. I was struck by a spasm lasting over five minutes, and even afterward, I could only gasp for air, bleeding profusely from my nose, ears, and eyes. The pigeons struggled in distress, while the cat staggered about, mewing piteously with its tongue lolling out as if poisoned. Realizing my reckless error too late, I was overcome with panic, fully expecting to die within minutes.

They are aware of his cleverness; he will be sent away for good. They will surely give the Artful a life sentence. What do you mean by lagging and a lifer? asked Mr. Bolter. Why speak in such a way to me; why not use plain language I can understand? Fagin prepared to explain these slang terms, which meant transportation for life, but the conversation was interrupted by Master Bates, who entered with his hands in his pockets and a look of mock misery on his face. It is all over, Fagin, Charley announced after being introduced to his new associate. What do you mean? They have located the owner of the snuffbox; others are coming to identify him, and the Artful is definitely being shipped off, Master Bates replied. I need a full mourning outfit and a hatband to visit him before he departs. To think of Jack Dawkins—the great Dodger—being sent away for a cheap, insignificant snuffbox! I expected him to go for a gold watch and chain at the very least. Why did he not rob a wealthy man of all his valuables and go abroad like a gentleman, rather than a common thief without honor or glory? Expressing his sympathy for his friend, Master Bates slumped into a chair, looking dejected. Why do you say he lacks honor or glory? Fagin snapped, glaring at his pupil. Was he not always the leader among you? Is there any one of you who could match his skill? Not one, Master Bates answered, his voice thick with sorrow. Then why are you complaining? Fagin demanded. Because it will not be on the record, Charley retorted, his grief turning into defiance; because it cannot be included in the indictment; because no one will ever know his true capabilities. How will he appear in the Newgate Calendar? Perhaps he will not be mentioned at all. Oh, what a terrible blow! Ha! ha! Fagin laughed, gesturing toward Mr. Bolter while shaking with a palsy-like tremor; observe the pride they take in their craft, my dear.

Certainly, he was quite entertaining, yet I felt deeply let down. When I inquired about the chainmail, he merely chuckled, claiming it was far too chilly for English weather. Oh, look, Mr. Podgers has arrived! Mr. Podgers, I insist you read the Duchess of Paisley’s palm. Duchess, please remove your glove. No, the other hand, not the left. My dear Gladys, I truly feel this is improper, the Duchess murmured, slowly unfastening a somewhat grimy kid glove. Nothing intriguing ever is, Lady Windermere replied, for that is how the world is made. Still, I must present you. Duchess, meet Mr. Podgers, my favorite palmist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley; if you claim her mount of the moon exceeds mine, I shall never trust your skills again. I am certain, Gladys, that my hand contains no such thing, the Duchess remarked solemnly. Your Grace is correct, Mr. Podgers noted, observing the small, plump hand with its stubby fingers, the mount of the moon is undeveloped. However, the life line is superb. Please flex your wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines on the rascette! You shall enjoy a long and very happy life, Duchess. Your ambition is modest, your intellect line is balanced, and your heart line— Do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers, Lady Windermere urged. Nothing would please me more, Mr. Podgers replied with a bow, had the Duchess ever been so, but I regret to observe a great constancy of affection paired with a profound sense of duty. Please continue, Mr. Podgers, the Duchess said, looking quite satisfied. Frugality is among your Grace’s many virtues, Mr. Podgers added, causing Lady Windermere to burst into laughter. Thrift is a commendable trait, the Duchess noted smugly; when I wed Paisley, he possessed eleven castles but not one habitable house. And now he owns twelve houses and not a single castle, Lady Windermere exclaimed. Well, my dear, the Duchess began, I prefer— Comfort, Mr. Podgers interjected, along with modern conveniences and hot water in every room. Your Grace is entirely right. Comfort is the sole gift our civilization offers. You have read the Duchess’s character perfectly, Mr. Podgers; now you must read Lady Flora’s. Following a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall young woman with sandy hair and prominent shoulder blades emerged awkwardly from behind the sofa, extending a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers. Ah, a pianist, I perceive, Mr. Podgers remarked, a skilled pianist, though perhaps not quite a musician.

I come from a small, cloudy island. When I think of the vast globe, my home seems like a tiny speck, yet in terms of intellectual power, it outweighs much larger and more populated nations. It is true that the human mind creates everything good and great, while nature merely serves as its assistant. England, located in the northern sea, often appears in my dreams as a massive, well-crewed ship mastering the waves. As a boy, this land was my entire universe. Standing on my native hills, looking out over the fields and homes shaped by my countrymen, I felt that this place was the center of the world, and everything else was just a story I could easily forget. My life has always demonstrated how much change can influence a person. This instability was almost an inheritance. My father was gifted with immense wit and imagination, but he lacked the reason to steer his life or the judgment to guide it. Though born into obscurity, he rose to public notice, quickly spending his small inheritance on a life of luxury. In his youth, he was adored by the elite and even the young king, who sought his company to escape the pressures of ruling. My father’s lack of self-control constantly led him into trouble, yet he used his cleverness to escape. He carried his massive debts with a light heart and constant cheer, and because the wealthy found his company so essential, they forgave his failings and showered him with flattery. However, this popularity was fleeting, and his mounting troubles soon far outpaced his ability to solve them.

I will submit to you. I see in your face that you know I have no other choice. I know you are honest. The old man kissed her, hurried her into his room, and locked the door. He then rushed back to the Doctor, opened the window and the blind, and placed a hand on the Doctor’s arm to look out into the courtyard together. They looked out at a crowd of about forty or fifty people. The guards had let them in, and they had rushed to use the grindstone, which had been set up in that secluded spot for their use. The workers and their work were terrifying. Two men turned the double-handled grindstone frantically. Their faces, revealed as their long hair whipped back, were more cruel and horrible than the wildest savages. They wore fake eyebrows and mustaches, and their faces were covered in blood and sweat, twisted by howling and wild, sleep-deprived excitement. As they turned the stone, women held wine to their mouths. Between the dripping blood, the spilled wine, and the sparks flying from the stone, the air seemed filled with gore and fire. Every person in the group was smeared with blood. Men stripped to the waist, men in rags, and men wearing stolen lace and silk ribbons all shoved each other to reach the stone, their bodies and clothes stained deep red. Hatchets, knives, bayonets, and swords were all covered in blood. Some hacked swords were tied to the owners' wrists with bloody strips of cloth. As these frantic people grabbed their sharpened weapons and tore into the streets, their eyes burned with the same red frenzy—eyes that any decent person would have given twenty years of their life to stop forever.

When Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, purchased Canterville Chase, everyone warned him he was making a mistake, as the property was undoubtedly haunted. Lord Canterville, a man of strict integrity, felt obligated to mention this during their negotiations. We have avoided living there ourselves, Lord Canterville explained, ever since my great-aunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, suffered a permanent shock when two skeletal hands touched her shoulders while she dressed for dinner. I must inform you that the ghost has been sighted by several family members and the local rector, Reverend Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. Following the Duchess’s incident, our younger staff refused to stay, and Lady Canterville frequently lost sleep due to mysterious noises in the library and corridor. My Lord, the Minister replied, I will take the furniture and the ghost at a fair price. I come from a modern nation where money buys everything. Given how our energetic young men are currently taking over the Old World and courting your finest actresses, I suspect that if a ghost truly existed in Europe, we would have already moved it to an American museum or put it on tour. I fear the ghost is real, Lord Canterville said with a smile, though it has eluded your enterprising showmen. It has been documented for three centuries, since 1584, and always appears before a family death. So does the family doctor, Lord Canterville. But ghosts do not exist, and I doubt the laws of nature are suspended for the British aristocracy. You are certainly very direct in America, Lord Canterville replied, clearly missing the point. If you do not mind a ghost, that is fine, but remember that I warned you. Weeks later, the sale was finalized, and at the end of the season, the Minister and his family moved to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, formerly the celebrated New York socialite Lucretia R. Tappan, was now a striking, middle-aged woman with beautiful eyes and a refined profile.

The day unfolded much like the previous one. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent part of the morning with the recovering patient, and that evening, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room. There was no card table set up. Mr. Darcy sat writing while Miss Bingley hovered nearby, frequently interrupting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley played piquet, watched by Mrs. Hurst. Elizabeth occupied herself with needlework, finding amusement in the interaction between Darcy and Miss Bingley. The lady’s constant praise of his penmanship and the indifference with which he met her remarks created a fascinating exchange that perfectly matched Elizabeth’s assessment of both individuals. How pleased Miss Darcy will be to get such a letter, she remarked. He did not reply. You write quite quickly, she noted. You are wrong, he said, I write rather slowly. Think of the many letters you must write annually, including business correspondence; how dreadful I should find that. It is fortunate, then, that the task falls to me rather than you, he replied. Please tell your sister I am eager to see her, she said. I have already conveyed that, as you requested, he answered. I fear you dislike your pen; let me mend it, as I am quite skilled at it. Thank you, but I always mend my own, he said. How do you manage to write so evenly? she asked. He remained silent. Tell your sister I am thrilled to hear of her harp progress and that I adore her table design, which is far better than Miss Grantley’s. May I postpone your enthusiasm until my next letter? I lack the space to do it justice now, he replied. It does not matter, as I shall see her in January, she said, but do you always write such delightful, lengthy letters to her, Mr. Darcy? They are usually long, he said, though whether they are delightful is not for me to judge. It is my belief that anyone who writes long letters with ease must write well, she stated. That is no compliment to Darcy, Caroline, her brother interjected, because he does not write with ease; he labors over his four-syllable words, do you not, Darcy? My writing style is quite unlike yours, he replied. Oh, Miss Bingley exclaimed, Charles writes in the most haphazard fashion imaginable.

He climbed onto the spirited steed that had carried him to triumph in Greece, exhausting himself with strenuous activity to drown his mental anguish in physical exertion. Gradually, he regained his composure, emerging from the haze of fever and obsession like one recovering from a toxin to find clarity in quiet thought. He considered his next steps, struck by how much time had passed while his actions were driven by insanity rather than reason. A month had vanished, and in that interval, he had not visited Evadne. Her influence, which had never truly taken root in his heart, had significantly waned. He was no longer bound to her as a lover or a servant; he resolved to avoid her entirely, hoping his total reformation would earn him Perdita’s trust. Yet, his imagination drifted to the Greek girl’s wretched dwelling—a place she had chosen to inhabit out of noble principle rather than accept a more luxurious life. He recalled her former splendor in Constantinople, contrasted with her current poverty, her grueling labor, and her hollow, gaunt features. Pity filled him; he decided to see her one last time to arrange for her restoration to society before parting ways permanently. He then reflected on his month of avoiding Perdita, a flight prompted by his own guilty conscience. Now fully alert, he vowed to correct his behavior and ensure his future devotion would erase this temporary stain on their happiness. Feeling optimistic, he mapped out his path. He recalled his promise to attend a festival that evening, October 19th, celebrating his election as Protector. He viewed this event as a positive omen for their future. He would briefly visit Evadne to offer some explanation for his long silence, then return to Perdita, his social obligations, and the exercise of his power. Following the events previously described, Perdita had anticipated a complete shift in Raymond’s demeanor. She looked forward to open communication and the restoration of the affectionate intimacy that had once defined their lives.

I am going, Master Will, I truly am, the man replied promptly. I am almost at the end now. At the end? Legrand shouted. Do you mean the end of that branch? I will be there soon, master. Oh, Lord have mercy! What is this on the tree? Well, Legrand cried, delighted, what is it? It is nothing but a skull. Someone left their head up here, and the crows have picked it clean. A skull? Very well. How is it attached to the branch? I must look, master. This is a curious circumstance. There is a large nail in the skull, pinning it to the tree. Jupiter, listen to me carefully. Do you hear? Yes, master. Pay attention. Find the left eye of the skull. There is no eye left at all. Curse your stupidity! Do you know your left hand from your right? Yes, I know that. It is the hand I use to chop wood. Exactly. Your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Can you find the left eye now? After a long pause, the man asked, Is the skull's left eye on the same side as its left hand? It does not have any hands. Never mind, I have the left eye now. What should I do with it? Drop the beetle through it as far as the string reaches, but do not let go of the string. That is done, Master Will. It was easy to put the bug through the hole. Look out below! Jupiter remained hidden, but the beetle descended, glistening like polished gold in the final rays of the setting sun. It hung clear of the branches, directly above our feet. Legrand used his scythe to clear a circular space three or four yards wide beneath the insect, then ordered Jupiter to release the string and climb down.

He was short but stood remarkably straight, and his voice was the most pleasant I had ever heard. He began his lecture by summarizing the history of chemistry and the advancements made by various scholars, speaking with passion about the most notable discoverers. He then gave a brief overview of the current state of the field and explained its basic terminology. After performing a few preliminary experiments, he concluded with a tribute to modern chemistry that I will never forget: The ancient teachers of this science promised the impossible and achieved nothing. Modern masters promise very little; they know metals cannot be transmuted and the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these scientists, whose hands seem meant only for dirt and whose eyes for microscopes or crucibles, have truly performed miracles. They delve into nature’s secrets, revealing how she works in her hidden places. They reach into the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and nearly limitless powers; they can command lightning, mimic earthquakes, and even replicate the invisible world with its own shadows. These were the professor’s words—or rather, the words of fate—spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were wrestling with a tangible enemy. One by one, the various components of my being were triggered; chord after chord was struck, and soon my mind was consumed by a single thought, a single purpose. So much has been done, my soul cried out—I will achieve far more. Following the path already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and reveal the deepest mysteries of creation to the world. I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in a state of rebellion and turmoil; I felt that order would eventually emerge, but I lacked the power to create it. Gradually, after dawn, sleep arrived. I awoke, and my thoughts from the night before felt like a dream. Only a resolution remained to return to my former studies and dedicate myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. That same day, I visited M. Waldman. His private manner was even more gentle and engaging than his public one, for the dignity he held during his lecture was replaced in his home by the greatest warmth and kindness.

He had been entirely unaware of his own influence. He followed her into the shrubbery without any plan to test it. Anxious to see how she handled Frank Churchill’s engagement, he arrived with no selfish agenda, hoping only to offer comfort or advice if she allowed it. The rest happened in an instant, driven by his immediate reaction to her words. The delightful realization that she felt nothing for Frank Churchill and that her heart was free sparked the hope that he might eventually win her affection. He had not expected immediate success; in a moment where eagerness overcame judgment, he only wanted her permission to try to win her over. The greater hopes that soon emerged were all the more enchanting. The love he had hoped to cultivate was already his. In half an hour, he had moved from deep distress to something indistinguishable from perfect happiness. Her transformation was just as profound. This brief time gave them both the precious certainty of being loved, clearing away their mutual ignorance, jealousy, and distrust. He had long been jealous, dating back to the arrival or even the anticipation of Frank Churchill. His love for Emma and his jealousy of Churchill had grown together, each emotion revealing the other. It was this jealousy that had driven him to leave the area; the Box Hill outing convinced him to go. He wanted to avoid witnessing such encouraged flirtations and hoped to learn indifference. However, he went to the wrong place. His brother’s home was filled with domestic happiness, and the women there were too amiable. Isabella reminded him so much of Emma—though lacking her brilliance—that he could not move on. He stayed stubbornly until the morning mail brought news of Jane Fairfax. Feeling a relief he did not hesitate to embrace, as he never believed Churchill deserved Emma, his concern for her became too intense to ignore. He rode home through the rain and walked over immediately after dinner to see how this wonderful woman, perfect despite her flaws, was handling the news.

To look at him was to imagine he had been struck by a divine curse. He stood frozen, his face a mask of marble sorrow. Having spent his youth in privileged, carefree luxury, he was suddenly confronted by the crushing weight of fate. It felt monstrous and insane. Was his future truly written in the lines of his palm, a hidden record of sin he could not decipher? Was he merely a pawn moved by unseen forces, a vessel shaped by a potter’s whim? His mind rebelled, yet he felt a looming tragedy, an unbearable burden placed upon him. Actors are lucky; they choose their roles, whether to laugh or weep. In reality, people are forced into parts they are ill-equipped to play. The world is a stage, but the casting is disastrous. Suddenly, Mr. Podgers entered. Seeing Lord Arthur, he recoiled, his face turning a sickly, jaundiced hue. They locked eyes in a tense silence. The Duchess left her glove, and I have come to retrieve it, Podgers said, spotting it on the sofa. Good evening. Mr. Podgers, I insist you answer my question directly. Another time, Lord Arthur; the Duchess is waiting. You are not leaving. The Duchess can wait. Ladies are often impatient, Podgers replied with a nauseating smile. Lord Arthur curled his lip in disdain; the Duchess meant nothing to him now. He approached Podgers and held out his hand. Tell me what you saw, he demanded. Tell me the truth. I am not a child.

Saturday at noon, I visited the well to observe. Merlin was still burning incense, waving his arms, and muttering nonsense, though he looked discouraged, having failed to produce even a drop of water. I asked him how things were progressing. He replied that he was attempting the most powerful Eastern enchantment, and if that failed, nothing would work, so I should remain silent. He produced a massive cloud of smoke that drifted toward the hermits' dens, followed by frantic gestures and chanting. After twenty minutes, he collapsed, exhausted. The abbot, a crowd of monks, nuns, pilgrims, and orphans arrived, drawn by the spectacle. When the abbot asked for results, Merlin claimed he had used the strongest magic possible. He declared that a spirit whose name cannot be spoken had cursed the well, and since no mortal could uncover the secret of that spell, the water was gone forever. He asked to be excused. The abbot, clearly distressed, turned to me and asked if it were true. I told him part of it was. When he pressed me, I confirmed that the spirit had indeed cursed the well. The abbot cried out in despair, fearing they were ruined. I suggested it was only a possibility. When he asked if that meant Merlin was wrong about the spell being unbreakable, I explained that while Merlin was mistaken, there remained a small, slim chance of success under the right conditions.

Do you intend to play? The spy turned toward Mr. Lorry with a servile air, suggesting that a man of his age and kindness might convince his younger companion that playing the mentioned Ace was beneath his station. He acknowledged his own disreputable role as a spy, yet questioned why a gentleman would stoop to such behavior. Carton checked his watch and replied that he would play his Ace without hesitation in a few moments. When the spy attempted to invoke respect for his sister, Carton countered that he could show no greater respect for her than by removing her brother from her life. The spy faltered, unable to penetrate Carton’s inscrutable demeanor. Carton then mused aloud about another card, asking after the associate who claimed to frequent the prisons. The spy quickly dismissed the man as a Frenchman of no importance. Carton repeated the words mechanically, claiming to recognize the face. Despite the spy’s denials, Carton suddenly realized the man was Cly, whom they had previously encountered at the Old Bailey. Barsad smiled, his nose tilting, and remarked that Carton was being hasty and granting him an advantage.

On the morning scheduled for Admiral and Mrs. Croft to tour Kellynch Hall, Anne felt it best to walk to Lady Russell’s house to avoid the encounter, only to regret missing the chance to meet them afterward. The meeting was a success, settling the matter immediately. Both women were eager to agree, viewing each other with mutual favor. The Admiral’s genuine, open-hearted nature impressed Sir Walter, who had been further flattered by Mr. Shepherd’s claims that the Admiral considered him a paragon of refinement. The house, grounds, and terms were all accepted without a single dispute, and the legal paperwork began immediately. Sir Walter declared the Admiral the most presentable sailor he had ever encountered, noting that with a better barber, he would be quite acceptable in public. Meanwhile, the Admiral remarked to his wife that the Baronet was harmless, if not particularly brilliant. These mutual assessments were equally balanced. The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas, and since Sir Walter planned to move to Bath the month before, preparations began in earnest. Lady Russell, knowing Anne would have no say in choosing their new home, hoped she might stay behind until after Christmas. However, Lady Russell had her own travel plans, and Anne, despite dreading the heat of Bath and mourning the loss of the autumn season in the country, ultimately felt it was best to leave.

Without pausing to think, and feeling a jumble of emotions, Elizabeth finished the first letter and immediately tore open the second, which had been written a day later. My dearest sister, you have likely received my first hurried note by now. I hope this one is clearer, though my mind is so overwhelmed that I cannot promise to be coherent. I have terrible news that cannot wait. As foolish as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate for it to be true, because we fear they never went to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday from Brighton. Although Lydia’s note to Mrs. Forster suggested they were heading to Gretna Green, a comment from Mr. Denny made the Colonel suspect that Wickham never intended to marry her at all. The Colonel immediately set out to track them. He followed them as far as Clapham, but there they switched to a public carriage and vanished. They were last seen heading toward London. I do not know what to think. After searching near London, the Colonel came to Hertfordshire to check the roads, but he found no trace of them. He then came to Longbourn to share his fears with us, acting with great kindness. I feel for him and his wife, but they are not to blame. We are in deep distress. Mother and Father fear the worst, but I cannot think so poorly of Wickham. Perhaps they chose to marry privately in London instead. Even if Wickham were capable of such a scheme, I cannot believe Lydia would be so foolish. Still, I am saddened that the Colonel does not share my hope; he shook his head and admitted he does not trust Wickham.

That served as sufficient encouragement. "Well, my dear, you should be aware that Mrs. Long reports Netherfield has been rented by a wealthy young gentleman from northern England. He arrived Monday in a carriage drawn by four horses to inspect the property, was quite pleased, and promptly reached an agreement with Mr. Morris. He intends to move in before Michaelmas, with his staff arriving late next week." "What is he called?" "Bingley." "Is he a bachelor?" "Certainly, my dear, he is single! A wealthy bachelor with an income of four or five thousand annually. What a wonderful prospect for our daughters!" "In what way? How does that concern them?" "My dear Mr. Bennet," his wife answered, "how can you be so exasperating? You know perfectly well I am considering him as a husband for one of them." "Is that his intention in moving here?" "Intention? Absurd, how can you say such things! Still, he might very well fall for one of them, so you must call upon him upon his arrival." "I see no reason for that. You and the girls can go, or perhaps send them alone, which might be better; since you remain as attractive as any of them, Mr. Bingley might prefer you to the rest." "You flatter me, my dear. I have certainly enjoyed my share of beauty, but I do not claim to be remarkable now. Once a woman has five adult daughters, she should stop dwelling on her own looks." "In such instances, a woman rarely has much beauty left to dwell upon." "Regardless, you must visit Mr. Bingley once he settles in the area." "I cannot promise that, I assure you." "But think of your daughters. Consider what a match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas intend to go for that reason alone, as they typically do not visit newcomers. You must go, for we cannot visit him otherwise." "You are being overly cautious. I am certain Mr. Bingley will be pleased to see you; I will provide a note confirming my full approval for him to marry whichever girl he prefers, though I must put in a good word for my dear Lizzy." "I forbid you from doing any such thing. Lizzy is no better than the others; she is certainly not as pretty as Jane, nor as cheerful as Lydia."

Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, began to wonder if an honest life was truly better. Deciding that it was, he left his past behind, determined to start fresh. He struggled and suffered for a while, but thanks to his cheerful nature and clear goals, he eventually succeeded. After working as a farmhand and a delivery boy, he is now the happiest young cattle farmer in all of Northamptonshire. My hand trembles as I reach the end of this story, wishing I could continue the narrative a little longer. I would love to stay with these characters and describe their happiness. I would show Rose Maylie in her graceful womanhood, bringing warmth and light to everyone around her. I would depict her as the heart of her family, following her through sunny fields and listening to her gentle voice on moonlit walks. I would watch her kindness toward others and her dedication at home, seeing her and her sister’s child share their love and memories of those they lost. I would bring back those happy children gathered at her knee and recall her clear laughter and compassionate tears. I wish I could capture every one of those moments. How Mr. Brownlow educated his adopted son, growing closer to him as the boy’s character blossomed, and how he saw reminders of his old friend in the boy’s actions—bringing him both sadness and comfort—is clear. How the two orphans, shaped by hardship, practiced mercy, love, and gratitude toward the One who protected them, are all things that need not be explained.

This must have been the period of Mr. Elliot’s life that has always piqued my curiosity, Anne remarked. It was around the time he first met my father and sister. I never met him myself, only heard of him, but his behavior toward them and the circumstances of his marriage never quite aligned with the man I see today. It suggested a completely different character. I know everything, Mrs. Smith exclaimed. He was introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, but he spoke of them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, yet he chose not to go. I can clarify things you would not expect, and I knew all about his marriage at the time. I was the friend he confided in regarding his hopes and plans. Although I did not know his wife beforehand—her lower social standing made that impossible—I knew her for the rest of her life and can answer any questions you have. No, Anne said, I have no specific questions about her. I always understood they were unhappy. I only want to know why he avoided my father’s acquaintance back then, when my father was clearly inclined to treat him with kindness. Why did he pull away? At that time, Mrs. Smith replied, Mr. Elliot had one goal: to make his fortune, and faster than a legal career would allow. He was determined to marry for money and avoid an imprudent match. He believed—rightly or wrongly—that your father and sister were trying to arrange a marriage between the heir and your sister, which did not fit his plans for wealth and independence. That was his reason for withdrawing, I assure you. He told me the entire story; he kept no secrets from me. It is ironic that after leaving you in Bath, my first major acquaintance upon marrying was your cousin, and through him, I constantly heard about your father and sister.

Emma Woodhouse, beautiful, intelligent, and wealthy, possessed a pleasant residence and a cheerful nature, appearing to enjoy life's finest gifts; she had spent nearly twenty-one years with almost nothing to trouble her. She was the younger daughter of a doting, lenient father, and following her sister's wedding, she had managed his household from a young age. Her mother had passed away when she was too small to recall much of her, and her role was filled by a wonderful governess who loved her like a parent. Miss Taylor had spent sixteen years with the Woodhouse family, acting more as a companion than a teacher, especially to Emma. Their bond resembled that of sisters. Even while Miss Taylor held her official title, her gentle nature prevented her from being strict, and with that authority long gone, they lived as devoted friends, with Emma following her own inclinations while valuing Miss Taylor's advice. The true drawbacks of Emma's life were her tendency to have her own way and a slight inclination toward vanity; these were the only flaws in her otherwise fortunate existence. Currently, she did not view these traits as problematic. Sorrow arrived, though it was mild and lacked any sense of personal regret. Miss Taylor married, and this loss caused Emma's first real sadness. After the wedding guests departed, Emma and her father dined alone, facing a long, quiet evening. As her father napped after the meal, she reflected on her loss. The marriage promised happiness for her friend, as Mr. Weston was a man of excellent character, comfortable means, and agreeable personality. Emma found some comfort in knowing she had selflessly encouraged the union, yet the day felt bleak. She would miss Miss Taylor constantly. She remembered sixteen years of affection, recalling how her friend had taught and played with her since she was five, dedicating herself to her amusement and caring for her through every childhood illness.

Consequently, I determined to disembark the moment we reached the town to escape his presence. I managed this plan easily. My small suitcase rested in the boot beneath my feet; I simply unlatched a hinge to retrieve it, dropped it to the ground, and followed, finding myself at the initial streetlamp on the town's edge. The convicts continued with the coach, and I understood where they would be taken to the river. In my mind, I pictured the boat with its prisoner crew waiting at the muddy steps, heard the harsh command to row, and envisioned the sinister vessel anchored on the dark water. I could not name my fear, as it remained formless and vague, yet I felt deeply unsettled. Walking toward the hotel, I sensed a dread far beyond the simple worry of an awkward encounter, which made me shake. I am certain it lacked a clear form, representing merely a brief resurgence of childhood terror. The Blue Boar's coffee-room was vacant, and I had already ordered and begun my meal before the waiter recognized me. After apologizing for his lapse in memory, he inquired if he should fetch Mr. Pumblechook. I refused firmly. The waiter, who had delivered the Commercials' complaint when I was apprenticed, seemed startled and promptly placed a grimy local newspaper before me. I picked it up and read a notice: Our readers will be interested to learn regarding the recent fortunate rise of a local blacksmith—a subject for our poet TOOBY—that the youth's first mentor and friend was a respected figure in the corn and seed trade, whose business is located near the High Street. We take pride in noting him as the guide to our young Telemachus, as it is heartening that our town fostered the architect of his success.

I went from shop to shop, buying what was needed to change his appearance. Once finished, I headed to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but stood up as I entered, moving to stand before his fireplace. "Now, Pip," he warned, "be careful." "I will, sir," I replied, having prepared my words. "Don't commit yourself," Jaggers said, "and don't commit anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don't tell me anything; I don't want to know, and I am not curious." It was clear he knew the man had arrived. "I only want to confirm what I have been told is true," I said. "I have no hope it is false, but I must verify it." Jaggers nodded. "Did you say 'told' or 'informed'?" he asked, tilting his head to listen to the floor. "'Told' implies verbal communication, and you cannot speak to a man in New South Wales." "I will say 'informed,' Mr. Jaggers." "Good." "I have been informed by Abel Magwitch that he is my long-unknown benefactor." "That is the man," Jaggers confirmed, "in New South Wales." "And only him?" I asked. "Only him." "I am not unreasonable enough to hold you responsible for my mistakes, but I always assumed it was Miss Havisham." "As you say, Pip," Jaggers replied, eyeing me coolly while biting his finger, "I am not responsible for that." "And yet it seemed so likely," I pleaded, feeling discouraged. "Not a shred of evidence, Pip," Jaggers said, shaking his head. "Never judge by appearances; judge by evidence. There is no better rule." "I have nothing more to say," I sighed after a silence. "I have verified the information, and that is the end of it." "And now that Magwitch has revealed himself," Jaggers continued, "you understand how strictly I have always adhered to the facts in our dealings. There has never been the slightest deviation. You are aware of that?" "Quite, sir." "I warned Magwitch when he first wrote to me from New South Wales that he must never expect me to deviate from the strict truth."

While reaching through the valve with water for the cat, my shirt sleeve caught the loop supporting the basket, instantly detaching it. The basket vanished from view as if it had dissolved into thin air. Less than a tenth of a second passed between the release and its total disappearance. I wished them well, though I held no expectation that the cat or her kittens would survive the fall. By six o'clock, I noticed a large section of the earth to the east shrouded in shadow, which spread quickly until the entire visible surface was cloaked in night by five minutes to seven. The setting sun continued to light the balloon long after this, a predictable yet deeply satisfying sight. It was clear that I would witness the sunrise hours before the people of Rotterdam, despite their more easterly position, and that my increased altitude would grant me progressively longer days. I resolved to record my journey, counting days as continuous twenty-four-hour periods regardless of darkness. At ten, feeling tired, I prepared to sleep, but a glaring problem occurred to me: how would the air in the cabin be refreshed while I rested? Breathing the same air for more than an hour or so would be impossible, potentially leading to fatal results. This realization caused me significant alarm; it may seem strange that after surviving so many perils, I would view this issue so gravely that I considered abandoning my mission and descending. Yet, this doubt lasted only a moment.

I walked quickly, reaching my college soon. I shivered, suddenly realizing the creature I left in my apartment might still be there. I dreaded seeing the monster, but feared even more that Henry might encounter him. Asking him to wait at the stairs, I rushed to my room. My hand was on the lock before I paused, trembling. I threw the door open, expecting a ghost, but the room was empty. Relieved, I ran back to Clerval. We went upstairs, but I could not contain my agitation. My pulse raced, and I paced frantically, laughing loudly. Clerval initially thought I was just happy to see him, but my wild eyes and hysterical laughter soon alarmed him. Victor, what is wrong? he asked. You look ill. Do not ask, I cried, shielding my eyes as I imagined the monster entering. Save me! I felt the creature grab me, struggled, and collapsed. Poor Clerval; our reunion had turned into a nightmare. I remained unconscious, unaware of his distress. This began a nervous fever that lasted months. Henry nursed me alone, shielding my father and Elizabeth from the truth of my condition.

What kind of life would they have while fate kept this terrifying fortune hanging in the balance? The wedding had to be delayed at any cost. He was firm on this. As much as he loved her—and the simple touch of her hand sent thrills through him—he saw his duty clearly. He had no right to marry until he had committed the murder. Once that was done, he could stand at the altar with Sybil Merton and offer her his life without fear of guilt. He could hold her, knowing she would never have to feel shame because of him. It had to be done, and the sooner, the better. Many men might have chosen an easy life over duty, but Lord Arthur was too principled to put pleasure first. His love was more than just passion; Sybil represented everything noble. Though he felt a brief, natural revulsion toward the task, it quickly faded. His heart told him it was a sacrifice, not a sin, and his reason confirmed there was no other way. He had to choose between his own desires and the needs of others. Though the task was horrific, he refused to let selfishness win. Everyone faces this choice eventually, but it came to him early, before cynicism or vanity could corrupt him. He did not hesitate. Fortunately, he was not a dreamer or a dilettante. Had he been, he might have wavered like Hamlet. Instead, he was practical. To him, life meant action, not just thought; he possessed the rare gift of common sense. The chaotic emotions of the previous night had vanished, and he looked back on his frantic wandering and agony with a sense of shame. His past suffering now felt unreal, and he wondered how he could have been so foolish as to despair over the inevitable.

I truly wish we owned a donkey. It would be ideal for Jane, Miss Bates, and myself to arrive on donkeys, with my dear husband walking alongside. I must discuss buying one with him. In the country, I consider it essential; regardless of a woman's interests, she cannot remain confined indoors forever, and long walks are plagued by summer dust and winter mud. You will encounter neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane remains free of dust and is currently quite dry. Nevertheless, arrive by donkey if you prefer; you are welcome to borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I want everything to suit your preferences. I am certain of that, and I truly appreciate your kindness. Despite your somewhat dry and blunt demeanor, I recognize your deeply affectionate heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are quite the eccentric. Believe me, Knightley, I am fully aware of your consideration in arranging this plan. It is exactly what I desired. Mr. Knightley had another motive for avoiding a shaded table. He hoped to convince Mr. Woodhouse to attend, knowing that dining outdoors would surely make the elderly man ill. He had to ensure Mr. Woodhouse was not lured into discomfort under the guise of a pleasant morning excursion. The invitation was genuine, and Mr. Woodhouse agreed. He had not visited Donwell in two years. He reasoned that on a fine morning, he, Emma, and Harriet could visit; he would sit with Mrs. Weston while the young women explored the gardens, assuming the ground was dry. He was eager to see the estate again and pleased to meet the Eltons and other neighbors. He found no fault in the plan, praising Mr. Knightley’s invitation as thoughtful and far superior to dining out, which he disliked. Mr. Knightley’s proposal met with universal approval. Everyone accepted the invitation as a personal compliment. Emma and Harriet expressed great anticipation, and Mr. Weston volunteered to bring Frank along, a gesture of gratitude that Mr. Knightley could have done without. Consequently, Mr. Knightley was forced to welcome the idea, and Mr. Weston promised to write immediately to persuade Frank to attend.

Lay down your weapons, brothers! Forgiveness, help, and friendship await your change of heart. You are precious to us because you share our fragile human form; each of you will find a friend among these ranks. Why should man fight man while the plague, our common enemy, looms over us, thriving on our slaughter and proving more cruel than we are? Both armies hesitated. On our side, soldiers gripped their weapons tightly, eyeing the enemy with stern resolve. The opposing troops had not dropped their arms, driven more by fear than a desire to fight; they looked to one another for a lead, but they had no commander. Adrian dismounted and approached a fallen soldier. He is a man, he cried, and he is dead. Quickly, bind the wounds of the fallen. Do not let another soul escape through your brutal cuts to tell God of this fratricide. Cast aside your savage hearts and drop these tools of hate. In this moment of shared destiny, let every man be a brother and guardian to the next. Discard those blood-stained weapons and help treat these wounds. As he spoke, he knelt and lifted a man whose lifeblood was pouring out. The poor soul gasped, and in the sudden silence of both armies, his moans were clearly heard. Every heart, recently set on massacre, now beat with anxious hope for this one man. Adrian tore off his scarf to bind the wound, but it was too late. The man sighed, his head fell back, and his body went limp. He is dead, Adrian said, bowing his head in sorrow. The fate of the world seemed tied to this single death. On both sides, soldiers dropped their weapons. Even the veterans wept, and our men reached out to their foes, filled with a sudden, profound sense of unity. The two forces merged, unarmed and hand in hand, discussing how to help one another. Regretting their past cruelty and recent violence, they followed the General’s orders to march toward London.

Further chances to observe them were inevitable. Anne spent enough time with the quartet to form her own conclusions, though she kept them to herself, knowing they would please neither spouse. While Louisa appeared to be the favorite, Anne suspected Captain Wentworth was not truly in love with either sister. Their feelings were merely a fleeting infatuation, though they might eventually lead to genuine affection. Charles Hayter seemed to sense his own neglect, yet Henrietta remained indecisive. Anne wished she could warn them of the potential consequences, though she believed none of them acted with malice. It comforted her to think the Captain was oblivious to the distress he caused; he showed no arrogance and likely remained ignorant of Charles Hayter’s prior claims. His only fault lay in welcoming the dual attentions of both young women. Eventually, Charles Hayter retreated. Three days passed without a visit, and he even declined a dinner invitation. When Mr. Musgrove found him buried in books, the family worried he was overworking himself. Mary hoped Henrietta had rejected him, while her husband expected his return daily. Anne simply thought Charles Hayter was acting prudently. One morning, while the men were out shooting, the sisters from the Great House visited the cottage. It was a beautiful November day, and the Miss Musgroves arrived merely to announce a long walk, assuming Mary would decline. When Mary insisted on joining them out of pride, Anne could see the sisters were disappointed. She marveled at the family’s rigid habit of sharing every activity, regardless of whether it was truly welcome or convenient.

Daylight arrived as I set the manuscript aside. The rain had nearly stopped, leaving the world gray and somber as the spent storm sighed itself into silence. I went to the stranger's room and listened at his door, which stood slightly open. Hearing his voice, I knocked, but received no response. I peeked inside to find him lying on his back, speaking in fragmented, spirited bursts while his arms thrashed with the restlessness of delirium. I entered quietly and leaned over him. As his muttering continued, I spoke a single word to catch his attention. His glassy eyes and pale face instantly brightened with joy and relief. Oh, Sandy, you have finally come. I have missed you so much. Sit by me and never leave again. Give me your hand; let me hold it. Now everything is peaceful and I am happy once more. You seem like a faint mist, but you are here, and that is enough. Don't pull away; I won't need it for long. Was that the child? Hello, Central? She doesn't answer. Bring her when she wakes so I can touch her hair and say goodbye. Sandy, you are still there. I drifted off and feared you had left. Have I been sick long? It feels like months. I have had such strange, terrifying dreams that felt entirely real. I dreamt the king was dead, that you were trapped in Gaul, and that a revolution had broken out. In my fever, I imagined Clarence and I fought and destroyed the entire chivalry of England. Even stranger, I felt like a man from a distant, future age. I seemed to have traveled back and forth through time, stranded as a lonely stranger in that foreign England, with thirteen centuries separating me from you, my home, and everything that makes life worth living.

You have nurtured an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am, unsuitable for his station; the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, being practical philosophers, will confirm this. What business have paupers with soul or spirit? It is sufficient that we permit them living bodies. Had you fed the boy only gruel, ma’am, this would not have occurred. Dear, dear! exclaimed Mrs. Sowerberry, piously lifting her eyes to the ceiling: this is the result of being generous! Mrs. Sowerberry’s generosity to Oliver had involved giving him all the scraps no one else would consume; thus, there was significant humility in her accepting Mr. Bumble’s harsh accusation, of which she was entirely innocent. Ah! said Mr. Bumble, once the lady looked down again; the only remaining option is to leave him in the cellar until he is sufficiently starved, then keep him on gruel throughout his apprenticeship. He comes from a bad family. Excitable natures, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both the nurse and doctor noted that his mother reached this place despite hardships that would have killed any decent woman weeks earlier. At this, Oliver, hearing enough to realize his mother was being discussed, resumed kicking with such force that all other sounds were drowned out. Sowerberry returned at this moment. After the ladies explained Oliver’s offense with exaggerations meant to provoke him, he quickly unlocked the cellar door and dragged his rebellious apprentice out by the collar. Oliver’s clothes were torn from the beating; his face was bruised and scratched, and his hair hung over his forehead. The angry flush remained, however, and as he was pulled from his prison, he glared defiantly at Noah, appearing entirely undaunted. Now, you are a fine young man, aren’t you? said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and boxing his ear. He insulted my mother, Oliver replied. Well, what if he did, you ungrateful wretch? said Mrs. Sowerberry. She deserved what he said, and worse. She did not, said Oliver. She did, said Mrs. Sowerberry. It is a lie! said Oliver. Mrs. Sowerberry began to weep profusely. This outburst left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Had he hesitated to punish Oliver severely, it would be clear to any experienced reader that he would have been, by all established marital precedents, a brute, an unnatural husband, and a base imitation of a man.

On Saturday at noon, I visited the well to watch. Merlin was still burning powders, waving his arms, and muttering nonsense, though he looked discouraged since he had not even dampened the well. I asked him how things were going. He replied that he was using the most powerful Eastern enchantment and demanded silence until he finished. He created a massive cloud of smoke that drifted toward the hermits, followed by more chanting and wild gestures. After twenty minutes, he collapsed, exhausted. Soon, the abbot, hundreds of monks and nuns, and a large crowd of pilgrims and orphans arrived, drawn by the smoke. When the abbot asked for the results, Merlin claimed he had used his strongest magic and failed. He declared that a powerful, nameless spirit had cursed the well, making it impossible for any mortal to restore the water. He asked to leave, claiming he had done all he could. The abbot was distressed and turned to me, asking if it was true. I told him part of it was. When he asked which part, I confirmed that the spirit had indeed cursed the well. The abbot cried out in despair, but I suggested that Merlin was not necessarily right about the spell being unbreakable. I explained that under certain conditions, there might still be a small chance of success.

Rising at dawn and once more eluding my creditors, I hurried to the bookseller to spend my remaining cash on texts regarding Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. Back home, I studied these volumes diligently, quickly gaining the expertise required for my scheme. During this time, I worked to appease the three creditors who plagued me. I eventually succeeded by selling off half my furniture to cover part of the debt and promising the remainder upon the completion of a project for which I requested their aid. Being simple men, they were easily persuaded. Once settled, I secretly arranged with my wife to sell my remaining belongings and borrowed significant sums under various pretexts, ignoring how I might repay them. With these funds, I acquired fine cambric muslin, twine, caoutchouc varnish, a custom wicker basket, and other materials for a massive balloon. I instructed my wife on its assembly while I fashioned the twine into a net, fitted it with a hoop and cords, and purchased a quadrant, compass, spyglass, modified barometer, and two obscure astronomical tools. Under cover of night, I transported to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam five fifty-gallon iron-bound casks, a larger one, six ten-foot tinned tubes, a specific semi-metal, and twelve demijohns of common acid. The gas produced from these is unique to my work, or at least never before used this way. I would reveal the secret, but it rightfully belongs to a citizen of Nantz, France, who shared it with me under conditions.

I cannot express the joy I felt returning from political turmoil and foreign hardships to the peace and love of my own home. Had I never left Windsor, these feelings would not be so strong, but my time in Greece was filled with fear and the loss of two people who represented greatness and virtue. Such misery could not touch the domestic life we enjoyed in our secluded forest. Time eventually left its mark on our happiness. Idris, my devoted wife, was a deeply loving mother. We had three children, but our second child died while I was in Greece, which deeply affected her. Before that, she felt her children were safe, but afterward, she lived in constant fear that death would take the others. Any minor illness caused her terror, and she was miserable whenever she was away from them. Fortunately, her fears were mostly unfounded. Alfred, now nine, was a strong, upright boy with a gentle nature. Our youngest was still an infant, but he was healthy and his laughter filled our home. Clara had grown past the age that caused Idris such worry. She was dear to us all, possessing a rare combination of intelligence, innocence, and beauty that made her a true treasure. At the start of winter, nine-year-old Alfred began school at Eton. He saw this as his first step toward manhood and was quite excited. Studying and playing with others helped develop his character, highlighting his perseverance, generosity, and steady nature.

Her face flushed, and she fell silent. Mrs. Gardiner stood slightly behind her, and when she paused, Darcy asked for an introduction to her companions. This unexpected politeness made her want to smile, knowing he sought to meet the very people his pride had previously rejected. She wondered how he would react once he realized who they were, assuming he currently mistook them for fashionable society. The introduction followed, and as she explained their relationship, she watched him closely, half-expecting him to flee from such embarrassing company. While clearly surprised, he remained composed and even began talking with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth felt a sense of triumph and relief that her relatives were people she could be proud of. She listened intently, taking pride in her uncle’s intelligence and good manners. Their conversation shifted to fishing, and Darcy politely invited Mr. Gardiner to fish on his property whenever he liked, offering him equipment and advice on the best spots. Mrs. Gardiner exchanged a look of amazement with Elizabeth. Though Elizabeth remained silent, she was deeply pleased, sensing the gesture was meant for her. She was stunned by his change in behavior, wondering if it could truly be for her sake, though she doubted her past criticisms could have caused such a transformation. As they walked, the group shifted when Mrs. Gardiner, feeling tired, decided to lean on her husband instead of Elizabeth.

Mr. Darcy spoke warmly of his sister’s musical talent. Lady Catherine replied that she was glad to hear it, but insisted that his sister would never excel without constant practice. Darcy assured her that his sister already practiced diligently. Lady Catherine insisted that one could never practice enough, adding that she often advised young ladies on the matter. She mentioned that she had told Miss Bennet she needed to practice more, and noted that Mrs. Collins was welcome to use the piano at Rosings whenever she liked. Mr. Darcy, embarrassed by his aunt’s rudeness, remained silent. After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam asked Elizabeth to play, and she sat at the piano. Lady Catherine listened briefly before turning to talk to Darcy, who eventually walked over to stand near Elizabeth, watching her closely. Elizabeth noticed him and, during a pause, smiled playfully. She told him that he was trying to intimidate her, but that she refused to be frightened, as her spirit only grew stronger when challenged. Darcy replied that he knew she did not truly believe he meant to scare her, noting that she enjoyed pretending to hold opinions she did not actually possess. Elizabeth laughed and told Colonel Fitzwilliam that his cousin was painting a poor picture of her, making it difficult for her to maintain the reputation she had hoped to establish.

Once that was done, he could stand at the altar with her, free from the fear of wrongdoing. He could hold her, knowing she would never have to feel ashamed of him. It had to be done, and the sooner, the better. Many men might have chosen pleasure over duty, but Lord Arthur was too principled for that.
