Unfortunate Jack was later killed in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara passed away from grief at Tunbridge Wells before the year concluded; thus, in every sense, the event was a triumph. It proved an arduous transformation, if one might apply such theatrical terminology to a profound mystery of the supernatural—or, more scientifically, the higher-natural realm—requiring three full hours of preparation. Finally, he was satisfied with his guise. The leather riding-boots were slightly oversized, and he located only one of the two horse-pistols, yet he felt content, gliding from the wainscoting at a quarter past one to creep down the hall. Upon arriving at the Blue Bed Chamber, where the twins slept, he noticed the door slightly open. Seeking a dramatic entrance, he threw it wide, only for a heavy water jug to tumble onto him, soaking him completely and narrowly missing his shoulder. Simultaneously, he heard muffled laughter erupting from the four-poster bed. The nervous shock drove him to retreat to his room immediately, and he spent the following day suffering from a severe cold. His only solace was that he had left his head behind; had he carried it, the outcome could have been dire. He abandoned all ambition to terrify the boorish American family, settling instead for shuffling through the corridors in soft slippers, a thick red muffler protecting his throat from drafts, and carrying a small arquebuse for defense against the twins. The final indignity occurred on September 19th. He had descended to the main entrance-hall, confident he would remain undisturbed, and was mocking the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife that had replaced the Canterville portraits. He wore a simple, tidy shroud stained with graveyard soil, his jaw bound with yellow linen, while he carried a lantern and a sexton’s spade.

To see a star clearly, one must look at it indirectly, using the outer edges of the retina, which are more sensitive to faint light. Looking directly at a star makes it appear dimmer. While more light hits the eye when staring straight on, the peripheral view offers a sharper perception. Excessive focus can weaken thought, just as staring too intently at Venus can make the planet disappear from the sky. Regarding these murders, let us investigate them ourselves before forming an opinion. It will be an interesting diversion, and Le Bon once did me a favor I have not forgotten. We will inspect the scene. I know the Prefect of Police and can easily get permission. Permission granted, we went to the Rue Morgue, a dreary street between Rue Richelieu and Rue St. Roch. It was late when we arrived, as it was far from our home. The house was easy to find, as a crowd still lingered across the street, staring at the closed shutters. It was a typical Parisian building with a concierge booth by the gate. Before entering, we walked around the block, with Dupin examining the neighborhood and the house with a level of detail I found inexplicable. Returning to the front, we rang the bell, showed our credentials, and were admitted by the police. We went upstairs to the room where the body of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been discovered and where the victims still lay. The room remained in its original state of disarray. I saw nothing that had not already been reported in the newspapers. Dupin examined everything, including the bodies. We then inspected the other rooms and the yard, accompanied by a gendarme throughout.

Is that everything? That is not much. Many fall under the Republic's wrath and must peer through the small window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he? I am he, as I am the last. Jarvis Lorry answers these inquiries while standing by the carriage door, addressing the officials. They inspect the vehicle and its roof luggage at a slow pace, while local onlookers crowd around to stare. A mother holds her child forward so the infant might touch the wife of an aristocrat destined for the guillotine. Here are your signed papers, Jarvis Lorry. May one leave, citizen? One may leave. Move on, postilions! Safe travels! I salute you, citizens. The first danger is behind us! Jarvis Lorry speaks these words, clasping his hands and looking up. Inside the carriage, there is weeping, terror, and the labored breathing of the unconscious passenger. Are we moving too slowly? Can they be made to go faster? Lucie asks, clutching the old man. It would appear like fleeing, my dear. I cannot press them too hard, or it will invite suspicion. Look back and see if we are followed! The road is empty, my dearest. We are not pursued yet. We pass scattered houses, farms, decaying structures, tanneries, and barren trees. The carriage rattles over uneven stones, occasionally veering into deep mud to avoid the jolting road, or becoming stuck in ruts. Our impatience is agonizing, and in our panic, we long to flee on foot. We pass through more ruins and desolate farms. Have they tricked us and returned us to the same spot? Thankfully, no. A village. Look back to see if we are pursued! Quiet! The posting-house. Our four horses are unhitched at a leisurely pace, leaving the coach motionless in the street. New horses arrive slowly, followed by postilions who idly toy with their whips, while the previous drivers count their coins, miscalculating and grumbling at the totals.

With a racing heart and an inexplicable dread, I sent away the servant, bolted my door, and sat to read my father’s letter. Its contents were as follows: My dear Child, I have violated your trust; I have sought to corrupt your thoughts, exposing your innocent heart to the gaze and speech of forbidden, monstrous desire. I must atone for these sins, attempting to match my penance to my transgression. You are surely ready for my announcement: we must part, separated forever. I strip you of your father and sole companion. You are abandoned, homeless; your prospects ruined, the tranquility of your pure spirit shattered. Memory will haunt you with visions of guilt and the pain of betrayed innocence. Yet I, who have brought this misery upon you, who have cast you out and cruelly branded my own child with agony, who with wicked flippancy tried to replace your beauty with the ugliness of sin—I, in my profound sorrow, beg your forgiveness. I do not seek your pity; you must loathe me. But pardon me, Mathilda, and do not pursue me into exile with unceasing wrath. I must never see you or hear your voice again, yet the gentle murmur of your pardon might soothe my fevered mind and heart; I believe I would feel it even in death. I venture to make this plea by explaining how wretchedly I was ensnared in this trap of torment and my efforts to escape. If your soul were less radiant, I would not try to justify myself, fearing that lessening your abhorrence might diminish your hatred of vice. However, speaking to you feels like addressing an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your absolution, or I shall fall into despair. I implore you to hear me; if guilt can be lessened by intense suffering and the madness of remorse, perhaps you might consider, though I dare not, that I deserve your compassion. I beg you to recall our early, joyful life by Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of weary travel, during which, despite many perils and hardships, my heart had remained entirely empty.

Basil, this is incredible! I have to meet Dorian Gray. Hallward stood up and paced the garden before returning. Harry, he said, Dorian Gray is simply an artistic inspiration to me. You might see nothing in him, but I see everything. He is present in my work even when his image is absent; he suggests a new style. I find him in the curves of certain lines and the subtlety of specific colors. That is all. Then why won't you exhibit his portrait? Lord Henry asked. Because I have unintentionally poured my own artistic obsession into it, something I have never mentioned to him. He knows nothing of it, and he never will. But the public might guess, and I refuse to expose my soul to their shallow scrutiny. I will not let them put my heart under a microscope. There is too much of myself in that painting, Harry. Poets are less careful, Lord Henry replied. They know passion sells. A broken heart often leads to many editions these days. I despise them for that, Hallward cried. An artist should create beauty without injecting his own life into it. We live in an era that treats art as autobiography, having lost the sense of abstract beauty. One day I will show the world what art truly is, and for that reason, they will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray. I think you are mistaken, Basil, but I will not argue. Only the intellectually lost argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray fond of you? The painter paused. He likes me, he said. I flatter him terribly, and I find a strange pleasure in saying things I later regret. Usually, he is charming, and we talk for hours in the studio. Occasionally, however, he is thoughtless and seems to enjoy hurting me. At those times, Harry, I feel I have surrendered my soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his lapel—a mere decoration to feed his vanity for a summer day.

Next, we built a wire fence. A wire fence? Yes. You suggested it yourself a few years ago. I remember now, back when the Church first challenged us and decided to wait for a better opportunity. How did you set it up? I ran twelve heavy, uninsulated wires from a large dynamo in the cave. The wires extend from the cave to enclose a flat area one hundred yards across. They form twelve separate circular fences, spaced ten feet apart, with both ends returning to the cave. The wires are attached to sturdy oak posts, spaced three feet apart and buried five feet deep. That sounds strong. The wires have no ground connection outside the cave. They run from the positive terminal, while the negative terminal is grounded. Each wire returns to the cave and is grounded separately. No, that is inefficient. You should only use the ground connection at the negative terminal. Bring the other ends back to the cave without any ground connection. This way, you save power. When a cavalry charge hits the fence, you are not wasting energy. The electricity waits like a loaded gun, costing nothing until the horses touch the wire and complete the circuit through the ground, killing them instantly. I see, that is much cheaper and more effective, especially if the wires break. Exactly, and we can monitor them from the cave. What about the Gatling guns? I have placed thirteen of them on a six-foot platform in the center of the inner circle, with plenty of ammunition. Perfect. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, they will face a deadly surprise. What about the cliff above the cave? I have installed a wire fence and a Gatling gun there as well.

Soon his voice called out in a shout. How much further must I go? How high are you? Legrand inquired. Ever so far, the man answered; I can see the sky through the treetops. Ignore the sky and listen to me. Look down the trunk and count the branches beneath you on this side. How many have you passed? One, two, three, four, five—I have passed five large limbs, master, on this side. Then climb one limb higher. Shortly, the voice returned, stating the seventh limb was reached. Now, Jup, Legrand shouted, clearly agitated, I need you to crawl out on that branch as far as possible. If you spot anything unusual, tell me. By then, any lingering doubt regarding my friend's sanity vanished. I felt certain he was suffering from madness and grew worried about returning him home. As I considered my options, Jupiter spoke again. I am quite afraid to venture far on this limb; it is mostly dead wood. Did you say it was a dead limb? Legrand asked, his voice trembling. Yes, master, it is dead as a doornail—certainly finished—it has departed this life. What on earth shall I do? Legrand asked, appearing deeply distressed. Do? I said, seizing the chance to speak, come home and go to bed. Come now, be a good fellow. It is getting late, and you recall your promise. Jupiter, he called, ignoring me entirely, do you hear me? Yes, Master Will, I hear you clearly. Test the wood well with your knife and see if it seems very rotten. It is rotten, master, for sure, the man replied after a moment, but not as bad as it could be. I might venture a little way out on the limb myself, that is true. Yourself? What do you mean? I mean the bug. It is a very heavy bug. Suppose I drop it first, then the limb will not break under just the weight of one man. You scoundrel! Legrand cried, seemingly relieved, what do you mean by such nonsense? If you drop that beetle, I will break your neck. Listen, Jupiter, do you hear me? Yes, master, no need to shout at me like that. Well, listen! If you venture out on the limb as far as you feel is safe, without dropping the beetle, I will give you a silver dollar once you return.

Reviewing his letter while drafting a response softened Harriet so much that Emma felt compelled to use firm language to steady her. Harriet’s deep concern for his feelings, coupled with her anxiety over what his mother and sisters might think of her, convinced Emma that had the young man appeared then, he might have been accepted. Nevertheless, the letter was completed, sealed, and dispatched. The matter was settled, and Harriet was secure. Though Harriet remained melancholy that evening, Emma indulged her gentle regrets, occasionally comforting her by affirming their own bond or shifting the focus to Mr. Elton. I shall never be asked to Abbey-Mill again, Harriet remarked sadly. Even if you were, I could not bear to lose you, my dear Harriet; you are far too essential at Hartfield to be spared. I am certain I would not wish to go there, for I am only content at Hartfield, she replied. Later, she mused that Mrs. Goddard and Miss Nash would be astonished, as Miss Nash considered her own sister well-married to a mere linen-draper. One would not wish for greater vanity in a schoolteacher, Harriet. Miss Nash would surely envy your chance at such a marriage. As for anything better, she remains ignorant. Mr. Elton’s attentions are not yet common gossip in Highbury; I suspect only we understand his true intentions. Harriet blushed, smiling at her own popularity. While the prospect of Mr. Elton provided comfort, she soon grew sympathetic toward the rejected Mr. Martin again. Now that he has my letter, she whispered, I wonder what they are doing. If he is miserable, his sisters will be too. I hope he does not take it too hard. Let us consider our absent friends who are more happily occupied, Emma urged. Perhaps Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his family right now, praising the beauty of the original, and after much insistence, finally revealing your name—your own dear name.

“However,” I replied, handing back the paper, “I remain entirely confused. Even if the treasures of Golconda were the reward for solving this puzzle, I am certain I could never claim them.” “Yet,” Legrand countered, “the answer is far less complex than a quick glance might suggest. These symbols clearly constitute a cipher, yet knowing Kidd, I doubted he could devise anything truly intricate. I concluded it was a basic type, meant to seem impossible to a simple sailor without the proper key.” “You actually deciphered it?” “Easily; I have cracked far more difficult ones. My inclinations have drawn me to such puzzles, and I doubt any human can create a riddle that human intellect cannot eventually unravel. Once I had clear, connected characters, the meaning was simple to extract. In any secret writing, the primary issue is the language, as the method of solution relies on the specific idiom. Usually, one must test various languages based on probability until the correct one appears. Here, the signature provided the answer. The pun on ‘Kidd’ only functions in English. Otherwise, I would have tested Spanish or French, as a pirate in the Spanish Main would likely use those. Instead, I proceeded assuming it was English. You will notice the lack of word breaks. Had they existed, the work would be simpler; I would have analyzed the short words, and a single-letter word like ‘a’ or ‘I’ would have guaranteed success. Without divisions, I began by identifying the most and least frequent characters.

One more word, Rose! Dearest Rose, just one! Harry cried, blocking her path. If I had been less fortunate—if a quiet, simple life had been my fate, or if I had been poor, sick, or helpless—would you have turned away? Or is it my potential wealth and status that causes your hesitation? Do not force me to answer, Rose replied. That situation does not exist and never will. It is unfair to push me. If your answer is what I hope, it will bring light to my lonely life, Harry insisted. It is not a small thing to offer such comfort to someone who loves you above all else. In the name of my deep devotion and all I have suffered for you, please answer me. If your life had been different, Rose said, if you had been only slightly above my station, and I could have been a comfort to you in a humble, peaceful home rather than a burden in your ambitious social circles, I would have been spared this pain. I have every reason to be happy now, but I admit I would have been happier then. Memories of old hopes from her girlhood flooded her mind as she spoke, bringing tears that offered some relief. I cannot help this weakness, but it makes my resolve stronger, Rose said, reaching out her hand. I must leave you now. I ask for one promise, Harry said. Within a year, I may speak to you on this subject one last time. Not to pressure me to change my mind, Rose replied with a sad smile, because that would be useless. No, Harry said. Just to hear you repeat your decision one final time. I will offer you whatever status or fortune I have, and if you still refuse, I will not try to change your mind again. Then let it be so, Rose agreed. It is only one more moment of pain, and by then, I may be better able to handle it. She held out her hand once more.

So you won't, won't you? Oh, you precious fool! It is naughty, isn't it, Oliver? Charley Bates asked. He will end up being hanged, won't he? I do not know what that means, Oliver replied. Something like this, old fellow, Charley said. As he spoke, he grabbed the end of his neckerchief, held it up, dropped his head to his shoulder, and made a strange sound through his teeth, clearly acting out a hanging. That is what it means, Charley said. Look how he stares, Jack! I have never seen such funny company as this boy; he will be the death of me. Charley laughed heartily and went back to his pipe with tears in his eyes. You have been raised poorly, the Artful Dodger said, looking at his boots with satisfaction after Oliver finished polishing them. Fagin will make something of you, or you will be the first one he ever had who was not profitable. You had better start right away, because you will join the trade sooner than you think, and you are just wasting time, Oliver. Charley Bates added his own moral advice, and then he and the Dodger described the many pleasures of their life, hinting that Oliver should win Fagin’s favor immediately. And always remember this, Nolly, the Dodger said as they heard the old man unlocking the door above, if you do not take handkerchiefs and watches— What is the point of talking like that? Charley interrupted. He does not know what you mean. If you do not take pocket handkerchiefs and watches, the Dodger said, simplifying his language for Oliver, someone else will. The people who lose them will be worse off, you will be worse off, and nobody will be any better except the person who takes them, and you have just as much right to them as they do. To be sure, to be sure! said the old man, who had entered without Oliver noticing. It is simple, my dear; take the Dodger’s word for it. He understands the lessons of his trade. The old man rubbed his hands together gleefully, agreeing with the Dodger’s logic and chuckling at his student’s skill. The conversation ended there, as the old man returned with Miss Betsy and a man Oliver had never seen before, whom the Dodger called Tom Chitling.

Mrs. Musgrove took a moment to speak privately with Anne. She expressed her wish that Mary had some of Anne’s skill with the children, noting how much better they behaved for her. She complained that they were spoiled and difficult to manage, which made her reluctant to host them. She felt Mary did not know how to handle them, often resorting to giving them too many sweets just to keep them quiet. Meanwhile, Mary complained to Anne that Mrs. Musgrove’s servants were constantly neglecting their duties to wander around the village. Mary claimed they were a bad influence on her own nursemaid, Jemima, though she trusted Jemima to remain steady. Conversely, Mrs. Musgrove told Anne that she avoided interfering in Mary’s affairs, but warned her that Mary’s nursemaid was unreliable and far too concerned with her own appearance. She urged Anne to keep a watchful eye on the situation. Finally, Mary grumbled that Mrs. Musgrove often failed to give her the proper social status she deserved when they dined together, treating her more like a family member than a guest.

We eventually decided to live together during my time in the city. Since my finances were more stable than his, I paid to rent and furnish a decaying, grotesque mansion in a desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain, a place long abandoned due to superstitions we chose not to investigate. If our daily routine had been public knowledge, people would have considered us mad, though perhaps harmlessly so. We lived in total seclusion, admitting no visitors. We kept our location secret from my former acquaintances, and Dupin had long since cut ties with Parisian society. We lived entirely within our own private world. It was a strange whim of my friend to be obsessed with the night, and I surrendered to his eccentricities completely. Since the darkness could not always be with us, we faked it. At dawn, we would close the heavy shutters of our old home and light a pair of scented candles that cast only a ghastly, dim glow. By their light, we spent our time reading, writing, or talking until the clock signaled the arrival of true night. Then, we would walk the streets arm in arm, discussing our earlier topics or wandering until late, seeking the mental stimulation that comes from observing the city’s shifting lights and shadows. During these walks, I admired Dupin’s remarkable analytical ability. He clearly took great pleasure in exercising it, often boasting with a low chuckle that most people had windows in their chests, allowing him to see right through them. He would follow such claims with startling proofs of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. At these moments, his manner was cold and detached, his eyes vacant, and his voice, usually a rich tenor, rose to a sharp treble that would have seemed petulant if not for his deliberate, precise way of speaking.

I want to see you well-settled, and it is best to limit your casual acquaintances. If you are still here when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with his sisters does not force you to know his wife, who will likely be an uneducated farmer’s daughter. Certainly. I do not think Mr. Martin would marry anyone without an education, but I will not argue with you. I value the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and would hate to lose them, as they are as well-educated as I am. But if he marries someone ignorant and vulgar, I will avoid her if I can. Emma watched her, seeing no signs of love. The young man had admired her first, but she trusted Harriet would not resist her own plans. They met Mr. Martin the next day on the Donwell road. He looked at Emma respectfully, then at her companion with genuine delight. Emma walked ahead to observe him. He looked neat and sensible, but lacked refinement. Compared to true gentlemen, he would surely lose Harriet’s interest. Harriet noticed manners, but Mr. Martin seemed to lack them entirely. They spoke for only a few minutes so as not to delay Miss Woodhouse. Harriet returned smiling and flustered, which Emma hoped to calm. Just think of meeting him! How strange! He said it was pure chance he did not go by way of Randalls, as he assumed we walked there most days.

He made it clear that Frank admired her immensely, finding her both beautiful and charming. Given his many positive qualities, she decided not to judge him too severely, agreeing with Mrs. Weston that all young people have their quirks. However, one person in Surrey was not so forgiving. While most in Donwell and Highbury were lenient toward such a handsome, polite young man, Mr. Knightley remained unmoved by his charm. When told the news at Hartfield, he stayed silent at first, but Emma soon heard him mutter to himself while reading the paper, "Hum! Just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for." She considered taking offense, but realized he was merely venting his own frustration rather than trying to provoke her, so she let it go. Although the Westons brought mixed news, their visit was timely. Emma needed advice on a specific matter, and their input proved exactly what she required. The Coles, a friendly and unpretentious family, had recently grown quite wealthy through trade. Having expanded their home and staff, they now lived in a style second only to the Hartfield estate. Their new dining room signaled their intent to host formal dinners, and they had already entertained some of the local bachelors. Emma doubted they would dare invite the area's elite families, such as those from Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. She was determined to refuse any such invitation, though she regretted that her father’s predictable habits would make her rejection seem less significant than she intended.

The studio was saturated with the heady fragrance of roses, while a gentle summer breeze carried in the potent aroma of lilacs and the subtle perfume of pink-flowering thorn through the doorway. Reclining on a divan of Persian saddle-bags and smoking his usual endless supply of cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton glimpsed the golden, honey-sweet blossoms of a laburnum, its delicate branches straining under the weight of such vibrant beauty. Occasionally, the fleeting shadows of birds crossed the tussore-silk curtains covering the large window, creating a transient Japanese aesthetic that reminded him of Tokyo artists who attempt to capture motion within static art. The persistent drone of bees navigating the tall, unkempt grass or circling the woodbine only deepened the heavy silence, while the distant hum of London resembled the low drone of an organ. Positioned in the middle of the room on an easel was a full-length portrait of a remarkably handsome young man. Seated nearby was the artist, Basil Hallward, whose mysterious vanishing years prior had sparked widespread intrigue and wild speculation. Observing the graceful figure he had captured so expertly, a satisfied smile crossed Basil's face. Suddenly, he stood and pressed his fingers to his closed eyes, as if trying to hold onto a fleeting vision he feared losing. "It is your finest work, Basil, truly your best," Lord Henry remarked lazily. "You must exhibit it at the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is far too crowded and common. I find it either too packed with people to see the art, or too full of art to see the people. The Grosvenor is the only suitable venue." "I do not intend to send it anywhere," Basil replied, tossing his head back with the peculiar gesture that had amused his peers at Oxford.

It is quite remarkable that she always hears Jane more clearly than she hears me. Jane speaks so distinctly! Still, she will find her grandmother no deafer than she was two years ago, which is saying a lot at my mother’s age. It has been two full years since she was last here. We have never gone so long without seeing her, and as I told Mrs. Cole, we will hardly know how to make enough of her now. Are you expecting Miss Fairfax soon? Oh yes, next week. Indeed, that must be a great pleasure. Thank you, you are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised and says such kind things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends in Highbury as they are to see her. She will arrive Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which because Colonel Campbell will need the carriage himself on one of those days. It is so kind of them to send her the whole way, but they always do. Yes, next Friday or Saturday. That is what she wrote about, which is why she wrote out of turn; normally, we would not have heard from her until next Tuesday or Wednesday. Yes, I imagined as much. I feared there was little chance of hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today. How kind of you! No, we would not have heard if not for this specific circumstance of her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted, as she is to stay with us for at least three months. She says so quite positively, as I am about to read to you. The situation is that the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to visit her immediately. They had not intended to go until summer, but she is impatient to see them again. Until she married last October, she had never been away from them for more than a week, so it must feel very strange to be in different countries. She wrote a very urgent letter—or perhaps Mr. Dixon wrote it, I am not sure, but we shall see in Jane’s letter—to press them to come over immediately. They would meet in Dublin and then travel to their country estate, Ballycraig, which I imagine is a beautiful place.

Jane admitted some surprise at the engagement, yet she spoke more of her sincere wishes for their joy than her shock, nor would she let Elizabeth convince her it was unlikely. Kitty and Lydia felt no jealousy toward Miss Lucas, as Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman, and they viewed the news only as gossip to share in Meryton. Lady Lucas took obvious pleasure in returning the favor to Mrs. Bennet by boasting of a well-married daughter, visiting Longbourn frequently to express her delight, despite Mrs. Bennet’s bitter glares and spiteful comments. A new reserve grew between Elizabeth and Charlotte, leaving them silent on the matter, and Elizabeth felt certain their former intimacy was gone. Disappointed in Charlotte, she turned with deeper affection toward her sister, whose integrity she trusted completely, though she worried increasingly for Jane’s happiness, as a week had passed since Bingley’s departure with no word of his return. Jane had replied promptly to Caroline’s letter and waited anxiously for a response. On Tuesday, Mr. Collins sent a formal letter of gratitude to their father, written with the gravity of a long-term houseguest. Having fulfilled that duty, he wrote ecstatically of his engagement to their neighbor, Miss Lucas, explaining that his eagerness to revisit Longbourn in two weeks was driven by a desire to see her. He noted that Lady Catherine fully supported the union and urged a swift wedding, which he hoped would persuade his dear Charlotte to set an early date. Mrs. Bennet no longer welcomed Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire; she complained of it as loudly as her husband. She found it bizarre and highly inconvenient that he intended to stay at Longbourn rather than Lucas Lodge, resenting the presence of guests while she felt unwell, especially those as tiresome as lovers.

“Starve? Oh, Sir Simon, are you famished? I have a sandwich in my bag if you would like it.” “No, thank you; I do not eat anymore. Still, it is kind of you, and you are far more pleasant than your dreadful, ill-mannered, and dishonest relatives.” “Stop!” Virginia exclaimed, stamping her foot. “You are the rude one. As for dishonesty, you stole my paints to touch up that absurd bloodstain in the library. You took my reds, so I could not paint sunsets, then my greens and yellows, leaving me only indigo and white for depressing moonlight scenes. I never reported you, though I was quite annoyed; besides, who has ever seen emerald-green blood?” “Well,” the Ghost replied meekly, “what was I to do? Real blood is hard to find, and since your brother started this with his detergent, I saw no reason not to use your paints. Color is a matter of taste; the Cantervilles have blue blood, though I know you Americans do not value such things.” “You know nothing. You should emigrate to improve your mind. My father would gladly provide a free passage, and since the customs officers are Democrats, there would be no trouble with the authorities. You would be a sensation in New York; many people there would pay a fortune for a family ghost.” “I do not think I would care for America.” “I suppose because we lack ruins and curiosities,” Virginia remarked sarcastically. “No ruins or curiosities? You have your navy and your manners,” the Ghost retorted. “Good evening. I am going to ask my father for an extra week of holiday for the twins.” “Please do not leave, Miss Virginia,” he pleaded. “I am lonely and miserable, and I cannot find rest.” “That is ridiculous! You simply need to go to bed and extinguish your candle.”

The gauge showed my altitude at 132,000 feet, or twenty-five miles, meaning I could see one three-hundred-twentieth of the Earth's total surface. By nine o'clock, the eastern land had vanished, and I noticed the balloon moving swiftly toward the north-northwest. The Earth's curvature was clearly visible, despite frequent interference from drifting clouds. I noted that even the thinnest mists never ascended beyond ten miles above sea level. At nine-thirty, I tested dropping a handful of feathers through the valve. Instead of floating, they plummeted straight down like lead weights, vanishing instantly. I was initially baffled, unable to grasp such a sudden increase in my ascent rate. I soon realized the air was too thin to support the feathers, and their rapid fall was compounded by my own swift upward movement. By ten o'clock, I had little to do. Everything proceeded smoothly, and I felt the balloon accelerating, though I lacked the means to measure it. I felt no discomfort and was in better spirits than at any time since leaving Rotterdam, alternating between checking my equipment and refreshing the cabin's air. I performed this ventilation every forty minutes, primarily for health. Meanwhile, my mind wandered to the moon. Unrestrained, my imagination explored a dreamlike landscape of ancient forests, jagged cliffs, and roaring, bottomless waterfalls. Then, I drifted into silent, windless noonday plains where vast fields of poppies and lilies stretched out, forever still.

I met a strange man at Warwick Castle who caught my attention with his simple honesty, his deep knowledge of ancient armor, and his easy conversation. As we trailed behind the tour group, he spoke so naturally about the past that I felt transported to a forgotten era. He discussed Sir Launcelot, Sir Galahad, and the other Knights of the Round Table as if they were his own neighbors. As he spoke, he seemed to grow incredibly old and weathered. He eventually turned to me and asked if I knew about the transposition of souls and bodies across time. I admitted I had not, but he seemed indifferent to my reply. Just then, the tour guide droned on about a sixth-century suit of armor, noting a mysterious hole in the chest that might have been caused by a bullet. My companion offered a smile that felt centuries out of date and whispered to himself that he had seen it happen—and that he was the one who had done it. Before I could process his shocking claim, he vanished. That evening at the Warwick Arms, I sat by the fire listening to the rain and wind, lost in a dream as I read Sir Thomas Malory’s tales of adventure and ancient chivalry.

May I pose two inquiries? Monks appeared surprised, noting that answering was his choice. That makes three, Mr. Bumble quipped. Is that your expectation? the matron asked. It is, Monks replied. What is the second? What is your plan for it, and could it be used against me? Never, Monks promised, warning them not to approach. He shoved the table away and lifted a trapdoor near Mr. Bumble, who retreated in haste. Look down, Monks commanded, lowering his lantern. I could have dropped you in earlier if I wished. The matron approached the edge, followed by a curious Mr. Bumble. Below, the rain-swollen river churned against rotting mill pilings. If a body were thrown in, where would it end up? Monks asked. Twelve miles downstream and mangled, Bumble answered, shuddering. Monks attached his packet to a lead weight and dropped it into the dark water, where it vanished instantly. The three breathed easier. Monks shut the trapdoor firmly. If the sea yields its dead, it will keep this trash, he remarked. Our meeting is concluded. Certainly, Mr. Bumble agreed quickly. Keep your silence, Monks warned with a menacing glare.

You have not been in Bath long enough to enjoy the evening parties, he remarked. Oh no, she replied. They do not interest me, as I do not play cards. I know you did not like them before, he said, but time changes many things. I have not changed that much, Anne said, then stopped, worried she might be misunderstood. After a pause, he added as if speaking from the heart, It is a long time. Eight and a half years is a long time. Anne wondered if he would have continued, but Henrietta interrupted, eager to leave before more visitors arrived. They had to move. Anne claimed she was ready, but she felt a deep reluctance to leave her seat. If Henrietta understood Anne’s regret, she might have pitied her. Their departure was halted by the arrival of Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose presence chilled the room. The comfort and joy of the gathering vanished, replaced by forced politeness and silence to match her father and sister’s cold elegance. Anne was mortified. She noticed that Captain Wentworth was acknowledged by both, with Elizabeth being surprisingly gracious. Elizabeth had a plan. After some small talk, she invited the Musgroves to a small gathering the next evening. She spoke gracefully and placed her invitation cards on the table, offering a special smile and an extra card to Captain Wentworth. Elizabeth had learned that in Bath, a man of his appearance was worth cultivating.

No sympathy was offered to Ireland. This oversight was returned in kind; when Lady Elliot passed away, Kellynch received no condolences, suggesting the Dalrymples considered the family tie severed. Restoring this connection was a priority for both Lady Russell and Mr. Elliot. Family ties were worth keeping, and Lady Dalrymple, having rented a home in Laura Place for three months, promised a sophisticated social life. Lady Russell had heard her described as charming, and they hoped to renew the acquaintance without sacrificing their dignity. Sir Walter insisted on handling it himself, sending a grand, overly explanatory letter to his cousin. Though Lady Russell and Mr. Elliot found the letter embarrassing, it succeeded in eliciting a brief, scrawled reply from the Dowager Viscountess, expressing her pleasure at the prospect of meeting. The effort paid off. They visited Laura Place and displayed the calling cards of the Viscountess and Miss Carteret prominently, frequently boasting of their high-status cousins to everyone they met. Anne felt embarrassed. Even if the women had been pleasant, the fuss was humiliating, but they were entirely unremarkable. Lady Dalrymple was only considered charming because she was polite to everyone, while Miss Carteret was so dull and awkward that her social standing was the only reason she was tolerated. Lady Russell admitted they were disappointing, yet insisted the connection held value. When Anne questioned Mr. Elliot, he conceded they lacked personal merit but argued their social status and ability to host others made them valuable. Anne smiled and replied that she defined good company as clever, well-informed people who could hold an engaging conversation.

She would be surrounded by people who loved her and possessed better judgment than she did; living in a safe, quiet environment while staying busy enough to remain cheerful. She would be protected from temptation and live a respectable, happy life. Everyone compares it not to the voice of a person from any nation whose language they know, but the opposite. The Frenchman assumes it was a Spaniard, claiming he might have understood words had he known Spanish. The Dutchman insists it was a Frenchman, though he required an interpreter because he does not speak French. The Englishman thinks it was a German, yet he does not understand German. The Spaniard is certain it was an Englishman, judging solely by the intonation, as he has no knowledge of English. The Italian believes it was a Russian, despite never having spoken to one. A second Frenchman disagrees with the first, certain the voice was Italian, but since he does not know that language, he relies entirely on the intonation. How remarkably strange that voice must have been to elicit such testimony, where residents of five European nations could recognize nothing familiar in its tones. You might suggest it was the voice of an Asian or an African. While those groups are not common in Paris, I will simply point out three things: one witness calls the voice harsh rather than shrill, two others describe it as quick and uneven, and no witness could distinguish any words or sounds resembling them. I do not know what impression I have made on you, Dupin continued, but I believe the logical deductions from this testimony regarding the gruff and shrill voices are enough to create a suspicion that should guide our investigation. I mean that these are the only proper deductions, and the suspicion arises inevitably from them. I will not state the suspicion yet, but keep in mind that it was strong enough to shape my inquiries in the room. Let us imagine ourselves in that chamber. What should we look for first? The means of escape used by the killers. It is safe to say that neither of us believes in supernatural events.

Anne remarked that this period of Mr. Elliot’s life had always piqued her interest, coinciding with his introduction to her father and sister. She had never met him personally, but his behavior toward her family and the details of his subsequent marriage seemed inconsistent with his current character, suggesting a very different man. Mrs. Smith exclaimed that she was fully aware of the situation. Although he had been introduced to Sir Walter and Elizabeth before she knew him, he spoke of them constantly. She confirmed he had been invited and encouraged to visit but chose not to, and she claimed to be privy to his private thoughts and plans regarding his marriage. While she had not known his wife beforehand due to her lower social standing, she knew her well afterward and offered to answer any questions. Anne clarified that she had no interest in the wife, having heard they were unhappy, but she remained curious why Mr. Elliot had shunned her father’s friendly overtures. Mrs. Smith explained that at that time, Mr. Elliot was focused on securing his fortune through marriage rather than his legal career. He feared that her father and sister were attempting to arrange a match between him and the young lady, which would not have met his requirements for wealth and independence. He had been completely open with her about these motives, and it was ironic that after leaving Anne in Bath, her cousin became her primary acquaintance, keeping her constantly informed about her family.

In my youth, discontent never troubled me. If I felt bored, the beauty of nature or the study of human achievement could always lift my spirits. Now, I am like a blasted tree, struck to the core. I realized then that I would remain only as a tragic example of ruined humanity, pathetic to others and unbearable to myself. We spent considerable time in Oxford, exploring the area and searching for sites linked to England's most inspiring history. Our excursions often stretched on as new sights caught our attention. We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the battlefield where he died. For a moment, my soul rose above its crushing fears to contemplate the noble ideals of liberty and sacrifice these places represented. I briefly dared to cast off my burdens and view the world with a free spirit, but the damage was too deep, and I soon sank back into my hopeless, miserable state. We left Oxford reluctantly for Matlock. The surrounding landscape resembled Switzerland, though on a smaller scale, lacking the distant, snow-capped Alps of my homeland. We toured the local caves and natural history displays, which were arranged like those in Servox and Chamounix. Hearing Henry mention the latter name made me tremble, and I hurried to leave Matlock to escape that painful association. Traveling north from Derby, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine I was back in the Swiss mountains. The lingering patches of snow, the lakes, and the rushing streams were all familiar and dear to me. We met people there who nearly tricked me into feeling happy. Clerval’s joy was even greater than mine; his mind flourished among talented people, and he discovered within himself capabilities he had never realized while surrounded by those of lesser intellect.

I recall the conditions during our nineteenth-century civil war. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars a day in gold, while in the South, he received fifty in nearly worthless Confederate currency. Since overalls cost a day's wages in the North but two days' wages in the South, Northern wages held significantly more purchasing power. I made various acquaintances in the village and was pleased to see our new currency circulating among the common people, including milrays, mills, cents, nickels, and some silver. Gold was only found at the goldsmith's shop. I stopped there while Marco was arguing over the price of salt and requested change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They scrutinized the coin, testing it with acid and ringing it on the counter, before interrogating me about my identity, origin, and destination. When their questions stalled, I volunteered irrelevant details about my dog, my late wife's religious background, and a man I once knew with extra thumbs. This eventually satisfied the curious clerk, though he seemed annoyed. He dared not challenge a man of my wealth, choosing instead to berate his subordinates. They changed my twenty, though it clearly strained their resources, much like asking a small-town shopkeeper to break a two-thousand-dollar bill. The goldsmith likely wondered how a traveler could carry such a sum, as he followed me to the door, watching me with reverent admiration.

Such reflections soothed me, and I fell into a deep slumber that afternoon; yet my feverish state precluded any tranquil visions. The ghastly events of the prior day played repeatedly in my mind—the women fleeing and Felix pulling me away from his father. I woke drained and, seeing it was night, emerged from my shelter to find sustenance. Once fed, I walked toward the familiar path leading to the cottage. Everything was quiet. I retreated to my shed, waiting in silence for the family to wake. The time passed and the sun climbed high, yet the residents did not emerge. I shook with dread, fearing some terrible calamity. The cottage remained dark and still; the torment of my uncertainty is beyond words. Soon, two men stopped by the house and spoke with agitated gestures, though I could not grasp their meaning as they used the local tongue rather than my protectors' language. Shortly after, Felix arrived with a stranger. I was startled, knowing he had not left earlier, and listened intently to discern the reason for these strange events. His companion asked if he realized he would forfeit three months' rent and his garden's yield, offering him time to reconsider. Felix insisted it was pointless, stating they could never return. He explained his father’s life was in peril due to the incident he had described, and that his wife and sister remained traumatized. He begged the man to stop arguing, urging him to reclaim the property so he could depart. Felix shook as he spoke. They entered the cottage briefly before leaving. I never saw the De Lacey family again. I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, consumed by a numb, hollow despair. My protectors had vanished, severing my only connection to humanity. For the first time, malice and vengeance flooded my heart, and rather than resist these impulses, I surrendered to them, focusing my thoughts on destruction and death.

I told myself I did not want to be involved in any of this. When I went downstairs the next morning, the parlor was closed and the people keeping watch were gone. Only the family, the Widow Bartley, and our group remained. I studied their faces for clues, but I could not tell if anything had happened. By midday, the undertaker and his assistant arrived. They placed the coffin on chairs in the center of the room and arranged our chairs in rows, borrowing more from neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were filled. I noticed the coffin lid was positioned as it had been before, but I was too afraid to look inside while others were present. People began to arrive, and the con artists and the girls sat in the front row near the coffin. For half an hour, the guests walked by in a single line to look at the dead man’s face. Some shed tears, and the room remained quiet and solemn, save for the girls and the men sobbing into their handkerchiefs. The only other sounds were the shuffling of feet and the blowing of noses, which always happens more at funerals than anywhere else except church. Once the room was packed, the undertaker moved about in his black gloves, making final adjustments with a quiet, soothing manner. He was as silent as a cat, guiding people and making space with only nods and hand gestures. He stood against the wall, the most stealthy and humorless man I have ever seen. They had borrowed a wheezy old organ, and when a young woman began to play it, the sound was squeaky and unpleasant. Everyone joined in to sing, though I thought Peter was the only one who sounded good. Then, Reverend Hobson began to speak slowly and solemnly, but suddenly, a terrible noise erupted from the cellar. It was only one dog, but he made such a powerful racket that he would not stop. The preacher had to stand there over the coffin and wait, as the noise made it impossible to hear anything else.

It is strange, but everyone who goes missing is supposedly seen in San Francisco. It must be a wonderful city, possessing all the charms of the afterlife. What do you think happened to Basil? Dorian asked, holding his wine to the light and wondering why he could discuss it so calmly. I have no idea. If Basil wants to hide, it is not my concern. If he is dead, I prefer not to think about it. Death is the only thing that terrifies me. I hate it. Why? the younger man asked wearily. Because, Lord Henry said, sniffing his perfume box, one can survive anything today except that. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts of the nineteenth century that cannot be explained away. Let us have coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran off with played it beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was fond of her. The house is lonely without her. Marriage is just a habit, a bad one. But one regrets losing even the worst habits. Perhaps one regrets them most, as they are essential to one's personality. Dorian said nothing, rose, and went to the piano, letting his fingers drift over the keys. After coffee arrived, he stopped and looked at Lord Henry. Harry, did it ever occur to you that Basil was murdered? Lord Henry yawned. Basil was popular and wore a cheap watch. Why would he be murdered? He was not clever enough to have enemies. He had a genius for painting, but a man can paint like a master and still be dull. Basil was dull. He only interested me once, when he told me years ago that he adored you and that you were the inspiration for his art. I was fond of Basil, Dorian said sadly. But do people not say he was murdered? Some newspapers do, but it seems unlikely. I know there are dangerous places in Paris, but Basil was not the type to go there. He lacked curiosity, which was his main flaw. What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I murdered Basil? the younger man asked.

That hardly matters. She replied, I might as well ask why you chose to tell me you loved me against your will, your reason, and your own character, if your clear intention was to insult me. Was that not justification enough for my rudeness? But I have other reasons. You know I do. Even if my own feelings had not been against you, even if I were indifferent or favorable, do you think I would ever accept the man who destroyed the happiness of my beloved sister? Darcy paled as she spoke, but he quickly composed himself and listened without interrupting. I have every reason to think poorly of you. Nothing excuses your unjust, ungenerous actions. You cannot deny that you were the primary cause of their separation, exposing one to public criticism for instability and the other to mockery, leaving them both in deep misery. She paused, noticing with indignation that he seemed entirely unrepentant, even offering a skeptical smile. Can you deny it? she repeated. He replied with forced calm, I have no desire to deny that I did everything possible to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. I was kinder to him than to myself. Those elderly, frail clerks were always seen bowing to the public, and it was widely believed that once they bowed a customer out, they continued bowing in the empty office until the next one arrived. The barrister realized the banker would not have spoken so firmly without moral certainty. Though the news was difficult to accept, he managed to process it. "Now," Mr. Stryver said, gesturing toward the Temple, "my strategy is to prove you all wrong." It was a classic courtroom tactic that brought him relief. "You will not make me the one in the wrong, young lady," he decided; "I will do that for you." When Mr. Lorry visited at ten that night, Mr. Stryver was surrounded by books and papers, acting as if the morning's topic was the furthest thing from his mind. He even feigned surprise at seeing Lorry, appearing entirely preoccupied. "Well!" said Lorry, after thirty minutes of failing to steer the conversation. "I have been to Soho." "Soho?" Stryver repeated coldly. "Oh, right! What was I thinking?" "I am certain my previous advice was correct," Lorry insisted. "My opinion is confirmed." "I assure you," Stryver replied with forced friendliness, "I am sorry for your sake and the father's. I know this is a sensitive subject; let us drop it." "I don't understand," Lorry said. "I imagine not," Stryver replied dismissively. "It doesn't matter." "But it does matter," Lorry urged. "It truly doesn't. Having mistakenly assumed there was sense and ambition where there was none, I am glad to be rid of the error. Young women have made such mistakes before, only to regret them in poverty. I am sorry it ended, as it would have been a poor worldly move for me, yet I am relieved it is over for the same reason—it is obvious I could have gained nothing from it."

Enough of this. I shall commence my narrative; it is my final duty, and I trust I possess the vigor to complete it. I recount no transgressions; my errors are easily forgiven, as they stemmed from poor judgment rather than malice. I suspect few would claim they could have escaped the calamities that have claimed me through better wisdom or conduct. My destiny was dictated by a grim, inescapable necessity. It demanded strength beyond my own—perhaps beyond any human capacity—to shatter the iron bonds that dragged me from a life of pure joy and virtue into this misery, which now nears its conclusion in death. But I digress; my story remains unshared. I will pause briefly, dry my weary eyes, and attempt to trade this dull, heavy sorrow for the sharper feelings of days gone by. I was born in England. My father was a nobleman who lost his own father young, raised by a doting mother who granted him every indulgence. He attended Eton and university, granted unrestricted access to wealth from childhood, gaining the independence such advantages typically foster in a public school boy. These conditions allowed his passions to take deep root, blossoming into either virtues or vices. Because he was always permitted to act on his own impulses, his character developed early and distinctly, revealing to the keen observer the seeds of both his noble traits and his eventual downfall. His reckless spending, which saw him waste fortunes on fleeting whims he grandly labeled as passions, often manifested as boundless generosity. Yet, while he busied himself with the needs of others, he never denied his own desires. He gave away money he did not miss, time he did not value, and affection he was pleased to exercise. I cannot say if he would have acted selfishly had his interests clashed with another's, for that test never arose. He was raised in prosperity, surrounded by every benefit, with everyone eager to please him.

Resting on the hearth lay several thick locks of grey hair, stained with blood and appearing as if torn out by the roots. Scattered across the floor were four Napoleons, a topaz earring, three large silver spoons, three smaller ones of Algerian metal, and two pouches holding nearly four thousand francs in gold. A bureau in the corner had its drawers pulled open and appeared ransacked, though many items remained inside. A small iron safe was found beneath the bed, left open with the key still in the lock; it contained only a few unimportant letters and papers. No sign of Madame L’Espanaye appeared, but after noticing an unusual amount of soot in the fireplace, a search of the chimney revealed the daughter’s corpse, which was dragged out headfirst after being forced deep into the narrow flue. The body remained warm. Examination showed numerous abrasions from the force used to shove and retrieve it, along with severe facial scratches and dark bruises on the throat with deep nail marks, suggesting she had been strangled. After searching the entire house without further findings, the group entered a small paved yard behind the building. There lay the old lady’s body, her throat so completely severed that her head detached when they tried to lift her. Both the head and torso were hideously mangled, the latter barely recognizable as human. We believe there is currently no lead in this gruesome mystery. The following day’s paper added these details: The Tragedy in the Rue Morgue. Many people have been questioned regarding this extraordinary and terrifying event, yet nothing has emerged to clarify the situation. We provide the essential testimony gathered below. Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, states she has known both victims for three years, having handled their laundry throughout that time. The mother and daughter appeared to have a very affectionate relationship and always paid promptly. She could not comment on their financial circumstances, though she believed Madame L. earned money by fortune-telling and was rumored to have savings.

My best customers no longer had time for me. They claimed they were too busy reading about revolutions and keeping up with the latest intellectual trends. If a fire needed fanning, a newspaper worked just fine, and as the government weakened, my leather and iron goods seemed to become indestructible; soon, no bellows in Rotterdam needed repairs. This situation was unbearable. I became penniless, and with a wife and children to support, my life felt like an impossible burden. I spent hours considering how to end it. Meanwhile, debt collectors gave me no peace. My house was constantly surrounded, making me pace like a caged tiger. Three men in particular harassed me, threatening legal action. I vowed to take bitter revenge on them if I ever had the chance, and only the hope of that vengeance kept me from shooting myself. I decided to hide my anger and appease them with empty promises until fate offered me a way to strike back. One day, after slipping away from my creditors, I wandered the backstreets in despair until I stumbled upon a bookseller’s stall. I sat in a nearby chair and aimlessly opened the first book I found. It was a pamphlet on speculative astronomy by Professor Encke or a French author with a similar name. Having some interest in the subject, I became completely absorbed, reading the entire volume twice before I finally noticed my surroundings again.

You ought to adopt some of my philosophy. Only dwell on the past when its memory brings you joy. I cannot attribute such a philosophy to you. Your reflections must be so entirely free of blame that your satisfaction stems not from philosophy, but from a much better source: ignorance. It is not so for me. Distressing memories arise that cannot and should not be dismissed. I have been selfish my entire life in practice, if not in principle. As a child, I was taught what was right, but never how to govern my temper. I was instilled with good principles but left to pursue them with pride and vanity. Being an only son for many years, I was indulged by parents who, though kind themselves, allowed and even encouraged me to be arrogant and selfish, to value only my own circle, and to look down upon the rest of the world. I remained that way from eight until twenty-eight, and I would likely still be that man if not for you, my dearest, loveliest Elizabeth. I owe you everything. You taught me a difficult but invaluable lesson. You humbled me. I approached you certain of my welcome, yet you revealed how inadequate my efforts were to please a woman truly worthy of admiration. Had you convinced yourself that I would accept? I truly had. What must you think of my vanity? I believed you were hoping for my proposal. My behavior must have been at fault, though never by design. I never intended to mislead you, but my high spirits may have led me astray. How you must have loathed me after that night! Loathe you? I was perhaps angry at first, but my resentment soon shifted toward a more appropriate target. I am hesitant to ask what you thought of me when we encountered one another at Pemberley. Did you resent my arrival? No, I felt only astonishment. Your surprise could not have exceeded my own at being acknowledged by you. My conscience whispered that I deserved no special courtesy, and I admit I expected no more than what was strictly necessary. My goal then, Darcy replied, was to demonstrate through every civility that I was not petty enough to harbor past grievances, and I hoped to earn your pardon and improve your opinion of me by showing that I had taken your rebukes to heart.

After unfastening a few more loops from the rim and feeding in more cloth, I reattached the loops to their buttons.
