While this seemed risky, the buttons were strong and spaced closely enough that each carried only a fraction of the load. Even if the weight had tripled, I would have felt secure. I then raised the hoop inside the rubberized covering, propping it up with three light poles to keep the bag expanded and the netting in place. Finally, I sealed the opening by gathering the fabric and twisting it tightly shut with a built-in tourniquet. Three thick glass windows were set into the sides of the enclosure, allowing me to see in every direction. A fourth window in the bottom, aligned with a hole in the floor, provided a view straight down. I could not install a window at the top due to the way the fabric bunched together, but this did not matter, as the balloon itself would have blocked the view anyway. About a foot below one side window, I placed an eight-inch circular opening fitted with a threaded brass rim. I screwed the condenser tube into this rim, keeping the machine itself inside the rubber chamber.

I wrapped him in paper and stuffed a piece in his mouth—that was the method. And you believe your master was truly bitten by the beetle, and that the bite caused his illness? I do not think anything about it—I know it. Why would he dream of gold if not for the gold-bug bite? I have heard of those gold-bugs before. But how do you know he dreams of gold? How do I know? Because he speaks of it while sleeping—that is how I know. Well, Jup, perhaps you are correct; but to what lucky event do I owe the pleasure of your visit today? What is the matter, master? Did you bring a message from Mr. Legrand? No, master, I brought this letter. Jupiter handed me a note that read: My dear friend, why have I not seen you lately? I hope you have not been foolish enough to take offense at my brief rudeness; though that is unlikely. Since we last met, I have been quite anxious. I have something to tell you, though I hardly know how to say it, or if I should at all. I have been unwell for days, and poor old Jup irritates me beyond measure with his well-intentioned care. Would you believe he prepared a large stick to punish me for slipping away to spend the day alone in the hills? I truly believe my sickly appearance saved me from a beating. I have added nothing to my collection since we met. If you can manage it, please come over with Jupiter. Do come. I must see you tonight regarding a matter of the highest importance. Ever yours, William Legrand. The tone of this note caused me significant distress. Its style was entirely unlike Legrand. What could he be imagining? What new obsession gripped his excitable mind? What business could be so vital? Jupiter’s report boded ill. I feared that persistent misfortune had finally unhinged my friend’s sanity. Without hesitation, I prepared to accompany the man. Upon reaching the dock, I observed a scythe and three new spades resting in the boat. What is the meaning of this, Jup?

I come from a small, cloud-covered island. When I consider the vast globe, my home seems like a tiny speck, yet in terms of intellectual influence, it outweighs far larger and more populous nations. It is true that the human mind creates all that is great, while nature merely serves as its instrument. England, situated in the northern seas, often appears in my dreams as a mighty, well-crewed ship mastering the waves. In my youth, she was my entire world. Standing on my native hills, looking out over the cultivated landscape, I felt that this place was the center of the earth, and the rest of the world was merely a myth I could easily ignore. My life has always demonstrated how change can dictate the course of human existence. This instability was almost an inheritance. My father was gifted with immense wit and imagination, but he lacked the reason to steer his life or the judgment to guide it. Though born into obscurity, he gained early public attention, quickly squandering his small inheritance on a life of luxury. In his youth, he was adored by the elite and even the young monarch, who sought his company to escape the pressures of state. My father’s lack of self-control constantly led him into trouble, yet his ingenuity always saved him. He carried the weight of mounting debts with a light heart and irrepressible humor, and because his presence was so desired at elite gatherings, his failures were excused and met with flattery. However, such popularity is fleeting, and the difficulties he faced soon grew far beyond his ability to manage.

I am uneducated, and it worries me, just a little. Tell me what is wrong. I have a cousin, my only relative and an orphan like me, whom I love dearly. She is five years younger and lives on a farm in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of my fate because I cannot write, and even if I could, how would I explain it? It is better this way. Yes, it is better. As we traveled, and as I look at your kind, strong face that gives me such support, I have been thinking: if the Republic truly helps the poor so they suffer less, she might live a long time, perhaps even to old age. What then, my gentle sister? Do you think, she asks, her eyes filling with tears, that it will feel like a long wait for me in the afterlife where I hope we will both find mercy? It cannot be, my child; there is no time or suffering there. You comfort me so much. I am so ignorant. Should I kiss you now? Is it time? Yes. She kisses his lips, he kisses hers, and they solemnly bless each other. His hand does not tremble as he lets her go; her face remains patient and constant. She goes before him and is gone; the knitting women count twenty-two. I am the Resurrection and the Life, says the Lord; he who believes in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. The murmuring voices, the upturned faces, and the pressing crowd surging forward like a wave all vanish. Twenty-three. That night, people in the city said his face was the most peaceful they had ever seen. Many added that he looked sublime and prophetic. Another notable victim of the same axe had recently asked at the scaffold for permission to write down her inspiring thoughts. If he had spoken his own, they would have been these: I see Barsad, Cly, Defarge, The Vengeance, the jury, and the judge, along with the new oppressors who rose from the ruins of the old, all perishing by this same instrument before its work is finally done.

April 7th. I woke early and, to my delight, finally saw what must be the North Pole. It was directly beneath me, yet I had ascended so high that I could see nothing clearly. Based on my altitude readings between April 2nd and the moment my barometer failed, I estimate that by 4:00 A.M. on April 7th, I had reached at least 7,254 miles above sea level. This figure may seem vast, but it is likely an underestimate. Regardless, I could see the Earth’s entire diameter; the northern hemisphere appeared like a flat map, with the equator forming my horizon. You can imagine that the unexplored Arctic regions, while directly below, were too small and distant to examine in detail. Still, what I saw was remarkable. North of the known world, an unbroken sheet of ice stretches out. It flattens, then levels into a plane, and finally becomes concave, ending at the Pole in a sharp, circular center. This spot, which spanned about sixty-five seconds of arc from my vantage point, was darker than the rest of the hemisphere, sometimes appearing as an impenetrable black. By noon, this circle had shrunk, and by 7:00 P.M., it vanished as my balloon drifted toward the equator. April 8th. The Earth’s apparent size has noticeably decreased, and its color and overall appearance have shifted significantly.

The area seemed to be a mix of back alleys, ditches, and small gardens, creating a rather quiet, dull atmosphere. Wemmick’s home was a tiny wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, with a roof carved and painted to resemble a fortress equipped with cannons. My own work, Wemmick said, looking pleased. It looks nice, doesn't it? I praised it highly. It was the smallest house I had ever seen, featuring strange gothic windows—mostly fake—and a door so small it was difficult to enter. That is a real flagpole, Wemmick explained, and I raise a real flag on Sundays. Look here. Once I cross this bridge, I pull it up like this and cut off access. The bridge was just a plank spanning a four-foot-wide, two-foot-deep ditch. It was charming to see the genuine pride he took in lifting it, smiling with real enjoyment rather than just going through the motions. At nine o'clock sharp, Greenwich time, the gun fires, Wemmick said. There it is! When you hear it, I think you will agree it is quite a powerful blast. The cannon sat in its own small fortress made of lattice, protected from the rain by a clever umbrella-like cover. In the back, out of sight so it does not ruin the fortification theme—because I believe if you have an idea, you should commit to it—there is a pig, along with chickens and rabbits. I also build my own frames to grow cucumbers, and you can judge my salad at supper. So, if you imagine this place under siege, it could hold out for a long time with all these supplies, he added with a serious, thoughtful smile. He then led me to a garden arbor about twelve yards away, reached by such winding paths that it took a while to arrive. Our glasses were already waiting there. Our punch was chilling in a small ornamental pond next to the arbor. This pond, which featured a tiny island that might have served as our salad, had a fountain he had built. When you started a small mill and pulled a cork from a pipe, it sprayed water with enough force to dampen the back of your hand.

In a certain town—which I will leave unnamed for good reason—there stands a building common to most communities: the workhouse. Within these walls, on a date that holds no significance for the reader at this moment, was born the individual whose name titles this story. For a long time after the parish surgeon brought him into this world of sorrow, it was uncertain if the child would survive long enough to be named. Had he perished, these memoirs would have been brief indeed, though perhaps remarkably concise and accurate. While being born in a workhouse is hardly an enviable start, it was, in this specific case, the best possible outcome for Oliver Twist. He struggled to take his first breath—a tiresome but necessary habit for survival—and lay gasping on a mattress, balanced precariously between life and death. Had he been surrounded by doting relatives and expert doctors, he would surely have been killed by their interference. Instead, with only a tipsy pauper and a contract-bound surgeon present, Oliver and nature fought the battle alone. After a few struggles, he breathed, sneezed, and announced his arrival to the workhouse by crying as loudly as any infant could who had possessed a voice for less than four minutes.

Ten minutes later, his face drained of color and eyes wide with sorrow, Lord Arthur Savile bolted from Bentinck House, pushing past the liveried servants beneath the striped awning as if oblivious to his surroundings. The air was freezing, and the streetlamps wavered in the sharp gale, yet his skin burned with a feverish heat. He stumbled forward with the unsteady rhythm of a man intoxicated. A constable watched him with suspicion, and a beggar emerging from a doorway recoiled, intimidated by a despair deeper than his own. Pausing beneath a light, he inspected his hands, imagining he saw bloodstains, and a soft moan escaped his shaking mouth. Murder was what the palmist had discovered. The word haunted the night, carried by the howling wind and lurking in every shadowed corner and rooftop. He reached the Park, drawn to its gloomy woods. Leaning against the cold, damp railings, he whispered the word repeatedly, as if repetition might soften its dread. His own voice startled him, yet he longed for the city to wake and hear his confession. He wandered toward Oxford Street and into squalid lanes. Painted women jeered at him, and from a dark yard came the sounds of violence and screaming. Seeing the bent, impoverished figures on a doorstep, he felt a sudden, strange sympathy. Were they, like him, merely fated pawns in a cruel performance? It was the absurdity of their suffering that struck him—its utter pointlessness and lack of logic. The world felt disjointed and discordant, a stark contrast to the superficial cheerfulness of his social circle. He was, after all, still very young. Eventually, he arrived at Marylebone Church, where the empty street stretched out like a silver ribbon, patterned by the shifting silhouettes of trees.

There was plenty of cold water to finish their meal. Soon, Becky suggested they move on. Tom hesitated, then asked if she could handle some bad news. Becky turned pale but nodded. Tom explained that they had to stay near the water because their last candle was nearly gone. Becky broke down in tears, and despite Tom’s attempts to comfort her, she remained inconsolable. She eventually asked if people would come looking for them. Tom agreed they certainly would, hoping the search had already begun. When Becky asked when they would be missed, Tom suggested it would be when the group returned to the boat. He then realized his mistake, mentioning that her mother would notice her absence as soon as she got home. Becky’s terrified expression confirmed she was not supposed to be home that night, and they both realized it might be Sunday morning before anyone noticed she was missing. They watched the candle burn down until the flame flickered and died, leaving them in total darkness. After an unknown amount of time, they drifted into a deep sleep, only to wake to their ongoing misery. Tom guessed it could be Sunday or Monday. He tried to talk to Becky, but she was too overwhelmed to respond. Tom attempted to shout for help, but the terrifying echoes in the dark silenced him. As time passed, hunger returned. They shared the last of their cake, but it only left them feeling hungrier than before.

He explained that he was wasting his time where he was, and that friends in London were urging his return to finalize the negotiations for his Indian venture. He could no longer delay his departure, but since his trip to London might soon be followed by a much longer voyage, he begged me to spend as much time with him as possible. He asked me to leave my isolated island and meet him in Perth so we could travel south together. This letter brought me back to life, and I decided to leave my island in two days. Before I left, however, I had to face a task that made me shudder: I needed to pack my chemical equipment. This required entering the room where I had performed my repulsive work and handling tools that now sickened me. At daybreak the next morning, I gathered my courage and unlocked the laboratory. The remains of the half-finished creature I had destroyed lay scattered on the floor, and I felt as if I had mutilated a living human being. After composing myself, I entered the room. With trembling hands, I removed the instruments, realizing I could not leave these remnants to horrify or alarm the local villagers. I placed them in a basket with heavy stones, intending to dump them into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach, cleaning and organizing my equipment. My perspective had shifted completely since the night the creature appeared. Previously, I had viewed my promise with gloomy despair, believing it had to be fulfilled regardless of the consequences. Now, it felt as if a veil had been lifted, and I saw things clearly for the first time. The thought of resuming my work never crossed my mind. Although the creature's threat weighed on me, I no longer believed my actions could prevent it. I had decided that creating another monster would be an act of the most atrocious selfishness, and I dismissed any thought that might lead me to a different conclusion.

I spent two years this way. Day after day passed without external change, yet these years slowly altered my mind as I drifted toward death. I studied more, empathizing with the ideas found in books and history, losing my sense of self among the people of the past. As my immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude lost its appeal, and I began to crave companionship—not from a crowd, but from one friend who would love me. You might think this prepared me to rejoin society, but I disagree. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure and free from worldly influence that I would inevitably be disappointed by the crude realities that taint even the best human feelings. I was less prepared for social interaction than ever. When I first left society, people tormented me like a sickness—something external I wanted to discard. Now, however, I craved a deep connection, which would only have invited more suffering, as I was as sensitive as a fragile plant. I did not want help with ambition or wisdom, but simple, mutual affection—smiles and gentle words. I wanted one heart to listen to my complaints, hoping something good might grow from such sorrow. Yet, how could I find this? True friendship is a rare spirit, usually found between those raised together or bonded by shared hardship. It comes to the chosen unexpectedly, like dew on barren ground, but it flees when pursued; it mocks those who beg for it. I knew this and did not go looking for it. Yet, there on my lonely heath, in my humble home, it found me like a winter sunbeam warming the snow. Sadly, the sun shone on ruined fruit; I could not revive under its light, for I was too broken to feel its kindness.

If you seek my patience and the mercy of those you have harmed, sit in that chair without speaking. It has been waiting for you for two days. Monks muttered something indistinct, still hesitating. You must be quick, Mr. Brownlow said. One word from me and your chance is gone forever. The man still wavered. I have no desire to negotiate, Mr. Brownlow continued, and since I represent the vital interests of others, I have no right to do so. Is there no middle ground? Monks asked, his voice trembling. None. Monks searched the old man’s face, but finding only stern resolve, he walked into the room and sat down with a shrug. Lock the door from the outside, Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, and return when I ring. They obeyed, leaving the two men alone. This is fine treatment from my father’s oldest friend, Monks said, tossing aside his hat and cloak. It is precisely because I was your father’s oldest friend, Mr. Brownlow replied, that I treat you with such restraint. My hopes were tied to him and to the woman who died young, leaving me alone. I stood with him at his sister’s deathbed when we were boys, the woman who would have been my wife had fate allowed. My heart clung to him through all his struggles until his death. Because those memories remain, and because even seeing you brings him to mind, I am moved to be gentle—even now, Edward Leeford—though I am ashamed of your unworthiness to bear that name. What does the name matter? Monks asked, watching his companion’s agitation with sullen confusion. What is the name to me? Nothing to you, Mr. Brownlow replied. But it was hers, and even now, it stirs the same thrill in me that I felt hearing it long ago. I am very glad you changed it. This is all very dramatic, Monks said after a long silence, during which he shifted in sullen defiance while Mr. Brownlow covered his face with his hand.

Emma felt quite pleased by her recent conversation with Mr. Knightley. As she strolled across the lawn the following morning, she savored the memory of the dance. She was delighted that they shared such similar views regarding the Eltons, and his kind words about Harriet were especially pleasing. The rudeness of the Eltons, which had briefly threatened to spoil her evening, had ultimately led to these pleasant outcomes, and she felt optimistic that Harriet would soon be cured of her foolish crush. Harriet’s own comments before leaving the ballroom suggested she finally realized Mr. Elton was not the perfect man she had imagined. With the infatuation fading and the Eltons’ future coldness likely to finish the job, Emma looked forward to a wonderful summer. She did not mind that Frank Churchill was not visiting that morning, as he had prior commitments. Having settled these thoughts, she prepared to return to her family duties when the gate opened to reveal Frank Churchill escorting a pale, trembling Harriet. They quickly entered the house, where Harriet promptly fainted. Emma soon learned the cause of the distress. Harriet and her friend Miss Bickerton had gone for a walk along the Richmond road, which grew unexpectedly secluded. After turning a corner shaded by trees, they had suddenly encountered a group of gypsies.

The day passed much like the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent the morning with the patient, who was slowly recovering, and Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room that evening. There was no card game. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley sat nearby, watching him and constantly interrupting to send messages to his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley played cards, watched by Mrs. Hurst. Elizabeth worked on her needlepoint, amused by the interaction between Darcy and Miss Bingley. The lady kept praising his handwriting and the length of his letter, while Darcy remained indifferent, which matched Elizabeth’s low opinion of both. Miss Bingley remarked on how happy Miss Darcy would be to receive the letter, but Darcy did not reply. She commented on how fast he wrote, but he corrected her, saying he wrote slowly. She complained about how tedious business letters would be, and he replied that it was fortunate they were his responsibility, not hers. When she asked him to tell his sister she wanted to see her, he noted he had already included that. She offered to fix his pen, but he declined, saying he always mended his own. When she asked how he wrote so neatly, he remained silent. She then asked him to tell his sister she loved her progress on the harp and her table design, but Darcy said he lacked the space to include such praise in this letter. She asked if he always wrote such long, charming letters, and he replied that while they were long, he could not judge if they were charming. Miss Bingley insisted that anyone who could write a long letter easily must write well. Her brother teased Darcy, saying he did not write with ease because he spent too much time choosing complex words. Darcy replied that his writing style was quite different from Bingley’s, to which Miss Bingley added that her brother wrote in a very careless manner.

The physician was an elderly, gentle-looking man once I roused him. I explained that my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday, camping on a raft fragment, when he accidentally discharged his firearm in his sleep, wounding his leg. I asked him to treat the injury discreetly so we could surprise our family upon our return that evening. When he asked who our people were, I named the Phelpses. He inquired again about the accident, and I repeated that a dream had caused the shooting, which he called a peculiar dream. He prepared his lantern and saddlebags, but hesitated at my canoe, deeming it unsafe for two. I assured him it had carried three of us—my brother, myself, and the guns—quite easily. He remained skeptical and searched for a larger vessel, but finding none, he took my canoe and told me to wait or return home. I declined, gave him directions to the raft, and he departed. I soon realized that if the treatment took several days, we would be exposed. I decided that if he needed to return, I would follow him, restrain him if necessary, and continue downriver until Tom was recovered, at which point we would compensate him and set him free. I fell asleep in a lumber pile and awoke to find the sun high. I rushed to the doctor's house, only to learn he had left during the night and had not yet returned.

The storm raged all night, but nothing notable happened. The next morning, however, the bloodstain had returned to the floor. Washington remarked that the detergent clearly was not to blame, suggesting it must be the ghost. He cleaned it again, but it reappeared the following morning. It returned a third time, despite Mr. Otis locking the library and keeping the key. The family grew intrigued; Mr. Otis reconsidered his skepticism, Mrs. Otis planned to join the Psychical Society, and Washington drafted a report on the persistence of bloodstains linked to crimes. That night, all doubt regarding the existence of ghosts vanished. After a warm, sunny day, the family went for an evening drive. They returned at nine for a light supper, discussing mundane topics like American actresses, the scarcity of specific American foods in England, the cultural importance of Boston, the efficiency of baggage checks, and the merits of the New York accent. No one mentioned the supernatural or Sir Simon de Canterville. The family retired at eleven, and by eleven-thirty, the house was dark. Later, Mr. Otis was awakened by a metallic clanking in the hallway that grew louder. He rose, lit a match, and checked the time: exactly one o’clock. Remaining calm and noting his steady pulse, he heard the noise continue alongside distinct footsteps. He put on his slippers, grabbed a small bottle from his dressing case, and opened the door.

She was an incredible talker. It would have been rude to mention that it was late and I was exhausted. I regretted not going to bed when I had the chance, but I had to endure it. She kept chattering in the silent, ghostly castle until a distant, muffled shriek rose from deep below, filled with such agony that my skin crawled. The queen paused, her eyes brightening with pleasure as she tilted her head like a listening bird. The sound pierced the stillness once more. I asked what it was. She replied that it was a stubborn soul who had been enduring the rack for hours. I asked what he was enduring, and she invited me to witness a cheerful sight, promising that if he did not yield his secret, I would see him torn apart. She was a smooth monster, perfectly serene while my own legs ached in sympathy with the victim. Escorted by armored guards with torches, we walked through echoing halls and down damp, moldy stone stairs. The journey was long and chilling, made worse by her casual talk about the prisoner's crime: killing a stag in the royal forest based on an anonymous tip. I suggested that anonymous testimony was unfair and that the accused should face his accuser. She dismissed this as unimportant, noting that the masked accuser had vanished after speaking to the forester. I asked if anyone else saw the killing, and she admitted no one had, only that this stranger saw the man near the carcass. I pointed out that the masked stranger might be the killer himself, but she ignored my logic, insisting that the man must confess to save his soul. She declared that while he would certainly be executed for his crime, she had to ensure he confessed and received absolution to protect her own soul.

The cycle of suffering that dictates existence must have been interrupted, yet the cruel destiny governing it would not tolerate such a violation of her ancient decrees. Why should I complain? Sorrow was my natural state, and only the wretched could draw near; had Woodville been content, our paths would never have crossed. Can I, who subsisted on tears and grew under the shadow of sorrow, hesitate to recount a narrative of grief and demise? Woodville was compelled to travel to the countryside, where he was held back for days, away from his beloved wife. He received a note from her mentioning a minor illness, yet urging him to return, claiming his presence would be her most effective cure. Delayed for three more days, he finally rushed to her. An inexplicable dread filled his heart; having heard nothing further, he feared her condition had worsened. This anxiety made him desperate to see her restored to health, even as a dark intuition murmured that he would never see her as she once was. Upon reaching her home, he found it deathly quiet. Passing through the rooms, he discovered a servant sobbing. Trembling with terror, he barely managed to ask if she had passed, only to hear the chilling reply, "Not yet." These words felt less devastating than he had anticipated; knowing she still lived offered a glimmer of hope. Recalling her letter, he clung to the desperate belief that his loving touch would restore her spirit and that she could not perish while he remained by her side. He hurried to her chamber, where she lay feverish and unresponsive. Embracing her, he pressed frantic kisses to her hot lips and whispered her name in agony, begging her to return to him. He pleaded for her to revive, insisting she could not die in his presence, for to lose her was to lose his own identity, his past, and his future.

But no, there was something even more exciting. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future seemed clear and brilliant. How his name would spread across the world and make people tremble! He imagined himself sailing the seas in a sleek, black ship called the Spirit of the Storm, his terrifying flag flying high. At the height of his fame, he would return to his old village and walk into church, tanned and rugged, wearing a black velvet outfit, a red sash, and a belt full of pistols and a sword. With his feathered hat and his skull-and-crossbones flag, he would listen with delight as people whispered, "It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!" Yes, his career was decided. He would run away from home the very next morning to begin his new life. He started preparing by gathering his supplies. He went to a nearby rotten log and dug under it with his pocketknife until he hit something hollow. He placed his hand there and recited a spell: "What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!" He cleared away the dirt to reveal a small wooden box. He opened it, expecting a fortune, but found only a single marble. Tom was shocked. He scratched his head, confused, and muttered, "Well, that beats everything!" He tossed the marble away and stood thinking. He and his friends had always believed that if you buried a marble with the right spell and left it for two weeks, all the marbles you had ever lost would gather there. The fact that it had failed shook his entire belief system. He had heard of it working many times but never failing. It didn't occur to him that he had tried this before and simply forgotten where he buried them. After thinking it over, he decided that a witch must have interfered and broken the charm.

He would never have escaped without my intervention. Morgan le Fay despised him completely and would never have shown mercy, even though his offense was born of thoughtlessness rather than malice. He had merely mentioned her red hair; while true, it was a social blunder, as such hair is properly called auburn among the elite. Consider that among the forty-seven captives, five had lost all record of their names, crimes, and arrival dates. These elderly, broken individuals had forgotten their own histories. The priests tasked with teaching them that God ordained their suffering for some divine purpose held only vague traditions about them, confirming only that they had been imprisoned for at least thirty-five years. The king and queen viewed these people as mere heirlooms, inherited assets with no known history, and thus felt no interest in them. When I asked the queen why she had not released them, she was baffled; the thought had never occurred to her. It became clear that, given her upbringing, she viewed these prisoners simply as property. We rarely discard property, even when it holds no value. When I finally led these human bats into the afternoon sun—having blindfolded them first to protect their long-darkened eyes—they were a harrowing sight. They were skeletal, wretched figures, the true products of a monarchy sanctioned by the church.

Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by ghosts. The perpetrators were physical beings who escaped in a physical way. How? There is only one logical path to follow, and it leads to a clear conclusion. Let us look at every possible exit. The killers were clearly in the room where Mademoiselle was found, or the one next to it, when the witnesses climbed the stairs. We only need to check those two rooms. The police inspected the floors, ceilings, and walls thoroughly, so no secret passages could have been missed. I checked myself to be certain, and there were no hidden exits. Both doors leading to the hallway were locked from the inside with the keys in the locks. Next, consider the chimneys. While wide near the fireplace, they narrow significantly higher up, making it impossible for even a large cat to pass through. Since these exits were impossible, the killers must have used the windows. No one could have escaped through the front windows without being seen by the crowd below. Therefore, they must have used the back windows. Since logic forces us to this conclusion, we cannot reject it just because it seems impossible. We must prove that these apparent impossibilities are not actually impossible. There are two windows in the room. One is clear, but the other is partially blocked by a large bed. The first window was locked from the inside and would not budge. A hole had been drilled into the frame, and a sturdy nail was driven in. The second window had an identical nail, and it also refused to open. The police were satisfied that no one escaped that way, so they did not bother to remove the nails. I examined them more carefully because I knew the solution to this mystery had to be found there.

Watching him in these moods, I often pondered the old theory of the dual soul, imagining a double Dupin—one creative and one analytical. Do not mistake this for a mystery or a work of fiction. What I observed in the Frenchman was simply the product of an intense, perhaps even strained, intellect. An example of his comments during these times will best illustrate my point. We were walking one night down a long, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Both lost in thought, we had not spoken for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly, Dupin remarked, "He is a very small man, it is true, and would be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés." "There is no doubt of that," I replied instinctively, not immediately realizing—so deep was my concentration—how perfectly he had aligned with my own thoughts. A moment later, I caught myself, and my astonishment was profound. "Dupin," I said seriously, "this is beyond my understanding. I am amazed and can hardly believe my senses. How could you possibly know I was thinking of—?" I paused, wanting to confirm if he truly knew whom I meant. "—of Chantilly," he said. "Why do you hesitate? You were thinking that his small stature made him unfit for tragedy." This was exactly what I had been considering. Chantilly was a former cobbler from the Rue St. Denis who, obsessed with acting, had attempted the role of Xerxes in Crébillon’s play and was famously mocked for it. "For heaven's sake, tell me the method—if there is one—by which you read my mind," I exclaimed, more startled than I cared to admit. "It was the fruit seller," my friend replied, "who led you to conclude that the cobbler was not tall enough for Xerxes and his like." "The fruit seller! You surprise me; I do not know any fruit seller." "The man who bumped into you as we entered the street—perhaps fifteen minutes ago." I then recalled that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples had accidentally nearly knocked me over as we turned onto the street, but I could not fathom what that had to do with Chantilly.

Must I be borne to heaven on beds of ease, while others struggle for the prize and navigate crimson seas? He was esteemed as an exceptional reader. At church gatherings, he was frequently asked to recite verse; upon finishing, the women would raise their hands, let them drop in their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, signaling that the beauty was beyond mortal expression. Following the hymn, Reverend Sprague acted as a bulletin board, announcing meetings and society events until the list seemed endless—a strange practice that persists in America despite the prevalence of newspapers. Often, the more baseless a tradition, the more difficult it is to abandon. Then, the minister offered a comprehensive prayer. It was a generous petition, covering the church, the village, the county, the State, the nation, the government, sailors at sea, the oppressed under foreign tyrannies, the spiritually blind, and the distant heathen, concluding with a plea that his sermon might bear fruit. Amen. As the congregation sat, the boy whose story this is merely endured the prayer. He was restless, tracking the familiar route of the minister’s petition and resenting any new additions as unfair. During the prayer, a fly landed on the pew ahead, tormenting him by grooming itself with such tranquil, vigorous precision—polishing its head and smoothing its wings like coat-tails—that it seemed entirely indifferent to its surroundings.

We finished our investigation at dusk and left. On the way home, my companion stopped briefly at a newspaper office. I have mentioned that my friend had many quirks, which I always humored. He chose not to discuss the murder until the following afternoon, when he suddenly asked if I had noticed anything peculiar at the crime scene. His emphasis on that word made me shudder for no apparent reason. I told him I saw nothing beyond what the papers reported. He dismissed the newspaper's account, arguing that the police found the case impossible only because its strange details made it seem difficult. They were confused by the lack of motive for such brutality and the impossibility of the suspects escaping the room. The chaotic state of the apartment, the body shoved up the chimney, and the horrific mutilation had completely baffled the authorities. They made the common mistake of confusing the unusual with the complex. However, it is through these strange deviations that reason finds the truth. In such cases, we should ask not what happened, but what has happened that is truly unprecedented. The ease with which I will solve this mystery is directly proportional to how impossible it seems to the police. I stared at him in silence, stunned. He looked toward our door and added that he was expecting someone who, even if not the killer, was certainly involved in the crime.

It was the best of times and the worst of times; an age of wisdom and foolishness; a period of belief and skepticism; a season of light and darkness; a spring of hope and a winter of despair. We had everything before us, yet we had nothing. We were all heading straight to Heaven or straight the other way. In short, that era was so similar to the present that some of its loudest leaders insisted it be viewed only in the most extreme terms. A king with a large jaw and a plain-faced queen sat on the English throne, while a king with a large jaw and a beautiful queen ruled France. In both nations, the powerful elite were certain that their status was secure forever. It was 1775. England was filled with spiritual claims, much like today. Mrs. Southcott had just turned twenty-five, and a prophetic soldier had announced that London and Westminster were destined to be destroyed. The Cock-lane ghost had only been silenced twelve years prior, after tapping out messages much like the unoriginal spirits of the past year. Meanwhile, messages of great importance had arrived for the English Crown from British subjects in America—events far more significant than any ghostly warnings. France, less focused on spiritual matters, slid smoothly toward ruin, printing and spending paper money. Guided by their religious leaders, the French also engaged in brutal acts, such as sentencing a young man to have his hands cut off, his tongue torn out, and his body burned alive simply for failing to kneel before a passing religious procession. It is likely that in the forests of France and Norway, trees were already growing that Fate would eventually harvest to build a certain wooden frame with a sack and a blade, destined to become a terrifying symbol in history.

It was well past noon when he woke. His valet had checked on him several times, wondering why his master slept so late. Finally, the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly with tea and a stack of letters on a china tray, pulling back the satin curtains from the tall windows. Monsieur has slept well, he said with a smile. What time is it, Victor? Dorian Gray asked sleepily. It is a quarter past one, Monsieur. How late! He sat up, sipped his tea, and looked through his mail. One letter was from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He hesitated, then set it aside. He opened the others listlessly, finding the usual invitations to dinners, art shows, and charity concerts that fashionable young men receive daily. There was a large bill for a silver toilet set he had not yet dared show his old-fashioned guardians, who failed to understand that in this age, luxuries are necessities. There were also polite offers from money-lenders in Jermyn Street. After ten minutes, he rose, put on an embroidered silk dressing gown, and went to the onyx bathroom. The cool water refreshed him, and he seemed to have forgotten his recent troubles. A vague memory of some strange tragedy flickered, but it felt like a dream. Once dressed, he went to the library for a light French breakfast at a small table by the open window. It was a beautiful day, the air filled with the scent of spices. A bee buzzed around a bowl of yellow roses. He felt perfectly happy. Suddenly, his gaze landed on the screen hiding the portrait, and he jumped. Is it too cold, Monsieur? his valet asked, placing an omelette on the table. Shall I shut the window? Dorian shook his head. I am not cold, he murmured.

The area seemed to be a maze of back alleys, ditches, and small gardens, offering a rather dull, secluded atmosphere. Wemmick’s home was a tiny wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, its roof carved and painted to resemble a battery equipped with cannons. My own work, Wemmick said. Looks nice, doesn't it? I praised it highly. It was the smallest house I had ever seen, featuring odd gothic windows—mostly fake—and a door so narrow it was difficult to enter. That is a real flagpole, Wemmick noted. On Sundays, I raise a real flag. And look here. Once I cross this bridge, I lift it up—like this—and cut off access. The bridge was just a plank spanning a four-foot-wide, two-foot-deep trench. It was charming to see the genuine pride he took in hoisting it, smiling with real satisfaction rather than just going through the motions. At nine o'clock sharp, Greenwich time, the gun fires, Wemmick explained. There it is! When you hear it, I think you will agree it packs a punch. The cannon sat in its own lattice-work fortress, shielded from the elements by a clever umbrella-like tarp. In the back, out of sight so it doesn't ruin the fortification theme—because I believe if you have a concept, you should commit to it, don't you agree? I told him I certainly did. In the back, I keep a pig, chickens, and rabbits. I also built my own cold frame to grow cucumbers, and you can judge my salad skills at supper. So, sir, Wemmick said, smiling seriously, if you imagine this place under siege, it could hold out for a long time with these provisions. He then led me to a garden bower a dozen yards away, reached by such winding paths that it took a while to arrive. Our glasses were already waiting. Our punch was chilling in an ornamental pond beside the bower. This circular pool featured a small island—perhaps the future salad—and a fountain he had built. When you started the small mill and unplugged the pipe, it sprayed with enough force to dampen the back of your hand.

Will you? His eyes brightened, and he declared, I will help you steal him! I was stunned, feeling as if I had been struck. It was the most shocking thing I had ever heard, and I must admit my opinion of Tom Sawyer dropped significantly. I simply could not believe it; Tom Sawyer, a person who would steal a slave? Oh, nonsense, I replied, you are teasing. I am not teasing at all. Well, I said, whether you are or not, if you hear any talk about a runaway, remember that neither of us knows anything about him. We loaded the trunk into my wagon, then parted ways. I was so preoccupied and elated that I forgot to drive slowly, arriving home much faster than expected. The old man met me at the door, exclaiming, This is incredible! Who would have thought the mare had it in her? I wish we had timed her. She is not even sweating. I would not take a hundred dollars for her now, even though I would have sold her for fifteen earlier. He was the most guileless, kindhearted man I have ever known. This was not surprising, as he was both a farmer and a preacher who maintained a small log church on his property, providing services and schooling for free. Such men were common in the South. About thirty minutes later, Tom’s wagon pulled up to the stile. Aunt Sally spotted it from the window and called out, Someone has arrived! I believe it is a stranger. Jimmy, tell Lize to set another plate. Everyone hurried to the door, as visitors were rare and far more exciting than an epidemic. Tom hopped over the stile and headed toward the house while his wagon sped off toward the village. We gathered at the entrance, watching Tom approach in his fine clothes, clearly relishing the attention.

In the pale moonlight, he saw an old man with a terrifying appearance. His eyes glowed like burning coals, his long grey hair hung in tangled locks, and his old-fashioned clothes were dirty and torn. Heavy, rusted chains hung from his wrists and ankles. Mr. Otis said, My dear sir, I must insist that you oil those chains. I have brought you a bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that purpose. It is said to work perfectly after one use, and there are several recommendations on the label from prominent local ministers. I will leave it here by your candles and can provide more if you need it. The American Minister placed the bottle on a marble table, closed his door, and went to bed. For a moment, the Canterville ghost stood still in shock. Then, he smashed the bottle against the floor and fled down the hallway, groaning and glowing with a ghostly green light. Just as he reached the top of the oak staircase, a door flew open, two children in white robes appeared, and a large pillow flew past his head. Realizing he had no time to waste, he escaped by slipping through the wall, leaving the house quiet. Reaching a secret room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and reflect on his situation. In three hundred years of a successful career, he had never been so insulted. He remembered the Duchess he had frightened into a fit, the four housemaids who had hysterical breakdowns when he grinned at them, the local priest whose candle he had blown out, and Madame de Tremouillac, who had been bedridden for six weeks after seeing a skeleton reading her diary by the fire.

Sir Walter had secured an excellent residence in Camden Place, a grand and elevated location befitting a man of his standing, and both he and Elizabeth were quite content there. Anne arrived with a heavy heart, dreading a long confinement and silently questioning when she might depart. Yet, the surprisingly warm reception she encountered lifted her spirits. Her father and sister greeted her kindly, eager to display their new home and its appointments, and they appreciated her presence at the dinner table. Mrs. Clay was as charming and smiling as ever, though her manners felt routine. While Anne had anticipated such behavior from her, the genuine pleasantness of her father and sister was unforeseen. They were in high spirits and eager to share their news, showing little interest in Anne’s own experiences. After fishing for compliments about how much they were missed in their former home—which Anne could not provide—they quickly turned the conversation to their own affairs, focusing entirely on Bath rather than Uppercross or Kellynch. They assured her that Bath exceeded their expectations in every way. Their house was clearly the finest in Camden Place, with drawing-rooms that surpassed all others in layout and decor. They were highly sought after, receiving constant visits from strangers despite their efforts to limit introductions. Anne understood why they were so pleased, yet she could not help but sigh at her father’s lack of regret for his former responsibilities and his vanity regarding such trivial urban matters. She watched with a mix of amusement and sadness as Elizabeth proudly paced between the folding doors, boasting of the space in a house that seemed tiny compared to the grandeur of Kellynch Hall. Beyond these comforts, they also had the company of Mr. Elliot.

Good God! Had I realized for a moment the hellish intent of my monstrous enemy, I would have exiled myself forever, wandering the earth as a friendless outcast, rather than agreeing to this wretched marriage. Yet, as if by magic, the creature blinded me to his true motives; while I believed I was merely preparing for my own death, I was actually hastening the demise of a far more precious victim. As our wedding date approached, whether from cowardice or intuition, my heart sank. I hid my dread behind a facade of cheerfulness that pleased my father, though it barely fooled the observant Elizabeth. She anticipated our union with calm contentment, tempered by a lingering fear that this tangible happiness might vanish like a dream, leaving only lasting regret. Preparations continued, and we received well-wishers, all while I suppressed the anxiety consuming me. I participated in my father’s plans, even as they felt like decorations for my own tragedy. Through his efforts, the Austrian government restored part of Elizabeth’s inheritance, including a small property on the shores of Lake Como. We agreed to spend our honeymoon at Villa Lavenza. Meanwhile, I took every precaution against an open attack, carrying a pistol and dagger, constantly alert for treachery. This vigilance brought me some peace. As the day neared, the threat seemed like a delusion, and our marriage felt increasingly inevitable. Elizabeth appeared happy, and my calm demeanor helped settle her nerves. Yet, on the day that was to seal my fate, she grew melancholy, filled with a sense of impending doom—perhaps because she was thinking of the terrible secret I had promised to reveal to her the following day.

Our investigation lasted until nightfall, at which point we left. While returning, my associate briefly stopped at a newspaper office. I have noted his many eccentricities and my tendency to indulge them. He chose to remain silent regarding the homicide until the following noon, when he abruptly inquired if I had noticed anything peculiar at the crime scene. His emphasis on that word made me shiver inexplicably. I replied that I had seen nothing beyond what the papers reported. He dismissed the press, arguing that the mystery was deemed unsolvable precisely because of its bizarre nature, whereas that should make it simple. The police are baffled by the lack of motive for such brutality, the conflicting accounts of voices heard, and the impossibility of the killer escaping unseen. The chaotic room, the body shoved up the chimney, and the gruesome mutilations have paralyzed the authorities. They err by confusing the unusual with the complex. Yet, it is through these departures from the ordinary that reason finds the truth. In such cases, one should ask not what happened, but what has never happened before. The ease with which I solve this mystery is proportional to its apparent difficulty for the police. I stared at him in silence. He looked toward our door and added that he was expecting someone who, while perhaps not the killer, was surely involved in the crimes.

After settling our friend into his new office, we headed toward Windsor. Because it was so close to London, leaving Raymond and Perdita did not feel like a painful separation. We said our goodbyes at the Protectoral Palace. It was charming to watch my sister embrace her new role, trying to carry herself with appropriate dignity. Her inner pride and humble manner were constantly at odds. Her shyness was genuine, stemming from a fear of being misunderstood and a sensitivity to the world's indifference, much like Raymond. However, Perdita was more considerate of others; her bashfulness came from a desire to ensure those around her did not feel inferior, a thought that never occurred to her. While Idris would have been more naturally suited to formal ceremonies due to her upbringing, she found such routines tedious. In contrast, Perdita clearly enjoyed her new position. She was so occupied with new ideas that she felt little sadness when we left. She said an affectionate goodbye and promised to visit, but she did not mind our departure. Raymond was in high spirits, overwhelmed by his new authority. His mind was full of plans, though he had not settled on any yet. He vowed to his friends and the world that his time as Protector would be marked by some act of great glory. We discussed them as we returned to Windsor Castle with a smaller group. We were relieved to escape the political chaos and returned to our quiet life with renewed appreciation. We kept busy, and I focused my energy on intellectual pursuits; hard study proved to be the perfect remedy for the restless spirit that would have otherwise plagued me. Perdita allowed us to take Clara back to Windsor, and she, along with my two children, provided constant joy. The only thing that troubled us was Adrian's health. He was clearly fading, though he showed no specific symptoms beyond bright eyes, an animated expression, and flushed cheeks, which made us fear consumption. Yet, he felt no pain or fear. He turned to his books with passion and spent his rest periods in the company he loved most: his sister and me.

Goodness, she was an expert conversationalist. It would have been rude to mention the late hour or my own exhaustion. I regretted not retiring earlier, but I was trapped now. She prattled on within the silent, ghostly castle until a distant, muffled scream rose from below, sounding so agonizing that it made my skin prickle. The queen paused, her eyes brightening with delight as she tilted her head like a listening bird. The noise pierced the stillness once more. I asked what it was. She replied that it was a stubborn soul enduring the rack for many hours. When I asked what he was enduring, she invited me to witness the spectacle, promising he would be torn apart if he did not reveal his secret. She was a polished monster, calm and serene, while my own legs ached in sympathy with the victim. Escorted by armored guards with torches, we descended through damp, moldy stone corridors that smelled of ancient darkness. The journey was long and unsettling, made worse by the sorceress discussing the prisoner's crime: killing a stag in the royal woods based on an anonymous tip. I suggested that anonymous accusations were unjust and that the accused should face his accuser. She dismissed this as trivial, noting the accuser had arrived masked at night and remained unknown to the forester. I asked if anyone else witnessed the act, and she admitted no one saw the killing, only that the informant spotted the man near the carcass. I pointed out that the masked informant might be the true culprit, but she insisted the torture was necessary to force a confession. She claimed that while his life was forfeit by law, she needed him to confess and receive absolution to protect her own soul.

Unless you call Miss Havisham a man. And I doubt you would go that far. Miss Havisham, in town? Joe asked. Is there any Miss Havisham out of town? my sister replied. She wants this boy to go and play there. Of course he is going. And he had better play there, she said, shaking her head at me to encourage me to be lively and cheerful, or I will deal with him. I had heard of Miss Havisham in town—everyone for miles around had—as an incredibly wealthy and stern woman who lived in a large, gloomy house barricaded against thieves, living a life of total seclusion. Well, I am amazed! Joe said. I wonder how she came to know Pip! Idiot! my sister cried. Who said she knew him? Some individual, Joe politely hinted, mentioned that she wanted him to go and play there. Could she not ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? Is it not just possible that Uncle Pumblechook is her tenant, and that he might sometimes—we will not say quarterly or half-yearly, as that would be asking too much of you—go there to pay his rent? And could she not then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? And could Uncle Pumblechook, always being considerate and thoughtful for us—though you may not think so, Joseph, she said with deep reproach, as if he were the most unfeeling of nephews—then mention this boy, standing here prancing—which I solemnly declare I was not doing—that I have always been a willing slave to? Good again! Uncle Pumblechook cried. Well put! Nicely stated! Good indeed! Now Joseph, you understand the situation. No, Joseph, my sister said, still reproachfully, while Joe apologetically wiped his nose with the back of his hand, you do not yet—though you may think you do—understand the situation. You may believe you do, but you do not, Joseph. For you do not know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that for all we know this boy’s fortune might be made by going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own cart, keep him overnight, and take him personally to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And good heavens! my sister cried, throwing off her bonnet in sudden desperation, here I am talking to simpletons, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the horse catching a cold at the door, and the boy covered in soot and dirt from head to toe!

Those elderly, frail clerks were always seen bowing to the public. People joked that after showing a customer out, they kept bowing in the empty office until the next person arrived. The lawyer realized the banker would not have spoken so firmly without being certain. Though the news was hard to accept, he managed to process it. Shaking his finger at the room, Mr. Stryver decided his best move was to prove everyone else wrong. It was a classic courtroom tactic that brought him comfort. He told himself he would be the one to reject the young lady before she could reject him. When Mr. Lorry visited that night at ten, Stryver acted as if he were busy with legal papers and had forgotten their earlier talk. He even feigned surprise at seeing Lorry. After half an hour of trying to bring up the topic, Lorry finally said he had been to Soho. Stryver responded coldly, pretending to have forgotten. Lorry insisted his previous advice was correct and still held true. Stryver replied in a friendly tone that he felt sorry for Lorry and the girl’s father, suggesting they drop the painful subject. When Lorry protested that it did matter, Stryver dismissed him with a wave. He claimed he had simply made a mistake in judgment. He remarked that many young women had made similar foolish choices before, only to regret them later in poverty. He concluded that while he was sorry for the family's sake, he was relieved to be finished with the matter, as it would have been a poor choice for his own career.

I must point out, Sir Walter, Mr. Shepherd remarked one morning at Kellynch Hall while setting aside his newspaper, that the current situation works in our favor. This peace will bring many wealthy naval officers back to shore, all of whom will need homes. There could not be a better time to secure reliable tenants. Many fortunes were made during the war, and if a rich admiral were to come our way, Sir Walter— He would be a very lucky man, Shepherd, Sir Walter replied. Kellynch Hall would be a prize to him, the greatest he has ever taken, would it not? Mr. Shepherd laughed as expected at the wit, then added, I would suggest that naval officers are excellent to deal with in business. They have liberal ideas and make desirable tenants. If rumors of your intentions were to spread—which is possible, as it is difficult to keep the affairs of a man of your standing private—I would not be surprised if word got out. Should that happen, I believe applications from wealthy naval commanders would be worth considering. I can be here in two hours to handle any inquiries, saving you the trouble. Sir Walter merely nodded. Soon after, he stood and paced the room, remarking sarcastically, I imagine few naval officers would not be surprised to find themselves in a house of this caliber. They would look around and count their blessings, Mrs. Clay added, having accompanied her father to Kellynch for her health. I agree with my father that a sailor would be a very desirable tenant.

After a brief silence, Mr. Lorry placed a hand on the Doctor’s arm. "To what do you attribute this episode?" he asked. The Doctor replied, "I believe it was triggered by a powerful resurgence of the memories that first caused his illness. Distressing associations were vividly brought to mind. He likely feared these triggers for a long time, and his attempt to brace himself may have only weakened his resolve." When Mr. Lorry asked if the patient would remember the relapse, the Doctor looked around the room and quietly shook his head. "Not at all." Regarding the future, the Doctor regained his composure. "I am hopeful. Since he recovered so quickly, I believe the worst has passed." Mr. Lorry expressed his relief, and the Doctor bowed his head in gratitude. "There are two other points I must discuss," Mr. Lorry continued. "You may proceed," the Doctor said, offering his hand. "He is studious and energetic, applying himself intensely to his work. Is he doing too much?" The Doctor considered this. "I think not. His mind requires constant occupation, perhaps due to his past trauma. Without healthy distractions, his thoughts might drift toward the unhealthy. He may have realized this himself." Mr. Lorry pressed further, "Are you certain he is not under too much strain?" The Doctor insisted he was sure, adding that his intense work served as a necessary counterweight to his past suffering. Mr. Lorry persisted, "If he were overworked, would it manifest as a return of this disorder?"

His temperament and intellect, while distinct from hers, would have fulfilled all her desires. Their partnership would have benefited both: her vivacity might have tempered his disposition and refined his conduct, while his wisdom and worldly experience would have offered her invaluable guidance. Yet, no such ideal union would now demonstrate true marital bliss to the world. Instead, a far less promising alliance was imminent within their household. She struggled to envision how Wickham and Lydia might maintain a decent living, though she easily surmised that a couple united solely by unchecked passion rather than virtue could find little lasting joy. Mr. Gardiner wrote to his brother once more. He briefly acknowledged Mr. Bennet’s thanks, expressing his commitment to the family’s welfare while requesting that the matter never be raised again. His letter primarily served to announce that Wickham intended to leave the militia. He noted that he had strongly encouraged this move once the marriage was settled, believing a transfer was essential for both Wickham and his niece. Wickham planned to join the Regulars, having secured an ensigncy in a regiment stationed in the north through the aid of old acquaintances. This distance from their current home was a distinct benefit. He seemed sincere, and Gardiner hoped that in a new environment, both might act with greater discretion to protect their reputations. He had contacted Colonel Forster to settle Wickham’s debts in Brighton, guaranteeing payment himself, and asked Mr. Bennet to provide similar assurances to creditors in Meryton based on an enclosed list. He trusted Wickham had been honest about his liabilities. Once Haggerston finalized these matters within the week, the couple would join the regiment, unless they visited Longbourn first, as Mrs. Gardiner indicated that her niece was eager to see the family before departing the south.

As the weeks passed, my fixation on you deepened. Initially, I depicted you as Paris in elegant armor or as Adonis carrying a boar-spear. You appeared crowned with lotus flowers on Adrian’s barge upon the Nile, or peering into a Greek woodland pool at your own reflection. Those works were everything art should be: ideal, remote, and unconscious. Eventually, I decided to paint you as you truly are, in modern attire. I cannot say if it was the realism or the raw intensity of your presence, but as I painted, every stroke seemed to expose my hidden devotion. I feared my idolatry was visible, so I resolved never to exhibit the portrait. You were annoyed, though you failed to grasp the significance. Harry mocked my concerns, yet I remained convinced I was right. Once the painting left my studio, however, I felt foolish for believing it held anything beyond your beauty and my technical skill. I suspect now that the passion of creation is never truly captured in the final work; art is more abstract than we assume. It often hides the artist rather than revealing him. Consequently, when the Paris offer arrived, I intended to feature your portrait, never imagining you would object. I realize now you were correct. The painting must remain hidden. Please do not be angry with me, Dorian, for my confession.

It was early February, and Anne had been in Bath for a month. She was anxious for news from Uppercross and Lyme, having heard nothing from Mary for three weeks. She only knew that Henrietta had returned home and that Louisa was recovering in Lyme. One evening, she received a thick letter from Mary, sent with the compliments of Admiral and Mrs. Croft. The Crofts were in Bath, which delighted Anne, as she was very fond of them. Sir Walter immediately asked about the letter, noting that he intended to visit his tenant, Admiral Croft. Anne ignored him, focused entirely on her letter, which had been started days earlier. Mary wrote that she had not written sooner because she assumed Anne was too busy enjoying Bath to care about dull Uppercross. She complained about a boring Christmas, noting that the Musgroves had hosted no parties. She also grumbled that the holidays had lasted too long and that the Harville children were still staying at the house, which she found strange. Mary disliked the children and felt Mrs. Musgrove favored them over her own grandchildren. She also complained about the terrible weather and mentioned that Charles Hayter had been visiting far too often. She added that she wished Henrietta had stayed in Lyme longer to avoid him.

There was no joy in the small town that quiet Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were in deep mourning, filled with grief and tears. An unusual silence hung over the village, which was already peaceful enough. The residents went about their business distractedly, speaking little and sighing often. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children, who lost interest in their games and eventually stopped playing altogether. That afternoon, Becky Thatcher wandered around the empty schoolyard, feeling deeply depressed. Finding no comfort there, she whispered to herself, "If only I still had that brass andiron knob. Now I have nothing to remember him by." She choked back a sob. She paused and added, "It happened right here. If I could do it over, I would never say that—not for anything. But he is gone, and I will never see him again." Overcome, she walked away with tears streaming down her face. Soon, a group of Tom and Joe’s friends gathered by the fence, speaking in hushed tones about the last time they saw the boys. They pointed out exactly where the missing lads had stood, recalling small, prophetic details. Each child described their own position, claiming they felt a strange, chilling sensation at the time, which they only now understood. A debate broke out over who had seen the boys last. Those who could prove they had spoken to them last gained a sense of solemn importance, envied by the others. One boy, lacking any other claim to fame, said proudly, "Well, Tom Sawyer beat me up once." The attempt at glory failed, as most of the boys could say the same. The group drifted away, still whispering memories of the lost boys.

Poor Jack was later killed in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended; in every sense, it was a complete success. It was, however, a difficult transformation to achieve, and it took him three full hours to prepare. Finally, he was satisfied with his appearance. The leather riding boots were slightly oversized, and he could only locate one of his two horse pistols, but he was pleased enough. At 1:15 a.m., he slipped from the wainscoting and crept down the hall. Reaching the twins' room, known as the Blue Bed Chamber for its curtains, he found the door slightly open. Hoping for a dramatic entrance, he threw it wide, only for a heavy water jug to fall on him, soaking him completely and narrowly missing his shoulder. Simultaneously, he heard muffled laughter from the four-poster bed. The shock sent him fleeing back to his room, and he spent the next day bedridden with a severe cold. He was only consoled by the fact that he had left his head behind; had he been wearing it, the outcome could have been disastrous. He abandoned all hope of terrifying the rude American family, settling for shuffling through the halls in soft slippers, wearing a thick red scarf to avoid drafts and carrying a small arquebus in case the twins attacked. The final indignity occurred on September 19th. He had gone to the main entrance hall, assuming he would be left alone, and was mocking the large Saroni photographs of the American Minister and his wife that had replaced the Canterville portraits. He was dressed simply in a burial shroud stained with grave dirt, his jaw bound with yellow linen, and he carried a small lantern and a sexton’s spade.

“I look forward to presenting my son to you before long,” Mr. Weston remarked. Mrs. Elton, pleased to interpret this as a personal tribute, offered a gracious smile. “You are likely familiar with Frank Churchill,” he added, “and aware that he is my son, despite his different surname.” “Indeed, I shall be delighted to meet him. Mr. Elton will certainly call upon him promptly, and we would both be pleased to welcome him to the Vicarage.” “You are very kind. Frank will be equally pleased. He is expected in town by next week, if not sooner. We received word today; I intercepted the mail this morning and, seeing his handwriting, took the liberty of opening the letter addressed to Mrs. Weston. She is his primary correspondent, I fear; I rarely receive one myself.” “You actually opened her mail! Oh, Mr. Weston,” she said with a playful laugh, “I must object. That sets a dangerous precedent! I hope your neighbors do not follow suit. If this is the standard, we wives must be on our guard! I never would have suspected you of such a thing.” “We men are indeed troublesome. You must be cautious, Mrs. Elton. This brief note informs us that they are traveling to town immediately for Mrs. Churchill’s sake. She has been unwell all winter and finds Enscombe too chilly, so they are relocating south without delay.” “From Yorkshire, I believe? Is Enscombe in Yorkshire?” “Yes, it is roughly one hundred and ninety miles from London—a significant trip.” “Quite significant, indeed. Sixty-five miles further than the distance from Maple Grove to London. Yet, what is distance to the wealthy? You would be astonished by how my brother, Mr. Suckling, travels. It is hard to believe, but he and Mr. Bragge once made the round trip to London twice in a single week using four horses.” “The trouble with the distance from Enscombe,” Mr. Weston noted, “is that Mrs. Churchill has reportedly been confined to her sofa for a week. In his recent letter, Frank mentioned she was too frail to reach her conservatory without the support of both his arm and his uncle’s.”

We endured a few miserable hours until the trial began at eleven. My father and the family had to attend as witnesses, so I went with them. Throughout this pathetic mockery of justice, I suffered absolute agony. It was to be decided if my reckless curiosity would lead to the deaths of two people: one an innocent, joyful baby, the other a victim of a horrific, infamous murder. Justine was a virtuous girl with a bright future, yet now she faced a shameful death because of me. I would have gladly confessed to the crime myself, but my absence made such a claim seem like the ravings of a madman, and it would not have saved her. Justine appeared calm. Dressed in mourning, her naturally engaging face looked exquisitely beautiful in its solemnity. She seemed confident in her innocence and did not tremble, despite being stared at and cursed by thousands who viewed her as a monster. Her tranquility was clearly forced; having been accused of guilt earlier due to her confusion, she now summoned a facade of courage. Entering the courtroom, she scanned the room and spotted us. A tear clouded her eye, but she quickly regained her composure, her sorrowful, affectionate gaze confirming her innocence. The trial commenced, and after the prosecutor presented the charges, witnesses were called. Several bizarre facts emerged that might have convinced anyone lacking my knowledge of her innocence. She had been out all night when the murder occurred, and a market woman had seen her near the crime scene toward morning. When asked what she was doing there, she had acted strangely and given a confused, incoherent reply. She returned home at eight o’clock, and when asked where she had been, she claimed she was searching for the child and anxiously inquired if he had been found.

Seeing the creature, the orangutan leaped through the door, down the stairs, and out an open window into the street. The Frenchman followed in despair, while the ape, still holding the razor, paused occasionally to gesture at him before darting away again. This chase continued through the quiet streets near three in the morning. Passing an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the ape noticed a light from Madame L’Espanaye’s fourth-story window. It rushed to the building, climbed the lightning rod with incredible speed, grabbed the open shutter, and swung onto the bed’s headboard in less than a minute, kicking the shutter as it entered. The sailor felt both relieved and worried. He hoped to trap the beast, as it could only escape by climbing back down the rod, but he feared what it might do inside. He followed, climbing the rod easily, but when he reached the window, he could only lean over to peer inside. What he saw nearly made him fall in terror. This was when the horrific screams began, waking the neighbors. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter were in their nightclothes, sorting papers from an open iron chest in the middle of the room. They had their backs to the window and likely did not notice the beast at first, assuming the shutter had been blown by the wind. As the sailor watched, the giant animal grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by her loose hair and waved the razor near her face, mimicking a barber.

They passed empty brickfields where the fog thinned, revealing bottle-shaped kilns glowing with orange fire. A dog barked, and a distant seagull cried out. The horse stumbled, then broke into a gallop. Soon, they left the dirt road for rough, paved streets. Most windows were dark, but he watched shadows dance behind lit blinds, hating their puppet-like movements. A dull rage grew within him. As they turned a corner, a woman shouted, and two men chased the carriage until the driver whipped them away. Passion often makes one think in circles. Dorian Gray repeatedly whispered the same words about soul and sense, finding in them a justification for his desires. A desperate hunger for life surged through him. He began to cherish the ugliness he once despised because it felt real. The crude violence and filth of the city were more vivid to him than art or music; they offered the distraction he craved. In three days, he would be free. The carriage stopped abruptly at a dark lane near the docks, where ship masts rose above the rooftops like ghostly sails. The driver asked if they had arrived. Dorian stepped out, paid the man, and hurried toward the quay. Lanterns flickered on merchant ships, their light reflecting in the puddles. A red glow shone from a nearby steamer, and the wet pavement glistened like oil.

“You don’t mean to say—” my sister began. “Yes, I do,” Pumblechook interrupted. “Go on, Joseph.” “What would you say to twenty pounds?” Joe asked. “That would be generous,” my sister replied. “Well,” Joe continued, “it’s more than twenty.” Pumblechook nodded, laughing patronizingly. “It’s more than that, indeed. Keep going, Joseph!” “To finish it,” Joe said, handing her the bag, “it’s twenty-five pounds.” “Twenty-five pounds,” Pumblechook echoed, standing to shake her hand, “and you deserve every penny. I wish you joy!” The villain then made things worse by seizing my arm with an air of ownership that eclipsed his previous behavior. “Now, Joseph and wife,” he said, gripping my elbow, “I always finish what I start. This boy must be apprenticed immediately. That’s my way.” “We are deeply grateful, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, clutching the cash. “Don’t mention it,” the man replied. “But we must get this boy bound. I promised I would see to it.” We went to the nearby Town Hall to finalize my apprenticeship. Pumblechook shoved me along as if I had just committed a crime. The crowd clearly assumed I was guilty; some asked what I had done, while others remarked on my supposedly wicked appearance. A kind-looking person even handed me a pamphlet titled To Be Read In My Cell, featuring an illustration of a young criminal in chains. The courtroom felt strange, with high pews and onlookers peering down. The Justices sat back, some reading newspapers or dozing, while dark portraits hung on the walls, appearing to my eyes like strange, hardened lumps.

They traveled past desolate brickyards. The mist thinned, revealing odd, bottle-shaped kilns glowing with orange flames. A dog bayed, and a distant gull cried out in the gloom. The horse tripped in a rut, then veered and began to gallop. Eventually, they left the dirt track for uneven cobblestones. Most windows remained dark, though occasionally strange silhouettes danced against illuminated blinds. He observed them with interest, finding their puppet-like movements repulsive. A simmering anger filled him. As they rounded a bend, a woman shouted from a doorway, and two men pursued the carriage briefly until the driver lashed out with his whip. Passion often traps the mind in repetitive cycles. Dorian Gray obsessively turned over the same phrases regarding soul and sense, seeking to justify his turbulent emotions through intellectualization.
