His desire to live intensified, sharpening his nerves. He began to cherish the ugliness he once despised, finding it more authentic than art or music. Such raw, chaotic reality offered the oblivion he craved. In three days, he would be liberated. The carriage stopped abruptly at the mouth of a dark alley. Beyond the jagged rooftops, ship masts loomed, draped in ghostly white fog. The driver asked if they had arrived. Dorian stepped out, paid the promised fare, and hurried toward the quay. Lanterns flickered on merchant vessels, their light fracturing in the puddles. A steamer nearby cast a red glow, and the damp pavement glistened like oilcloth.

In English, the letter e appears most often. The remaining frequency follows this order: a, o, i, d, h, n, r, s, t, u, y, c, f, g, l, m, w, b, k, p, q, x, z. E is so dominant that it is rare to find a sentence of any length where it does not appear most frequently. This provides a solid foundation for more than just a guess. While the table is generally useful, we only need it partially here. Since 8 is our most frequent character, we will assume it represents e. To verify this, we check if 8 appears in pairs, as e often does in words like meet, fleet, or speed. In this short cipher, it appears doubled five times. Let us assume 8 is e. The word the is the most common in our language, so we should look for three characters appearing together in that order, ending with 8. If we find such a pattern, it likely represents the. We find seven instances of the sequence ;48. We can assume ; is t, 4 is h, and 8 is e. This is a significant step. Having identified one word, we can determine the starts and ends of others. Look at the second-to-last instance of ;48 near the end of the cipher. We know the following ; starts a new word, and we already recognize five of the six characters following that the. Writing them out with known letters and a blank space, we get t eeth. We can discard the th as part of the word starting with the first t, because testing the alphabet shows no word fits that structure. This leaves us with t ee, and by testing the remaining letters, we identify the word as tree.

“Never!” the girl replied. “Tell me why?” “For one reason,” she said firmly, “the lady knows and will support me; I have her promise. Also, I have lived a bad life, just like the others I have known. I will not betray them, even though they are criminals, because they never betrayed me.” “Then,” the gentleman said quickly, “give me Monks, and let me handle him.” “What if he turns against the others?” she asked. “If the truth is forced from him, the matter will end there. Oliver’s history contains painful details that should not be made public. If we get the truth, the others will go free.” “And if not?” she asked. “Then,” the gentleman continued, “Fagin will not be prosecuted without your consent. I believe I could convince you to agree if it came to that.” “Do I have the lady’s promise?” she asked. “You do,” Rose replied. “My sincere pledge.” “Monks will never know how you found out?” the girl asked after a pause. “Never,” the gentleman said. “He will never even guess.” “I have been a liar since I was a child,” she said, “but I will trust your word.” After they assured her she was safe, she spoke in a low voice, describing the tavern she had left that night. As she paused, the gentleman took quick notes. Once she explained the location, how to watch it without being seen, and when Monks usually visited, she paused to recall his appearance. “He is tall and well-built, but not heavy,” she said. “He walks cautiously, constantly looking over his shoulder.”

My father stood by me, offering comfort and replacing painful recollections with optimistic prospects; I found a strange solace in my sadness, knowing he would soothe my weeping. He further diverted my mind by contrasting my grief with his own anguish upon losing my mother. I trembled at his vivid descriptions, for he possessed a poet's imagination, rendering his past emotional turbulence with such lifelike intensity that I felt his terror. I marveled that he could return to ordinary existence after such profound, almost supernatural experiences; his concepts seemed too vast for a mortal heart to contain, better suited to a spirit dwelling in cataclysms than a man of flesh and blood. Yet, he had transformed; he was now entirely gentle and affectionate, his smile revealing a heart governed by kindness. Two months following my aunt's passing, we relocated to London, where my father guided me toward more rigorous academic pursuits. He took great joy in my progress, participating in every lesson. We socialized frequently, and he constantly sought to brighten our days with new diversions. Our mutual devotion created a delightful atmosphere; we lived so fully that a single week felt like months, with every experience enriched by novelty. We traveled often, whether to admire landscapes, view art, or simply seek spontaneous enjoyment, and I was always content in his presence. I disliked when others joined us, yet a single tender glance from my father would instantly restore my happiness. Those moments of profound joy were fleeting, yet in retrospect, obscured by the subsequent fog of sorrow, they seem to span an entire lifetime.

I agree. It is the best plan. Will you just join hands and promise that we— Oh no, that will not suffice for this. That is fine for trivial, common matters—especially with girls, because they betray you regardless and gossip if they get angry—but there ought to be a written record for a significant thing like this. And blood. Tom’s entire spirit cheered this notion. It was profound, dark, and ominous; the time, the situation, and the environment were all appropriate. He grabbed a smooth pine shingle resting in the moonlight, retrieved a small piece of red chalk from his pocket, caught the moonlight on his task, and laboriously scratched these words, stressing every deliberate downward stroke by biting his tongue and easing the pressure on the upward strokes. Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will remain silent about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot. Huckleberry was struck with awe at Tom’s writing skill and the grandeur of his prose. He immediately pulled a pin from his lapel and prepared to pierce his skin, but Tom intervened. Wait! Do not do that. A pin is brass. It might have verdigris on it. What is verdigris? It is poison. That is what it is. You just swallow some of it once—you will see. So Tom unspooled thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked his thumb pad, squeezing out a drop of blood. Eventually, after much squeezing, Tom managed to sign his initials, using his little finger as a pen. Then he instructed Huckleberry on how to form an H and an F, and the vow was finished. They interred the shingle near the wall with somber rituals and chants, and the chains binding their tongues were deemed locked with the key discarded. A figure crept quietly through a gap at the far end of the derelict structure, but they remained unaware. Tom, Huckleberry whispered, does this prevent us from ever telling—always? Certainly it does. It makes no difference what happens, we must stay silent. We would drop down dead—do you not know that? Yes, I suppose that is true. They continued whispering for a while. Suddenly, a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—within ten feet of them. The boys grabbed each other instantly, paralyzed by terror. Which one of us is he signaling? Huckleberry gasped. I do not know—look through the crack. Quickly! No, you do it, Tom! I cannot—I am unable to, Huck!

With their business settled, the agreement was sealed with another cup of peppermint, which the lady required to calm her nerves. As she drank, she informed Mr. Bumble of the old woman’s passing. That gentleman, sipping his drink, promised to notify Sowerberry to collect the body the next day, asking if that news had caused her distress. She evaded the question, promising to explain after their wedding. When Mr. Bumble suggested a male pauper might have insulted her, she quickly denied it. He grew indignant, threatening to punish any man who dared look at her, a display of devotion that moved the lady to call him a dove. The dove then donned his hat and coat, embraced his bride-to-be, and ventured into the night. He stopped briefly in the paupers’ ward to berate the residents, confirming his own capacity for the necessary harshness of a workhouse master. Satisfied, he headed toward the undertaker’s shop, his mind filled with dreams of advancement. Finding the shop open and the Sowerberrys away, he tapped his cane on the counter. Receiving no response, he peered into the back parlor and was quite astonished by what he witnessed.

“Tom!” Silence. “TOM!” Silence. “Where has that boy gone? You, TOM!” Still no reply. The elderly woman adjusted her glasses to peer around the room, though she rarely used them for spotting a mere boy; they were for show, not utility, and she could have seen just as clearly through iron lids. Puzzled, she muttered, loud enough for the room to hear, “If I catch you, I’ll—” She left the threat unfinished, busy jabbing her broom beneath the bed. She only managed to retrieve the cat. “I have never seen the likes of that child!” She stepped to the doorway to survey the garden of tomato plants and weeds. Tom was nowhere to be seen. She raised her voice to carry across the yard: “Y-o-u-u TOM!” A rustle behind her made her spin around, catching a small boy by his jacket just as he tried to bolt. “I should have checked the closet. What were you doing in there?” “Nothing.” “Nothing? Look at your hands and mouth. What is that?” “I don’t know, Aunt.” “I know. It is jam. I have told you forty times to leave it alone or I would tan your hide. Give me that switch.” As the rod hung in the air, the danger peaked. “Oh! Look behind you, Aunt!” The woman turned quickly, pulling her skirts aside. The boy vanished instantly, scaling the tall fence and leaping over. Aunt Polly stood stunned, then began to chuckle. “Confound the boy, will I never learn? Has he not tricked me enough that I should expect this? Yet old fools are the worst. You cannot teach an old dog new tricks. Still, he never repeats the same prank, so how is one to anticipate him? He seems to know exactly how far to push me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me or make me laugh, my anger vanishes and I cannot strike him.”

Mr. Darcy spoke warmly of his sister’s musical skill. Lady Catherine remarked that she must practice diligently to excel. Darcy assured her that his sister already practiced constantly. Lady Catherine insisted that one could never practice enough, noting that she frequently advised Miss Bennet to do the same and offered Mrs. Collins use of the piano at Rosings. Darcy appeared embarrassed by his aunt’s rudeness and remained silent. After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam asked Elizabeth to play, and she complied. Lady Catherine chatted with Darcy until he moved toward the piano to watch Elizabeth. Elizabeth noticed him and teased that he intended to intimidate her with his presence, though she refused to be cowed. Darcy replied that she did not truly believe he meant to frighten her, noting her habit of expressing opinions she did not actually hold. Elizabeth laughed and told the Colonel that his cousin was painting a poor picture of her, lamenting that she had hoped to maintain a better reputation in this part of the country.

I wrapped him in paper and stuffed a piece in his mouth—that was the way. And you believe your master was truly bitten by the beetle, and that the bite caused his illness? I do not think anything about it—I know it. Why would he dream of gold if not because he was bitten by that gold-bug? I have heard of those bugs before. But how do you know he dreams of gold? How do I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that is how I know. Well, Jupiter, perhaps you are right; but to what good fortune do I owe your visit today? What is the matter, sir? Did you bring a message from Mr. Legrand? No, sir, I brought this letter. Jupiter handed me a note that read: My dear friend, why have I not seen you in so long? I hope you have not been foolish enough to take offense at my recent abruptness; though that is unlikely. Since we last met, I have had great cause for anxiety. I have something to tell you, though I hardly know how to say it, or if I should say it at all. I have not been well lately, and poor old Jupiter annoys me beyond endurance with his well-meaning care. Would you believe he prepared a large stick to punish me for slipping away to spend the day alone in the hills? I truly believe my poor appearance alone saved me from a beating. I have added nothing to my collection since we met. If you can, please come over with Jupiter. Do come. I must see you tonight regarding a matter of the highest importance. Yours, William Legrand. The tone of this note caused me great unease. Its style differed significantly from Legrand’s usual manner. What could he be dreaming of? What new obsession had taken hold of his excitable mind? What business could possibly be of such importance? Jupiter’s account boded no good. I feared that the constant pressure of misfortune had finally unsettled my friend’s reason. Without hesitation, I prepared to accompany the man. Upon reaching the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all seemingly new, lying in the bottom of the boat. What is the meaning of all this, Jupiter?

“So, I own a few knights now,” I remarked as we rode away. “Who would have thought I’d end up with assets like these? I have no idea what to do with them, unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?” “Seven, sir, along with their squires.” “That’s a decent haul. Who are they, and where are they based?” “Where are they based?” “Yes, where do they live?” “Ah, I didn’t understand you. I will tell you shortly.” She repeated the phrase to herself, savoring the sound. “Where are they based? It has a charming, elegant ring to it. I shall practice it while I’m idle so I might learn it. Where are they based? It already rolls off my tongue quite easily.” “Don’t forget the knights, Sandy.” “Knights?” “Yes, you were going to tell me about them. Let’s get to the point.” “I will begin,” she said. “So, the two of them departed and rode into a vast forest. And—” “Good grief!” I realized my mistake immediately. I had started her off, and it was my own fault; she would take a month to reach the facts. She usually started without an introduction and finished without a conclusion. If I interrupted, she would either ignore me or repeat the sentence from the beginning. Interruptions were counterproductive, yet I had to make them to survive; the sheer monotony of her storytelling was unbearable. “Good grief!” I exclaimed in frustration. She simply started over. “So, the two of them departed and rode into a vast forest. And—” “Which two?” “Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. They arrived at an abbey of monks, where they were well lodged. The next morning, they heard mass and rode until they reached a great forest. There, Sir Gawaine noticed twelve beautiful damsels and two armed knights on large horses in a valley near a tower, with the damsels walking back and forth by a tree.”

Farewell, Uncle George. I must depart or I shall miss lunch. Thank you for the details I requested; I prefer learning about new acquaintances while ignoring the old. Where are you dining, Harry? At Aunt Agatha’s. I invited myself and Mr. Gray, her current favorite. Tell her to stop pestering me with her charitable requests, Harry. I am tired of her assuming I exist only to fund her whims. I will tell her, Uncle, though it will be futile. Philanthropists lack all humanity; it is their defining trait. The old man grunted in agreement and summoned his servant. Lord Henry walked through the arcade toward Berkeley Square. So that was the history of Dorian Gray’s birth. Despite the blunt delivery, the tale of a strange, modern romance intrigued him. A beautiful woman sacrificing all for a reckless passion, followed by brief happiness ended by a treacherous crime. Then, months of silent suffering, a painful birth, the mother’s death, and a boy left to the cold rule of a loveless guardian. It was a compelling history that framed the youth perfectly. Every beautiful thing requires a tragic foundation; the world must suffer for a flower to bloom. How charming he had been the previous evening, his eyes wide and lips parted in delight as he sat across from him, the candlelight deepening the wonder on his face. Conversing with him felt like playing a fine violin, responsive to every movement. The power of influence was deeply captivating. To project one’s soul into another, to hear one’s own thoughts returned with the music of youth, to infuse one’s temperament into another like a delicate perfume—this was a profound joy in an era so vulgar and limited. This lad, discovered by chance in Basil’s studio, was a marvelous specimen, or at least, one that could be molded into such.

I examined the skull closely. The outer edges, nearest the vellum’s border, were sharper than the rest, suggesting the heat had been applied unevenly. I lit a fire and exposed the entire parchment to the warmth. Initially, only the skull’s faint lines darkened, but as I persisted, a figure appeared in the corner diagonally opposite the skull. I first thought it was a goat, but closer inspection convinced me it was a kid. I laughed, telling Legrand that while a fortune was no laughing matter, he shouldn't try to link pirates to goats, as they were agricultural creatures. He corrected me, noting it was not a goat. I replied that a kid was essentially the same. He explained that he viewed the animal as a punning signature for Captain Kidd, given its placement. The skull, positioned diagonally, seemed like a seal. Still, I was frustrated by the lack of accompanying text. I assumed he had hoped for a letter between the seal and signature. He agreed, admitting he felt a strong premonition of great fortune. He confessed that Jupiter’s foolish remark about the golden bug had sparked his imagination. He marveled at the series of coincidences, noting how the rare cool weather allowed for a fire, and how, without that fire or the dog’s timely arrival, he would never have discovered the skull or the treasure.

It was marvelous even to read about the opulence of the deceased. He then shifted his focus to embroideries and the tapestries that served as frescoes in the cold chambers of northern Europe. As he studied these—possessing a unique talent for total immersion in his current interest—he felt a melancholy regarding the decay time inflicts upon exquisite objects. He, however, had avoided such a fate. Seasons passed, flowers withered, and nights of dread recounted their disgrace, yet he remained unaltered. No winter touched his youthful complexion. How starkly this contrasted with physical items. Where had they vanished? Where was the saffron robe depicting the gods battling giants, crafted by dark-skinned maidens for Athena? Where was the massive velarium Nero spanned over the Colosseum, that purple sail showing the starry heavens and Apollo’s chariot? He yearned to behold the intricate napkins of the Priest of the Sun, featuring every imaginable feast delicacy; King Chilperic’s burial shroud with its three hundred golden bees; the eccentric garments that angered the Bishop of Pontus, adorned with beasts and hunters; or the coat of Charles of Orleans, its sleeves embroidered with a song’s lyrics and musical notes fashioned from pearls. He learned of Queen Joan of Burgundy’s Rheims palace chamber, decorated with over a thousand golden parrots and hundreds of butterflies bearing royal crests. Catherine de Medicis owned a mourning-bed of black velvet covered in crescents and suns, draped in damask and pearl-fringed embroidery, set within a room hung with her emblems. Louis XIV featured fifteen-foot-tall gold-embroidered caryatids in his quarters.

In that harsh critique of Chantilly published in yesterday’s Musée, the writer made shameful remarks about the cobbler changing his name for the stage, citing a Latin line we have discussed: Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum. I had explained that this referred to Orion, once spelled Urion, and I knew you remembered it. It was obvious you would connect Orion with Chantilly. Your smile confirmed you had, and I saw you thinking of the poor cobbler’s demise. You straightened your posture, clearly reflecting on Chantilly’s small stature. I interrupted your thoughts to suggest that, given his size, he would be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés. Shortly after, we were reading the evening Gazette des Tribunaux when these paragraphs caught our eye: Extraordinary Murders. At three this morning, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by terrifying screams from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue, occupied by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Camille. After failing to gain entry, neighbors broke down the door with a crowbar and entered with two police officers. The screams had stopped, but as they climbed the stairs, they heard two rough voices arguing above. By the second landing, silence had returned. The group searched the rooms, eventually forcing open a locked back chamber on the fourth floor. The scene inside horrified and astonished them. The room was in total disarray, with furniture smashed and scattered. The bed had been stripped, its mattress thrown into the center of the floor. A blood-stained razor lay on a chair.

I wish we had a donkey. It would be perfect for Jane, Miss Bates, and me to ride, with my dear husband walking alongside. I really must discuss buying one with him. In the country, I consider it a necessity; no matter how many interests a woman has, she cannot stay indoors forever, and long walks are difficult—there is always dust in summer and mud in winter. You will find neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and it is perfectly dry right now. Still, come by donkey if you prefer; you can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I want everything to be exactly to your liking. I am sure you do. I truly appreciate you, my friend. Beneath your dry, blunt exterior, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are quite the character. Believe me, Knightley, I am fully aware of your thoughtfulness in planning this. You have suggested exactly what I wanted. Mr. Knightley had another reason to avoid sitting in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse and Emma to join, and he knew that eating outdoors would inevitably make Mr. Woodhouse ill. He could not let him be tempted into misery under the guise of a pleasant morning drive. He was invited in good faith, with no hidden traps. He agreed. He had not visited Donwell in two years. He thought that on a fine morning, he, Emma, and Harriet could go; he could sit with Mrs. Weston while the girls walked the gardens. He doubted the ground would be damp in the middle of the day. He would love to see the old house again and meet the Eltons and other neighbors. He saw no objection to the trip. He thought Mr. Knightley’s invitation was kind and sensible—much better than dining out, which he disliked. Mr. Knightley was fortunate that everyone agreed so readily. The invitation was so well received that everyone seemed to take it as a personal compliment. Emma and Harriet expressed great excitement, and Mr. Weston promised to bring Frank along if possible—a gesture of approval that Mr. Knightley could have done without. He was forced to say he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston vowed to write immediately to persuade him.

Why, you don't mean to say— my sister began. Yes I do, Mum, said Pumblechook, but wait a bit. Go on, Joseph. Good in you! Go on! What would present company say, Joe continued, to twenty pounds? Handsome would be the word, my sister replied. Well, then, said Joe, it is more than twenty pounds. That hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and said with a patronizing laugh, It is more than that, Mum. Good again! Follow her up, Joseph! Then to make an end of it, Joe said, happily handing the bag to my sister, it is twenty-five pounds. It is twenty-five pounds, Mum, echoed that swindler Pumblechook, rising to shake her hand, and it is no more than you deserve, as I said when asked, and I wish you joy of the money! If the villain had stopped there, his behavior would have been bad enough, but he made it worse by taking me into custody with a sense of authority that surpassed his previous offenses. Now you see, Joseph and wife, Pumblechook said, grabbing my arm, I am one of those people who always finish what they start. This boy must be apprenticed immediately. That is my way. Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook, my sister said, clutching the money, we are deeply grateful to you. Never mind me, Mum, the corn-dealer replied. A pleasure is a pleasure. But this boy, you know, we must have him apprenticed. I said I would see to it. The Justices were sitting in the nearby Town Hall, so we went over to have me officially apprenticed to Joe. I say we went over, but Pumblechook shoved me along as if I had just committed a crime. The crowd clearly thought I had been caught red-handed, as people asked what I had done and remarked that I looked like a bad kid. One kind person even gave me a religious pamphlet about a young criminal in prison. The Hall was a strange place with high pews like a church, onlookers leaning over the sides, and powerful Justices who were busy reading, sleeping, or taking snuff. On the walls hung dark portraits that looked to my untrained eyes like lumps of candy and adhesive.

Winters near Sullivan’s Island are rarely harsh, and a fire is seldom needed in autumn. However, in mid-October of that year, a day of unusual cold arrived. Just before sunset, I pushed through the evergreens to my friend’s cabin. I had not visited in weeks, as I lived in Charleston nine miles away, and travel was far more difficult then. Finding no answer to my knock, I retrieved the hidden key, unlocked the door, and entered. A fire blazed on the hearth, a welcome surprise. I removed my coat, sat by the logs, and waited for my host. He arrived after dark, greeting me warmly. Jupiter, grinning broadly, hurried to prepare marsh-hens for dinner. Legrand was in one of his typical states of intense excitement. He had discovered a new genus of bivalve and, with Jupiter’s help, had captured a beetle he believed was entirely new, though he wanted my opinion on it the next day. Why not tonight? I asked, warming my hands and wishing the beetle elsewhere. If I had known you were coming, Legrand replied, but it has been so long. I foolishly lent the specimen to Lieutenant G from the fort, so you cannot see it until morning. Stay the night, and I will have Jup fetch it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing in existence. What, sunrise? I asked. No, the bug! he insisted. It is brilliant gold, the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end and a longer one at the other. The antennae are... There is no tin in it, Massa Will, I keep telling you, Jupiter interrupted. The bug is solid gold, inside and out, except for its wings. I have never felt a bug so heavy in my life.

Raymond paced the room in a fury. I stood prepared to face his accusations. Adrian leaned against the wall. "This is absurd," he cried. "If you were schoolboys, you could not act more unreasonably." "You do not understand," Raymond said. "This is part of a system of tyranny I will never accept. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in the empire? My privacy is invaded, my actions criticized, and my friends insulted. I am finished with it all." He took the star, the symbol of his office, from his chest and threw it onto the table. "I renounce my position. I abdicate my power. Let whoever wants it take it." "Let someone take it," Adrian exclaimed, "if they can prove themselves your superior. No one in England has the arrogance to try. Know yourself, Raymond, and your anger will fade. Months ago, we prayed for the country's prosperity and for the Protector's welfare as one. You dedicated your time to our benefit and sought our approval. You improved our towns, built useful institutions, and made the land fertile. The powerful feared your judgment, and the poor thrived under your protection. Can you wonder that we are shocked and grieving now that this has changed? This bad mood has passed; resume your duties. Your supporters will cheer, your enemies will be silenced, and we will show you our love and respect again. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world is yours." "That would be sensible if said to someone else," Raymond replied moodily. "Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the highest peer in the land, could become its sovereign. You are good, wise, and just; you could rule all hearts. But I realize, too late for England, that I took on a task I cannot handle. I cannot rule myself. My passions are my masters. Do you think I renounced the Protectorate in a fit of temper? I swear by the living God that I will never pick up that trinket again, nor burden myself with the weight of the misery it represents."

He thought so, at least, but who could be sure? No, there was nothing more. He had spared her out of vanity and acted the part of a good man out of hypocrisy. He had practiced self-denial only to satisfy his curiosity. He understood that now. But would this murder haunt him forever? Was he destined to be burdened by his past? Confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained: the portrait itself. He had to destroy it. Why had he kept it so long? It once brought him pleasure to watch it age, but lately, it only caused him distress and kept him awake. When away, he lived in terror that someone might see it. It had cast a shadow over his passions and ruined his joy. It had become his conscience. He would destroy it. He spotted the knife he had used to kill Basil Hallward. He had polished it until it shone. Just as it had killed the painter, it would now destroy the painter’s work and everything it represented. It would kill the past, and with that dead, he would be free. It would end this monstrous existence, and without its hideous warnings, he would finally find peace. He grabbed the blade and stabbed the canvas. A cry of agony rang out, followed by a crash. The sound was so horrific that the terrified servants woke and crept from their rooms. Two men passing through the square below stopped to look at the mansion. They found a policeman and brought him back. He rang the bell repeatedly, but there was no answer. Aside from a light in an upper window, the house remained dark. Eventually, the officer moved to a nearby portico to watch. Whose house is that, Constable? the older man asked. It belongs to Mr. Dorian Gray, the officer replied. The men exchanged a sneer as they walked away. One was the uncle of Sir Henry Ashton. Inside, the servants whispered to one another in their nightclothes. Mrs. Leaf wept and wrung her hands while Francis looked deathly pale. After fifteen minutes, he gathered the coachman and a footman and crept upstairs.

He shuddered and retreated, shutting the window. Upon reaching the door, he unlocked it and stepped out, deliberately avoiding a look at the corpse. He believed the key to his composure was to ignore the reality of the scene. The man who had created the portrait responsible for his suffering was gone; that sufficed. He then recalled the Moorish lamp, crafted of silver and steel with turquoise accents. Fearing his servant might notice its absence, he returned to retrieve it. He could not avoid seeing the body, noting how motionless it lay and how ghastly white the hands appeared, resembling a macabre wax figure. After locking the door, he descended the stairs, the floorboards groaning under his weight. He paused frequently, but the house remained silent. In the library, he gathered the coat and bag, stowing them in a hidden wall compartment where he kept his costumes, intending to burn them later. Checking his watch, he saw it was nearly two. He pondered his situation, reflecting on the frequency of executions for such crimes. Yet, he reasoned, there was no proof. Basil had departed at eleven, and no one had witnessed his return. With the staff away and his valet asleep, he could claim Basil had taken the midnight train to Paris. Given the artist's reclusive nature, months would pass before anyone grew suspicious, providing ample time to erase all traces. A sudden idea occurred to him. Donning his coat and hat, he moved to the hall, pausing as a policeman’s lantern flashed against the window. He held his breath until the officer passed, then quietly unlatched the door, slipped outside, and began to ring the bell.

So, let us hear the whole story. Well, it happened like this. Miss Watson was always nagging me and treating me harshly, yet she insisted she would never sell me down to New Orleans. Still, I noticed a slave trader hanging around the property quite a bit lately, which made me nervous. One night, I crept up to the door and found it slightly ajar. I overheard Miss Watson telling the widow that she intended to sell me to New Orleans. She claimed she did not want to, but the offer of eight hundred dollars was too much money to turn down. The widow tried to talk her out of it, but I did not wait to hear the rest. I left in a hurry. I ran down the hill, intending to steal a skiff along the shore somewhere above town, but people were still moving about, so I hid in the old, dilapidated cooperage by the riverbank to wait for the area to clear. I stayed there all night. People were around constantly. By six in the morning, boats began passing, and by eight or nine, everyone in every skiff was talking about how your father had come to town claiming you were murdered. These later boats were filled with ladies and gentlemen heading over to see the scene. Sometimes they would pull up to the shore to rest before crossing, so through their conversations, I learned all about the killing. I was deeply sorry you were dead, Huck, but I am not anymore. I lay there under the wood shavings all day. I was hungry, but I was not afraid, because I knew Miss Watson and the widow would head to the camp meeting right after breakfast and be gone all day. They knew I usually went out with the cattle at dawn, so they would not expect to see me around the house and would not miss me until after dark. The other servants would not notice my absence either, as they would sneak off to take a holiday as soon as the owners were out of sight. When darkness fell, I headed up the river road for two miles or more to where there were no houses. I had decided on my plan. You see, if I kept trying to escape on foot, the dogs would track me. If I stole a skiff to cross the river, they would notice it missing and know exactly where I landed on the other side, allowing them to pick up my trail.

At that moment, our eyes landed on a scrap of parchment, which I initially mistook for paper. It lay half-buried in the sand with one corner exposed. Nearby, I noticed the rotted remains of what appeared to be a ship’s longboat, so weathered that its structure was barely recognizable. Jupiter retrieved the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Shortly after, we encountered Lieutenant G. I showed him the insect, and he eagerly asked to take it to the fort. When I agreed, he quickly shoved the beetle into his waistcoat pocket, leaving behind the parchment I had been holding. Knowing his obsession with natural history, he likely feared I would change my mind. Meanwhile, I must have absentmindedly tucked the parchment into my own pocket. You recall that when I sat down to sketch the beetle, I could not find any paper in its usual place or in the drawer. While searching my pockets for a scrap of paper, I discovered the parchment. I recount these details because the sequence of events struck me as significant. You may think me imaginative, but I had already begun connecting the pieces. A boat lay on the coast, and nearby was a piece of parchment—not paper—bearing a skull. You might ask how they relate, but the skull is a classic pirate emblem, often displayed on their flags. I noted that the material was durable, nearly indestructible parchment, which is rarely used for trivial notes. This suggested the skull held real importance. I also observed that despite a missing corner, the parchment was originally oblong.

The connection between soul and body was truly mysterious. The soul possessed animal instincts, while the body experienced moments of spirituality. Senses could refine a person, while the intellect could corrupt. It was impossible to define where physical impulses ended and mental ones began, despite the shallow claims of psychologists. Whether the soul was trapped in a house of sin or the body existed within the soul remained an unsolvable puzzle. He wondered if psychology could ever become an exact science that explained every detail of human life. Currently, we constantly misunderstand ourselves and others. Experience held no moral value; it was simply a label people gave their mistakes. While moralists argued that experience shaped character and taught us what to avoid, it actually lacked any real power to change us. It only proved that our future would mirror our past, and that sins we once committed with regret, we would eventually repeat with pleasure. He believed the experimental method was the only way to analyze human passions, and Dorian Gray was the perfect subject. Dorian’s sudden, intense love for Sibyl Vane was a fascinating psychological case. While curiosity and a desire for new experiences played a role, the emotion was complex. The raw instincts of youth had been transformed by his imagination into something that felt spiritual, making it all the more dangerous. We are most controlled by the passions we fail to understand. Often, when we believe we are experimenting on others, we are actually experimenting on ourselves. As Lord Henry pondered these thoughts, his valet knocked to remind him it was time to dress for dinner.

I examined the skull drawing closely. The outer edges were clearer than the rest, suggesting the heat had not been applied evenly. I lit a fire and heated the entire parchment. At first, only the skull lines darkened, but as I continued, a figure appeared in the opposite corner. I initially thought it was a goat, but closer inspection revealed it was a kid. I laughed, telling Legrand that while a fortune was no laughing matter, he would not find a connection between pirates and a goat, as goats belonged to farmers. He corrected me, noting it was a kid, not a goat. I replied that they were essentially the same, but Legrand insisted they were different. He explained that he saw the animal as a punning signature for Captain Kidd, while the skull acted like a seal. He was frustrated by the lack of any accompanying text. I asked if he had hoped to find a letter between the seal and the signature. He admitted he had, driven by a strong feeling of impending good fortune. He confessed that Jupiter’s foolish comment about the gold bug had sparked his imagination. He marveled at the series of coincidences, noting that if it had not been cool enough for a fire that day, or if the dog had not appeared at that exact moment, he would never have discovered the skull or the treasure.

I turn now to my own history. My early years offer little to recount, yet I must linger on my childhood to show how the loss of one hope rendered my life a void, and how the destruction of my only cherished affection extinguished my spirit. My aunt differed greatly from my father. While not malicious, she possessed the coldest heart imaginable, entirely devoid of warmth. She assumed my guardianship out of duty, yet having lived long in solitude, she would not permit my youthful presence to disrupt her peace. Unmarried, she had spent five years alone on her inherited estate by Loch Lomond in Scotland. Though my father requested she live with me at our family home near Richmond, she refused. Once she settled her brother’s affairs, she left England, taking me to her Scottish residence. Until I turned eight, my mother’s former servant, who had joined us in our seclusion, cared for me. I lived in a distant wing, seeing my aunt only twice daily: once at noon in my nursery, and again after her dinner. She never showed affection, appearing anxious that my childish behavior might disturb her. My nurse coached me thoroughly before these visits, and the dread inspired by my aunt’s icy demeanor ensured I remained perfectly still and obedient. Under my nurse’s guidance, I roamed the park and fields freely. Born of profound love, I was a sensitive child, possessed by an intense passion for everything around me, even the inanimate.

In my youth, I was never unhappy. If I ever felt bored, the beauty of nature or the study of human achievement could always lift my spirits. Now, however, I am like a blasted tree; my soul has been struck by lightning. I realized then that I would live on only as a broken shell of a person, a miserable sight to others and unbearable to myself. We spent a long time in Oxford, wandering the area and trying to find places connected to important moments in English history. Our trips were often extended by the interesting things we found. We visited the tomb of the famous Hampden and the battlefield where he died. For a moment, my soul rose above my fears to consider the noble ideas of liberty and sacrifice that these sites represented. For an instant, I dared to feel free, but the weight of my suffering returned, and I sank back into hopelessness. We left Oxford for Matlock. The landscape there resembled Switzerland, though on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the distant, snow-capped peaks of my homeland. We visited a famous cave and small natural history displays, which were arranged like those in Servox and Chamounix. Hearing the name of that place made me tremble, and I quickly left Matlock to escape the painful memory. Traveling north from Derby, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine I was back in the Swiss mountains. The patches of snow on the hills, the lakes, and the rushing streams were all familiar and dear to me. We met people there who almost tricked me into feeling happy. Clerval was even more delighted than I was; his mind grew in the company of talented people, and he discovered strengths in himself he had never realized he possessed.

The refined gentlemen of high society wore small hanging trinkets that chimed as they moved. These golden ornaments, combined with the rustle of silk and fine linen, created an atmosphere that kept the starving people of Saint Antoine at a distance. Fashion was the primary tool used to maintain social order. Everyone dressed as if they were attending a never-ending costume party. From the royal palace and the court down to the legal system and even the public executioner, everyone followed this trend. The executioner himself was expected to perform his duties while wearing a powdered wig, a gold-trimmed coat, and white silk stockings. In 1780, it seemed impossible that a system built on such absurd formality could ever collapse. After finishing his chocolate, Monseigneur opened the doors to his private chambers and emerged. The crowd responded with extreme submission and fawning, bowing so low that they seemed to have no devotion left for God, whom they largely ignored. Monseigneur moved through the rooms, offering empty promises and smiles to his followers before retreating back into his sanctuary. Once the display ended, the crowd dispersed, their jewelry jingling as they left. Only one man remained, walking slowly past the mirrors with his hat and snuffbox. Stopping at the final door, he looked toward the sanctuary and muttered, I devote you to the Devil. He brushed the snuff from his fingers and calmly walked downstairs.

Listen! His father fell ill in Rome, and my mother, from whom he had long been separated, traveled from Paris with me to join him. She likely came only to secure his assets, as there was no love between them. He was unconscious when we arrived and died the following day. Among his desk papers were two documents addressed to you, Mr. Brownlow, marked to be delivered only after his death: a letter to Agnes and a will. The letter was a frantic, repetitive confession. He had deceived Agnes, claiming a secret mystery prevented their marriage, leading her to trust him until she was ruined and pregnant. He begged her not to curse his memory or fear their child would suffer for his sins. He recalled the locket and the ring he had given her, asking her to keep them close, writing as if he had lost his mind. The will mirrored the letter. He lamented the misery his wife had caused and the malice of you, his son, whom he claimed had been raised to hate him. He left you and your mother small annuities, while dividing the bulk of his estate equally between Agnes Fleming and their child, provided the infant survived to adulthood.

These deputies had been sent to Adrian, the chosen arbiter. They traveled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and desolate landscapes, harboring intense mutual hatred, and now they argued their cases with fierce partisanship. By questioning the deputies separately, we discovered the true situation in Paris. Since parliament named him Ryland’s deputy, the remaining English had deferred to Adrian as their leader, lawgiver, and protector. Originally, we intended to stay together under the Earl of Windsor’s command, but unforeseen events forced us to split for nearly two months. Upon arriving in Paris in two separate groups, conflict erupted. They found Paris a wasteland. While early plague reports reached us, communication eventually ceased as mortality rates climbed. Even within England, travel became rare. No ships crossed from Calais to Dover; those who tried were often lost at sea or arrived already infected, dying before they could describe the devastation. We had hoped to find many survivors on the continent, but the plague had been even more destructive there. France was empty; we saw no one on the road from Calais to Paris. In the capital, perhaps a hundred people remained, wandering the streets or gathering to discuss the past with their characteristic, resilient spirit. The English took over the silent city. A few pale figures at the Tuileries wondered why we had come to their doomed home, for in deep misery, people always believe their own suffering is the worst, wishing only to trade their specific agony for any other.

I had not yet fully swallowed the bitter cup of my reality. I was not yet convinced of my total loss, nor did I feel in every heartbeat and thought that I was truly the last human left of my kind. The sky turned gray, and a cold rain began at sunset. I wondered if the heavens wept, why should a man be ashamed of his own tears? I recalled old myths of people melting into fountains from their sorrow and wished for such a fate, hoping to join Adrian and Clara in their watery end. Grief is a strange force; it projects its own patterns onto the world, coloring everything it touches. I wandered away from the shore until I found an Italian watchtower. I was relieved to see something built by human hands after staring at the empty wilderness. I climbed the winding stairs to the guardroom. Fortunately, there were no grim reminders of the previous occupants. A makeshift bed of planks and dried corn husks awaited me, along with a chest of moldy biscuits that stirred a hunger I had not realized I felt. I was also parched from the seawater and exhaustion. Nature provided a brief, soothing relief as I ate the meager food and drank sour wine from a discarded flask. I lay down on the bed, grateful for the dry, earthy scent of the leaves after the stench of seaweed. For a moment, I forgot my isolation. I stopped dwelling on the past or fearing the future. My mind quieted, and I fell into a deep sleep, dreaming of childhood scenes: haymakers, a shepherd whistling to his dog, and the familiar sights and sounds of the mountains I had long ago forgotten.

While these events unfolded at the workhouse, Fagin sat in his old hideout—the same place from which the girl had taken Oliver—brooding over a dim, smoky fire. He held a pair of bellows on his lap, having tried to stir the flames, but he had drifted into deep thought, resting his chin on his folded arms while staring blankly at the rusty grate. At a table behind him, the Artful Dodger, Charley Bates, and Mr. Chitling were focused on a game of whist, with the Dodger playing dummy against the other two. The Dodger’s face, always sharp, grew even more intense as he studied the game and peeked at Chitling’s hand, adjusting his own strategy based on what he saw. Because it was cold, the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did indoors. He also kept a clay pipe in his teeth, removing it only to sip gin-and-water from a quart pot on the table. Charley Bates was also focused, but being more excitable than his friend, he drank more frequently and made constant, distracting jokes that were hardly appropriate for a serious game. The Dodger, relying on their friendship, occasionally scolded him for his behavior, but Bates just laughed it off, telling his friend to get lost or offering some other witty retort that clearly impressed Mr. Chitling. It was notable that Chitling and his partner always lost, yet this didn't bother Bates, who laughed loudly after every hand, claiming he had never had so much fun. That is two doubles and the rubber, Chitling said with a long face, pulling half-a-crown from his pocket. I have never seen anyone like you, Jack; you win everything.

Upon my return, I found this letter from my father: My dear Victor, you have likely been waiting for me to set a date for your homecoming. I considered writing only a brief note, but that would be a cruel kindness. How could I let you arrive expecting a joyful welcome only to find us in tears? I cannot spare you this pain, though I know you are already scanning these lines for the terrible truth. William is dead. That sweet, gentle, happy child has been murdered. I will not try to comfort you, but will simply explain what happened. Last Thursday, May 7th, I went for a walk in Plainpalais with my niece and your brothers. The evening was warm, and we stayed out longer than planned. As it grew dark, we realized William and Ernest were missing. We waited for them, but soon Ernest returned alone, explaining that William had run off to hide and never came back. We searched until nightfall, then assumed he had gone home. When he was not there, we searched with torches, terrified for his safety. At five the next morning, I found my boy, who had been so full of life, lying motionless on the grass. The marks of a killer’s fingers were on his neck. We brought him home, and my grief revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She insisted on seeing the body, and when she looked at his neck, she clasped her hands and cried out, O God!

Knights in heavy armor could not move quickly. Even on firm ground without snow or mud, they would likely maintain a pace of seven miles an hour. After changing horses twice, they should arrive around six o'clock. There would still be enough daylight to spot the white cloth on my arm, allowing me to take command. We would surround the prison and rescue the king immediately. It would be a dramatic scene, though I would have preferred doing it at noon for more theatrical effect. To improve my chances, I decided to find people I recognized and reveal my identity, which might resolve our situation without needing the knights. However, I had to be careful. I needed to acquire fine clothing, but I could not simply put it on all at once. I had to buy increasingly expensive outfits from different shops until I reached silk and velvet. I began my plan, but it failed instantly. Turning a corner, I ran into one of our slaves with a watchman. I coughed, and he looked at me with a piercing gaze, as if he recognized the sound. I ducked into a shop and pretended to browse while watching them. They stopped to talk while looking toward the door. I decided to escape through the back. I told the shopkeeper I was an undercover officer searching for an escaped slave and asked her to tell my partner at the door to move to the end of the alley to intercept the fugitive. Eager to see a notorious criminal, she hurried off to deliver the message.

Your father might spare you, if your mother agrees. Daughters matter less to a father. If you stay another full month, I could take one of you to London when I go in early June. Since Dawson does not mind the carriage box, there is room for one, or even both if the weather is cool and you remain small. You are very kind, but we must stick to our original plan. Lady Catherine accepted this. Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. I always speak my mind, and it is highly improper for two young women to travel alone. You must arrange for someone to go. I dislike such things; young women should always be properly attended based on their status. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate, I insisted she have two men-servants. Miss Darcy could not have traveled otherwise. You must send John with them; it would be shameful for you to let them go alone. My uncle is sending a servant for us. Oh, your uncle has a man-servant? I am glad someone is thinking of these things. Where will you change horses? Bromley, of course. Mention my name at the Bell, and they will take care of you. Lady Catherine asked many questions about the trip, and Elizabeth found it fortunate that she had to pay attention, or she might have forgotten where she was. She saved her thoughts for her solitary walks, where she could dwell on her unpleasant memories. She nearly knew Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings toward him shifted. She felt indignant remembering his tone, but when she considered how unfairly she had judged him, her anger turned toward herself, and she felt pity for his disappointment.

Mrs. Otis, whose expertise in Art is significant given her winters in Boston during her youth, informs me that these jewels possess considerable value and would command a high price if sold. Consequently, Lord Canterville, I am certain you understand why I cannot permit my family to keep them. Such frivolous ornaments, while perhaps fitting for the British aristocracy, are entirely inappropriate for those raised on the rigorous, enduring tenets of republican simplicity. I should add that Virginia wishes to keep the box as a keepsake of your ill-fated ancestor. Since it is quite aged and somewhat damaged, you might see fit to grant her request. Personally, I am surprised my daughter shows sympathy for medievalism, though I attribute it to her birth in a London suburb shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from Athens. Lord Canterville listened to the Minister with solemnity, tugging his grey moustache to conceal a smile. Once Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly and replied, My dear sir, your delightful daughter performed a vital service for my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, and my family owes her a great debt for her remarkable bravery. The jewels are hers; indeed, if I were cruel enough to reclaim them, the old spirit would likely rise from his grave within a fortnight to torment me. They are not heirlooms, as they were never mentioned in any legal document and remained unknown until now. I have no more right to them than your butler, and I imagine Miss Virginia will enjoy wearing them when she is older. Furthermore, you purchased the furniture and the ghost at a valuation, meaning anything belonging to the spirit became yours; legally, Sir Simon was deceased, and you acquired his assets through that transaction.

Meanwhile, gravity would constantly weaken as the square of the distance increased. Consequently, I would accelerate rapidly toward the regions where the moon’s pull replaces the earth’s. Given this, I saw no reason to pack more than forty days of supplies. Another concern troubled me, however. Balloonists reaching great heights often suffer from painful breathing, bodily discomfort, and nosebleeds, which worsen with altitude. I wondered if these symptoms might prove fatal. I eventually decided they would not. These issues stem from the loss of atmospheric pressure causing blood vessels to swell, rather than a fundamental breakdown of the body’s systems. Since breathing is merely a muscular action, I believed life could persist even in a vacuum. I assumed my body would eventually adjust to the lack of pressure, and I trusted my own physical toughness to endure the initial pain. Your Excellencies, I have now explained the reasoning behind my lunar voyage. I will now describe the outcome of this bold and unprecedented attempt. After reaching an altitude of three and three-quarters miles, I tossed out some feathers and found I was still rising quickly, so I did not need to drop any ballast. I was pleased, as I wanted to keep as much weight as possible for reasons I will explain later.

After dinner, the group went to the sandbar to hunt for turtle eggs. They poked sticks into the sand, and whenever they found a soft spot, they knelt down to dig with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. The eggs were perfectly round, white, and slightly smaller than walnuts. They enjoyed a large feast of fried eggs that night and again on Friday morning. After breakfast, the boys ran out onto the sandbar, shouting and chasing each other. They shed their clothes until they were naked, continuing their game in the shallow water against the strong current, which frequently knocked them over and added to the fun. Occasionally, they gathered in a group to splash water at each other, turning their faces away to avoid the spray. Eventually, they would grab and wrestle until someone was dunked, leaving them all in a tangled heap of limbs, surfacing to laugh and catch their breath. Once exhausted, they sprawled on the hot, dry sand to bury themselves before returning to the water to repeat the cycle. Eventually, they decided their bare skin looked like flesh-colored tights, so they drew a ring in the sand and held a circus, with all three boys insisting on being clowns. Next, they played marbles until they grew bored. Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom refused, realizing he had lost the rattlesnake rattle he wore as a protective charm. He worried he had avoided cramps only because of the charm, so he refused to swim until he found it. By the time he recovered it, the other boys were tired. They wandered off, feeling homesick as they gazed across the river at the sleepy village. Tom found himself writing "BECKY" in the sand with his toe. He quickly scratched it out, annoyed by his own sentimentality, but he soon wrote it again. Unable to stop himself, he finally erased it once more and rejoined the other boys to distract himself.

My friend carefully drove a peg into the ground exactly where the beetle had landed, then pulled out a tape measure. He attached one end to the nearest point on the tree trunk and stretched it out to the peg, continuing for another fifty feet in the same line while Jupiter cleared away the brush with a scythe. At that spot, he drove a second peg and marked a rough circle about four feet wide around it. He handed spades to Jupiter and me, urging us to start digging immediately. Honestly, I had no desire for this task. Night was falling, and I was exhausted, but I saw no way out and did not want to upset my friend. I considered forcing him home, but I knew Jupiter would never help me fight his master. I assumed Legrand had fallen victim to local superstitions about buried treasure, fueled by the discovery of the beetle and Jupiter’s insistence that it was made of real gold. His talk about the insect being the key to his fortune seemed like the delusions of a troubled mind. Still, I decided to cooperate, hoping that digging would quickly prove his theories wrong. We lit our lanterns and began working with surprising energy. As the light shone on us and our tools, I realized how strange and suspicious we must have looked to any outsider. We dug steadily for two hours.

He acted with extreme stubbornness, repeating only "that cursed bug" throughout our journey. I carried two lanterns, while Legrand swung the beetle on a piece of string like a magician. Seeing this clear sign of his mental instability, I nearly cried. I decided to play along for now, hoping to find a better way to help him later. My attempts to ask about our destination failed; he refused to discuss anything else, answering only with "we shall see!" We crossed the creek in a small boat and climbed the mainland hills, heading northwest through wild, empty land. Legrand led us confidently, stopping briefly to check landmarks he had set previously. After two hours, as the sun set, we reached a desolate plateau near the top of a steep, wooded hill. The area was filled with large, loose boulders held in place only by the trees, and deep ravines added to the grim atmosphere. The ground was covered in thick brambles that we could only clear with a scythe. Jupiter followed Legrand’s orders to cut a path to a massive tulip tree. It stood among several oaks, towering over them with its majestic shape and wide, beautiful branches.

I felt no concern for her. She was a capable woman who handled worldly affairs without my help. Honestly, she likely viewed me as an aimless youth, useful only for daydreaming, and was pleased to see me go. It was a pitch-black night when I departed, accompanied by the three creditors who had plagued me. We transported the balloon and its gear via a circuitous route to the storage site. Finding everything undisturbed, I set to work. It was April first. The night remained dark and starless, with intermittent drizzle causing us misery. My main worry was the balloon, which grew heavy with moisture despite its varnish, and the risk to the gunpowder. I kept my three duns busy packing ice around the central cask and stirring the acid. They constantly pestered me about my intentions, complaining about the grueling labor and the pointlessness of getting soaked for such strange rituals. I grew anxious, working feverishly, as I suspected these fools believed I was consorting with the devil and that my actions were sinister. I feared they might abandon me, but I managed to calm them by promising full payment once my task was complete. They interpreted this in their own way, assuming I would soon possess great wealth; as long as they were paid, they likely cared little for my fate. After four and a half hours, the balloon was inflated. I secured the car and loaded my equipment, including the condenser, plenty of water, and compact, nutrient-dense provisions like pemmican.

She left everything behind, except the memory that such things had occurred. Anne had not visited Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s home in September. It had not been necessary, and she had managed to avoid the few opportunities she had to go to the Hall. Her return was meant to resume her place in the elegant rooms of the Lodge and please its mistress. Lady Russell felt some anxiety along with her joy at seeing Anne. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. Fortunately, Anne looked healthier, or at least Lady Russell thought so. As Anne accepted these compliments, she amused herself by linking them to her cousin’s silent admiration, hoping she might enjoy a renewed sense of youth and beauty. As they talked, Anne realized her own perspective had shifted. The concerns that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, which she had felt ignored and forced to hide among the Musgroves, now seemed less important. She had recently lost interest in her father, her sister, and their life in Bath. Their affairs had been overshadowed by those at Uppercross. When Lady Russell discussed their old hopes and fears, mentioning her satisfaction with the house in Camden Place and her regret that Mrs. Clay was still with them, Anne felt ashamed of how much more she was thinking about Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and her new acquaintances there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick felt far more interesting to her than her father’s house or her sister’s friendship with Mrs. Clay. She had to force herself to show equal concern for topics that should have been her priority. Their conversation felt slightly awkward when they turned to the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had heard the full story shortly after arriving the day before, but they still had to discuss it. She asked questions, expressed regret over the recklessness, and lamented the outcome. Both women had to mention Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne felt she handled it less naturally than Lady Russell. She could not say his name while looking directly at her until she decided to briefly share her thoughts on the attachment between him and Louisa.

Yet how could I, a bewildered country boy, escape that strange contradiction that even the wisest men encounter daily? I told Biddy that while her words might be true, I adored her intensely. I buried my face in my hands, clutching my hair and pulling it in frustration. I was fully aware of my own foolishness, feeling that my face deserved to be struck against the stones for being part of such a fool. Biddy, being incredibly sensible, stopped arguing. She placed her work-roughened but comforting hand over mine, pulling them away from my hair. She patted my shoulder as I wept into my sleeve, much like I had in the brewery yard, feeling a vague sense of being mistreated by the world. Biddy expressed gratitude that I trusted her, promising to keep my secrets. She remarked that if her former self—a poor teacher needing instruction—were still my mentor, she would assign a difficult lesson, though I had surpassed her now. Sighing, she stood up and asked if we should continue our walk or return home. I stood, embraced her, and kissed her, promising to always share everything with her. She replied that I would do so until I became a gentleman. I insisted I never would, meaning I would always tell her everything, as she already knew my secrets. She whispered softly while gazing at the ships, then asked again if we should walk further or head back. I chose to continue our stroll, and as the summer afternoon faded into a beautiful evening, we walked on.

His only concern was selecting a victim, as he understood that murder, like ancient pagan rituals, required both a priest and a sacrifice. Lacking the imagination to have enemies, and recognizing that his grave mission left no room for petty grudges, he drafted a list of friends and family. After careful thought, he chose Lady Clementina Beauchamp, his elderly second cousin living on Curzon Street. He was fond of her, and since he had inherited Lord Rugby’s fortune, he stood to gain nothing financially from her death. Convinced she was the perfect choice and unwilling to delay for Sybil’s sake, he began his preparations. First, he settled his debt with the palmist, writing a check for 105 pounds to Mr. Septimus Podgers and sending it via his valet. He then ordered his carriage and dressed to leave. Before departing, he glanced at Sybil Merton’s photograph, vowing to keep his self-sacrificing secret hidden forever. On his way to the club, he sent Sybil a basket of narcissus. Upon arrival, he went to the library and ordered a lemon-and-soda along with a book on toxicology. He decided poison was the most discreet method; he found physical violence distasteful and wanted to avoid the public scandal of a sensational murder investigation, fearing the unwanted attention of society columns.

The ringmaster gave a brief speech, asking for no further disruptions and promising to let the man ride if he could stay mounted. The crowd laughed, and the man climbed on. Immediately, the horse began bucking and rearing while two circus workers struggled to hold the bridle. The drunk man clung to the horse’s neck, his legs flailing as the audience roared with laughter. Eventually, the horse broke free and galloped around the ring with the man swaying dangerously, his limbs dangling. I felt terrified for him, but soon he pulled himself upright, grabbed the reins, and stood tall on the galloping horse as if he were perfectly sober. He began shedding layers of clothing, tossing seventeen suits into the air until he stood slim and handsome in a brilliant, ornate costume. He whipped the horse into a frenzy, then leaped off, bowed, and danced away while the crowd cheered in disbelief. The ringmaster, realizing he had been tricked by one of his own performers, looked utterly humiliated. I felt foolish for being deceived, but I would not have traded places with that ringmaster for anything. It was the best circus I have ever seen, and I will certainly return whenever I find it again.

This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to retain at Lady Canterville’s urgent insistence. She greeted them with a deep curtsey as they arrived, stating in a formal, archaic style, ‘I welcome you to Canterville Chase.’ They followed her through the Tudor hall into the library, a long, dark-paneled room featuring a large stained-glass window. Tea was prepared there, and after removing their coats, they sat and surveyed the room while Mrs. Umney served them. Mrs. Otis soon noticed a dull red mark on the floor near the hearth and, unaware of its meaning, remarked, ‘I fear something has been spilled there.’ ‘Yes, madam,’ the housekeeper whispered, ‘blood has been spilled on that spot.’ ‘How dreadful,’ Mrs. Otis exclaimed; ‘I dislike bloodstains in a living room. It must be cleaned immediately.’ The woman smiled, replying in a hushed, cryptic tone, ‘It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered there by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine more years before vanishing under mysterious circumstances. His remains were never found, but his spirit haunts the Chase. The stain is admired by visitors and cannot be removed.’ ‘That is nonsense,’ Washington Otis declared; ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover will clear it instantly.’ Before the horrified housekeeper could stop him, he knelt and scrubbed the floor with a black stick. Soon, the stain vanished. ‘I knew Pinkerton would succeed,’ he boasted to his family, but as he spoke, a brilliant flash of lightning illuminated the room, a loud crack of thunder startled them, and Mrs. Umney fainted. ‘What a terrible climate!’ the American Minister noted, lighting a cigar. ‘I suppose England is so crowded they lack sufficient weather for everyone. Emigration is the only solution.’ ‘My dear Hiram,’ Mrs. Otis asked, ‘what shall we do with a woman who faints?’ ‘Bill her for it like broken china,’ the Minister replied; ‘she will not faint again.’ Shortly after, Mrs. Umney regained consciousness.

Upon returning, I discovered this note from my father: My dear Victor, you have surely been awaiting word regarding your homecoming. I considered sending a brief note with a date, but that would be a heartless mercy. How could I surprise you with sorrow when you anticipated a joyful reunion? I cannot shield you from this tragedy, though I know your eyes are already racing to find the terrible truth. William is dead. That dear, cheerful boy has been murdered. I will not offer hollow comfort, but will explain what occurred. Last Thursday, May 7th, I went to Plainpalais with my niece and your brothers. The evening was pleasant, and we stayed out longer than intended. As dusk fell, we realized William and Ernest were missing. We waited, but only Ernest returned, explaining that William had run off to hide and failed to reappear. Alarmed, we searched until nightfall, then checked the house. He was gone. We searched with torches through the night, fearing for his safety. At five in the morning, I found my beautiful boy, who had been so vibrant, lying lifeless on the grass, his neck marked by the killer’s grip. We brought him home, and my grief revealed the truth to Elizabeth. Despite my protests, she insisted on seeing him. Upon viewing the body and the marks on his throat, she clasped her hands and cried out, O God!

You have encouraged a spirit in him that is unsuitable for his station, ma'am. The board members are practical men, and they would tell you that paupers have no need for soul or spirit. It is enough that we provide them with bodies. If you had fed the boy only gruel, this would not have happened. Oh dear, Mrs. Sowerberry sighed, looking toward the ceiling. This is what comes of being generous. Her generosity had actually consisted of giving Oliver the scraps no one else would eat, so she showed great humility in accepting Mr. Bumble’s false accusation. The only solution now, Mr. Bumble continued, is to leave him in the cellar until he is starved into submission, then keep him on gruel for the rest of his apprenticeship. He comes from a bad family. His mother arrived here after enduring hardships that would have killed any decent woman weeks earlier. Hearing his mother mentioned, Oliver began kicking the door so violently that no other sound could be heard. Mr. Sowerberry returned just then, and after hearing an exaggerated account of Oliver’s behavior, he unlocked the cellar and dragged the boy out by his collar. Oliver’s clothes were torn, his face was bruised, and his hair was disheveled, but he still glared defiantly at Noah. You are a fine young man, aren't you? Sowerberry said, shaking him and boxing his ears. He insulted my mother, Oliver replied. What if he did, you ungrateful wretch? Mrs. Sowerberry cried. She deserved what he said and worse. She did not, Oliver insisted. She did, she countered. It is a lie, Oliver shouted. Mrs. Sowerberry burst into tears. This left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. If he had hesitated to punish Oliver severely, he would have been branded a brute and a terrible husband by all standards of marital disputes.

“What is it?” “It is ten o’clock, sir.” “What? Ten at night?” “Yes, sir. You asked to be awakened.” “Ah, I recall. Very well.” Failing to drift back to sleep while his servant noisily tended the fire, he rose, donned his hat, and departed. He wandered through the Temple, pacing King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings to clear his head, before heading to Stryver’s chambers. The clerk had departed, so Stryver himself answered the door, dressed in slippers and a loose robe, his throat exposed. He possessed the strained, haggard look around the eyes common to men of his indulgent habits, a trait visible in portraits of heavy drinkers throughout history. “You are slightly late, Memory,” Stryver remarked. “About the usual time, perhaps fifteen minutes past.” They entered a dim, book-lined room cluttered with documents and warmed by a roaring fire. A kettle hissed on the hearth, and a table was set with wine, spirits, sugar, and lemons. “I see you have finished your bottle, Sydney.” “Two tonight, I believe. I dined with today’s client, or watched him dine—it makes no difference.” “That was a brilliant point you made regarding the identification. How did you discover it?” “I thought he was a handsome man, and that I might have been just like him, had I possessed any luck.” Stryver laughed, his belly shaking. “Always with the luck, Sydney! Get to work.” The jackal, looking sullen, fetched a basin of cold water and some towels. He soaked the cloths, wrung them out, wrapped them around his head in a grotesque fashion, and sat down. “I am ready.” “Not much to condense tonight, Memory,” Stryver said cheerfully, sorting through his papers. “How much?” “Only two cases.” “Give me the most difficult one first.” “Here you are, Sydney. Proceed.” The lion reclined on a sofa beside the table, while the jackal took his place at the desk, surrounded by papers and the waiting bottles.

It is impossible to convey the sheer joy I felt returning from domestic political strife and the hardships of foreign lands to my own sanctuary of kindness, affection, and peaceful connection. Had I never left Windsor, these feelings would lack such depth; yet in Greece, I had been haunted by fear and tragic upheaval, witnessing the loss of two individuals who embodied greatness and virtue. Such sorrows, however, could not breach the domestic circle I maintained within our secluded forest, where we lived in quiet harmony. Time inevitably left its mark on our joys and hopes. Idris, a devoted wife, sister, and friend, was also a deeply loving mother. For her, motherhood was not merely a pastime but a profound passion. We had three children, but the second passed away during my time in Greece, tempering her maternal joy with persistent anxiety. Previously, she viewed our children as secure, but now she feared the cruel hand of death might claim her remaining ones. Minor illnesses triggered intense terror; she could not bear to be away from them, guarding her happiness as if protecting precious gems from a thief. Fortunately, her fears were largely unfounded. Alfred, now nine, was a sturdy, upright boy with a bright expression and a gentle, independent spirit. Our youngest was still an infant, yet he thrived with rosy health and a lively nature that filled our home with laughter. Clara had grown past the age that initially caused Idris such worry. She was cherished by all for her blend of intelligence and innocence, sensitivity and patience, and a serious yet cheerful disposition. Her transcendent beauty and endearing simplicity made her a true treasure in our lives. As winter began, nine-year-old Alfred started at Eton. He viewed this as his first real step toward adulthood and was delighted. Engaging in shared studies and play helped cultivate his finest traits: steady perseverance, generosity, and disciplined resolve.

Will you? His eyes brightened as he replied, I will help you steal him! I was stunned, feeling as if I had been shot. It was the most shocking thing I had ever heard, and I must admit my opinion of Tom Sawyer dropped significantly. I simply could not believe it. Tom Sawyer, a person who would steal a slave? Oh, stop, I said. You are joking. I am not joking at all. Well then, I replied, joking or not, if you hear anything about a runaway slave, remember that you know nothing about him, and neither do I. We loaded the trunk into my wagon and went our separate ways. I was so excited and lost in thought that I drove much faster than I should have, arriving home far too quickly. The old man was at the door and exclaimed, This is incredible! Who would have thought that mare could do it? I wish we had timed her. She is not even sweating. I would not take a hundred dollars for her now, even though I would have sold her for fifteen earlier. He was the most innocent, kind-hearted man I have ever met. This was not surprising, as he was not just a farmer but also a preacher. He had built a small log church behind the plantation at his own expense to serve as a school and house of worship, never charging for his services.
