There were many such farmer-preachers in the South. About thirty minutes later, Tom’s wagon arrived at the front gate. Aunt Sally saw it from the window and said, Someone is here! I wonder who it is? It looks like a stranger. Jimmy, run and tell Lize to set another plate for dinner. Everyone rushed to the front door, as a visitor was a rare and exciting event. Tom climbed over the gate and headed toward the house while his wagon drove off toward the village. We all gathered at the door. Tom was wearing his best clothes and had an audience, which was exactly what he loved.

It was well past noon when he woke. His valet had checked on him repeatedly, puzzled by his master’s late slumber. When the bell finally rang, Victor entered quietly with tea and a stack of letters on a Sevres china tray, pulling back the olive-satin curtains to reveal the tall windows. You slept well this morning, Monsieur, he said with a smile. What time is it, Victor? Dorian Gray asked sleepily. A quarter past one, Monsieur. It was so late. He sat up, sipped his tea, and glanced at his mail. One letter from Lord Henry, delivered by hand, he set aside. He opened the others listlessly: invitations to dinners, private viewings, and charity concerts—the usual flurry of social obligations for a fashionable young man. There was a steep bill for a silver toilet set he dared not show his old-fashioned guardians, who failed to grasp that in this age, luxuries are necessities. There were also polite offers from money-lenders on Jermyn Street. After ten minutes, he rose, donned an embroidered cashmere dressing gown, and entered the onyx bathroom. The cool water refreshed him, and his recent troubles seemed to fade, feeling as unreal as a dream. Once dressed, he went to the library for a light breakfast by the open window. It was a beautiful day, the air heavy with spice. A bee buzzed around a bowl of yellow roses. He felt entirely content. Suddenly, his gaze landed on the screen hiding the portrait, and he flinched. Too cold for you, Monsieur? his valet asked, placing an omelette on the table. Should I close the window? Dorian shook his head. I am not cold, he murmured.

Reading about the opulence of the deceased was truly remarkable. He then focused on the embroideries and tapestries that served as wall hangings in the cold northern European palaces. As he researched—possessing a unique talent for total immersion in his current interest—he felt a melancholy reflection on how time inevitably destroys beautiful objects. He, however, had avoided such a fate. Seasons passed, flowers bloomed and withered, and nights of terror repeated their shameful tales, yet he remained untouched. No winter aged his face or faded his youthful glow. How different it was for material things. Where had they vanished? Where was the saffron robe depicting the gods battling giants, crafted by artisans for Athena? Where was the massive purple canopy Nero stretched over the Colosseum, featuring a starry sky and Apollo driving his chariot? He yearned to see the intricate napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, displaying every imaginable feast; King Chilperic’s burial shroud with its three hundred golden bees; the scandalous robes adorned with lions, bears, and hunters that angered the Bishop of Pontus; or the coat of Charles of Orleans, its sleeves embroidered with song lyrics and musical notes formed from pearls. He read of Queen Joan of Burgundy’s room at Rheims, decorated with over thirteen hundred embroidered parrots and five hundred butterflies, all bearing royal crests in gold. Catherine de Medici owned a mourning bed of black velvet covered in crescents and suns, with damask curtains and pearl-fringed embroidery, set in a room draped with her emblems. Louis XIV even possessed fifteen-foot-tall gold-embroidered caryatids in his private chambers.

The young people were desperate to visit Lyme. Captain Wentworth mentioned returning there himself, as it was only seventeen miles from Uppercross. Despite it being November, the weather was decent. Louisa, the most enthusiastic of the group, decided they would go. Pleased to have her own way and convinced of the virtue in asserting her independence, she overcame her parents' desire to postpone the trip until summer. The party—Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth—would go to Lyme. The initial plan to return the same night was rejected by Mr. Musgrove to spare his horses. Once they considered the logistics, they realized a November day would leave little time for sightseeing after accounting for the seven-hour round trip. They decided to stay overnight, returning the following day. This was a welcome improvement. Although they met for an early breakfast and departed promptly, it was well past noon by the time the two carriages—Mr. Musgrove’s coach carrying the four ladies and Charles’s curricle with Captain Wentworth—descended the long hill into Lyme. It was clear they would barely have time to explore before the daylight faded. After checking into an inn and ordering dinner, they immediately walked to the sea. They had arrived too late in the season for the typical attractions of a resort town. The public rooms were closed, the visitors had departed, and only the locals remained. Since the architecture was unremarkable, the town’s unique geography was the main draw. The main street seemed to rush toward the water, and the walk to the Cobb, which curved around the bay, offered beautiful views. Even without the seasonal crowds and bathing machines, the historic Cobb, the recent improvements, and the stunning cliffs to the east made the area captivating to any visitor.

Get up! What are you doing? I opened my eyes, confused about my surroundings. It was past sunrise, and I had been fast asleep. Pap stood over me, looking grumpy and ill. He asked what I was doing with the gun. Realizing he did not remember his actions from the night before, I told him someone had tried to break in, so I was waiting for them. He asked why I had not woken him, and I explained that I could not move him. He told me to stop talking and go check the fishing lines for breakfast, promising to follow shortly. He unlocked the door, and I headed up the riverbank. I noticed branches and bark floating by, signaling that the river was rising. I thought about how the June rise usually brought good luck, as logs and firewood would drift down for me to catch and sell. I walked along the bank, watching for Pap and any useful debris. Suddenly, I spotted a beautiful canoe, about fourteen feet long, floating by. I dove into the water and swam out to it. I expected someone to be hiding inside to play a trick, but it was empty. I paddled it to shore, thinking Pap would be pleased with a ten-dollar find. However, he was not around, so I decided to hide the boat in a vine-covered creek. I realized this was my chance to escape by river instead of running away on foot. I quickly hid the canoe, constantly worried that Pap might appear. After securing it, I peeked through the willows and saw him down the path, aiming his gun at a bird.

The two ladies were thrilled to see their friend, remarking that it had been ages since they last met and repeatedly asking how she had been. They ignored the rest of the family, avoiding Mrs. Bennet, saying little to Elizabeth, and nothing to the others. They soon left, rising with a sudden energy that surprised their brother, and hurried away as if eager to escape Mrs. Bennet’s politeness. The upcoming Netherfield ball delighted every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet felt it was held in honor of her eldest daughter and was flattered that Mr. Bingley had invited them personally. Jane looked forward to spending the evening with her friends and their brother, while Elizabeth anticipated dancing with Mr. Wickham and observing Mr. Darcy’s behavior. Catherine and Lydia were excited simply because it was a ball, and even Mary agreed to attend, noting that she found social recreation acceptable in moderation. Elizabeth was in such high spirits that she asked Mr. Collins if he planned to attend and dance. She was surprised to learn he had no objections, fearing no criticism from his superiors for participating. He assured her that a ball hosted by a respectable man was perfectly fine and even asked for the first two dances with her, hoping Jane would not take offense at his preference.

I am not eating at home, so I will not need you. Thank you, sir, the man replied, leaving the room. Now, Alan, we have no time to waste. This chest is heavy; I will carry it. You bring the rest. He spoke quickly and with authority. Campbell felt overwhelmed by him, and they left together. Upon reaching the landing, Dorian unlocked the door, then hesitated, a look of distress crossing his face. He shuddered. I do not think I can go in, Alan, he whispered. It makes no difference to me. I do not need you, Campbell said coldly. Dorian opened the door slightly. He saw his portrait leering in the sunlight, the torn curtain lying on the floor before it. He realized he had forgotten to cover the canvas the night before and started to rush forward, but recoiled in horror. What was that disgusting red dew glistening on one of the hands, as if the painting were sweating blood? It was more terrifying than the silent figure he knew lay on the table, whose distorted shadow on the carpet confirmed it had not moved. Taking a deep breath, he opened the door wider and stepped inside with his eyes half-closed and his head turned away, determined not to look at the corpse. He picked up the gold-and-purple cloth and threw it over the picture. He stood there, afraid to turn around, staring at the fabric pattern. He heard Campbell bring in the chest and the tools needed for his grim task. He wondered if Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever met. Leave me now, a stern voice commanded. He turned and hurried out, catching a glimpse of the dead man pushed back into the chair and Campbell staring at a glistening yellow face. As he descended the stairs, he heard the key turn in the lock. It was well past seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale but composed. I have done what you asked, he muttered.

Enough of this. I will begin my story; it is my final task, and I hope I have the strength to finish it. I have committed no crimes; my mistakes are easily forgiven, as they came from poor judgment rather than malice. I believe few could claim they would have avoided the misfortunes that have claimed me, had they been in my place. My fate was dictated by a cruel necessity—a force stronger than any human power—that bound me, once a person of joy and goodness, to a misery that will only end in death. But I digress. I will pause to compose myself and try to lose my current sorrow in the memories of the past. I was born in England to a nobleman. Having lost his own father early, he was raised by an indulgent mother who gave him everything he wanted. He attended Eton and college, where he was granted large sums of money, gaining the independence typical of a wealthy schoolboy. These circumstances allowed his personality to take deep root. Because he was always permitted to act on his own impulses, his character developed early, showing both potential for virtue and the seeds of future misfortune. His reckless spending, which he mistook for passion, often appeared as great generosity. While he was eager to help others, he never had to sacrifice his own desires to do so. He gave away his time and money freely, but only because he had plenty of both. I cannot say if he would have been selfish had he ever been forced to choose between his needs and those of others, but that test never came. He was raised in constant prosperity, surrounded by people who loved him and sought only to please him.

I will submit to you. I see in your expression that you know I have no other choice. I trust you. The old man kissed her, hurried her into his room, and locked the door. He then rushed back to the Doctor, opened the window and partially raised the blind, and placed a hand on the Doctor’s arm as they looked into the courtyard. They saw a crowd of forty or fifty people. The house’s occupants had admitted them, and they had rushed in to use the grindstone, which had been set up in that secluded spot. The workers and their work were terrifying. Two men turned the double-handled grindstone with frantic intensity. Their faces, revealed as their long hair whipped back, were more cruel than those of the most savage barbarians. Wearing fake eyebrows and mustaches, their hideous features were slick with blood and sweat, twisted by howling, and wild with sleep-deprived excitement. As they turned the stone, women held wine to their mouths. Between the dripping blood, the spilled wine, and the sparks flying from the stone, the air seemed filled with gore and fire. Every person in the group was stained with blood. Men stripped to the waist, men in rags, and men adorned with stolen lace and silk ribbons all shoved each other to reach the stone, their bodies and clothing soaked in red. Hatchets, knives, bayonets, and swords were all being sharpened, each coated in blood. Some hacked blades were tied to their owners' wrists with strips of linen or fabric, all stained the same deep color. As these frantic individuals snatched their weapons from the sparks and tore into the streets, that same red hue burned in their frenzied eyes—eyes that any decent person would have given twenty years of their life to stop forever.

Three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a fashionable crowd for the wedding. The Dean of Chichester officiated, and everyone remarked on what a striking couple the bride and groom made. More importantly, they were genuinely happy. Lord Arthur never regretted his sacrifices for Sybil, and she offered him her complete devotion and love. Reality did not diminish their romance; they remained forever young at heart. Years later, after they had two children, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, the Duke’s wedding gift to his son. While sitting under a lime tree watching the children play, she took Sybil’s hand and asked if she was happy. Sybil confirmed she was, but Lady Windermere claimed she lacked the time for happiness, noting that she quickly grew bored with people once she knew them. When Sybil asked if her social favorites satisfied her, Lady Windermere dismissed them as dull once their novelty faded. She recalled the fraud Mr. Podgers, noting that while she could forgive his financial requests, his romantic advances had ruined palmistry for her; she now preferred telepathy. Sybil warned her not to mock palmistry, as Arthur took it quite seriously. When Lady Windermere questioned this, Sybil directed her to Arthur, who was approaching with their children and a bouquet of yellow roses. Lady Windermere asked if he truly believed in palmistry. Smiling, Arthur confirmed he did, explaining as he sat down that he owed his entire life’s happiness to it.

I encountered several funerals, sparsely attended and viewed by onlookers as grim omens. Some watched with frantic intensity, others fled in fear, and some wept openly. Adrian’s primary goal, beyond immediate medical aid, was to hide the plague's progression from London’s residents. He understood that fear and despair fueled the disease, making people more vulnerable to infection. Consequently, he kept shops open and maintained a semblance of normal traffic to avoid visible signs of decay. Yet, to me, the city felt profoundly altered. Carriages were absent, grass grew in the streets, and houses looked desolate with shuttered windows. The people I passed wore a look of haunted terror, a stark contrast to the usual industrious nature of Londoners. My lone carriage drew attention as I traveled toward the Protectoral Palace, where the elite streets seemed even more abandoned. I found Adrian’s waiting room packed. Unwilling to interrupt, I watched the petitioners—mostly working-class people whose livelihoods had vanished with the collapse of trade. Their anxiety and terror contrasted sharply with the calm, satisfied expressions of those leaving after meeting him. I could see his influence in their renewed hope. When the clock struck two, he stopped taking visitors, and I entered his office. I was struck by Adrian’s improved health. He no longer appeared fragile or weighed down; his eyes were bright, his expression composed, and he radiated a focused energy. He sat with secretaries, organizing petitions and notes. I admired his patience and fairness as he advised those who could afford to leave London to do so immediately, providing them with the necessary resources.

Raymond felt energized by his returning health. As general of the Athenians, he believed he held a position worthy of his ambition. He viewed the potential conquest of Constantinople as a historic milestone, an achievement unparalleled in human records. He envisioned this city, renowned for its beauty and long held by the Muslims, being liberated from oppression and restored to a people celebrated for their intellect, culture, and love of freedom. Perdita found comfort in his recovery, his affection, and his rising fame, feeling as relaxed as if resting on a luxurious couch; every thought brought her joy, and every emotion felt perfectly at peace. We reached Kishan on July 7th after a journey marked by calm weather. Each day, we departed before dawn, watching the shadows vanish from the hills and valleys as the sun rose in golden splendor. Our soldiers greeted the beauty of nature with lively enthusiasm, hailing the sunrise with triumphant music, while birds filled the gaps in their melodies. At noon, we rested in shaded valleys or wooded mountain groves, where the sound of babbling brooks invited sleep. Our evening marches were even more delightful than the mornings. When the band played, they chose gentle, emotional tunes—songs of love or longing—often concluding with solemn hymns that harmonized with the evening’s tranquility and inspired deep, spiritual reflection. Sometimes, we fell silent to listen to nightingales, watching fireflies dance while the aziolo’s soft call promised fair weather. In the valleys, we were surrounded by soft shadows and colorful rocks. From the mountains, Greece appeared like a living map beneath us, its famous peaks piercing the sky and its rivers winding like silver threads through the fertile land. We English travelers watched this magnificent landscape with ecstasy, struck by how different it was from the muted, somber beauty of our homeland. Leaving Macedonia, we crossed the flatter, fertile plains of Thrace; though less picturesque, the journey remained engaging. An advance guard announced our arrival, and the local people gathered to honor Lord Raymond.

His deeply tanned face was largely obscured by a thick beard and mustache. He carried a heavy oak club but seemed to possess no other weapons. He offered an ungainly bow and greeted us in French, his accent clearly Parisian despite a slight Neufchatel inflection. Sit down, my friend, Dupin invited. I assume you are here regarding the orangutan. I must say, I almost envy you owning such a magnificent and valuable creature. What is your estimate of his age? The sailor exhaled deeply, as if shedding a heavy weight, and answered confidently: I cannot say for certain, but he is likely no more than four or five. Is he here? Oh no, we lacked the facilities to house him, Dupin replied. He is at a nearby stable on Rue Dubourg. You may collect him tomorrow. Naturally, you are ready to prove ownership? Certainly, sir. I shall regret losing him, Dupin remarked. I do not expect you to go to such trouble for nothing, the man insisted. I am happy to offer a reasonable reward for his recovery. That is quite fair, Dupin agreed. Let me consider. My reward shall be this: you must provide all the information you possess concerning the murders in the Rue Morgue. Dupin spoke these final words softly. With equal composure, he walked to the door, locked it, and pocketed the key. He then produced a pistol from his coat and placed it calmly upon the table. The sailor turned crimson, appearing as if he were choking. He leaped up and seized his club, but immediately collapsed back into his chair, shaking uncontrollably and looking deathly pale. He remained silent. I felt profound pity for him. My friend, Dupin said gently, you are distressing yourself without cause. We intend you no harm. I give you my word as a gentleman and a Frenchman that we mean you no injury. I am fully aware that you are innocent of the crimes in the Rue Morgue. Nevertheless, you cannot deny that you are involved in them to some degree.

It is just a tick. Where did you find him? In the woods. What will you take for him? I do not know. I do not want to sell him. Fine. It is a very small tick anyway. Anyone can catch a tick that is not theirs. I am happy with this one. It is good enough for me. There are plenty of ticks. I could have a thousand if I wanted. Well, why do you not? Because you know you cannot. This is an early tick. It is the first one I have seen this year. Huck, I will give you my tooth for him. Let me see it. Tom unwrapped a piece of paper. Huckleberry looked at it longingly. The temptation was strong. Finally, he asked if it was real. Tom lifted his lip to show the gap. All right, it is a trade. Tom put the tick in the small box that used to hold a beetle, and the boys parted, both feeling richer. When Tom arrived at the schoolhouse, he walked in quickly, acting as if he had hurried. He hung up his hat and sat down. The teacher, sitting in his large chair, was dozing off to the sound of the students studying. The noise woke him. Thomas Sawyer! Tom knew that being called by his full name meant trouble. Sir! Come here. Why are you late again? Tom was about to lie when he saw two yellow braids hanging down a back he recognized. That girl was sitting in the only empty seat on the girls' side. He immediately said, I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn! The teacher stared in shock. The room went silent. The students wondered if Tom had lost his mind. The teacher asked what he had done. I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn. Thomas Sawyer, this is the most shocking confession I have ever heard. A simple punishment will not do for this. Take off your jacket. The teacher whipped him until his arm was tired and the switches were worn down. Then he ordered, Go and sit with the girls! Let this be a warning. The laughter that spread through the room seemed to embarrass Tom, but in reality, he was overwhelmed by his awe for the girl and the thrill of his good fortune.

In the middle of the gap, I noticed a white object. After adjusting my telescope, I realized it was a human skull. I felt confident that the mystery was solved. The instructions about the seventh limb and the left eye of the skull clearly pointed to a method for finding buried treasure. I assumed the plan was to drop a bullet through the skull's left eye, then draw a straight line from the tree trunk through that landing spot, extending fifty feet to mark where the treasure was hidden. I told him the plan seemed clever yet straightforward, and asked what happened after he left the Bishop’s Hotel. He explained that he headed home, but the circular gap disappeared the moment he left the rock ledge. He noted that the opening was only visible from that specific vantage point. He had been accompanied by Jupiter, who had been watching him closely, but he managed to sneak away the next morning to find the tree. He returned that night, and Jupiter threatened to punish him for leaving. I asked if he missed the treasure because Jupiter dropped the beetle through the wrong eye of the skull. He confirmed that this small mistake shifted the target by two and a half inches. While that seems minor, it threw their entire fifty-foot measurement off, causing them to search in the wrong place.

It was an era of extremes: simultaneously the finest and most wretched of times, an age of profound sagacity and utter folly, a period of faith and deep skepticism, a season of illumination and shadow, a spring of optimism and a winter of hopelessness. We possessed everything and yet nothing; we were destined for paradise or its opposite. In essence, that era so closely resembled our own that its most vocal leaders demanded it be viewed only in the most extreme terms. England was ruled by a king with a prominent jaw and a plain-faced queen, while France had a king with a similar jaw and a beautiful queen. To the ruling classes in both nations, it seemed perfectly evident that the existing order was permanent. The year was 1775. England experienced spiritual manifestations much like our own; Mrs. Southcott had just turned twenty-five, and a prophetic soldier had foretold the destruction of London. The Cock-lane ghost had been silenced only twelve years prior, having communicated much like the unoriginal spirits of the previous year. Meanwhile, messages of far greater consequence arrived from British subjects in America, proving more significant to humanity than any spectral warnings. France, though less spiritually inclined, slid effortlessly toward ruin, printing and squandering currency. Under the watch of her clergy, she amused herself with brutal acts, such as torturing a youth for failing to kneel before a passing religious procession. It is probable that in the forests of France and Norway, trees were already being marked by Fate to be fashioned into the grim, historical apparatus of execution that would eventually claim its victims.

Keeping in mind the strange voice, the remarkable agility, and the lack of motive in this horrific crime, let us examine the murder itself. A woman was strangled by hand and shoved headfirst into a chimney. Such methods are not used by typical killers, nor do they dispose of victims in this manner. The act of forcing the body into the flue was bizarre and defies human logic, even for the most depraved. Consider the immense strength required to wedge the corpse so tightly that it took several men to pull it out. Consider also the evidence of extraordinary power. Thick clumps of grey hair were ripped out by the roots, leaving scalp tissue attached—a sign of immense force. The victim’s throat was not just cut; her head was severed with a simple razor. Note the savage cruelty involved. The bruises on Madame L’Espanaye were caused by the stone pavement, as she fell from the window. The police missed this simple fact because their focus on the nails blinded them to the possibility that the window had been opened. When you combine the chaotic state of the room with the astounding agility, superhuman strength, brutal ferocity, lack of motive, grotesque horror, and the unintelligible, foreign voice, the evidence points to a singular conclusion.

The mental traits identified as analytical are difficult to analyze themselves; we recognize them solely through their manifestations. We understand that for those who possess them in abundance, they provide immense satisfaction. Just as a robust individual takes pride in physical exertion, the analyst delights in the mental labor of unraveling complexities. They find joy in applying their skills to even minor tasks, showing a keenness for puzzles and ciphers that seems supernatural to the average observer. Their conclusions, reached through rigorous methodology, often appear to be the result of pure intuition. While mathematical study, particularly the branch termed analysis, may strengthen this faculty, calculation is not synonymous with analysis. A chess player, for instance, calculates without necessarily analyzing. Consequently, the impact of chess on the mind is frequently misjudged. Without intending to write a formal treatise, I will note that the reflective intellect is better served by the humble game of draughts than by the intricate triviality of chess. In chess, the varied and strange movements of the pieces lead many to mistake complexity for depth. The game demands intense focus; a momentary lapse results in defeat. Because the potential moves are both numerous and tangled, errors are common, and victory often goes to the player who is more focused rather than more sharp. In draughts, where moves are uniform and simple, the risk of oversight is low. With attention less taxed, success depends entirely on superior insight. Consider a game of draughts limited to four kings, where mistakes are impossible. In such a scenario, victory between equal opponents must inevitably stem from a sophisticated maneuver born of intense intellectual effort.

Ten minutes later, his face pale with terror and eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile rushed from Bentinck House, pushing past the crowd of footmen under the striped awning, oblivious to his surroundings. The night was freezing, and the streetlights flickered in the sharp wind, yet his hands were feverish and his forehead burned. He walked with the unsteady gait of a drunkard. A policeman watched him with curiosity, and a beggar emerging from an archway retreated, intimidated by a misery deeper than his own. Stopping under a lamp, he examined his hands, imagining he saw bloodstains, and a faint cry escaped his lips. Murder. That was what the palmist had seen. The night seemed to know it, and the wind howled the word. It lurked in dark corners and grinned from the rooftops. He reached the Park, drawn to its somber woods. Leaning against the wet metal railings to cool his brow, he whispered the word repeatedly, as if repetition could dull its horror. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he longed for an echo to wake the sleeping city. He felt a desperate urge to stop a stranger and confess everything. He wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, squalid alleys. Two women with heavy makeup mocked him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came the sound of swearing and violence, followed by shrill screams, and he saw the hunched figures of the elderly poor huddled on a damp doorstep. A strange pity stirred within him. Were these people destined for their fate, just as he was for his? Were they, like him, merely puppets in a grotesque performance? It was the absurdity of suffering that struck him—its utter pointlessness and lack of meaning. Everything felt incoherent and discordant. He was stunned by the gap between the day's shallow optimism and the harsh reality of existence. He was still very young. Eventually, he found himself before Marylebone Church. The silent road stretched out like a ribbon of polished silver, patterned by the dark, swaying shadows.

Men marry out of exhaustion; women, out of curiosity: both end in disappointment. I doubt I will marry, Harry. I am too much in love. I am applying your own aphorism to my life. Who is she? Lord Henry asked. An actress, Dorian Gray replied, blushing. Lord Henry shrugged. That is a common start. You would not say that if you saw her. Who is she? Sibyl Vane. I have never heard of her. No one has yet, but they will. She is a genius. My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are merely decorative. They have nothing to say, yet they say it charmingly. They represent the triumph of matter over mind, just as men represent the triumph of mind over morals. Harry, how can you say that? It is true. I am currently analyzing women, so I should know. It is not as complex as I thought. There are only two kinds: the plain and the colorful. The plain are useful for gaining a reputation for respectability. The others are charming but make the mistake of using makeup to look young. Our grandmothers used makeup to appear witty. Now, as long as a woman looks younger than her daughter, she is satisfied. There are only five women in London worth talking to, and two are social outcasts. Tell me about your genius. How long have you known her? Your views terrify me. Never mind that. How long? About three weeks. Where did you meet her? I will tell you, but do not be unsympathetic. It never would have happened if I had not met you. You filled me with a desperate desire to know everything about life. For days, something throbbed in my veins. As I walked through the park or down the street, I looked at everyone and wondered about their lives with a frantic curiosity. Some fascinated me; others terrified me. There was a beautiful poison in the air. I craved sensations.

I told myself I wanted no part in such affairs. Descending the stairs the next morning, I found the parlor closed and the vigil keepers departed. Only the family, Widow Bartley, and our group remained. I scanned their expressions for signs of recent events, but found none. By midday, the undertaker and his assistant arrived, placing the coffin on chairs in the center of the room. They arranged our chairs in rows, supplementing them with borrowed ones until the hall, parlor, and dining room were crowded. I noticed the coffin lid remained as it had been, yet I dared not peek inside while others were present. As guests arrived, the con artists and the girls occupied the front row. For thirty minutes, mourners filed past in a single line, pausing to gaze at the deceased. Some shed tears in the heavy silence, broken only by the sobbing of the girls and the shuffling of feet or blowing of noses—a common funeral occurrence. Once the room was filled, the undertaker moved about in black gloves, his manner soothing and feline. He managed the crowd and the arrangements with silent gestures and nods, eventually taking his place against the wall. He was the most stealthy, humorless man I had ever encountered. A wheezing melodeon was brought in, and after a young woman played it, the congregation sang, though in my opinion, only Peter sounded decent. Reverend Hobson began his solemn address, but was immediately interrupted by a tremendous commotion from the cellar. A single dog created such a deafening racket that the parson was forced to pause, unable to compete with the noise.

He explained that he was wasting his time where he was and that friends in London wanted him back to finalize his Indian business venture. He could not delay his departure any longer, but since his trip to London might soon be followed by a much longer voyage, he begged me to spend as much time with him as possible. He asked me to leave my lonely island and meet him in Perth so we could travel south together. This letter brought me back to life, and I decided to leave my island in two days. Before I left, I had a task to perform that made me shudder: I had to pack my chemical tools. This meant entering the room where I had done my hateful work and touching the equipment that sickened me. At dawn the next morning, I gathered my courage and unlocked the laboratory door. The remains of the half-finished creature I had destroyed lay scattered on the floor, and I felt as if I had mangled a living human being. I paused to compose myself before entering. With trembling hands, I moved the tools out of the room. Realizing I could not leave these remains to horrify the local peasants, I placed them in a basket with heavy stones, planning to dump them into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach cleaning my equipment. My feelings had changed completely since the night the monster appeared. Before, I had viewed my promise with gloomy despair, believing it had to be fulfilled regardless of the consequences. Now, it felt as if a veil had been lifted from my eyes and I could see clearly for the first time. The thought of resuming my work never crossed my mind. Although the monster's threat weighed on me, I no longer believed my own actions could prevent it. I decided that creating another creature like the first would be an act of pure, selfish cruelty, and I refused to consider it any further.

Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire read only one book for pleasure: the Baronetage. It occupied his idle hours and comforted him in distress. It stirred his admiration for the oldest titles and allowed him to view the newer, more common creations of the last century with pity and disdain. Most of all, he never tired of reading his own entry. The book always fell open to this page: ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL. Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq. of South Park, Gloucestershire. By this lady (who died in 1800), he had issue: Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; and Mary, born November 20, 1791. Sir Walter had updated the original text, adding the date of his wife’s death and noting that Mary married Charles, heir to Charles Musgrove, Esq. of Uppercross, Somerset, on December 16, 1810. The entry continued with the family’s history: their origins in Cheshire, their service as high sheriffs, their parliamentary seats, and their loyalty rewarded by a baronetcy in the first year of Charles II. It listed the various marriages and concluded with their coat of arms, motto, and the location of Kellynch Hall. In his own hand, Sir Walter had added: Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter. Vanity defined Sir Walter’s character, both regarding his appearance and his social standing. He had been a handsome youth and remained a striking man at fifty-four. Few women were as obsessed with their looks as he was, and he took as much pride in his social position as any servant of a newly titled lord. He believed beauty was second only to a baronetcy, and he held himself in the highest regard for possessing both. His looks and rank were his greatest assets, having secured him a wife far superior to anything he deserved.

Keeping in mind the points I have highlighted—the strange voice, the unusual agility, and the baffling lack of motive in such a brutal murder—let us examine the crime itself. A woman was strangled and shoved headfirst up a chimney. Ordinary killers do not commit murder this way, nor do they dispose of bodies like this. You must admit that forcing a corpse into a chimney is bizarre and defies all human logic, even for the most depraved individuals. Consider the immense strength required to shove the body into such a tight space, especially since it took several men working together to pull it back out. Consider the evidence of extraordinary physical power. Thick clumps of grey hair were torn out by the roots. You know how much force is needed to pull out even a few hairs; the roots were still attached to pieces of scalp, proving the massive force used to rip out thousands of hairs at once. The victim’s throat was not just cut; her head was completely severed by a simple razor. Note the savage ferocity of these acts. I will not dwell on the bruises on Madame L’Espanaye’s body. Monsieur Dumas and Monsieur Etienne correctly identified that they were caused by a blunt object, which was clearly the stone pavement where she landed after falling from the window. This simple explanation eluded the police, just as the width of the shutters did, because their obsession with the nails blinded them to the possibility that the windows could have been opened. If you combine these facts with the strange disorder of the room, we have identified a culprit with astounding agility, superhuman strength, brutal ferocity, and no clear motive. We are looking for a horror that defies human nature, accompanied by a voice that sounds foreign to every nationality and lacks any intelligible speech.

It was some time before I regained my composure enough to check the balloon. To my relief, it was undamaged. My equipment was secure, and I had lost neither ballast nor supplies, as I had fastened them too well for such a mishap. Checking my watch, I saw it was six o'clock. I was still climbing rapidly, and my barometer indicated an altitude of three and three-quarter miles. Directly below, a small, dark, oblong object floated on the ocean, looking much like a child's domino. Through my telescope, I identified it as a British ninety-four-gun ship, sailing close-hauled and pitching heavily, headed west-southwest. Beyond that, there was only the sea, the sky, and the sun, which had long since risen. It is time to explain the purpose of my dangerous journey. You must understand that financial ruin in Rotterdam had driven me to consider suicide. I did not hate life itself, but I was exhausted by the misery of my circumstances. Caught between the desire to live and the weariness of existence, a book I found at a stall sparked my imagination. I decided to leave the world while continuing to live; in short, I resolved to attempt a voyage to the moon. Lest you think me entirely mad, I will explain why I believed this difficult and perilous feat was possible for a bold spirit. First, I considered the moon's distance. The average interval between the centers of the two bodies is about 237,000 miles. However, because the moon's orbit is elliptical and the earth sits at its focus, I realized that if I could intercept the moon at its perigee, that distance would be significantly reduced.

Their arrival sparked a sudden tension in Saint Antoine, visible in the faces watching from every doorway. No one followed them, and the wine-shop fell silent as they entered, though every gaze fixed upon them. Monsieur Defarge greeted the room, prompting a collective, hesitant response. When Defarge remarked on the poor weather, the men exchanged uneasy glances and looked away, save for one who promptly left. Defarge then introduced his companion, a road-mender named Jacques, to his wife, asking her to serve him wine. A second man departed. The road-mender drank and ate his coarse bread near the counter, while a third man left the shop. Defarge drank sparingly, waiting for the stranger to finish. Neither he nor his wife, who had returned to her knitting, acknowledged the others. Once the man finished, Defarge led him through the streets, across a courtyard, and up a steep staircase to a small attic room. This was the same place where an old man had once sat making shoes. The old man was gone, but the three men who had left the wine-shop were waiting inside. Defarge shut the door and spoke quietly, introducing the road-mender to the others as the witness he had been sent to find.

I do not understand why she wanted to be close to me, but I would likely be fooled again if the situation repeated itself. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday, and I heard nothing from her in the meantime. When she finally arrived, it was clear she did not enjoy the visit. She offered a brief, formal apology for the delay, said nothing about wanting to see me again, and acted so differently that I decided to end our acquaintance. I pity her, even though I blame her. She was wrong to single me out, as she initiated every step toward our friendship. I pity her because she must know she acted wrongly, and I am certain her anxiety about her brother is the cause. I need not explain further; while we know her worry is unnecessary, it explains her behavior. Given how much she loves her brother, her concern is natural. Still, I am surprised she has these fears, because if he cared for me, we would have met long ago. She let slip that he knows I am in town, yet she talks as if she wants to convince herself he prefers Miss Darcy. I cannot understand it. If I were not afraid of being too harsh, I would call her behavior deceitful. I will try to set aside these painful thoughts and focus on what makes me happy: your affection and the kindness of our aunt and uncle. Write to me soon. Miss Bingley mentioned he might never return to Netherfield and might give up the house, but she was not certain. We should not mention it. I am glad you have good news from our friends at Hunsford. Please visit them with Sir William and Maria; I am sure you will be comfortable. This letter troubled Elizabeth, but she felt better knowing Jane would no longer be deceived by the sister. Any hope regarding the brother was now completely gone.

The powerful, unearthly voice—impossible to link to any instrument—ceased its resonance, and the girl, turning to help her elderly companion, finally noticed us. He was her father, and she had guided his sightless steps since childhood. They were Saxons who had emigrated years earlier, forming bonds with local villagers. When the plague began, a young German student joined them. Their story was clear: a nobleman who loved the musician’s daughter and followed them to escape his family’s disapproval. But the great equalizer arrived, and the youth was an early victim. She lived on for her father’s sake, keeping him unaware that the world had emptied, leaving them as the only listeners to her music. The day we arrived, she fell ill. Terrified of leaving her blind father alone, she hid her condition, driven by desperation to perform one last time. At vespers, she led him to the chapel and played a hymn to creation, her own impending funeral song, with perfect precision. We appeared to her like divine messengers, and her fragile composure shattered. She rushed to us, clutched Adrian’s knees, and begged him to save her father before collapsing into tears. Poor girl. She and her father now lie beside her lover beneath the walnut tree she identified before she died. Her father, finally realizing her state, held her hand until it grew cold in death. He remained motionless until he followed her into rest twelve hours later. They sleep beneath the tree, framed by the Jura mountains and the distant Alps. The church spire still rises above the trees, and though her hands are still, I imagine the music they loved continues to drift there, comforting their gentle spirits.

No, that is for tomorrow, and I specifically needed to see Knightley today for that reason. It is such a scorching morning, and I walked across the fields, which made it even worse. To find him gone is unacceptable. There was no apology and no message. The housekeeper claimed she did not know I was expected, which is very strange. Nobody knew where he went—perhaps to Hartfield, the Abbey Mill, or his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley. Can you explain it? Emma pretended to agree that it was very strange and that she had no excuse for him. I cannot imagine, Mrs. Elton said, feeling insulted on her husband's behalf, how he could treat you this way, especially you. My dear Mr. Elton, he must have left a message. Knightley could not be that rude; his servants must have forgotten. That is typical of the Donwell staff, who are always clumsy and careless. I would never allow someone like his servant Harry in our house. As for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her; she promised a recipe and never sent it. I met William Larkins near the house, Mr. Elton continued, and he told me his master was out, but I did not believe him. William seemed grumpy and said he could hardly ever speak to his master lately. I do not care about William's problems, but it is very important that I see Knightley today, so this hot, wasted walk is a serious inconvenience. Emma decided it was best to go home immediately. She was likely expected there, and Mr. Knightley might be spared further criticism from Mr. Elton, if not from William Larkins. As she left, she was pleased that Miss Fairfax followed her out of the room and downstairs, giving her a chance to speak privately.

She studied me intently for a moment before asking softly, "What is your price for them?" I replied, "Only that you distinguish them from the rest. Though they share the same blood, they possess a different nature." Miss Havisham persisted, "What do you want for them?" Feeling my face flush, I answered, "I am not clever enough to conceal that I do want something. If you would provide the funds to assist my friend Herbert in a way he must never discover, I could explain how." She rested her hands on her cane to watch me more closely and asked, "Why must it remain secret?" I told her, "Because I began this aid two years ago without his awareness, and I cannot be exposed. My inability to complete it involves a secret that is not mine to share." She turned her gaze toward the fire, watching the embers fade in the candlelight. When the coals shifted, she looked back at me with renewed focus. As Estella continued knitting, Miss Havisham asked, "What else?" I turned to Estella, my voice wavering, and said, "You know I have loved you long and deeply." She looked up, her expression indifferent as her needles kept moving. Miss Havisham watched us both. I continued, "I would have spoken sooner, but I mistakenly believed Miss Havisham intended us for each other. I held back while I thought you had no choice in the matter, but I must speak now." Estella shook her head without pausing her work. I replied to her gesture, "I understand. I have no expectation that you will ever be mine, Estella."

To observe him was to imagine Nemesis had seized Pallas's shield, revealing the Gorgon’s visage. He appeared petrified, his countenance marble-like in its sorrow. Having enjoyed a refined existence of wealth and privilege, free from common worries and marked by youthful ease, he now grasped the grim enigma of Fate and the dire significance of Doom. How irrational and grotesque it appeared! Was some dark secret of transgression or a crimson mark of guilt inscribed upon his palm, legible only to others? Was there no flight? Were humans merely pawns shifted by an invisible hand, or clay molded by a potter for glory or disgrace? His intellect rebelled, yet he sensed an impending tragedy and an unbearable weight placed upon him. Actors are lucky; they select their roles, whether tragic or comic. In reality, however, people often play parts for which they are ill-suited. Our minor characters act as leads, and our leads must play the fool. The world is a stage, but the casting is flawed. Suddenly, Mr. Podgers walked in. Upon seeing Lord Arthur, he recoiled, his bloated face turning a sickly greenish-yellow. Their gazes locked in a silent moment. The Duchess left a glove, and I am here to retrieve it, Mr. Podgers eventually stated, spotting it on the sofa. Good evening. Mr. Podgers, I demand a direct answer to my question. Another time, Lord Arthur; the Duchess is waiting. You shall not leave. The Duchess can wait. Ladies should not be delayed, Mr. Podgers replied with a nauseating grin. They are prone to impatience. Lord Arthur’s lips curled in scorn. The Duchess seemed trivial to him then. He approached Mr. Podgers and extended his hand. Tell me what you saw, he commanded. Speak the truth. I must know. I am no child.

No raising by hand, then. Not at all! Joe offered me more gravy, which I hesitated to accept. He was quite a burden to you, ma’am, Mrs. Hubble remarked to my sister. Burden? my sister repeated, launching into a terrifying list of my various illnesses, sleepless nights, falls from heights and depths, self-inflicted injuries, and the many times I had stubbornly refused her wishes for my demise. I suspect the Romans were constantly irritated by their noses, perhaps explaining their restless nature. Regardless, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose so vexed me during this account of my sins that I longed to pull it until he screamed. Yet, my suffering was minor compared to the dread I felt when the silence following her speech left everyone staring at me with visible disgust. Still, Mr. Pumblechook gently steered the conversation back, asking if boiled pork was also rich. Have some brandy, uncle, my sister suggested. Oh heavens, the moment had arrived! He would discover it was diluted, declare it so, and I would be ruined. I gripped the table leg beneath the cloth, bracing for the end. My sister fetched the stone bottle and poured his drink. The wretched man toyed with his glass, prolonging my agony while the others cleared the table. I watched him, still clutching the table leg, as he playfully swirled his drink, smiled, tilted his head back, and swallowed. Suddenly, the room erupted in horror as he leaped up, spun in a spasmodic, whooping dance, and bolted outside. Through the window, I saw him plunging about and spitting, making grotesque faces as if he had lost his senses. I held on tight while Joe and his wife rushed to his aid.

I hurried toward my college, suddenly chilled by the realization that the creature I had abandoned in my rooms might still be roaming there. Terrified of encountering the monster—and even more fearful that Henry might see him—I asked my friend to wait downstairs while I rushed up. My hand gripped the lock before I hesitated, overcome by a freezing tremor. I flung the door open with the frantic energy of a child expecting a ghost, but the room was vacant. My bedroom was likewise deserted. Scarcely daring to believe in such luck, I confirmed my enemy had vanished and raced back down to Clerval, clapping my hands in relief. We went up to my room, but as the servant served breakfast, I could not compose myself. Overwhelmed by a frantic sensitivity and a racing pulse, I paced restlessly, leaping over furniture and laughing with a hollow, wild intensity. Clerval initially mistook my behavior for excitement at his arrival, but my erratic eyes and jarring laughter soon filled him with alarm. My dear Victor, he pleaded, what is wrong? You are clearly unwell. Do not laugh like that. I covered my eyes, screaming for him to save me as I hallucinated the monster entering the room. I struggled against an imagined grasp until I collapsed in a fit. Poor Clerval; the reunion he had anticipated with such delight had turned into a nightmare. I remained unconscious, oblivious to his distress, for a long time. This marked the start of a nervous fever that kept me bedridden for months. Throughout my illness, Henry acted as my sole caretaker. I later discovered that he had shielded my father and Elizabeth from the truth of my condition, sparing them the agony of knowing how severe my breakdown had become.

I recall the conditions during our nineteenth-century civil war. In the North, a carpenter earned three dollars daily in gold, while in the South, he received fifty in nearly worthless Confederate currency. Since a pair of overalls cost a day's pay in the North but two days' wages in the South, Northern earnings effectively held double the purchasing power. During my time in the village, I was pleased to see our new currency circulating among the common people, including mills, cents, nickels, and silver. Gold remained at the goldsmith's shop. While Marco was busy arguing over salt prices, I requested change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. The staff scrutinized the coin, testing its weight and purity, before subjecting me to an exhaustive interrogation about my identity and travels. When their questions ceased, I provided unsolicited details about my dog, my late wife's religious background, and an acquaintance with extra thumbs, until the inquisitive clerk seemed both satisfied and annoyed. Though he dared not challenge a man of my means, he vented his frustration on his subordinates. They eventually broke my twenty, though the transaction clearly taxed their resources, much like asking a small-town merchant to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. The goldsmith likely wondered how a traveler possessed such wealth, as he stood at the door watching me depart with a look of awestruck respect.

My father stayed by my side to comfort me, replacing my bitter memories with hopeful thoughts. It felt sweet to grieve simply because he was there to dry my tears. He distracted me from my sorrow by comparing it to the despair he felt when he lost my mother. I shuddered at his description of that time; he had a poet's imagination, and his account of his emotional turmoil was so vivid that I trembled as I listened. I marveled that he could ever return to normal life after experiencing such intense, almost supernatural feelings. His emotions seemed too vast for a human heart, better suited to a spirit of fire and earth than a mortal man. Yet, he had changed. He was now entirely gentle and loving, and his warm smile showed that his heart was filled with kindness. Two months after my aunt died, we moved to London, where my father encouraged me to pursue more serious studies. He took great joy in my progress, assisting me with every lesson. We socialized often, and my father worked to make every day enjoyable. Our deep mutual love and respect made every moment special. We lived so fully that a single week felt like months, with every new experience adding excitement to our lives. We frequently went on excursions together, whether to see beautiful landscapes, admire art, or simply find amusement. I was always happiest when I was with him. I disliked it when others joined us, but if I looked at my father with concern, his tender gaze would instantly restore my happiness. Those hours of intense joy were brief, yet looking back on them through the fog of later grief, they feel as long as a lifetime.

I told him I required the watermelon, but he argued that I did not need it for a prison escape, which was the point of contention. He claimed it would be acceptable if I intended to conceal a blade inside to help Jim slay the jailer. I dropped the subject, though I found little benefit in playing the part of a prisoner if I had to debate such trivialities whenever I spotted a watermelon. As I mentioned, we waited that morning until the yard was deserted. Tom carried the sack into the shed while I kept watch. He soon emerged, and we sat on the woodpile to confer. He stated that everything was prepared except for the tools. When I asked what tools were for, he explained we needed them to dig, as we could not simply gnaw Jim out. I suggested the old, broken picks in the shed should suffice, but he looked at me with such pity that it was nearly heartbreaking. He asked if I had ever heard of a prisoner being provided with modern digging equipment, noting that such tools would ruin any chance of him being a hero. He insisted that even a king would not be given picks and shovels. When I asked what we should use instead, he specified a pair of case-knives. I protested that using knives to dig out a cabin foundation was absurd, but he maintained it was the correct and standard method. He claimed to have read every relevant book on the subject, asserting that prisoners always dig through solid rock with case-knives, a process that takes ages. He asked how long I thought a prisoner in the Castle d'If took to dig his way out, and when I could not guess, he pressed me for an answer. I replied that I had no idea, perhaps a month and a half.

He had never oppressed or imprisoned anyone. Far from demanding his dues, he had voluntarily relinquished them, venturing into a harsh world to earn his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the struggling estate under instructions to assist the tenants, providing whatever fuel and produce the creditors allowed. Gabelle had surely documented these efforts for his own protection, and this evidence would now be clear. This bolstered Charles Darnay’s growing resolve to travel to Paris. Like the sailor in the legend, he felt drawn toward the magnetic rock, pulled by an irresistible force. Every thought pushed him faster toward that dangerous destination. He felt a nagging guilt that while wicked men committed atrocities in his homeland, he—who knew he was better than them—remained absent, failing to advocate for mercy or prevent bloodshed. This internal conflict, combined with the contrast between his own inaction and the duty shown by others, was sharpened by the stinging insults of Monseigneur and the coarse mockery of Stryver. Finally, Gabelle’s letter arrived, a desperate plea from an innocent man facing death, appealing to Darnay’s sense of honor. His decision was final: he had to go to Paris. The magnetic pull was absolute. He failed to see the true danger, believing instead that his past intentions would be recognized and appreciated upon his arrival. He was seduced by the idealistic vision that he might exert influence over the chaotic Revolution and steer it toward a more humane path.

Every properly fashioned boy eventually feels an intense urge to search for buried treasure. This impulse struck Tom suddenly. He went to find Joe Harper but failed, and his search for Ben Rogers also proved fruitless as the boy had gone fishing. Eventually, he encountered Huck Finn the Red-Handed, who proved receptive. Tom brought him to a secluded spot to share his secret plan. Huck agreed, as he was always ready for any venture that promised amusement without requiring money, possessing an excess of time that held no monetary value. Where shall we dig, Huck asked. Oh, almost anywhere, Tom replied. Is it hidden everywhere, Huck wondered. Certainly not, Tom explained. It is buried in specific locations, like islands, inside decaying chests beneath the boughs of dead trees where shadows fall at midnight, or under the floorboards of haunted houses. Robbers hide it, Tom clarified, dismissing Huck's suggestion of Sunday-school superintendents. Huck mused that he would rather spend such wealth, but Tom insisted robbers always leave it behind. They often forget the markers or perish, leaving the treasure to rust until someone discovers an old, cryptic map filled with hieroglyphics that require weeks to decipher. When Huck asked if Tom possessed such a map, Tom admitted he did not. He planned to search haunted houses, islands, and dead trees with protruding limbs. When Huck pointed out that checking every tree would take all summer, Tom countered by describing the potential reward of a brass pot filled with rusty coins or a chest of diamonds. Huck’s eyes brightened, declaring that a hundred dollars would be plenty for him.

I hope to introduce my son to you soon, Mr. Weston said. Mrs. Elton, assuming this was a special compliment, smiled graciously. You have heard of Frank Churchill, I assume, and know he is my son, even if he does not use my name. Oh yes, I look forward to meeting him. Mr. Elton will certainly visit him, and we would love to host him at the Vicarage. You are very kind, and Frank will be delighted. He arrives in town next week, or perhaps sooner. We received a letter today; I saw his handwriting and opened it, even though it was addressed to Mrs. Weston. She is his main correspondent, and I rarely hear from him. You actually opened her mail? Mrs. Elton laughed affectedly. I must protest! That is a dangerous precedent. I hope our neighbors do not follow your lead. We married women will have to be more careful! I could not have believed it of you. We men are troublesome, Mr. Weston replied. You must be careful, Mrs. Elton. The letter is brief, just to let us know they are moving south immediately because Mrs. Churchill has been unwell all winter and finds Enscombe too cold. Indeed, from Yorkshire, I believe? Yes, it is about one hundred and ninety miles from London, quite a long trip. It is significant, certainly. Sixty-five miles further than Maple Grove is from London. But distance means little to the wealthy. You would be amazed at how my brother, Mr. Suckling, travels. He and Mr. Bragge once went to London and back twice in one week with four horses. The trouble with the distance from Enscombe, Mr. Weston noted, is that Mrs. Churchill has been unable to leave her sofa for a week. In his last letter, Frank mentioned she was too weak to reach her conservatory without help from both him and his uncle.

On the morning Admiral and Mrs. Croft were scheduled to view Kellynch Hall, Anne decided to walk to Lady Russell’s house to stay out of the way. Later, she felt regret for missing the chance to meet them. The meeting went perfectly, and the deal was settled immediately. Both women were eager to agree, so they viewed each other favorably. The Admiral’s friendly, open nature impressed Sir Walter, especially since Mr. Shepherd had flattered him by claiming the Admiral already considered him a model of good manners. The house, grounds, and furniture were all accepted, and the legal paperwork began without any disagreements. Sir Walter even declared the Admiral the best-looking sailor he had ever met, joking that he would be proud to be seen with him if only his hair were styled better. Meanwhile, the Admiral told his wife that Sir Walter was harmless, even if not particularly brilliant. These mutual, backhanded compliments were essentially equal. The Crofts were set to move in at Michaelmas, and since Sir Walter planned to relocate to Bath the month before, they had to act quickly. Lady Russell knew Anne would have no say in choosing their new home and wanted her to stay behind until after Christmas. However, Lady Russell had her own travel plans and could not host her. Although Anne dreaded the heat of Bath and felt sad about leaving the countryside in autumn, she ultimately decided it was best to go.

On that matter, I shall remain silent, and you may be certain that I will never speak unkindly of you once we are married. Elizabeth had to interrupt him. You are moving too quickly, sir, she exclaimed. You forget that I have not yet answered. Let me do so now. Thank you for the compliment, and I appreciate the honor of your proposal, but I must decline. Mr. Collins waved his hand formally. I know it is common for young women to reject a man at first even when they intend to accept him, and sometimes they refuse several times. I am not discouraged and hope to lead you to the altar soon. Elizabeth replied that his hope was strange given her clear answer. I am not one of those women who risk their happiness by playing games. I am serious. You could not make me happy, and I am the last woman who would make you happy. Even Lady Catherine would agree that I am ill-suited for the role. Mr. Collins replied gravely that he doubted Lady Catherine would disapprove. When I see her again, I will speak highly of your modesty and other fine qualities. Mr. Collins, please do not praise me. You must let me judge for myself and believe what I say. I wish you happiness and wealth, and by refusing you, I am doing my best to ensure you find both. You have fulfilled your duty to your feelings regarding my family, so you may take the Longbourn estate when it falls to you without guilt. This matter is settled. She stood to leave, but Mr. Collins spoke again. When I address this subject again, I hope for a more favorable answer. I do not accuse you of cruelty, as I know it is the custom for women to reject a man at first, and you have likely said as much as is proper to encourage me.

Observing a star indirectly—by shifting one's gaze so the outer retina catches the light—allows for a clearer view and a better sense of its brilliance, which fades when stared at directly. While more light hits the eye when looking straight on, the peripheral vision offers a more nuanced perception. Excessive intensity can confuse and weaken the mind; even Venus can disappear from sight if scrutinized with too much focus or persistence. Regarding these killings, let us investigate them ourselves before forming a judgment. It will be an interesting diversion, and Le Bon once helped me, so I owe him a debt. We shall visit the scene. I am acquainted with G—, the Prefect of Police, and can easily secure access. Permission was granted, and we traveled to the Rue Morgue, a dreary street between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late when we arrived, as the location was far from our home. The house was easy to spot, as a crowd still lingered across the way, staring at the shuttered windows with aimless curiosity. It was a typical Parisian building featuring a gateway and a concierge's booth. Before entering, we walked the street, turned into an alley, and circled behind the structure, while Dupin inspected the area and the house with a level of detail I found inexplicable. Returning to the front, we rang the bell, presented our papers, and were let in by the officers. We ascended to the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been discovered and where the victims remained. The disarray had been left undisturbed. I observed nothing beyond what the Gazette had reported. Dupin examined everything, including the corpses, before we toured the remaining rooms and the yard, escorted by a gendarme.

It was well past midday when he roused. His valet had tiptoed into the chamber repeatedly to check for movement, puzzled by his master’s prolonged slumber. At last, the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly, bearing tea and a stack of mail on a delicate Sevres tray. He pulled back the olive-satin curtains, lined with shimmering blue, which covered the three large windows. Monsieur has slept quite late, he remarked with a smile. What time is it, Victor? Dorian Gray inquired sleepily. A quarter past one, Monsieur. How late! He sat up, sipped his tea, and examined his correspondence. One note from Lord Henry had been hand-delivered that morning; he paused, then set it aside. He opened the rest indifferently, finding the usual array of invitations, private view tickets, and charity programs typical for a fashionable man during the season. There was a substantial bill for a chased silver toilet set he dared not show his conservative guardians, who failed to grasp that in our era, luxuries are our only true necessities. Other letters included polite offers from Jermyn Street lenders to provide funds at a moment’s notice. Ten minutes later, he rose, donned an ornate cashmere dressing gown, and entered the onyx bathroom. The cold water revived him, and he seemed to shed his recent experiences. A vague memory of some dark tragedy flickered, but it felt as unreal as a dream. Once dressed, he moved to the library for a light French breakfast served at a small table by the open window. It was a beautiful day, the air heavy with spice. A bee buzzed around the blue-dragon bowl of yellow roses before him, and he felt entirely content. Suddenly, his gaze landed on the screen hiding the portrait, and he recoiled. Is it too cold for you, Monsieur? his valet asked, placing an omelette on the table. Shall I close the window? Dorian shook his head. I am not cold, he whispered.

Ten minutes later, his face pale with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile rushed out of Bentinck House. He pushed through the crowd of footmen by the entrance, seeing and hearing nothing. The night was freezing, and the gas lamps flickered in the sharp wind, but his hands were feverish and his forehead burned. He walked like a drunkard. A policeman watched him with curiosity, and a beggar who stepped out to ask for money grew frightened, seeing misery worse than his own. Once, he stopped under a lamp to look at his hands. He imagined he saw bloodstains on them and let out a soft cry. Murder. That was what the palm reader had seen. The night seemed to know it, and the wind howled it in his ears. The dark corners of the streets were full of it, and it seemed to grin from the rooftops. He reached the park, where the dark trees drew him in. He leaned against the wet metal railings to cool his brow, listening to the quiet of the woods. He kept repeating the word murder, as if saying it over and over could lessen the horror. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he almost wanted to wake the city and tell everyone. He wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, grim alleys. Two women with heavy makeup mocked him as he passed. From a dark courtyard came the sound of swearing and fighting, followed by screams. On a damp doorstep, he saw the hunched figures of the poor and elderly. A strange pity filled him. Were these people destined for their suffering just as he was for his? Were they, like him, just puppets in a cruel play? Yet it was not the mystery of suffering that struck him, but its comedy—its total uselessness and lack of meaning. Everything seemed disconnected and chaotic. He was amazed by the gap between the shallow optimism of society and the harsh reality of life. He was still very young. Eventually, he found himself in front of Marylebone Church. The empty road looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, marked by the dark, waving shadows of the trees.

The small man possessed a disproportionately wide frame, lending his entire appearance a comical roundness. His feet remained hidden, though a suspicious, horny material occasionally poked through a tear in the base of his vehicle, or more accurately, the crown of his hat. His hands were massive. His hair, quite gray, was pulled into a queue at the back. His nose was remarkably long, hooked, and inflamed; his eyes were full, sharp, and bright; his chin and cheeks, while aged and wrinkled, were wide, puffy, and double; yet no trace of ears could be found anywhere on his head. This peculiar gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin frock coat with matching tight breeches, secured by silver knee buckles. His vest was a vibrant yellow; a white taffeta cap sat rakishly on his head; and to finish his attire, a blood-red silk scarf wrapped his neck, cascading over his chest in a massive, elaborate bow. Having descended to roughly one hundred feet above the ground, the little man was suddenly gripped by anxiety, seemingly unwilling to get any closer to solid earth. He struggled to heave a bag of sand from his craft, causing his ascent to halt immediately. In a flustered state, he pulled a large morocco wallet from his coat pocket. He weighed it suspiciously, appearing shocked by its heft. Finally, he opened it, removed a bulky letter sealed in red wax and bound with red tape, and dropped it right at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to retrieve it. However, the aeronaut, still deeply rattled and seemingly finished with his business in Rotterdam, began preparing to leave. Needing to shed weight to rise again, he tossed out half a dozen bags without emptying them, which unfortunately landed squarely on the burgomaster, rolling him over twenty-one times before the entire population of Rotterdam. One should not assume, however, that the great Underduk allowed this insolence from the little man to go unpunished.

He rode the spirited horse that had carried him to victory in Greece, exhausting himself with physical exertion to numb his troubled mind. Slowly, he recovered, emerging from the fog of fever and passion into a state of calm reflection. He realized that for the past month, madness rather than reason had guided him. He had not seen Evadne during this time, and her influence over him had faded. He was no longer her slave or her lover; he resolved to never see her again and to earn back Perdita’s trust. Yet, he could not help but picture the Greek girl’s miserable living conditions. He remembered her former life of oriental luxury in Constantinople and contrasted it with her current poverty and gaunt appearance. Compassion filled him, and he decided to visit her one last time to help restore her to her proper social standing before ending their relationship for good. He also reflected on how he had avoided Perdita out of guilt, but he was determined to fix this and prove his devotion. Feeling optimistic, he planned his next steps. He remembered he was expected at a festival that evening to celebrate the anniversary of his election as Protector. He decided he would briefly visit Evadne to explain his long absence and then return to Perdita, his public duties, and his life of power. Following these events, Perdita hoped for a complete change in Raymond’s behavior, expecting a return to the open, affectionate communication that had once defined their life together.

For years, Dorian Gray remained under the spell of that book, or perhaps he simply chose not to break free. He ordered nine copies from Paris, binding them in various colors to match his shifting moods and his increasingly erratic nature. The protagonist, a young man who blended romanticism with science, felt like a mirror of his own life, as if his story had been written before he lived it. In one way, Dorian was luckier than the book’s hero. He never suffered from the strange fear of mirrors or reflective surfaces that plagued the character after his beauty faded. Dorian read the tragic end of the book with a cruel sense of satisfaction, finding pleasure in the despair of someone who had lost the beauty he valued most. Yet, the beauty that had captivated Basil Hallward never left Dorian. Even when scandalous rumors about his lifestyle circulated through London clubs, people could not believe the gossip once they saw him. He always appeared untouched by the world. His face was so pure that it silenced vulgar men, reminding them of the innocence they had lost. They wondered how someone so charming could remain untainted by such a sordid, sensual age. Often, after returning from his mysterious and long absences, Dorian would sneak upstairs to his locked room. He would unlock the door, stand before the portrait Basil had painted, and hold up a mirror. He would compare the aging, wicked face on the canvas to the youthful, laughing reflection staring back at him.

We grew up together, less than a year apart in age. We never experienced any conflict; harmony defined our bond, and our contrasting personalities only brought us closer. Elizabeth possessed a calm, focused nature, while I was more passionate, driven by intense focus and a deep thirst for knowledge. She found joy in the poetic and the beauty of our Swiss home—the mountains, the changing seasons, and the Alpine landscape. While she admired the world’s surface, I sought to understand its underlying causes. The world was a mystery I longed to solve, and my earliest memories are filled with the thrill of uncovering nature’s hidden laws. When my brother was born seven years later, my parents settled permanently in Switzerland. We split our time between a house in Geneva and a country home on Lake Belrive. My parents lived quietly, and I, preferring a small circle to crowds, avoided most schoolmates. I formed one deep friendship with Henry Clerval, a merchant’s son. Henry was imaginative and bold, drawn to hardship and adventure. He loved tales of chivalry, writing heroic songs and stories about knights and enchantment. He often organized plays and masquerades based on legends of King Arthur and the crusaders. I had an exceptionally happy childhood. My parents were kind and indulgent, acting not as strict rulers, but as the loving architects of our many joys.

I am very ignorant, and it troubles me a little. Tell me what it is. I have a cousin, an orphan like me, whom I love dearly. She is five years younger and lives on a farm in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of my fate because I cannot write. It is better this way. Yes, it is better. As we traveled, I kept thinking, while looking at your kind, strong face, that if the Republic truly helps the poor so they suffer less, she might live a long time. She might even grow old. What then, my gentle sister? Do you think, she asked, her eyes filling with tears, that it will feel like a long wait for me in heaven, where I hope we will both find peace? It cannot be, my child; there is no time or trouble there. You comfort me so much. Am I to kiss you now? Is it time? Yes. She kisses his lips, and he kisses hers; they bless each other. His hand is steady as he lets her go, and her face remains calm and bright. She goes before him and is gone; the knitting women count twenty-two. I am the Resurrection and the Life, says the Lord.
