The murmuring voices, the sea of faces, and the pressing crowd all fade away. Twenty-three. That night, people said his face was the most peaceful they had ever seen, looking both sublime and prophetic. Another victim had recently asked to write down her final thoughts. If he had spoken his, they would have been: I see the new oppressors who rose from the ruins of the old, all perishing by this same blade before its work is finally done.

We declared ourselves free men so loudly and earnestly that we drew the attention of a grandstanding orator and his patriotic followers, who surrounded us with a menacing air. The orator declared, "If you are truly free, you have nothing to fear; Britain's God-given liberties protect you. Show us your proof." When I asked what proof he meant, he insisted we prove our status as free men. I suddenly remembered my situation and stayed silent, but the king exploded, "You are insane. It would be more reasonable for this thief to prove we are not free." He understood the law only in theory, not in practice; laws become vivid only when they apply to you personally. The crowd looked disappointed and began to lose interest. The orator spoke again, this time with cold, professional detachment: "If you do not know the laws of this land, it is time you learned. You are strangers here. You might be free, but you might also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove you are slaves; it requires you to prove you are not." I pleaded, "Sir, just give us time to send word to Astolat or the Valley of Holiness." He dismissed me, claiming such requests were unreasonable and would inconvenience our master. "Master, you idiot!" the king roared. "I have no master, I am the m--" I cut him off just in time. We were in enough trouble; we did not need them thinking we were insane. There is no point in detailing the rest. The earl had us auctioned off. This same wretched law existed in the American South thirteen centuries later, where countless free men were sold into lifelong slavery without me giving it much thought. Yet, once the law and the auction block became my personal reality, what had seemed merely improper became truly hellish. That is simply how we are built. We were sold like livestock. In a bustling market, we might have fetched a decent price, but this town was so stagnant that we sold for an amount that still shames me to recall.

The daughter lay still, having fainted. The elderly woman’s frantic screams and resistance, which resulted in her hair being ripped out, transformed the orangutan’s likely peaceful intent into violent rage. With a single powerful stroke, the beast nearly decapitated her. The sight of blood drove it into a frenzy. Gnashing its teeth and with eyes ablaze, it attacked the girl, sinking its claws into her throat until she died. Its wild gaze then landed on the bed’s headboard, where its master’s face, frozen in terror, was visible. The creature’s fury, tempered by the memory of the whip, shifted to fear. Aware of its guilt, it sought to hide the carnage, pacing the room in a nervous panic, smashing furniture and pulling the bed from its frame. Finally, it shoved the daughter’s body up the chimney and hurled the old woman’s corpse out the window. As the ape neared the window with the body, the sailor recoiled in horror, slid down the lightning rod, and fled home, abandoning the animal in his terror. The noises heard on the stairs were the Frenchman’s cries of shock mixed with the beast’s demonic chattering. I have little to add. The orangutan must have escaped down the rod just before the door was broken, closing the window behind it. Its owner later recaptured it and sold it for a high price to the Jardin des Plantes. Le Bon was released immediately after we explained the events to the Prefect. Though the Prefect was friendly toward my companion, he could not hide his annoyance at the outcome, offering a few sarcastic remarks about people minding their own affairs. Let him talk, Dupin remarked, choosing not to respond. It eases his conscience. I am content to have outwitted him in his own domain. That he failed to solve this mystery is not as surprising as he believes; in reality, our friend the Prefect is far too clever to be truly profound.

“What is wrong?” Oliver asked. “Quiet!” the Dodger answered. “Do you notice that elderly man at the bookstand?” “The gentleman across the street?” Oliver asked. “Yes, I see him.” “He will serve,” the Dodger said. “An excellent target,” remarked Charley Bates. Oliver stared at them in bewilderment, but before he could question them, the two boys crept across the street and slipped behind the man. Oliver followed a few steps, then paused, watching in stunned silence. The gentleman appeared quite respectable, with powdered hair, gold spectacles, a bottle-green coat with a velvet collar, and white trousers, carrying a bamboo cane. He was so absorbed in a book from the stall that he seemed to believe he was in his own study, oblivious to his surroundings as he read with intense focus. Oliver watched in horror as the Dodger reached into the man’s pocket, pulled out a handkerchief, passed it to Charley Bates, and then both boys sprinted around the corner. Suddenly, the truth about the stolen goods and the old man dawned on Oliver. Terrified, he felt as though his blood were boiling, and he fled in a panic, running as fast as he could. This all occurred in a moment. As Oliver bolted, the gentleman reached for his pocket, realized his handkerchief was gone, and turned around. Seeing the boy racing away, he assumed Oliver was the thief and, shouting “Stop thief!” at the top of his lungs, chased after him with his book still in hand.

It is only fair to note that the young lady did not flatly refuse, but instead expressed a strong desire to be damned if she would. This polite evasion showed her natural good manners, as she could not bear to cause anyone the pain of a blunt rejection. The Jew’s face fell. He turned from this woman, who was dressed in a bright red gown, green boots, and yellow hair curlers, to the other. Nancy, my dear, the Jew said soothingly, what do you say? It won’t work, so don’t bother trying, Fagin, Nancy replied. What do you mean by that? Mr. Sikes asked, looking up grumpily. Just what I said, Bill, Nancy answered calmly. You are the perfect person for this, Sikes argued, since nobody around here knows you. And since I don’t want them to, it is a firm no from me, Bill, Nancy replied. She will go, Fagin, Sikes insisted. No, she won’t, Fagin, Nancy countered. Yes, she will, Fagin, Sikes repeated. Sikes was right. Through a mix of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman was eventually convinced to take the job. She did not share her friend’s hesitation, as she had recently moved from a distant neighborhood and did not fear being recognized. With a clean white apron over her dress and her hair curlers hidden under a straw bonnet provided by the Jew, Nancy prepared to leave. Stop a minute, my dear, the Jew said, handing her a small basket. Carry that; it looks more respectable. Give her a door key for the other hand, Sikes added, it looks more genuine. Yes, that is perfect, the Jew said, hanging a large key on her finger and rubbing his hands together. Oh, my brother! My poor, sweet, innocent little brother! Nancy cried, bursting into tears while clutching the basket and key in apparent distress. What has happened to him? Where have they taken him? Please, gentlemen, have pity and tell me what has become of the dear boy!

As summer progressed, the sun intensified, and the plague spread its deadly reach across the world. Nations suffered and perished. Crops rotted in the fields while those who went to harvest them collapsed, struck down by the sickness. The forests remained lush, providing shade for the dying, whose cries disrupted the peaceful woods. While birds and animals thrived, death claimed only humanity. Our fear grew alongside the summer heat. Looking at my wife, Idris, and our children, I vowed to protect them. I promised that one day we would tell them of these dark times, ensuring they would survive and remain healthy. Our eldest son occasionally asked about the widespread suffering, but his youth allowed him to quickly return to his play. Little Evelyn remained a joyful, innocent child, filling our home with laughter. Our daughter, Clara, was our greatest comfort. She dedicated herself to helping the sick, the elderly, and the grieving, moving through our home like a guardian angel. Despite her gentle nature and simple kindness, she possessed remarkable courage and wisdom. We endured the long summer, praying that winter would slow the disease. We dared not hope it would vanish entirely, for even mentioning such a possibility brought forth tears and overwhelming grief from those who had lost all sense of security.

He was dressed as Jonas the Graveless, a character from one of his most famous performances that had once caused a major feud between the Cantervilles and their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was past two in the morning, and he believed the house was quiet. As he walked toward the library to check for the bloodstain, two figures jumped from the shadows, waving their arms and shouting 'BOO!' in his ear. Terrified, he ran for the stairs, only to find Washington Otis waiting with a large garden syringe. Trapped, he escaped into a cold iron stove and crawled through the chimneys, reaching his room covered in soot and deeply humiliated. He did not venture out again. The twins tried to lure him out by scattering nutshells in the halls, but he remained hidden, his pride clearly wounded. Mr. Otis returned to his history of the Democratic Party, Mrs. Otis hosted a successful clam-bake, the boys played American games, and Virginia rode her pony with the young Duke of Cheshire, who was visiting. Everyone assumed the ghost had left, and Mr. Otis even wrote to Lord Canterville to confirm it, much to the Lord's relief. However, the family was mistaken. The ghost remained in the house, and though weak, he was determined to act, especially after learning that the young Duke of Cheshire was a guest. The Duke’s great-uncle had once bet he could play dice with the ghost, only to be found the next morning paralyzed and unable to speak anything but 'Double Sixes' for the rest of his life.

Oh, bother my hat! I want Virginia! the little Duke laughed as they galloped toward the station. Mr. Otis asked the station-master if anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen, but he had no news. The official promised to alert the line and keep a watch. After buying the Duke a new hat from a nearby shop, Mr. Otis rode to Bexley, a village four miles away known for its gypsy camps. They woke the local policeman, but he offered no help. After searching the common, they returned home by eleven o’clock, exhausted and heartbroken. Washington and the twins met them at the gate with lanterns, but they had found no trace of her. The gypsies had been located in a nearby meadow, but Virginia was not with them; they explained they had left in a hurry to reach a fair on time. They were genuinely upset to hear she was missing and had even left four men behind to help search. The pond had been dragged and the entire estate scoured, but to no avail. It was clear that Virginia was truly lost for the night. Mr. Otis and the boys walked to the house in deep despair, followed by the groom. Inside, the servants were terrified, and Mrs. Otis lay on the library sofa, nearly hysterical, while the housekeeper tended to her. Mr. Otis insisted she eat and ordered supper for everyone. It was a somber meal; even the twins were quiet and subdued. Once finished, Mr. Otis sent everyone to bed despite the Duke’s protests, promising to contact Scotland Yard for detectives in the morning.

The group was split across two adjacent benches. Anne sat on the front one, where Mr. Elliot, aided by his friend Colonel Wallis, had successfully secured a seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by cousins and receiving the Colonel’s full attention, was perfectly satisfied. Anne was in the ideal frame of mind to enjoy the evening; the concert provided just enough distraction. She felt receptive to the music’s tenderness, the gaiety of the mood, the technical skill of the performers, and the tediousness of the duller moments. She had never enjoyed a concert more, at least during the first half. As the interval following an Italian song began, she used their program to explain the lyrics to Mr. Elliot. This is roughly the meaning, she said, or at least the gist of it, since one shouldn't look for deep sense in an Italian love song. It is as close as I can manage, as I am a poor Italian scholar. He laughed, telling her that her modesty was unnecessary, as her ability to translate those complex lines into elegant English on the spot was proof enough of her skill. She replied that she would accept his kindness but would hate to be tested by an expert. He countered that he had known Miss Anne Elliot long enough to recognize that she was too modest for the world to appreciate her true talents, and too talented for such modesty to be natural in anyone else. Embarrassed by the flattery, she turned back to the program to see what was next. Lowering his voice, Mr. Elliot suggested he had known her character longer than she realized. Surprised, she asked how that could be, given they had only met in Bath. He explained that he had known her by reputation for years, having heard her described by those who knew her well, making her personality and accomplishments familiar to him long before they met. Mr. Elliot succeeded in piquing her interest, for few can resist the allure of such a mystery.

This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to keep on at Lady Canterville’s request. She curtsied as they arrived and said in an old-fashioned way, 'I welcome you to Canterville Chase.' They followed her through the Tudor hall into the library, a long room with black oak panels and a stained-glass window. Tea was waiting, and they sat down to look around while Mrs. Umney served them. Suddenly, Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor near the fireplace. Not knowing what it was, she said, 'I am afraid something has been spilled there.' 'Yes, madam,' the housekeeper replied quietly, 'blood has been spilled on that spot.' 'How horrid,' Mrs. Otis cried. 'I do not want bloodstains in a sitting room. It must be removed.' The old woman smiled and said in a mysterious voice, 'It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered there by her husband, Sir Simon, in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine more years before disappearing under mysterious circumstances. His body was never found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the house. The stain is admired by tourists and cannot be removed.' 'That is nonsense,' Washington Otis declared. 'Pinkerton’s Stain Remover will clean it up immediately.' Before the terrified housekeeper could stop him, he knelt and scrubbed the floor with a cleaning stick. In moments, the stain was gone. 'I knew Pinkerton would work,' he said triumphantly. Just then, a flash of lightning lit the room, a loud thunderclap made everyone jump, and Mrs. Umney fainted. 'What a terrible climate,' the American Minister said calmly, lighting a cigar. 'I suppose this country is so crowded they do not have enough good weather for everyone. Emigration is the only solution for England.' 'My dear Hiram,' Mrs. Otis cried, 'what can we do with a woman who faints?' 'Charge it to her like broken items,' the Minister replied. 'She will not faint again.' Soon after, Mrs. Umney regained consciousness.

The artist suddenly emerged at the studio entrance, gesturing sharply for them to approach. They exchanged smiles. I am waiting, he called out. Please enter. The lighting is ideal, and you are welcome to bring your refreshments. They stood and walked down the path together. A pair of green-and-white butterflies drifted by, and a thrush began singing in the garden pear tree. You are pleased to have met me, Mr. Gray, Lord Henry remarked, observing him. Yes, I am pleased now. I wonder if I shall always feel this way. Always! That is a terrible word. It makes me shiver. Women love using it, ruining every romance by insisting it endure forever. It is also empty. The sole distinction between a whim and a lifelong passion is that the whim persists slightly longer. As they walked into the studio, Dorian Gray touched Lord Henry’s arm. In that case, let our friendship be a whim, he whispered, blushing at his own audacity, before climbing onto the platform to resume his pose. Lord Henry collapsed into a wicker armchair to watch. The rhythmic strokes of the brush against the canvas were the only sounds in the quiet, save for Hallward occasionally stepping back to study his progress. Dust motes danced like gold in the slanted light pouring through the doorway. The thick fragrance of roses seemed to hang over the room. After fifteen minutes, Hallward ceased painting, staring intently at Dorian and then at the portrait, chewing his brush and frowning. It is finished, he finally announced, leaning down to sign his name in bright red letters in the corner. Lord Henry approached to inspect the work. It was truly a remarkable piece of art and an excellent likeness. My dear fellow, I offer my sincere congratulations, he said. It is the greatest portrait of our time. Mr. Gray, come see yourself. The young man started as if roused from a dream. Is it truly done? he asked, stepping down. Quite finished, the painter replied. You sat wonderfully today. I am very grateful. That is entirely my doing, Lord Henry interjected. Is it not, Mr. Gray? Dorian did not reply, but walked listlessly toward the painting and turned to face it.

Reading about the luxuries buried with the dead was fascinating. He then turned his focus to embroideries and the tapestries that served as wall decorations in cold northern European rooms. As he studied these, he possessed a unique ability to become completely immersed in his interests, yet he felt a touch of sadness regarding how time eventually ruins all beautiful things. He, however, had avoided that fate. Seasons passed, flowers bloomed and withered, and nights of terror came and went, but he remained the same. No winter touched his face or faded his youthful appearance. How different this was from physical objects. Where had they all gone? He wondered about the golden robe depicting the gods fighting giants, crafted for Athena, or the massive purple canopy Nero stretched over the Roman Colosseum, showing the starry sky and Apollo’s chariot. He longed to see the intricate napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, featuring every imaginable feast dish; the burial cloth of King Chilperic, covered in three hundred golden bees; or the strange robes that angered the Bishop of Pontus, decorated with lions, bears, hunters, and forests. He thought of the coat worn by Charles of Orleans, with song lyrics embroidered on the sleeves in gold thread, each musical note formed by four pearls. He read about Queen Joan of Burgundy’s room at Rheims, decorated with over thirteen hundred embroidered parrots and five hundred butterflies, all featuring royal emblems in gold. Catherine de Medici owned a mourning bed of black velvet covered in crescents and suns, with damask curtains and pearl fringe, displayed in a room hung with black velvet symbols on silver cloth. Even Louis XIV had fifteen-foot-tall gold embroidered figures decorating his private chambers.

He sprang up and gripped her arm harshly. "Point him out. Which one is he? I must see him!" he cried, but the Duke of Berwick’s coach blocked their view, and by the time it passed, the carriage had vanished from the park. "He is gone," Sibyl whispered mournfully. "I wish you had seen him." "I wish I had, for as surely as God exists, if he ever harms you, I will kill him." She stared at him, terrified. He repeated the threat, his words sharp as a blade. Bystanders began to stare, and a nearby woman giggled. "Come away, Jim," she urged. He followed her stubbornly through the throng, satisfied with his declaration. Near the Achilles Statue, she turned to him, her eyes filled with pity that soon turned to a smile. She shook her head. "You are foolish, Jim; just a bad-tempered boy. How can you say such awful things? You are merely jealous and unkind. I wish you would fall in love; it makes people good, and your words were wicked." "I am sixteen," he replied, "and I know my mind. Mother cannot help you; she does not know how to protect you. I regret leaving for Australia. I would abandon the plan if my papers were not already signed." "Do not be so serious, Jim. You sound like the heroes in the melodramas Mother used to act in. I will not fight with you. Seeing him is perfect happiness. You would never harm someone I love, would you?" "Not while you love him, I suppose," he muttered. "I shall love him forever!" she declared. "And he?" "Forever, too!" "He had better." She recoiled, then laughed and touched his arm, dismissing him as a mere boy. At Marble Arch, they boarded an omnibus toward their modest Euston Road home. It was past five, and Jim insisted Sibyl rest before her performance. He preferred to say goodbye without their mother present, as he loathed the scenes she was prone to creating.

Mrs. Otis, who is quite an expert on art after spending several winters in Boston as a girl, tells me these jewels are very valuable. Under these circumstances, Lord Canterville, I am sure you understand that I cannot let my family keep them. Such flashy trinkets, while perhaps fitting for the British aristocracy, are entirely out of place for those raised on the strict, timeless principles of republican simplicity. Virginia would very much like to keep the box as a keepsake of your unfortunate ancestor. Since it is quite old and damaged, I hope you will agree. I am surprised my daughter feels any sympathy for medieval customs, though I suppose it is because she was born in a London suburb shortly after her mother returned from a trip to Athens. Lord Canterville listened seriously, tugging at his grey moustache to hide a smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly and said, My dear sir, your daughter did my ancestor, Sir Simon, a great service, and my family owes her a debt of gratitude for her courage. The jewels are hers. If I were heartless enough to take them, I suspect the old ghost would rise from his grave within two weeks to make my life miserable. These items are not legal heirlooms, as they were never mentioned in a will and their existence was unknown. I have no more claim to them than your butler does. When Virginia grows up, I am sure she will enjoy wearing them. Besides, you bought the furniture and the ghost together; legally, anything belonging to Sir Simon became yours when you purchased the property, as he was officially dead regardless of his nightly activities in the hallway.

Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest the city is in a state of intense intellectual agitation. Events have occurred there so unexpected, so novel, and so contrary to established beliefs, that I am certain all of Europe is currently in an uproar, with the fields of physics, reason, and astronomy thrown into total disarray. It appears that on a certain day, a large crowd gathered in the Exchange square of Rotterdam for reasons not clearly stated. The weather was unusually warm for the season with little wind, and the people were in good spirits, occasionally cooled by brief showers falling from white clouds scattered across the blue sky. Around noon, however, a noticeable stir rippled through the assembly. A sudden clamor of voices erupted, and instantly, ten thousand faces turned toward the heavens. Ten thousand pipes were removed from ten thousand mouths, and a roar, comparable only to the sound of Niagara Falls, echoed loudly throughout the city. The cause of this commotion soon became clear. Emerging from behind a large cloud into the clear blue sky was a strange, solid object, shaped so whimsically and constructed so oddly that the sturdy citizens below could neither comprehend nor sufficiently admire it. What could it be? What could it possibly mean? No one knew, and no one could guess. Even the mayor, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, had no clue to solve the mystery. Lacking a better course of action, everyone replaced their pipes, tilted their heads to study the phenomenon, puffed, paused, paced about, and grunted significantly before repeating the process. Meanwhile, the object of such curiosity and smoke descended lower toward the city. Within minutes, it was close enough to be clearly identified. It was, without a doubt, a type of balloon, yet surely no such craft had ever been seen in Rotterdam before.

By eight o’clock, I had reached seventeen miles above the earth. It was clear my ascent was accelerating, even without dropping more ballast. My head and ears throbbed with sharp, recurring pain, and my nose bled occasionally, though I felt better than expected. Breathing became increasingly difficult, with each breath causing my chest to spasm. I prepared my condensing equipment for use. The view below was stunning. To the west, north, and south, a vast, calm ocean stretched out, turning a deep blue and appearing slightly curved. Far to the east, I could see Great Britain, the coasts of France and Spain, and part of Africa. Human cities and buildings had vanished entirely. Gibraltar looked like a tiny speck, and the Mediterranean, filled with islands like stars in the sky, stretched until it seemed to pour over the horizon’s edge, making me strain to hear the sound of a great waterfall. Above, the sky was pitch black, and the stars shone brightly. The pigeons were suffering, so I decided to release them. I placed a gray-mottled bird on the edge of the basket. It looked around anxiously, fluttering and cooing, but refused to leave. When I tossed it a few yards away, it did not fly down as I expected. Instead, it struggled frantically to return, crying out shrilly. It managed to land back on the rim, but immediately collapsed and died inside the basket.

Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay, was finally brought to trial. The judges wore feathered hats, but the rough red caps and tricolor badges of the revolutionaries were everywhere else. Looking at the jury and the rowdy crowd, Darnay felt as if the world had turned upside down, with criminals judging honest men. The city’s most brutal citizens dominated the room, shouting their opinions and cheering for a conviction without restraint. Many men carried weapons, while some women held knives or daggers. Others ate, drank, or knitted as they watched. One woman, knitting steadily, sat near a man Darnay recognized as Defarge. She whispered to her husband, yet neither of them ever looked at Darnay. They stared only at the jury, waiting with grim focus. Doctor Manette sat quietly below the President, dressed in his usual clothes, appearing alongside Mr. Lorry as one of the few people not wearing the coarse revolutionary uniform. The prosecutor accused Darnay of being an emigrant, a crime punishable by death under the Republic’s new laws. It did not matter that the law was passed after he had returned to France; he was there, and they wanted his head. The crowd screamed for his execution, calling him an enemy of the Republic. The President rang his bell for order and asked if Darnay had lived in England for many years. Darnay admitted he had. The President then asked if that made him an emigrant. Darnay replied that he hoped not, as he had voluntarily given up his title and status, leaving France to earn his own living in England rather than profiting from the labor of the French people.

They brought in a distinguished-looking older man and a younger companion with his arm in a sling. The crowd roared with laughter, but I saw nothing funny, and I doubted the duke and king would either. I expected them to turn pale, yet they remained unfazed. The duke acted blissfully unaware, while the king stared down at the newcomers with a sorrowful expression, as if the existence of such frauds pained his very soul. He performed brilliantly. Many prominent citizens gathered around the king to show their support. The older man appeared utterly bewildered. Soon he began to speak, and I immediately noticed his authentic English accent, which differed from the king’s decent imitation. He addressed the crowd, saying: This is an unexpected surprise, and I admit I am ill-prepared to respond, as my brother and I have suffered misfortunes; he has a broken arm, and our luggage was mistakenly left at a town upstream last night. I am Harvey Wilks, brother of Peter, and this is William, who is deaf and mute, and now struggles to communicate with only one hand. We are who we claim to be, and I shall provide proof once our baggage arrives. Until then, we will retire to the hotel. As he and his silent brother departed, the king scoffed, mocking the broken arm as a convenient excuse for a fraud unable to use sign language, and dismissing the lost luggage story as a clever fabrication. He laughed, joined by most of the crowd. Only a few remained serious, including the doctor, a sharp-looking lawyer named Levi Bell who had just arrived from Louisville, and a large, rugged man who listened intently to both the newcomer and the king.

I reasoned backward. If the killers escaped through these windows, they could not have locked them from the inside, yet the police found them secured. Since the windows were locked, they had to be self-locking. I approached the clear window, removed the nail, and tried to lift the sash. It would not budge. I suspected a hidden spring, and finding it confirmed my theory, even if the nails remained a mystery. I pressed the spring but left the sash closed. I replaced the nail and studied it. A killer could close the window, triggering the spring, but they could not have replaced the nail from the outside. The killers must have used the other window. Assuming the springs were identical, there had to be a difference in the nails or how they were fixed. I climbed onto the bed to examine the second window. I found the identical spring behind the headboard. The nail looked just as sturdy and well-fitted as the first. You might think I was stumped, but my logic remained sound. I had followed the trail perfectly, and it led directly to this nail. Despite its appearance, the fact that the trail ended here meant something was wrong. I touched the nail, and its head, along with a small piece of the shank, snapped off in my hand.

“Halt the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Halt the larboard! Advance the starboard! Stop her! Let the outer wheel rotate slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Throw out that headline! Quickly now! Come—release the spring-line—what are you doing? Loop the bight around that stump! Prepare the stage—let it drop! Engines finished, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (testing the gauge-cocks). Tom kept whitewashing, ignoring the steamboat. Ben watched for a moment and remarked: “Hi-Yi! You are in a predicament, aren't you!” Tom offered no reply. He examined his latest stroke with an artist’s gaze, brushed again, and inspected the result. Ben moved closer. Tom craved the apple but remained focused. Ben asked: “Hello, friend, forced to work, are you?” Tom spun around. “Oh, it’s you, Ben! I didn't see you.” “Listen, I am going swimming. Don't you wish you could? But you would rather work, wouldn't you? Of course you would!” Tom studied him briefly. “What do you define as work?” “Well, isn't that work?” Tom continued painting, answering casually: “Maybe it is, maybe it isn't. All I know is that it suits Tom Sawyer.” “Come now, you don't expect me to believe you enjoy it?” The brush kept moving. “Enjoy it? I don't see why I shouldn't. Does a boy get the opportunity to whitewash a fence every day?” This changed Ben’s perspective. He ceased eating his apple. Tom brushed delicately, stepped back to observe, added finishing touches, and critiqued his progress while Ben watched, increasingly fascinated. Finally, Ben asked: “Tom, let me whitewash a little.” Tom hesitated, nearly agreeing, but changed his mind. “No, I don't think that would work, Ben. Aunt Polly is extremely particular about this fence, since it faces the street. If it were the back fence, I wouldn't mind, and neither would she. She is very strict; it must be done perfectly. I doubt one boy in two thousand could handle it properly.” “Really? Is that so? Oh, please, let me try. Just a little—I would let you if you were me, Tom.” “Ben, I would like to, truly, but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she refused; Sid wanted to as well, and she wouldn't allow him either.”

No imagination could capture how magnificent this sight would have been in the dark of night; it would have looked like hell itself. Even in the daylight, my hair stood on end as I stared into the deep, fiery abyss, picturing myself wandering through those strange, glowing caverns. I had narrowly escaped disaster. If I had stayed in the cloud a moment longer—or if I had not decided to drop my ballast to avoid the dampness—I would have certainly perished. These dangers are often overlooked, yet they are the most significant risks of ballooning. By now, however, I had reached such a height that I no longer worried about that. By seven o'clock, my barometer showed I had reached an altitude of nine and a half miles. I began to struggle for air. My head throbbed, and I soon realized the moisture on my cheeks was blood leaking from my ears. My eyes felt painful and seemed to bulge from their sockets, making everything in the balloon look distorted. These symptoms alarmed me. In a moment of poor judgment, I threw out fifteen pounds of ballast. This caused me to rise too quickly into the thin upper atmosphere, nearly killing me. I suffered a violent spasm lasting five minutes, and even afterward, I could only gasp for air while bleeding heavily from my nose, ears, and eyes. The pigeons were clearly distressed, and the cat staggered around the car, mewing piteously with its tongue hanging out as if it had been poisoned. I realized too late how reckless I had been to drop the ballast, and I was terrified, expecting to die within minutes.

Mary never wrote to Bath herself, leaving the tedious task of corresponding with Elizabeth entirely to Anne. Shortly after breakfast, Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick joined them for a final walk around Lyme before the group departed for Uppercross at one o'clock. Once they reached the street, Captain Benwick gravitated toward Anne. They continued their previous discussion about Scott and Byron, finding themselves just as unable to agree on the poets' merits as before, until the group shifted and Captain Harville took his place beside her. Speaking quietly, he told Anne that she had done a kindness by drawing Benwick out of his shell. He worried about his friend's isolation but noted they could not bear to be apart. Anne suggested that time would eventually ease his grief, noting that he had only lost his partner the previous summer. Harville sighed, confirming it was only June. He explained that Benwick did not learn of the tragedy until August, when he returned from the Cape. Harville admitted he could not bring himself to deliver the news, so Captain Wentworth had taken on the burden. Wentworth traveled day and night to Portsmouth to reach Benwick, staying by his side for a week to help him through the shock. Harville emphasized how much this proved Wentworth's loyalty. Anne agreed wholeheartedly, though her own emotions made it difficult to say much more. Harville, clearly moved by the memory, soon changed the subject to something else.

Should I summon them? Or perhaps Miss Bates? She is closer, and I suspect she understands the group's preferences as well as anyone. We require a broader consensus. Shall I invite Miss Bates to assist us? If you wish, Mrs. Weston replied with some hesitation, provided you believe she will be helpful. You will gain nothing useful from Miss Bates, Emma remarked. She will be entirely overwhelmed with joy and thanks, but she will offer no insight and will likely ignore your inquiries. I see no benefit in consulting her. But she is so entertaining! I truly enjoy her conversation, and I need not invite the entire family. Mr. Weston then arrived, and upon hearing the proposal, he offered his full support. Yes, Frank, go fetch Miss Bates and settle this immediately. She will appreciate the plan, and she is an excellent example of how to overcome obstacles. Bring them both. Both, sir? Can the elderly lady manage? The elderly lady? No, the young lady, of course. I shall consider you quite foolish, Frank, if you return with the aunt but not the niece. I apologize, sir. I did not recall. I shall certainly attempt to persuade them both. He departed at once. Long before he returned with the brisk, neat aunt and her graceful niece, Mrs. Weston, acting as a patient wife, had re-evaluated the hallway and determined the issues were far less significant than she had initially feared. The remaining details, at least in theory, were easily resolved. Minor logistics regarding furniture, lighting, music, and refreshments settled themselves or were left for Mrs. Stokes to manage. Every invitee was expected to attend, and Frank had already requested an extension of his stay at Enscombe, which was sure to be granted. It promised to be a wonderful dance. Miss Bates arrived and heartily agreed that it would be a success. While her advice was unnecessary, her enthusiastic approval was most welcome. Her praise, both broad and specific, was constant and pleasing. For another half-hour, they paced between the rooms, offering suggestions and anticipating the event with shared delight.

Three or four months passed, and it was deep into winter. I had been attending school regularly, learning to read, write, and spell a little. I could recite the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five, but I doubt I could ever learn more, even if I lived forever. I never cared much for math anyway. At first, I hated school, but eventually, I grew used to it. When I felt tired, I would skip class, and the punishment I received the next day actually cheered me up. As time went on, school became easier. I was also getting accustomed to the Widow’s rules, which didn't bother me as much anymore. Living indoors and sleeping in a bed felt restrictive, but before the weather turned cold, I would occasionally sneak out to sleep in the woods for a break. I still preferred my old ways, but I was starting to enjoy the new ones too. The Widow said I was making slow but steady progress and that she was proud of me. One morning at breakfast, I accidentally knocked over the salt shaker. I reached to throw some over my left shoulder to ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson stopped me, scolding me for making a mess. The Widow tried to defend me, but I knew that wouldn't stop the bad luck from coming. I left the house feeling anxious, wondering what kind of trouble was headed my way. Since there was no way to prevent this specific misfortune, I just walked along, feeling gloomy and alert. I went to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the high board fence. There was an inch of fresh snow on the ground, and I noticed someone’s footprints. They had come from the quarry, lingered by the stile, and then walked around the garden fence. It was strange that they hadn't come inside after waiting there so long. I couldn't understand it. It seemed very odd, so I knelt down to examine the tracks more closely.

Back home, we gathered funds through tariffs, and citizens falsely believed foreign importers bore the burden. In reality, the American public paid, with the cost distributed so precisely that a millionaire and a laborer's infant paid the same six dollars. I find that perfectly equitable. Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, with the British Isles holding under a million people. A laborer earned three cents daily, covering his own expenses. Consequently, the government required ninety thousand dollars annually, or roughly two hundred fifty dollars a day. By swapping gold for nickels during the king's healing ceremony, I satisfied everyone while saving four-fifths of the daily budget—a sum equivalent to eight hundred thousand dollars in my own time. I utilized a lesson from my youth: I used to donate buttons to missionaries instead of coins. The buttons satisfied the ignorant, while the coins served me better; everyone benefited. Marinel processed the patients. He screened them, and those who qualified were sent to the king. A priest recited scripture while the monarch touched the sores. Finally, the patient received a nickel, hung around their neck by the king, and was sent away. You might doubt the efficacy of this, but it worked. Any ritual cures if the patient possesses sufficient faith. Near Astolat, a chapel stands where a goose-girl claimed the Virgin appeared. Despite a frightening painting of the event, thousands of sick and crippled pilgrims visit annually and depart fully restored.

Master Charles Bates, horrified by the brutality of Sikes, began to contemplate whether a virtuous existence might be superior. Concluding that it was, he abandoned his former life, determined to seek a fresh start elsewhere. Despite enduring significant hardship and struggle, his cheerful temperament and firm resolve eventually led to success; having transitioned from a farmhand and delivery boy, he is currently the most jovial young cattleman in Northamptonshire. Now, the hand writing these lines hesitates, nearing the end of its labor, wishing to extend the narrative a while longer. I desire to remain with those I have accompanied for so long, sharing in their joy by describing it. I would depict Rose Maylie in the full radiance of her youth, casting a gentle, warming light upon all who walked beside her. I would portray her as the heart of every gathering, following her through sunlit fields and listening to her soft voice during evening strolls. I would observe her charitable deeds and her diligent care for her home, illustrating the deep affection between her and her late sister’s child as they fondly remembered those they had lost. I would gather those happy children around her once more, listening to their laughter and recalling the sympathetic tears in her blue eyes. Every smile and nuance of her character, I would gladly preserve. How Mr. Brownlow educated his adopted son, growing ever more fond of him as his character blossomed into the man he hoped for, and how he recognized echoes of his old friend in the boy—stirring both sad and comforting memories—or how the two orphans, tempered by hardship, practiced mercy and gratitude, are stories that need not be recounted.

We visited your home, the first man stated, but missing you there and hearing you had walked this way, we followed to catch you. Please step into the carriage. Their demeanor was commanding, and they positioned themselves to block my path to the door. They carried weapons; I did not. Gentlemen, I replied, forgive me, but I typically ask who seeks my help and what the situation entails. The second man answered, Doctor, your clients are of high standing. Regarding the case, our faith in your expertise convinces us you will determine the details better than we could explain. Enough. Please enter the carriage. I had no choice but to obey and climbed in silently. Both men followed, the last one pulling up the steps. The carriage turned and resumed its pace. I recount this dialogue precisely as it happened, word for word. I describe events exactly as they occurred, keeping my focus steady. Where I insert these breaks, I am pausing to conceal my notes. The carriage exited the city, passed the North Barrier, and reached the country road. About two miles from the barrier—a distance I calculated later—it left the main route and stopped at a secluded house. We all stepped out and walked along a damp garden path past an overflowing, neglected fountain to the entrance. The door did not open instantly when the bell rang, and one of my escorts struck the servant who answered across the face with his heavy riding glove. This violence did not surprise me, as I had often seen commoners treated worse than animals. However, the second man, also irritated, struck the servant in the same fashion. Their identical expressions and movements revealed they were twin brothers. From the moment we arrived at the locked outer gate, which they had unlocked and secured behind us, I had heard cries coming from an upstairs room.

The little man possessed a disproportionately broad frame, giving his figure a comical roundness. His feet were hidden, though a suspicious, horny substance occasionally poked through a tear in the bottom of his hat. His hands were massive, his hair gray and tied in a queue. His nose was long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes were sharp and brilliant; his cheeks and chin were wrinkled, puffy, and double. Remarkably, he had no visible ears. He wore a loose sky-blue satin coat with matching breeches buckled at the knees, a bright yellow vest, and a white taffeta cap worn jauntily. A large, blood-red silk handkerchief was tied in a flamboyant bow around his throat. Upon descending to about one hundred feet above the ground, the man grew suddenly anxious and reluctant to land. He struggled to toss sand from a canvas bag, causing his craft to hover. Agitated, he pulled a heavy leather pocketbook from his coat, examined it with surprise, and removed a large letter sealed with red wax and tied with tape. He dropped it at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. As the official bent to retrieve it, the aeronaut, eager to leave, dumped six full bags of ballast to gain altitude. They struck the burgomaster, rolling him over twenty-one times before the entire city. Naturally, Underduk would not let such an insult go unpunished.

Everyone lives like that, Huck. Tom, it makes no difference. I am not everyone, and I cannot stand it. Being tied down is miserable. Food comes too easily, so I have no appetite for it. I have to ask permission to go fishing or swimming; I have to ask to do everything. I had to speak so politely that it was no comfort at all. I had to go up to the attic and curse just to feel like myself, or I would have died. The widow would not let me smoke, yell, yawn, stretch, or scratch in front of people. And she prayed constantly! I have never seen such a woman. I had to leave, Tom; I just had to. Besides, school is starting, and I would have been forced to go. I would not stand for that. Look, Tom, being rich is not what people claim. It is just constant worry and sweat, and wishing you were dead. These clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I am never giving them up. I would never have gotten into this mess if not for that money. Take my share along with yours, give me a dime now and then—not often, because I do not care for things unless they are hard to get—and you go convince the widow to let me be. Oh, Huck, you know I cannot do that. It is not fair, and if you try it a little longer, you will grow to like it. Like it? Yes, the way I would like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I will not be rich, and I will not live in those suffocating houses. I like the woods, the river, and these barrels, and I am sticking to them. Just when we had guns, a cave, and everything ready to start robbing, this foolishness has to ruin it all! Tom saw his chance. Look, Huck, being rich will not stop me from becoming a robber. Really? Are you serious, Tom? As serious as I am sitting here. But Huck, we cannot let you into the gang if you are not respectable. Huck’s joy vanished. You cannot let me in, Tom?

Forget my hat, I want Virginia! the young Duke laughed as they galloped toward the station. Mr. Otis asked the station-master if anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen, but received no information. The official promised to alert the line and keep a watch. After buying the Duke a new hat from a shopkeeper closing for the night, Mr. Otis rode to Bexley, a village four miles away known for its gypsy encampments. They woke the local policeman, but he knew nothing. After searching the common, they returned to the Chase by eleven, exhausted and devastated. Washington and the twins waited at the gate with lanterns, but there was no sign of Virginia. The gypsies had been found in Brockley meadows, but she was not with them; they explained they had simply miscalculated the date of the Chorton Fair. They were genuinely distressed by her disappearance, grateful for the permission to camp on the estate, and four of them remained to assist in the search. The pond had been dragged and the grounds scoured to no avail. It was clear she was lost for the night. Mr. Otis and the boys walked to the house in despair, followed by the groom. Inside, the servants were terrified, and Mrs. Otis lay on the library sofa, hysterical with anxiety, while the housekeeper tended to her. Mr. Otis insisted she eat and ordered supper for everyone. It was a somber meal; even the twins were uncharacteristically quiet. Afterward, despite the Duke’s protests, Mr. Otis sent everyone to bed, promising to contact Scotland Yard for detectives in the morning.

She was discovered dead in her bed the next morning, seemingly having passed without pain. Sir Mathew Reid was summoned immediately, but nothing could be done, and her funeral was scheduled for the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. Shortly before her death, she had drafted a will leaving Lord Arthur her Curzon Street home, furniture, and personal belongings, excluding her miniatures for Lady Margaret Rufford and an amethyst necklace for Sybil Merton. The estate held little value, yet her solicitor, Mr. Mansfield, urged Lord Arthur to return promptly to settle numerous unpaid bills, as Lady Clementina had never maintained organized records. Lord Arthur was deeply moved by her generosity and blamed Mr. Podgers for the circumstances. Still, his devotion to Sybil eclipsed all else, and the knowledge that he had fulfilled his duty brought him peace. He felt entirely content upon arriving at Charing Cross. The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise that nothing would ever separate them again, and they set their wedding date for June 7th. Life appeared bright once more, and his former joy returned. One day, while clearing out the Curzon Street house with the solicitor and Sybil—burning old letters and sorting through drawers—Sybil suddenly cried out in delight. "What have you found?" Lord Arthur asked with a smile. "This lovely little silver candy box, Arthur. Isn't it quaint? Please let me have it! I know amethysts won't suit me until I'm eighty." It was the container that had held the aconitine. Lord Arthur started, his face flushing. He had nearly forgotten his actions, and it felt like a strange coincidence that Sybil, the very reason for his past torment, should be the one to remind him. "Of course you can have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself." "Oh, thank you! And may I have the candy inside, too? I had no idea Lady Clementina liked sweets; I thought she was far too intellectual." Lord Arthur turned deathly pale as a horrific realization struck him.

Get up! What are you doing? I opened my eyes, disoriented. It was past sunrise, and I had been fast asleep. Dad stood over me, looking miserable and ill. He asked, What are you doing with this gun? Realizing he had no memory of his actions, I replied, Someone tried to break in, so I was waiting for him. Why didn't you wake me? I tried, but I couldn't move you. Fine. Stop talking and go check the fishing lines for breakfast. I will be there shortly. He unlocked the door, and I headed up the riverbank. I saw branches and bark floating by, signaling the river was rising. I thought about how much fun I would have if I were in town; the June rise always brought good luck, as logs and firewood drifted down for me to catch and sell. I walked along the bank, watching for Dad and any debris. Suddenly, a beautiful canoe, about thirteen feet long, drifted by. I dove into the water, clothes and all, and swam toward it. I expected someone to be hiding inside to play a trick, but it was empty. I paddled it to shore. I thought Dad would be pleased, as it was worth ten dollars. However, he was nowhere to be seen. As I hid the boat in a vine-covered creek, I had a new idea: I would keep it hidden and use it to escape fifty miles downriver instead of traveling on foot. I worked quickly, constantly fearing Dad would appear. Once the canoe was concealed, I peeked through the willows and saw him down the path, aiming his gun at a bird.

They were her existence, more precious than any sanctuary of love or anything else on earth. The boys received news of our departure with youthful joy, while Clara inquired if we were headed to Athens. I answered that it was possible, and her face lit up with delight. There, she would finally see her parents' grave and the lands steeped in her father’s renown. She had long contemplated these places in quiet, a preoccupation that had replaced her childhood playfulness with a grave, ambitious spirit. We had many humble friends we could not abandon, including the spirited horse Lord Raymond had gifted his daughter, Alfred’s dog, and an aging pet eagle. Yet, listing these favorites brought sorrow for our greater losses and the many things we were forced to leave behind. Idris wept, while Alfred and Evelyn insisted on packing rose bushes and carved vases, lamenting that we could not bring the castle, the forest, and all our familiar treasures. I told the foolish ones that we had already lost far greater things and were leaving these behind to protect what truly mattered. I urged them to focus on our purpose to stem their regret for such trifles. The children were soon distracted by thoughts of future fun, but Idris had vanished. She had fled to the park to hide her distress, and I found her embracing an old oak tree, sobbing uncontrollably. My heart broke to see her so consumed by grief. I pulled her close, and as she felt my embrace, she remembered what she still possessed. She thanked me for my kindness, admitting that while her heart was torn by sorrow, she remained happy because I and our children were still by her side.

There was plenty of cold water to finish their meal. Soon, Becky suggested they keep moving, but Tom hesitated. Becky, can you handle some bad news? he asked. Her face went pale, but she nodded. We have to stay here near the water, Tom explained. That little piece of candle is all we have left. Becky began to cry and wail. Tom tried to comfort her, but it did little good. Eventually, Becky asked if people would search for them. Tom agreed they certainly would. She wondered if they were looking now, and Tom hoped they were. When would they realize we are gone? she asked. Tom guessed it would be when they returned to the boat. Becky worried it might be dark by then, but Tom assured her that her mother would notice her absence as soon as she got home. Seeing the fear on her face, Tom realized his mistake; Becky was not supposed to be home that night. They fell silent, both realizing that it might be Sunday morning before anyone noticed Becky was missing. They watched their candle burn down until the flame flickered and died, leaving them in total darkness. They eventually fell into a deep, exhausted sleep. When they woke, they had no idea how much time had passed. Tom guessed it could be Sunday or even Monday. He tried to talk to Becky, but she was too hopeless to respond. Tom suggested they shout for help, but the terrifying echoes in the dark cave made him stop. As time dragged on, hunger returned. They shared the last of Tom’s cake, but it only made them hungrier.

While events unfolded at the rural workhouse, Fagin remained in his familiar hideout—the same place from which the girl had taken Oliver—meditating before a dim, smoky fire. He rested a pair of bellows on his knees, having seemingly tried to stir the flames, but he had lapsed into a profound reverie, staring blankly at the iron grate with his arms crossed and his chin propped on his thumbs. Behind him, the Artful Dodger, Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling were engrossed in a game of whist, with the Dodger playing dummy against the other two. The Dodger’s face, always sharp, grew even more intense as he scrutinized the game, frequently stealing glances at Mr. Chitling’s hand to guide his own strategy. Because of the chill, the Dodger kept his hat on, as was his habit indoors. He also kept a clay pipe in his mouth, removing it only to sip from a quart pot of gin-and-water placed on the table for everyone. Master Bates also focused on the cards, but being more volatile than his friend, he drank more often and made frequent, inappropriate jokes that disrupted the serious nature of the match. The Dodger occasionally lectured him on his behavior, but Bates merely brushed off the advice with colorful insults or witty retorts that greatly amused Mr. Chitling. Curiously, Chitling and his partner always lost, yet Bates found this hilarious, laughing loudly after every hand and declaring it the most enjoyable game he had ever played. That is two doubles and the rubber, Chitling remarked gloomily, pulling half-a-crown from his pocket. I have never known anyone like you, Jack; you win at everything.

“Darn it, Tom,” I said, “you could at least tell me. What is a bar sinister?” “Oh, I don’t know. But he has to have one. All the nobility does.” That was just how he was. If he did not feel like explaining something, he would not do it. You could pester him for a week and it would not make a difference. He had the coat of arms figured out, so he started planning a mournful inscription, insisting Jim needed one just like the others. He wrote several on a piece of paper and read them aloud: 1. Here a captive heart broke. 2. Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and friends, spent his sorrowful life. 3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit found rest after thirty-seven years of solitary confinement. 4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV. Tom’s voice shook as he read them, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he could not decide which one Jim should carve into the wall because they were all so good, so he decided Jim should carve them all. Jim complained it would take him a year to scratch all that onto the logs with a nail, and he did not know how to write letters anyway. Tom promised to outline them so Jim only had to follow the lines. Then he said, “Actually, logs will not work; dungeons do not have log walls. We need to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We will get a rock.” Jim argued that a rock was even worse than logs, saying it would take so long to carve that he would never get out. Tom said he would let me help. He then checked on how Jim and I were doing with the pens. It was incredibly tedious, slow work that kept my hands from healing, and we were barely making progress, so Tom said, “I know how to fix this. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the inscriptions, so we can kill two birds with one stone.”

Raymond felt invigorated by his returning health, viewing his role as Athenian general as a position befitting his aspirations. He anticipated the capture of Constantinople as a monumental achievement in history, a feat unparalleled, where a city of such renown and beauty, long held by the Moslems, would be liberated from oppression and returned to a people celebrated for their intellect and love of freedom. Perdita found comfort in his presence, his affection, and his rising glory, finding every thought and emotion steeped in pure delight. We reached Kishan on July 7th after a journey marked by calm weather. Each morning, we departed before daybreak, observing the shadows vanish as the sun emerged. Our soldiers greeted the dawn with spirited enthusiasm, their music mingling with the songs of birds. At midday, we rested in shaded valleys or mountain woods, lulled to sleep by the sound of babbling brooks. Our evening travels were even more serene; the soldiers played gentle melodies of love and longing, followed by solemn hymns that suited the peaceful twilight. Often, we fell silent to hear the nightingale, watching fireflies flicker while the aziolo’s call promised fair skies. Whether passing through shadowed valleys or crossing mountains that revealed Greece like a living map of silver rivers and towering peaks, we English travelers were captivated by the vibrant landscape, so distinct from the muted tones of our homeland. As we left Macedonia for the flatter plains of Thrace, the scenery grew less dramatic, yet our progress remained engaging. Our vanguard announced our arrival, and the local inhabitants gathered to pay tribute to Lord Raymond.

Each witness compares the sound not to a language they know, but to one they do not. The Frenchman claims it was Spanish, yet admits he would have known the words had he spoken the tongue. The Dutchman insists it was French, though he required an interpreter to testify. The Englishman identifies it as German, despite his ignorance of that language. The Spaniard is certain it was English, relying solely on intonation since he lacks knowledge of the speech. The Italian guesses Russian, having never spoken to a Russian native. A second Frenchman contradicts the first, asserting it was Italian, yet he too relies on intonation, being unfamiliar with that language. How peculiar that voice must have been to baffle citizens from five European nations! You might suggest an Asian or African origin, though such people are rare in Paris. Regardless, consider three facts: one witness calls it harsh rather than shrill, two describe it as quick and uneven, and no one could distinguish any recognizable words. Dupin continued, stating that while he was unsure of my impression, the deductions drawn from these conflicting accounts regarding the voices were enough to form a suspicion that would guide his investigation. He emphasized that these were the only logical conclusions, though he would not yet reveal the nature of his suspicion. He only wanted me to remember that it gave a clear direction to his search of the room. Let us imagine ourselves in that chamber. What should we look for first? The escape route used by the killers. It is safe to say that neither of us believes in the supernatural.

I avoid rushing him, which might lead to a clumsy failure. Instead, I approach from the side, moving slowly so he remains unaware of my intentions. Suddenly, he finds himself on his back, completely bewildered by the turn of events. That was my strategy with brother Dowley. I began speaking in a relaxed, casual manner, as if merely killing time, ensuring no one could possibly predict where my argument would lead. Boys, there are many fascinating aspects to law, custom, and tradition, as well as the evolution of human thought. Written laws fade, but unwritten ones endure. Consider the unwritten law of wages: it dictates a gradual, centuries-long increase. We observe current wages, calculate an average, and compare it to historical data from one or two centuries past. This provides a clear pattern of growth, allowing us to estimate wages from even further back without any written records. We then apply this same logic to the future. I can predict wage levels for centuries to come. What, goodman, what! Yes. In seven hundred years, wages in this region will increase sixfold, with farmhands earning three cents a day and mechanics six. I wish I could die now and be reborn then, exclaimed Smug the wheelwright, his eyes gleaming with greed. And that is not all; they will also receive board, though it will be meager. Two hundred and fifty years later, pay attention, a mechanic's wages will be twenty cents a day, and this is a certainty, not a guess. A collective gasp of amazement filled the room, and Dickon the mason murmured, his eyes and hands lifted in wonder.

Good God! If I had realized for even a second what my monstrous enemy was planning, I would have chosen to live as a lonely exile forever rather than agree to this wretched marriage. The creature had used some dark power to blind me to his true motives; I thought I was only preparing for my own death, but instead, I was rushing toward the destruction of someone far more precious. As our wedding date approached, I felt my heart sink, whether from fear or a dark premonition. I hid my dread behind a fake cheerfulness that pleased my father, though it barely fooled Elizabeth. She looked forward to our marriage with quiet hope, tempered by the fear that our happiness might vanish like a dream, leaving only regret. We made preparations and received guests, all while I hid my inner turmoil and acted as if I were excited for a future that felt like a trap. My father managed to recover some of Elizabeth’s inheritance, including a small property on the shores of Lake Como, where we planned to spend our honeymoon. Meanwhile, I took every precaution to defend myself, carrying a pistol and dagger at all times. This vigilance brought me some peace, and as the day neared, the monster’s threats began to feel like a delusion. Elizabeth seemed happy, and my calm behavior helped settle her nerves. Yet, on the day of our wedding, she was melancholy and filled with a sense of impending doom, perhaps because she was thinking of the terrible secret I had promised to reveal to her the following day.

Yet how could I, a confused village boy, escape the very inconsistency that even the wisest men fall into daily? I told Biddy, It may all be true, but I admire her intensely. I buried my face in my hands, pulling my hair in frustration. I knew my obsession was foolish and misplaced, and I felt my face deserved to be punished for belonging to such an idiot. Biddy, the wisest of girls, stopped trying to reason with me. She placed her rough, hardworking hand over mine, gently pulling them from my hair. She patted my shoulder as I wept into my sleeve, just as I had in the brewery yard, feeling vaguely victimized by everyone. I am glad you trusted me with this, Pip, Biddy said. I am also glad you know you can rely on my discretion. If your first teacher—poor and uneducated as she was—were teaching you now, she knows what lesson she would assign. But it would be difficult, and you have outgrown her, so it is useless. Sighing, Biddy stood up and asked if we should walk further or head home. Biddy, I cried, hugging her and kissing her cheek, I will always tell you everything. Until you become a gentleman, Biddy replied. I will never be one, so that means always, I insisted. You already know everything I know. Ah, Biddy whispered, looking toward the ships. She repeated her question about walking further or going home. I chose to walk, and as the summer afternoon faded into a beautiful evening, we continued on.

No raising him by hand then. Not at all! Joe offered me more gravy, but I was afraid to accept. He was a great burden to you, ma'am, Mrs. Hubble said, sympathizing with my sister. Burden? my sister repeated. She then listed every illness I had caused, every sleepless night I had forced on her, every fall I had taken, and every time she had wished me dead only for me to stubbornly survive. I think the Romans must have annoyed each other with their noses, which perhaps made them such a restless people. Regardless, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose irritated me so much during my sister’s lecture that I wanted to pull it until he screamed. Yet, my suffering was nothing compared to the dread I felt when the silence following her speech left everyone staring at me with disgust. Still, Mr. Pumblechook said, steering the conversation back, boiled pork is rich, isn't it? Have some brandy, uncle, my sister offered. It had finally happened. He would realize the brandy was weak, and I would be ruined. I gripped the table leg under the cloth and waited for my fate. My sister brought the stone bottle and poured his drink. The man toyed with his glass, looking at it against the light and prolonging my agony while the others cleared the table. I could not look away. Holding the table leg tightly, I watched him smile, tilt his head back, and swallow the drink. Suddenly, the room erupted in shock as he jumped up, performed a frantic, coughing dance, and bolted out the door. Through the window, I saw him gasping and making hideous faces as if he had lost his mind. I held on tight while my sister and Joe ran to help him.

Her circumstances were truly fraught with unusual hardship. While she burned with a desperate need to uncover the secrets of Oliver’s past, she felt bound to honor the trust placed in her by the wretched woman she had just met. The woman’s demeanor had moved Rose Maylie deeply; alongside her devotion to her young ward, she felt a sincere, fervent desire to guide the outcast toward redemption. They intended to stay in London for only three days before traveling to the coast. It was already midnight on the first day. How could she act within forty-eight hours, or delay their departure without raising questions? Mr. Losberne was accompanying them, but Rose knew his impulsive nature too well. She feared his immediate, fiery reaction toward the person responsible for Oliver’s abduction, and she dared not confide in him without an experienced ally to plead the girl’s case. These same concerns made her wary of telling Mrs. Maylie, who would surely consult the doctor at once. Seeking legal counsel was equally unthinkable for similar reasons. She briefly considered turning to Harry, but the memory of their final parting stopped her. It felt improper to summon him—and as tears filled her eyes, she wondered if he had already moved on and found happiness in her absence. Troubled by these conflicting thoughts, Rose endured a restless, anxious night. After further deliberation the following day, she reached the difficult decision to reach out to Harry. If his return is painful for him, she reasoned, it will be equally difficult for me. Yet he might not come; he could write, or visit without seeking her out, just as he had done before. She set down her pen and turned away, as if the very letter meant to carry her message should not witness her sorrow.

No, that is for tomorrow, and I specifically needed to see Knightley today for that reason. What a sweltering morning! I walked across the fields, which made it even worse. To find him gone! I am not at all pleased. No apology, no message left for me. The housekeeper claimed she knew nothing of my visit. It is very strange, and no one knew where he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, the Abbey Mill, or his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley. Can you explain it? Emma agreed that it was indeed strange and that she had nothing to say in his defense. I cannot imagine, Mrs. Elton said, feeling the slight as a wife should, how he could treat you this way, of all people. My dear Mr. Elton, he must have left a message. Knightley could not be that eccentric; his servants must have forgotten. That is likely the case with the Donwell staff, who are always awkward and careless. I would not have his servant Harry in our house for anything. As for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her; she promised a recipe and never sent it. I met William Larkins near the house, Mr. Elton continued, and he told me I would not find his master, but I did not believe him. William seemed irritable and said he did not know what had come over his master lately, as he could rarely speak to him. I do not care about William’s issues, but it is vital that I see Knightley today, so this hot walk has been a serious inconvenience. Emma decided she should head home immediately. She was likely expected there, and Mr. Knightley might be spared further conflict with Mr. Elton, if not with William Larkins. She was pleased when Miss Fairfax insisted on walking her out, giving her an opportunity she immediately used to speak.

They brought in a distinguished-looking older gentleman and a younger man with his arm in a sling. The crowd cheered and laughed loudly, but I saw nothing funny about it. I expected the duke and the king to look nervous, but they did not. The duke acted perfectly content, while the king looked down at the newcomers with a pained expression, as if the existence of such frauds broke his heart. He played the part perfectly. Many prominent citizens gathered around the king to show their support. The older man looked completely confused. He soon began to speak, and I noticed immediately that he sounded like a genuine Englishman, unlike the king’s imitation. He addressed the crowd, saying, This is an unexpected surprise, and I admit I am unprepared to respond. My brother and I have faced misfortune; he has a broken arm, and our luggage was mistakenly left at a town upriver last night. I am Harvey Wilks, brother of Peter, and this is my brother William, who is deaf and mute and cannot use signs well with only one hand. We are who we claim to be, and I will prove it once our luggage arrives. Until then, we will wait at the hotel. As he and his brother left, the king laughed and mocked them, calling the broken arm and lost luggage convenient excuses for a fraud who had not learned sign language. The king laughed, and most of the crowd joined in. Only a few did not, including the doctor, a sharp-looking lawyer named Levi Bell who had just arrived from the steamboat, and a large, rough man who had been listening intently to both sides.

The doctor was a kind, elderly man. I woke him up and explained that my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday. I told him my brother accidentally shot himself in the leg with his gun while dreaming, and we needed him to treat the wound secretly so we could surprise our family back home that evening. When he asked who our family was, I told him the Phelpses. He asked again how the accident happened, and I repeated that it was a strange dream. He grabbed his lantern and medical bag, but he hesitated when he saw my canoe, worried it was too small for two people. I quickly claimed it had carried the three of us—my brother, myself, and the guns—without trouble. He remained skeptical and looked for a larger boat, but since all others were locked, he took mine. He told me to wait or go home, but I insisted on staying. I gave him directions to the raft and he left. I worried that if the injury took days to heal, he might reveal our secret. I decided that if he had to return to the raft, I would follow him, tie him up if necessary, and keep him until my brother was ready to leave, at which point we would pay him and let him go. I fell asleep in a pile of lumber, and when I woke, the sun was high. I rushed to the doctor’s house, but was told he had left during the night and had not yet returned.

During his brief visit, Emma had barely seen him, yet it was enough to notice he had not improved; he now carried an air of irritation and arrogance. She wondered how she had ever found him charming. Seeing him was so unpleasant that, unless she viewed it as a moral lesson in humility, she would have preferred never to see him again. She wished him well, but he caused her distress, and she would be happiest knowing he was far away. His upcoming marriage would at least make his presence in Highbury easier to bear. A Mrs. Elton would provide a reason to change their social interactions, allowing their former intimacy to fade naturally. Emma gave little thought to the woman herself. She was likely good enough for Mr. Elton and Highbury, though probably plain compared to Harriet. Emma was confident that, despite Mr. Elton’s earlier arrogance regarding Harriet, he had not married into a superior family. Aside from her ten thousand pounds, Miss Hawkins seemed no better than Harriet. She had no notable family name or connections. Her father was a merchant from Bristol, though his modest wealth suggested his business was equally unremarkable. She had spent time in Bath, but her home was in Bristol with an uncle who worked in the legal field—likely a low-level clerk. The height of her family's prestige rested on her older sister, who had married a man near Bristol wealthy enough to own two carriages. That was the extent of Miss Hawkins's social standing.

April 12th. The balloon shifted its course, a change I had anticipated and which brought me immense relief. After reaching the twentieth parallel south, it veered sharply eastward, maintaining a path aligned with the lunar ellipse. This maneuver caused a noticeable, persistent swaying of the car that lasted for several hours. April 13th. The loud, crackling noise from the tenth returned, causing me great alarm. I pondered its cause without success. The earth’s apparent size has shrunk significantly, now spanning an angle of just over twenty-five degrees. The moon is hidden directly above me. I remain on the elliptical path but have made little eastward progress. April 14th. The earth is shrinking rapidly. I am convinced the balloon is traveling along the line of apsides toward the perigee, heading directly for the moon’s closest point to earth. The moon remains obscured overhead. I have spent considerable effort condensing the atmosphere. April 15th. The earth’s continents and seas are no longer distinguishable. Around noon, I heard that terrifying sound for the third time. It grew in intensity until the car shook violently. A massive, flaming object roared past me like thunder. Once my shock faded, I concluded it was a volcanic fragment ejected from the moon—likely the same type of substance known on earth as a meteoric stone. April 16th. Looking through the side windows, I was delighted to see the edges of the moon’s disk finally emerging from behind the balloon’s massive frame.

I rushed to her, cradling her in my arms while showering her with affection and pleading, "Speak to me, dear, what is wrong?" Her head slumped against my chest as she whispered barely audibly, "Hello-Central!" I yelled to Clarence to summon the king's homeopath immediately. Within moments, I was at the child's bedside while Sandy sent servants scurrying throughout the palace. I recognized the ailment instantly: membranous croup. I leaned in and murmured, "Wake up, sweetheart. Hello-Central." She opened her eyes slowly and managed to say, "Papa." That brought me relief; she was still fighting. I ordered sulfur treatments and prepared the croup-kettle myself, as I never wait for physicians when my family is ill. I was experienced in nursing them, having held this little one for much of her life, often soothing her tears when even her mother could not. Sir Launcelot, dressed in his finest armor, marched through the hall toward the stock-board. As president, he occupied the Siege Perilous, which he had purchased from Sir Galahad for the Knights of the Round Table to conduct their business. Though he was a bear currently cornering a market and preparing to squeeze the shorts, he abandoned his financial schemes the moment he saw his favorite was unwell.
