He tossed his helmet aside and immediately began tending the alcohol lamp for the croup-kettle. Sandy had already constructed a blanket canopy over the crib. Launcelot and I added unslaked lime, carbolic acid, and a dash of lactic acid to the kettle, filled it with water, and directed the steam spout under the canopy. With everything prepared, we sat on either side of the crib to begin our vigil.

They were her life, more precious than any sanctuary of love or anything else on earth. The boys were delighted by the news of our departure, and Clara asked if we were moving to Athens. When I told her it was possible, her face lit up with joy. She longed to see her parents' tomb and the land where her father had earned his fame. She had spent so much time quietly thinking about those places, and those memories had turned her childhood playfulness into a serious, restless ambition. We had many humble friends we could not leave behind, including the spirited horse Lord Raymond had given his daughter, Alfred’s dog, and an aging pet eagle. Yet, making this list of favorites only reminded us of the heavy losses we had suffered and the many things we were forced to abandon. Idris wept, while Alfred and Evelyn brought me a favorite rose tree and a carved marble vase, insisting they must come with us and lamenting that we could not take the entire castle, forest, and wildlife. I told them they were being foolish, as we had already lost far greater treasures and were leaving these behind to protect what truly mattered. I urged them to focus on our goal, which would help ease their regret over such trifles. The children were easily distracted and soon returned to their excitement. Idris, however, had disappeared to hide her sadness. I found her in the park, clinging to an old oak tree and sobbing uncontrollably. It broke my heart to see her in such pain. I pulled her close, and as she felt my arms around her, she remembered what she still had. She thanked me for not scolding her, admitting that while her grief was sharp, she remained happy because I and our children were still by her side, unlike so many others who had lost their entire families.

Had she realized her sister intended to ruin such prospects, her reaction would have been intense, understood only by her mother. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was the only comfort for her mother, who knew her husband would never visit. They remained unaware of the truth, and their excitement lasted until the day Lydia departed. Elizabeth was seeing Mr. Wickham for the final time. Having spent much time with him recently, her former feelings had faded. She now found his once-charming gentleness affected and tiresome. His attempt to renew his past attentions only annoyed her. She felt insulted that he assumed his renewed interest would flatter her vanity regardless of his previous neglect. On the regiment’s final day in Meryton, Wickham dined at Longbourn. Elizabeth, eager to distance herself, mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had spent three weeks at Rosings, asking if he knew the Colonel. Wickham looked startled and uneasy, but quickly regained his composure, calling the Colonel a gentleman and asking for her opinion. Elizabeth praised him warmly. Wickham then asked, with feigned indifference, how long he had stayed. When she confirmed it was nearly three weeks and that they met daily, he remarked on the difference between the cousins. Elizabeth noted that Mr. Darcy improved upon acquaintance. Wickham looked visibly disturbed, then asked with a forced, lighthearted tone if it was his manner that improved.

There was a strangeness in all this that captivated me. He seemed to have awakened from a long, dreamlike slumber, feeling much like a character from an ancient legend. Diana was gone, his friends were either changed or dead, and upon his return, I was the only person left for him to love. How precious the landscapes of Loch Lomond became with such a companion. I explored every island, waterfall, and shaded path with my father, whose conversation expanded my perspective. I felt reborn, as if transported from a confined existence into a limitless universe. Previously, my life had been a small, quiet stream destined to vanish unnoticed; now, it felt like a vibrant river winding through a beautiful landscape. I did not yet foresee the desert ahead, the jagged rocks that would tear at its current, or the distorted reflections that awaited. Life was brilliant, and I began to hope—yet what brings more bitter despair than hope destroyed? Is it not strange how quickly grief follows such divine happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, only to find bitterness at the bottom. I had no concept that love could cause such misery, yet I was forced to learn this lesson in a way few ever must. I still mourn those few months of paradise; I broke no rules, yet I was ruthlessly cast out. My companion faltered, and I was pulled down with him. But I digress; let sorrow wait, for I may still speak of happiness at this point in my story. Three months of this delightful connection passed before my aunt fell ill. I spent a month nursing her, but her condition was terminal. Her death left me inconsolable for a time. Death is so terrifying to the living; the bonds of habit are so powerful that their breaking inevitably agonizes the heart, even when affection is not the primary link.

Biddy wept, and the darkening garden, the lane, and the emerging stars blurred in my own vision. Nothing was ever discovered, Biddy? Nothing. Do you know what became of Orlick? Based on his clothing, I suspect he works in the quarries. You have seen him, then? Why are you staring at that dark tree? I saw him there the night she died. That was not the last time, was it? No, I have seen him there since we began walking here. It is useless, Biddy said, touching my arm as I moved to run out, you know I would not lie to you; he was only there for a moment and is gone. My indignation flared to learn she was still pursued by him, and I felt a deep hatred. I told her I would spend any amount or effort to drive him from the area. Gradually, she calmed me, speaking of how Joe loved me and never complained—she did not say of me, but I understood—always doing his duty with a strong hand, quiet tongue, and gentle heart. It is hard to praise him enough, I said, and Biddy, we must discuss these things often, as I will be here frequently now. I will not leave poor Joe alone. Biddy said nothing. Biddy, do you hear me? Yes, Mr. Pip. Aside from you calling me Mr. Pip, which seems in poor taste, what do you mean? What do I mean? Biddy asked timidly. Biddy, I said with self-righteous insistence, I must know what you mean by this. By this? Biddy repeated. Do not echo me, I retorted. You never used to echo. Used not! Biddy exclaimed. Oh, Mr. Pip! Used! I decided to drop that point. After another silent walk, I returned to my main concern. Biddy, I said, I mentioned coming here often to see Joe, which you met with silence. Please tell me why. Are you certain you will come to see him often? Biddy asked, stopping in the garden path and looking at me under the stars with clear, honest eyes.

He would never have escaped without my help. Morgan le Fay hated him deeply and would never have shown him mercy. His crime was mostly thoughtless, though; he had simply mentioned her red hair. While true, it was a social blunder, as people of her status are said to have auburn hair. Consider that among these forty-seven prisoners, five had been forgotten entirely. These elderly, frail people could no longer recall their own names or why they were imprisoned. The priests who visited them only taught them to accept their suffering as God's will, and even their records were lost. We only knew they had been locked away for at least thirty-five years. The king and queen viewed them as mere inherited property, like old furniture, and never thought to release them. When I asked the queen why they remained, she was puzzled; the idea of freeing them had never occurred to her. To her, they were simply assets, and people rarely discard property even when it lacks value. I led these human ghosts out into the sunlight, having blindfolded them first to protect their sensitive eyes. They were a tragic sight—skeletal, withered figures who stood as the true legacy of the monarchy and the church.

I regretted hearing Jim say that; it diminished my respect for him. My conscience pricked me so severely that I finally promised myself I would row to shore at dawn and report him. Immediately, I felt relieved and lighthearted, my worries vanished. I kept a sharp lookout for a light, humming to myself until one appeared. Jim shouted, "We are safe, Huck! Jump for joy! That is Cairo at last, I am certain!" I replied, "I will take the canoe to check, Jim. It might not be the place." He eagerly prepared the canoe, placing his coat inside for me to sit on. As I pushed off, he said, "Soon I will be shouting for joy, and I will say it is all because of Huck. I am a free man, and I never could have been without you. Jim will never forget you; you are the best friend I have ever had, and the only one I have now." I was paddling away, desperate to betray him, but his words drained my resolve. I slowed down, no longer certain if I was glad to be leaving. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called out, "There you go, the true Huck; the only white gentleman who ever kept his word to old Jim." I felt sick, yet I told myself I had to go through with it. Just then, a skiff with two armed men approached. They stopped, and I did too. One asked, "What is that over there?" "A piece of a raft," I replied. "Are you on it?" "Yes, sir." "Any men on it?" "Only one, sir." "Well, five slaves ran off tonight up the river. Is your man white or black?" I hesitated, unable to speak. I tried to gather the courage to tell the truth, but I lacked the nerve. Realizing I was failing, I finally said, "He is white." "We will go see for ourselves," the man said. "I wish you would," I answered, "because it is my father on board, and perhaps you could help me tow the raft to the light."

He was attired as Jonas the Graveless, the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn, a role that had famously sparked the Cantervilles' feud with Lord Rufford. It was past two in the morning, and the house seemed silent. While heading to the library to check for the bloodstain, two figures suddenly sprang from the shadows, flailing their arms and shouting 'BOO!' in his ear. Terrified, he bolted for the stairs, only to find Washington Otis waiting with a garden syringe. Cornered, he escaped into an unlit iron stove, crawling through the flues to reach his room, covered in soot and misery. He never ventured out at night again. Despite the twins' efforts to trap him by scattering nutshells, he remained in hiding, his pride deeply injured. Mr. Otis returned to his history of the Democratic Party, Mrs. Otis hosted a successful clam-bake, the boys played American games, and Virginia rode her pony with the visiting Duke of Cheshire. Believing the ghost had departed, Mr. Otis informed Lord Canterville, who expressed his relief. Yet, the ghost remained, though weakened. He was particularly agitated by the presence of the young Duke, whose great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet he could play dice with the spirit, only to be discovered the next day paralyzed and capable of uttering nothing but 'Double Sixes.'

She now wished the situation had never occurred. Convinced he had consumed too much of Mr. Weston’s wine, she expected him to talk nonsense. To keep him in check, she prepared to speak with calm gravity about the weather, but as soon as they passed the gate and reached the carriage, he seized her hand and began making aggressive advances. He declared his feelings, claiming he would be devastated by a refusal while insisting his intense passion must surely move her. He was determined to be accepted immediately. Without hesitation or apology, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s supposed suitor, was professing his love for her. She tried to stop him, but he persisted. Angry, she decided to remain composed, hoping his behavior was merely the result of intoxication. With a tone blending seriousness and playfulness, she replied, "I am astonished, Mr. Elton. You forget yourself; you mistake me for my friend. I will gladly deliver any message to Miss Smith, but please, say no more of this to me." He repeated her words with a feigned, boastful amazement that forced her to respond sharply, "Mr. Elton, this is extraordinary. I can only assume you are not yourself, or you would not speak this way to me or of Harriet. Control yourself, and I will try to forget this." However, Mr. Elton had only drunk enough to boost his spirits, not to cloud his mind. He knew exactly what he was doing. After dismissing her suspicion as insulting and briefly mentioning his respect for Miss Smith—while expressing confusion as to why she was even brought up—he returned to his own feelings and pressed her urgently for a favorable answer.

But no, there was something even more spectacular. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future was clear and shining with incredible brilliance. How his name would echo across the world and make people tremble! How gloriously he would sail the lively seas in his long, low, black-hulled ship, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grim flag flying high! At the height of his fame, he would return to the old village and march into church, tanned and weathered, wearing a black velvet suit, tall boots, a crimson sash, a belt full of pistols, a scarred cutlass at his side, and a plumed hat, while his skull-and-crossbones flag waved. He imagined the thrill of hearing the whispers, “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!” Yes, his path was set. He would run away from home to begin his career the very next morning. He started gathering his supplies, digging under a rotten log with his pocketknife until he hit hollow wood. He recited a solemn incantation: “What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!” He cleared the dirt to reveal a small wooden box. Inside lay a single marble. Tom was stunned, scratching his head in confusion. “Well, that beats everything!” he muttered, tossing the marble away in frustration. He stood there thinking. His superstition, which he and his friends considered foolproof, had failed. The belief was that if you buried a marble with the right words and waited two weeks, all the marbles you had ever lost would gather there. Since it had failed, his entire worldview was shaken. He had heard of it working many times but never failing. It did not occur to him that he had tried this before and simply forgotten where he buried them. After pondering, he concluded that a witch must have interfered and broken the spell.

Their arrival ignited a spark throughout Saint Antoine, quickly igniting faces at every doorway and window. Still, no one pursued them, and silence reigned as they stepped into the wine-shop, despite every gaze fixing upon them. Good day, gentlemen, Monsieur Defarge announced. This seemed to break the collective reserve, prompting a chorus of replies. It is poor weather, gentlemen, Defarge added, shaking his head. At this, the men exchanged glances before lowering their eyes in silence, save for one who rose and departed. My wife, Defarge called out to Madame Defarge, I have journeyed some distance with this road-mender, Jacques. I encountered him by chance a day and a half from Paris. He is a fine fellow, this Jacques. Serve him some wine! A second man stood and left. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender, who tipped his blue cap and drank. He pulled coarse bread from his blouse, eating between sips near the counter. A third man rose and exited. Defarge took a modest drink himself, then waited for the traveler to finish. He ignored the others, and they ignored him, even Madame Defarge, who was busy with her knitting. Have you finished your meal, friend? he eventually asked. Yes, thank you. Then come! You shall see the room I mentioned. It will suit you perfectly. They moved from the shop to the street, through a courtyard, up a steep flight of stairs, and into a garret—the same room where an elderly man once sat hunched over, crafting shoes. The old man was gone, but the three men who had left the shop were waiting. The only connection to the former occupant was the memory of them peering through the wall's cracks. Defarge shut the door and whispered, Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness I, Jacques Four, have brought by appointment.

My father’s surname was Pirrip and my first name was Philip, but as a toddler I could only manage the name Pip. So, I called myself Pip, and that is how everyone knew me. I know my father’s name from his tombstone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the local blacksmith. Since I never met my parents or saw any portraits of them—as they lived long before photography—my early impressions of them came entirely from their graves. The blocky lettering on my father’s stone made me imagine him as a stout, dark man with curly hair. From the inscription regarding my mother, Georgiana, I childishly concluded she was sickly and freckled. Beside their grave stood five small stones for my brothers who died in infancy. I grew up believing they had been born lying on their backs with their hands in their pockets, never having taken them out during their short lives. We lived in the marshlands near the river, about twenty miles from the sea. My first clear realization of the world occurred on a raw, late afternoon. That was when I understood that the nettle-choked field was a graveyard, that my parents and brothers were buried there, and that the dark, flat landscape beyond was the marshes. I saw the river as a leaden line and the distant, howling wind as the sea. I realized the small, shivering boy crying in fear was me. Suddenly, a terrifying voice shouted, "Quiet!" A man jumped up from behind the church porch. "Stay still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!" He was a frightening figure dressed in coarse grey, with a heavy iron shackle locked around his leg.

I haven't mentioned the most important point. What is that, Harry? the boy asked listlessly. The obvious consolation. Stealing someone else's partner when you lose your own. In high society, that always redeems a woman. But honestly, Dorian, Sibyl Vane must have been so different from the women we usually meet. There is something quite beautiful about her death. I am glad to live in an era where such wonders occur. They make the concepts we toy with—romance, passion, and love—feel real. I was terribly cruel to her, you forget that. I suspect women appreciate cruelty, genuine cruelty, above all else. They possess remarkably primitive instincts. We may have emancipated them, but they remain slaves seeking masters. They love being dominated. I am sure you were magnificent. I have never seen you truly furious, but I can imagine how striking you looked. Besides, you said something to me the day before yesterday that I thought was merely fanciful, but now realize is the absolute truth. What was that? You said Sibyl Vane represented every romantic heroine to you—that she was Desdemona one night and Ophelia the next; that if she died as Juliet, she was reborn as Imogen. She will never come to life again, the boy muttered, burying his face in his hands. No, she is finished. She has played her final role. But you must view that lonely death in her cheap dressing-room as a dark, dramatic fragment from a classic tragedy. She never truly lived, so she never truly died. To you, she was always a dream, a phantom drifting through Shakespeare’s plays, making them more beautiful. The moment she touched reality, she ruined it, and it ruined her, so she vanished. Mourn Ophelia if you wish. Grieve for Cordelia. Cry out against heaven for Desdemona. But do not waste tears on Sibyl Vane. She was less real than they were. Silence filled the room as evening deepened. Shadows crept in from the garden like silent, silver-footed ghosts. The colors faded from the room. After a while, Dorian Gray looked up.

At that instant, both our gazes landed on the fragment of parchment, which I initially mistook for paper. It lay partially submerged in the sand, with one edge protruding. Nearby, I noticed the decaying remains of what seemed to be a ship’s longboat. The wreckage appeared ancient, as the structure of the timbers was barely discernible. Jupiter retrieved the parchment, used it to wrap the beetle, and handed it to me. Shortly after, we headed home and encountered Lieutenant G——. I displayed the insect, and he requested to bring it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately tucked it into his waistcoat, leaving behind the parchment I had held throughout his examination. Perhaps he feared I might retract my offer, eager to secure his prize, given his intense passion for natural history. Unknowingly, I must have slipped the parchment into my own pocket. You recall that when I approached the table to sketch the beetle, I found no paper in its usual place. I checked the drawer and my pockets, hoping for a scrap of paper, only to discover the parchment. I recount these details precisely because the sequence of events struck me as significant. You may find me imaginative, but I had already forged a connection. I linked two pieces of a larger puzzle: a boat on the shore and a parchment—not paper—bearing a skull. You might ask where the connection lies. I contend that the skull is the quintessential pirate emblem, flown on their flags during battle. I noted the material was parchment, not paper. Parchment is remarkably durable, nearly indestructible. Trivial matters are seldom recorded on it, as it is less suited for routine writing than paper. This observation implied a deeper significance to the death’s-head. I also noted the shape of the parchment; despite a damaged corner, it was clearly oblong.

I thanked him and apologized. He replied, "Not at all," and continued. "Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and naturally considered a great catch. Her half-brother had regained his wealth, but he quickly squandered it again through debts and reckless behavior. There was intense conflict between them, and it is believed he held a deep grudge against her for influencing their father’s anger. Now, I reach the cruel part of the story—though I must pause, my dear Handel, to note that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a glass." I have no idea why I was trying to force mine into the tumbler, only that I was working with strange determination to make it fit. I thanked him and apologized again, and he cheerfully replied, "Not at all!" before resuming. "A man appeared—perhaps at the races or a public ball—who began courting Miss Havisham. I never met him, as this was twenty-five years ago, but my father described him as a flashy man, well-suited for his schemes. My father insisted he was no gentleman, arguing that true manners must come from the heart. He believed that no amount of polish can hide a person's true nature; in fact, the more you try to cover it, the more obvious it becomes. This man pursued Miss Havisham relentlessly, and she, having shown little interest in anyone before, fell passionately in love with him. She truly idolized him. He manipulated her feelings so effectively that he extracted large sums of money from her. He even convinced her to buy out her brother’s share of the brewery at an inflated price, claiming that as her husband, he needed full control. Your guardian was not involved in her affairs at the time, and she was far too proud and infatuated to listen to anyone else.

I uncovered the embers, and a light breeze quickly fanned them into flame. I used a branch to keep the fire alive when it began to fade. By night, I realized the fire provided both light and warmth, and it improved my food; the scraps left by travelers tasted far better roasted than the raw berries I gathered. I tried cooking other items, finding that while berries were ruined, nuts and roots were much improved. Food eventually became scarce, and I often spent entire days searching for acorns to satisfy my hunger. I decided to leave my current home to find a place where my needs were more easily met. I deeply regretted losing the fire, as I did not know how to recreate it. After much thought, I gave up on trying to restart it, wrapped myself in my cloak, and headed west. After three days of wandering, I reached open country. A heavy snowfall had covered the fields in white, and the cold, damp ground chilled my feet. Around seven in the morning, desperate for food and shelter, I spotted a small shepherd's hut on a hill. I examined the structure with curiosity and entered through the open door. An old man sat by a fire, preparing breakfast. Upon seeing me, he shrieked and fled across the fields with surprising speed for his frail frame. His reaction and flight puzzled me, but I was captivated by the hut. It was dry and protected from the elements, appearing to me as a divine sanctuary after my long suffering.

The two women were thrilled to see their friend, remarking that it had been ages since they last met and repeatedly asking how she had spent her time. They ignored the rest of the family, avoiding Mrs. Bennet, speaking little to Elizabeth, and saying nothing to the others. They soon departed, rising with a suddenness that surprised their brother and hurrying away as if desperate to escape Mrs. Bennet’s politeness. The prospect of the Netherfield ball delighted every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet viewed it as a tribute to her eldest daughter, feeling flattered that Mr. Bingley had extended the invitation personally rather than by card. Jane looked forward to a pleasant evening with her friends and their brother, while Elizabeth anticipated dancing with Mr. Wickham and observing Mr. Darcy’s behavior. Catherine and Lydia were excited simply by the event itself, as any ball was welcome, and even Mary claimed she did not mind attending. She noted that as long as her mornings remained private, she was happy to participate in social engagements, believing recreation was healthy for everyone. Elizabeth was in such high spirits that she asked Mr. Collins if he planned to attend and whether he felt dancing was appropriate. She was surprised to learn he had no objections and feared no criticism from his patrons for participating. He assured her that a ball hosted by a respectable man was perfectly acceptable. He added that he enjoyed dancing and hoped to partner with all his cousins, specifically requesting the first two dances with Elizabeth, hoping Jane would understand his choice was not meant as a slight.

I call upon the spirits of the dead and the agents of vengeance to help me in my mission. Let that cursed monster suffer deeply; let him feel the same despair that now torments me. I began my plea with a solemnity that made me feel as if my murdered friends were listening and approving, but by the end, my rage was so intense that I could barely speak. The silence of the night was broken by a loud, demonic laugh. It echoed through the mountains, and I felt as if hell itself were mocking me. I might have lost my mind and ended my life right then, but I knew my vow had been heard and that I was destined for revenge. The laughter faded, and a familiar, hated voice whispered near my ear, "I am satisfied, you miserable wretch! You have chosen to live, and that is enough for me." I lunged toward the sound, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly, the moon rose, illuminating his distorted figure as he fled with superhuman speed. I chased him, and this has been my life for many months. I followed his trail along the Rhone, but in vain. When I reached the Mediterranean, I saw him board a ship heading for the Black Sea. I followed on the same vessel, yet he still managed to slip away. I have tracked him through the wilderness of Russia and Tartary. Sometimes frightened peasants told me which way he went, and sometimes he left clues himself, fearing that if I lost his trail, I might give up and die. As snow fell, I followed his massive footprints across the plains. To you, who are young and have not yet known true suffering, how can I explain what I have endured? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my pains. I felt cursed, carrying my own personal hell with me. Yet, a sense of goodness still guided my steps, and whenever I felt hopeless, I was miraculously saved from impossible situations. Sometimes, when I was near death from starvation, I would find food waiting for me in the wilderness, giving me the strength to continue.

They know how clever he is; he will be sent away for life. They will make sure the Artful Dodger gets a life sentence. What do you mean by lagging and a lifer? asked Mr. Bolter. Why talk to me like that? Why not speak so I can understand you? Fagin was about to explain that these terms meant transportation for life, but the conversation was interrupted by Master Bates, who entered with his hands in his pockets and a look of mock misery on his face. It is all over, Fagin, Charley said after being introduced to the new companion. What do you mean? They found the man who owns the snuffbox, and others are coming to identify him. The Artful Dodger is definitely being sent away, Master Bates replied. I need a full mourning suit and a hatband to visit him before he leaves. To think of Jack Dawkins—the great Dodger—being sent away for a cheap, two-penny snuffbox! I never thought he would go for anything less than a gold watch and chain. Why didn't he rob a rich man of all his valuables and go out like a gentleman, instead of a common thief with no honor? With this lament for his friend, Master Bates sat down, looking dejected. Why do you say he has no honor? Fagin snapped, glaring at his pupil. Was he not always the best among you? Is there one of you who could match him? Not one, Master Bates replied, his voice thick with regret. Then what are you complaining about? Fagin demanded. Why are you crying? Because it will not be on the record, Charley said, emboldened by his grief. It cannot be in the indictment, and no one will ever know how great he truly was. How will he be remembered in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe he will not be there at all. Oh, what a blow this is! Ha! ha! Fagin laughed, turning to Mr. Bolter while shaking with excitement. See how much pride they take in their profession, my dear.

He never tried again. The boys lay there counting the slow seconds until it felt as though time itself had stopped, and they were relieved when the sun finally began to set. Suddenly, a snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, and gave a grim smile at his partner, whose head was resting on his knees. He nudged him with his foot and said, "You're a great watchman, aren't you? Still, nothing happened." "My, was I asleep?" "A little bit. It's almost time to go. What should we do with the rest of our loot?" "I don't know. Leave it here like we always do, I suppose. No point in carrying six hundred and fifty dollars in silver until we head south." "Fine, but we might need to come back once more." "True, but we should come at night like before; it's safer." "Maybe, but it could be a while before I get my chance at that job. Things happen, and this isn't the best spot. Let's bury it deep." The partner agreed, walked over, and lifted a hearthstone to reveal a jingling bag. He took out some cash for both of them and handed the bag to Joe, who was already digging in the corner with his knife. The boys watching forgot their fear and misery instantly. They watched with wide eyes, amazed by their luck. Six hundred dollars was a fortune! This was treasure hunting at its best, with no guesswork involved. They nudged each other, silently celebrating their decision to stay. Joe’s knife hit something hard. "Hello!" he said. "What is it?" his partner asked. "A rotten board, or maybe a box. Help me out, I’ve broken a hole in it." He reached inside and pulled out a handful of gold coins. The boys above were just as thrilled as the men. Joe’s partner said, "Let's finish this quickly. I saw an old rusty pick in the weeds by the fireplace a moment ago."

He explained that while traveling from home through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke rising from the inn's chimney. Expecting to find fellow travelers, he knocked and was let in. Only Lucy and her mother were there; the mother was bedridden with rheumatism, and as the remaining locals departed one by one, they were left behind. Lucy begged the man to stay until her mother recovered in a week or two so they could leave together, warning that they would otherwise perish. The man refused, insisting he had to rejoin his wife and children among the emigrants. As a final plea, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, which he successfully delivered. Idris read it with deep emotion: Honoured Lady, I hope you remember and pity me, for I have no other hope. Please forgive my confused writing. A month ago, my mother lost the use of her limbs. She is improving and would be ready to travel in a month with the help you promised, but everyone else has abandoned us. Three days ago, I went to Samuel Woods, hoping his family might wait for us, but their house was empty. I have seen no one until this man arrived. What will become of us? I have hidden our situation from my mother. Will you send someone? We will surely perish here. If I moved her now, she would die on the road, and even if she recovered, I have no way to navigate the long journey to the sea, only to find you have already crossed the ocean to France.

Good heavens, the Duchess thought, he is a foot doctor after all. How dreadful. I hope he is a foreigner; that would be slightly better. I must introduce him to you. Introduce him? the Duchess cried. You do not mean he is here? She began searching for her fan and shawl, ready to leave immediately. Of course he is here; I would never host a party without him. He says I have a psychic hand and that if my thumb were shorter, I would be a pessimist living in a convent. Oh, I see, the Duchess said, feeling relieved. He tells fortunes, I suppose? And misfortunes, Lady Windermere replied. Next year, I am in danger by land and sea, so I plan to live in a balloon and pull my dinner up in a basket. It is written on my finger or palm, I forget which. But surely that is tempting fate, Gladys. My dear Duchess, surely fate can resist temptation by now. Everyone should have their palms read monthly to know what to avoid. We do it anyway, but it is pleasant to be warned. If someone does not fetch Mr. Podgers, I shall go myself. Let me go, said a handsome young man standing nearby with an amused smile. Thanks, Lord Arthur, but I fear you would not recognize him. If he is as wonderful as you say, I cannot miss him. Describe him, and I will bring him to you. He does not look like a palm reader. He is not mysterious or romantic. He is a short, stout man with a bald head and gold-rimmed glasses, looking like a mix between a doctor and a lawyer. I am sorry, but it is not my fault. People are annoying. My pianists look like poets, and my poets look like pianists. Last season, I invited a dangerous conspirator who had blown up many people and carried a dagger, yet he arrived looking like a nice clergyman and told jokes all evening.

He bowed and left. The street was empty at that hour; it is a secluded, quiet lane. William Bird, a tailor, testified that he was among those who entered the residence. He is English and has resided in Paris for two years. He was among the first to climb the stairs and heard voices arguing. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman; he recalled hearing 'sacré' and 'mon Dieu.' He also noted sounds of a struggle, like scraping and scuffling. The shrill voice was louder than the gruff one and did not sound English; he suspected it was German, though he does not speak the language, or perhaps it was a woman's. Four witnesses confirmed that the door to Mademoiselle L.'s room was locked from the inside when they arrived. Everything was quiet, with no groans or other sounds. Upon breaking the door open, they found no one. The windows in both rooms were shut and secured from within. The door connecting the rooms was closed but unlocked, while the door to the hallway was locked with the key inside. A small, cluttered room at the top of the passage was found with its door ajar, but a thorough search of the entire house, including the chimneys, revealed nothing. The building had four stories and an attic; the roof trapdoor was nailed shut and had clearly not been opened in years. Estimates of the time between hearing the argument and forcing the door varied from three to five minutes, and the door itself proved difficult to open. Alfonzo Garcio, an undertaker living on the Rue Morgue, testified that he was part of the group but stayed downstairs due to his nervous disposition. He heard the argument and identified the gruff voice as French, but he was certain the shrill voice belonged to an Englishman.

They were her life, more precious than any sacred place or earthly treasure. The boys were thrilled by the news of our departure, and when Clara asked if we were moving to Athens, my affirmative reply made her face glow with joy. She longed to see her parents' tomb and the land defined by her father’s legacy, memories that had long ago replaced her childhood playfulness with a restless, solemn ambition. We had many humble friends to consider: the spirited horse Lord Raymond had gifted his daughter, Alfred’s dog, and an aging pet eagle. Yet, listing these favorites only deepened our sorrow for what we had already lost and what we were forced to abandon. Idris wept, while Alfred and Evelyn begged to bring along rose bushes and marble vases, lamenting that we could not pack the castle, the forest, and the wildlife. I told them they were being foolish, as we were leaving behind mere trifles to protect far greater treasures. I urged them to focus on our hope, which would surely stem the tide of our regret. The children were soon distracted, but Idris had vanished. I found her in the park, clinging to an old oak tree, sobbing uncontrollably. My heart broke to see her in such despair. As I held her and kissed her eyelids, she regained her composure. She thanked me for my kindness, admitting that while her grief was agonizing, she remained happy because I and our children were still by her side, unlike so many others who had lost everything.

So, let's hear the whole story. Well, it happened like this. Miss Watson was always picking on me and treating me poorly, but she insisted she would never sell me down to New Orleans. Still, I noticed a slave trader hanging around the property lately, which made me uneasy. One night, I crept to the door and heard her telling the widow that she intended to sell me for eight hundred dollars. She claimed she did not want to, but the money was too much to resist. The widow tried to talk her out of it, but I did not wait to hear the rest. I left immediately. I hurried down the hill, intending to steal a skiff along the shore, but people were still active, so I hid in an old, dilapidated cooper shop on the bank. I stayed there all night. By six in the morning, boats began passing by, and by eight or nine, everyone was talking about how your father had come to town claiming you were murdered. I heard all the details from the people stopping at the shore. I was truly sorry you were killed, Huck, but I am not anymore. I stayed hidden under the wood shavings all day. I was hungry, but not afraid, because I knew Miss Watson and the widow would be at a camp meeting all day. They assumed I was out with the cattle, so they would not miss me until dark. The other servants would be gone as well. When night fell, I headed up the river road for two miles to where there were no houses. I had decided on my plan. If I kept traveling on foot, the dogs would track me; if I stole a skiff to cross, they would notice it missing and know exactly where to find my trail.

Count Rouvaloff stared at him in disbelief, then realizing he was sincere, wrote an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and passed it across the table. Scotland Yard would pay dearly for this address, he remarked. They will not get it, Lord Arthur laughed. After shaking the Russian’s hand, he hurried downstairs, checked the note, and instructed his driver to head to Soho Square. He dismissed the carriage there and walked down Greek Street until he reached Bayle’s Court. Passing under the archway, he entered a strange dead-end street dominated by a French laundry, where clotheslines crisscrossed the space, fluttering with white linen. He reached the end and knocked on a small green house. After a pause, during which neighbors peered from every window, a rough-looking man opened the door and asked in broken English what he wanted. Lord Arthur presented the paper. The man bowed and led him into a shabby parlor. Moments later, Herr Winckelkopf entered, wearing a wine-stained napkin and holding a fork. Count Rouvaloff recommended me, Lord Arthur said, bowing. I need to discuss business. My name is Robert Smith, and I require an explosive clock. Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur, the cheerful German laughed. Do not be alarmed; it is my job to know everyone. I recall seeing you at Lady Windermere’s. I hope she is well. Would you mind joining me for breakfast? The pâté is excellent, and my friends claim my Rhine wine surpasses what is served at the German Embassy. Before Lord Arthur could recover from the shock of being recognized, he was seated in the back room, sipping fine wine from a monogrammed glass and chatting easily with the notorious conspirator. Explosive clocks, Winckelkopf explained, are difficult to export. Even if they clear customs, the train schedules are so unreliable that they often detonate before reaching their intended target.

I shall submit to you. Your expression confirms you realize I have no other choice. I trust you are sincere. The elderly man kissed her, ushered her into his chamber, and locked the door. He then rushed back to the Doctor, opened the window and partially raised the blind, and, placing a hand on the Doctor’s arm, gazed with him into the courtyard. They looked down upon a crowd of perhaps forty or fifty people. Those occupying the house had admitted them, and they had hurried in to operate the grindstone, which had been positioned there as a secluded and practical location. The workers and their labor were truly terrifying. Two men turned the double-handled grindstone with frantic intensity. As their long hair whipped back, their faces appeared more cruel and grotesque than the most savage warriors. Adorned with fake eyebrows and mustaches, their hideous features were slick with blood and sweat, twisted by howling, and wild with animalistic fervor and exhaustion. As these brutes labored, women offered them wine; between the dripping blood, the spilled wine, and the sparks flying from the stone, the air seemed filled with gore and flame. Every person in the group was stained with blood. Men stripped to the waist, others in tattered clothing, and some wearing stolen lace and silk ribbons—all were covered in the same crimson mark as they jostled to reach the sharpening stone. Hatchets, knives, bayonets, and swords were all coated in red. Some damaged blades were bound to the owners' wrists with blood-soaked rags. As these frenzied individuals snatched their sharpened weapons and rushed into the streets, their eyes burned with the same murderous intensity—a gaze that any civilized observer would have gladly ended with a single shot.

He chose Friday, August 17th, for his debut, dedicating much of the day to reviewing his attire. He eventually settled on a wide, slouched hat adorned with a red plume, a shroud featuring frills at the neck and wrists, and a corroded dagger. As evening approached, a fierce rainstorm erupted, with winds strong enough to rattle every door and window in the ancient manor. It was precisely the sort of weather he favored. His strategy was precise: he would slip into Washington Otis’s chamber, mock him from the bed’s foot, and pierce his own throat three times while accompanied by somber music. He held a particular resentment toward Washington, knowing he was the one who repeatedly scrubbed away the legendary Canterville bloodstain using Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. Once he had reduced the reckless youth to a state of utter dread, he intended to visit the Minister and his wife, placing a cold, damp hand upon Mrs. Otis’s brow while whispering the grim secrets of the grave into her husband’s ear. Regarding young Virginia, he remained undecided. She had never offended him and possessed a gentle, pretty nature. He reasoned that a few mournful groans from her wardrobe would suffice, or perhaps he might claw at her bedcovers with trembling fingers should she remain asleep. As for the twins, he was resolved to discipline them. He planned to sit upon their chests to simulate the suffocating weight of a nightmare. Since their beds were adjacent, he would stand between them as a frigid, green corpse until they were frozen with terror, then discard his shroud to crawl about the room as ‘Dumb Daniel, the Suicide’s Skeleton’—a performance that had proven highly effective in the past and which he deemed as impressive as his renowned ‘Martin the Maniac.’ By half-past ten, he heard the family retiring. He was briefly annoyed by the twins’ boisterous laughter, but by eleven-fifteen, silence reigned. As the clock struck midnight, he emerged. An owl struck the glass, a raven called from the yew, and the wind wailed around the house like a wandering spirit; yet the Otis family slumbered, unaware of their fate, while the American Minister’s rhythmic snoring rose above the tempest.

Reading his letter again made Harriet so sympathetic that Emma had to use firm language to keep her focused. Harriet worried so much about hurting him, and about what his family would think of her, that Emma feared she might have accepted him if he had appeared right then. However, the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She felt down that evening, but Emma understood her gentle regrets, comforting her by talking of their friendship or mentioning Mr. Elton. I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again, Harriet said sadly. Even if you were, I could not bear to part with you, Emma replied. You are far too important to Hartfield to be spared. I would never want to go there anyway, because I am only happy at Hartfield, Harriet said. Later, she wondered if Mrs. Goddard or Miss Nash would be surprised, noting that Miss Nash thought her own sister was well-married to a mere shopkeeper. Emma dismissed this, suggesting that Miss Nash would likely envy Harriet’s prospects. She added that Mr. Elton’s interest was still a secret known only to them. Harriet blushed, pleased by the thought of Mr. Elton, yet she still felt pity for Mr. Martin. Now that he has my letter, she whispered, I wonder if he is unhappy, and if his sisters know. I hope he is not too upset. Let us think of happier things, Emma interrupted. Perhaps Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his family right now, telling them how much more beautiful you are, and finally sharing your name with them.

“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped his temple, signaling his disappointment in Joseph. “My dear young friend,” Mr. Pumblechook said, “you must be starving. Sit down. I have brought chicken, tongue, and other delicacies from the Boar that I hope you will enjoy. But am I truly looking at the boy I once played with during his happy childhood? May I—may I?” This meant he wanted to shake my hand. I agreed, and he shook it fervently before sitting down again. “Here is wine,” he continued. “Let us drink to Fortune, and may she always choose her favorites as wisely as she has today! And yet, I cannot look at you—or drink to you—without again asking, may I—may I?” I gave him permission, and he shook my hand again, drained his glass, and turned it upside down. I followed suit, and the wine went straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook served me the best portions of chicken and tongue, neglecting his own plate. “Ah, poultry! You never imagined, as a fledgling, that you would provide refreshment under this humble roof for someone who—call it a weakness if you like—but may I? May I?” He began doing it without waiting for my consent. I do not know how he avoided cutting himself with my knife. “And your sister,” he added after eating, “who had the honor of raising you by hand! It is sad to think she is no longer capable of appreciating that honor. May—” I saw him preparing to reach for me again and stopped him. “Let us drink to her health,” I said. “Ah!” Mr. Pumblechook cried, leaning back in admiration, “that is how you recognize them, sir! That is how you know the noble-minded, sir!”

One day, while I was occupied with my studies and Mr. Pocket, I received a letter that immediately unsettled me. Although I had never seen the handwriting, I instinctively knew who had sent it. It lacked any formal salutation, simply stating: I am arriving in London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you would meet me. Regardless, Miss Havisham expects it, and I am writing accordingly. She sends her regards. Yours, Estella. Had there been time, I would have ordered new clothes, but I had to settle for what I owned. My appetite disappeared, and I found no peace until the day arrived. Even then, I was more anxious than ever, haunting the coach office in Wood Street long before the coach could have possibly left town. Despite knowing better, I felt I could not leave the office for more than five minutes. I had been waiting for half an hour when Wemmick bumped into me. Hello, Mr. Pip, he said. How are you? I would not have expected to see you here. I explained I was meeting someone arriving by coach and asked after his home and his father. Both are doing well, thank you, Wemmick replied, especially the old man. He is in great spirits and will be eighty-two soon. I am considering firing my cannon eighty-two times, provided the neighbors do not complain and the weapon holds up. But this is not business talk. Where do you think I am headed? To the office? I asked. Something like that, Wemmick said. I am going to Newgate. We are handling a bank robbery case, and after inspecting the scene, I need to speak with our client. Did your client commit the robbery? I asked. Goodness no, Wemmick replied dryly. But he is accused of it. You or I could just as easily be accused of the same thing.

Emma found no reason to change her negative opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her initial assessment proved accurate; every meeting confirmed that the woman was self-important, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and rude. While Mrs. Elton possessed some beauty and minor talents, she lacked the judgment to realize she was not the sophisticated expert she imagined herself to be. She arrived in the country believing she was there to improve the neighborhood, convinced that her own social standing was superior to everyone else's. Mr. Elton appeared just as misguided, seeming not only happy with his wife but genuinely proud of her. He acted as though he had brought a woman to Highbury who surpassed even Emma in quality. Most of their new acquaintances, influenced by Miss Bates’s enthusiasm or simply willing to accept the bride at face value, were easily satisfied. Consequently, praise for Mrs. Elton spread freely, while Emma kept her own counsel, politely describing her as pleasant and well-dressed. Over time, Mrs. Elton’s behavior worsened. Offended by Emma’s lack of interest in a close friendship, she became cold and distant. Although this distance was a relief, the hostility behind it only deepened Emma’s dislike. Furthermore, both Mr. and Mrs. Elton treated Harriet with sneering neglect. Emma hoped this would help Harriet move on, but the couple’s behavior revealed their poor character. It was clear they had shared details of Harriet’s past with each other, likely painting Emma in the worst possible light to soothe Mr. Elton’s ego. As a result, the couple united in their dislike of Emma, frequently mocking her when they had nothing else to discuss. Since they dared not show open disrespect to Emma herself, they vented their spite by treating Harriet with contempt. Meanwhile, Mrs. Elton took an immediate liking to Jane Fairfax. She was not content with merely admiring her; she insisted on acting as a patron, offering unwanted help and friendship. By their third meeting, Emma had already heard all about Mrs. Elton’s self-appointed mission to champion Jane.

Do you visit often? I have not returned since. Neither have I. As the moon ascended, I recalled the serene expression on the ceiling that had vanished, and the firm grip on my hand when I uttered his final earthly words. Estella eventually interrupted our quiet. I frequently intended to return, but various matters hindered me. Poor, sad place. Moonlight caught the silver mist and the tears falling from her eyes. Unaware I noticed, she composed herself and asked if I wondered why the property remained in such disrepair. Yes, Estella. The land is mine. It is the sole thing I have not surrendered. Everything else faded away, but I held onto this. It was the one thing I stubbornly defended during those miserable years. Will it be developed? Finally, yes. I came to bid it farewell before it changes. And you, she asked with gentle concern, do you still reside abroad? Still. And you are doing well, I trust? I labor diligently for a modest living, so yes, I am doing well. I have thought of you often, Estella remarked. Have you? Lately, quite often. There was a long, difficult period when I pushed away the memory of what I discarded before realizing its value. But since my obligations allow it, I have welcomed that memory back. You have always remained in my heart, I replied. We fell silent until she spoke again. I never imagined I would bid you farewell while saying goodbye to this place, Estella said. I am very glad to do so. Glad to separate again? Parting is painful to me; the memory of our last goodbye has always been sorrowful. But you told me, God bless you, God forgive you, she replied earnestly. If you could say that then, you will not hesitate to say it now, when suffering has taught me to understand your heart. I have been bent and broken, but I hope, into a better form.

Mr. Darcy spoke warmly of his sister’s musical skill. I am pleased to hear it, Lady Catherine said, but tell her she cannot expect to excel without frequent practice. I assure you, he replied, she does not need that advice; she practices constantly. So much the better, she continued. I will remind her of it when I write. I often tell young ladies that musical excellence requires constant effort. I have told Miss Bennet repeatedly that she will never play well without more practice. Although Mrs. Collins lacks an instrument, I have often invited her to use the piano in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room at Rosings. She would not be in anyone’s way there. Mr. Darcy, embarrassed by his aunt’s rudeness, remained silent. After coffee, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth of her promise to play, and she sat at the instrument. He pulled a chair close. Lady Catherine listened briefly before resuming her conversation with her other nephew, until he walked away and stood where he could watch Elizabeth play. Noticing him, she paused and said with a playful smile, You intend to intimidate me, Mr. Darcy, by listening so intently, but I will not be frightened, even if your sister plays so well. I am too stubborn to be intimidated; my courage only grows when someone tries to scare me. I will not say you are mistaken, he replied, because you know I have no such intention. I have known you long enough to realize you enjoy expressing opinions you do not actually hold. Elizabeth laughed and told Colonel Fitzwilliam, Your cousin is giving you a poor impression of me and teaching you to doubt my words. It is unfortunate to meet someone so capable of exposing my true character in a place where I hoped to be well-regarded.

When I finally caught Tom alone, I asked what his plan had been for the escape—specifically, what he intended to do if we successfully freed a man who was already legally free. He explained that his original vision was to take Jim downriver on the raft, seeking adventures until we reached the mouth of the river. Then, we would reveal his freedom, return him home in style on a steamboat, compensate him for his time, and arrange a grand celebration with a torchlight procession and a brass band to make him a hero. I decided things turned out well enough as they were. We freed Jim quickly, and once the family realized how much he had helped nurse Tom, they treated him with great kindness, providing him with plenty of food and leisure. In the sickroom, Tom gave Jim forty dollars for his patience as our prisoner. Jim was overjoyed, exclaiming that his earlier signs had proven true and that he knew he would be rich again. Tom then suggested the three of us sneak out soon to get gear and head into the Territory for a few weeks of adventure. I agreed, though I worried I lacked the money for supplies, assuming my father had returned to steal my funds from Judge Thatcher. Tom assured me the money was still there, over six thousand dollars, and that my father had not returned.

Mrs. Clay’s feelings for the young man outweighed her own interests, leading her to abandon her long-term plans to manipulate Sir Walter. However, she is as clever as she is affectionate, and it remains unclear whether his cunning or hers will ultimately prevail. After stopping her from marrying Sir Walter, he might eventually be charmed into marrying her himself. Sir Walter and Elizabeth were certainly shocked and embarrassed by her departure and by the realization that they had been deceived. While they could seek comfort from their wealthy cousins, they had to accept that flattering others without receiving any admiration in return was a hollow experience. Anne, confident that Lady Russell had come to appreciate Captain Wentworth, felt only one regret: she had no family to offer him that a sensible man would value. She felt this inferiority deeply. The difference in their wealth did not bother her, but having no respectable, harmonious family to welcome him—especially when his own siblings had been so warm—caused her genuine pain. She had only two friends to introduce to him: Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. He was happy to accept both. He could now sincerely value Lady Russell, and while he did not agree with her past interference, he was willing to praise her in other ways. Mrs. Smith, meanwhile, had earned his lasting favor. Her recent kindness to Anne was enough to secure their friendship, and their marriage gained Anne two friends instead of losing one. Mrs. Smith was their first visitor once they settled down. Captain Wentworth fully repaid her kindness by helping her recover her husband’s property in the West Indies, acting with the energy and determination of a true friend to resolve her legal difficulties.

Well, everyone lives that way, Huck. Tom, it makes no difference. I am not everyone, and I cannot stand it. It is terrible to be so restricted. Food comes too easily, and I have no appetite for it. I have to ask permission to go fishing or swimming; I have to ask to do everything. I had to speak so politely that it was no comfort at all. I had to go to the attic and vent my frustration every day just to feel like myself, or I would have died. The widow would not let me smoke, yell, yawn, stretch, or scratch in front of people. She prayed all the time! I had to leave, Tom; I just had to. Besides, school is starting, and I would have had to go. I would not stand for that. Look, being rich is not what people claim. It is just constant worry and effort, making you wish you were dead. These clothes and this barrel suit me, and I am never giving them up. I would never have had this trouble if not for that money. Take my share along with yours, give me a dime now and then, and please convince the widow to let me go. Oh, Huck, you know I cannot do that. It is not fair, and if you try it a little longer, you will learn to like it. Like it? Yes, the way I would like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I will not be rich, and I will not live in those suffocating houses. I like the woods, the river, and my barrel, and I am sticking to them. Just when we had guns, a cave, and everything ready for robbing, this nonsense has to ruin it all! Tom saw his chance. Look, Huck, being rich will not stop me from becoming a robber. Really? Are you serious, Tom? As serious as I am sitting here. But Huck, we cannot let you into the gang if you are not respectable. Huck’s joy vanished. You cannot let me in, Tom?

With a racing heart and an unexplained dread, I dismissed my servant, locked the door, and sat to read my father’s letter. It read as follows: My dear child, I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and exposed your innocent heart to the language of monstrous, illicit passion. I must atone for these crimes and ensure my punishment matches my guilt. You are surely prepared for what I must announce: we must separate forever. I am depriving you of your parent and only friend, casting you out into the world without shelter. Your hopes are ruined, and the peace of your pure mind is destroyed. Memory will haunt you with images of my guilt and the pain of betrayed love. Yet I, who have brought this misery upon you, who have remorselessly branded my own child with agony and replaced your beauty with the deformity of sin, I beg you in my own anguish to forgive me. I do not ask for pity, for you must abhor me. But pardon me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts follow me into exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you or hear your voice again, but the soft whisper of your forgiveness might cool my disordered brain and heart, even in the grave. I dare to make this request by explaining how I was trapped in this web of anguish and how I struggled to escape. If your soul were less pure, I would not attempt to justify myself, fearing that by lessening your hatred for me, you might hate vice less. But in addressing you, I feel I am appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, which I must gain or fall into despair. I implore you to listen; if guilt can be mitigated by sharp agony and remorse that borders on madness, perhaps you might think I have some claim to your compassion. I entreat you to remember our happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had arrived after sixteen years of weary wandering, during which, despite many dangers, my affections had remained a blank.

For an instant, I was too stunned to reason clearly. While my own design differed in detail, the general shape bore a striking resemblance. I took a candle to the far side of the room to examine the parchment more carefully. Flipping it over, I discovered my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had drawn it. Initially, I was simply astonished by the remarkable similarity of the outlines and the strange coincidence that a skull, unknown to me, existed on the reverse side directly beneath my scarab, matching it in both size and form. This oddity left me momentarily paralyzed, as the mind often struggles to find a causal link in such events and falters when it cannot. Yet, as my shock faded, a far more unsettling realization emerged. I distinctly recalled that the parchment was blank when I drew the beetle. I was certain of this, as I remembered checking both sides for a clean surface. Had the skull been present, I surely would have seen it. This mystery felt inexplicable, though a faint, distant intuition of the truth—which last night’s events would later confirm—began to stir in my mind. I stood up, secured the parchment, and set aside further thought until I could be alone. After you left and Jupiter fell asleep, I began a systematic investigation. I first considered how the parchment came into my hands. We found the scarab on the mainland coast, a mile east of the island, just above the high-tide line. When I picked it up, it bit me, causing me to drop it. Jupiter, with his usual wariness, searched for a leaf to grasp the insect after it flew toward him.

I spent two years this way. The days passed without external change, yet they slowly altered my mind as I drifted toward death. I studied more, empathized with the thoughts found in books, read history, and lost my sense of self among those who came before. As my immediate suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude lost its appeal; I began to crave connection. I did not want to join the masses, but I longed for one friend. You might think I was becoming ready to rejoin society, but I disagree. The sympathy I craved had to be so pure and free from external influence that I would inevitably have been disappointed by the crude realities of the world. I was less prepared for human interaction than ever. When I first left society, people tormented me like a sickness—something external I wanted to discard. Now, I would have sought a deep soul-connection, only to invite further suffering, for I had become as sensitive as a raw nerve. I did not want help with ambition or wisdom, but simple, mutual affection—smiles and gentle words. I wanted one heart to receive my complaints, hoping something good might grow from such sorrow. Yet, how could I find it? True friendship is a delicate spirit, rarely found unless two people are bonded from youth or through shared hardship. It arrives unbidden to the fortunate, like dew on barren ground, but it flees when pursued; it mocks those who beg for it. I understood this and did not go looking for it. Yet, there on my lonely heath, under my humble roof in that desolate place, it arrived like a winter sunbeam, illuminating the snow even as it melted it. Alas, the light shone on withered fruit; I could not revive under its warmth, for I was too broken to feel its kindness.

He kept one secret from his dear friends, a private devotion nurtured since childhood that he dared not share, fearing they might mock the intensity of a passion he considered his very lifeblood. Near his family estate lived a man of modest means with three lovely daughters. The eldest, Diana, possessed not only striking beauty but a sharp intellect and a gentle spirit. Having been playmates since infancy, she was a favorite of his mother, and they spent every school vacation together. Influenced by literature that introduced the concept of romance to the impressionable, he began speaking the language of love to her by age eleven. Though two years his senior, Diana was less worldly; she accepted his youthful declarations with innocent ignorance. As she matured and realized the nature of their bond, her heart was already committed, leaving her only to fear his potential inconstancy. Their affection deepened as they grew, becoming an inseparable part of his existence. Despite his dread that peers might judge him for loving someone of lower social standing, he remained steadfast in his resolve to marry her once he could overcome the necessary obstacles. Diana was entirely deserving of his profound devotion.

In our village, Saturday nights brought a pleasant feeling of tidying up and pausing before starting fresh, which encouraged Joe to stay out thirty minutes past his usual time. When his rum and water were finished, Joe stood up to leave and took my hand. Stop a moment, Mr. Gargery, the stranger said. I believe I have a shiny new shilling in my pocket, and if I do, the boy shall have it. He found it among his change, wrapped it in crumpled paper, and handed it to me, insisting it was mine to keep. I thanked him while staring rudely, clutching Joe’s hand. He said goodnight to Joe and Mr. Wopsle, who left with us, but gave me only a strange look with his one good eye, closing the other as if to signal something. On the walk home, Mr. Wopsle left us at the tavern door, and Joe walked in silence, mouth agape to air out the taste of rum. I was too stunned by this encounter with a man from my past to speak. My sister was in a decent mood when we reached the kitchen, so Joe told her about the shilling. She immediately claimed it must be counterfeit, but when I unwrapped it, the coin was genuine. Then she noticed two one-pound notes inside the paper. They were dirty and worn from heavy use. Joe grabbed his hat and rushed back to the tavern to return the money. While he was gone, I sat on my stool, certain the man would be long gone. Joe soon returned, confirming the stranger had left, though he had alerted the tavern staff about the lost notes.

Are you talking about Mr. Knightley? Of course I am. I never meant anyone else, and I assumed you knew. When we discussed him, it seemed perfectly clear. Not quite, Emma replied, trying to stay calm. Everything you said seemed to point to someone else. I could have sworn you named Mr. Frank Churchill, especially when you mentioned how he saved you from the gypsies. Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how you forget! My dear Harriet, I remember our conversation perfectly. I told you that I understood your feelings because of his kindness, and you agreed, speaking warmly about how he rescued you. I remember it clearly. Oh, Harriet cried, now I understand, but I was thinking of something else entirely. It was not the gypsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. I was thinking of a much more meaningful moment: when Mr. Knightley asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused, and when no one else would. That was the kind, generous act that made me realize how superior he is to everyone else. Good heavens, Emma exclaimed, this has been a terrible, unfortunate mistake! What can we do? You would not have encouraged me if you had understood? At least I am no worse off than I would have been otherwise, and now, it is possible. She paused, and Emma could not speak. I am not surprised, Miss Woodhouse, that you see a huge difference between the two men, Harriet continued. You must think one is infinitely above me. But I hope, even if it seems strange, that you will not oppose it. You said yourself that more unlikely matches have happened than one between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. If I am lucky enough that Mr. Knightley does not mind the difference in our status, I hope you will not try to stand in our way.

With a racing heart and a sense of dread I could not explain, I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. It read as follows: My dear child, I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and exposed your innocent heart to the language of forbidden and monstrous passion. I must pay for these crimes, and I must try to make my punishment fit my guilt. I am sure you are prepared for what I am about to say: we must separate and be divided forever. I am taking away your parent and only friend. You are cast out into the world without shelter; your hopes are ruined, and the peace of your pure mind is destroyed. Memory will bring you frightening images of guilt and the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who have brought all this misery upon you, who have cast you out and cruelly marked my own child with distrust and agony, who have tried to steal your beauty and replace it with the ugliness of sin—I, in the depths of my suffering, beg you to forgive me. I do not ask for your pity, for you must hate me. But pardon me, Mathilda, and do not follow me into exile with constant anger. I must never see you again or hear your voice, but the soft whisper of your forgiveness will reach me and soothe my troubled mind. I am sure I would feel it even in my grave. I dare to make this request by explaining how I was trapped in this web of agony and how I struggled to escape it. If your soul were less pure, I would not try to justify myself, as I would fear that making you hate me less might make you hate evil less. But in speaking to you, I feel as if I am appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must try to earn it or I will despair. I beg you to listen to my words. If guilt can be lessened by sharp agony and the remorse that drives one to madness, perhaps you might think—though I dare not—that I deserve some compassion. I ask you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had arrived after sixteen years of weary wandering, during which, despite many dangers and misfortunes, my heart had remained empty.

Must I be carried to the skies on flowery beds of ease, while others fight to win the prize and sail through bloody seas? He was considered an excellent reader. At church gatherings, he was always asked to read poetry. When he finished, the ladies would clasp their hands, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say the words were too beautiful for this world. After the hymn, Reverend Sprague acted like a bulletin board, reading announcements for meetings and societies until it felt like the list would last forever. This strange custom persists in America, even in cities, despite the availability of newspapers. Often, the less a tradition makes sense, the harder it is to stop. Then the minister prayed. It was a long, thorough prayer, covering the church, the village, the county, the state, the nation, the government, sailors at sea, the oppressed under foreign dictators, those who ignore the truth, and people in distant lands. He finished by asking that his upcoming sermon be well-received. The congregation sat down. The boy in this story did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it. He was restless, mentally tracking the familiar path of the minister’s words. He resented any new additions as unfair. During the prayer, a fly landed on the pew in front of him, grooming itself so calmly that it seemed to know it was perfectly safe, which only added to the boy's irritation.

We both loved Adrian, though she, still a child, could not fully grasp his merits or share my deep connection to his ideas. I was constantly by his side. His gentle, sensitive nature lent a tender, ethereal quality to our talks. He was as joyful as a singing bird, as ambitious as an eagle, and as innocent as a dove. He could lighten Perdita’s seriousness and soothe my own restless, tortured spirit. I viewed my past struggles as a troubled dream, feeling as transformed as if I had entered a new body that perceived the world differently. Yet, I remained the same in my strength and my craving for connection. My masculine virtues endured, softened and humanized by his influence. Adrian taught me more than just history and philosophy; while helping me tame my reckless spirit, he revealed his own heart, allowing me to understand its remarkable depth. The former queen of England had tried since his infancy to instill ambition in her son. Recognizing his genius, she nurtured it to serve her own ends. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his courage, hoping his love of freedom would eventually turn into a desire for power. She tried to foster resentment toward those who had forced his father’s abdication, but she failed. Despite her biased accounts, he admired the nation’s choice to govern itself and became a republican by principle. Still, she did not despair. Combining his pride of birth with her own patience and ambition, she studied his character closely. She used praise and criticism to manipulate him, and though the results disappointed her, she relied on his talents, certain she would eventually prevail.

The nephew glanced at him, unsuccessfully, while heading for the door. Good night, the uncle remarked. I anticipate seeing you tomorrow. Sleep well! Light my nephew to his room! And burn him in his bed, if you wish, he muttered to himself before ringing his bell to summon his valet. Once the valet departed, the Marquis paced in his dressing gown, preparing for sleep on that sweltering night. Moving silently in his slippers, he paced like a sophisticated tiger, resembling a wicked nobleman from a fable whose transformation into a beast was either fading or beginning. He traversed his luxurious bedroom, reflecting on the day’s journey: the arduous climb at sunset, the mill, the crag-top prison, the village, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender pointing at the carriage chain. That fountain brought to mind the one in Paris, the bundle on the step, the women hovering over it, and the tall man shouting, Dead! I am calm now, the Marquis declared, and ready for bed. Leaving a single light on the hearth, he drew his thin curtains and listened to the night sigh as he drifted off. The stone faces on the exterior walls stared into the darkness for three long hours; the horses stamped, dogs barked, and the owl hooted in a way that defied poetic convention. For three heavy hours, the stone lions and human faces gazed blindly into the night. Total darkness blanketed the landscape and the dusty roads. The graveyard became a blur of indistinguishable grass mounds, and the figure on the Cross vanished into the gloom. In the village, both the tax-collectors and the taxed slept soundly, perhaps dreaming of feasts and rest, finding temporary liberation in their slumber.

I had tucked my handkerchief inside my helmet, along with a few other items, forgetting that I could not remove the helmet on my own. The fact that the cloth was so close yet impossible to reach made my situation unbearable. It is human nature to crave what we cannot have, and this thought consumed me. For miles, I could think of nothing but that handkerchief while salty sweat stung my eyes. It sounds trivial, but it was genuine misery. I decided that next time I would carry a small bag, regardless of what the knights of the Round Table thought. I prioritized comfort over their rigid standards of style. As we traveled, clouds of dust made me sneeze and cry, leading me to use language I probably should have avoided. We encountered no one in that desolate land, not even an ogre. If we had, I would have gladly traded his armor for his handkerchief. Meanwhile, the sun beat down, turning my iron suit into an oven. Every minor detail became a source of irritation. When I trotted, my armor rattled like a crate of dishes, and my shield banged against my body. If I slowed to a walk, my joints screeched like a rusty wheelbarrow, and the lack of airflow made me feel as though I were being cooked alive. The slower I moved, the heavier the iron felt, pressing down on me with increasing weight.

Mr. Wickham was so satisfied with their talk that he never brought up the subject again, much to Elizabeth’s relief. Soon, the day arrived for him and Lydia to leave. Mrs. Bennet had to accept the separation, as her husband refused to let the whole family move to Newcastle, meaning they would likely be apart for a year. Oh, my dear Lydia, when will we see each other again? Mrs. Bennet cried. Oh, I don’t know. Maybe not for two or three years, Lydia replied. Write to me often, her mother urged. I will when I can, but married women are busy. My sisters can write to me; they have nothing else to do. Mr. Wickham’s farewells were far warmer than his wife’s.
