He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things. He is a fine fellow, Mr. Bennet remarked once they had left. He charms us all. I am very proud of him. I doubt Sir William Lucas has a son-in-law as impressive. Mrs. Bennet was miserable for several days after Lydia left. I think there is nothing worse than parting with friends, she lamented. It makes one feel so lonely. This is the result of having a married daughter, Elizabeth noted. Surely this makes you glad your other four are still single? Not at all, her mother insisted. Lydia is only leaving because her husband’s regiment is stationed so far away. If they were closer, she would not have left so soon. Mrs. Bennet’s sadness soon vanished, replaced by excitement when news began to spread. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been told to prepare for her master’s arrival; he was coming to hunt for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was restless, glancing at Jane with knowing smiles. Well, Mr. Bingley is returning, she told her sister, Mrs. Philips. That is fine, though I do not care about it. He means nothing to us, and I certainly do not need to see him again. Still, he is welcome to visit Netherfield if he wishes.

Mr. Elliot gazed upward with profound respect. How charming! Mrs. Clay exclaimed, though she dared not glance at Anne. It is just like a father and son! My dear Miss Elliot, may I not call them father and son? I place no restrictions on what people say, but I hardly feel his attentions exceed those of any other gentleman. My dear Miss Elliot! Mrs. Clay cried, raising her hands and eyes before falling into a convenient, astonished silence. Well, Penelope, you need not be so concerned. I invited him, after all. When I learned he was visiting friends at Thornberry Park tomorrow, I took pity on him. Anne marveled at her friend’s performance, managing to display such delight at the arrival of the very man who hindered her own ambitions. Mrs. Clay surely loathed the sight of Mr. Elliot, yet she maintained a placid, obliging expression, appearing content to spend only half as much time with Sir Walter as she might have otherwise. For Anne, Mr. Elliot’s entrance was distressing, and his approach was painful. She had previously suspected his sincerity, but now she perceived falsehood in everything. His deferential behavior toward her father, so contrary to his earlier remarks, was repulsive. Recalling his heartless treatment of Mrs. Smith, she could barely endure his mild smiles or his hollow, virtuous sentiments. She hoped to avoid any change in demeanor that might invite his questioning. Her goal was to evade any scene or scrutiny, yet she intended to remain as cool as their relationship allowed, quietly withdrawing from the unnecessary intimacy she had been drawn into. Consequently, she was more guarded and distant than the previous evening. He attempted to pique her curiosity once more regarding where he had heard her praised, hoping for further encouragement, but the spell had vanished. He realized that the excitement of a public setting was required to stir his cousin’s vanity, or at least that his current efforts were ineffective amidst the competing demands of the others.

I had tucked my handkerchief inside my helmet, along with a few other items, forgetting that I could not remove the helmet on my own. The realization that the cloth was so close yet completely inaccessible made my situation unbearable. It is a universal truth that we desire most what we cannot reach. My entire focus narrowed to that handkerchief, and as salty sweat dripped into my eyes, I was powerless to wipe it away. While it sounds trivial, it was genuine misery. I decided that in the future, I would carry a bag regardless of what the knights of the Round Table thought; comfort would take precedence over their rigid standards of style. As we traveled, clouds of dust forced me to sneeze and weep, leading me to curse in frustration. We encountered no one in that desolate landscape, which was fortunate for any ogre who might have crossed my path, as I would have gladly traded his life for a simple cloth. Meanwhile, the sun heated my iron armor until I felt like I was being baked alive. Every movement was an irritation; trotting caused a clattering sound like a crate of dishes, while the shield banged incessantly against my body. If I slowed to a walk, my joints screeched like a rusted wheelbarrow, and the lack of airflow made the heat stifling. The slower I moved, the heavier the armor felt, pressing down on me with the weight of a thousand tons.

Emma felt no remorse for her decision to attend the Coles' party. The following day, she reflected on the visit with pleasure, convinced that the loss of her usual reserved dignity was well compensated by the glow of public favor. She had surely brought joy to the deserving Coles and secured a lasting reputation among them. Yet, perfect contentment is rare, and two matters troubled her. She questioned if she had acted improperly by sharing her suspicions regarding Jane Fairfax’s emotions with Frank Churchill. While it felt like a breach of sisterly duty, the impulse had been overwhelming, and his deference to her insight made it hard to regret speaking. Her second concern was more certain: she genuinely lamented her own musical shortcomings. Deeply regretting her youthful lack of discipline, she sat down to practice with renewed intensity for ninety minutes. Her efforts were cut short by Harriet’s arrival, whose admiration offered little solace. When Harriet compared her skill to Jane’s, Emma insisted they were incomparable, likening her own performance to a lamp beside Jane’s sunshine. Harriet countered that she preferred Emma’s playing and noted that others had praised her taste. Emma maintained that Jane possessed both taste and technical mastery. Harriet remained unconvinced, dismissing Jane’s Italian singing as incomprehensible and suggesting that Jane’s proficiency was merely a professional necessity for her future as a governess.

I swear by the sun, the blue sky, and the fire of love in my heart, that if you grant my request, you will never see me again as long as they live. Go home and begin your work; I will watch your progress with intense anxiety. Do not fear; I will appear when you are ready. With that, he left, perhaps afraid I might change my mind. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle, quickly vanishing into the icy landscape. His story had taken all day, and the sun was setting as he left. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness fell, but my heart was heavy and my pace slow. Navigating the mountain paths was difficult, as I was preoccupied with the day's events. It was late when I reached the halfway point and sat by the fountain. Stars flickered between passing clouds, and the dark pines and fallen trees created a solemn, unsettling scene. I wept bitterly, wringing my hands in agony, and cried out to the stars, clouds, and winds, begging them to either end my consciousness or leave me in darkness. These were desperate thoughts, but I cannot explain how the constant starlight burdened me, or how I feared every gust of wind as if it were a destructive force. Morning had broken by the time I reached Chamounix. I did not rest, but returned immediately to Geneva. I could not articulate my feelings; they weighed on me like a mountain, crushing my spirit. I returned home and faced my family. My haggard, wild appearance alarmed them, but I could barely speak or answer their questions. I felt as though I were cursed, unworthy of their sympathy, and forever barred from their companionship.

“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped his temple, signaling his low opinion of Joseph’s intellect. “My dear young friend,” Mr. Pumblechook declared, “you must be famished. Sit. I have brought chicken, tongue, and other delicacies from the Boar, which I hope you will enjoy. But do I truly see before me the boy I once played with in his happy youth? May I—may I?” This request meant a handshake, which I granted. He shook my hand fervently before sitting once more. “Here is wine,” he continued. “Let us toast to Fortune and her wise choices! Yet, I cannot look upon you and drink without again asking—may I—may I?” I agreed, and he shook my hand again, draining his glass and inverting it. I followed suit, and the wine went straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook served me the best portions of chicken and tongue, neglecting his own plate. “Ah, poultry! You little imagined as a fledgling what fate awaited you—to provide sustenance under this humble roof for one who—call it a weakness, but may I? May I?” He did not wait for my permission again. I marveled that he did not cut himself with my knife during these frequent interruptions. “And your sister,” he added after a pause, “who raised you by hand! It is tragic that she can no longer appreciate that honor. May—” Seeing he was about to lunge for my hand again, I interrupted. “Let us drink to her health,” I suggested. “Ah!” Mr. Pumblechook exclaimed, leaning back in admiration, “that is how you recognize them, sir! That is how you know the noble-minded, sir!”

I expressed my gratitude and offered an apology. He dismissed it with a polite, "Not at all," and continued. "Miss Havisham had become an heiress, attracting much attention as a desirable match. Her half-brother had regained his wealth, only to squander it once more through debts and reckless behavior. Tensions between them surpassed those he had with his father, and it is believed he harbored a lethal resentment toward her, blaming her for their father's hostility. Now, I reach the heart of this tragic tale—pausing briefly, my dear Handel, to note that a dinner napkin will not fit inside a glass." I have no explanation for why I was attempting to force my napkin into the tumbler, only that I was laboring with misplaced determination to cram it inside. I thanked him and apologized once more, to which he replied with cheerful ease, "Not at all, I assure you!" and proceeded. "A man appeared—perhaps at the races or a ball—and began courting Miss Havisham. I never met him, as this occurred twenty-five years ago, before your time or mine, but my father described him as a flashy individual perfectly suited for his schemes. My father insists he could never be mistaken for a gentleman, maintaining that one who lacks a gentleman's heart can never truly possess a gentleman's manners. He argues that varnish cannot conceal the wood's grain; in fact, the more polish applied, the more the grain shows through. This man pursued Miss Havisham relentlessly, claiming deep devotion. Though she had previously shown little romantic interest, she became utterly captivated and adored him. He exploited her feelings systematically, extracting large sums of money and persuading her to purchase her brother's share of the brewery at an exorbitant cost, under the pretense that he would manage the entire business once they were wed. Your guardian was not involved in her affairs then, and she was far too proud and infatuated to accept any counsel."

Jupiter could barely contain his delight at the sight, though his master looked deeply disappointed. He pressed us to keep digging, and I had barely started again when I tripped over a large iron ring partially hidden in the dirt. We then labored with renewed intensity, experiencing ten minutes of profound excitement. We uncovered a rectangular wooden chest, remarkably preserved and hardened, likely by a mineral treatment. Measuring three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep, the box was reinforced with riveted iron bands in a trellis pattern. Six iron rings, three on each side, allowed for a firm grip, yet our combined strength barely shifted the heavy coffer. Realizing we could not move it, we slid back the two bolts on the lid with trembling hands. A fortune of immense value was revealed. As our lantern light hit the pit, the pile of gold and jewels shimmered with a brilliance that blinded us. I cannot describe my reaction, though amazement was foremost. Legrand was drained by the intensity, barely speaking. Jupiter’s face turned as pale as possible, and he appeared completely stunned. He knelt in the pit, plunging his bare arms into the gold as if bathing in it. Finally, he sighed and muttered to himself about the gold-bug, expressing shame for how he had treated the creature. Eventually, I had to urge them to focus on moving the treasure. It was getting late, and we needed to secure everything before dawn. We spent considerable time deliberating, our thoughts too scattered to decide on a plan.

It was past two when I suddenly found myself near the lake, where a small boat was tied up. Seeing my father and aunt on the lawn nearby, I jumped into the skiff. Used to such things, I pushed off and rowed with all my might. Dressed in white with only a tartan shawl over me and my hair flowing, I moved so quickly that my father later told me I looked more like a spirit than a girl. As I reached the shore, he caught the boat, and I leaped into his arms. My life truly began then. Everything shifted from dullness to pure joy. The happiness of being with my father surpassed my wildest hopes. We were inseparable, and our conversations never ended. During his sixteen years away, he had traveled through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, living among people few Europeans ever saw. His stories about their customs and the landscapes he visited filled our hours when we weren't discussing our own future. The sound of his affection was so new that I listened intently as he described his feelings during those long years of silence. He told me that at first, he could not bear to think of me, but as his grief faded and hope returned, he constantly imagined my small form. He felt as though the northern breeze carried my spirit, and he dreamed of taking me to a peaceful island. As he traveled home, his excitement was mixed with painful fear that I might be dead. But he told me, no, it was not so; he had his Mathilda, his comfort, and his hope.

As they left the dining room, the clock tower struck midnight. The final chime was followed by a crash, a shrill cry, and a thunderclap that rattled the house. Eerie music filled the air as a wall panel at the top of the stairs flew open. Virginia stepped out onto the landing, pale and holding a small casket. Her family rushed to her; Mrs. Otis hugged her tightly, the Duke kissed her repeatedly, and the twins danced around them. Mr. Otis, annoyed and assuming she had played a prank, asked where she had been, noting that he and Cecil had searched everywhere while her mother was terrified. He told her not to play such jokes again. The twins shouted that she should only play them on the ghost. Mrs. Otis kissed her trembling daughter and smoothed her hair, telling her never to leave her side. Virginia calmly explained that she had been with the ghost, who was now dead. She told them he had been wicked but was sorry, and had given her the jewels before passing away. The family stared in amazement, but Virginia remained serious. She led them through the wall into a narrow secret hallway, with Washington carrying a candle. They reached a heavy oak door with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it opened to reveal a small, vaulted room with a tiny window. A skeleton was chained to an iron ring in the wall, stretched out on the floor. It seemed to be reaching for a plate and pitcher just beyond its grasp. The pitcher was covered in mold, and the plate held only dust. Virginia knelt and prayed silently while her family watched, stunned by the tragic secret finally revealed.

The shock and confusion I felt at this sudden shift in circumstances were perhaps the most difficult parts of the experience to explain. The reversal was natural and inevitable, long anticipated for the moment my balloon reached the point where the moon’s gravity overcame the earth’s. Waking from a deep sleep, I was startled by a phenomenon I knew would happen, though not exactly when. The transition must have been gradual; even had I been awake, I doubt I would have felt any physical sensation of the inversion. Once I regained my senses and moved past the initial terror, I focused entirely on the moon’s appearance. It lay below like a map, and though still distant, its surface features were remarkably clear. The total lack of oceans, lakes, or rivers was the most striking geological detail. Strangely, I saw vast, flat alluvial plains, though most of the visible hemisphere was covered in countless conical volcanic mountains that looked almost artificial. The tallest rose less than four miles high, but a map of the Phlegraean Fields would give you a better sense of the terrain than I could describe. Most were actively erupting, and I was terrified by the frequent, thunderous roar of volcanic debris rushing past my balloon with increasing intensity.

After lightening the chest by removing two-thirds of its load, we managed, with significant effort, to lift it from the pit. We hid the removed items in the brush, instructing Jupiter to guard them and remain silent until we returned. We hauled the chest home, reaching our hut at one in the morning, exhausted by the labor. We rested until two, ate, and then headed back to the hills with three sturdy sacks. Arriving at the pit shortly before four, we split the remaining loot and returned to the hut, depositing our golden cargo just as dawn broke over the eastern horizon. Though completely drained, our intense excitement prevented us from sleeping. After a restless nap of a few hours, we woke simultaneously to inspect our fortune. The chest had been filled to capacity, and we spent the entire day and most of the following night sorting through the chaotic heap. We discovered our wealth was even greater than anticipated. We held over four hundred and fifty thousand dollars in gold coins, calculated by contemporary tables. There was no silver, only antique gold from France, Spain, Germany, and England, along with unfamiliar tokens. Some heavy coins were too worn to identify, and there was no American currency. Estimating the jewels proved harder. We found one hundred and ten large, fine diamonds, eighteen brilliant rubies, three hundred and ten beautiful emeralds, twenty-one sapphires, and an opal. These gems had been pried from their settings, which we found crushed and mangled among the gold, likely to obscure their origins.

Had she realized her sister intended to deprive her of such prospects and realities, her reaction would have been understood only by her mother, who likely shared those feelings. Lydia’s departure for Brighton was the only comfort for her mother, who was sadly convinced her husband would never visit the town himself. Yet, they remained unaware of these developments, and their excitement persisted until the day Lydia departed. Elizabeth prepared to see Mr. Wickham for the final time. Having spent much time with him since her return, her previous agitation had faded, along with her former partiality. She now recognized the same gentleness that once charmed her as mere affectation, becoming tiresome and wearying. Furthermore, his attempt to renew the attentions he had shown earlier in their acquaintance only annoyed her. She lost all sympathy for him, finding his idle gallantry insulting. While she firmly discouraged his advances, she felt offended that he assumed her vanity would be easily flattered by his renewed interest, regardless of his past neglect. On the regiment's final day in Meryton, Wickham dined at Longbourn. Elizabeth, feeling little desire to part on friendly terms, mentioned Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy’s three-week stay at Rosings when he asked about her time at Hunsford, then inquired if he knew the Colonel. Wickham appeared surprised, annoyed, and alarmed, but quickly recovered with a smile, noting he had known him well. After calling him a gentleman, he asked for her opinion. She praised him warmly. Wickham then asked with feigned indifference how long he had stayed at Rosings. Upon learning it was nearly three weeks and that she had seen him daily, he remarked on the difference between the cousins' manners. When Elizabeth noted that Mr. Darcy improved upon acquaintance, Wickham’s reaction was telling. He began to ask a question but stopped himself, instead asking with forced cheerfulness if it was in his manner that Darcy improved.

As they left the dining room, the clock tower struck midnight. The final chime was followed by a crash, a sharp cry, and a thunderous tremor that rattled the house. Eerie music filled the air as a wall panel at the top of the stairs burst open. Virginia emerged onto the landing, pale and clutching a small casket. The family rushed to her; Mrs. Otis embraced her, the Duke kissed her repeatedly, and the twins danced wildly. Mr. Otis, annoyed and assuming she had played a prank, demanded to know where she had been, noting that he and Cecil had searched everywhere while her mother was terrified. He insisted she stop such behavior. The twins shouted that she should only prank the ghost. Mrs. Otis, kissing her trembling daughter and smoothing her hair, thanked God she was safe and told her never to leave her side again. Virginia calmly explained that she had been with the ghost, who was now dead. She claimed he had been wicked but felt remorse, gifting her the jewels before passing. Stunned, the family followed her through the wall into a narrow, hidden corridor, Washington leading with a candle. They reached a heavy oak door reinforced with rusty nails. It swung open to reveal a small, vaulted room with a single grated window. A skeletal figure was chained to an iron ring in the wall, stretched out on the floor. It appeared to be reaching for a bowl and pitcher just beyond its grasp. The pitcher was coated in mold, and the bowl held only dust. Virginia knelt and prayed silently while her family watched, stunned by the grim secret finally revealed.

He also considered Sybil’s traditional parents, who might oppose the union if scandal arose, though he believed they would understand his motives if fully informed. Poison seemed the ideal choice; it was secure, certain, and discreet, sparing him the unpleasant confrontations that most Englishmen naturally detest. Lacking any knowledge of toxicology, he searched the library himself after the waiter failed to assist. He discovered a fine edition of the Pharmacopoeia and Erskine’s Toxicology, edited by Sir Mathew Reid—a man whose membership in the Buckingham club resulted from a clerical error that led the committee to reject the actual physician out of spite. Confused by the technical jargon and wishing he had studied harder at Oxford, Lord Arthur eventually found a clear description of aconitine in Erskine’s second volume. It was the perfect substance: rapid, painless, and easily ingested via a gelatine capsule. He noted the lethal dosage on his cuff, returned the books, and walked to Pestle and Humbey’s pharmacy. Mr. Pestle, accustomed to serving the elite, initially hesitated and requested a medical certificate. Once Lord Arthur claimed the poison was for a rabid Norwegian mastiff that had bitten his coachman, the chemist was satisfied, praised his toxicological expertise, and prepared the order. Lord Arthur placed the capsule into a silver bonbonnière purchased on Bond Street, discarded the pharmacy’s container, and departed for Lady Clementina’s.

Get up! What are you doing? I opened my eyes, disoriented. It was past sunrise, and I had been fast asleep. Pap stood over me, looking ill and irritable. He asked what I was doing with the gun. Assuming he had no memory of his actions, I told him someone had tried to enter, so I was waiting for them. He asked why I had not woken him, and I replied that I had tried but could not move him. He told me to stop talking and go check the fishing lines for breakfast, promising to follow shortly. He unlocked the door, and I hurried up the riverbank. Seeing debris and bark floating by, I realized the river was rising. I thought of the good fortune the June rise usually brought, as it carried cordwood and logs downstream that I could catch and sell to the mills. I walked along the bank, watching for Pap and any useful drift. Suddenly, a beautiful canoe, about fourteen feet long, appeared, bobbing on the water. I dove in like a frog, fully clothed, and swam to it. I feared someone might be hiding inside to play a trick, but it was truly a drift-canoe. I paddled it to the bank, thinking Pap would be pleased with its ten-dollar value. However, as I hid it in a vine-covered creek, a new plan formed: I would conceal it well and use it to escape downriver fifty miles instead of traveling on foot. I worked quickly, constantly expecting Pap to appear. After hiding the boat, I peered through the willows and spotted him down the path, aiming his gun at a bird.

In a certain town—which I shall leave unnamed for discretion—there stands a building common to most municipalities: a workhouse. Within these walls, on a date I need not specify as it holds no immediate relevance, was born the individual whose name titles this chapter. For some time after the parish surgeon brought him into this world of woe, it was uncertain if the infant would survive long enough to be named. Had he perished, these memoirs would either never exist or would have been remarkably brief, serving as a uniquely concise biography. While being born in a workhouse is hardly an enviable start, it proved the best possible outcome for Oliver Twist. He struggled initially to draw breath, a tedious but necessary habit, lying on a mattress while teetering between life and death. Had he been surrounded by doting relatives and expert physicians, he surely would have been killed by their interference. Instead, with only a tipsy pauper and a contract surgeon present, Oliver and Nature settled the matter themselves. After a few efforts, he breathed, sneezed, and announced his arrival to the workhouse by crying as loudly as any infant could after only three minutes of life.

Hear me! You! Monks replied. When his father fell ill in Rome, my mother, from whom he had long been estranged, traveled from Paris with me to join him. She likely came to secure his assets, as there was little love between them. He remained unconscious until his death the following day. Within his desk, we discovered two documents dated from the onset of his sickness, addressed to you, Mr. Brownlow. They were accompanied by a note instructing that they only be delivered after his passing. One was a letter to Agnes, the other a will. What of the letter? Mr. Brownlow inquired. It was a page filled with remorseful confessions and pleas for divine mercy. He had deceived the girl, claiming a secret mystery prevented their marriage, leading her to trust him until she suffered an irreparable loss. She was then nearing her delivery. He detailed his plans to conceal her disgrace had he survived, begging her not to curse his memory or fear their child would suffer for his sins. He recalled the locket and ring he had given her, inscribed with her name and a space for the one he hoped to provide, urging her to keep them close. He wrote frantically, as if losing his mind, which I believe he was. The will, Mr. Brownlow prompted as Oliver wept. Monks remained quiet. The will, Mr. Brownlow continued, mirrored the letter. He spoke of the misery his wife caused, the malice and vice of you, his son, whom he claimed was raised to despise him. He bequeathed you and your mother annuities of eight hundred pounds each. The remainder of his estate was split equally between Agnes Fleming and their child, provided the infant survived and reached maturity.

If I cannot survive on that, I will not ask for help. Is that acceptable? A massive roar of applause erupted, and the king’s voice rose above it: Remove his bonds and set him free! Let everyone, high and low, pay him homage, for he is now the king’s right hand, vested with authority and seated at the highest level of the throne! Now, banish this creeping night and restore the light so the world may bless you. I replied: It is nothing for a common man to be shamed, but it would dishonor the king if those who saw his minister humiliated did not also see him vindicated. If I might request that my clothes be returned. They are not suitable, the king interrupted. Bring him different attire; dress him like a prince! My plan worked. I needed to maintain the status quo until the eclipse was total, or they would pressure me to end the darkness, which I could not do. Sending for the clothes bought some time, but not enough, so I made another excuse. I suggested it would be natural for the king to reconsider his impulsive decision; therefore, I would let the darkness persist, and if he remained resolute after a reasonable time, I would dismiss it. No one was satisfied, but I held my ground. It grew increasingly dark while I struggled with those awkward sixth-century garments. Eventually, it became pitch black, and the crowd groaned in horror as cold, eerie breezes blew and stars appeared in the sky. When the eclipse finally became total, I was relieved, though everyone else was miserable. I announced: The king, by his silence, upholds the terms. I raised my hands, stood still for a moment, and declared with solemnity: Let the enchantment dissolve and pass away! There was no response in the graveyard silence of the darkness. But when the sun’s silver rim emerged moments later, the crowd erupted in a massive shout, rushing toward me with blessings and gratitude; Clarence was certainly among the first to reach me.

It was past two when I rounded a bend and spotted a small skiff moored near the lake, close to our home. Seeing my father and aunt on the lawn, I jumped into the boat and rowed with all my might. Dressed in white with my tartan shawl and hair flowing behind me, I moved with such speed that my father later told me I looked more like a spirit than a girl. I reached the shore, and he caught the boat as I leapt into his arms. My life truly began then. Everything shifted from dull monotony to vibrant joy. The happiness of being with my father surpassed my wildest hopes. We were inseparable, our conversations endless. He had spent sixteen years traveling through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, living among locals in ways few Europeans ever could. His stories of their customs and landscapes filled our hours when we weren't discussing our future. The sound of his affection was so new that I cherished every word as he described his feelings during those long years of separation. He told me that while he initially struggled to think of me, hope eventually returned, and my image haunted him in cities and deserts alike. He felt my spirit in the northern breeze and dreamed of taking me to a peaceful island. As he finally traveled home, his anticipation was marred by agonizing fear that he might find my grave instead of me. But he held me close, calling me his consolation and his hope.

That powerful, unnatural voice—devoid of any mechanical origin—ceased its resonant vibration, and the young woman, turning to help her elderly companion, finally noticed our presence. It was her father, whom she had guided since her youth. They were Saxons who had settled nearby only a few years prior. When the plague emerged, a young German student had joined them. Their story was clear: a nobleman who loved the musician’s daughter and followed them to escape his family’s disapproval, only to be claimed by the pestilence. She survived solely for her father, shielding him from the truth of their isolation so he believed his music still reached an audience beyond the silent landscape. On the day we arrived, she fell ill. Terrified of leaving her blind father alone, she summoned her remaining strength to lead him to the chapel at vespers, performing a hymn to the earth that would soon become her grave. Seeing us felt like a divine intervention; her fragile resolve shattered, and she collapsed at Adrian’s feet, begging him to protect her father. Sadly, she and her father now rest together under the walnut tree beside her lover. Upon realizing her condition, the father held her hand until she passed, remaining motionless until he too succumbed twelve hours later. They lie beneath that tree, framed by the Jura mountains and the distant Alps, while the church spire rises above the trees, and I like to imagine their favorite music still lingers to comfort their spirits.

Perdita’s name went unspoken, yet I knew his indecision stemmed from his love for her. Who was more worthy of his affection than my noble sister? Who better deserved this self-important leader than she, whose regal presence commanded respect and who loved him in return, even as disappointment dampened her feelings and ambition warred with his own? We arrived at the House that evening. Raymond, aware that his future would be decided during the debate, remained lighthearted. A roar like a swarm of bees greeted us in the coffee-room, where anxious politicians gathered in clusters. The aristocratic faction, England’s wealthiest men, seemed calm, as the debate would proceed without their direct interference. Near the fire stood Ryland and his allies. Ryland, a man of humble origins who had amassed a fortune from his father’s manufacturing business, had spent his life championing the democratic shifts that followed the king’s abdication. While he initially welcomed Lord Raymond’s influence as a way to weaken his rivals, the situation had escalated. The lesser nobility, eager to regain their lost power, embraced the return of monarchy. Though some remained steadfast, the term republic had lost its appeal, and many longed for the pageantry of a crown. Ryland, finally moved to action, declared that his patience had ended and he would soon dismantle this royalist movement. When Raymond entered the room, his supporters cheered, gathering around him to tally their votes and discuss the new members who had yet to declare their allegiance.

I do not rush at my opponent, risking a clumsy failure. Instead, I move to the side and approach slowly, so he never suspects I plan to strike. Then, in a flash, he is on his back, completely bewildered by how it happened. That is how I handled brother Dowley. I began speaking in a relaxed, casual tone, as if just passing the time. No one could have guessed where my argument was heading. Boys, there are many strange things about laws, customs, and the way human opinion evolves. Written laws fade, but unwritten ones are eternal. Consider the unwritten law of wages: they must rise gradually over the centuries. We know current wages, and we know what they were one or two hundred years ago. That history reveals the rate of progress, allowing us to estimate wages from centuries past. We do not stop there; we apply this law to the future. I can predict wages for hundreds of years to come. What, goodman, what! Yes. In seven hundred years, wages here will be six times higher; farmhands will earn three cents a day, and mechanics six. I wish I could die now and live then, interrupted Smug the wheelwright, his eyes glowing with greed. And that is not all; they will get their meals, too, though they will not be filling. Two hundred and fifty years later, pay attention, a mechanic’s wages will be twenty cents a day. The group gasped in astonishment, and Dickon the mason murmured, eyes and hands raised to the sky.

We finished our inspection by nightfall and left. On the way home, my companion stopped briefly at a newspaper office. I have mentioned that my friend had many quirks, and I always humored them. He chose not to speak of the murder until the following afternoon, when he suddenly asked if I had noticed anything peculiar at the crime scene. His emphasis on the word peculiar made me shudder for no apparent reason. I replied that I had seen nothing beyond what the papers reported. He dismissed the press, arguing that the police found the case impossible only because its bizarre nature should have made it easy to solve. They were baffled by the lack of motive for such brutality, the conflicting accounts of voices heard, and the fact that no one else was found in the room. The chaotic state of the apartment, the body shoved up the chimney, and the horrific mutilations had paralyzed the authorities. They made the common mistake of confusing the unusual with the complex. Yet, it is through these very deviations from the ordinary that reason finds the truth. In such cases, one must ask not what happened, but what has happened that is unprecedented. The ease with which I will solve this mystery is directly proportional to how impossible it seems to the police. I stared at him in silence. He looked toward our door and added that he was waiting for someone who, while perhaps not the killer, was certainly involved in the crimes.

Please consider, ma'am, Oliver said, tears welling despite his efforts. Think of how young and kind she is, and the joy she brings to everyone. I am certain that for your sake, and for hers, she will not die. Heaven would never let her pass so young. Hush, Mrs. Maylie said, resting a hand on his head. You speak like a child, but you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it, but I hope to be forgiven; I am old and have seen enough death to know the pain of losing those we love. I also know that the youngest and best are not always spared. Yet this brings comfort, for Heaven is just, and these trials remind us of a brighter world beyond. God's will be done. I love her, and He knows how deeply. Oliver was surprised to see Mrs. Maylie suddenly compose herself, her grief replaced by firm resolve. He was even more astonished that this strength held throughout the following days; she remained collected and diligent, performing her duties with a steady, almost cheerful demeanor. He was young and did not yet understand what strong minds can endure under pressure. An anxious night passed, and by morning, Mrs. Maylie's fears were confirmed. Rose had fallen into a dangerous fever. We must be active, Oliver, and avoid useless grief, Mrs. Maylie said, looking him in the eye. This letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne immediately. Take it to the market town four miles away by the footpath, and have them send an express rider to Chertsey. The inn staff will handle it, and I know I can trust you to see it done. Oliver could not speak, but his expression showed his eagerness to leave at once.

Elizabeth was deeply depressed, finding no joy in her usual activities. She felt that any happiness was a betrayal of the dead, believing that endless grief was the only proper response to such a tragic loss. She was no longer the cheerful girl who once walked by the lake with me, dreaming of our future. This first great sorrow had arrived, dimming her spirit and stealing her smiles. She told me, "When I think of Justine Moritz’s miserable death, my view of the world changes. I used to think of injustice as something distant or fictional, but now that misery has struck so close, people seem like monsters hungry for blood. I know I am being unfair, as everyone believed she was guilty. If she had actually murdered the child she helped raise for a few jewels, she would have been truly depraved. I could never support an execution, but I would have thought such a person unfit for society. Yet, I know she was innocent, and your agreement confirms it. Victor, when lies look so much like the truth, how can anyone be happy? I feel like I am walking on the edge of a cliff, surrounded by people trying to push me into the abyss. William and Justine were murdered, yet the killer remains free and perhaps even respected. Even if I were to face the scaffold for these crimes, I would never trade places with such a monster." I listened in agony, knowing that while I did not commit the act, I was the true cause of these deaths. Elizabeth saw my pain and took my hand, saying, "My dear friend, you must calm yourself. These events have hurt me deeply, but I am not as miserable as you are."

I do not have the nerves for this sort of thing. But could you really be comfortable spending the whole evening away from the poor boy? Yes, his father can, so why shouldn't I? Jemima is very careful and can send us updates every hour. I think Charles should have told his father we were all coming. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terrified yesterday, but today is different. Well, if you do not think it is too late, why not go with your husband? Leave little Charles in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove will not think it wrong if I am with him. Are you serious? Mary asked, her eyes brightening. That is a wonderful idea. I might as well go, as I am of no use at home and it only stresses me out. You, who do not have a mother's feelings, are the best person for this. You can make little Charles do anything; he always listens to you. It will be much better than leaving him with only Jemima. I will certainly go. They want me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being alone. What an excellent thought, Anne. I will tell Charles and get ready immediately. You can send for us if anything happens, but I am sure there will be no trouble. I would not go if I were not completely at ease about my dear child. A moment later, she was knocking at her husband's door. As Anne followed her upstairs, she heard Mary say excitedly, I am going with you, Charles, because I am no more useful at home than you are. If I stayed with the child forever, I could not make him do anything he disliked. Anne will stay; she offered to look after him. It is her own idea, so I will go with you, which is much better since I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday. This is very kind of Anne, her husband replied, and I would be glad to have you go, but it seems unfair that she should be left alone to nurse our sick child.

The day unfolded much like the previous one. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent the morning with the patient, who was recovering, albeit slowly. In the evening, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room. There was no card game; Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley sat nearby, watching him and repeatedly interrupting to send messages to his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley played piquet, watched by Mrs. Hurst. Elizabeth picked up some needlework, amused by the interaction between Darcy and Miss Bingley. The lady’s constant praise of his handwriting, the straightness of his lines, or the length of his letter, contrasted with his complete indifference, made for an interesting exchange that confirmed Elizabeth’s assessment of them both. "Miss Darcy will be so pleased to receive this!" He did not respond. "You write incredibly fast." "You are mistaken. I write quite slowly." "You must have to write so many letters every year! Business letters, too! I would find them detestable." "It is fortunate, then, that they fall to me rather than you." "Please tell your sister I look forward to seeing her." "I have already told her that, as you requested." "I fear you do not like your pen. Let me sharpen it; I am quite good at it." "Thank you, but I always sharpen my own." "How do you manage to write so evenly?" He remained silent. "Tell your sister I am thrilled to hear of her progress on the harp, and that I am absolutely delighted with her design for a table; it is far superior to Miss Grantley’s." "May I save your praise for my next letter? I have no room to include it now." "Oh, it does not matter. I will see her in January. But do you always write such wonderful, long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?" "They are usually long, but whether they are wonderful is not for me to say." "I believe that anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write poorly." "That is not much of a compliment to Darcy, Caroline," her brother interjected, "because he does not write with ease. He struggles too much to find complex words. Don't you, Darcy?" "My writing style is quite different from yours." "Oh," Miss Bingley exclaimed, "Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable."

Do you visit often? I have never returned since. Neither have I. As the moon rose, I remembered the calm expression on his face before he passed, and the pressure of his hand when I spoke his final words. Estella broke the silence. I have often intended to return, but circumstances prevented me. This poor, old place. Moonlight caught the mist and the tears falling from her eyes. Unaware I saw them, she composed herself and asked, Were you wondering why it was left like this? Yes, Estella. The land is mine. It is the only thing I kept. Everything else is gone, but I held onto this despite years of misery. Is it being developed? Finally, yes. I came to say goodbye before it changes. And you, she asked with genuine concern, do you still live abroad? Still. And you are doing well, I hope? I work hard for a living, so yes, I am doing well. I have thought of you often, Estella said. Have you? Lately, yes. For a long time, I suppressed the memory of what I discarded before I understood its value. But now that I am free to remember, I have made room for you in my heart. You have always held a place in mine, I replied. We fell silent until she spoke again. I never imagined I would say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place, she said. I am glad I did. Glad to part again? Parting is painful for me; the memory of our last farewell has always been sorrowful. But you told me, God bless you, God forgive you, she replied earnestly. If you could say that then, you will say it now, now that suffering has taught me to understand your heart. I have been bent and broken, but I hope I have been reshaped into something better.

We declared our freedom so boisterously that the liberty-obsessed orator and his followers took notice, surrounding us with a menacing air. The speaker declared that if we were truly free, Britain’s divine protections would shield us, and demanded we present evidence. When I hesitated, the king erupted, calling the man mad and insisting the burden of proof lay with the accuser. The king understood the law only in theory, not in practice, as people often do until it affects them personally. The crowd grew disinterested as the orator shifted to a practical tone, explaining that since we were strangers, the law required us to prove we were not slaves. I pleaded for time to send for verification, but he dismissed the request as an unreasonable inconvenience to our master. When the king began to shout that he had no master, I silenced him, fearing we would be branded lunatics. Ultimately, the earl auctioned us off. This same cruel law had existed in the American South centuries later, yet it only felt truly demonic once I was the one on the block. We were sold like livestock; because the market was stagnant, we fetched a price so low it still shames me to recall.

Nearly twelve months had elapsed since my father came home, and the year had nearly completed its cycle. It was late May; the forests were dressed in vibrant green, and the scent of freshly cut hay filled the air. I hoped the gentle atmosphere and the beauty of the landscape might help soften his disposition, fostering the tranquility and affection necessary for the trust I intended to earn. I selected an evening for this purpose, inviting him for a stroll. I guided him to a nearby beech grove, where the delicate shade protected us from the sun’s low, brilliant rays. After walking silently, we sat upon a mossy mound. I can still picture the location vividly: slender, smooth trunks wrapped in dark, glossy ivy, contrasting with the pale bark and bright foliage of young beech shoots. The ground was a mix of grass, moss, and scattered autumn leaves gathered by the wind, punctuated by weathered stumps. The breeze stirred the canopy, revealing the azure sky above. As twilight approached, the distant trees glowed red in the sunset, the wind vanished, and birds flew toward their nests. We sat there, and when you learn of the horrors that later shattered our souls in that serene place—a spot that could have been a paradise—you will understand why I recall it so clearly. I observed the scenery, hoping its stillness would grant me composure and eloquence. My heart raced as I prepared to speak, resolute yet fearful of his reaction. Finally, I began with hesitation: Your kindness and the profound affection you showed me upon your return will, I hope, forgive my boldness in addressing you not only as a daughter, but with the candor of a friend and equal.

Do not misunderstand; I was never truly insane. I remained aware of my condition even when frantic thoughts pushed me toward madness, keeping them hidden in silence and solitude. Those around me noticed nothing. They saw only a broken-spirited girl who spoke softly, her eyes often downcast to hide tears. I was someone who craved isolation, avoided attention, and never smiled—that was all. Eventually, I escaped. I left my guardian’s home and vanished; based on the letters I left behind, people assumed I had taken my own life. Consequently, the search for me was half-hearted, and I was soon forgotten. I departed London on a small ship bound for northern England. Once I succeeded, peace returned. As the ship glided over calm seas, I sat on deck beneath the open sky, feeling transformed. I was no longer the raving, miserable Mathilda, but a young hermit dedicated to seclusion, determined to keep my heart free from turmoil and despair. My simple, nun-like attire, the secret of my survival, and the prospect of a solitary future soothed my wounded spirit. The breeze refreshed me, and I watched the sun glinting off the waves and birds skimming the water. I slept without dreams and woke to enjoy my quiet freedom. After four days, we reached port. I moved inland immediately, seeking a solitary house on a vast plain, far from others, where I could view the horizon and wander undisturbed. I was not a misanthrope, but I knew my peace required solitude. I settled in a desolate, stony heath, where short grass grew and rushes clustered around a small pool.

Mr. Merton felt quite troubled by the wedding’s second delay, and Lady Julia, having already purchased her gown, urged Sybil to end the engagement. Despite her deep devotion to her mother, Sybil had committed her future to Lord Arthur and remained steadfast. Lord Arthur struggled for days with his frustration, his nerves frayed by the setback. Eventually, his practical nature prevailed, and he concluded that since poison had failed, an explosive device was the logical next step. He reviewed his acquaintances and decided to target his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a scholar with a passion for antique clocks, a hobby Lord Arthur believed provided the perfect opening for his plan. Finding an explosive proved difficult; the London Directory offered no leads, and he doubted Scotland Yard would be helpful, as they rarely anticipated such events. Years ago, I became close with William Legrand. He came from an old Huguenot family and was once wealthy, but a string of misfortunes left him destitute. To escape the shame of his losses, he left New Orleans, his ancestral home, and moved to Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston, South Carolina. This island is unique, consisting mostly of sea sand, three miles long and less than a quarter-mile wide. It is separated from the mainland by a narrow creek winding through reeds and mud, a haven for marsh hens. Vegetation is sparse and stunted. Aside from the western tip near Fort Moultrie, where some modest summer cottages for Charleston residents stand among palmettos, the island is covered in dense thickets of sweet myrtle. These shrubs grow up to fifteen feet high, forming nearly impenetrable groves that fill the air with scent. Deep within these thickets, near the island's eastern end, Legrand built a small hut where he lived when I first met him by chance. Our acquaintance quickly grew into friendship, as the recluse was a man of deep intellect and character. However, he was prone to misanthropy and erratic shifts between intense enthusiasm and deep melancholy. Though he owned many books, he rarely read them, preferring to hunt, fish, or wander the beach and myrtle groves searching for shells and insects. His collection of specimens would have impressed any expert. He was usually accompanied by an elderly man named Jupiter, a formerly enslaved person who had been freed before the family's decline. Jupiter refused to leave his young master’s side, regardless of threats or promises. It is likely that Legrand’s relatives, fearing he was mentally unstable, had encouraged Jupiter’s stubborn loyalty to ensure the wanderer was watched over.

Felix’s sorrow vanished, replaced by an ecstatic joy that made him appear as radiant as she. The woman wiped away tears and extended her hand, which Felix kissed passionately, calling her his sweet Arabian. She smiled, seemingly unaware of his language. He helped her dismount, dismissed the guide, and led her inside. After a brief exchange with his father, the stranger knelt at the old man’s feet; he lifted her up and embraced her warmly. Soon, a group of Tom and Joe’s friends gathered by the fence. They spoke in hushed, reverent tones about the last things the boys had said or done, pointing out exactly where they had stood. Each child recounted their final interactions, claiming they felt a strange, ominous sensation at the time that they only now understood. A debate broke out over who had seen the boys last, with many children competing for the grim honor. Those who could prove they were the final people to speak to the lost boys gained a sense of sacred importance, envied by the others. One boy even tried to claim status by bragging that Tom Sawyer had once beaten him up, but the others dismissed this, as most of them had shared that experience. The group eventually drifted away, continuing to share memories of their lost friends in hushed, awed voices.

When I first caught Tom alone, I inquired about his original plan for the escape—what he intended to do if we successfully freed a man who was already legally liberated. He explained that his vision had always been to float Jim downriver on the raft, seeking adventures until we reached the river's mouth. Afterward, we would reveal his freedom, return him home in style via steamboat, compensate him for his time, and organize a grand procession with torches and a brass band to welcome him as a hero. I decided, however, that things turned out for the best as they were. We freed Jim from his shackles quickly. Once Aunt Polly, Uncle Silas, and Aunt Sally learned how diligently he had assisted the doctor in nursing Tom, they treated him with great kindness, providing him with excellent food and leisure. We visited him in the sickroom for a long conversation, where Tom gave Jim forty dollars for his patient cooperation. Jim was overjoyed, exclaiming that his earlier predictions on Jackson's Island had come true, proving that his signs were indeed accurate. Tom then suggested that the three of us sneak away soon to acquire gear and embark on wild adventures among the Indians in the Territory for a few weeks. I agreed, though I noted I lacked the funds for supplies and doubted I could get any from home, assuming my father had returned to seize my money from Judge Thatcher. Tom assured me that my six thousand dollars remained untouched and that my father had not returned.

Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay, was finally brought to trial. The judges wore feathered hats, but the rough red cap and tricolor cockade were the standard attire. Observing the jury and the rowdy crowd, he felt as if the natural order had inverted, with criminals judging the innocent. The city's most vicious elements dominated the room, shouting, cheering, and dictating the outcome without restraint. Many men carried weapons, while some women brandished knives or daggers, and others ate or knitted. Among the knitters sat a woman beside Defarge, a man Darnay recognized from his arrival. She whispered to her husband, yet neither ever glanced at the prisoner, staring only at the jury with grim resolve. Below the President sat Doctor Manette, who, along with Mr. Lorry, remained dressed in ordinary clothes, unlike the others who had adopted the coarse style of the revolution. The prosecutor charged Darnay as an emigrant, subject to the death penalty under a decree that banished all such individuals. It mattered little that the law postdated his return; he was in France, and they demanded his life. The crowd roared for his execution, branding him an enemy of the Republic. When the President silenced the room, he questioned Darnay about his years in England. Darnay admitted to living there but denied being an emigrant in the legal sense. He argued that he had voluntarily abandoned his title and status, leaving France before the term was even defined, choosing to support himself through his own labor rather than exploit the burdened people of his homeland.
