The letter is brief, just to give us notice. It says they are all coming to town immediately because of Mrs. Churchill. She has been unwell all winter and finds Enscombe too cold, so they are moving south quickly. Indeed, from Yorkshire? Yes, about one hundred and ninety miles from London, quite a journey. It is significant, certainly. Sixty-five miles further than from Maple Grove to London. But distance means little to the wealthy. You would be amazed at how my brother, Mr. Suckling, travels. He and Mr. Bragge once went to London and back twice in a single week with four horses. The trouble with the distance from Enscombe, Mr. Weston noted, is that Mrs. Churchill has reportedly been unable to leave her sofa for a week. In his last letter, Frank mentioned she was too weak to reach her conservatory without the support of both his arm and his uncle’s.

“Certainly not,” Duff answered. “And, interpreting the term yokel for the ladies, I assume you mean this attempt was not the work of a countryman?” Mr. Losberne asked with a smile. “That is it, sir,” Blathers replied. “This concerns the robbery, does it?” “Entirely,” the doctor said. “Now, what is this regarding the boy the servants are discussing?” Blathers inquired. “Nothing at all,” the doctor replied. “A frightened servant imagined he was involved in the break-in, but it is pure nonsense.” “Easily dismissed, then,” Duff remarked. “He is right,” Blathers added, nodding while toying with his handcuffs. “Who is the boy? What is his story? Where is he from? He did not fall from the sky, did he?” “Of course not,” the doctor said, glancing nervously at the ladies. “I know his history, but we can discuss that later. You would prefer to see where the thieves attempted entry first, I suppose?” “Certainly,” Blathers agreed. “We should inspect the premises before questioning the servants. That is standard procedure.” Lights were brought, and Blathers and Duff, accompanied by the constable, Brittles, Giles, and the others, entered the small room to examine the window. They then circled the lawn to view it from outside, inspected the shutter with a candle, traced footprints with a lantern, and poked the bushes with a pitchfork. Once finished, they returned inside, where Giles and Brittles reenacted their roles from the previous night’s events, performing the scene six times and contradicting each other more frequently with each repetition. When finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room for a private consultation, which was conducted with a gravity far exceeding that of a medical board. Meanwhile, the doctor paced the adjacent room in distress, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious expressions. “Upon my word,” he said, stopping after many rapid turns, “I hardly know how to proceed.”

Upon waking, Tom initially felt disoriented. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and surveyed his surroundings, soon realizing where he was. The woods were bathed in the cool, gray light of dawn, offering a profound sense of tranquility and stillness. Nature seemed lost in meditation, with no breeze to stir the leaves. Dew clung to the vegetation, while the campfire lay beneath a blanket of ash, sending a slender plume of blue smoke upward. Joe and Huck remained fast asleep. Soon, a bird chirped in the distance, followed by a reply and the rhythmic tapping of a woodpecker. As the gray morning light brightened, the forest stirred with life. Tom watched in wonder as nature awakened. A small green worm crawled across a leaf, periodically arching its body as if measuring the distance. Tom sat motionless as the creature approached, his excitement growing until it finally climbed onto his leg, which he took as a certain omen that he would soon possess a new, flamboyant pirate costume. Nearby, ants busily went about their tasks, one hauling a spider several times its size up a tree. Tom recited a rhyme to a ladybug, prompting it to fly away, a result he expected given the insect's known gullibility. A tumblebug rolled its ball, feigning death when Tom touched it. By now, the birds were clamorous. A catbird sang from above, mimicking its peers, while a vibrant blue jay landed nearby to inspect the boys with intense curiosity. Squirrels darted about, pausing to chatter at the intruders, clearly unaccustomed to the presence of humans.

Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, knights of the castle, clashed with Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay, shattering their spears upon impact. Sir Pertolope then emerged from the castle to face Sir Lionel, whom the green knight promptly unhorsed. Heralds carefully recorded the performance of every combatant. Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth but was himself thrown to the ground. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin challenged Gareth, only to be struck down as well. Sir Galihud attempted to avenge his brother, but Gareth defeated him just as he had the others, along with Sir Dinadan, La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore, and Sir Dodinas, all of whom he unhorsed with a single spear. King Agwisance of Ireland watched in amazement as the knight shifted colors between green and blue with every pass, making him impossible to identify. Gareth then unhorsed King Agwisance, King Carados of Scotland, King Uriens of Gore, and Sir Bagdemagus. When Bagdemagus’s son, Meliganus, broke a spear against him, Prince Galahault challenged the multicolored knight to a duel. Gareth struck the prince’s helmet so forcefully that he nearly fell, saved only by his men. King Arthur praised the knight’s skill and asked Sir Launcelot to challenge him. Launcelot refused, stating that the knight had already endured enough labor for one day. He argued that it would be dishonorable to interrupt such a display of prowess, especially since the knight was clearly fighting for a lady’s favor. Launcelot declared that he would not deny the man his well-earned glory.

Mrs. Musgrove seized a moment alone with Anne to remark, "Oh, Miss Anne, I truly wish Mrs. Charles possessed your way with those children. They behave like entirely different beings when they are with you! They are generally so coddled, it is a shame you cannot teach your sister how to handle them. They are such robust, healthy little things, but Mrs. Charles has no idea how to manage them. They can be so vexing that I hesitate to invite them over as often as I might. I suspect Mrs. Charles is annoyed by my reluctance, but it is exhausting to constantly correct children or bribe them with excessive sweets just to keep them quiet." Mary also shared her own grievances, claiming, "Mrs. Musgrove believes her servants are paragons of virtue, but her housemaid and laundry-maid are constantly wandering the village instead of working. I see them everywhere, and they are always trying to lead Jemima astray. If she were not so reliable, they would certainly ruin her." Conversely, Mrs. Musgrove confided to Anne, "I never interfere in my daughter-in-law's affairs, but I must tell you that I distrust her nursery-maid. She is always out and about, and her obsession with fine clothing is a bad influence on the other staff. Mrs. Charles trusts her implicitly, but I wanted to warn you so you might keep a watchful eye and speak up if you notice anything wrong." Finally, Mary complained that Mrs. Musgrove frequently failed to grant her the social precedence she deserved during dinners at the Great House, failing to see why her status as family should cost her proper recognition.

The next morning, the Otis family discussed the ghost over breakfast. Mr. Otis was annoyed that his gift had been rejected. He stated that while he did not want to hurt the ghost, throwing pillows at him was rude, considering how long he had lived there. The twins laughed at this, but Mr. Otis insisted that if the ghost refused to use the lubricant, they would have to take his chains away because the noise made sleeping impossible. For the rest of the week, they were left alone, though the bloodstain on the library floor kept reappearing. This was odd because Mr. Otis locked the doors and windows every night. The stain also changed colors, shifting from dull red to vermilion, purple, and even bright emerald-green. The family found these changes amusing and often bet on the next color, though little Virginia was always distressed by the stain and nearly cried when it turned green. The ghost appeared again on Sunday night. A loud crash in the hall brought the family downstairs, where they found a suit of armor on the floor and the ghost sitting in a chair, rubbing his knees in pain. The twins immediately shot pellets at him, while Mr. Otis pointed his revolver and ordered him to put his hands up. The ghost shrieked in anger and vanished through them like mist, blowing out Washington’s candle and leaving everyone in the dark.

The youth were desperate to visit Lyme. Captain Wentworth mentioned returning, as it was merely seventeen miles from Uppercross. Despite it being November, the weather remained fair. Louisa, the most enthusiastic of the group, decided they must go. Pleased to have her own way and convinced of the virtue in her persistence, she overcame her parents' desire to delay the trip until summer. Thus, Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth prepared to depart. The initial plan to travel and return in a single day was rejected by Mr. Musgrove to protect his horses. Upon reflection, a November day offered little time for sightseeing once the seven-hour journey was subtracted. They agreed to stay overnight, returning the following day. This change was welcomed. Although they gathered early at the Great House and departed promptly, it was well past noon when the two carriages—Mr. Musgrove’s coach carrying the ladies and Charles’s curricle with the Captain—descended the long hill into Lyme. It was clear they would have little daylight left to explore. After settling into an inn and ordering dinner, they immediately walked toward the sea. Arriving late in the season, they found none of the typical diversions of a public resort. The rooms were closed, and most visitors had departed. Since the architecture offered little interest, the town’s unique geography became the focus. The main street plunging toward the water, the path to the Cobb along the bay, and the striking cliffs to the east were the primary attractions. Only a very peculiar traveler would fail to find the surroundings of Lyme captivating enough to warrant further exploration.

Jupiter could barely contain his joy at the sight, but his master looked deeply disappointed. He urged us to keep digging, and I had barely started again when I tripped over a large iron ring half-buried in the loose soil. We began working in earnest, and I have never experienced ten minutes of such intense excitement. We unearthed an oblong wooden chest, preserved so well and hardened by some mineral process that it remained perfectly intact. The box measured three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep. It was reinforced with riveted iron bands forming a trellis pattern. Six iron rings, three on each side, allowed for a firm grip, yet our combined strength barely budged the heavy coffer. We realized moving it was impossible. Fortunately, the lid was held only by two sliding bolts. We pulled them back, trembling with anxiety. Instantly, a treasure of immense value was revealed. As our lantern light hit the pit, a dazzling glow erupted from a chaotic pile of gold and jewels. I cannot describe my feelings; amazement was the primary emotion. Legrand seemed exhausted and spoke little. Jupiter’s face turned as pale as possible, and he looked completely stunned. He fell to his knees, plunged his bare arms into the gold up to his elbows, and let them rest there as if bathing. Finally, he sighed and muttered to himself, "And this all came from the gold-bug! The pretty gold-bug! The poor little gold-bug I treated so roughly! Aren't you ashamed of yourself? Answer me that!" Eventually, I had to remind them that we needed to move the treasure. It was getting late, and we had to secure everything before dawn. We were all so disoriented that we spent a long time debating what to do next.

Count Rouvaloff stared at him in astonishment for a moment, then realizing his sincerity, scribbled an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and passed it over. Scotland Yard would pay dearly for this information, he remarked. Lord Arthur laughed, declaring they would never obtain it. After shaking the Russian’s hand, he hurried out, checked the address, and instructed his driver to head for Soho Square. Dismissing the carriage, he wandered down Greek Street until he reached Bayle’s Court. Passing through the archway, he entered a strange dead-end street filled with a French laundry, where clotheslines crisscrossed the space, fluttering with white linen. He reached the end and knocked at a small green house. Following a pause, during which curious faces appeared in every window, a disheveled foreigner opened the door and demanded his business in broken English. Lord Arthur presented the paper from Count Rouvaloff. The man bowed and ushered him into a worn parlor. Shortly after, Herr Winckelkopf entered, wearing a wine-spotted napkin and holding a fork. Lord Arthur introduced himself as Robert Smith and requested an explosive clock. The German laughed, greeting him as Lord Arthur and mentioning he had seen him at Lady Windermere’s. He invited his guest to join him for breakfast, offering pâté and fine Rhine wine. Before Lord Arthur could recover from the shock of being identified, he was seated in the back room, enjoying excellent wine and conversing with the notorious conspirator. Herr Winckelkopf noted that explosive clocks were poor exports, as unreliable train schedules often caused them to detonate prematurely.

Mr. Otis was troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the peer remained firm. He eventually convinced the Minister to let his daughter keep the ghost’s gift. In the spring of 1890, when the young Duchess of Cheshire was presented at the Queen’s first drawing-room following her wedding, her jewels were universally admired. Virginia had received the coronet, the reward for all good American girls, and married her childhood sweetheart once he came of age. They were so charming and devoted that everyone was delighted, except for the Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had unsuccessfully tried to secure the Duke for one of her seven daughters, and, oddly, Mr. Otis himself. While fond of the young Duke, Mr. Otis theoretically opposed titles, fearing that the influence of a pleasure-seeking aristocracy might erode republican simplicity. His objections were overruled, and as he walked his daughter down the aisle at St. George’s, Hanover Square, he was surely the proudest man in England. After their honeymoon, the couple visited Canterville Chase. The day after arriving, they walked to the secluded churchyard near the pine woods. After much debate, Sir Simon’s tombstone was engraved only with his initials and the verse from the library window. Virginia scattered roses on the grave before they wandered into the ruined abbey. She sat on a fallen pillar while her husband lounged at her feet, smoking. He soon discarded his cigarette, took her hand, and asked her to share the secrets she had kept from him. He pressed her to reveal what occurred while she was locked away with the ghost. Virginia replied solemnly that she had never told anyone.

Biddy wept, and the darkening garden, the lane, and the emerging stars blurred in my own vision. Nothing was ever discovered, Biddy? Nothing. Do you know what became of Orlick? Based on his clothing, I believe he works in the quarries. You have seen him, then? Why are you staring at that dark tree in the lane? I saw him there the night she died. That was not the last time, was it? No, I have seen him there since we have been walking here. It is useless, Biddy said, placing a hand on my arm as I prepared to run out. You know I would not deceive you; he was only there for a minute and is gone now. I was filled with indignation that she was still being pursued by him, and I felt a deep hatred toward him. I told her I would spend any amount of money or effort to drive him from the area. Gradually, she guided me toward a calmer conversation, telling me how much Joe loved me and how he never complained, though she did not explicitly mention my own failings. I understood her meaning; Joe simply did his duty with a strong hand, a quiet tongue, and a gentle heart. It would be hard to praise him enough, I said. Biddy, we must speak of these things often, as I intend to visit here frequently. I am not going to leave poor Joe alone. Biddy said nothing. Biddy, do you not hear me? Yes, Mr. Pip. Aside from you calling me Mr. Pip, which I find in poor taste, what do you mean? What do I mean? Biddy asked timidly. Biddy, I said with self-righteousness, I must know what you mean by this. By this? Biddy asked. Do not echo me, I retorted. You used to not echo, Biddy. Used not! Biddy exclaimed. Oh, Mr. Pip! Used! I decided to drop that point. After another silent walk in the garden, I returned to my main concern. Biddy, I said, I mentioned that I would come here often to see Joe, and you received that with silence. Please tell me why. Are you quite sure that you will come to see him often? Biddy asked, stopping in the garden path and looking at me under the stars with clear, honest eyes.

Mrs. Clay’s feelings had outweighed her ambition, leading her to sacrifice her long-term schemes for Sir Walter for the sake of a young man. Yet, she possesses both heart and intellect, leaving it uncertain whose manipulation will ultimately prevail; having prevented her from marrying Sir Walter, the young man might still be charmed into making her the wife of Sir William. Sir Walter and Elizabeth were undoubtedly shaken and humiliated by the loss of their companion and the realization of her duplicity. While they could seek comfort from their prominent cousins, they were left to realize that flattering others without receiving the same in return offers only a hollow satisfaction. Anne, confident that Lady Russell had come to appreciate Captain Wentworth, felt only one shadow over her future: the lack of a family she could offer him that a sensible man would value. She felt this inferiority deeply. The financial disparity meant nothing to her, but having no respectable, harmonious family to welcome him—unlike the warmth she received from his own siblings—caused her genuine distress. She had only two friends to introduce to him: Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. He was happy to embrace both. He could now sincerely value Lady Russell, and while he did not have to agree with her past interference, he was prepared to praise her in every other regard. Mrs. Smith, meanwhile, had earned her place through her own merits. Her recent kindness toward Anne was sufficient, and their marriage gained Anne a second friend rather than losing one. Mrs. Smith was their first visitor once they settled down. Captain Wentworth fully repaid her past kindness by helping her recover her husband’s West Indian property, acting with the resolve of a loyal friend to guide her through every legal complication.

Though it is merely four, the winter sun has vanished. The sky is clear and freezing, lacking clouds to catch the light, yet the air holds a faint pink hue that mirrors onto the snow-dusted earth. I dwell in a solitary cottage upon a vast, empty heath, isolated from all human sound. The barren plain is blanketed in white, broken only by dark spots where the midday sun cleared the sharp hilltops. A few birds forage on the frozen pools, remnants of a long-standing frost. My mental state is peculiar. I am entirely alone, withered by the touch of misfortune. Knowing my end is near, I feel a strange joy. My pulse races, and my thin hand burns against my cheek; the flickering spirit within me is casting its final sparks. I will not witness another winter or feel the summer sun again, and with this certainty, I begin to record my tragic story. Perhaps this history should perish with me, but an indefinable urge compels me, and I lack the strength to resist. When I was vibrant, I believed my tale held a sacred horror that forbade speech, yet now, facing death, I reveal its dark secrets. It is a grove reserved for the dying, and like Oedipus, I approach my end. What am I setting down? I must gather my thoughts. I assume only you, my friend, will read these pages after I pass. I write as if for strangers, though I cherish our bond. You have frequently questioned my isolation, my tears, and my guarded silence. I dared not speak while living, but in death, I disclose the truth. While others may discard these pages, to you, Woodville, they will be precious—a testament from a broken-hearted girl who, even in death, feels warmth from your kindness. I know you will weep over these accounts of my suffering, and for that sympathy, I am grateful while I still draw breath.

I now move to the most emotional part of my story. I will describe events that shaped me into the person I am today. Spring arrived quickly with clear skies and pleasant weather. I was amazed that the once gloomy landscape was now filled with beautiful flowers and greenery. My senses were delighted by the many pleasant scents and sights. One day, while the family rested and the old man played his guitar, I noticed Felix looked deeply sad. He sighed often, and when his father asked why, Felix answered with a forced cheerfulness. Suddenly, someone knocked at the door. A lady on horseback arrived with a guide. She wore a dark outfit and a thick black veil. When Agatha asked who she was, the stranger simply said the name Felix in a sweet, melodic voice. Hearing this, Felix rushed to her. She lifted her veil, revealing a face of angelic beauty with dark, braided hair, gentle eyes, and a fair complexion with rosy cheeks. Felix was overjoyed, his sadness replaced by an intense happiness that made him look as radiant as she was. The lady wiped away tears and held out her hand, which Felix kissed passionately, calling her his sweet Arabian. She smiled, though she did not seem to understand his words. He helped her down, sent the guide away, and brought her inside. After a brief conversation, the young woman knelt before the old man, who kindly lifted her up and embraced her. I soon realized that while she spoke a language of her own, she and the cottagers could not understand one another.

There was a peculiar fascination in all this that captivated me. He seemed to have roused from a lengthy, dreamlike slumber, feeling much like one of the seven sleepers or Nourjahad from that charming oriental fable. Diana had vanished, his acquaintances were altered or deceased, and upon his awakening, I remained his sole object of affection. How precious the landscapes of Loch Lomond became with such a cherished companion for my excursions. I explored every enchanting location with my father, from the islands to the shaded waterfalls and fern-covered paths. His discourse broadened my perspective, making me feel reborn with the vitality of a new existence; his arrival had shifted me from a confined corner of the world into an expansive universe. My life had previously resembled a modest stream destined to vanish quietly within its native fields, but it had transformed into a diverse river winding through a lush, ever-changing landscape. I remained unaware of the barren wilderness ahead, the jagged rocks that would lacerate its currents, and the grotesque reflections that would haunt its surface. Life shone brightly then, and as I began to embrace hope, I learned that nothing brings deeper despair than hope shattered. Is it not odd that such sublime joy should be so swiftly followed by sorrow? I sipped from a magical chalice, only to find bitterness lurking beneath its lingering sweetness. My heart overflowed with profound, tranquil affection, oblivious to the possibility that love could breed misery—a lesson I was forced to learn in a uniquely harsh manner. I mourn, and shall always mourn, those brief months of Edenic bliss; I broke no rules and tasted no forbidden fruit, yet I was cruelly cast out. My companion transgressed, and I was plunged into his ruin. But I digress; let grief arrive in its own time, for I may still speak of happiness at this point in my narrative. Three months of this delightful companionship elapsed before my aunt fell ill. I spent a month nursing her, but her ailment proved fatal, and her death left me inconsolable for a time. Death is terrifying to the living; the bonds of habit are so potent, even without the ties of affection, that their severance inevitably agonizes the heart.

I walked beside a burly man with a cheerful face, hoping to strike up a conversation and learn more, but he immediately began telling that same tired anecdote Sir Dinadan had shared when I first clashed with Sir Sagramor. I excused myself and fell to the back of the group, feeling disheartened and weary of this life of struggle and defeat, yet fearing the finality of death and the prospect of encountering that same story in eternity. By early afternoon, we caught up to another group of pilgrims, but this one was devoid of any joy or laughter. It included people of all ages, from the elderly to infants, yet every face was marked by the hollow hopelessness born of long-term suffering. They were slaves. Shackles bound their hands and feet to waist belts, and the adults were chained together by their collars. They had walked three hundred miles in eighteen days on meager rations, sleeping huddled together like animals. They wore only rags, and their irons had caused festering, maggot-ridden sores on their ankles. Their feet were raw, and every one of them limped. Originally a group of one hundred, half had been sold along the way. The trader in charge rode a horse, carrying a heavy, multi-tailed whip. He never spoke, using the lash to strike the shoulders of anyone who stumbled from exhaustion, forcing them back into line.

The woman wiped away tears and held out her hand, which he kissed passionately, calling her his sweet Arabian. She smiled, seemingly not understanding his words. Raymond felt energized by his return to health. He believed his role as general of the Athenians matched his ambition, and he viewed the potential conquest of Constantinople as a historic achievement—a feat unmatched in human records. He envisioned rescuing this beautiful, ancient city from Muslim control and restoring it to a people known for their genius and love of liberty. Perdita found comfort in his recovery, his love, and his growing fame, feeling as relaxed as if she were resting on a luxurious couch. Every thought brought her joy, and her emotions felt perfectly at peace. We reached Kishan on July 7th. The weather throughout our journey was calm. Each day, we broke camp before dawn, watching the shadows fade as the sun rose in golden splendor. Our soldiers greeted the beauty of nature with lively enthusiasm, singing triumphant songs at sunrise while birds filled the gaps in their music. At noon, we rested in shady valleys or wooded mountains, lulled to sleep by the sound of streams flowing over pebbles. Our evening marches were even more delightful than the mornings. When the band played, they chose gentle melodies about love or longing, often ending with solemn hymns that matched the peaceful evening and inspired deep, spiritual thoughts. Sometimes, we fell silent to listen to nightingales, watching fireflies dance while the soft call of the aziolo promised good weather. In the valleys, we were surrounded by soft shadows and colorful rocks. From the mountains, Greece appeared like a living map beneath us, with its famous peaks piercing the sky and rivers winding like silver threads through the fertile land. We English travelers watched this magnificent landscape in awe, struck by how different it was from the muted, somber beauty of our homeland. As we left Macedonia, the flat plains of Thrace offered fewer sights, yet the journey remained engaging. An advance guard announced our arrival, and the local people hurried to welcome Lord Raymond.

For a moment, I was too stunned to think clearly. I knew my own sketch differed in detail from this one, though the general outline was similar. I took a candle to the other side of the room to examine the parchment more closely. Turning it over, I found my own drawing on the back, exactly as I had left it. At first, I was merely surprised by the remarkable coincidence that a skull—matching my scarab in size and shape—had been on the other side of the paper all along. Such coincidences often leave the mind paralyzed as it struggles to find a logical connection. Once I recovered, however, a far more startling realization dawned on me. I clearly remembered that the parchment was blank when I drew the scarab. I was certain of this because I had checked both sides to find a clean spot. If the skull had been there, I would have seen it. This mystery felt impossible to explain, yet a faint intuition began to stir in my mind—a glimmer of the truth that last night’s events would eventually confirm. I stood up, secured the parchment, and stopped thinking about it until I could be alone. After you left and Jupiter fell asleep, I began a methodical investigation. I first considered how I acquired the parchment. We found the scarab on the mainland coast, a mile east of the island, just above the high-tide mark. When I picked it up, it bit me, causing me to drop it. Jupiter, with his usual caution, searched for a leaf to grab the insect after it flew toward him.

The surrounding oaks sheltered a colony of nightingales—I am transported back there now; young Idris, in the bloom of her youth, stands beside me—recall that I am merely twenty-two, and my beloved has seen barely seventeen summers. The river, bloated by autumn storms, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian was occupied in his preferred vessel with the perilous sport of snapping the highest branch from a sunken oak. Do you tire of existence, Adrian, that you toy so recklessly with peril? He secured his trophy and navigated the deluge; we watched him with anxious eyes, but the current swept him away, forcing him to dock downstream and travel a long path to rejoin us. He is safe, Idris remarked as he jumped ashore, brandishing the branch in triumph; we shall await him here. We remained alone; the sun had vanished, the nightingales commenced their melody, and the evening star glowed brightly within the lingering western light. My angelic companion gazed at that lovely symbol with her blue eyes. How the light flickers, she observed, as if it were the star’s own vitality. Its unsteady radiance suggests that its existence, much like our own, is uncertain; I believe it fears and loves. Do not study the star, my dear, selfless friend, I implored, nor seek love in its shivering beams; ignore distant spheres and mere fantasies of emotion. I have remained quiet for too long; I have yearned to speak to you, to surrender my soul and my entire being to your care. If you must look at the star, let its eternal glow plead my case; let it serve as my silent witness—love is to me what light is to that star; as long as it remains unextinguished, I shall love you. The ecstasy of that instant must remain hidden from the world’s indifferent gaze. I still feel her elegant frame pressed against my overflowing heart—my senses still falter at the memory of that initial kiss. We walked quietly to find Adrian, whose approach we heard nearby. I begged Adrian to return after escorting his sister home. That same night, as we strolled along the moonlit forest trails, I revealed my entire heart, its joy and its expectations, to my companion. For an instant, he appeared troubled. I should have anticipated this, he remarked, what conflict will follow now!

Once finished, additional loops were detached from the rim, more fabric was fed through, and the freed loops were secured to their corresponding buttons. This allowed the entire upper section of the bag to be positioned between the netting and the hoop. Clearly, the hoop would then descend into the car, leaving the total weight of the vessel and its cargo supported solely by the buttons. While this might appear insufficient, it was quite secure, as the buttons were robust and spaced closely enough that each bore only a fraction of the load. Even with triple the weight, I would have felt no concern. I then lifted the hoop back inside the rubberized covering, bracing it near its original height with three slender poles. This maintained the bag's upper tension and kept the lower netting correctly aligned. Finally, I sealed the enclosure's mouth by gathering the fabric folds and twisting them firmly from within using a fixed tourniquet. Three circular panes of thick, clear glass were set into the sides of the covering, providing a full horizontal view. A fourth window was placed in the bottom fabric, aligning with a small floor opening to allow a downward view. I could not install a similar overhead window due to the fabric folds at the closure, though this was inconsequential, as the balloon itself would have obstructed any upward sight. About a foot beneath one side window, an eight-inch circular opening with a threaded brass rim was installed. The condenser's large tube was screwed into this rim, with the device itself housed inside the gum-elastic chamber.

The refined gentlemen of noble lineage sported small hanging ornaments that chimed with their sluggish movements; these golden chains sounded like tiny bells. Between that tinkling and the soft swish of silk, brocade, and linen, the air held a lightness that kept the starving masses of Saint Antoine at a distance. Attire served as the constant charm to maintain social order. Everyone appeared dressed for an endless masquerade. From the Tuileries Palace, through the Court and legal chambers, down to the common executioner, the costume persisted. Even the hangman was expected to perform his duties while powdered, frizzled, and adorned in a gold-trimmed coat with silk stockings and pumps. At the gallows, Monsieur Paris presided in this elegant garb. In that year of our Lord seventeen hundred and eighty, who could doubt that a society anchored by a daintily dressed executioner would endure forever? After finishing his chocolate, Monseigneur had his inner sanctum doors opened and emerged. The display of groveling, fawning, and total servility was absolute; the courtiers bowed so deeply that they left nothing for Heaven, which perhaps explains why they never sought divine favor. Offering scattered promises and smiles, Monseigneur moved through his chambers before eventually retreating back into his sanctuary, hidden away by his attendants. When the spectacle concluded, the atmosphere grew restless, and the bells jingled as the crowd departed. Only one man remained, walking slowly past the mirrors with his hat tucked away and a snuff-box in hand. Pausing at the final exit, he turned toward the sanctuary and declared, I consign you to the Devil. He flicked the snuff from his fingertips as if shaking off dust and calmly descended the stairs.

No, that is for tomorrow; I specifically needed to speak with Knightley today regarding that matter. What a scorching, miserable morning! I walked across the fields, which only made it worse. To find him absent! I am quite displeased. No note, no message left for me. The housekeeper claimed she was unaware of my visit. It is very strange, and no one knew his destination. Perhaps Hartfield, the Abbey Mill, or his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is unlike our friend Knightley. Can you account for it? Emma feigned agreement that it was indeed odd, offering no defense for him. I cannot fathom, Mrs. Elton remarked, feeling the slight as a wife should, how he could treat you so, of all people! The last person one would expect him to neglect. My dear Mr. E., he surely left a message; his servants must have forgotten. That is likely the case, as the Donwell staff are notoriously clumsy and negligent. I would never tolerate such a person as his Harry at our sideboard. As for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks little of her; she promised a recipe and never delivered it. I encountered William Larkins near the house, Mr. Elton added, and he warned me his master was away, but I doubted him. William seemed irritable, complaining that he could rarely speak with his master lately. I care little for William’s grievances, but it is vital that I see Knightley today; this hot, fruitless walk is a serious inconvenience. Emma decided it was best to depart immediately. She was likely expected at home, and her absence might prevent Knightley from further offending Mr. Elton or William Larkins. She was glad when Miss Fairfax insisted on escorting her out, providing a moment for her to speak.

She would reside among those who cherished her and possessed greater wisdom than she; sufficiently secluded for security and busy enough to remain content. She would avoid temptation, neither seeking it nor being sought by it. She would lead a respectable, happy life, and Emma conceded that she was the most fortunate soul alive to have inspired such steadfast devotion in such a man—or, if not the absolute luckiest, second only to herself. Harriet, increasingly occupied by her commitments to the Martins, visited Hartfield less frequently, which was for the best. Their intimacy was destined to fade, transitioning into a more moderate goodwill, a shift that fortunately seemed to be occurring naturally and by degrees. By late September, Emma accompanied Harriet to the altar, witnessing her union with Robert Martin with a contentment that no recollection of Mr. Elton could diminish. Indeed, she barely noticed Mr. Elton, viewing him only as the minister whose benediction might soon be bestowed upon her own marriage. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, though the last to become engaged, were the first to wed. Jane Fairfax had departed Highbury, returning to the comforts of the Campbells, while the Churchills remained in town, awaiting November. Emma and Mr. Knightley had tentatively settled on the intervening month for their own nuptials, hoping to marry while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield so they might enjoy a two-week seaside excursion. Their friends fully supported the plan, but Mr. Woodhouse presented a challenge; he had always spoken of their union as a remote possibility. When first approached, his distress was so profound that they nearly despaired. A subsequent mention caused less agony, as he began to accept the inevitability of the event—a hopeful sign of resignation. Yet he remained unhappy, and his visible suffering sapped his daughter’s resolve. Unable to bear his pain or the thought that he felt abandoned, Emma hesitated, despite the reassurances of both Mr. Knightleys that his misery would prove fleeting once the wedding had passed.

Story! He seemed to deliberately misunderstand her, quickly adding, Yes, clients; in banking, we refer to our connections as clients. He was a French gentleman, a man of science and great learning—a doctor. Not from Beauvais? Yes, from Beauvais. Like your father, Monsieur Manette, he was well-regarded in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our relationship was professional, though confidential. I was working at our French branch then, as I had been for twenty years. At that time—may I ask when that was, sir? I am speaking of twenty years ago, miss. He married an Englishwoman, and I served as one of his trustees. His affairs, like those of many French families, were managed entirely by Tellson’s. I have acted as trustee for many clients in similar ways. These are strictly business matters; there is no friendship, no sentiment involved. I move from one to another just as I do throughout my workday. In short, I have no feelings; I am merely a machine. To continue— But this is my father’s story, sir; and I am beginning to think, she said, her brow furrowed in concentration, that when I was orphaned after my mother died two years after my father, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost certain it was you. Mr. Lorry took her hesitant hand, kissed it with formal grace, and led her back to her chair. Holding the back of the chair, he rubbed his chin and adjusted his wig, looking down at her as she gazed up at him. Miss Manette, it was I. You will see how truthfully I described myself as having no feelings, and that my connections to others are purely professional, when you consider that I have not seen you since. You have been a ward of Tellson’s, and I have been occupied with the firm’s other affairs. Feelings! I have no time or opportunity for them. I spend my entire life, miss, operating a vast financial machine.

She studied me intently for a moment before asking quietly, "What do you want for them?" I replied, "Only that you do not group them with the others. They may share the same blood, but they are not the same in nature." She persisted, "What do you want for them?" Feeling myself blush, I admitted, "I am not clever enough to hide that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would provide the funds to help my friend Herbert in a way he must never discover, I could show you how." She rested her hands on her cane to watch me more closely. "Why must he not know?" she asked. "Because I began helping him two years ago without his knowledge, and I do not want to be exposed. I cannot explain why I cannot finish the task; it is someone else's secret." She turned her gaze to the fire. After a long silence, the coals shifted, and she looked back at me with renewed focus. Estella continued knitting. Miss Havisham asked, "What else?" I turned to Estella, my voice shaking. "Estella, you know I love you. I have loved you for a long time." Estella looked up, her expression indifferent as her needles kept moving. Miss Havisham watched us both. "I would have said this sooner, but I was mistaken in thinking Miss Havisham intended us for each other. I held back while I believed you had no choice in the matter, but I must speak now." Estella kept knitting and shook her head. I responded to her gesture, "I know. I have no hope that you will ever be mine, Estella."

As we rode away, I remarked that I was now the owner of several knights. I wondered what I would do with such assets, perhaps raffle them off. I asked Sandy how many there were. She replied there were seven, along with their squires. I asked who they were and where they lived. Sandy seemed confused by my slang, repeating the phrase "hang out" with delight, testing the words as if they were a new discovery. I urged her to focus and tell me about the knights, but she began a long, rambling story. I realized my mistake; she was prone to endless, circular narratives that lacked a clear beginning or end. Interrupting her only made her restart the same sentence, yet I felt I had to try, as her monotonous storytelling was unbearable. When I exclaimed in frustration, she simply started over. I asked her to specify which knights she meant. She explained that Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine had stayed at an abbey before riding into a forest, where Gawaine spotted twelve young women and two armed knights near a tower.

I encountered the peculiar stranger I intend to describe at Warwick Castle. He drew my attention through his guileless nature, his extraordinary knowledge of historical armor, and the ease of his presence, as he carried the entire conversation. We gravitated toward one another at the rear of the tour group, and he immediately began sharing fascinating observations. As he spoke in a gentle, fluid manner, he seemed to slip away from the present, transporting me into a distant, forgotten age. He cast such a charm that I felt as though I were wandering among the ghosts and remnants of a gray antiquity, conversing with a survivor of that era. He discussed Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot, Sir Galahad, and the other legends of the Round Table with the familiarity one reserves for neighbors or acquaintances. As he continued, he appeared increasingly ancient, withered, and faded. Eventually, he turned to me and remarked as casually as if discussing the weather, "You are familiar with the transmigration of souls; are you aware of the transposition of epochs and bodies?" I replied that I had not, though he was so indifferent that he did not seem to notice my response. A brief silence followed, broken by the guide's monotonous voice: "Ancient hauberk, sixth century, era of King Arthur; attributed to Sir Sagramor le Desirous; note the hole in the left breast, likely caused by a bullet from Cromwell's soldiers." My companion offered a smile—one that seemed to have vanished centuries ago—and murmured to himself, "Know well, I saw it happen. I did it myself." Before I could process the shock of his claim, he had vanished. That evening, I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, lost in visions of the past while rain lashed the windows and wind howled outside. I occasionally turned to Sir Thomas Malory's captivating work, immersing myself in its tales of wonder and the evocative charm of its archaic names.

He had been entirely unaware of his own power. He followed her into the garden without any intention of testing it, driven only by a desire to see how she handled Frank Churchill’s engagement. He had no selfish agenda, hoping only to offer comfort or advice if she permitted. The rest happened spontaneously, a direct reaction to her words. The wonderful realization that she felt nothing for Frank Churchill sparked the hope that he might eventually win her heart. It was not an immediate expectation; in a moment of impulsive eagerness, he had merely sought permission to try to win her. The greater hopes that followed were all the more magical. The love he had hoped to cultivate was already his. In thirty minutes, he had moved from deep distress to near-perfect happiness. Her transformation was just as profound. This half-hour granted both the same precious certainty of mutual love, dispelling their shared ignorance and doubt. He had long been jealous of Frank Churchill, a feeling that emerged alongside his love for Emma. This jealousy had driven him away, with the Box Hill excursion finally prompting his departure to escape witnessing their interactions. He had left to learn indifference, but his brother’s home proved a poor environment for that goal. Isabella’s presence, while distinct, only served to highlight Emma’s brilliance. He remained until the morning post brought news of Jane Fairfax. Feeling justified in his belief that Frank Churchill was unworthy of her, his concern for Emma became too intense to ignore. He rode home through the rain and walked over after dinner to see how this wonderful woman, perfect despite her flaws, was coping with the news.

The cycle of misery should have been broken, yet cruel fate would not allow such a violation of her eternal laws. Why should I complain? Misery was my natural state, and only the wretched could ever reach me; if Woodville had been happy, we would never have met. Having spent years fed by tears and raised in grief, how can I hesitate to tell this story of sorrow and death? Woodville had to travel to the country, where he was held back for days, away from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her mentioning she was slightly ill, but urging him to return, claiming his presence would be her best medicine. Delayed for three more days, he finally rushed to her. He felt a strange sense of dread; having heard nothing further, he feared she had worsened. This fear made him restless, yet a dark voice whispered that he would never see her as she once was. When he reached her home, everything was silent. He walked through the rooms and found a servant weeping bitterly. Faint with fear, he barely managed to ask if she was dead, only to hear the reply, "Not yet." These words were less terrifying than he had expected; knowing she was still alive gave him a glimmer of hope. Recalling her letter, he clung to the desperate belief that his love could restore her spirit and that she could not die while he was near. He hurried to her room, where she lay feverish and unconscious. He wrapped her in his arms, kissing her burning lips and calling her name with quiet anguish. "Return, Elinor; I am here with you. You promised me that I would bring you health. Let your spirit revive; you cannot die while I am near. What is death? To see you no more? To lose the part of myself without whom I have no past or future?"

Listen to me; I have mastered the language of despair. I am despair itself, a strange, triumphant force. Yet that is a lie, for the dark wave is not bitter. We simply close our eyes in a gentle sleep, and upon waking, we are free. Do not delay, you slow one! Look at this inviting potion. I am a spirit of mercy, not a mere woman, urging you to drink. As I spoke, I watched his face. His exquisite beauty and the heavenly compassion in his eyes, filled with earnest wonder, shattered my resolve. My stern despair dissolved into soft grief. His own eyes grew moist as he took my hands and sat beside me. This is a tragic path you propose, my dear friend, and your suffering must be profound to drive you to such thoughts. You crave death, yet you fear it and want me to join you. I lack your courage; I dare not die, even with you. Listen to me before you try to convince me, even if your desperate eloquence could make death seem more inviting than heaven. I have harbored such dark thoughts myself and longed for the end, but I have overcome that phantom. Just as you played the role of Despair, I will be your guide to lead you safely from this cavern. Listen and let your heart soften. We do not understand this world’s strange mix of good and evil, yet we are placed here to live and hope. I do not know what we should hope for, but there is some greater good we must seek; that is our purpose. If misfortune strikes, we must fight it and continue our search. Whether this hope prepares us for another life or simply allows us to smooth the path for those who follow, I cannot say.

He remained indoors the following day, largely confined to his room, paralyzed by a frantic fear of death while simultaneously feeling detached from existence. A sense of being pursued and trapped consumed him. The slightest rustle of the tapestry made him tremble, and withered leaves tapping against the windowpanes mirrored his own squandered intentions and bitter regrets. Whenever he shut his eyes, the sailor’s visage appeared behind the glass, and dread gripped his heart once more. Perhaps, however, he had merely conjured vengeance from the darkness. While reality is chaotic, the imagination possesses a grim logic, driving remorse to haunt wrongdoing and forcing every transgression to spawn its own wretched consequences. In the mundane world, virtue and vice rarely meet their just deserts; strength brings success, and weakness invites failure. Surely, had a stranger lurked nearby, the staff would have noticed, or the gardeners would have discovered footprints. It was only a delusion. Sibyl Vane’s brother had not returned for revenge; he had likely perished at sea. He was safe, for the man could not possibly recognize him behind his youthful facade. Yet, if it were only an illusion, the power of conscience to manifest such terrifying specters was harrowing. What existence awaited him if shadows of his guilt were to haunt his every moment, mocking him from the darkness or waking him with freezing touches? As this realization took hold, he turned pale, and the room seemed to chill. In a moment of frantic insanity, he had murdered his friend, and the memory returned now with unbearable clarity. From the depths of the past, his sin emerged, vivid and stained in crimson.

It is only four o’clock, but winter has already brought an early sunset. The sky is clear and frosty, casting a soft pink glow over the snow-covered ground. I live in a lonely cottage on a vast, empty heath where no human voice ever reaches me. The desolate plain is white, except for a few dark patches on the hilltops where the snow is thinner. A few birds peck at the ice covering the pools, hardened by a long, bitter frost. I am in a strange state of mind. I am completely alone in the world, withered by misfortune. I know I am dying, and I feel strangely happy. My pulse races, and my thin hand feels hot against my cheek. My inner spirit is burning out its final sparks. I will not live to see another winter or feel the warmth of another summer. Believing this, I begin to write my tragic story. Perhaps it should die with me, but I am too weak to resist the urge to tell it. While I was strong, I felt my story was too dark to share, but now that I am dying, I feel compelled to reveal its terrors. I must gather my thoughts. I do not know who will read these pages besides you, my friend, who will receive them after my death. I am writing as if for strangers, though I address you. You have often asked about my solitary life, my tears, and my silence. In life, I could not speak, but in death, I reveal the mystery. Others may discard these pages, but to you, Woodville, my kind friend, they will be precious. They are the memories of a heartbroken girl who, even in death, is warmed by gratitude for your sympathy.

That reflection, which once bolstered me at the start of my path, now only drags me deeper into despair. My dreams and expectations have vanished; like the fallen angel who sought godlike power, I am bound in an everlasting torment. My mind was creative, yet my capacity for logic and execution was profound; combining these, I envisioned and brought a man to life. Even now, I recall with intense emotion the daydreams I held while my work remained unfinished. I felt divine in my musings, alternating between pride in my abilities and excitement over their consequences. From childhood, I was filled with grand ambitions, but how far I have fallen! My friend, had you known me in my former state, you would not recognize this ruined man. Hope seldom left me; a great purpose seemed to guide me, until I collapsed, never to recover. Must I lose this remarkable person? I have craved a friend, someone to share my life and affection. Here, on these desolate waters, I found such a man, yet I fear I have discovered his worth only to lose him. I attempt to persuade him to live, but he refuses. I appreciate your kindness toward a wretch like me, Walton, he replied, but when you suggest new bonds, do you believe anyone can replace those I have lost? Can anyone truly be to me what Clerval was, or any woman take the place of Elizabeth? Even when bonds are not forged by exceptional character, the companions of our youth hold a sway over us that later friends rarely achieve. They understand our early nature, which, though altered by time, is never truly erased; they judge our deeds with a clearer sense of our true intentions. A sibling can never suspect the other of deceit unless it was evident from the start, whereas a newer friend might harbor doubts despite their devotion. I was blessed with friends who were dear both through long association and their own virtues; wherever I go, the gentle voice of my Elizabeth and the words of Clerval will echo in my mind. They are gone, and only one purpose in this isolation could convince me to continue living. If I were committed to some noble task of great benefit to humanity, I might survive to see it through.

Tom joined the Cadets of Temperance, drawn by their flashy uniforms. He pledged to avoid smoking, chewing tobacco, and swearing while a member. He quickly discovered that promising to abstain only made him crave those very things. His urge to drink and curse became so intense that only the prospect of wearing his red sash kept him in the group. He looked forward to a grand public funeral for the dying Judge Frazer, but the Judge kept recovering. Tom grew frustrated and resigned, only for the Judge to die that same night. Tom felt betrayed by the man's inconsistency. The funeral was impressive, and the Cadets marched in a way that would have made Tom jealous, but he was relieved to be free. Surprisingly, once he was allowed to drink and swear again, he lost all interest in doing so. Soon, Tom found his newfound freedom boring. He tried keeping a diary, but gave up after three days of inactivity. A traveling minstrel show arrived, and Tom and Joe Harper organized their own troupe, enjoying it for two days. Even the Fourth of July was a letdown; it rained, canceling the parade, and the visiting U.S. Senator, Mr. Benton, was a massive disappointment because he was nowhere near the twenty-five feet tall Tom had imagined. Then, a circus came to town.

On the hearth lay several thick locks of grey human hair, stained with blood and seemingly torn out by the roots. The floor held four gold coins, a topaz earring, three large silver spoons, three smaller ones made of base metal, and two bags containing nearly four thousand francs in gold. A desk in the corner had been ransacked, though many items remained inside. A small iron safe found under the bed was open with the key still in the lock, containing only unimportant papers. No trace of Madame L’Espanaye was found, but after noticing soot in the fireplace, searchers looked up the chimney and pulled out the daughter’s body, head-first. She had been forced deep into the narrow space. The body was still warm and covered in scrapes from the struggle. Her face was scratched, and her throat bore deep bruises and fingernail marks, suggesting she had been strangled. After searching the rest of the house, the group entered a small backyard where the old lady’s body lay. Her throat was so severely cut that her head detached when they tried to lift her. Both the body and head were horribly mutilated, barely recognizable as human. There is currently no clue to this mystery. The next day’s paper added that many people had been questioned regarding the tragedy, but nothing had shed light on the case. Pauline Dubourg, a laundress, testified that she had known the women for three years and found them affectionate toward each other and reliable with payments. She did not know how they earned their living, though she believed the mother told fortunes and was rumored to have saved money.

He chose Friday, August 17th, for his appearance, spending the day choosing his outfit: a wide-brimmed hat with a red feather, a ruffled burial shroud, and a rusted dagger. By evening, a fierce rainstorm rattled the house, creating the perfect atmosphere for his plans. He intended to sneak into Washington Otis’s room, haunt him from the foot of the bed, and stab himself in the throat to the sound of slow music. He held a grudge against Washington for repeatedly cleaning the Canterville bloodstain with detergent. After terrifying the young man, he planned to visit the Minister and his wife, placing a cold hand on her forehead while whispering gruesome secrets to her husband. He was undecided about Virginia, who had always been kind, so he settled on merely groaning from her wardrobe or scratching at her bedsheets. He was determined to punish the twins by sitting on their chests to induce nightmares, then standing between their beds as a frozen, green corpse before revealing his skeletal form as 'Dumb Daniel,' a role he had perfected over the years. At ten-thirty, he heard the family heading to bed. The twins’ laughter delayed him, but by midnight, the house was silent. As the wind howled and the owl cried, he crept out, while the Otis family slept soundly, unaware of the ghost stalking the halls.

“Come on, Tom,” I said, “you could at least tell me. What is a bar sinister?” “I don’t know. But he has to have one. All the nobility does.” That was just how he was. If he didn’t want to explain something, he wouldn’t. You could pester him for a week and it wouldn’t matter. With the coat of arms settled, he started planning a mournful inscription, insisting Jim needed one just like the others. He wrote several on a piece of paper and read them aloud: 1. Here a captive heart burst. 2. Here a poor prisoner, forsaken by the world and friends, fretted out his sorrowful life. 3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity. 4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV. Tom’s voice trembled as he read, and he nearly broke down. When he finished, he couldn’t decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall, so he decided Jim should scratch them all. Jim argued it would take him a year to carve all that into the logs with a nail, and he didn’t even know how to form letters, but Tom promised to outline them so Jim only had to follow the lines. Then he added, “Actually, logs won’t work; dungeons don’t have log walls. We need to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll get one.” Jim complained that a rock was even worse, saying it would take so long he would never get out. Tom offered to let me help. He then checked our progress on the pens. It was incredibly tedious, slow work that kept my hands from healing, and we were barely making any progress, so Tom said, “I know how to fix this. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the inscriptions, so we can kill two birds with one stone.”

I had not yet fully accepted my situation. I did not yet feel in every heartbeat and thought that I was truly the last human left on earth. The sky turned gray, and a light rain began to fall at sunset. I wondered if it was shameful for a man to cry when even the heavens wept. I recalled old stories of people who turned into fountains from their tears and wished that were my fate, as it would connect me to the deaths of Adrian and Clara. Grief is strange; it colors everything around me and finds meaning in every object. I had wandered far from where I landed and found one of the watchtowers that line the Italian coast. I was relieved to find something built by human hands after seeing only the empty wilderness. I climbed the winding stairs to the guardroom. Fortunately, there were no grim reminders of the people who once lived there. I found a simple bed made of planks and dried corn husks, along with a chest containing some stale biscuits. These items triggered a hunger I had not realized I felt. I was also suffering from a parching thirst caused by the seawater I had swallowed and my physical exhaustion. I felt refreshed and calmed as I ate the simple food and drank the sour wine left in a flask. I lay down on the bed, grateful for the shelter. The earthy scent of the dried leaves was a relief after the smell of seaweed. For a moment, I forgot my loneliness. I stopped thinking about the past or the future and drifted into a peaceful sleep, dreaming of the mountain life and simple country scenes from my childhood.

Eventually, the Westminster tower clock struck twelve, its deep chimes making the night shudder. The railway lights extinguished, leaving only one lamp glowing like a ruby on a mast, while the city’s din subsided. At two, he rose and walked toward Blackfriars. The scene appeared surreal, like a dream; the buildings across the river seemed constructed of shadows. The dome of St. Paul’s emerged like a bubble in the twilight. Near Cleopatra’s Needle, he spotted a man leaning on the parapet. As he drew closer, the gaslight illuminated the face of Mr. Podgers, the palmist, with his unmistakable flabby features, gold spectacles, and weak, sensual expression. Lord Arthur approached stealthily from behind, seized the man by his legs, and tossed him into the Thames. A harsh curse and a splash followed, then silence. Lord Arthur watched as the man’s hat spun in the moonlit water before sinking. He briefly feared he saw the bulky figure swimming toward the stairs, but it was merely a reflection. Convinced he had fulfilled his destiny, he sighed with relief and whispered Sybil’s name. A policeman with a lantern suddenly asked if he had dropped something. Nothing important, he replied, then hailed a hansom cab to Belgrave Square. Over the following days, he fluctuated between hope and dread, fearing Podgers might reappear yet trusting in his fate. He visited the palmist’s street twice but lacked the courage to knock, caught between a desire for certainty and a fear of it. The answer arrived while he sat in his club, listening to Surbiton discuss a song, as a waiter entered with the evening papers.

Since my father’s surname was Pirrip and my given name Philip, my baby speech could manage nothing more distinct than Pip. Thus, I named myself Pip, and that is how I became known. I cite Pirrip as my father’s name based on his headstone and the word of my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, the blacksmith’s wife. Having never seen my parents or any portrait of them—as they lived long before photography—my initial notions of their appearance were absurdly formed by their graves. The lettering on my father’s stone suggested a stout, square, dark man with curly hair. From the phrasing regarding Georgiana, his wife, I childishly inferred my mother was sickly and freckled. Five small stone markers nearby, dedicated to my five brothers who died in infancy, led me to believe they were born lying on their backs with hands in their pockets, never removing them throughout their lives. We lived in the marshlands near the river, roughly twenty miles from the sea. My first clear understanding of the world came on a raw, late afternoon. That was when I realized this nettle-choked spot was the churchyard, where my parents and brothers lay buried. I saw the dark, flat wilderness of the marshes, the leaden river, the distant sea, and realized the small, shivering, weeping child was myself. "Quiet!" a harsh voice shouted as a man emerged from behind the church porch. "Stay still, you little wretch, or I will slit your throat!" He was a frightening figure, dressed in coarse grey, with a heavy iron shackle on his leg.

Soon, his voice called out from above. How much further do I go? How high are you? Legrand asked. Very far, the man replied. I can see the sky through the treetops. Never mind the sky, Legrand said. Look down the trunk and count the branches you have passed on this side. One, two, three, four, five, the man said. I have passed five big branches. Then go up one more, Legrand instructed. A few minutes later, the man announced he had reached the seventh branch. Now, Jupiter, Legrand shouted, clearly excited, climb out on that branch as far as you can. If you see anything unusual, tell me. By now, I was certain my friend had lost his mind, and I worried about how to get him home. While I considered what to do, Jupiter spoke again. I am afraid to go far on this branch. It is mostly dead wood. Is it really dead? Legrand asked, his voice shaking. Yes, sir, it is completely dead, Jupiter replied. What shall I do? Legrand asked, sounding distressed. Do? I said, happy to speak up. Come home and go to bed. It is getting late, and you promised. Jupiter, Legrand shouted, ignoring me, do you hear me? Yes, Master Will, I hear you clearly. Test the wood with your knife and see if it is very rotten, Legrand said. It is rotten, Jupiter replied after a moment, but not too bad. I might be able to go out a little way. By yourself? What do you mean? I mean the bug, Jupiter said. It is a very heavy bug. If I drop it first, the branch will not break under just my weight. You fool! Legrand cried, sounding relieved. What are you talking about? If you drop that beetle, I will break your neck. Do you hear me? Yes, sir, no need to shout at me like that. Listen, Legrand said. If you go out on the branch as far as is safe without dropping the beetle, I will give you a silver dollar when you come down.

I examined the skull closely. The edges near the parchment's border were sharper, suggesting the heat had been applied unevenly. I lit a fire and heated the entire parchment. Initially, only the skull's lines darkened, but as I continued, a figure appeared in the opposite corner. I first thought it was a goat, but closer inspection revealed it was a kid. I laughed, telling Legrand that while a fortune was no laughing matter, he could not possibly link pirates to a goat, as they were hardly farmers. He corrected me, noting it was a kid, not a goat. I conceded the point, but he explained he saw it as a punning signature for Captain Kidd. The skull seemed like a seal, yet I was frustrated by the lack of any accompanying text. I asked if he expected a letter between the seal and the signature. He admitted he felt a strong premonition of great fortune, fueled by Jupiter’s comment about the gold bug and the series of bizarre coincidences. He marveled at how the fire, the dog, and the rare cool weather had all aligned perfectly to reveal the skull and lead him to the treasure.

The mental traits we call analytical are difficult to analyze themselves; we only understand them through their results. We know that for those who possess them in abundance, they provide immense pleasure. Just as a strong person takes pride in physical exercise, the analyst delights in the mental activity of untangling problems. They find joy in even the smallest tasks that utilize their skills. They love riddles, puzzles, and codes, solving them with a sharpness that seems supernatural to others. Their conclusions, reached through rigorous method, often appear to be mere intuition. While mathematical study strengthens this problem-solving ability, calculation is not the same as analysis. A chess player, for instance, calculates without necessarily analyzing. Chess is often misunderstood; I believe the humble game of checkers actually exercises the reflective mind more effectively than the complex frivolity of chess. In chess, where pieces move in strange ways with varying values, people often mistake complexity for depth. The game demands intense focus; if a player loses concentration for a moment, they make a mistake that leads to defeat. Because the possible moves are so numerous and tangled, errors are common, and the player who is more focused usually wins rather than the one who is more insightful. In checkers, where moves are simple and consistent, the chance of a careless error is low. With less need for constant, rigid attention, victory is determined by true mental sharpness. If we imagine a game of checkers reduced to only four kings, where mistakes are impossible, it becomes clear that victory between equal players can only be achieved through a clever, superior intellectual effort.

Many American women abroad pretend to be sickly, thinking it looks sophisticated, but Mrs. Otis avoided this mistake. She was healthy and energetic. In many ways, she was quite English, proving that America and England share everything except language. Her eldest son, Washington, was a handsome, fair-haired man who prepared for diplomacy by dancing at Newport. He was sensible, though he loved flowers and the nobility. Virginia, his fifteen-year-old sister, was graceful and lovely with bright blue eyes. A skilled rider, she once beat Lord Bilton in a race, which so impressed the young Duke of Cheshire that he proposed to her immediately, only to be sent back to school by his guardians. Finally, there were the twins, nicknamed the Stars and Stripes because they were constantly in trouble. They were the only true republicans in the family besides their father. Since Canterville Chase was seven miles from the train station, Mr. Otis hired a carriage. They set off in high spirits on a beautiful July evening, enjoying the scent of pine and the sight of wildlife. As they reached the estate, however, the sky turned dark, the air grew still, and birds flew silently overhead. Rain began to fall just before they arrived. An elderly woman in a black silk dress, white cap, and apron stood on the steps to greet them.

After a brief silence, Mr. Lorry placed a hand on the Doctor’s arm and asked what had caused the episode. The Doctor replied that he believed a painful memory had been triggered. He suspected the patient had long feared this specific association would return under certain conditions, and that his attempt to prepare for it had only weakened his ability to cope. When Mr. Lorry asked if the man would remember the relapse, the Doctor looked around the room and quietly shook his head. Regarding the future, the Doctor regained his composure and expressed great hope. He believed that since the man had recovered so quickly after facing a long-dreaded burden, the worst was likely behind him. Mr. Lorry expressed his gratitude, and the Doctor bowed his head in agreement. Mr. Lorry then asked if he might address two other concerns. The Doctor encouraged him, offering his hand. Mr. Lorry noted that the man was studious and energetic, often working intensely on his professional research. He asked if this was too much. The Doctor disagreed, suggesting that the man’s mind required constant occupation to remain healthy. He believed the man understood his own needs well. When Mr. Lorry pressed him on whether the man was under too much strain, the Doctor remained confident that he was not. Mr. Lorry persisted, asking if overwork would inevitably lead to a return of the disorder.

I thought this charming falsehood was told with grace and simplicity, though perhaps its novelty for me was the reason; it had surely delighted the others when first heard. Sir Dinadan the Humorist stirred first, waking the group with a crude prank. He fastened metal cups to a dog's tail and released the panicked animal, which bolted through the room followed by a pack of barking dogs, causing a chaotic, deafening uproar. The crowd roared with laughter, some falling from their seats and rolling on the ground in delight, acting much like children. Dinadan, immensely proud, recounted the origin of his inspiration repeatedly until everyone grew weary, yet he continued to chuckle long after the others had ceased. He then insisted on delivering a humorous speech, which consisted of the most tiresome, exhausted jests I had ever endured. He was more tedious than any minstrel or circus clown. It was melancholy to sit there, thirteen centuries before my own time, hearing the same stale, ancient jokes that had irritated me as a boy in the future. It confirmed my suspicion that no truly original joke exists. Everyone laughed at these relics, as people always do, though the boy did not; he mocked them, declaring most of Dinadan's humor rotten and the rest fossilized. I remarked that 'fossilized' was apt, as I felt those jokes could only be categorized by geologic eras. The boy was confused, as geology had not yet been conceived, but I recorded the thought, intending to teach the public once I had the chance. One should not discard a clever idea simply because the time is not yet right. Then, Sir Kay stood and began to spin his tales, using me as his subject.

I must go, unsure of what will happen, but I will return or find you as soon as I can. A single word or look will decide if I ever step foot in your father’s house again. Recovering from such a letter was impossible. Ten minutes of solitude were not enough to calm her; instead, her excitement only grew. Before she could process her emotions, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta arrived. She tried to act normal, but soon she could not follow their conversation and had to claim she felt unwell. They were shocked by her pale appearance and refused to leave her side, which only made her more anxious. Desperate for peace, she decided to go home. Mrs. Musgrove insisted she take a sedan chair, but Anne refused. She could not bear the thought of losing her chance to run into Captain Wentworth on her walk through town. After Mrs. Musgrove confirmed Anne had not suffered a head injury, she finally let her go. Determined to ensure everything was clear, Anne added, Please tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party tonight. I am worried there was a misunderstanding, so please assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we expect them both. Oh, my dear, it is perfectly understood, I promise you.

Heavily armored knights and horses were limited in speed. With the ground firm and free of snow or mud, they might manage a seven-mile pace, requiring a few horse changes. They should arrive around six, while daylight remained, spotting the white cloth on my arm so I could assume command. We would quickly surround the prison and liberate the king. It promised to be a dramatic spectacle, though I would have preferred the theatricality of high noon. To bolster my options, I considered revealing my identity to former acquaintances to resolve our predicament without the knights. However, the risk required caution. I needed to acquire fine clothing gradually, purchasing increasingly luxurious garments at distant shops until I reached silk and velvet. I began my task, but the plan collapsed instantly. Turning a corner, I encountered one of our slaves with a watchman. My cough drew a piercing look from him, as if he recognized the sound. I ducked into a shop, feigning interest in merchandise while watching them confer at the entrance. Deciding to escape through the rear, I told the shopkeeper I was an undercover officer hunting a fugitive. I claimed my partner was outside with a captured murderer and asked her to tell him to move to the far end of the alley to intercept the suspect once I flushed him out. Eager to see a notorious criminal, she hurried off to deliver the message.

When Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, acquired Canterville Chase, everyone warned him he was acting imprudently, as the estate was undoubtedly haunted. Lord Canterville, a man of impeccable integrity, felt obligated to disclose this when they negotiated the sale. We have avoided living there, Lord Canterville explained, ever since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, suffered a permanent breakdown after two skeletal hands touched her shoulders while she dressed. I must inform you that the specter has been witnessed by several relatives and the parish rector, Reverend Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College. Following the Duchess’s ordeal, our younger staff refused to remain, and Lady Canterville frequently lost sleep due to strange sounds emanating from the library and hallway. My Lord, the Minister replied, I shall accept the furniture and the phantom at an appraised value. I hail from a modern nation where money buys everything; with our energetic youth conquering the Old World and courting your finest performers, I suspect that if a ghost existed in Europe, we would have already secured it for a museum or a traveling exhibit. I believe the ghost is real, Lord Canterville said with a smile, even if it has eluded your enterprising showmen. It has been documented since 1584 and invariably appears before a family death. So does the family physician, Lord Canterville. Regardless, ghosts do not exist, and I doubt the laws of nature are suspended for the British nobility. You are certainly quite natural in America, Lord Canterville replied, failing to grasp the remark, but if you are comfortable with a ghost, that is your affair. Just remember that I provided a warning. Weeks later, the transaction concluded, and after the season ended, the Minister and his family traveled to Canterville Chase.
