Mrs. Otis, formerly the renowned New York beauty Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, was now a striking, middle-aged woman with beautiful eyes and a magnificent profile.

She would be a delightful companion for Emma. Mr. Woodhouse agreed, but added that their friend Harriet Smith was also a lovely young person whom Emma would enjoy. While the other guest praised Jane Fairfax for her accomplishments and age, the conversation remained pleasant. Later, the arrival of gruel sparked a lengthy discussion about its health benefits and the difficulty of finding a cook who could prepare it properly. The daughter mentioned her own recent struggle with a cook at South End, which immediately worried Mr. Woodhouse. He looked at her with concern, implying that her trip to South End had been a mistake. Emma hoped he would drop the subject, but after a few minutes, he insisted that he regretted her decision to visit the sea instead of coming to see him. When Emma defended the trip by noting how well the children had fared, Mr. Woodhouse argued that South End was unhealthy, citing his doctor, Perry, as an authority. Emma tried to reassure him by mentioning her own doctor, Mr. Wingfield, who considered the location perfectly safe. Undeterred, Mr. Woodhouse insisted that she should have chosen Cromer, which Perry considered the superior seaside destination.

This knot is one only sailors can tie, and it is unique to the Maltese. I found the ribbon near the lightning rod, and it could not have belonged to either victim. If my deduction that the Frenchman is a sailor from a Maltese ship is wrong, my advertisement does no harm. If I am mistaken, he will simply assume I was misled. However, if I am right, I have gained a significant advantage. Even if he is innocent of the murder, the Frenchman will hesitate to claim his orangutan. He will think: I am innocent and poor, and this animal is worth a fortune. Why lose it to groundless fear? It was found far from the crime scene. How could anyone suspect a beast committed such a murder? The police have no leads. Even if they find the animal, they cannot prove I was involved. Most importantly, I am known. The advertiser knows I own the beast. If I do not claim such valuable property, I only invite suspicion. It is safer to claim the animal and keep it hidden until this blows over. Just then, we heard footsteps on the stairs. Be ready with your pistols, Dupin said, but do not show or use them until I signal. The front door was open, and the visitor had entered without ringing. He hesitated on the stairs, then started to descend, but soon turned and walked up with purpose, knocking on our door. Come in, Dupin said cheerfully. A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—tall, muscular, and possessing a bold, daring look that was not entirely unpleasant.

In reality, as one climbs to any specific elevation, the weight of the air overcome during further ascent does not correspond to the added height gained, but follows a steadily declining ratio. Consequently, no matter how high we travel, we cannot reach a point where the atmosphere ceases to exist. I maintained that it must persist, even if in a state of extreme thinning. Conversely, I knew that many have argued for a definitive boundary to the atmosphere. However, a factor often overlooked by these proponents seemed to me a subject deserving careful study. By analyzing the intervals between Encke’s comet reaching its perihelion, while accounting for planetary gravitational disturbances, it is clear the periods are shrinking; the major axis of the comet’s orbit is shortening in a slow, consistent manner. This is exactly what one would expect if the comet encountered resistance from a highly rarefied ethereal medium throughout its path. Such a medium would slow the comet, weakening its centrifugal force and allowing the sun’s gravity to pull it closer with each orbit. There is no other explanation for this shift. Furthermore, the comet’s nebulosity contracts as it nears the sun and expands as it moves away. Was I not correct to assume, like M. Valz, that this volume change results from compression by that same ethereal medium, which grows denser near the sun? The zodiacal light also demanded consideration. This glow, visible in the tropics and distinct from meteoric light, stretches obliquely from the horizon, generally aligning with the sun’s equator. It seemed clearly to be a thin atmosphere radiating from the sun, reaching at least past Venus and likely much further. I could not imagine this medium restricted solely to the comet’s path or the sun’s immediate vicinity.

Colonel Grangerford was a true gentleman, as was his entire family. He came from a good background, which the Widow Douglas considered as valuable in a man as in a horse, a sentiment even my father agreed with, despite his own lack of refinement. The Colonel was tall and slender with a pale complexion, free of any flush. He shaved his thin face daily, revealing sharp features: thin lips, narrow nostrils, a prominent nose, and heavy eyebrows over deep-set, dark eyes that seemed to peer from caverns. His hair was black, straight, and shoulder-length. He wore pristine white linen suits daily and a blue tail-coat with brass buttons on Sundays, always carrying a silver-headed mahogany cane. He was serious, quiet, and genuinely kind, which made people trust him. While his smile was pleasant, his stern, upright posture and flashing eyes were intimidating enough to make anyone seek safety. He never had to demand respect; his presence naturally encouraged good behavior. He brought a sense of warmth to any room, and his rare moments of anger were brief yet effective in restoring order. Each morning, the family stood when he and his wife entered, remaining standing until the couple was seated. His sons, Tom and Bob, would prepare drinks at the sideboard. They would wait for the Colonel to join them, offering a formal toast before they all drank. Even we boys, Buck and I, were included in this ritual, receiving a small portion of the drink to toast the elders.

Directly before him, illuminated by the pale moonlight, stood an old man of terrifying appearance. His eyes glowed like burning coals, his long grey hair hung in matted tangles, and his antique, tattered clothing was complemented by heavy, rusted shackles on his wrists and ankles. Mr. Otis remarked that he must insist the man oil his chains, offering a bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. He noted its effectiveness, citing testimonials from prominent local clergy, and left the bottle on a marble table by the candles before retiring to bed. The Canterville ghost stood motionless in shock, then smashed the bottle against the floor and fled, groaning and glowing with a sickly green light. As he reached the oak staircase, a door swung open, and two figures in white robes threw a pillow at his head. Realizing he had no time to waste, he vanished through the wall, leaving the house silent. Reaching a secret room, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath, struggling to process the situation. In three hundred years of a successful career, he had never been so insulted. He recalled the Dowager Duchess he had terrified, the housemaids he had sent into hysterics, the rector whose candle he had extinguished, and Madame de Tremouillac, who had fallen ill for weeks after finding a skeleton reading her diary, eventually turning to the Church and abandoning her friendship with Voltaire.

Sydney Carton halted in the street, uncertain of his destination. “Tellson’s at nine,” he mused. “Should I make an appearance meanwhile? Yes, it is a wise precaution for them to know I am present. But I must be careful.” He paced the dimming street, weighing the implications of his choice. Convinced of his plan, he headed toward Saint Antoine. Defarge had identified his wine-shop in that district, and Carton found it easily. After dining and sleeping soundly—abstaining from strong spirits for the first time in years—he awoke at seven. He tidied his cravat, collar, and hair in a shop mirror before entering the wine-shop. Only Jacques Three, the juror with the nervous hands, was present with the Defarges and The Vengeance. Carton sat and requested wine in poor French. Madame Defarge scrutinized him, then approached to confirm his order. When she asked if he were English, he stared as if struggling with the language before replying in a thick, foreign accent.

If I cannot survive on that, I shall not request assistance from anyone. Is that acceptable? A massive wave of cheering erupted, through which the monarch’s voice emerged, declaring: Release his shackles and grant him liberty! Let all, whether noble or humble, wealthy or destitute, pay him honor, for he is now the king’s primary advisor, vested with authority and seated upon the throne’s highest tier! Dispel this encroaching darkness and restore the light and joy, so that the entire world may offer you its blessings. I replied: It is of no consequence if a commoner is humiliated before the world, but it would be a disgrace to the king if those who witnessed his minister in such a state did not also see him redeemed from that shame. If I might request that my garments be returned. They are unsuitable, the king interrupted. Bring attire of a different quality; dress him as a prince! My plan succeeded. I needed to maintain the status quo until the eclipse reached totality, lest they attempt to force me to end the darkness, which I was unable to do. Requesting the clothes provided a brief delay, but insufficient time. I had to invent another pretext. I claimed it would be expected for the king to reconsider his impulsive actions; therefore, I would allow the darkness to persist briefly, and if the king remained resolute after a suitable interval, the darkness would be lifted. Neither the king nor the crowd was pleased with this, but I remained firm. The gloom deepened until it was pitch black, while I wrestled with those cumbersome medieval garments. The crowd moaned in terror as cold, unnatural breezes swept through and stars appeared in the sky. When the eclipse finally became total, I felt relieved, though everyone else was miserable, as expected. I announced: The king, by his silence, upholds the agreement. I raised my hands, paused, and declared with profound gravity: Let the spell dissolve and vanish without harm! There was no immediate reaction in that profound darkness and deathly silence. However, as the sun’s silver edge emerged moments later, the crowd erupted in a thunderous roar and surged forward like a flood to overwhelm me with gratitude; Clarence was certainly among the first to reach me.

He was short but stood remarkably straight, and his voice was the most pleasant I had ever heard. He began his lecture by summarizing the history of chemistry and the advancements made by various scholars, speaking with passion about the most famous discoverers. He then gave a brief overview of the current state of the field and explained its basic terms. After performing a few introductory experiments, he concluded with high praise for modern chemistry, the words of which I will never forget: The ancient teachers of this science promised the impossible and achieved nothing. Modern masters promise very little; they know that metals cannot be changed and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these scientists, whose hands seem meant only for dirt and whose eyes for microscopes or crucibles, have truly performed miracles. They explore nature’s secrets and reveal how she works in hiding. They reach into the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and nearly unlimited powers; they can command lightning, mimic earthquakes, and even imitate the invisible world. These were the professor’s words—or rather, the words of fate—spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were fighting a physical enemy. One by one, the various parts of my being were stirred, and soon my mind was filled with a single purpose. So much has been done, my soul exclaimed, but I will achieve far more. Following the path already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and reveal the deepest mysteries of creation to the world. I did not sleep that night. My mind was in a state of chaos, and though I felt that order would eventually emerge, I could not create it myself. By dawn, sleep finally came. When I awoke, my thoughts from the night before felt like a dream, yet I remained determined to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. That same day, I visited M. Waldman. His private manner was even more gentle and engaging than his public one, as the dignity he displayed during his lecture was replaced at home by great warmth and kindness.

The surrounding oaks sheltered a colony of nightingales—I am there now, with Idris, in the prime of youth, by my side. I am twenty-two, and she has seen barely seventeen summers. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian was busy in his boat, dangerously reaching for the highest branch of a submerged oak. I wondered if he was tired of living to toy with such peril. He secured his prize and navigated the flood. We watched anxiously as the current swept him away, forcing him to land far downstream and take a long path back to us. Idris cheered when he finally jumped ashore, waving the branch in triumph. We decided to wait for him. Alone together as the sun set, we listened to the nightingales while the evening star glowed in the fading western light. Idris gazed at it, remarking on how its flickering light seemed to mirror the wavering, uncertain nature of our own lives, full of fear and love. I begged her not to look at the star or seek meaning in its light, but to look at me instead. I told her I had long been desperate to confess my feelings and surrender my entire being to her. I asked the star to witness my vow: my love for her was as essential as light to that star, and it would endure until my end. The joy of that moment remains private. I still feel her against me and my breath still hitches at the memory of that first kiss. We walked in silence to meet Adrian. Later, after he took his sister home, I asked him to return. Walking through the moonlit woods, I confessed my love and hope to him. He looked troubled for a moment and said he should have seen this coming, noting the conflict that would surely follow.

Back home, we collected taxes through tariffs, and citizens liked believing foreign importers paid them. In reality, the American public paid, with the burden distributed so evenly that a millionaire and a laborer’s infant paid the exact same six dollars. I suppose that is as fair as it gets. Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, with the British Isles holding under a million people. A mechanic earned three cents daily, covering his own expenses. National costs were ninety thousand dollars annually, or two hundred fifty daily. By swapping gold for nickels during the king’s healing ceremonies, I satisfied everyone while saving four-fifths of the daily budget, equivalent to eight hundred thousand dollars in my time. I drew on childhood wisdom, realizing that a true statesman values all insight; I used to donate buttons to missionaries instead of coins, keeping the money for myself. Everyone was satisfied, and no one suffered. Marinel processed the patients. If they qualified, they went to the king. A priest recited scripture while the king touched the ulcers. Finally, the patient received a nickel, hung around their neck by the king, and left. You might doubt the efficacy, but it worked. Any ritual cures if the patient has faith. Near Astolat, a chapel stood where a goose-girl claimed to see the Virgin. Despite a disturbing painting of the event, thousands of sick and lame visited annually, leaving fully recovered, while even the healthy remained unharmed.

This union is entirely appropriate. I doubted it initially, but I concede the point now. The gods fashioned Sibyl Vane for you; without her, you would remain unfinished. Dorian Gray squeezed his hand in gratitude, replying that he knew Basil would grasp his meaning. He noted that Harry’s cynicism frightened him, then gestured toward the orchestra, which he dismissed as awful but brief. He promised that once the curtain ascended, Basil would behold the woman to whom he had pledged his existence and all his virtues. Fifteen minutes later, Sibyl Vane appeared to thunderous applause. She was undeniably beautiful, possessing a fawn-like grace and startled eyes that struck Lord Henry as remarkable. A delicate flush touched her cheeks as she surveyed the cheering audience, and she retreated slightly, her lips quivering. Basil Hallward stood to clap, while Dorian remained transfixed, staring at her as if in a trance. Lord Henry observed through his spectacles, whispering his approval. The scene depicted the Capulet hall, where Romeo arrived with his companions. Amidst the clumsy, poorly costumed cast, Sibyl moved with ethereal elegance, her form swaying like a plant in a current, her throat and hands reminiscent of lilies and ivory. Yet, she appeared strangely detached, showing no delight upon seeing Romeo. She delivered her lines with a hollow, artificial cadence. Though her voice was lovely, its tone was entirely false, draining the poetry of its vitality and rendering the emotion counterfeit. Dorian Gray turned pale, watching with growing confusion and distress. His companions remained silent, both recognizing her performance as utterly inept.

The line of flickering streetlights stretched far into the distance, where a lone taxi waited outside a small walled house, its driver asleep. He walked quickly toward Portland Place, glancing back occasionally as if fearing pursuit. At the corner of Rich Street, two men studied a poster on a wooden fence. Driven by sudden curiosity, he crossed the street. As he approached, the word 'Murder' in bold black letters caught his eye. He flinched, his face flushing deeply. It was a reward notice for a man of medium height, aged thirty to forty, wearing a bowler hat, black coat, and plaid trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it repeatedly, wondering if the man would be caught and how he had earned his scar. Perhaps one day his own name would be plastered on London’s walls, with a price on his head. The thought sickened him. He turned and hurried into the night. He wandered aimlessly through a maze of grim houses and dark streets, eventually reaching Piccadilly Circus at dawn. Walking toward Belgrave Square, he passed wagons heading to Covent Garden. Carters in white smocks, their faces sunburnt and hair curly, strode along cracking whips and calling to one another. A chubby boy sat atop a massive grey horse, laughing as he gripped the mane, a bunch of primroses tucked into his battered hat. The piles of vegetables appeared like jade against the morning sky. Lord Arthur felt strangely moved, finding the delicate beauty of the dawn deeply pathetic. He reflected on how many days begin in beauty only to end in storms. He wondered what these simple, good-humored workers saw in this city—a pale, ghost-like place, free from the night's sins and the day's smoke. He questioned if they understood London’s hidden splendor and shame, its intense joys, its desperate hunger, and all it creates or destroys from sunrise to sunset.

With these screams, many women, driven into a blind frenzy, spun around, striking and tearing at their own companions until they collapsed in a passionate swoon, saved from being trampled only by their men. Yet, not a moment was wasted. Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville and might be released. Not if Saint Antoine remembered its own suffering and insults. Armed people poured out of the district so quickly, dragging even the stragglers with them, that within fifteen minutes, only a few elderly women and crying children remained in Saint Antoine. By then, the crowd was choking the Hall of Examination where the wicked old man was held, spilling into the surrounding streets. The Defarges, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three were in the front, near him in the hall. Look, Madame cried, pointing with her knife. See the old villain tied with ropes. Tying a bundle of grass to his back was well done. Let him eat it now. She tucked her knife away and clapped as if at a theater. The people behind her explained her satisfaction to those further back, and soon the neighboring streets echoed with applause. During hours of tedious debate, Madame Defarge’s impatience was mirrored by the crowd, relayed by men who had climbed the building’s exterior to watch through the windows. Finally, the sun rose high, casting a ray of light onto the prisoner’s head. The crowd could no longer be contained; the barrier of dust and tension vanished, and Saint Antoine seized him. The news spread instantly. Defarge leaped over a railing and table to grab the wretch, while Madame Defarge twisted her hand into his ropes. Before the others could even reach him, a cry went up across the city: Bring him out!

Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by ghosts. The perpetrators were physical beings who made a physical escape. How? Fortunately, there is only one logical way to approach this, and it must lead to a firm conclusion. Let us examine every possible exit. The killers were clearly in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was found, or the adjacent one, when the witnesses climbed the stairs. We need only search those two rooms. The police have inspected the floors, ceilings, and walls thoroughly; no hidden exits could have escaped them. Still, not trusting their eyes, I checked myself. There were no secret passages. Both doors leading to the hallway were locked from the inside with the keys in the locks. As for the chimneys, while they are wide near the hearth, they narrow so much that even a large cat could not pass through. Since these exits are impossible, we must look to the windows. No one could have escaped the front windows without being seen by the crowd below. The killers must have used the back windows. Having reached this conclusion, we cannot reject it simply because it seems impossible. We must prove that these apparent impossibilities are not impossible at all. There are two windows in the room. One is unobstructed and fully visible. The other is partially blocked by the head of a heavy bed pushed against it. The first window was locked from the inside and resisted all attempts to open it. A large hole had been drilled into the frame, and a sturdy nail was driven in. The second window had an identical nail, and it also refused to budge. The police were satisfied that no one had escaped through them, so they saw no reason to remove the nails and open the windows. My own investigation was more thorough, precisely because I knew that the apparent impossibilities had to be explained.

Put down your weapons, brothers! Forgiveness and friendship await your change of heart. You are precious to us because we share the same fragile humanity. Why should man fight man when a deadly plague already threatens us all, thriving on our violence? Both armies hesitated. Our soldiers held their weapons tightly, watching the enemy with stern eyes. The opposing troops had not dropped their arms, mostly out of fear rather than a desire to fight, waiting for a leader to show them what to do. Adrian jumped from his horse and knelt by a fallen soldier. He is a man, and he is dead, he cried. Quickly, tend to the wounded. Do not let another soul die or go before God to tell the story of this brotherly slaughter. Replace your cruel hearts with kindness and discard your weapons. In this moment of shared fate, let us be guardians to one another. As he spoke, he knelt and lifted a man whose life was bleeding away. The soldier gasped, and in the sudden silence, his moans were heard by everyone. Hearts that had been set on killing now beat with anxious hope for this one life. Adrian used his scarf to bind the wound, but it was too late. The man sighed and went limp. He is dead, Adrian said, bowing his head in grief. The fate of the world seemed to rest on that single death. Soldiers on both sides dropped their weapons. Even the hardened veterans wept, and our men reached out to their former enemies with love. The two armies merged, unarmed and holding hands, discussing how to help one another. Regretting their past violence, they followed the General’s orders and began the journey toward London.

He also considered Sybil’s old-fashioned parents, who might oppose the marriage if a scandal occurred. Still, he felt sure they would understand his motives if he explained everything. He decided that poison was the best choice; it was safe, certain, and quiet, avoiding the painful scenes that he, like most Englishmen, deeply disliked. Knowing nothing about poisons, he searched the library himself after the waiter failed to help. He found a medical textbook and a copy of Erskine’s Toxicology. The technical language confused him, and he regretted not studying harder at Oxford, but he eventually found a clear description of aconitine. It was fast, painless, and easy to take in a gelatin capsule. He noted the lethal dose on his shirt cuff, returned the books, and walked to a prominent chemist. The owner, Mr. Pestle, was surprised by the request and mentioned needing a medical certificate. Lord Arthur explained that the poison was for a Norwegian mastiff showing signs of rabies that had already bitten his coachman. Satisfied by this excuse, the chemist praised Lord Arthur’s knowledge and prepared the dose. Lord Arthur placed the capsule into a silver candy box he bought on Bond Street, discarded the chemist’s container, and drove to Lady Clementina’s.

He always pretended Peter wrote those letters, but that was a lie; he had gotten every single detail from the simpleton we had taken by canoe to the steamboat. Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud, weeping over the contents. It bequeathed the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls, while leaving the profitable tannery, other properties worth seven thousand dollars, and another three thousand in gold to Harvey and William, noting exactly where the six thousand dollars in cash was hidden in the cellar. The two frauds insisted on retrieving the money to ensure everything was handled transparently, and they told me to follow with a candle. Once we shut the cellar door, they dumped the bag onto the floor, revealing a beautiful pile of gold coins. The king’s eyes lit up as he slapped the duke on the shoulder, exclaiming that this was incredible and surpassed all their previous schemes. The duke agreed. They sifted the gold through their fingers, letting the coins jingle against the floor. The king remarked that posing as brothers to a wealthy deceased man and representing foreign heirs was their most successful strategy, proving that trusting in Providence was the best approach. Most people would have been satisfied with the haul, but they insisted on counting it, only to find it was four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king cursed, wondering where the missing money had gone. After searching in vain, the duke suggested that the sick man had likely made a mistake, and they should just let it go. The king agreed they could afford the loss, but he was obsessed with the count. He insisted they needed to be completely transparent, planning to take the money upstairs and count it in front of everyone to avoid suspicion, though he worried that presenting a sum different from what the deceased had specified would look wrong.

Smallpox! I rushed to the king and whispered, "Leave immediately, sire! The woman is dying of the same plague that devastated Camelot two years ago." He did not move. "I shall stay and help," he insisted. I urged him again, "King, you must go." He replied, "You mean well, but it would be shameful for a king to show fear or for a knight to withhold aid. I will not leave. You must go, as the Church forbids your presence here, and they will punish you severely if they find out." It was a dangerous situation that could cost him his life, but I knew arguing was useless once he felt his honor was at stake. I dropped the subject. The woman spoke, "Kind sir, would you climb that ladder and tell me what you find? Do not fear to tell me, for a mother's heart can break only once." The king set down his pack and said, "Stay and feed her. I will go." He started up, then paused, looking down at a man lying in the shadows who had not spoken. "Is this your husband?" the king asked. "Yes," she replied. "Is he asleep?" "Thank God, yes, for three hours. My heart is full of gratitude for his rest." I promised, "We will be careful not to wake him." She answered, "You cannot, for he is dead." "Dead?" I asked. "Yes, and what a triumph that is! No one can harm or insult him now. He is in heaven, or if he is in hell, he is content, for he will find no bishops there. We were together for twenty-five years, never separated until today. Think of how long we loved and suffered. This morning he was delirious, imagining we were children wandering in happy fields, and in that innocent conversation, he wandered into the afterlife and left my sight."

You will be pleased to learn that no misfortune has marred the start of a venture you viewed with such apprehension. I reached this place yesterday, and my primary duty is to reassure my dear sister of my safety and my growing belief in the triumph of my mission. I am already well north of London, and as I stroll through the streets of Petersburgh, a chilly northern wind brushes my face, strengthening my resolve and filling me with joy. Do you grasp this sensation? This breeze, blowing from the very lands I approach, offers a preview of those frozen territories. Encouraged by this promising wind, my fantasies grow more intense. I struggle unsuccessfully to believe the pole is merely a place of ice and emptiness; in my mind, it remains a realm of splendor. There, Margaret, the sun never sets, its massive disk grazing the horizon and casting constant light. There—if I may trust the accounts of earlier explorers—snow and frost are absent; sailing across tranquil waters, we might reach a land more wondrous and beautiful than any yet found. Its natural features may be unique, just as the celestial phenomena surely are in those unexplored wastes. What might one find in a land of perpetual light? I may uncover the mysterious force that draws the compass needle and clarify countless astronomical observations, turning their apparent irregularities into consistent laws. I shall satisfy my intense curiosity by witnessing a part of the world never before seen, perhaps walking on soil untouched by human feet. These prospects are my motivation, enough to overcome any dread of peril or death and to inspire me to begin this arduous journey with the delight of a child setting out in a small boat with friends to explore a local river. Even if these theories prove incorrect, you cannot deny the immense value I will provide to all humanity by finding a polar route to distant lands, currently requiring months of travel, or by unlocking the secrets of magnetism, which can only be achieved through a voyage like mine. These thoughts have calmed the unease I felt when starting this letter, and my heart now burns with an enthusiasm that lifts my spirit, for nothing settles the mind like a firm objective upon which the soul can focus.

Citizens, butchers, cattle-dealers, peddlers, youths, criminals, and loafers of every sort formed a dense, chaotic mob. The whistling of drovers, barking dogs, bellowing cattle, bleating sheep, squealing pigs, hawkers' cries, and the constant shouting, swearing, and fighting created a deafening, discordant roar. Between the ringing bells, the clamor from taverns, and the shoving, beating, and yelling of the unwashed, disheveled masses surging through the market, the scene was utterly overwhelming and disorienting. Mr. Sikes, pulling Oliver along, pushed through the densest part of the throng, ignoring the sights and sounds that bewildered the boy. He acknowledged a few acquaintances with nods and declined several offers of a drink, moving purposefully until they escaped the chaos, passing through Hosier Lane into Holborn. Now, youngster, Sikes remarked, glancing at St. Andrew’s clock, it is nearly seven. You must hurry. Do not start lagging now, Lazy-legs. Sikes punctuated this with a sharp tug on the boy’s wrist, forcing Oliver to trot to keep pace with the house-breaker’s long strides. They maintained this speed past Hyde Park Corner toward Kensington, where Sikes slowed until an empty cart approached. Noting the sign for Hounslow, he politely asked the driver for a ride to Isleworth. Climb in, the man said, asking if the boy was his. Yes, he is mine, Sikes answered, staring at Oliver while his hand drifted toward his hidden pistol. Your father moves a bit fast for you, does he not? the driver asked, noticing Oliver’s exhaustion. Not at all, Sikes interrupted. He is accustomed to it. Here, grab my hand, Ned. Get in. He helped Oliver into the cart, where the driver told the boy to rest on a pile of sacks. As they passed each milestone, Oliver grew increasingly anxious about their destination. They traveled steadily through Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, showing no signs of stopping.

I wrapped him in paper and stuffed some in his mouth—that was the way. And you think your master was bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him sick? I do not think anything about it—I know it. Why would he dream about gold if he was not bitten by the gold-bug? I have heard of those gold-bugs before. But how do you know he dreams about gold? How do I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that is how I know. Well, Jupiter, perhaps you are right; but why are you visiting me today? What is the matter, master? Did you bring a message from Mr. Legrand? No, master, I brought this letter. Jupiter handed me a note that read: My dear friend, why have I not seen you lately? I hope you have not taken offense at my recent behavior. I have been anxious and have something to tell you, though I am unsure how to explain it. I have not been well, and Jupiter annoys me with his constant attention. He even prepared a stick to punish me for spending the day alone in the hills. I believe my poor health saved me from a beating. I have not added to my collection since we met. Please come over with Jupiter tonight. I need to see you regarding a matter of the highest importance. The tone of this note worried me. It was unlike Legrand. What was he thinking? What new obsession filled his mind? Jupiter’s story did not sound good. I feared that his recent misfortunes had finally affected his sanity. Without hesitation, I prepared to go with Jupiter. At the wharf, I saw a scythe and three new spades in the boat. What is the meaning of all this, Jupiter?

What outcome has followed? What impression have I left on your imagination? I felt a shiver as Dupin posed the query. A lunatic, I suggested, committed this act—some raving soul fled from a nearby asylum. In some ways, he answered, your notion is not off base. Yet the cries of madmen, even in their most frantic states, never match that strange voice heard on the stairs. Lunatics belong to a nation, and their speech, however garbled, maintains the consistency of syllables. Furthermore, the hair of a madman is not like this tuft I hold, which I pulled from the tightly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you think of it. Dupin, I said, shaken, this hair is highly strange; it is not human. I did not claim it was, he replied, but before we conclude, look at this sketch I have drawn. It is a copy of what witnesses described as bruises and deep nail indentations on the throat of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, or as livid spots left by fingers. You will see, my friend continued, laying the paper down, that this drawing suggests a firm, unmoving grip. There is no sign of slipping. Each finger held its position until the victim died. Try to place your own fingers into these marks. I tried and failed. We are perhaps not testing this fairly, he noted. The paper is flat, but a throat is cylindrical. Here is a wooden rod with a similar circumference. Wrap the drawing around it and try again. I did so, but the impossibility was even clearer. This, I said, is not the mark of a human hand. Read this passage from Cuvier, Dupin replied. It was a detailed anatomical description of the large fulvous orangutan of the East Indian Islands. The immense size, incredible strength, wild ferocity, and imitative nature of these animals are well known. I grasped the full horror of the murder immediately. The description of the fingers, I said, finishing the text, matches this drawing perfectly.

Without pausing to think and barely processing her emotions, Elizabeth finished the first letter and immediately tore open the second, which had been written a day later. My dearest sister, you have likely received my rushed note by now. I hope this one is clearer, though my mind is so scattered that I cannot promise coherence. Lizzy, I have terrible news that cannot wait. As unwise as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate for confirmation that it happened, as there is reason to fear they never went to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton shortly after the initial alarm. Although Lydia’s note to Mrs. Forster suggested they were heading to Gretna Green, Denny hinted that Wickham never intended to marry her at all. The Colonel immediately set out to track them. He followed them easily to Clapham, but there they switched to a hackney coach and vanished. We only know they continued toward London. I am at a loss. After searching that area, the Colonel came to Hertfordshire, checking every tollgate and inn along the way, but no one had seen them. He arrived at Longbourn to share his fears with great compassion. I feel for him and his wife, but they are not to blame. Our distress is immense. My parents fear the worst, but I cannot think so poorly of him. Perhaps they chose a private London wedding instead. Even if he were capable of such a scheme, I cannot believe Lydia would be so foolish. Still, I am saddened that the Colonel does not share my optimism; he shook his head when I spoke of marriage, fearing Wickham is not a man to be trusted.

The daughter lay motionless, having fainted. The older woman’s screams and struggles, during which her hair was torn out, turned the orangutan’s likely peaceful intentions into rage. With one powerful swipe, it nearly decapitated her. The sight of blood drove the beast into a frenzy. Gnashing its teeth and with eyes flashing, it attacked the girl, burying its claws in her throat until she died. Its wild gaze then fell upon the head of the bed, where its master’s face, frozen in horror, was visible. The beast, still fearing the whip, was suddenly terrified. Aware of its guilt, it tried to hide the carnage, pacing the room in agitation, smashing furniture, and dragging the bed from its frame. Finally, it shoved the daughter’s body up the chimney and hurled the older woman’s corpse through the window. As the ape approached the window with the body, the sailor retreated in terror, sliding down the lightning rod and fleeing home, abandoning the beast. The sounds heard on the stairs were the Frenchman’s horrified cries mixed with the animal’s savage jabbering. There is little to add. The orangutan must have escaped down the rod just before the door was broken, closing the window behind it. The owner later captured it and sold it for a large sum to the Jardin des Plantes. Le Bon was released immediately after we explained the circumstances to the Prefect of Police. Though the Prefect was friendly toward my friend, he could not hide his annoyance at how things turned out, offering a few sarcastic remarks about people minding their own business. Let him talk, Dupin said, choosing not to respond. Let him speak; it will ease his conscience. I am satisfied with having outplayed him in his own domain. His failure to solve this mystery is not as surprising as he thinks; in truth, our friend the Prefect is far too cunning to be truly profound.

Nearly a year had passed since my father returned, and the seasons had almost completed their cycle. It was late May; the woods were lush with fresh growth, and the scent of newly mown grass filled the fields. I hoped the mild air and the beauty of nature might soften his mood, fostering the peace and love I needed before I could earn his trust. I chose an evening for my attempt, inviting him for a walk in a nearby beech grove where the light shade protected us from the setting sun. After walking in silence, we sat on a mossy mound. I can still see that spot clearly: the slender, smooth trunks wrapped in ivy, their dark, glossy leaves contrasting with the pale bark and bright new beech sprouts. The grass was mixed with moss and scattered with last autumn’s dead leaves, gathered by the wind into small piles. The breeze stirred the canopy, revealing the bright blue sky above. As evening fell, the distant trees glowed red in the sunlight, the wind faded, and birds flew past toward their nests. We sat together in that place, and when you hear of the terrible events that tore our souls apart in what should have been a paradise, you will understand why I remember it so vividly. I hoped its tranquility would grant me the courage and persuasive words I needed. I observed these details distractedly while organizing my thoughts. My heart raced as I prepared to speak, determined not to be turned away, yet terrified of his reaction. Finally, with great hesitation, I began: “Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the immense affection you showed upon your return, will hopefully excuse my boldness in speaking to you not just as a daughter, but with the openness of a friend and equal.”

I considered faking my death; my satisfied heirs would claim my fortune, and I would finally be free. Yet, the plan required careful execution; I could not be left penniless, so I had to secure funds. What wretched measures I was forced to take! A life of deception seemed my only path. Whenever guilt made me hesitate, a visit from an aunt or cousin would solidify my resolve. They would claim death is inevitable, then suggest my father had lost his mind since my mother’s passing. They called him insane and told me I was lucky he had not killed me during one of his episodes. They spoke with delicate, whispered hints, downcast eyes, and sympathetic whimpers. I listened calmly while trembling inside, unable to challenge their cruel words. What a delightful life, entirely devoid of honesty! I wore a gentle expression while harboring a cunning heart, feeling only the shame of my lies rather than the comfort of innocence. I, who once valued sincerity, now had to adopt a deceptive persona. It felt awkward at first, but I learned to lie with grace, staining my soul until its true nature was hidden. Oh, beloved father, accept your daughter’s pure heart; let me join you untainted, or you will not recognize me. Just as grief transformed Constance, deceit has changed me, until you might say in heaven, “This is not my child.” To be happy now and when we reunite, I must escape this mocking life. Only in solitude can I be myself and belong to you. Even now, I look back with disgust at the schemes I used to secure my independence and stage my own death. I could detail the painful struggles I endured to ensure my survival and convince the world I had perished, but I will not.

Mrs. Musgrove took the first chance to speak privately with Anne. She remarked that she wished Mrs. Charles possessed Anne’s way with the children, noting how they behaved differently around her. She lamented that they were generally spoiled and wished Anne could teach her sister how to manage them. While she considered them healthy and fine, she admitted their behavior was often difficult, which discouraged her from inviting them over as frequently as she might otherwise. She suspected Mrs. Charles was unhappy about this, but explained that it was exhausting to constantly correct children or bribe them with sweets to keep them quiet. Mary, meanwhile, complained to Anne that Mrs. Musgrove’s servants were constantly wandering the village instead of working, which she felt was a bad influence on her own reliable nursemaid, Jemima. Conversely, Mrs. Musgrove told Anne she avoided interfering in her daughter-in-law’s affairs, but warned her that Mary’s nursemaid was unreliable and overly concerned with her appearance, hoping Anne might keep a watchful eye on the situation. Finally, Mary expressed her frustration that Mrs. Musgrove often failed to grant her the social precedence she felt she deserved when they dined together at the Great House.

He thought so, at least, but who could be sure? There had been nothing more. He had spared her out of vanity and acted good only to hide his hypocrisy. He realized now that his self-denial had been mere curiosity. Would this murder haunt him forever? Must he always carry this burden? Confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained: the portrait. He had to destroy it. He had once enjoyed watching it age, but lately, it only brought him dread. It had become a conscience he could not escape. He grabbed the knife he had used to kill Basil Hallward. It was clean and bright. Just as it had killed the painter, it would destroy the painting and his past. Once the past was dead, he would finally be free. He stabbed the canvas. A terrible cry rang out, followed by a crash. The servants woke in terror. Two men passing by noticed the house, alerted a policeman, and waited. The officer rang the bell, but the house remained dark, save for a single light upstairs. When the officer left, the men walked away, mocking the owner, Dorian Gray. Inside, the servants whispered in fear. Mrs. Leaf wept while Francis stood pale. Eventually, he gathered the coachman and a footman to head upstairs.

I told myself I wanted no part of such business. When I went downstairs the next morning, the parlor was closed and the night watchers had left. Only the family, the widow Bartley, and our group remained. I studied their faces for any sign of what might have occurred, but I could tell nothing. By midday, the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They placed the coffin on chairs in the center of the room and arranged our chairs in rows, borrowing more from neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were filled. I noticed the coffin lid remained as it was, but I dared not look inside while others were present. People began to arrive, and the con artists and the girls took the front row. For half an hour, the mourners filed past in a single line to gaze at the dead man’s face. Some shed tears in the heavy silence, while the girls and the men sobbed with heads bowed. The only sounds were the shuffling of feet and the blowing of noses, which always seems more frequent at funerals than anywhere else except church. Once the room was packed, the undertaker moved about in black gloves with a smooth, soothing manner, making final adjustments without a sound. He guided people into place with silent nods and hand gestures before taking his position against the wall. He was the most stealthy, gliding man I have ever seen, completely devoid of any expression. They had borrowed a wheezing melodeon, and when a young woman began to play, it sounded strained and discordant. Everyone joined in the singing, though in my opinion, only Peter sounded decent. Then Reverend Hobson began his slow, solemn address. Suddenly, the most outrageous noise erupted from the cellar. It was only one dog, but he created such a powerful racket that the parson had to stand over the coffin and wait, as it was impossible to hear oneself think.

I agree. It is for the best. Will you just hold hands and swear that we— Oh no, that will not suffice for this. That is fine for trivial matters, especially with girls, because they always go back on their word and talk if they get upset, but there ought to be a written record for something this significant. And blood. Tom was thrilled by this idea. It was profound, dark, and ominous; the time and the setting were perfectly suited to it. He picked up a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, took a piece of red chalk from his pocket, and carefully scrawled these lines, biting his tongue in concentration as he pressed down on the strokes. Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about this and they wish they may drop dead in their tracks if they ever tell and rot. Huckleberry was filled with admiration for Tom’s writing skill and the gravity of his language. He immediately took a pin from his lapel to prick his finger, but Tom stopped him. Wait! Do not do that. A pin is brass. It might have verdigris on it. What is verdigris? It is poison. That is what it is. You swallow some of that and you will see. So Tom unwound thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked his thumb to squeeze out a drop of blood. After much effort, Tom signed his initials using his fingertip as a pen. He then showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was complete. They buried the shingle near the wall with somber rituals, believing their secret was now sealed forever. A figure crept stealthily through a gap in the other end of the ruined building, but they did not notice. Tom, Huckleberry whispered, does this keep us from ever telling, always? Of course it does. It does not matter what happens, we have to stay silent. We would drop dead, do you not know that? Yes, I suppose that is so. They whispered for a while longer. Suddenly, a dog let out a long, mournful howl just ten feet away. The boys clutched each other in terror. Which one of us does he mean? Huckleberry gasped. I do not know, look through the crack. Quick! No, you do it, Tom! I cannot, I cannot do it, Huck!

Mr. Wopsle’s eyes were glaring in such a strange, confused way that I could not understand him. I pondered this long after he had finished his performance, and I was still thinking about it when I left the theater and found him waiting for me outside. We shook hands and walked down the street together. I mentioned that I had seen him looking at me, but he seemed preoccupied. He asked if I had noticed anyone else in the audience. When I asked who he meant, he looked lost and insisted he could swear he saw someone. I grew uneasy and asked him to explain. He rambled on, saying he might not have noticed the man if I had not been there. I looked around nervously, feeling a chill. He assured me the man was gone, having left before the show ended. Because of my own secrets, I suspected Mr. Wopsle might be trying to trick me into saying something incriminating, so I remained silent. He continued, saying he had imagined the man was with me until he realized I was unaware of him sitting behind me like a ghost. I felt cold again but stayed quiet, fearing he was trying to link me to Provis. I knew for certain Provis had not been there. He told me I would find his story hard to believe. He asked if I remembered that Christmas Day from my childhood when soldiers came to the Gargery house to fix handcuffs. I told him I remembered it well. He asked if I recalled the hunt for the two convicts, when Gargery carried me on his back and I struggled to keep up with him as he led the way.

The following day, the ghost felt exhausted and frail. The intense strain of the past month had taken its toll, leaving his nerves frayed and his disposition jumpy. After remaining in his quarters for five days, he decided to abandon the library bloodstain. Since the Otis family lacked the refinement to appreciate such symbolic phenomena, they were clearly unworthy of it. While he could not control his astral manifestations, he felt bound by duty to haunt the corridor weekly and wail from the oriel window twice a month. Despite his wicked past, he remained diligent regarding his supernatural obligations. For the next three Saturdays, he crept through the hall between midnight and three, taking great care to remain undetected. He discarded his boots, stepped softly on the creaking floorboards, donned a velvet cloak, and used the Rising Sun Lubricator to silence his chains. Though initially humiliated, he eventually recognized the utility of the oil. Nevertheless, he faced constant harassment. The twins frequently rigged the corridor with tripwires, and he suffered a painful tumble after stepping on a butter-slide they had placed near the Tapestry Chamber while he was disguised as Black Isaac. Enraged by this indignity, he vowed to reclaim his status by terrorizing the boys the following night as Reckless Rupert, the Headless Earl. He had not donned this costume in seventy years, not since he had frightened Lady Barbara Modish so severely that she abandoned her engagement to Lord Canterville’s grandfather and eloped with Jack Castleton, refusing to marry into a family plagued by such a ghastly specter.

From the moment we embarked at the stairs, I had kept a vigilant watch for signs of suspicion, yet found none. We were certainly not being shadowed by any vessel; had we been, I would have steered for the bank to force their hand. Instead, we proceeded without interference. Wrapped in his boat-cloak, he appeared entirely at home in the surroundings. It was striking—perhaps a result of his harsh existence—that he remained the most composed among us. He was not unconcerned, expressing a wish to see his gentleman thrive abroad, nor was he merely resigned, yet he refused to anticipate trouble. He met adversity only when it arrived. "If you knew, dear boy," he remarked, "what it is to sit here with you and smoke, after years confined within four walls, you would envy me. You cannot truly understand." I replied that I appreciated the joys of liberty. He shook his head solemnly. "You cannot know it as I do. You must have been imprisoned to grasp it fully, but I will not be melancholy." It seemed contradictory that he would risk his life and liberty for a singular purpose, yet I realized that safety without peril was perhaps too foreign to his nature. He confirmed this after a pause: "When I was across the world, I constantly looked toward this side. Growing wealthy there felt hollow, for everyone knew Magwitch, and no one cared where he went. They are not so indifferent here, at least if they knew my whereabouts." I assured him that if all proceeded as planned, he would be secure and free within hours. He drew a deep breath and replied, "I hope so." I asked, "And do you believe it?"

Dorian, you must care about your reputation. Every gentleman does. You wouldn't want people calling you vile. Wealth and status aren't everything. I don't believe these rumors, especially when I look at you. Sin always leaves a mark on a man's face; it cannot be hidden. There is no such thing as a secret vice. If a man is corrupt, it shows in his mouth, his eyes, or even his hands. Last year, a man I didn't know offered me a fortune to paint him, but I refused because I hated the shape of his fingers. I later learned his life was truly dreadful. But you, with your innocent face and youthful glow, seem incapable of such things. Yet, I rarely see you now, and when I hear these terrible whispers, I don't know what to think. Why does the Duke of Berwick leave the room when you enter? Why do so many gentlemen avoid you? Lord Staveley told me recently that while you have artistic taste, no decent woman should be allowed to know you. He said it right in front of everyone, and it was horrible. Why is your friendship so destructive? Think of the young soldier who killed himself, or Sir Henry Ashton, who had to flee England in disgrace.

Knights in heavy armor were slow. With the ground clear of snow and mud, they could manage a seven-mile pace, swapping horses twice to arrive by six. There would be enough daylight to spot the white cloth on my arm, allowing me to take command. We would surround the prison and rescue the king quickly. It would be a dramatic scene, though I would have preferred noon for the added theatrical effect. To improve my odds, I decided to find people I recognized and reveal my identity, potentially solving our problem without the knights. However, I had to be careful. I needed to acquire fine clothing gradually, buying increasingly expensive outfits at distant shops until I reached silk and velvet. I began my plan, but it failed instantly. Turning a corner, I ran into one of our slaves with a watchman. I coughed, and his sharp look suggested he recognized me. I ducked into a shop, pretending to browse while watching them talk and peer through the door. I decided to escape through the back. I told the shopkeeper I was an undercover officer hunting an escaped slave and asked her to tell my partner at the door to move to the end of the alley to intercept the fugitive. Eager to see a notorious criminal, she hurried off to deliver the message.

He kept one secret from his dear friends, nurtured since childhood. Despite his affection for his peers, he dared not trust them with his feelings, fearing they would mock the intensity of a passion he considered the very essence of his life. A man of modest means lived near his family estate with three lovely daughters. The eldest was the most beautiful, possessing a sharp intellect and an angelic temperament. She and my father had been childhood playmates; his mother had always favored her, ensuring they spent every vacation together. Influenced by novels that introduced the concept of romance to the impressionable, he was deeply affected. By age eleven, he spoke the language of love to her. Though she was two years his senior, her sheltered upbringing left her naive; she accepted his declarations innocently, unaware of their weight. She had read no novels and knew nothing of the distinction between love and friendship. By the time she understood the nature of their bond, her heart was already his, and she feared only that his interest might eventually fade. Their love grew more ardent and tender with time, becoming inseparable from his very being. They kept their secret, and though he feared his companions might judge him for loving someone of lower social standing, he remained steadfast in his resolve to marry her as soon as he could overcome the inevitable obstacles. Diana was truly worthy of his devotion.

She and the children could easily stay. Ah, papa, that is something you have never managed, and I doubt you ever will. Isabella cannot bear to be away from her husband. This was undeniable. Though he disliked the thought, Mr. Woodhouse could only sigh in resignation. Seeing his spirits dampen at the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband, Emma quickly shifted the conversation to cheer him. Harriet must spend as much time with us as possible while my brother and sister are visiting. I am sure she will adore the children. We are quite proud of them, aren't we, papa? I wonder which she will find more handsome, Henry or John? Yes, I wonder. Poor little things, they will be so happy to visit. They love being at Hartfield, Harriet. I am sure they do, sir. I cannot imagine who would not. Henry is a fine boy, but John looks just like his mother. Henry is the eldest, named after me rather than his father. John, the second, is named after his father. Some were surprised the eldest was not, but Isabella insisted on Henry, which I thought was very sweet. He is a clever boy, indeed. They are all remarkably bright and have such charming ways. They stand by my chair and ask, Grandpapa, can you give me some string? Once, Henry asked for a knife, but I told him knives are only for grandpapas. I think their father is often too rough with them. He seems rough to you, Emma replied, because you are so gentle. If you compared him to other fathers, you would not think so. He wants his boys to be active and hardy, and while he may be sharp when they misbehave, he is an affectionate father. Mr. John Knightley is truly devoted. The children love him. And then their uncle comes in and tosses them toward the ceiling in a terrifying way! But they love it, papa; it is their favorite thing. They enjoy it so much that if their uncle did not make them take turns, they would never stop. Well, I cannot understand it. That is true for all of us, papa. Half the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other.

I reasoned backward. The killers escaped through one of these windows, yet the sashes were found locked from the inside. This obvious fact had stopped the police from investigating further, but I knew the windows must be capable of locking themselves. I went to the first window, removed the nail with effort, and tried to lift the sash. It would not budge. I realized a hidden spring must exist, and finding it confirmed my theory. I pressed the spring but left the window closed. I replaced the nail and studied it. A killer could close the window so the spring would catch, but they could not have replaced the nail from the outside. This meant they must have escaped through the other window. Assuming the springs were identical, there had to be a difference in the nails or how they were secured. I climbed onto the bed to examine the second window. I found the identical spring behind the headboard, but the nail looked just as sturdy and well-fitted as the first. You might think I was confused, but I was not. My logic remained sound, and I had followed the trail directly to the nail. Despite its appearance, the fact that the trail ended here meant something was wrong. I touched the nail, and its head, along with a small piece of the shank, snapped off in my hand.

I decided to get off as soon as we reached town to avoid him. I managed this easily. My small bag was under my feet, so I simply opened the latch, grabbed it, and stepped onto the pavement by the first streetlamp. The convicts continued on the coach toward the river. In my mind, I pictured the boat waiting for them at the muddy stairs, heard the harsh command to row, and saw the dark, ominous ship on the black water. I could not explain my fear, but it was intense and vague. As I walked to the hotel, I felt a dread far worse than just worrying about being recognized. It was formless, like a sudden return of a childhood terror. The Blue Boar’s coffee room was empty, and I had already started my dinner before the waiter recognized me. After apologizing for his poor memory, he asked if he should fetch Mr. Pumblechook. I told him absolutely not. The waiter, who had served me when I was first apprenticed, looked surprised. He quickly placed a dirty local newspaper in front of me. I picked it up and read a paragraph about my recent rise in fortune. It claimed that my earliest mentor was a respected local man in the corn and seed trade, whose business was located near the High Street. The article praised him as the guide behind my success, clearly taking pride that our town had produced the man who started my career.

It is only fair to note that the young woman did not explicitly decline, but rather voiced a fervent wish to be damned if she would; a refined way of dodging the plea, revealing a natural courtesy that recoiled from the cruelty of a blunt rejection. The Jew’s face darkened. He shifted his gaze from this lady, dressed in a vibrant red gown, green boots, and yellow hair-papers, to the other woman. Nancy, my dear, Fagin asked coaxingly, what is your answer? It will not work, so do not bother, Fagin, Nancy replied. What do you mean by that? Mr. Sikes asked, glancing up with a scowl. Exactly what I said, Bill, Nancy answered calmly. You are the perfect person for this, Sikes argued, as no one around here knows you. Since I intend to keep it that way, my answer is more no than yes, Bill, Nancy replied with equal composure. She will go, Fagin, Sikes insisted. No, she will not, Fagin, Nancy countered. Yes, she will, Fagin, Sikes repeated. Sikes was correct. Through a mix of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman was finally persuaded to accept the task. She lacked the hesitations of her friend, for having moved recently from the distant but respectable Ratcliffe to the area near Field Lane, she feared no recognition from her many acquaintances. Thus, with a clean white apron over her dress and her hair-papers hidden beneath a straw bonnet—both items supplied from the Jew’s vast collection—Miss Nancy prepared to depart. Wait a moment, my dear, the Jew said, producing a small covered basket. Carry this in one hand. It appears more respectable. Give her a door-key for the other hand, Sikes added; it looks authentic. Yes, that is perfect, the Jew agreed, hanging a large key on the woman’s right forefinger. Excellent, he said, rubbing his hands. Oh, my brother! My poor, sweet, innocent little brother! Nancy cried, breaking into tears while clutching the basket and key in a display of feigned distress. What has become of him! Where have they taken him! Please, have pity and tell me what has happened to the dear boy, gentlemen; I beg you, gentlemen!

Citizens, butchers, cattle drivers, street vendors, children, thieves, and vagrants of every sort were packed into a chaotic mass. The whistling of drovers, barking dogs, bellowing oxen, bleating sheep, and squealing pigs mixed with the shouts, curses, and arguments of the crowd. Bells rang, taverns roared with noise, and people shoved and yelled in a hideous, discordant din. The unwashed, disheveled figures darting through the throng created a scene so overwhelming it dazed the senses. Mr. Sikes dragged Oliver through the thickest part of the crowd, ignoring the sights and sounds that stunned the boy. He nodded to a few acquaintances and declined several offers for a drink, pushing forward until they reached Holborn. Look here, kid, Sikes said, checking the church clock. It is nearly seven. Keep moving and do not lag behind, you lazy boy. Sikes jerked Oliver’s wrist, forcing the boy to trot to keep pace with his long strides. They continued until they passed Hyde Park Corner toward Kensington, where Sikes slowed down to wait for an approaching cart. Seeing Hounslow written on the side, he politely asked the driver for a ride to Isleworth. Jump in, the driver said. Is that your boy? Yes, he is my boy, Sikes replied, staring at Oliver while his hand drifted toward his pocketed pistol. Your father walks a bit fast for you, does he not? the driver asked, noticing Oliver was breathless. Not at all, Sikes interrupted. He is used to it. Come on, take my hand, Ned. Get in. Sikes helped Oliver into the cart, where the driver told him to rest on a pile of sacks. As they passed each milestone, Oliver wondered where he was being taken. They traveled through Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, and Brentford, continuing as steadily as if they had only just begun.

Four days later, a funeral procession departed Canterville Chase at eleven o’clock at night. Eight black horses pulled the hearse, their heads adorned with nodding ostrich plumes, while the leaden coffin lay beneath a purple pall embroidered with the golden Canterville crest. Servants carrying torches walked alongside the carriages, creating a somber and striking scene. Lord Canterville, having traveled from Wales, served as chief mourner, riding with young Virginia. The American Minister and his wife followed, then Washington and the boys, with Mrs. Umney in the final carriage; having endured the ghost’s presence for fifty years, she was deemed entitled to witness his final rest. The Reverend Augustus Dampier conducted the service at a grave beneath the churchyard’s ancient yew tree. As the coffin was lowered, Virginia placed a cross of white and pink almond blossoms upon it. Suddenly, the moon emerged from the clouds, bathing the churchyard in silver light as a nightingale sang from a nearby thicket. Recalling the ghost’s description of the Garden of Death, Virginia wept silently and remained quiet for the journey home. The following morning, Mr. Otis met with Lord Canterville to discuss the jewels the ghost had gifted Virginia. They were magnificent, particularly a sixteenth-century Venetian ruby necklace, and their immense value caused Mr. Otis to hesitate about his daughter keeping them. He told Lord Canterville that he believed the jewels should be considered family heirlooms and requested that he take them to London as recovered property. He added that his daughter was merely a child with no interest in such luxuries.

His personality and temperament, though different from hers, would have perfectly suited her. But such a happy marriage would not be the example of true marital bliss for others to admire. Instead, a different, less promising union was about to take place within her family. She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would support themselves, but she knew that a couple brought together only by passion rather than virtue could not expect lasting happiness. Mr. Gardiner wrote to Mr. Bennet again. He briefly acknowledged Mr. Bennet's thanks, expressed his desire to help the family, and asked that the matter never be mentioned again. His main point was that Wickham had decided to leave the militia. He noted that he wanted this change as soon as the marriage was settled, as it was best for both Wickham and his niece. Wickham intended to join the regular army, and friends were helping him secure a position as an ensign in a regiment stationed in the north. It was better for them to be far away. He seemed sincere, and Mr. Gardiner hoped that in a new place, where they had reputations to maintain, they would be more careful. He had written to Colonel Forster to explain the plan and to promise that Wickham’s debts in Brighton would be paid. He asked Mr. Bennet to do the same for the creditors in Meryton, using a list he provided. He hoped Wickham had been honest about his debts. Everything would be settled within a week.
