Good heavens, the Duchess thought, he is just a palm reader after all. How dreadful. I hope he is at least a foreigner; that would make it slightly more acceptable. I must introduce him to you. Introduce him? the Duchess exclaimed. You don't mean he is here? She began searching for her tortoise-shell fan and tattered lace shawl, prepared to leave immediately. Of course he is here; I would never host a party without him. He claims I have a pure psychic hand and that if my thumb were slightly shorter, I would be a confirmed pessimist living in a convent. Oh, I see, the Duchess said, feeling relieved. He tells fortunes, I suppose? And misfortunes, Lady Windermere replied. Plenty of them. Next year, I am in great danger by land and sea, so I plan to live in a balloon and hoist my dinner up in a basket. It is all written on my finger or palm, I forget which. But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys. My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their palms read monthly to know what to avoid. We do it anyway, but it is pleasant to be warned. If someone doesn't fetch Mr. Podgers, I shall have to go myself. Let me go, Lady Windermere, said a tall, handsome young man standing nearby, listening with an amused smile. Thanks, Lord Arthur, but I fear you wouldn't recognize him. If he is as wonderful as you say, I couldn't miss him. Describe him, and I will bring him to you. He doesn't look like a palmist at all. He isn't mysterious or romantic. He is a short, stout man with a bald head and gold-rimmed spectacles, looking like a cross between a family doctor and a country lawyer. It is not my fault; people are so annoying. My pianists look like poets, and my poets look like pianists. Last season, I invited a dangerous conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up many people and wore chainmail with a dagger in his sleeve—and he arrived looking like a pleasant clergyman, cracking jokes all evening.

I cannot determine how long I stayed in that condition. It was certainly a significant duration, for when I regained consciousness, dawn was arriving, the balloon soared at an immense altitude above an endless sea, and no land appeared anywhere along the horizon. My feelings upon waking were not as painful as one might expect. In fact, a touch of budding insanity colored the detached way I assessed my predicament. I lifted my hands to my face, one by one, pondering why my veins were swollen and my fingernails turned a ghastly black. I then inspected my head, shaking it and touching it thoroughly until I felt certain it had not grown larger than the balloon, as I had briefly feared. With a knowing air, I searched my pockets, and upon finding my tablets and toothpick case missing, I felt strangely annoyed by my inability to explain their loss. I then noticed a sharp discomfort in my left ankle, and a vague awareness of my circumstances began to dawn on me. Curiously, I felt neither shock nor terror. If I experienced any emotion, it was a smug satisfaction regarding the ingenuity I would soon employ to escape this trap; I never once doubted my eventual survival. I sat in deep thought for several minutes, recalling how I pressed my lips together and touched my nose, mimicking the gestures of a man pondering complex matters from the comfort of his chair. Having gathered my thoughts, I carefully reached behind me to unfasten the heavy iron buckle on my trousers. The three teeth were rusted and stiff, but I managed to pivot them to a right angle and keep them steady. Gripping this tool between my teeth, I began to untie my cravat, a task that required several pauses before I finally succeeded.

I have neglected to mention the most significant point. What is that, Harry? asked the youth apathetically. The obvious comfort, of course. Stealing another person's suitor after losing one's own. In high society, that always redeems a woman. Yet, Dorian, how distinct Sibyl Vane must have been from the women we usually encounter! Her death possesses a genuine beauty to me. I am pleased to live in an era where such marvels occur, as they validate the concepts we merely toy with, like romance, passion, and love. I was dreadfully cruel to her, you forget. I suspect women value cruelty, sheer cruelty, above all else. They possess remarkably primitive instincts. Despite our efforts to emancipate them, they remain slaves seeking masters. They enjoy being controlled. I am certain you were magnificent. I have never witnessed your true rage, but I can imagine how captivating you appeared. Furthermore, you remarked something to me two days ago that I initially dismissed as whimsical, but now recognize as profound; it explains everything. What was that, Harry? You claimed Sibyl Vane embodied every romantic heroine for you—that she was Desdemona one evening and Ophelia the next; that if she perished as Juliet, she revived as Imogen. She shall never revive again, the youth murmured, hiding his face in his hands. No, she will not. Her final performance is over. View her solitary death in that cheap dressing-room as a vivid, dark fragment of a Jacobean tragedy, a striking scene from Webster, Ford, or Tourneur. The girl never truly lived, and thus she never truly died. To you, she remained a dream, a phantom drifting through Shakespeare’s works, enhancing their beauty and enriching the music of his verse. Once she touched reality, she ruined it, and it ruined her, leading to her departure. Grieve for Ophelia if you must. Cover your head in ashes because Cordelia was strangled. Rail against Heaven because Brabantio’s daughter perished. But do not squander tears on Sibyl Vane. She was less real than they. Silence followed. The room grew dim as evening approached. Shadows crept in from the garden with silent, silver steps. The colors slowly drained from the surroundings. Eventually, Dorian Gray raised his head.

I call upon you, spirits of the dead and ministers of vengeance, to guide me in my task. Let that hellish monster suffer the same agony and despair that now torment me. I began my plea with a solemnity that made me feel my murdered friends were listening, but by the end, rage choked my voice. A loud, fiendish laugh broke the silence of the night. It echoed through the mountains, and I felt as if hell itself were mocking me. I would have ended my miserable life then, had I not been bound by my vow of vengeance. The laughter faded, and a familiar, hated voice whispered near my ear, I am satisfied, wretch! You have chosen to live, and I am satisfied. I lunged toward the sound, but the devil escaped. The moon rose, illuminating his ghastly form as he fled with supernatural speed. I have pursued him for months. I followed his trail along the Rhone, but in vain. I tracked him to the Mediterranean, where I saw him board a ship bound for the Black Sea, yet he slipped away again. Through the wilds of Russia and Tartary, I have followed his path. Sometimes terrified peasants told me of his movements; sometimes he left clues himself, fearing that if I lost his trail, I would give up and die. As snow fell, I followed his massive footprints across the plains. To you, just beginning your life, how can I explain the agony I have endured? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my burdens; I carried my own personal hell with me. Yet, a benevolent spirit often guided my steps, rescuing me from impossible situations. When I was near death from starvation, I would miraculously find food in the wilderness to restore my strength.

Sir Walter had rented a fine house in Camden Place, a grand and elevated location befitting a man of his status, and both he and Elizabeth were quite pleased with their new home. Anne arrived with a heavy heart, dreading a long stay and wondering when she might finally escape. However, the unexpectedly warm welcome she received lifted her spirits. Her father and sister were genuinely glad to see her, if only to show off their new residence and furnishings, and they treated her with kindness. They even appreciated having a fourth person at the dinner table. Mrs. Clay was pleasant and smiling, though her manners felt routine. Anne had expected such performative politeness from her, but the friendliness of her father and sister was a surprise. They were in high spirits and eager to share their news, showing no interest in hearing about Anne’s life. After fishing for compliments about how much they were missed in their old neighborhood—which Anne could not provide—they quickly turned the conversation back to themselves. Uppercross and Kellynch held no interest for them; they only cared about Bath. They assured her that Bath exceeded all their expectations. Their house was clearly the best in Camden Place, with drawing rooms that surpassed any others in layout and decor. They were highly sought after, with strangers constantly leaving calling cards despite their efforts to limit new acquaintances. Anne understood why they were happy, yet she sighed to see her father feel no shame in his diminished circumstances. He seemed to have forgotten the responsibilities of a landowner, finding vanity instead in the trivialities of city life. She could only sigh and smile as Elizabeth proudly paced between the folding doors, boasting about the space of rooms that were barely thirty feet apart—a woman who had once been the mistress of Kellynch Hall. Yet, their happiness did not end there; they also had Mr. Elliot.

He does not understand English, but judges by tone. Alberto Montani, a confectioner, testified that he was among the first to climb the stairs. He heard the voices in question; the gruff one was French and seemed to be arguing. He could not understand the shrill voice, which spoke quickly and unevenly; he assumes it was Russian, though he has never spoken to a Russian. He confirms the general testimony. Several witnesses confirmed that the fourth-floor chimneys were too narrow for a person. The brushes used to clean them were passed through every flue, and there was no back exit for anyone to escape while the group ascended. Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was wedged so tightly in the chimney that it took several men to pull it down. Paul Dumas, a physician, testified that he examined the bodies at daybreak. The young woman’s corpse was bruised and scraped, likely from being forced up the chimney. Her throat was chafed, with deep scratches under the chin and livid finger-shaped bruises. Her face was discolored, her eyes protruded, and her tongue was bitten. A bruise on her stomach suggested pressure from a knee. Dr. Dumas concluded she was strangled by unknown persons. The mother’s body was horribly mutilated, with shattered bones in her right leg and arm, a splintered left tibia, and broken ribs. Her entire body was bruised. Such injuries could only be inflicted by a very powerful man using a heavy, blunt object like a club, iron bar, or chair. A woman could not have caused such damage. The victim’s head was severed and shattered, and her throat had been cut with a sharp instrument, likely a razor.

Without pausing to reflect, and barely aware of her own emotions, Elizabeth finished the first letter and immediately grabbed the second. She opened it with great impatience and began to read; it had been composed a day after the first. My dearest sister, you have surely received my rushed note by now. I hope this one is clearer, though my mind is so confused that I cannot guarantee coherence. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know how to begin, but I must share some urgent, distressing news. While a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be imprudent, we now desperately hope it has occurred, as there is grave reason to fear they never headed for Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having departed Brighton shortly after the express. Although Lydia’s brief note to Mrs. Forster suggested they were bound for Gretna Green, Denny let slip his belief that Wickham never intended to go there or marry her at all. The Colonel, immediately alarmed, set out to track them. He followed their path as far as Clapham, where they abandoned their carriage for a hackney-coach. From there, they were only seen continuing toward London. I am at a loss. After searching that area, the Colonel traveled to Hertfordshire, checking every turnpike and inn in Barnet and Hatfield, yet found no trace of them. He came to Longbourn with great kindness to share his fears. I feel deeply for him and Mrs. Forster, though they are blameless. Our distress is profound. While my parents fear the worst, I cannot think so poorly of him. Perhaps they chose a private London wedding over their original plan. Even if he could harbor such designs against a girl of Lydia’s standing—which seems unlikely—could she truly be so lost? It is impossible. Still, I am saddened that the Colonel does not share my optimism; he shook his head when I voiced my hopes, admitting he feared Wickham was not a man to be trusted.

Back home, we collected taxes through tariffs, and citizens liked to believe foreign importers paid them. In reality, the American people paid, and the cost was distributed so perfectly that a millionaire and a laborer's infant paid the exact same amount: six dollars. I thought that was quite fair. In Arthur's time, Scotland and Ireland were under his rule, with a total population of under one million. A worker earned three cents a day, covering his own expenses. The government's annual budget was ninety thousand dollars, or about two hundred fifty dollars a day. By using nickels instead of gold for the king's healing ceremony, I satisfied everyone and saved four-fifths of the daily budget, which would equal eight hundred thousand dollars in my time. I used a lesson from my childhood: I used to donate buttons to missionaries instead of pennies. The buttons satisfied the distant recipients just as well as coins, and keeping the coins benefited me. Everyone was happy, and no one was harmed. Marinel processed the patients. He checked their eligibility, then sent the qualified ones to the king. A priest recited scripture while the king touched the patients' ulcers. Finally, the king hung a nickel around each patient's neck, and they were dismissed. You might wonder if that could actually cure anyone, but it did. Any ritual works if the patient has enough faith. Near Astolat, there was a chapel built where a goose girl claimed to have seen the Virgin Mary. A painting of the event hung there; it was so poorly done that you might think it would make a sick person worse. Instead, thousands of sick and lame people prayed before it every year and left fully recovered, and even healthy people could look at it without harm.

He said nothing about the matter until their guest left for the night. Once they were alone, he turned to his daughter and said, "Jane, congratulations. You will be a very happy woman." Jane immediately went to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness. "You are a good girl," he replied, "and it gives me great pleasure to think you will be so well settled. I have no doubt you will do very well together. Your temperaments are quite similar. You are both so accommodating that you will never decide on anything, so easygoing that every servant will cheat you, and so generous that you will always spend more than you earn." "I hope not," Jane said. "Financial recklessness would be inexcusable for me." "Spend more than they earn? My dear Mr. Bennet," his wife exclaimed, "what are you talking about? He has four or five thousand a year, if not more." Turning to her daughter, she added, "Oh, my dear Jane, I am so happy! I am sure I won't sleep a wink tonight. I knew this would happen. I always said it would. I knew you couldn't be that beautiful for nothing! I remember thinking the moment I saw him arrive in Hertfordshire last year that you two would end up together. He is the handsomest young man I have ever seen!" Wickham and Lydia were forgotten. Jane was undeniably her favorite child, and for the moment, she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters soon began asking her for favors she might be able to grant in the future. Mary requested access to the library at Netherfield, and Kitty pleaded for a few balls there every winter. From then on, Bingley was a daily visitor at Longbourn, arriving before breakfast and staying until after supper, unless some annoying neighbor forced him to accept a dinner invitation. Elizabeth had little time to talk to her sister, as Jane had no attention for anyone else while he was present. However, she proved useful to both during their brief separations. When Jane was away, Bingley would talk to Elizabeth about her, and when he left, Jane would seek the same comfort. "He has made me so happy," Jane said one evening, "by telling me he had no idea I was in town last spring!"

What a wonderful opportunity for our daughters! How so? How does that concern them? My dear Mr. Bennet, how can you be so annoying? You know I am thinking of him marrying one of them. Is that his plan for moving here? Nonsense, how can you say that? But it is very likely he might fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives. I see no reason for that. You and the girls can go, or you can send them on their own, which might be even better. Since you are as pretty as any of them, Mr. Bingley might prefer you. My dear, you flatter me. I once had my share of beauty, but I do not claim to be anything special now. When a woman has five grown daughters, she should stop worrying about her own looks. In such cases, a woman rarely has much beauty left to worry about. But you really must visit Mr. Bingley when he arrives. I cannot promise that, I assure you. Think of your daughters. Consider what a great match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are going for that very reason, even though they usually do not visit newcomers. You must go, because we cannot visit him unless you do. You are being overly cautious. I am sure Mr. Bingley will be happy to see you, and I will write a note giving my full consent for him to marry whichever girl he chooses, though I must put in a good word for my favorite, Lizzy. I forbid you to do that. Lizzy is no better than the others, and she is certainly not as pretty as Jane or as cheerful as Lydia.

Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, began to wonder if an honest life was truly superior. Concluding that it was, he abandoned his past, determined to start fresh elsewhere. He struggled significantly for a time, but his contented nature and clear purpose eventually led to success. Having worked as a farmhand and delivery boy, he is now the most cheerful young cattle farmer in Northamptonshire. My hand falters as I reach the end of this task, wishing to extend these adventures a little longer. I would gladly linger with those I have known so long, sharing their happiness by describing it. I would show Rose Maylie in the grace of her youth, casting a gentle light on everyone around her. I would depict her as the heart of her social circle, following her through sunny fields and hearing her soft voice on moonlit walks. I would observe her charity, her domestic devotion, and the love she shares with her late sister’s child as they fondly remember those they lost. I would summon those joyful children who gathered at her knee, listening to their laughter and recalling the sympathetic tears in her eyes. I wish to remember every smile and thought. How Mr. Brownlow educated his adopted son, growing closer as the boy’s character flourished and mirrored his old friend, bringing Brownlow both melancholy and comfort—and how the two orphans, shaped by hardship, practiced mercy and gratitude—these are stories that need not be told.

Roughly ten minutes later, the tea bell sounded, and since Virginia failed to appear, Mrs. Otis dispatched a footman to summon her. He soon returned, reporting that Miss Virginia was nowhere to be found. Initially, Mrs. Otis felt no alarm, as her daughter frequently gathered garden flowers for the table, but by six o’clock, she grew truly distressed. She sent the boys to search while she and Mr. Otis combed the house. By half-past six, the boys returned empty-handed. In their mounting panic, Mr. Otis recalled granting a group of gypsies permission to camp in the park days earlier. He immediately departed for Blackfell Hollow with his eldest son and two farmhands. The young Duke of Cheshire, frantic with worry, pleaded to join them, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing potential violence. Upon arrival, they discovered the gypsies had fled in haste, leaving behind a smoldering fire and scattered plates. After sending Washington and the men to search the area, Mr. Otis hurried home to wire police inspectors throughout the county regarding a kidnapped girl. He then ordered his horse, insisted his wife and sons dine, and rode toward Ascot Road with a groom. He had traveled only two miles when he heard hoofbeats; the young Duke was galloping after him on his pony, hatless and flushed. The boy gasped that he could not eat while Virginia remained missing and begged not to be sent away, suggesting their engagement might have prevented this crisis. Amused by the spirited youth and moved by his loyalty, the Minister leaned down to pat his shoulder, agreeing to let him join the search provided they stopped in Ascot for a hat.

Those elderly and frail individuals were constantly observed by the public bowing, and it was widely assumed that after escorting a client out, they continued to bow in the vacant office until the next visitor arrived. The barrister was perceptive enough to realize the banker would not have spoken so definitively without absolute moral certainty. Though the news was difficult to accept, he managed to process it. "Now," Mr. Stryver declared, gesturing toward the Temple, "my strategy is to prove you all mistaken." It was a classic maneuver for an Old Bailey strategist, providing him significant comfort. "You will not make me the one in the wrong, young lady," he remarked; "I shall handle that for you." Consequently, when Mr. Lorry visited at ten that night, Mr. Stryver, surrounded by a clutter of books and documents, appeared entirely unconcerned with the morning's topic. He even feigned surprise at seeing Mr. Lorry, acting distracted and preoccupied. "Well!" the good-natured messenger noted, after thirty minutes of futile attempts to steer the conversation. "I have been to Soho." "To Soho?" Mr. Stryver asked coldly. "Oh, of course! My mind was elsewhere!" "I am certain," Mr. Lorry continued, "that our previous discussion was accurate. My view remains unchanged, and I repeat my counsel." "I assure you," Mr. Stryver replied cordially, "that I regret this for your sake and for the father's. I realize this is a sensitive family matter; let us drop it." "I do not follow you," Mr. Lorry stated. "I imagine not," Stryver replied, nodding dismissively; "it is of no consequence." "But it does matter," Mr. Lorry insisted. "It truly does not. Having assumed there was wisdom where there is none, and ambition where there is none, I am relieved to be rid of the error. Young women have made such mistakes before, often ending in poverty and obscurity. Unselfishly, I regret the matter is closed, as it would have been disadvantageous for me; selfishly, I am glad it is over, as it would have been a poor worldly prospect—it goes without saying I would have gained nothing from it."

No imagination could capture the majesty of such a spectacle occurring in the dead of night; it would have resembled hell itself. Even in daylight, my hair bristled as I peered into the gaping depths, picturing my mind wandering through those strange, vaulted chambers and crimson chasms of unfathomable fire. I had narrowly avoided disaster. Had the balloon lingered in the cloud a moment longer—or had I not been prompted by the dampness to drop my ballast—certain destruction would have followed. Such dangers are often overlooked, yet they remain the most significant risks of ballooning. By now, however, I had reached an altitude where such concerns were no longer pressing. By seven o'clock, I was ascending swiftly, and the barometer marked a height of nine and a half miles. Breathing became arduous, and my head throbbed with intense pain. Feeling moisture on my cheeks, I realized it was blood flowing steadily from my ears. My eyes caused me further distress; they felt as though they had bulged from their sockets, and everything I saw appeared warped. These unexpected symptoms alarmed me. In a moment of reckless haste, I discarded fifteen pounds of ballast. This sudden surge upward thrust me too quickly into thin air, nearly ending my life and my journey. A spasm gripped me for over five minutes, and even afterward, I could only gasp for air, bleeding profusely from my nose, ears, and eyes. The pigeons were clearly suffering, struggling to break free, while the cat staggered about, mewing piteously with her tongue lolling out as if poisoned. I realized too late the folly of my actions and was overcome with agitation, expecting death to arrive at any moment.

I must warn you that I intend to tell Sybil everything. She is joining me for lunch tomorrow to discuss hats, and if Mr. Podgers discovers you have a short temper, gout, or a secret wife in Bayswater, I will certainly inform her. Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. I am not afraid, he replied. Sybil knows me as well as I know her. I am sorry to hear that. A successful marriage requires mutual misunderstanding. I am not being cynical, merely experienced, which is essentially the same. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile wants his palm read. Do not mention his engagement to one of London's most beautiful women, as that was in the Morning Post a month ago. Dear Lady Windermere, the Marchioness of Jedburgh cried, let Mr. Podgers stay. He just told me I should be an actress, and I am fascinated. If he said that, I am taking him away. Come here, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand. Lady Jedburgh pouted as she rose. If I cannot be an actress, I must at least be in the audience. We all will be, Lady Windermere said. Now, Mr. Podgers, tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is a favorite of mine. When Mr. Podgers examined Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned pale and fell silent. A shudder passed through him, and his bushy eyebrows twitched in that strange, irritating way they did when he was confused. Beads of sweat broke out on his yellow forehead like poisonous dew, and his fingers turned cold and clammy. Lord Arthur noticed this agitation and felt fear for the first time. He wanted to flee the room but forced himself to stay. It was better to know the worst than to endure this agonizing uncertainty. I am waiting, Mr. Podgers, he said. We are all waiting, Lady Windermere added impatiently, but the palmist remained silent. I suspect Arthur is going on the stage, Lady Jedburgh remarked, and Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him after your scolding.

He stood and left the chamber with my nurse, and my father walked in immediately. Nothing could have delighted me more than his arrival. I reached out my hand and asked if he, Elizabeth, and Ernest were safe. My father comforted me by confirming their well-being, hoping to lift my spirits, yet he soon realized a prison is no place for joy. He gazed sadly at the barred windows and dismal room, remarking on the misfortune that seemed to follow me, and mentioned poor Clerval. The mention of my murdered friend overwhelmed my fragile state, and I wept. I told him that some terrible fate hung over me, and I had to survive to meet it, or I would have perished beside Henry. We could not speak long, as my health required absolute rest. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted I avoid overexertion. Still, my father’s presence acted like a guardian angel, and I slowly regained my strength. As my illness faded, a dark, impenetrable melancholy took hold. Clerval’s murdered image haunted me, and my distress often worried my friends that I might relapse. I wondered why they kept me alive, concluding it was only to fulfill a destiny nearing its end. Soon, death would silence my suffering, and I would find peace through justice. At that time, death felt distant, though I constantly desired it, often sitting motionless for hours and praying for a catastrophe to destroy both me and my enemy. The assizes drew near. Having spent three months in jail, I was still frail, yet I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county town for my trial. Mr. Kirwin took charge of gathering witnesses and preparing my defense.

Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest the city is gripped by intense intellectual fervor. Extraordinary and unprecedented events have occurred there, defying all established theories and surely throwing European scientific and astronomical circles into complete chaos. On an unspecified date, a massive throng gathered in the Exchange square of Rotterdam. The weather was unseasonably warm and still, with the crowd enjoying occasional brief showers from scattered white clouds. Around midday, however, a sudden stir rippled through the assembly. A cacophony of voices erupted, and instantly, ten thousand faces turned skyward, ten thousand pipes dropped from ten thousand mouths, and a roar akin to Niagara Falls echoed throughout the city. The cause of this commotion was soon clear. Emerging from behind a cloud into the clear blue sky was a strange, solid, and oddly constructed object that baffled the gaping citizens below. What was it, and what did it signify? Nobody, including the burgomaster Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, had any explanation. Lacking a better response, everyone replaced their pipes, squinted upward at the phenomenon, and paced about, grunting and puffing in contemplation. Meanwhile, the object descended steadily toward the city, drawing more smoke and curiosity. Within minutes, it was close enough to identify: it was a balloon, though unlike any ever witnessed in Rotterdam before.

The stars were still bright when I woke at midnight, shaken by a nightmare. I had dreamt of a feast where Raymond, transformed into a monstrous, plague-bearing phantom, chased me while throwing foul-smelling vessels. The vision grew until it seemed to threaten the very sky. Shaking off the terror, I regained my senses and thought only of Perdita. I knew I had to return to her, to comfort her broken heart and guide her through her grief with both duty and compassion. Guided by the stars, I escaped the ruins of the Golden City. Outside the walls, I borrowed a horse from a group of soldiers and rode toward my sister. The landscape had changed; the army was gone, and the scattered soldiers I passed looked stunned and fearful. I entered the palace with a heavy heart, dreading what I would find. Perdita sat on the marble floor, her hair messy and her face pale with agony. When she looked up, a flicker of hope crossed her eyes, which only deepened my pain. I could not speak, and my forced smile told her everything. She bowed her head again, her fingers twisting nervously. When I finally found my voice, it frightened her; she did not want to hear the confirmation of her tragedy spoken aloud. Instead, she stood up and whispered, "Hush, Clara is finally sleeping after all her crying; we must not wake her."

After sharing their distress over the disastrous outcome, which Elizabeth viewed as inevitable and Jane could not deny was possible, Elizabeth pressed for more details. She asked what Colonel Forster had said and if he had suspected anything before the elopement, given how often the couple was seen together. Jane explained that the Colonel had noticed some mutual interest, particularly from Lydia, but felt no alarm. He had been very kind and was already traveling to see them to express his regret before the rumors of their flight to Scotland surfaced. Elizabeth asked if Denny knew of their plans or if he still believed Wickham would not marry her. Jane replied that when questioned, Denny claimed ignorance and refused to share his true thoughts, though he no longer insisted they would not marry, which gave her some hope. Elizabeth asked if they had truly believed the couple was married until the Colonel arrived. Jane admitted they had no reason to suspect otherwise, though she had worried about Lydia’s happiness because of Wickham’s past behavior. Their parents only saw the match as imprudent. Kitty later revealed that Lydia had hinted at this in her last letter, having known of their affection for weeks. When Elizabeth asked if this predated their time in Brighton, Jane said she believed not. Elizabeth then asked if the Colonel understood Wickham’s true character. Jane admitted he no longer spoke well of him, noting that Wickham was considered reckless and was rumored to have left Meryton with significant debts. Elizabeth lamented that if they had only been more open about what they knew of him, this might have been avoided. Jane agreed it might have been better, but noted that exposing someone’s past faults without knowing their current state of mind had felt wrong.

I reasoned backward. The killers fled through these windows, yet the sashes were found locked from within, a fact that baffled the police. Since the windows had to lock themselves, I examined the clear casement, removed the nail, and tried to lift the sash. It held firm, confirming my theory of a hidden spring. I soon located the mechanism, pressed it, and left the window closed. I replaced the nail and studied it. A killer could close the window, but could not replace the nail from outside. Thus, they must have exited through the other window. Assuming the springs were identical, I climbed onto the bed to inspect the second casement. I found the matching spring behind the headboard, but the nail appeared identical to the first, driven deep into the frame. You might assume I was stumped, but my logic remained sound. I had followed the trail to the nail itself. Despite its appearance, the nail was the key to the mystery. I touched it, and the head, along with a small portion of the shank, snapped off in my hand.

With no work to occupy him, he rhythmically clasped his hands together, alternating knuckles and palms, while rubbing his bearded chin in a constant, repetitive motion. Pulling him out of the mental drifting that followed his speech was like reviving someone from a faint or trying to catch the final words of a dying man. "Did you ask for my name?" "I certainly did." "One Hundred and Five, North Tower." "Is that all?" "One Hundred and Five, North Tower." With a weary sound, he returned to his work until the silence was broken again. "You are not a shoemaker by trade?" Mr. Lorry asked, watching him closely. The man looked to Defarge for help, but receiving none, he turned back to Mr. Lorry. "I am not a shoemaker? No, I was not. I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to--" He drifted off again, his hands continuing their mechanical movements. Eventually, his eyes returned to Mr. Lorry, and he started as if waking from a dream. "I asked permission to teach myself, and after a long time, I finally got it. I have made shoes ever since." As he reached for his shoe, Mr. Lorry asked, "Monsieur Manette, do you remember me at all?" The shoe fell from his hand as he stared at Mr. Lorry. Placing a hand on Defarge’s arm, Mr. Lorry continued, "Monsieur Manette, do you remember this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does any memory of an old banker, your past business, a servant, or a different time come to mind?" As the long-time prisoner stared between them, faint signs of his former intelligence flickered across his forehead, struggling through the mental fog. They appeared, faded, and vanished, but for a brief moment, they had been there.

No message of sympathy had reached Ireland. This oversight fell upon the offender; for when Lady Elliot passed away, Kellynch received no such letter, suggesting the Dalrymples viewed the kinship as ended. Restoring this connection was a matter Lady Russell and Mr. Elliot deemed significant. Family ties were worth keeping, and Lady Dalrymple, having rented a residence in Laura Place for three months, promised a stylish social life. Lady Russell had heard her described as a delightful woman, and it seemed prudent to renew the acquaintance if it could be managed with proper dignity. Sir Walter insisted on his own approach, composing an elaborate letter of explanation and regret to his noble cousin. Though Lady Russell and Mr. Elliot found the letter lacking, it successfully elicited a brief, polite reply from the Dowager Viscountess. The effort concluded, and the rewards followed. They visited Laura Place and displayed the cards of the Viscountess and Miss Carteret prominently, frequently mentioning their cousins to all acquaintances. Anne felt embarrassed. Even had the visitors been pleasant, she would have disliked the fuss, but they were unremarkable. They possessed no notable grace or intellect. Lady Dalrymple was deemed charming merely for her pleasant demeanor, while Miss Carteret was so dull and clumsy that only her lineage made her presence in Camden Place acceptable. Lady Russell admitted disappointment, yet insisted the connection held value. When Anne shared her assessment with Mr. Elliot, he conceded they were personally uninteresting but argued they remained valuable for their social standing and ability to gather good company. Anne smiled and replied that her definition of good company involved intelligent, well-informed individuals capable of engaging conversation.

Long ago, I became close with a man named William Legrand. Descended from an old Huguenot line, he was once affluent, but a string of calamities left him destitute. To escape the shame of his ruin, he departed New Orleans, his ancestral home, and settled on Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston, South Carolina. This island is quite unique, composed mostly of sea sand, stretching three miles long and never exceeding a quarter-mile in width. A barely visible creek, winding through a marshy thicket of reeds and mud favored by marsh hens, separates it from the mainland. Vegetation is sparse or stunted, with no large trees. Near the western tip, where Fort Moultrie and some modest summer cottages for Charleston residents stand, one finds the bristly palmetto. Otherwise, the island is blanketed in thick sweet myrtle, a shrub prized by English gardeners that grows up to twenty feet high, creating a fragrant, dense, and nearly impassable thicket. Deep within this brush, near the island's eastern end, Legrand constructed a small hut where he lived when we first met by chance. Our acquaintance quickly grew into friendship, as the recluse possessed qualities that commanded respect. He was highly educated and brilliant, though plagued by misanthropy and prone to erratic shifts between zeal and gloom. He owned many books but seldom read them, preferring to hunt, fish, or wander the beach and myrtle groves searching for shells and insects—his collection of which would have impressed a naturalist like Swammerdamm. He was usually joined on these outings by an elderly freedman named Jupiter. Despite the family's financial collapse, Jupiter refused to leave his young master, ignoring all threats or entreaties to depart. It is likely that Legrand’s relatives, fearing for his mental stability, encouraged this stubborn loyalty to ensure the wanderer remained under watch.

I traveled to the plantation and resumed my questioning of the elderly laborers. Eventually, one aged woman mentioned she knew of Bessop’s Castle, though she clarified it was actually a tall rock rather than a building. I promised her payment, and after some hesitation, she agreed to lead me there. Once we arrived, I sent her away and began my inspection. The site was a cluster of crags, one of which stood out for its height and unnatural, isolated shape. I climbed to the top, uncertain of my next move. While pondering, I noticed a narrow shelf on the eastern side, about a yard below where I stood. It was roughly eighteen inches long and a foot wide, and a nearby niche gave it the look of an antique chair. I felt certain this was the 'devil’s seat' mentioned in the manuscript, and the mystery began to unravel. I realized 'good glass' referred to a telescope, a common term among sailors. It was clear I needed to use a telescope from this exact spot. I concluded that the specific degrees and compass directions were instructions for aiming the instrument. Thrilled, I rushed home to retrieve my telescope and returned to the rock. I lowered myself onto the ledge, finding I could only sit in one specific way, which reinforced my theory. I began using the glass, interpreting the degrees as the elevation above the horizon, while the compass provided the horizontal bearing. After setting the direction, I adjusted the elevation until I spotted a circular gap in the leaves of a distant, towering tree.

Upon arriving at the stairhead, he composed himself and prepared his famous demonic cackle. This performance had proven quite effective previously, having reportedly whitened Lord Raker’s hair overnight and caused three of Lady Canterville’s governesses to resign prematurely. He unleashed his most terrifying laugh, causing the vaulted ceiling to vibrate, but the echo had barely faded when Mrs. Otis emerged in a blue dressing-gown. She offered him a bottle of Dr. Dobell’s tincture, suggesting it would cure his apparent indigestion. Enraged, the ghost prepared to transform into a large black dog—a feat credited with causing the permanent mental decline of the Hon. Thomas Horton—but the sound of footsteps forced him to reconsider. Instead, he merely glowed with a faint phosphorescence and vanished with a mournful groan just as the twins arrived. Back in his chamber, he collapsed in a state of intense agitation. While the twins’ rudeness and Mrs. Otis’s materialism were irritating, he was most distressed by his failure to wear his suit of mail. He had expected even Americans to be impressed by a Spectre in Armour, perhaps out of deference to Longfellow, whose poetry had often occupied his lonely hours. Furthermore, it was his own armor, worn successfully at the Kenilworth tournament and praised by the Virgin Queen. Yet, the weight of the breastplate and helmet had proven too much, causing him to collapse and suffer bruised knees and knuckles. He remained unwell for several days, rarely leaving his room except to maintain the bloodstain. Eventually, he recovered and determined to attempt a third time to terrify the American Minister and his family.

Smallpox! I rushed to the king and whispered, "Leave at once, sire! The woman is dying of the same disease that devastated Camelot two years ago." He did not move. "I will stay and help," he insisted. I urged him again, "King, you must go." He replied, "You mean well, but it would be shameful for a king to show fear or for a knight to ignore those in need. I will not leave. You should go, as the Church forbids your presence here, and they will punish you severely if they find out." It was a dangerous situation that could cost him his life, but I knew arguing was useless. If he felt his honor was at stake, he would not budge. I let the matter drop. The woman spoke, "Kind sir, would you climb the ladder and tell me what you find? Do not fear to tell me, for a mother's heart can break only once." The king set down his bag and said, "Stay and feed her. I will go." He started up, then paused to look at a man lying in the shadows who had not spoken. "Is this your husband?" the king asked. "Yes," she replied. "Is he asleep?" "Thank God, yes, for three hours now. I am so grateful for his rest." I promised, "We will be careful not to wake him." She answered, "You cannot, for he is dead. It is a relief to know he is safe from harm and insult. He is in heaven now, or perhaps in hell, where he will at least be free from bishops and abbots. We were together for twenty-five years and never parted until today. This morning, he was delirious, imagining we were children wandering in happy fields, and in that state, he slipped away from this life."

Plenty of cold water remained to conclude their meal. Soon, Becky proposed they continue, but Tom hesitated before speaking. He asked if she could handle some difficult news. Becky grew pale but signaled her readiness. Tom explained that they needed to remain near the water, as their remaining candle was nearly gone. Becky broke into sobbing, and despite Tom’s efforts to soothe her, she remained inconsolable. She eventually asked if people would search for them, and Tom assured her they certainly would. Becky wondered if the search had already begun, and Tom expressed his hope that it had. When she asked when they would be missed, Tom suggested it would be upon the group's return to the boat. Becky worried they might not notice their absence in the dark, but Tom countered that her mother would surely realize she was missing once home. Seeing Becky’s sudden terror, Tom realized his mistake; she was not supposed to have been home that evening. The children fell silent, both realizing the grim truth that it might be Sunday morning before her mother discovered she was not at the Harpers'. They watched their final candle flicker and fade until the wick stood bare, the flame climbed a wisp of smoke, and total darkness consumed them. Neither could say how much time passed before Becky realized she was weeping in Tom’s arms. After a long, death-like slumber, they awoke to their renewed suffering. Tom speculated it could be Sunday or even Monday. He attempted to engage Becky in conversation, but she was overwhelmed by despair. Tom insisted they must have been missed and that a search was likely underway, but when he shouted for help, the eerie echoes in the dark discouraged him from trying again. As time dragged on, hunger returned to plague them. They shared the remainder of Tom’s cake, yet their hunger only intensified.

In the middle of the gap, I noticed a white object, though I could not initially identify it. After adjusting my telescope, I realized it was a human skull. Upon this realization, I felt confident the mystery was resolved. The instructions regarding the seventh limb and the east side clearly pointed to the skull's location, while the direction to shoot from the left eye of the death's head could only mean one thing for finding buried treasure. I understood that a bullet dropped from that eye would mark a spot, and a straight line drawn from the trunk through that point and extended fifty feet would reveal where the treasure was hidden. I remarked that the plan was clever yet straightforward, and asked what happened after he departed the Bishop's Hotel. He explained that after noting the tree's position, he headed home. Once he left the devil's seat, the circular gap disappeared and could not be seen again from any other vantage point. Jupiter had been shadowing him, worried by his recent distracted behavior, but he managed to sneak away the next morning to locate the tree. After a difficult search, he succeeded, though his valet threatened to punish him upon his return. I suggested that his initial failure to find the treasure was due to Jupiter dropping the beetle through the right eye of the skull instead of the left. He agreed, noting that this minor error of two and a half inches in the initial placement caused the entire fifty-foot line of direction to be significantly misaligned, leading them far from the actual target.

Few possessed a heart so untainted or a spirit so genuinely humble, paired with such steadfast faith in her own virtue and that of others. Raised in seclusion, she lost her mother early, leaving her father to oversee her upbringing. His unconventional methods left her well-versed in the legends of antiquity and English history, yet largely unaware of contemporary affairs. While she had read little from the last half-century, her broader literary knowledge was profound. Though she seemed less worldly than he, her wisdom was grounded in deeper truths; even had her beauty not captivated him, her intellect would have commanded his devotion. He viewed her as his mentor, finding joy in the sense of inferiority she occasionally inspired. Following his mother's death when he was nineteen, he left university and withdrew from his peers, finding solace in her presence. This brief isolation emboldened him to claim his independence. Believing his friends would not openly mock a marriage already finalized, he secured his guardian's reluctant consent and her father's ready approval. By his twentieth birthday, he had wed Diana in secret. He adored her with intense passion, finding her affection so enchanting that he could focus on nothing else. Though he initially invited college acquaintances to visit, their superficiality repelled him. Diana had stripped away his youthful illusions; he had matured into a man, marveling that he had ever adopted the trivial habits of his peers or feared their judgment. He abandoned those old connections not out of caprice, but because he recognized they were beneath him.

The refined gentlemen of high status wore small hanging charms that chimed with their languid movements. These golden ornaments rang like bells, and combined with the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, they created a sensory distraction that kept the starving masses of Saint Antoine at a distance. Fashion served as the primary tool for maintaining social order. Everyone appeared dressed for an endless masquerade. From the Tuileries Palace and the Court down to the legal chambers and the executioner, the mandate for elaborate attire remained absolute. Even the hangman was required to perform his duties while powdered, wearing a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings. At the gallows, this official presided in such delicate finery. In that year of 1780, no one at the reception doubted that a system anchored by a powdered, gold-clad executioner would endure forever. After Monseigneur finished his chocolate, he opened the doors to his inner sanctum and emerged. The resulting display of submission, fawning, and servility was absolute; the guests offered such total humiliation that they left nothing for Heaven, which perhaps explains why they never sought divine intervention. Offering vague promises and smiles to his followers, Monseigneur moved through his rooms before eventually retreating back into his sanctuary, hidden away by his attendants. Once the spectacle ended, the atmosphere calmed, and the guests departed. Only one man remained, walking slowly past the mirrors with his hat tucked under his arm and a snuffbox in his hand. Stopping at the final doorway, he looked toward the sanctuary and whispered, I consign you to the Devil. He flicked the remaining snuff from his fingers as if shaking off dust and quietly walked away.

Few possessed a heart as pure or a spirit as humble, paired with such steadfast integrity and faith in others. Raised in seclusion after losing her mother early, she was educated by her father according to his unconventional theories. She knew the heroes of ancient Greece, Rome, and early England intimately, yet remained oblivious to contemporary affairs, having read almost nothing published in the last half-century. While she seemed less worldly than her suitor, her knowledge was deeper and more grounded. Had her beauty not captivated him, her intellect surely would have. He viewed her as his guide, finding joy in the sense of inferiority she occasionally inspired. Following his mother's death when he was nineteen, he left college and withdrew from his social circle, finding solace in her presence. This brief isolation gave him the courage to claim his independence. Believing his friends would not dare mock a marriage once it was finalized, he secured permission from his guardian and her father. By his twentieth birthday, he had married Diana without informing anyone else. He loved her passionately, and her tenderness consumed his thoughts. When he invited college friends to visit, their frivolity repulsed him. Diana had stripped away his youthful naivety; he was now a man, bewildered that he had ever adopted the shallow jargon of his peers or feared their judgment. He abandoned those old friendships, not out of fickleness, but because he had outgrown them.

The lieutenant once asked why he had traveled so far across the ice in such an unusual sled. The stranger’s face turned deeply somber as he replied, "I am searching for someone who fled from me." When asked if the man he pursued traveled the same way, he confirmed it. I mentioned that we had seen a man on a sled pulled by dogs the day before we rescued him. This caught his attention, and he asked many questions about the path the creature had taken. Later, when we were alone, he noted that I must be curious but was too polite to ask questions. I agreed that prying would be rude, especially after I had saved his life. He then asked if the shifting ice might have destroyed the other sled. I told him I could not be sure, as the ice did not break until midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety by then. This news gave the stranger a new sense of purpose. He was eager to go on deck to watch for the sled, but I convinced him to stay in the cabin, as he was too weak for the cold. I promised to have someone watch for him instead. This is my record of these events. The stranger is slowly recovering, though he remains quiet and uneasy around others. Still, his gentle nature has won over the crew. I have grown to care for him like a brother, and his profound sorrow moves me deeply. He must have been a remarkable man in his prime. I once wrote to you, Margaret, that I would find no friends at sea, yet I have met a man whom I would have been proud to call a brother.

Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest the city is in a state of intense intellectual agitation. Events have occurred there so unexpected and contrary to established beliefs that I am certain all of Europe is now in an uproar, with the fields of physics and astronomy thrown into total confusion. It seems that on a recent day, a large crowd gathered in the Exchange square of Rotterdam. The weather was unusually warm with little wind, and the people were in good spirits despite occasional light showers falling from scattered white clouds. Around noon, however, a sudden stir moved through the assembly. A roar of conversation erupted, and instantly, ten thousand faces turned toward the sky. Ten thousand pipes were removed from mouths, and a shout like the roar of Niagara Falls echoed throughout the city. The cause of this commotion soon became clear. Emerging from behind a large cloud into the clear blue sky was a strange, solid object. Its shape was so odd and whimsical that the sturdy citizens below could neither understand nor stop staring at it. What could it be? What did it mean? No one knew, and even the mayor, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, had no explanation. Lacking any better option, everyone carefully replaced their pipes, tilted their heads to study the object, and paced about, grunting in confusion. Meanwhile, the object drifted lower toward the city, generating even more smoke from the crowd. Within minutes, it was close enough to be clearly identified. It was a balloon, but certainly nothing like any balloon ever seen in Rotterdam before.

I wonder how long you would have waited if left to your own devices. I wonder when you would have spoken had I not prompted you. My decision to thank you for your kindness toward Lydia clearly had a significant impact. Perhaps too much, I fear; for what becomes of the moral if our comfort stems from a broken promise? I should not have brought it up. This is not right. You need not worry. The moral remains sound. Lady Catherine’s unreasonable attempts to keep us apart actually cleared away all my doubts. I do not owe my current happiness to your sudden urge to express gratitude. I was not in the mood to wait for you to start. My aunt’s news gave me hope, and I was determined to know the truth immediately. Lady Catherine has been incredibly useful, which should please her, as she loves to be helpful. But tell me, why did you come to Netherfield? Was it just to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward, or did you intend something more serious? My true purpose was to see you and determine if I could ever hope for your love. My stated purpose, or at least what I told myself, was to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and if so, to make the confession to him that I have since made. Will you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what is coming? I am more likely to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. But it must be done; if you provide paper, I will do it now. If I did not have a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire your penmanship, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt who must not be ignored any longer. Because she was reluctant to admit how much her closeness with Mr. Darcy had been exaggerated, Elizabeth had not yet replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter. Now, however, having news she knew would be most welcome, she felt ashamed that her aunt and uncle had already missed three days of joy, and she wrote: My dear aunt, I should have thanked you sooner for your long, kind, and detailed letter, but to be honest, I was too annoyed to write. You assumed more than was true. But now, assume whatever you like; let your imagination run wild, and unless you believe I am already married, you cannot be far from the truth.

Once our friend was settled in his new office, we looked toward Windsor. Its proximity to London softened the sting of parting from Raymond and Perdita, whom we left at the Protectoral Palace. It was charming to watch my sister embrace her role, striving to inhabit her position with appropriate grace. Her inner pride and humble demeanor were in constant conflict. Her shyness was genuine, stemming from a fear of being misunderstood and a disregard for public opinion, much like Raymond. Yet, Perdita was more considerate of others; her reserve was partly an attempt to spare those around her from feeling inferior—a sentiment she herself never harbored. While Idris’s upbringing might have better suited her for formal duties, she found such rituals tedious, whereas Perdita clearly relished her new status. Occupied by fresh ideas, she bid us a warm farewell, promising a visit without lingering on the sadness of our departure. Raymond was brimming with boundless energy, his mind racing with ambitious plans to mark his Protectorship with some glorious achievement. We discussed them as we returned to Windsor Castle, relieved to leave political strife behind and eager for our quiet life. I focused my restless energy on intellectual pursuits, finding that rigorous study calmed the spirit. Perdita allowed us to bring Clara to Windsor, and she, along with my two children, provided constant joy. The only shadow on our peace was Adrian’s failing health. Though he showed no clear symptoms, his bright eyes and flushed cheeks suggested consumption, yet he remained free of pain or anxiety. He devoted himself to his books, finding rest in the company of his sister and me.

Indeed, and I would have claimed him had I been larger; I spotted him initially. Who captured him? It was an elderly stranger who traded his opportunity for forty dollars because he had to travel upriver immediately. Imagine that! I would have waited seven years for such a prize. I agreed, though I wondered if the deal was legitimate given the low price. It is perfectly honest, he insisted. I saw the flyer myself; it describes him precisely, including the plantation he escaped from near New Orleans. There is no doubt about the legality of this venture. Could you spare some chewing tobacco? I had none, so he departed. I retreated to the raft and sat in the shelter to ponder, but I reached no conclusion. I exhausted my mind trying to find a solution, yet everything seemed ruined. After our long journey and all our efforts for those villains, it was devastating that they would betray Jim for forty miserable dollars, condemning him to lifelong slavery among strangers. I briefly considered writing to Tom Sawyer to inform Miss Watson of Jim's location, thinking it better for him to be enslaved near his family. I quickly dismissed this, realizing she would be furious at his perceived ingratitude and likely sell him further down the river. Furthermore, people despise an ungrateful runaway, and Jim would suffer constant humiliation. Then there was my own reputation; if word spread that Huck Finn assisted a slave in escaping, I would be utterly shamed if I ever encountered anyone from home. That is the way of it: a person commits a shameful act and then avoids the consequences, believing secrecy prevents disgrace. That was my exact situation. The more I contemplated this, the more my conscience tormented me, leaving me feeling increasingly wicked and degraded.

Few possessed such a pure heart and genuine humility, combined with a firm belief in her own integrity and the goodness of others. She had lived a quiet life since birth. Although she lost her mother early, her father dedicated himself to her education, following his own unconventional methods. She was well-versed in the heroes of ancient Greece, Rome, and historical England, yet she knew little of current events. She had read few modern authors, but her education was otherwise extensive. While she seemed less experienced in the ways of society than he, her knowledge was deeper and more grounded. Even if her beauty and sweetness had not captivated him, her intellect would have held him spellbound. He looked to her as his guide, finding joy in the sense of inferiority she sometimes inspired in him. When he was nineteen, his mother died. He left college, distanced himself from his old friends, and sought comfort in the company of his beloved Diana. This brief separation gave him the courage to assert his independence. Believing his friends would not dare mock his marriage once it was official, he secured his guardian’s consent with some difficulty and her father’s approval more easily. Without telling anyone else, he married Diana by his twentieth birthday. He loved her passionately, and her tenderness consumed his thoughts. He invited some college friends to visit, but their frivolity disgusted him. Diana had opened his eyes, helping him transition into manhood. He was surprised he had ever adopted the shallow attitudes of his peers or feared their judgment. He abandoned his old friendships not out of fickleness, but because he realized they were truly unworthy of him.

The painter suddenly appeared at the studio door, gesturing for them to enter. They exchanged smiles. I am waiting, he called out. Please come in. The light is perfect, and you may bring your drinks. They stood and walked down the path together. Two butterflies fluttered by, and a thrush began to sing in the garden pear tree. You are glad you met me, Mr. Gray, Lord Henry said, watching him. Yes, I am glad now. I wonder if I always will be. Always! That is a terrible word. It makes me shudder. Women love using it, ruining every romance by trying to make it permanent. It is meaningless, too. The only difference between a whim and a lifelong passion is that the whim lasts a little longer. As they entered the studio, Dorian Gray touched Lord Henry’s arm. In that case, let our friendship be a whim, he murmured, blushing at his own boldness, before stepping onto the platform to resume his pose. Lord Henry threw himself into a wicker armchair to watch. The sound of the brush against the canvas filled the silence, broken only when Hallward stepped back to study his work. Dust motes danced in the golden light streaming through the doorway, and the heavy scent of roses hung in the air. After fifteen minutes, Hallward stopped, staring at Dorian and then at the painting, biting his brush and frowning. It is finished, he finally announced, signing his name in vermilion letters on the canvas. Lord Henry approached to examine the work. It was a remarkable piece of art and a perfect likeness. My dear fellow, I congratulate you, he said. It is the finest portrait of our time. Mr. Gray, come see yourself. The young man started as if waking from a dream. Is it really finished? he murmured, stepping down. Quite, said the painter. You sat splendidly today. I am very grateful. That is entirely due to me, Lord Henry interrupted. Isn’t it, Mr. Gray? Dorian did not answer, but walked listlessly toward the portrait.

Wickham was so content with their talk that he never again bothered himself or annoyed Elizabeth by bringing it up, and she was glad her words had been enough to silence him. The day of his and Lydia’s departure arrived, and Mrs. Bennet had to accept a separation that, since her husband refused to move the whole family to Newcastle, would likely last at least a year. Oh, my dear Lydia, she cried, when will we see each other again? Goodness, I don’t know. Maybe not for two or three years. Write to me often, my dear. As often as I can, but you know married women don’t have much time to write. My sisters can write to me; they will have nothing else to do. Wickham’s goodbyes were far warmer than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things. He is as fine a man as I have ever seen, Mr. Bennet remarked once they had left. He simpers and flirts with us all. I am incredibly proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to produce a more valuable son-in-law. The loss of her daughter left Mrs. Bennet feeling quite down for several days. I often think there is nothing worse than parting with friends, she said. One feels so lonely without them. This is the result of marrying off a daughter, Elizabeth noted. It should make you more content that your other four are still single. Not at all. Lydia is not leaving because she is married, but only because her husband’s regiment is stationed so far away. If they were closer, she would not have left so soon. However, her low spirits were soon lifted by a new rumor. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been ordered to prepare for her master’s arrival; he was coming in a few days to shoot for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was in a state of excitement, alternating between smiling at Jane and shaking her head. Well, so Mr. Bingley is returning, she told her sister, Mrs. Philips, who had brought the news. That is fine. Not that I care, of course. He means nothing to us, and I am sure I never want to see him again. Still, he is welcome to visit Netherfield if he wishes.

His temperament and intellect, though different from hers, would have fulfilled all her desires. It was a match that would have benefited both: her ease and vivacity might have softened his disposition and refined his manners, while she would have gained significantly from his judgment and worldly wisdom. Yet, no such ideal marriage would now demonstrate true marital bliss to the world. A different, inevitable union was soon to occur within their family instead. She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would maintain any independence, but she easily foresaw that a couple united only by passion rather than virtue could find little lasting happiness. Mr. Gardiner wrote to Mr. Bennet again. He briefly acknowledged Mr. Bennet’s thanks, expressed his commitment to the family’s welfare, and requested that the matter never be raised again. His main point was that Wickham had decided to leave the militia. He noted that he had strongly encouraged this once the marriage was settled, as leaving the regiment was advisable for both Wickham and his niece. Wickham intended to join the regular army, and former friends were willing to help him secure an ensigncy in a regiment stationed in the north. Being so far away was an advantage. Wickham made fair promises, and he hoped that among new acquaintances, where they would need to maintain their reputations, both would act more prudently. He had contacted Colonel Forster to settle Wickham’s debts in Brighton, for which he had personally vouched. He asked Mr. Bennet to provide similar assurances to Wickham’s creditors in Meryton, based on a list he provided. He hoped Wickham had been honest about his debts. Haggerston had their instructions, and everything would be finalized within a week. They would then join the regiment, unless they were first invited to Longbourn, as Mrs. Gardiner indicated that his niece was very eager to see the family before leaving the south.

Your father can surely spare you, if your mother agrees. Daughters matter less to fathers. If you stay another full month, I could take one of you to London when I go in early June. Since Dawson does not mind the carriage box, there is room for one, or even both if the weather is cool and you remain small. You are very kind, but we must stick to our original plan. Lady Catherine accepted this. Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant. I speak my mind, and it is improper for two young women to travel alone. You must arrange for someone to go. I despise such things; young women require proper protection. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate, I insisted on two men-servants. Miss Darcy could not have traveled otherwise. I am very particular. You must send John with them, Mrs. Collins; it would reflect poorly on you to let them go alone. My uncle is sending a servant for us. Oh, your uncle has a man-servant? I am glad someone considers these things. Where will you change horses? Bromley, of course. Mention my name at the Bell and you will be well served. Lady Catherine asked many questions about the trip, and Elizabeth found it fortunate she had to pay attention, or she might have lost track of her surroundings. She saved her reflections for solitary walks, where she could dwell on her unpleasant memories. She nearly knew Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She analyzed every sentence, her feelings shifting constantly. She felt indignant at his tone, yet when she considered how unfairly she had judged him, her anger turned inward, and she felt compassion for his disappointment.

It is only four o’clock, but winter has already brought an early sunset. The sky is clear and frosty, lacking clouds to catch the light, yet the air holds a faint rose tint that reflects off the snow-covered ground. I live in a solitary cottage on a vast, empty heath where no human voice reaches me. The desolate plain is blanketed in white, broken only by dark patches atop sharp hillocks where the snow is thin. A few birds peck at the ice covering the pools, hardened by a long, relentless frost. I am in a strange state of mind. I am entirely alone in the world, withered by the blight of misfortune. I know I am dying, and I feel a sense of joy. My pulse races, and my thin hand burns against my cheek; the quick spirit within me is emitting its final sparks. I will not see another winter’s snow or feel the warmth of another summer sun. Convinced of this, I begin to record my tragic history. Perhaps it should die with me, but an indefinable urge drives me, and I am too weak to resist. When I was strong, I believed my story was too sacred and horrific to share, but now, facing death, I feel compelled to reveal its terrors. It is like the grove of the Eumenides, which only the dying may enter; I am like Oedipus, nearing my end. What am I writing? I must gather my thoughts. I do not know if anyone will read these pages except you, my friend, who will receive them after I am gone. I do not address them to you alone, as dwelling on our friendship in this way feels more natural than a private letter. I will tell my story as if for strangers. You have often asked about my solitary life, my tears, and my impenetrable silence. In life, I dared not speak; in death, I unveil the mystery. Others may discard these pages, but to you, Woodville, my kind and affectionate friend, they will be precious memorials of a heartbroken girl who, even in death, is warmed by gratitude. I know your tears will fall upon these words, and while I still live, I thank you for your sympathy.

The Attorney-General told the jury that the defendant, despite his youth, was a veteran of treasonous activities punishable by death. He argued that this communication with the enemy was not a recent development but had persisted for years, with the prisoner frequently traveling between France and England for clandestine purposes he could not justify. Had such treachery been successful, the defendant’s true malice might have remained hidden; however, Providence had inspired an irreproachable individual to uncover these schemes and report them to the King’s Secretary and the Privy Council. This patriot, the Attorney-General explained, would testify before them. He described the witness as a figure of sublime character who, having once been the prisoner’s friend, had chosen to sacrifice that bond for the sake of his country upon discovering the man's infamy. While Britain lacked the tradition of erecting statues to such benefactors, the Attorney-General insisted the man deserved one. He remarked that virtue, particularly patriotism, was contagious, noting the jury’s apparent lack of familiarity with the poetic references he cited. This noble example had inspired the prisoner’s own servant to search his master’s belongings and seize his documents. The Attorney-General anticipated attempts to discredit this servant, yet he declared he held the man in higher regard than his own family. He urged the jury to follow this example. Finally, he asserted that the testimony of these two witnesses, alongside the recovered documents detailing the King’s military forces and their strategic positions, would prove beyond doubt that the prisoner had consistently provided intelligence to a hostile nation.

With these cries, many women, driven into a blind frenzy, spun around, striking and tearing at their own friends until they collapsed in a faint, saved from being trampled only by their own men. Still, not a moment was wasted. Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville and might be released. If Saint Antoine remembered its own suffering and insults, that would never happen. Armed men and women poured out of the district so quickly, pulling even the stragglers along, that within fifteen minutes, only a few old women and crying children remained in Saint Antoine. By then, the crowd was choking the Hall of Examination where the wicked old man was held, spilling out into the nearby streets. The Defarges, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three were at the front, close to him. Look, Madame cried, pointing with her knife. See the old villain tied with ropes. Tying a bundle of grass to his back was a good touch. Let him eat it now! She tucked her knife away and clapped like she was at a theater. The people behind her explained her satisfaction to those further back, and soon the surrounding streets echoed with applause. During the long hours of waiting and endless talk, Madame Defarge’s impatience was quickly mirrored by the crowd, aided by men who had climbed the building’s exterior to watch through the windows and signal her reactions to those outside. Finally, the sun rose high enough to cast a ray of light directly onto the prisoner’s head. The crowd could no longer be held back; the barrier of people broke, and Saint Antoine had him. The news spread instantly. Defarge jumped over a railing and a table to grab the miserable man, and Madame Defarge followed, twisting her hand into his ropes. Before the others could even reach him, a cry went up across the entire city: Bring him out!

When we returned to the raft and the king counted his earnings, he had eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He also brought back a three-gallon jug of whiskey he found under a wagon while walking through the woods. The king claimed it was his most successful day of missionary work, insisting that heathens were no match for pirates when it came to swindling a camp meeting. The duke had felt proud of his own efforts until the king arrived. He had printed two horse-sale flyers for farmers, earning four dollars. He also collected ten dollars in advertising fees by offering a discount for advance payment. He sold three newspaper subscriptions for half a dollar each, insisting on cash instead of the usual payment of wood or onions. He even wrote and typeset a sad three-verse poem titled, "Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart," which he included for free. In total, he made nine dollars and a half and felt satisfied with his day. Then, he showed us a flyer he had printed for our own use. It featured a picture of a runaway slave with a bundle on a stick and offered a two-hundred-dollar reward. The text described Jim perfectly, claiming he had escaped from a plantation near New Orleans and was heading north. The duke explained that this would allow us to travel during the day. If we saw anyone approaching, we could tie Jim up, hide him in the shelter, and show the flyer to claim we had captured him and were taking him back to collect the reward.

He was a poet who published his first work at twenty-three, earning immediate, nationwide acclaim. His success was unprecedented, with both the public and intellectuals praising his work without reservation. At the peak of his fame, he met Elinor, a beautiful young heiress living with her guardian. They seemed destined for each other. While Elinor lacked Woodville’s creative genius, she was noble and virtuous, possessing a natural grace and deep, expressive eyes that reflected both wisdom and sensitivity. They fell in love instantly, finding profound joy in their mutual devotion. Woodville, the son of a modest clergyman, was a celebrated figure, while Elinor was wealthy. Her guardian approved of their relationship, acknowledging Woodville’s stature, but her father’s will prohibited her from marrying until she came of age. Though only twenty, they accepted the wait, spending their time together in blissful anticipation, studying and planning their future. As Woodville’s reputation grew, Elinor flourished under his guidance. With her twenty-first birthday only two months away, their wedding preparations were underway. It is painful to recount the tragedy that followed, yet perhaps it was inevitable; in a world defined by sorrow, such perfect happiness as theirs could not be permitted to endure. To allow them their union would have required a fundamental change in the nature of our existence.

Basil, this is incredible! I must meet Dorian Gray. Hallward stood up and paced the garden before returning. Harry, he said, Dorian Gray is simply an artistic inspiration to me. You might see nothing in him, but I see everything. He influences my work even when he is not physically present. He suggests a new style, appearing in the curves of my lines and the subtlety of my colors. That is all. Then why won't you exhibit his portrait? Lord Henry asked. Because I have unintentionally poured my own deep artistic devotion into it, and I have never spoken to him about it. He knows nothing, and he never will. The public might guess, however, and I refuse to expose my soul to their shallow curiosity. I will not let them examine my heart under a microscope. There is too much of myself in that painting. Poets are less careful, Lord Henry replied. They know that passion sells. Nowadays, a broken heart can lead to many book sales. I hate them for that, Hallward cried.
