An artist should create beauty without putting their own life into it. We live in an era where people treat art like an autobiography. We have lost the true sense of abstract beauty. One day I will show the world what art should be, and for that reason, the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray. I think you are wrong, but I will not argue. Only those who are intellectually lost argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray fond of you? The painter paused. He likes me, he said. I flatter him constantly, and I find a strange pleasure in saying things I later regret. Usually, he is charming, and we talk for hours in the studio. Occasionally, however, he is thoughtless and seems to enjoy hurting me. At those times, I feel I have given my entire soul to someone who treats it like a simple flower for his lapel—a mere decoration for his vanity.

Shortly after midday, the boys took a small boat belonging to an absent neighbor and set off. Once they were several miles past Cave Hollow, Tom spoke up. "Notice how this bluff looks identical all the way from the hollow—no dwellings, no wood-yards, just uniform brush. But see that white patch where the earth slid away? That is one of my markers. We will go ashore here." They disembarked. "Now, Huck, you could reach the hole I escaped from with a fishing pole from where we stand. Try to locate it." Huck searched the area thoroughly but found nothing. Tom marched triumphantly into a dense cluster of sumac bushes and declared, "Here it is! Look, Huck; it is the most hidden spot in the region. Keep this to yourself. I have long wanted to be a robber, but finding a place like this was the challenge. We have it now, and we will keep it secret, though we shall include Joe Harper and Ben Rogers—a gang is essential for any real prestige. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds magnificent, doesn't it, Huck?" "It certainly does, Tom. And who are we going to rob?" "Oh, just about anyone. We will waylay travelers—that is the usual method." "And kill them?" "Not always. We will hold them in the cave until they pay a ransom." "What is a ransom?" "Money. You force them to collect all they can from their friends; if they cannot pay after a year, then you kill them. That is the standard procedure. You never kill the women, though. You lock them up, but you do not harm them. They are always beautiful, wealthy, and terrified. You take their jewelry, but you always remove your hat and speak courteously. Robbers are the most polite people—you will see that in any book. Eventually, the women grow to love you, and after a week or two in the cave, they stop weeping and refuse to leave. If you tried to drive them out, they would return. That is how it happens in all the stories." "Why, that is truly excellent, Tom. I think it is even better than being a pirate." "Yes, it has advantages, since it is near home and the circus and such." With preparations complete, the boys entered the opening, Tom leading the way. They struggled to the far end of the tunnel, secured their knotted kite strings, and pressed onward.

After mourning the terrible outcome that Elizabeth felt was certain and Jane could not deny was possible, Elizabeth asked for more details. She wanted to know what Colonel Forster had said and if anyone had suspected the elopement, given how often the couple was seen together. Jane explained that the Colonel had noticed Lydia’s interest in Wickham but had not been alarmed. He felt terrible about the situation and had come to reassure them of his concern before realizing the couple had not actually gone to Scotland. When asked if Denny knew of their plans, Jane said that Denny had denied knowing anything when questioned by the Colonel. He had not repeated his earlier claim that they would not marry, which gave Jane some hope. Elizabeth asked if they had assumed the couple was married, and Jane admitted that such a thought had never occurred to them. She had been worried about Lydia’s happiness because of Wickham’s past behavior, though her parents only saw the match as imprudent. Kitty then revealed that Lydia had hinted at this in her last letter, having known about their romance for weeks. When Elizabeth asked if the Colonel thought poorly of Wickham, Jane admitted he no longer spoke of him favorably. He considered Wickham reckless and in debt, though Jane hoped the rumors of his financial troubles were untrue. Elizabeth lamented that if they had been more open about what they knew of Wickham, this might have been avoided. Jane agreed it might have been better, but noted that exposing someone’s past mistakes without knowing their current intentions had felt wrong.

Good heavens! Had I for a moment suspected the diabolical purpose of my enemy, I would have chosen a life of lonely exile over agreeing to this wretched union. Yet, the monster used some dark art to obscure his true motives; in my attempt to prepare for my own demise, I inadvertently accelerated the destruction of someone far more precious. As the wedding date approached, I felt my spirit falter, whether from fear or intuition. I masked my dread with a forced cheerfulness that pleased my father, though it failed to fully convince the perceptive Elizabeth. She anticipated our marriage with calm hope, tempered by the lingering fear that such happiness might prove fleeting. Preparations proceeded, and I hid my inner turmoil, participating in my father's arrangements as if they were not merely the trappings of my own ruin. Through his efforts, Elizabeth regained some of her inheritance, including a property on Lake Como, where we planned to spend our honeymoon. Meanwhile, I armed myself with pistols and a dagger, remaining vigilant against any overt assault. This vigilance brought me some peace, and as the day neared, the threat seemed less substantial, making our union feel inevitable. Elizabeth appeared content, and my composed manner helped soothe her, yet on our wedding day, she was somber, haunted by a sense of impending doom and perhaps the weight of the secret I had vowed to share with her the following day.

She left everything behind, save for the memory that it had once existed. Anne had not stepped foot in Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s home in September. She had avoided the Hall whenever possible, but now she returned to the elegant Lodge to delight its mistress. Lady Russell felt a mix of joy and anxiety, aware of Anne’s time at Uppercross. Fortunately, she thought Anne looked healthier, and Anne privately hoped this meant she was regaining her youthful bloom. As they talked, Anne realized her priorities had shifted. The concerns that once consumed her at Kellynch now felt secondary. Even her father and sister in Bath seemed distant compared to her experiences at Uppercross. When Lady Russell discussed their family affairs, Anne felt guilty for being far more preoccupied with her friends in Lyme, particularly the Harvilles and Captain Benwick. She had to force herself to show interest in her own family’s matters. Discussing the accident at Lyme was initially awkward. Lady Russell had already heard the details, but they still needed to process the event, the imprudence involved, and the mention of Captain Wentworth. Anne struggled to remain composed while speaking his name, only finding relief once she explained her perspective on his attachment to Louisa Musgrove.

He constantly pretended Peter had written him those details, but it was a falsehood; he had extracted every single bit of information from that dim-witted youth we had ferried to the steamboat. Mary Jane then produced the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud, weeping over the contents. It bequeathed the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls, while granting the profitable tanyard, additional property worth seven thousand, and another three thousand in gold to Harvey and William, specifying that the six thousand in cash was concealed in the cellar. The two impostors claimed they would retrieve it to ensure everything was transparent, instructing me to accompany them with a candle. Once we closed the cellar door and located the bag, they emptied it onto the floor, revealing a magnificent pile of gold coins. The king’s eyes gleamed as he slapped the duke on the shoulder, exclaiming that it was truly impressive and surpassed the Nonesuch. The duke agreed. As they handled the gold, letting it clink against the floor, the king remarked that posing as brothers to a wealthy deceased man and representatives of foreign heirs was their most successful strategy, proving that trusting in Providence was ultimately the superior path. Rather than accepting the sum as it was, they insisted on counting it, only to find it four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king cursed, wondering where the missing amount had gone. After searching in vain, the duke suggested the sick man had simply miscalculated and that they should remain silent about the discrepancy since they could afford the loss. The king dismissed the loss itself, focusing instead on the importance of the count; he insisted they needed to present the full amount upstairs to avoid any suspicion, noting that they could not contradict the dead man’s stated total of six thousand dollars.

Two years elapsed in this manner. Though my external circumstances remained static, my internal state shifted as I drifted toward my end. I immersed myself in study and literature, finding connection in historical narratives and losing my sense of self among the ghosts of the past. As the sharpness of my immediate agony faded, I grew more human. Solitude, once appealing, began to feel hollow; I craved companionship, not from the masses, but from a single devoted friend. You might assume this prepared me for society, but I disagree. The purity of the connection I sought could not exist in a world tainted by coarse, worldly concerns. I was, in truth, less prepared for human interaction than ever. Previously, my torment was external, like a sickness I longed to shed. Now, I yearned for a soul to bind to my own, a desire that would have only invited further misery, for I had become fragile and hypersensitive. I did not seek intellectual validation, but rather tender affection—a heart to receive my confessions, hoping that even from my wretched state, something beautiful might bloom. Yet, such friendship is elusive, often born of shared youth or mutual hardship. It descends unbidden like dew upon the chosen, but flees from those who actively pursue it. I understood this and refrained from searching, yet in my desolate isolation, a glimmer of connection arrived like a winter sunbeam upon the snow. Alas, it illuminated only decay; I was too far broken to be revived by its warmth.

They passed desolate brickfields where the fog thinned, revealing bottle-shaped kilns breathing orange flames. A dog barked, a distant gull cried, and their horse stumbled before breaking into a gallop. Soon they left the dirt road for rough cobblestones. Most windows were dark, but he watched the strange, puppet-like shadows dancing behind lit blinds with growing resentment. A woman shouted from a doorway, and two men chased the carriage until the driver whipped them away. Passion often traps the mind in cycles, and Dorian Gray obsessively repeated phrases about soul and sense, using them to justify his dark impulses. His desire to live intensified, turning his nerves into live wires. He now embraced the ugliness he once despised, finding the raw reality of crime and squalor more vivid than art or poetry. These things offered the oblivion he craved; in three days, he would be free. The carriage stopped abruptly at a dark lane near the docks, where ship masts rose above the rooftops like ghostly sails. The driver asked if they had arrived, and Dorian stepped out, paid him, and hurried toward the quay. Lanterns flickered on merchant ships, their light shattering in the puddles, while a nearby steamer cast a red glow over the slick, wet pavement.

I considered faking my death; my happy heirs would take my fortune, and I would finally be free. My plan had to be clever, though, as I needed to secure enough money to survive. What disgusting schemes I was forced to adopt! I would have lived a life of lies, yet whenever I felt guilty about the deception, a visit from an aunt or cousin would harden my resolve. They would tell me that death comes for everyone, then claim my father had lost his mind since my mother died. They called him insane and told me I was lucky he had not killed me during one of his episodes. They said this with soft whispers, downcast eyes, and fake sympathy, while I sat quietly, trembling inside, unable to challenge their cruel words. What a wonderful life of honesty this was! I wore a gentle expression while hiding a cunning heart. I felt only the shame of lying, not the comfort of innocence. I had to learn to weave complex webs of deceit until I could lie gracefully, masking my true self entirely. Oh, beloved father, accept your daughter’s pure heart; let me return to you untainted, or you will not recognize me. Just as grief changed Constance, deceit would change me until you would not know me in heaven. To be happy now and when we meet again, I must escape this mocking life. Only in solitude can I be myself and be yours. Even now, I look back with disgust at the schemes I used to escape after many painful struggles. I could explain how I secured my living and faked my death, but I will not.

I uncovered the fire, and a light breeze quickly fanned it into a flame. I made a fan out of branches to keep the embers alive when they began to fade. By night, I was pleased to find that the fire provided both light and warmth. It also helped with my food; I discovered that some scraps left by travelers had been roasted and tasted much better than the berries I gathered. I tried cooking my own food on the embers, finding that while it ruined the berries, it greatly improved the nuts and roots. Food eventually became scarce, and I often spent all day searching for acorns to satisfy my hunger. I decided to leave my home to find a place where my needs would be easier to meet. I deeply regretted losing the fire, as I did not know how to start it again. After thinking about it for hours, I gave up, wrapped myself in my cloak, and headed west through the woods. After three days of wandering, I reached open country. A heavy snowfall had covered the fields in white, and the cold, damp ground chilled my feet. Around seven in the morning, desperate for food and shelter, I spotted a small shepherd's hut on a hill. I examined the building with curiosity and, finding the door open, went inside. An old man sat by a fire, preparing breakfast. When he heard me, he turned, shrieked, and ran across the fields with surprising speed for his frail frame. His appearance and sudden flight surprised me, but I was delighted by the hut. It was dry and protected from the snow and rain, feeling like a perfect sanctuary to me.

He explained that while traveling from his home through Datchet, he noticed smoke rising from the inn's chimney. Expecting to find fellow travelers, he knocked and entered. Only Lucy and her mother were present; the older woman was bedridden with rheumatism, and as the remaining local residents departed one by one, they were left behind. Lucy begged the man to stay until her mother recovered in a week or two, warning that they would otherwise perish in their helpless state. The man refused, insisting he had to rejoin his wife and children among the emigrants. As a final plea, Lucy entrusted him with a letter for Idris, which he successfully delivered. Idris read the following with great feeling: Honoured Lady, I trust you will recall and pity me, and I dare hope for your assistance, as I have no other recourse. Forgive my writing, for I am quite distraught. A month ago, my mother lost the use of her limbs. She is improving, and I am certain she could travel within another month using the arrangements you kindly offered. However, everyone has now departed. Three days ago, I visited Samuel Woods, hoping his family might wait for us, but found their home abandoned. I have seen no one since until this man arrived. What will become of us? My mother is too ill to know our true situation. Will you send someone to help? We will surely perish here. If I moved my mother now, she would die on the journey, and even if she recovered, I have no way to navigate the miles to the sea, only to find you in France with the vast, terrifying ocean between us.

On Saturday at midday, I visited the well to observe. Merlin continued his ritual, burning powders, gesturing wildly, and chanting nonsense, though he appeared quite discouraged, having failed to produce even a drop of moisture. I eventually asked, "How is the work progressing, partner?" He replied, "I am currently testing the most potent enchantment practiced by Eastern occult masters; if this fails, nothing will. Be silent until I conclude." He generated a thick, dark cloud that drifted toward the hermits' dwellings, accompanied by frantic movements and a torrent of incantations. After twenty minutes, he collapsed, utterly spent. A large crowd of monks, nuns, pilgrims, and orphans gathered, stirred by the massive smoke. When the abbot asked for the outcome, Merlin declared, "If any human effort could release these waters, my recent attempt would have succeeded. It failed, confirming my fears: a spirit so powerful that its name is lethal has cursed this well. No living mortal can uncover the secret required to break this spell. The water is lost forever, Father. I have done my utmost. Allow me to depart." The abbot was visibly distressed and turned to me, asking, "You heard him. Is it accurate?" I replied, "Partially." He pressed, "Which part?" I said, "That the spirit with the unpronounceable name has indeed cursed the well." He cried, "Then we are ruined!" I answered, "Possibly." He asked, "But not certainly?" I confirmed, "Exactly." He continued, "So when he claims the spell is unbreakable--" I interrupted, "He is not necessarily correct. There are circumstances under which an attempt might have a slight, albeit slim, chance of success."

Please consider, ma'am, Oliver said, tears filling his eyes despite his efforts to stop them. Think of how young and kind she is, and the joy she brings to everyone. I am certain that for your sake, and for her own, she will not die. Heaven would never let her pass away so young. Hush, Mrs. Maylie said, resting her hand on Oliver's head. You think like a child, but you remind me of my duty. I had forgotten it for a moment, but I hope to be forgiven. I am old and have seen enough illness to know the pain of losing those we love. I also know that the youngest and best are not always spared, but this should comfort us. Heaven is just, and these trials remind us that there is a better world than this. God's will be done. I love her, and He knows how much. Oliver was surprised to see Mrs. Maylie suddenly stop her grieving and stand tall, appearing calm and firm. He was even more amazed that this strength lasted. Throughout the long care that followed, she remained composed and ready, performing her duties steadily and even cheerfully. He was young and did not understand what strong minds can endure during difficult times. A restless night followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie’s fears were confirmed. Rose was suffering from a severe and dangerous fever. We must be active and not give in to useless grief, Mrs. Maylie said, looking firmly at him. This letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne immediately. Take it to the market town four miles away by the footpath, and have it sent by horseback to Chertsey. The people at the inn will handle it, and I know I can trust you to see it done. Oliver could not speak, but his expression showed his eagerness to leave at once.

The storm raged all night, but nothing unusual happened. The next morning, however, the bloodstain had returned to the floor. Washington remarked that the detergent must not be at fault, suggesting it had to be the ghost. He cleaned it again, but the stain reappeared the following morning. It returned a third time, even though Mr. Otis had locked the library and kept the key. The family became intrigued; Mr. Otis reconsidered his skepticism, Mrs. Otis planned to join a psychical society, and Washington wrote a detailed letter about the persistence of bloodstains linked to crimes. That night, all doubt regarding ghosts vanished. The day had been warm, and the family went for a drive, returning at nine for a light supper. They did not discuss ghosts, avoiding any atmosphere of expectation. As Mr. Otis later noted, they talked about typical topics for cultured Americans: the acting skills of Fanny Davenport versus Sarah Bernhardt, the lack of American food like corn and buckwheat cakes in England, the global importance of Boston, the efficiency of the baggage check system, and the pleasantness of the New York accent. No one mentioned the supernatural or Sir Simon de Canterville. The family went to bed by eleven, and the house was dark by half-past. Later, Mr. Otis was woken by a strange metallic clanking in the hallway that grew louder. He stood up, lit a match, and checked the time; it was exactly one o’clock. Remaining calm and checking his steady pulse, he listened to the noise and the sound of footsteps. He put on his slippers, grabbed a small bottle from his dressing case, and opened the door.

As they exited the dining hall, the clock tower struck midnight. Following the final chime, a crash and a sharp scream echoed, accompanied by a thunderous tremor that rattled the house. Ethereal music drifted by, a staircase panel snapped open, and Virginia emerged onto the landing, pale and clutching a small casket. The family hurried to her; Mrs. Otis embraced her, the Duke kissed her repeatedly, and the twins danced wildly. Good heavens, where have you been? Mr. Otis demanded, annoyed, assuming she had played a prank. Cecil and I searched everywhere, and your mother was terrified. Do not pull such stunts again. Except on the Ghost! the twins shouted. My darling, thank God you are safe; never leave me again, Mrs. Otis whispered, stroking her daughter's hair. Papa, Virginia said calmly, I was with the Ghost. He has passed away, and you must see him. He was wicked, but he felt remorse and gave me these jewels before he died. The family stared in stunned silence as she led them through the wall into a secret passage, Washington lighting the way with a candle. They reached a heavy oak door reinforced with rusted nails. It swung open to reveal a small, vaulted chamber with a single barred window. A skeletal figure was chained to an iron ring in the wall, lying prone on the floor, its bony fingers reaching toward a trencher and ewer just beyond its grasp. The jug held only mold, and the platter was covered in dust. Virginia knelt to pray silently while the others watched, awestruck by the grim mystery finally revealed.

“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped it, signaling his disappointment in Joseph. “My dear young friend,” Mr. Pumblechook said, “you must be hungry and exhausted. Sit down. I have brought chicken, tongue, and other treats from the Boar that I hope you will enjoy. But am I truly looking at the boy I used to play with during his happy childhood? May I—may I?” This meant he wanted to shake my hand. I agreed, and he shook it enthusiastically before sitting down again. “Here is wine,” he said. “Let us drink to Fortune, and may she always choose her favorites wisely! Yet I cannot look at you and drink without again asking—may I—may I?” I gave him permission, and he shook my hand again, then drained his glass. I did the same, and the wine went straight to my head. Mr. Pumblechook served me the best parts of the chicken and tongue, barely eating anything himself. “Ah, poultry! You never thought when you were a chick that you would provide a meal under this humble roof for someone who—call it a weakness if you like—but may I? May I?” He kept asking to shake my hand so often that I stopped answering, and he simply did it anyway. I am surprised he did not cut himself with my knife. “And your sister,” he continued after eating, “who had the honor of raising you! It is sad to think she can no longer appreciate that honor. May—” I saw he was about to reach for me again, so I interrupted. “Let us drink to her health,” I said. “Ah!” Mr. Pumblechook cried, leaning back in his chair, overwhelmed with admiration. “That is how you recognize them, sir! That is how you know the noble-minded, sir!”

I had no concerns for her. She was a capable woman who managed her affairs well without me. In truth, she likely viewed me as an idle dreamer and was relieved to see me go. It was a dark night when I said goodbye, taking the three creditors who had plagued me as my assistants. We transported the balloon and its gear to the station where the rest of my equipment was stored. Finding everything undisturbed, I began my work. It was April first. The night was dark and starless, with a cold, drizzling rain that made us miserable. My main worry was the balloon, which was becoming heavy with moisture despite its varnish, and the risk to my gunpowder. I kept my three creditors busy packing ice around the central cask and stirring the acid in the others. They constantly pestered me about my plans, complaining about the grueling labor and getting soaked for what they called these dark rituals. I grew anxious, working frantically, as I suspected these fools believed I was in league with the devil. Fearing they might abandon me, I calmed them by promising to pay all my debts in full once the task was finished. They interpreted this as a sign that I would soon possess vast sums of money; as long as they were paid, they clearly did not care about my soul or my safety. After four and a half hours, the balloon was sufficiently inflated. I attached the basket and loaded my equipment, including the condensing unit, plenty of water, and compact, nutrient-dense provisions like pemmican.

Daylight arrived as I set the manuscript down. The rain had nearly stopped, leaving the world gray and somber as the spent storm sighed into silence. I approached the stranger's room and listened at his partially open door. Hearing him speak, I knocked, but received no reply. I peered inside to find him lying on his back, rambling with feverish intensity while his arms moved restlessly. I entered quietly and leaned over him. When I spoke his name, his glassy eyes and pale face suddenly brightened with joy and relief. Oh, Sandy, you have finally arrived; I have missed you so much. Stay beside me and never leave again. Give me your hand; holding it brings me peace and happiness. You appear as a faint mist, yet your presence is enough. Do not pull away, for I will not need it for long. Was that the child? Hello, Central? She does not answer. Bring her to me when she wakes so I may say goodbye. Sandy, are you still there? I drifted off and feared you had vanished. Have I been ill for a long time? It feels like months. I have had such terrifyingly vivid dreams. In my delirium, I imagined the king had died, you were trapped in Gaul, and a revolution had broken out. I even dreamt that Clarence and I, with a few cadets, wiped out the entire English chivalry. Stranger still, I felt like a man from a distant, future age. I seemed to have traveled back and forth across time, stranded as a lonely outsider in that strange England, separated from you and everything I hold dear by thirteen centuries.

Smallpox! I rushed to the king and murmured, "Leave at once, sire! The woman suffers from the same plague that ravaged Camelot two years past." He stood firm. "I shall stay and assist." I pressed him again, "King, you must depart." He replied, "Your intentions are good, but a king cannot show fear, nor a knight ignore those in need. I will not leave. You must go, for the Church forbids your presence here, and they will punish you severely if they learn of your intrusion." It was a perilous situation that could claim his life, but arguing was futile. If he felt his knightly honor was involved, he would not budge. I ceased my protests. The woman spoke, "Kind sir, would you climb the ladder and tell me what you see? Do not fear to speak, for a mother's heart can break no further." "Stay," the king commanded, "and feed the woman. I will go." He set down his pack. I turned to move, but the king had already begun. He paused, looking at a man lying in the shadows who had remained silent. "Is this your husband?" the king inquired. "Yes." "Is he sleeping?" "Thank God, yes—for three hours. I am so grateful for his rest." I added, "We will be quiet so as not to wake him." "You need not worry, for he is dead." "Dead?" "Yes, and what a victory that is! No one can harm or insult him now. He is in heaven, or perhaps hell, where he will find no abbots or bishops to torment him. We were childhood sweethearts and married for twenty-five years, never apart until today. Think of the years we spent loving and suffering together. This morning, he lost his senses and imagined we were children wandering through happy fields again. In that innocent state, he drifted further away, eventually crossing into the unknown and vanishing from mortal sight."

It is only fair to note that the young woman did not explicitly refuse, but instead expressed a fervent hope that she might be damned if she complied. This delicate evasion demonstrated a natural refinement, as she wished to spare her companion the sting of a blunt rejection. The old man’s face dropped. He turned from this woman, who was dressed in a vibrant red gown, green boots, and yellow hair curlers, to the other. Nancy, my dear, what do you say? he asked soothingly. It won’t work, Fagin, so stop trying, Nancy replied. What do you mean by that? Bill Sikes asked, looking up with a scowl. Exactly what I said, Bill, she answered calmly. You are the perfect person for this, Sikes argued, since nobody around here knows you. And since I intend to keep it that way, it is a firm no, Bill, she replied. She will go, Fagin, Sikes insisted. No, she will not, Nancy countered. Yes, she will, Sikes repeated. Sikes was correct. Through a combination of threats, promises, and bribes, the woman was eventually persuaded to take the job. Unlike her friend, she had recently moved to the area from a distant suburb and did not fear being recognized by her acquaintances. With a clean white apron over her dress and her curlers hidden beneath a straw bonnet provided by the old man, Nancy prepared to leave. Wait a moment, the man said, handing her a small covered basket. Carry that; it looks more respectable. Give her a door key for the other hand, Sikes added, it looks authentic. Yes, that is perfect, the man said, hanging a large key on her finger. Very good indeed! Oh, my poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother! Nancy cried, bursting into tears while clutching the basket and key in apparent agony. What has become of him? Where have they taken him? Please, gentlemen, have pity and tell me what has happened to the dear boy!

I recited the beautiful passage describing Dante’s arrival in the terrestrial Paradise, imagining how wonderful it would be to wander those banks and see the chariot of light descend, bringing my long-lost father back to me. I pictured myself weaving a wreath from the lovely flowers there to celebrate our reunion. I would sing my father’s favorite song, 'sul margine d’un rio,' and my voice, drifting through the still air, would tell him I had arrived. The marks of my sorrow would vanish, and I would look fearlessly into his eyes, which always shone with innocent love. Thinking of his gaze made me weep, though I kept my sobs quiet to avoid breaking the spell. I was so lost in this daydream that I didn't notice where I was walking until I reached down to pick a flower on that barren plain where nothing grew. I woke from my reverie, realizing I was completely lost. The sun had set, and the pink glow of the clouds had faded. A cold wind blew across the plain, and I could not find my way in the gathering dark. Eventually, night fell completely. Knowing my servant was staying in a nearby village and would not worry, and feeling safe from intruders in this wild place, I decided to stay where I was. I was too exhausted to continue. The air was cold, but I was used to the elements after two years of solitary wandering. I lay on the grass in total darkness. The night was silent, as even the insects were still in this desolate place devoid of trees or shrubs. This profound silence calmed my senses while stirring my soul, and my mind raced through endless thoughts.

She would make such a charming friend for Emma. Mr. Woodhouse concurred, yet added, Our young friend Harriet Smith is also a lovely sort of girl. You will enjoy Harriet. Emma could not ask for a better companion. I am delighted to hear it, but Jane Fairfax is known to be exceptionally talented and refined, and she is precisely Emma’s age. This subject was discussed quite pleasantly, followed by other topics of equal importance that passed with similar accord. However, the evening did not conclude without a brief moment of distress. The arrival of the gruel prompted extensive commentary, including praise for its health benefits and harsh criticism of households that failed to prepare it properly. Unfortunately, the daughter cited her own cook at South End as a prime example of such incompetence, noting the woman could never grasp the concept of a smooth, perfectly thin basin of gruel. This remark created a precarious situation. Ah, Mr. Woodhouse sighed, shaking his head with sympathetic concern. To Emma, his tone implied that the consequences of her trip to South End were truly endless and best left unmentioned. She hoped he would remain silent, allowing him to return to his own meal, but after a few minutes, he began again. I shall always regret that you chose the seaside this autumn rather than visiting us. Why should you be sorry, sir? It was very beneficial for the children. Furthermore, if you had to go to the coast, South End was a poor choice. It is considered unhealthy, and Perry was surprised you selected it. I am aware that many hold that opinion, but it is a misconception. We were perfectly healthy there and experienced no issues with the mud. Mr. Wingfield confirms the location is not unhealthy; he understands the climate well, and his own brother has visited repeatedly. You ought to have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you had to travel at all. Perry spent a week there once and considers it the finest of all the seaside resorts.

The following day, the ghost felt exhausted. The stress of the past month had shattered his nerves, leaving him jumpy at every sound. After staying in his room for five days, he decided to stop trying to maintain the bloodstain in the library. Since the Otis family did not want it, they clearly did not deserve it; they were far too practical to appreciate such symbolic displays. While he could not control his ghostly appearances, he felt a duty to haunt the corridor weekly and moan from the window twice a month. Despite his wicked past, he took his supernatural responsibilities seriously. For the next three Saturdays, he crept through the halls between midnight and three in the morning, taking great care to remain unseen. He removed his boots, walked softly on the creaky floorboards, wore a velvet cloak, and even used the Rising Sun Lubricator to silence his chains. Though he felt humiliated using the oil, he eventually admitted it was practical. Nevertheless, the family continued to harass him. They stretched strings across the hallway to trip him, and the twins once created a butter-slide that caused him to fall while he was dressed as the Huntsman of Hogley Woods. Furious at this final insult, he decided to reclaim his dignity by appearing the next night as his most famous persona: Reckless Rupert, the Headless Earl. He had not used this disguise in seventy years, not since he had terrified Lady Barbara Modish so badly that she broke off her engagement to the current Lord Canterville’s grandfather and eloped with Jack Castleton, refusing to marry into a family haunted by such a creature.

Shortly after noon, the boys borrowed a small skiff from an absent owner and set off. Several miles past Cave Hollow, Tom spoke. This bluff looks identical all the way from the hollow, with no houses or wood-yards, just uniform brush. But see that white patch where a landslide occurred? That is one of my markers. We will go ashore here. They landed. Now, Huck, you could touch the hole I escaped from with a fishing pole from where we stand. Try to find it. Huck searched the area but found nothing. Tom marched proudly into a thicket of sumac and said, Here it is. Look, Huck; it is the most hidden spot in the country. Keep this quiet. I have always wanted to be a robber, but finding a place like this was the challenge. We have it now, and we will keep it secret, though we will include Joe Harper and Ben Rogers. We need a gang to have any real style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds magnificent, doesn't it? It really does, Tom. Who will we rob? Oh, almost anyone. We will waylay people; that is the usual method. And kill them? No, not always. We will hold them in the cave until they pay a ransom. What is a ransom? Money. You make them collect all they can from their friends. If they cannot pay after a year, then you kill them. That is the standard way. You do not kill the women, though. You lock them up, but you do not kill them. They are always beautiful, wealthy, and terrified. You take their watches and valuables, but you always remove your hat and speak politely. Robbers are the most polite people—you see that in every book. Eventually, the women fall in love with you. After a week or two in the cave, they stop crying and refuse to leave. If you tried to drive them out, they would just come back. That is how it works in all the books. It is fantastic, Tom. I think it is better than being a pirate. Yes, it is better in some ways because it is closer to home, circuses, and everything else. Everything was ready, so the boys entered the opening with Tom leading. They struggled to the far end of the tunnel, secured their spliced kite strings, and moved forward.

He shivered and retreated, shutting the window. At the door, he turned the key and stepped out, refusing to look at the corpse. He felt that ignoring the reality of the situation was his only path forward. The friend who had painted the portrait responsible for his ruin was gone; that was sufficient. He then remembered the Moorish lamp, a silver piece inlaid with steel and turquoise. Fearing his servant might notice its absence, he returned to retrieve it. He could not avoid seeing the body; it lay perfectly still, its hands a ghastly, waxen white. After locking the door, he crept downstairs. The floorboards groaned under his weight, making him pause repeatedly, though he soon realized the sounds were only his own. In the library, he found the bag and coat. He hid them in a secret wall compartment where he kept his disguises, intending to burn them later. Checking his watch, he saw it was nearly two in the morning. He sat to reflect. Men were frequently executed in England for such crimes, yet what proof existed against him? Basil Hallward had left at eleven, and no one had seen him return. With most servants away and his valet asleep, he reasoned that Basil’s supposed trip to Paris would delay any suspicion for months. That was plenty of time to destroy the evidence. A sudden thought occurred to him. He donned his coat and hat, entering the hall just as a policeman’s lantern flashed against the window. He held his breath until the heavy footsteps faded. Finally, he slipped out, closed the door quietly, and rang the bell.

Winters near Sullivan’s Island are rarely harsh, and fires are seldom needed during the autumn. However, in mid-October of that year, a day arrived with an unusual chill. Shortly before dusk, I pushed through the evergreens to reach my friend’s cabin. I had not visited in weeks, as I lived in Charleston nine miles away, and travel was far more difficult then than it is now. Finding no response to my knock, I retrieved the hidden key, unlocked the door, and entered. A pleasant fire burned in the hearth, a welcome surprise. I removed my coat, sat by the logs, and waited for my host. He returned after dark, greeting me warmly. Jupiter, beaming, hurried to prepare marsh-hens for our meal. Legrand was in one of his characteristic states of excitement. He had discovered a new bivalve and, with Jupiter’s help, captured a beetle he believed to be a unique species, which he wanted me to examine the next day. Why not tonight? I asked, warming my hands and wishing the insect elsewhere. Legrand explained that he had foolishly lent the specimen to Lieutenant G from the fort, so I would have to wait until morning. He urged me to stay, promising to send Jupiter for it at dawn, calling it the most beautiful creature imaginable. When I asked if he meant sunrise, he clarified he was speaking of the bug, describing its brilliant gold color, its size, and its black markings. Jupiter interrupted, insisting the creature was solid gold, noting its remarkable weight.

Mr. Merton was quite upset by the second delay of the wedding. Lady Julia, having already purchased her dress, tried hard to convince Sybil to end the engagement. Despite her deep love for her mother, Sybil had committed her life to Lord Arthur and refused to change her mind. Lord Arthur was devastated for days, his nerves completely shattered. Eventually, his common sense returned, and he quickly decided on his next move. Since poison had failed, he concluded that an explosive was the logical solution. He reviewed his list of relatives and decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a cultured man who loved collecting clocks, which gave Lord Arthur an idea. Finding an explosive device was difficult. The London Directory offered no help, and he knew the police were useless at tracking such things. He suddenly remembered his friend Count Rouvaloff, a young Russian with revolutionary leanings he had met at a party. While the Count claimed to be researching Peter the Great, many suspected he was a Nihilist agent. Lord Arthur visited his Bloomsbury lodgings to ask for help. When Lord Arthur explained his goal, the Count asked if he was getting into politics. Lord Arthur, disliking pretense, admitted he had no interest in social issues and only needed the explosive for a private family matter.

Three or four months passed, and winter had fully arrived. I had attended school regularly, learning to read, write, and spell a little, though I could never master the multiplication tables past six times seven. I never cared much for mathematics anyway. Initially, I despised school, but eventually, I grew accustomed to it. When I felt overwhelmed, I would skip class, and the subsequent punishment actually improved my mood. Over time, school became easier, and I grew used to the widow’s habits, which no longer bothered me as much. While living indoors and sleeping in a bed felt restrictive, I occasionally slipped out to sleep in the woods before the weather turned cold, which provided some relief. I still preferred my old life, but I was beginning to appreciate the new one. The widow told me I was progressing steadily and that she was proud of me. One morning at breakfast, I accidentally knocked over the salt cellar. I reached to throw some over my left shoulder to ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson stopped me, scolding me for the mess. Although the widow defended me, I knew the bad luck was inevitable. I left the house feeling anxious, wondering what misfortune awaited me. There was no way to prevent this specific curse, so I walked along, feeling discouraged and vigilant. I went to the front garden and climbed over the stile in the high board fence. A fresh inch of snow covered the ground, and I noticed footprints. Someone had come from the quarry, lingered by the stile, and then walked around the fence. It was strange that they had not entered after waiting there so long. I could not understand it. It was quite mysterious, so I knelt down to examine the tracks more closely.

Yes, it is, and I could have had it if I were big enough; I saw him first. Who caught him? I agreed, but wondered if the chance was worth so little because something was wrong. No, it is perfectly legitimate. I saw the flyer myself. It describes him exactly, including the plantation he is from near New Orleans. There is no doubt about that deal. Give me some chewing tobacco, will you? I had none, so he left. After our long journey and all we did for those scoundrels, everything was ruined because they could betray Jim for forty dirty dollars and make him a slave for life among strangers. I briefly thought it would be better for Jim to be a slave back home with his family, so I considered writing to Tom Sawyer to tell Miss Watson where he was. I quickly dismissed this for two reasons: she would be furious at his escape and sell him further down the river, and everyone would despise him for being ungrateful, making his life miserable. Then I thought of myself. It would get out that Huck Finn helped a slave escape, and I would be so ashamed that I would want to hide from anyone I knew. That is how it goes; a person does something wrong and then tries to avoid the consequences, thinking that as long as it stays hidden, it is not shameful. That was my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience bothered me, and the more wicked and low-down I felt.

A beautiful woman risking everything for passion, a few weeks of happiness cut short by a treacherous crime, months of agony, and a child born in pain. The mother died, leaving the boy to the tyranny of a loveless man. It was an interesting background that made the lad seem more perfect. Every exquisite thing has a tragic origin; worlds must suffer for a flower to bloom. How charming he had been at dinner, sitting opposite him with wide, wonder-filled eyes. Talking to him was like playing a violin; he responded to every touch. There was something enthralling about exerting influence. To project one’s soul into another, to hear one’s own ideas echoed back with the music of youth, to infuse one’s temperament into another like a subtle perfume—that was a true joy in an age so vulgar and limited. The doctor was an elderly, kind-looking man once I woke him. I explained that my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday, camping on a raft we found. Around midnight, he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, causing it to discharge and wound his leg. I asked the doctor to treat him secretly so we could return home that evening and surprise our family. When he asked who my family was, I told him the Phelpses. He paused, then asked again how the shooting happened. I repeated that a dream caused the gun to fire, which he called a strange dream. He grabbed his lantern and saddlebags, but hesitated when he saw my canoe, doubting it was safe for two people. I insisted it had carried the three of us—my brother, myself, and the guns—without issue. He remained skeptical and tried to find a larger boat, but since all others were locked, he took mine. He suggested I wait or head home to prepare for the surprise, but I declined and gave him directions to the raft instead. Once he left, I worried about what we would do if the injury took days to heal. I decided that if he needed to return, I would follow him, even if I had to swim, and we would hold him captive until Tom was treated, then pay him and let him go. I fell asleep in a lumber pile and woke to find the sun high in the sky. I rushed to the doctor’s house, only to learn he had left during the night and had not yet returned.

Among the forty-seven prisoners, five had lost all record of their identities, crimes, and arrival dates. These four men and one woman were withered, elderly, and senile, possessing only hazy, inconsistent memories of their pasts. The priests tasked with preaching submission and patience to the captives held only vague legends regarding these individuals, confirming only that they had been imprisoned for at least thirty-five years. The monarchs viewed them merely as inherited property, like furniture passed down with the crown, and thus felt no curiosity regarding their histories. When I asked the queen why she had never released them, she was baffled, as the thought had never crossed her mind. It became clear that, given her upbringing, she saw these captives strictly as assets; one does not discard property simply because it lacks utility. After shielding their eyes to protect them from the sudden brightness, I led these wretched, skeletal figures into the afternoon sun. They were a haunting sight, the true offspring of a system governed by divine right and the established church.

Yet upon witnessing you become the focus of another’s affection, or imagining you might be cherished as something less than a divine icon of beauty, or that you might return such passion more fervently than you did mine, the monster stirred inside me. I sent your suitor away, and since that hour, tranquility has eluded me. Sleep fled, my eyes remained open, and my blood surged in constant agitation. I emerged into a new existence, much like a soul dying in hope might awaken in damnation. I shall not stain your mind by detailing my inner battles, my self-loathing, or my misery. Let a shroud cover the indescribable torments of a sinful father; such tortured secrets must not be cheapened. Everything was chaos, transgression, regret, and malice, yet mingled with the deepest tenderness. What finally spurred my resolve to master this passion and return to my daughter as a father was witnessing your own profound, empathetic grief. This brought me here; I believed that by rekindling the sorrow I felt at your mother’s passing, along with the memories dormant for seventeen years, my affection for her child would vanish. In a burst of resolve, I chose to depart alone, leaving you—the very essence of my life—until I could return without guilt. But it failed; I overestimated my strength or underestimated my love. I would surely have perished had you not come to me. Would that I had truly ceased to exist! And now, Mathilda, I offer my final admission. I was wretchedly wrong to think I could overcome my love for you; it is impossible. The sight of this home, these fields and woods where my first love once lived, seems only to have intensified it. In my delirium, I dared to tell myself that Diana died to bring you forth, that her spirit resides within you, and you should be as Diana to me. Despite every attempt to discard it, this affection clings tighter—a forbidden love, more unnatural than hatred, which blights your future and ruins me eternally. Better to have embraced despair or kissed death itself. Neither time nor distance can sever from my soul that which has become part of it. Since arriving, I have not for an instant escaped the hellish passion planted within me, destined to burn until all is cold, rigid, and lifeless.

I handed the slip back and said, "I am still completely lost. Even if the jewels of Golconda were the reward for solving this puzzle, I am certain I could never claim them." Legrand replied, "The solution is not as difficult as a quick glance might suggest. These symbols are clearly a cipher, but given what we know of Kidd, I doubted he could create anything truly complex. I assumed it was a simple code, designed to look impossible to an uneducated sailor without the key." "You actually solved it?" I asked. "Easily," he said. "I have cracked far more difficult ones. My background and interests draw me to such puzzles, and I doubt there is a riddle human ingenuity can create that it cannot also resolve. Once I had legible characters, the meaning was secondary. In any secret writing, the first step is identifying the language, as the method of solution depends on the specific idiom. Usually, one must test various languages based on probability until the right one is found. However, the signature here made it simple. The pun on 'Kidd' only works in English. Otherwise, I would have started with Spanish or French, as a pirate in the Spanish Main would likely use those. Instead, I assumed it was English. Notice there are no spaces between words. If there were, the task would be much simpler. I would have analyzed the short words first; finding a single-letter word like 'a' or 'I' would have guaranteed success. Without spaces, my first step was to identify the most and least frequent letters.

“Do you play?” The spy turned to Mr. Lorry with a humble air. “Sir, I appeal to a man of your age and kindness. Please ask this younger gentleman if he can justify playing the Ace he mentioned. I admit I am a spy, a disreputable job that someone must do, but he is not. Why should he lower himself to act like one?” “I will play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” Carton replied, checking his watch, “without hesitation in a few minutes.” The spy tried to involve Mr. Lorry again. “I had hoped, gentlemen, that your respect for my sister—” “I could show no greater respect for your sister than by finally removing her brother from her life,” Sydney Carton interrupted. “You think so, sir?” “I have fully decided.” The spy’s smooth tone, which clashed with his rough clothes, faltered against Carton’s mysterious demeanor. Carton looked at his cards and said, “Thinking again, I recall another card. That fellow who claimed to be working in the country prisons; who was he?” “He was French. You don’t know him,” the spy said quickly. “French, eh?” Carton mused, echoing him. “Perhaps.” “He is, I assure you, though it is not important,” the spy insisted. “Though it is not important,” Carton repeated mechanically. “Yet I know the face.” “I think not. I am sure not. It cannot be,” the spy said. “It cannot be,” Sydney Carton muttered, swirling his glass. “It cannot be. He spoke good French, yet like a foreigner, I thought?” “Provincial,” the spy suggested. “No, foreign!” Carton cried, striking the table as he realized the truth. “Cly! He was disguised, but it is the same man. We saw him at the Old Bailey.” “Now, you are being hasty, sir,” Barsad said with a crooked smile. “You are really giving me an advantage over you.”

Anne soon had plenty of chances to observe the group. She formed her own opinions, though she kept them to herself to avoid conflict at home. When Mr. Musgrove found him studying intensely, he worried that Charles was overworking himself. Mary hoped Henrietta had rejected him, while her husband expected to see him the next day. Anne simply thought Charles was acting wisely. One morning, while the men were out shooting, the sisters from the Great House visited the cottage. It was a beautiful November day, and the Miss Musgroves stopped by to announce they were going for a long walk, assuming Mary would not want to join. Lacking standard tools, the analyst adopts his opponent's mindset, identifying with them so completely that he often spots the simple, sometimes absurd, ways to lead them into mistakes. Whist has long been recognized for testing analytical power, and brilliant minds often prefer it over chess, which they dismiss as trivial. Nothing else challenges the analytical faculty quite like it. While a great chess player might only be skilled at that specific game, a master of whist possesses the mental agility required for any competitive endeavor. By mastery, I mean understanding every possible advantage, many of which are hidden from the average person. While a good memory and following the standard rules are often considered enough, true analytical skill goes beyond the basics. The analyst silently gathers observations and inferences. While others may do the same, the difference lies in the quality of what they notice. The key is knowing what to observe. The analyst looks beyond the game itself, studying his partner's face and comparing it to his opponents'. He watches how they hold their cards, counting trumps and honors based on their glances. He tracks every shift in their expressions—certainty, surprise, triumph, or frustration. From how a player collects a trick, he judges their future potential. He identifies bluffs by how cards are played. A stray word, a fumbled card, the way tricks are arranged, or signs of hesitation and eagerness all provide him with clear insight into the true state of the game.

Once my tears stopped, my mind cleared and I began to think calmly about my situation. Only a few hours had passed, yet my life had completely changed. It felt as though years had gone by; my father was dead to me, and I mourned him as if he were already in his grave. But he was not dead to the world, only to me. I had to run from him, avoiding him more carefully than my worst enemy. The thought left me breathless with pain, making it impossible to focus. I decided I would live in total isolation, perhaps moving to the Continent to join a convent—not for religious reasons, but simply to hide from the world and weep in peace. Yet, what about my father? Would he ever overcome the intense anger that controlled him? Perhaps, years from now, when age had cooled his temper, he could be a father to me again. This thought brought a sad smile to my face and gave me hope. I could wait. Let him wander for another sixteen years, shouting his complaints to the forests and waterfalls of distant lands. Let him endure hardships and the harsh elements of the world. I surrender you to this miserable life, Father. Go, live among savages, sleep under the open sky, and let your body grow weary and your heart grow cold until your youth is entirely gone.

“Tom!” No answer. “TOM!” No answer. “Where has that boy gone? You, TOM!” No answer. The old lady lowered her glasses to peer around the room, then pushed them up to look underneath. She rarely looked through them for something as small as a boy; they were for show, not for seeing. She looked confused, then said, loud enough for the furniture to hear, “Well, if I catch you, I’ll—” She stopped to poke under the bed with her broom, needing her breath for the effort. She found only the cat. “I have never seen the likes of that boy!” She went to the door and looked out at the garden. No Tom. She shouted, “Y-o-u-u TOM!” A noise behind her made her turn just in time to grab a small boy by his jacket. “I should have thought of the closet. What were you doing in there?” “Nothing.” “Nothing! Look at your hands and your mouth. What is that?” “I don’t know, Aunt.” “Well, I know. It’s jam. I’ve told you forty times to leave that jam alone. Hand me that switch.” As the switch hovered in the air, the boy cried, “Look behind you, Aunt!” The old lady spun around, and the boy immediately scrambled over the high fence and vanished. Aunt Polly stood surprised, then laughed softly. “Darn the boy, will I never learn? Hasn’t he played enough tricks for me to be ready? But old fools are the biggest fools. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks. Still, he never plays the same trick twice, so how is a person to know what’s coming? He seems to know exactly how long he can annoy me before I get angry, and he knows that if he can distract me or make me laugh, my anger fades and I can’t hit him.”

April 19th. This morning at nine, to my relief, the moon loomed terrifyingly close, and my condenser pump finally signaled a change in the atmosphere. By ten, the air density had clearly increased. By eleven, the apparatus required little effort, and at noon, I cautiously unscrewed the tourniquet. Finding no ill effects, I opened the rubber chamber and dismantled it from the car. As expected, this reckless experiment caused immediate spasms and a violent headache. Yet, since these breathing difficulties were not life-threatening, I endured them, knowing I was rapidly descending into the denser layers near the moon. My descent remained dangerously fast, and it became clear that while the moon possessed an atmosphere, it was far too thin to support the weight of my balloon, despite my earlier calculations regarding gravity and air density. My plummeting speed confirmed this, likely due to the geological anomalies I previously suspected. I was falling with terrifying speed. I immediately jettisoned my ballast, water kegs, condenser, and every item in the car, but it was useless. I continued to fall at a horrific rate, now less than half a mile from the surface. As a final resort, I discarded my coat, hat, and boots, then cut the heavy car loose. Clinging to the netting, I barely had time to see a landscape filled with tiny dwellings before I crashed into the center of a bizarre city. I landed amidst a crowd of grotesque little people who stood like idiots, arms akimbo, grinning and staring at me and my balloon without offering a word or any assistance.

At the top of the stairs, he composed himself, ready to unleash his signature demonic laugh. He had found it effective before; it had turned Lord Raker’s hair white overnight and caused three of Lady Canterville’s governesses to quit within a month. He laughed his most terrifying laugh, echoing through the vaulted ceiling, but as the sound faded, Mrs. Otis opened a door in a light blue robe. She offered him a bottle of Dr. Dobell’s tincture, suggesting it would cure his indigestion. Furious, the ghost prepared to transform into a large black dog—a feat that had once left Lord Canterville’s uncle permanently mentally disabled. Hearing footsteps, he hesitated and instead chose to glow faintly, vanishing with a mournful groan just as the twins arrived. Back in his room, he collapsed in distress. The twins’ rudeness and Mrs. Otis’s practicality were irritating, but he was most upset that he could not wear his suit of armor. He had hoped the Americans would respect a Spectre in Armor, perhaps even out of appreciation for Longfellow’s poetry, which he had enjoyed during his time with the Cantervilles. It was his own suit, worn successfully at the Kenilworth tournament and praised by the Queen herself. Yet, the weight of the breastplate and helmet had been too much; he had fallen on the stone floor, bruising his knees and knuckles. He remained ill for several days, rarely leaving his room except to maintain the bloodstain. Once recovered, he prepared a third attempt to terrify the American minister and his family.

I had tucked my handkerchief and other items inside my helmet, forgetting that I could not remove the headpiece myself. The knowledge that the cloth was so near yet completely unreachable became an unbearable obsession. As everyone knows, the things we cannot possess are exactly what we desire most. My focus narrowed entirely to that trapped handkerchief, and for miles, I fixated on it while salty sweat stung my eyes. Though it sounds trivial, this was genuine misery. I resolved that in the future, I would carry a handbag regardless of what the knights of the Round Table thought; I preferred comfort over their rigid standards of style. We continued our journey, occasionally hitting dusty patches that filled my nose and forced me to sneeze and curse, though I admit my language was far from perfect. We encountered no one in that desolate land, not even an ogre. Given my state of mind, it was fortunate for any ogre that he lacked a handkerchief, as I would have gladly traded his armor for one. Meanwhile, the sun heated my iron suit until I felt like I was cooking. Every sensation became an irritation. When I trotted, the rattling of my armor annoyed me, and the shifting shield banged against my chest and back. If I slowed to a walk, my joints groaned like a rusty wheelbarrow, and the lack of airflow made the heat stifling. Furthermore, moving slowly only made the heavy iron feel as though it were crushing me with increasing weight every passing minute.

I gathered sulfur and prepared the croup-kettle myself; I never wait for doctors when my family is ill. I had nursed this child often, and I knew how to soothe her when even her mother could not. Sir Launcelot, dressed in his finest armor, strode past on his way to the stock exchange. He was the board's president, holding the seat he had purchased from Sir Galahad, as the Knights of the Round Table now used their table for business. Despite his intense focus on market maneuvers, he stopped when he saw his favorite child was ill. He tossed his helmet aside, immediately helping to light the lamp and prepare the kettle. Sandy built a blanket canopy over the crib, and we were ready. Launcelot and I added lime, carbolic acid, and lactic acid to the water, positioning the steam spout under the canopy. With everything prepared, we sat on either side of the crib to begin our watch.

At that moment, we both noticed a scrap of parchment half-buried in the sand. Nearby lay the rotted remains of a ship’s longboat, so decayed that its structure was barely recognizable. Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. On our way home, we met Lieutenant G——, who asked to take the insect to the fort. I agreed, and he quickly pocketed the beetle, leaving me holding the parchment. He was so eager to secure his prize for his natural history collection that he didn't notice I kept the scrap, which I absentmindedly tucked into my own pocket. Later, when I sat down to sketch the beetle, I couldn't find any paper. While searching my pockets for a scrap to use, I discovered the parchment. I recall these details clearly because they struck me as significant. You might think me imaginative, but I had begun to connect the pieces. A boat on the shore and a parchment marked with a skull—the universal symbol of pirates—seemed linked. I noted that the material was durable parchment rather than paper, which is rarely used for unimportant notes. This suggested the skull had a specific, hidden meaning. Although one corner was torn, the original shape of the parchment was clearly oblong.

When Tom woke up, he was momentarily disoriented. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and realized where he was. It was a cool, gray dawn, and the woods were filled with a profound, peaceful stillness. Nothing moved; the forest seemed lost in meditation. Dew clung to the grass, and the campfire was reduced to white ash with a thin trail of blue smoke rising into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep. Soon, birds began to call to one another, followed by the rhythmic tapping of a woodpecker. As the morning light brightened, the forest came to life. Tom watched in wonder as nature stirred. A green inchworm crawled over a leaf, measuring the distance as it moved. Tom sat perfectly still, hoping the creature would crawl onto him, which would signify he was destined for a new suit of clothes—specifically, a flashy pirate costume. When the worm finally climbed onto his leg, he was delighted. Nearby, a line of ants marched past, one struggling to carry a dead spider up a tree. Tom whispered a rhyme to a ladybug, and when it flew away, he smiled, knowing how easily it was fooled. A tumblebug rolled its ball, curling up to play dead when Tom touched it. By now, the birds were active. A catbird sang from above, mimicking its neighbors, while a blue jay landed nearby to inspect the boys with curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large fox squirrel scurried past, pausing to chatter at the intruders, likely having never encountered humans before.

Despite her efforts, the boy grew increasingly pale and despondent. She tried various baths and treatments, but he remained as gloomy as ever. She then supplemented these with a strict oatmeal diet and medicinal plasters, force-feeding him various quack remedies. Tom had become indifferent to her interference, which deeply worried his aunt. She felt this apathy had to be shattered. Hearing of a new remedy called Pain-killer, she bought some and, after tasting its fiery intensity, abandoned all other treatments in its favor. She gave Tom a spoonful and watched anxiously. The effect was immediate; the boy reacted with such explosive energy that her worries vanished. Tom realized he needed a new strategy. He decided to pretend he enjoyed the medicine, asking for it so frequently that his aunt eventually told him to help himself. She noticed the bottle emptying, never suspecting he was pouring the liquid into a floorboard crack. One day, as Tom was dosing the floor, her yellow cat, Peter, begged for a taste. Tom warned him, but the cat insisted. Tom pried the cat's mouth open and poured the medicine in. Peter leaped high into the air, let out a screech, and began racing around the room, crashing into furniture and causing total chaos.

The beetle was remarkably heavy, and I could understand why Jupiter thought it was special. However, I could not fathom why Legrand agreed with him. When I finished looking at the insect, Legrand spoke grandly. He said he had summoned me to help him follow the path set by fate and the beetle. I interrupted him, telling him he was clearly unwell and needed to rest. I offered to stay with him for a few days until he recovered. He told me to check his pulse, and to my surprise, he had no fever. I insisted he was still ill, but he claimed he was simply excited and needed me to help him calm down. He explained that he and Jupiter were heading into the hills on the mainland and needed a trusted companion. He insisted I was the only one he could rely on. I asked if the beetle was involved in this trip, and he confirmed it was. I refused to take part in such a ridiculous plan. He expressed his regret, saying they would have to go alone. Worried he had lost his mind, I asked how long they would be gone. He said they would leave immediately and return by sunrise. I made him promise that once this obsession was settled, he would listen to my medical advice. He agreed, and we left at four o'clock. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, seemingly more concerned about keeping the tools away from his master than out of any desire to work.

Watching him in these moods, I often thought about the old idea of a dual soul, imagining Dupin as two people: the creative and the analytical. Do not think I am describing a mystery or writing fiction. What I saw in him was simply the result of an intense or perhaps troubled mind. An example of his comments will best explain this. One night, we were walking down a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. We had both been silent for at least fifteen minutes, lost in thought. Suddenly, Dupin spoke: "He is a very small man, it is true, and would be better suited for the Variétés Theater." I replied without thinking, not immediately realizing how perfectly he had matched my own thoughts. A moment later, I was stunned. "Dupin," I said seriously, "this is beyond me. I am amazed and can hardly believe it. How could you know I was thinking of—?" I paused to be sure he knew who I meant. "—of Chantilly," he said. "Why do you pause? You were thinking that his small size made him unfit for tragedy." That was exactly what I had been thinking. Chantilly was a former shoemaker who had become obsessed with acting, tried to play Xerxes in a tragedy, and was widely mocked for it. "For heaven's sake, tell me the method you used to read my mind," I exclaimed, more startled than I cared to admit. "It was the fruit seller," my friend replied, "who led you to conclude that the shoemaker was too short for Xerxes." "The fruit seller? You surprise me. I do not know any fruit seller." "The man who bumped into you when we entered the street fifteen minutes ago." I remembered then that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples had nearly knocked me over as we turned onto the street, but I could not understand what that had to do with Chantilly.

He believed so, at least, though who could be certain? No, nothing further had occurred. He had spared her out of vanity and donned a mask of virtue through hypocrisy. He had practiced self-denial merely to satisfy his curiosity, a truth he now acknowledged. Yet, would this murder haunt him forever? Must he always carry the weight of his history? Confess? Never. Only one piece of proof remained: the portrait. He had to destroy it. Why had he preserved it? It once delighted him to witness its decay, but lately, it only brought him sleepless nights. In his absence, he feared prying eyes would discover it. It had cast a shadow over his desires and poisoned his joy; it had become his conscience. He would end it. He spotted the blade that had slain Basil Hallward. He had polished it until it shone, free of any stain. Just as it had ended the artist, it would now destroy the artist’s creation and all it represented. It would slay the past, granting him freedom. It would extinguish this grotesque existence, and without its grim reminders, he would finally find rest. He grabbed the weapon and plunged it into the canvas. A harrowing cry of agony rang out, followed by a crash. The sound terrified the servants, who emerged from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing the square paused to gaze at the mansion. They summoned a policeman, who rang the bell repeatedly to no avail. The house remained dark, save for a single light in an upper window. Eventually, the officer retreated to a nearby portico to keep watch. Whose residence is this, Constable? the older gentleman inquired. It belongs to Mr. Dorian Gray, the officer replied. The men exchanged sneering glances as they departed; one was the uncle of Sir Henry Ashton. Within the servants' quarters, the staff whispered in hushed tones. Mrs. Leaf wept, wringing her hands, while Francis stood deathly pale. After fifteen minutes, he gathered the coachman and a footman to ascend the stairs.

He had never oppressed or imprisoned anyone. Far from demanding his dues, he had voluntarily given them up, venturing into a harsh world to earn his own living. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the struggling estate under instructions to help the people, providing whatever fuel and produce the creditors allowed. Gabelle had surely documented these efforts for his own protection, and this would now be clear. This supported Charles Darnay’s growing resolve to travel to Paris. Like the sailor in the legend, he felt drawn toward the magnetic rock, pulled by an irresistible force. His mind drifted steadily toward this dangerous attraction. He had long felt uneasy that his homeland was suffering under cruel leadership, and he worried that he, who knew he was better than those in power, was not there to advocate for mercy. This guilt, combined with the stinging insults of Monseigneur and the coarse mockery of Stryver, weighed on him. Then came Gabelle’s letter, a desperate plea from an innocent man facing death. His decision was final: he had to go to Paris. He felt the pull of the magnetic rock and believed he must sail toward it, blind to the true danger. He convinced himself that his past actions, though incomplete, would be recognized and appreciated in France. He was captivated by the idealistic vision of doing good, imagining he might even have the influence to guide the chaotic Revolution toward a better path.

Years ago, I became close friends with William Legrand. He came from an old, wealthy Huguenot family, but a string of bad luck left him penniless. To escape the embarrassment of his situation, he left his home in New Orleans and moved to Sullivan’s Island, near Charleston, South Carolina. This island is quite unique. It is a narrow strip of sea sand about three miles long and less than a quarter-mile wide. A small, muddy creek separates it from the mainland, where marsh birds often gather. The plant life is sparse and stunted. Aside from some palmettos near the western end—where Fort Moultrie and a few summer cottages stand—the island is covered in thick, fragrant myrtle bushes that grow up to twenty feet tall, creating a dense, tangled forest. Legrand built a small hut deep within this thicket, where I first met him by chance. Our acquaintance soon grew into a deep friendship, as I found him to be a highly intelligent man, though he was also a recluse prone to sudden shifts between intense excitement and deep sadness. He owned many books but rarely read them, preferring to spend his time hunting, fishing, or walking the beach to collect shells and insects. His collection of bugs would have impressed any expert. He was usually joined by an elderly man named Jupiter, a former slave who had been freed before the family lost their fortune. Jupiter refused to leave Legrand’s side, regardless of any threats or promises. It is likely that Legrand’s family, worried about his mental state, encouraged Jupiter to stay and keep a watchful eye on him.

What is the matter? Ten o’clock, sir. What do you mean? Ten at night? Yes, sir. You told me to wake you. Oh, I remember. Very well. After failing to fall back asleep while his servant noisily stirred the fire, he got up, grabbed his hat, and left. He walked to the Temple, paced the pavement twice to wake himself up, and headed to Stryver’s chambers. The clerk had already left, so Stryver opened the door himself, wearing slippers and a loose robe. He had the strained, bloodshot eyes common to men who live as hard as he did. You are a bit late, Memory, Stryver said. About the usual time, maybe fifteen minutes late. They entered a messy, book-lined room with a roaring fire. A kettle steamed on the stove, and a table was covered with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons. I see you have had your bottle, Sydney. Two tonight, I think. I was dining with today’s client, or watching him eat, which is the same thing. That was a clever point you made about the identification, Sydney. How did you think of it? I just thought he was a handsome fellow and that I would be like him if I had any luck. Stryver laughed, shaking his belly. You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work. Looking annoyed, the jackal loosened his clothes, went to the next room, and returned with a jug of cold water, a basin, and some towels. He soaked the towels, wrung them out, wrapped them around his head, and sat down. Now I am ready! Not much to do tonight, Memory, Stryver said cheerfully while sorting his papers. How much? Only two sets. Give me the worst one first. There they are, Sydney. Get to it! Stryver relaxed on a sofa by the table, while Sydney sat at his own desk, surrounded by papers and bottles.

Mr. Bennet remained largely silent throughout dinner, but once the staff departed, he sought to engage his visitor by remarking on his good fortune regarding his patroness. He noted that Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s kindness and concern for his welfare were truly exceptional. Mr. Collins responded with fervent praise, his demeanor growing unusually grave as he insisted he had never encountered such grace and humility in a noblewoman. He recounted how she had kindly commended his sermons, invited him to dine at Rosings on two occasions, and even summoned him to join her card games. While some deemed her haughty, he maintained she was nothing but affable, treating him as an equal and encouraging his social life and family visits. She had even advised him to marry wisely and had personally visited his parsonage to approve his renovations, even suggesting the addition of upstairs shelving.
