Mrs. Bennet expressed her approval, remarking that it was a shame more noblewomen were not so pleasant, and inquired if she lived nearby. Mr. Collins explained that his garden was separated from Rosings Park only by a lane. When Mrs. Bennet asked if the widow had any children, he mentioned her only daughter, the heiress to a vast estate. Mrs. Bennet sighed, noting the girl’s good fortune, and asked if she were beautiful. Mr. Collins described her as a charming young lady, adding that Lady Catherine considered her superior to all other women in beauty, as her features clearly reflected her noble lineage.

“Everyone lives that way, Huck.” “Tom, it makes no difference. I am not everyone, and I cannot endure it. Being confined is dreadful. Food comes too easily, so I have no appetite for it. I must ask permission to fish, to swim, to do anything at all. I had to speak so politely that it offered no comfort; I had to retreat to the attic to vent my frustrations daily just to feel like myself, or I would have perished. The widow forbade me from smoking, yelling, yawning, stretching, or scratching in public.” [He added with a surge of annoyance] “And confound it, she prayed constantly! I never encountered such a woman. I had to leave, Tom; I simply had to. Furthermore, school is starting, and I would have been forced to attend. I would not tolerate that. Listen, Tom, being wealthy is not as wonderful as people claim. It is nothing but constant worry and toil, making one wish they were dead. These clothes and this barrel suit me, and I will never abandon them. I would never have faced this trouble if not for that money. Take my share along with yours, give me a dime occasionally—not often, because I do not care for things unless they are difficult to obtain—and please convince the widow to let me be.” “Oh, Huck, you know I cannot do that. It is not fair, and if you try this life a little longer, you will grow to enjoy it.” “Enjoy it! Yes, the way I would enjoy sitting on a hot stove. No, Tom, I will not be rich, and I will not live in those stifling houses. I prefer the woods, the river, and my barrel, and I am staying with them. Confound it! Just as we had secured guns and a cave, ready to begin our robberies, this foolishness has to ruin everything!” Tom saw his chance. “Listen, Huck, being rich will not stop me from becoming a robber.” “No! Oh, goodness; are you truly serious, Tom?” “As serious as I am sitting here. But Huck, we cannot allow you into the gang unless you are respectable.” Huck’s joy vanished. “You cannot let me in, Tom?”

I drew near a stout man with a jovial expression, hoping to strike up a conversation and learn more, but I had barely introduced myself before he clumsily attempted to recount that same tiresome story Sir Dinadan had told me when I first clashed with Sir Sagramor. I retreated to the back of the group, feeling despondent and weary of this life of struggle and sorrow, yet fearing the finality of death, knowing how many souls in eternity had already heard that anecdote. By early afternoon, we encountered another group of pilgrims, though this one lacked all joy or levity. It included people of every age, from gray-haired elders to nursing infants, yet every face was marked by the profound hopelessness born of long-standing misery. They were slaves. Shackles bound their hands and feet to waist belts, and the adults were connected in a line by chains running from collar to collar. They had marched three hundred miles in eighteen days on meager scraps of food, sleeping huddled like animals while still in irons. Their clothing was nothing but rags, and their skin was raw and infested where the metal had rubbed. Their feet were mangled, forcing every one of them to limp. Originally numbering a hundred, half had been sold along the way. Their overseer rode nearby, wielding a heavy, multi-tailed whip; he never spoke, using the lash to strike the shoulders of any who faltered from exhaustion, forcing them back into line.

Our village possessed a pleasant atmosphere of tidying up and pausing before a fresh start on Saturday evenings, which emboldened Joe to linger half an hour past his usual time. As the rum and the extra time vanished, Joe rose to leave, gripping my hand. Wait a moment, Mr. Gargery, the stranger said. I believe I have a shiny new shilling, and if so, the lad shall have it. He retrieved it from his coins, wrapped it in creased paper, and handed it to me, insisting it was mine alone. I thanked him, gazing at him with unrefined intensity while clinging to Joe. He bade Joe and Mr. Wopsle goodnight, then offered me only a glance from his aiming eye—or rather, he closed it, though he could convey much by concealing it. Walking home, I remained silent, as Mr. Wopsle had left us and Joe was busy airing his mouth to clear the taste of rum. I felt dazed by this sudden reappearance of my past acquaintance and misdeed. My sister was in a decent mood when we arrived, prompting Joe to mention the shilling. She declared it a counterfeit, but upon inspecting the paper, she discovered two one-pound notes tucked inside. These notes appeared well-worn from extensive circulation. Joe immediately rushed back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them. While he was gone, I sat on my stool, certain the man would be long gone. Joe soon returned, confirming the man had departed, though he had left a message regarding the money.

Should you require one for personal use, I can provide a superior item and promise your complete satisfaction. May I inquire as to the recipient? If it is for the police or anyone associated with Scotland Yard, I cannot assist. English detectives are our greatest allies; their incompetence allows us to act with impunity, and I would hate to lose them. Lord Arthur replied that the police were not involved, explaining that the clock was meant for the Dean of Chichester. Herr Winckelkopf expressed surprise at such religious devotion in a young man, though Lord Arthur blushed and admitted he knew nothing of theology. Confirming the matter was strictly private, the man left and returned with a small dynamite disc and an elegant French clock topped with an ormolu figure of Liberty. Lord Arthur was delighted and asked how it functioned. Winckelkopf kept his methods secret, offering to calibrate the device for any desired moment. Lord Arthur requested it be set for Friday at noon, when the Dean would be home. The maker noted this in his ledger. When asked for the cost, Winckelkopf dismissed the labor, charging only for the materials and shipping, noting his pleasure in helping a friend of Count Rouvaloff. Lord Arthur then asked about compensation for his effort.

In a certain town, which I will not name, there stands a building common to most places: a workhouse. Inside this workhouse, on a date that does not matter to the reader, the boy whose name titles this story was born. For a long time after the parish surgeon brought him into this world of trouble, it was uncertain if the child would live long enough to be named. Had he died, this biography would have been incredibly short, though perhaps quite accurate. While being born in a workhouse is hardly a stroke of luck, it was actually the best thing that could have happened to Oliver Twist. He struggled to take his first breath, lying on a thin mattress, caught between life and death. Had he been surrounded by doting relatives and expert doctors, he surely would have been fussed to death. Instead, he was left with only a tipsy pauper and a busy parish surgeon. Oliver and nature fought it out alone. Eventually, he breathed, sneezed, and announced his arrival to the workhouse with a cry as loud as any newborn could manage after only three minutes of life.

He was powerless to stop it. It infuriated him to believe that Becky Thatcher was unaware he was even alive. Yet she saw him clearly, aware that her strategy was succeeding, and she took pleasure in his pain. Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom suggested he had urgent matters to attend to, but the girl kept talking. He silently cursed her, desperate to escape. When he finally left, she innocently promised to be nearby after school, and he departed, resenting her presence. He seethed, wishing it were any boy other than that arrogant Saint Louis dandy. He recalled beating the newcomer before and vowed to do it again, acting out a violent thrashing against the empty air to satisfy his rage. Tom hurried home at midday, unable to tolerate Amy’s joy or his own jealousy. Meanwhile, Becky’s interest in the pictures faded as Tom failed to appear. Her triumph turned to gloom and then misery, regretting her actions. When Alfred tried to show her another drawing, she snapped at him, weeping as she walked away. Alfred attempted to comfort her, but she told him to leave her alone, declaring her hatred for him. Confused and hurt, Alfred watched her go, eventually realizing he had merely been a tool for her to spite Tom Sawyer.

We finally lightened the box by removing two-thirds of its contents, which allowed us to lift it from the hole with some effort. We hid the items in the bushes and left the dog to guard them, with Jupiter strictly ordering him not to move or bark until we returned. We hurried home with the chest, reaching the hut safely but exhausted at one in the morning. Too tired to continue, we rested until two, ate, and then headed back to the hills with three sturdy sacks we found at the hut. Shortly before four, we reached the pit, divided the remaining treasure, and returned to the hut with our heavy loads just as dawn broke over the trees. We were exhausted, but our excitement kept us from sleeping. After a restless nap of a few hours, we woke up to examine our treasure. The chest had been packed to the top, and we spent the entire day and most of the next night sorting through it. Everything had been thrown in without order. Once organized, we realized we were even wealthier than we had imagined. We estimated the gold coins to be worth over four hundred and fifty thousand dollars. There was no silver, only antique gold from France, Spain, Germany, and England, along with some unfamiliar coins. Some large, heavy pieces were too worn to identify, and there was no American currency. The jewels were harder to value. We found one hundred and ten large, high-quality diamonds, eighteen brilliant rubies, three hundred and ten beautiful emeralds, twenty-one sapphires, and an opal. These stones had been pried from their settings, which we found hammered flat, likely to hide their origin.

The lieutenant eventually asked why he had traveled so far across the ice in such an unusual craft. His face darkened instantly, and he replied, "I am searching for someone who fled from me." When asked if the man he pursued traveled the same way, he confirmed it. The lieutenant mentioned seeing a man in a dog-drawn sledge crossing the ice the day before they rescued him. This caught the stranger's attention, and he began asking many questions about the route taken by the creature he called a demon. Later, alone with me, he remarked that he had surely piqued our curiosity, though we were too polite to pry. I assured him that it would be rude and heartless to question him, especially after we had saved his life. He then asked if the ice breaking might have destroyed the other sledge. I told him I could not be certain, as the ice did not break until near midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety by then. Since that conversation, a new energy has filled the stranger. He is desperate to go on deck to watch for the sledge, but I have insisted he stay in the cabin, as he is too weak for the freezing air. I promised to have someone watch for him. This is my record of these events. The stranger is slowly recovering but remains quiet and anxious when others enter his cabin. His gentle, winning manner has charmed the crew, despite their limited contact. I have grown to love him like a brother; his profound grief moves me deeply. He must have been a remarkable man in his prime, for even in his broken state, he is captivating. I once wrote to you, Margaret, that I would find no friend at sea, yet I have met a man who, had he not been crushed by sorrow, would have been the brother of my heart.

Shortly after noon, the boys borrowed a small boat from an absent owner and set off. Several miles past Cave Hollow, Tom pointed to a landslide on the bluff. He explained it was a landmark and steered them to the shore. Tom told Huck the cave entrance was nearby, but Huck could not find it. Tom walked into a thicket of bushes and revealed the opening. He told Huck to keep it a secret, noting that they would form a gang with Joe Harper and Ben Rogers. Tom Sawyer’s Gang, he declared, sounded impressive. Huck asked who they would rob, and Tom explained they would waylay people. When Huck asked if they would kill them, Tom said they would hold them for ransom. He explained that a ransom is money collected from friends, and if it is not paid after a year, the captives are killed. He added that women are never killed, only held captive, and that they eventually fall in love with the robbers because of their polite manners. Huck agreed that being a robber sounded better than being a pirate because it was closer to home. The boys then entered the cave, with Tom leading the way. They reached the end of the tunnel, tied their kite strings to a rock, and continued inside.

I handed the paper back and said, "I am still just as confused. Even if the jewels of Golconda were my reward for solving this puzzle, I am certain I could never earn them." Legrand replied, "The solution is not as difficult as it first appears. These symbols are clearly a code, but knowing Kidd, I doubted he could create anything truly complex. I assumed it was a simple cipher that would seem impossible to an uneducated sailor without the key." "And you actually solved it?" I asked. "Easily," he said. "I have solved far more difficult ones. My mind is naturally drawn to such riddles, and I doubt there is any puzzle human intelligence can create that it cannot also solve. Once I had the characters, the meaning was simple to find. In any secret writing, the first step is identifying the language, as the method of solving depends on the specific tongue. Usually, you must test different languages based on probability until you find the right one. However, the signature here made it clear. The pun on the name 'Kidd' only works in English. Otherwise, I would have started with Spanish or French, as those would be common for a pirate. Because of that, I assumed the code was in English. Notice there are no spaces between the words. If there were, the task would be much easier. I would have analyzed the short words first, and if a single-letter word like 'a' or 'I' appeared, the solution would be certain. Since there are no divisions, my first step was to identify which letters appeared most and least frequently.

I lack the nerves for such matters. But could you truly feel at ease spending the entire evening away from the poor child? Yes; his father manages it, so why shouldn't I? Jemima is quite attentive, and she could update us hourly. I really believe Charles should have told his father we would all attend. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terribly frightened yesterday, but today the situation is quite changed. Well, if you do not think it too late to send word, why not go along with your husband? Leave the boy in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove could not object while I am here with him. Are you in earnest? Mary exclaimed, her eyes lighting up. How wonderful! That is a brilliant idea. I might as well go, as I am of no use here, and it only distresses me. You, lacking a mother's sensibilities, are far better suited for this. You can make little Charles obey instantly. It will be much better than leaving him with only Jemima. I shall certainly go; I ought to, just as much as Charles, since they are so eager for me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left alone. A marvelous suggestion, Anne. I will inform Charles and prepare at once. You can summon us immediately if anything happens, though I am certain there will be no cause for alarm. I would not dream of going if I were not perfectly comfortable regarding my dear child. Moments later, she was knocking at her husband’s door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she overheard the entire exchange, which began with Mary declaring triumphantly, I intend to accompany you, Charles, for I am no more useful here than you are. If I remained shut up with the child forever, I could never persuade him to do anything against his will. Anne will stay; she has offered to remain and look after him. It was her own proposal, so I shall join you, which is much better, as I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday. This is very kind of Anne, her husband replied, and I would be glad to have you come, but it seems rather unfair that she should be left alone to nurse our sick child.

The nephew glanced at him, but continued toward the door. Good night, the uncle said. I look forward to seeing you in the morning. Sleep well. Light the way for my nephew to his room. And burn him in his bed if you like, he whispered to himself before ringing for his valet. Once the valet left, the Marquis paced his room in a loose robe, preparing for sleep on that hot, quiet night. Moving silently in his slippers, he paced like a refined tiger, appearing like a wicked nobleman from a fairy tale who might transform into a beast at any moment. He walked across his luxurious bedroom, reflecting on the day: the slow climb up the hill, the sunset, the mill, the prison on the cliff, the village, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender pointing at the carriage. These memories brought to mind the fountain in Paris, the bundle on the step, and the tall man crying out that the child was dead. I am cool now, the Marquis said, and ready for bed. He left one light burning by the hearth, drew his thin curtains, and drifted off as the night sighed. For three long hours, the stone faces on the exterior walls stared into the darkness. The horses shifted in the stables, dogs barked, and an owl hooted in a way that defied poetic convention. For those three hours, the stone carvings of lions and men watched the night. Total darkness covered the landscape and the dusty roads. The graveyard became a blur of indistinguishable mounds, and the figure on the cross vanished into the gloom. In the village, both the tax collectors and the taxed slept soundly. Perhaps dreaming of feasts and freedom, the starving and the overworked found a temporary escape in sleep.

Sydney Carton stood in the street, unsure of his next move. "Tellson's at nine," he mused. "Should I show myself before then? It is a wise precaution for these people to know I am here. I must be careful." He paced the darkening street, weighing the consequences of his plan. Convinced it was the right choice, he headed toward Saint Antoine. Defarge owned a wine shop in that district, and Carton found it easily without asking for directions. After locating the shop, he ate a meal and fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in years, he avoided strong spirits, having poured his brandy away the previous night. He woke at seven, feeling refreshed. On his way to Saint Antoine, he stopped at a mirror to straighten his messy cravat, collar, and hair. He then walked straight into Defarge’s shop. Only Jacques Three, the man he had seen on the jury, was there, drinking and talking with the Defarges and The Vengeance. Carton sat down and ordered a small wine in broken French. Madame Defarge glanced at him, then looked again with sharper interest. She approached him and asked what he wanted. He repeated his order. "English?" she asked, raising her eyebrows. He looked at her as if struggling to understand, then replied with a heavy foreign accent.

Early February arrived, and Anne, having spent a month in Bath, felt a growing urgency for updates from Uppercross and Lyme. Mary’s correspondence had been sparse, and three weeks had passed since Anne last heard anything. She knew only that Henrietta had returned home and that Louisa, while mending, remained in Lyme. She was deep in thought about them one evening when a substantial letter from Mary arrived, accompanied by the compliments of Admiral and Mrs. Croft. The Crofts were in Bath, a development that stirred her interest, as she held them in high regard. Sir Walter immediately questioned the arrival of his Kellynch tenants, but Anne, distracted by her letter, could barely attend to his remarks. The letter, dated February 1st, began with Mary offering no excuse for her silence, assuming Anne was too preoccupied with Bath’s pleasures to miss Uppercross. Mary complained of a tedious Christmas, noting the lack of dinner parties and dismissing the Hayters. She expressed frustration that the holidays had finally ended and remarked with surprise that the Harville children remained at the house, criticizing Mrs. Harville’s parenting and the children’s behavior. Mary also lamented the harsh weather and the lack of visitors, save for the unwelcome and frequent appearances of Charles Hayter, suggesting that Henrietta should have stayed in Lyme longer to avoid his company.

He was brought to you. You see, I am aware of the details. That is true, Defarge replied. His wife had nudged him while she knitted, signaling him to keep his answers brief. The spy continued, It was to you that his daughter came, and from your care that she took him, along with that man from Tellson’s Bank, Mr. Lorry, to England. That is true, Defarge repeated. Very interesting, the spy said. I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England. Do you hear much about them now? No, Defarge said. Actually, Madame Defarge added, looking up from her knitting, we never hear about them. We heard they arrived safely and received a letter or two, but since then, we have gone our separate ways. Quite right, the spy replied. She is going to be married. Going to be? Madame asked. She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English seem cold. You know I am English, the spy said. I can tell by your accent, Madame replied, and I assume the man matches the tongue. He did not take this as a compliment but laughed it off. After finishing his drink, he added, Yes, Miss Manette is getting married, but not to an Englishman. She is marrying a Frenchman, the nephew of the Marquis for whom Gaspard was executed. He lives in England under the name Charles Darnay, though his mother’s family name was D’Aulnais. Madame Defarge kept knitting, but the news clearly affected her husband. As he tried to light his pipe, his hands shook. The spy noticed his reaction immediately. Having made his point, and with no other customers arriving, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and left, politely mentioning that he looked forward to seeing the Defarges again.

The stars were still bright when I woke, and Taurus high in the southern sky marked midnight. I had been troubled by nightmares. I dreamt I was at Timon’s final feast, arriving hungry only to find the dishes filled with nothing but steam. I fled from my host, who took the form of Raymond, while the objects he threw at me seemed to reek of decay. His figure distorted into a massive phantom marked by the sign of plague, growing until it threatened to shatter the very sky. The nightmare became unbearable, and I forced myself awake to regain my senses. My first thought was of Perdita; I had to return to her, to support her and guide her through her grief with both duty and tenderness. Guided by the stars, I turned away from the ruins of the Golden City and managed to escape. Outside the walls, I borrowed a horse from a group of soldiers. The landscape had shifted; the encampment was gone, and the scattered remnants of the army moved about with faces full of shock and despair. With a heavy heart, I entered the palace, afraid to move or speak. Perdita sat on the marble floor, her head bowed, her hair wild, and her fingers twisting together. She was pale, her face twisted in agony. When she looked up, the brief spark of hope in her eyes was heartbreaking. I could not speak, and my forced smile only confirmed her fears. She understood, and her head dropped again. When I finally found my voice, it frightened her; she did not want her misery confirmed by words. Instead, she tried to distract me, rising from the floor and whispering, “Hush, Clara is finally sleeping after so much crying; we must not wake her.”

In the middle of the gap, I noticed a white object, though I could not initially identify it. After adjusting the telescope, I realized it was a human skull. I felt confident the mystery was solved. The instructions regarding the seventh limb and the east side clearly referred to the skull's position, while the mention of the left eye suggested a specific method for locating the treasure. I understood that dropping a bullet through that eye socket would create a line of sight; extending that path fifty feet from the tree trunk would mark the exact spot where the treasure might be buried. I remarked that the logic was clever yet straightforward, and asked what happened after he left the Bishop's Hotel. He explained that once he stepped away from the ledge, the circular gap disappeared and could not be seen from any other vantage point. He had been accompanied by Jupiter, who had been watching him closely, but he managed to slip away the next morning to find the tree. He eventually located it, though his valet threatened to punish him for his disappearance. I suggested that their initial failure to find the treasure was due to Jupiter dropping the beetle through the wrong eye. He agreed, noting that the small error in the starting position caused a significant deviation over the fifty-foot distance, leading them completely off course.

She felt a sudden urge to check the weather at the door, dismissing any suspicion of hidden intentions. Captain Wentworth had surely departed. She rose, determined to stop her mind from constantly second-guessing itself. Before she could reach the door, however, Captain Wentworth arrived, accompanied by a group of his friends. He appeared visibly startled and flustered upon seeing her, his face flushing. For the first time since their reunion, she felt more composed than he, having had a moment to brace herself against the initial shock. Yet, she remained deeply moved, experiencing a complex blend of pain and pleasure. He addressed her briefly before turning away, his demeanor clearly awkward rather than cold or friendly. Soon, he returned to exchange polite, trivial remarks, though neither truly absorbed the conversation. Anne noted his unusual lack of composure; he seemed unable to maintain the practiced indifference they had recently adopted. Whether due to time or Louisa, he was clearly unsettled. Though he appeared healthy and spoke of the Musgroves and Louisa with a fleeting touch of his old playfulness, he remained visibly ill at ease. Anne was saddened, though not surprised, to see Elizabeth pointedly ignore him. She witnessed their mutual recognition and knew he expected a greeting, making it all the more painful to watch her sister turn away with icy indifference. Finally, the servant arrived to announce that Lady Dalrymple’s carriage had arrived, much to Elizabeth’s relief.

He always pretended Peter wrote those letters, but that was a lie; he got all the information from that young fool we took to the steamboat. Mary Jane brought out the letter her father left, and the king read it aloud, pretending to cry. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls, and the profitable tanyard, other property worth seven thousand, and three thousand in gold to Harvey and William. It also mentioned where the six thousand dollars in cash was hidden in the cellar. The two frauds told me to bring a candle so they could retrieve it and appear honest. We locked the cellar door, and when they found the bag, they dumped the gold on the floor. It was a beautiful sight. The king’s eyes lit up as he slapped the duke on the shoulder and exclaimed that this was better than their previous scams. The duke agreed. They played with the gold coins, letting them jingle through their fingers. The king remarked that acting as brothers to a wealthy dead man and representatives for foreign heirs was their best strategy, proving that trusting in Providence always pays off. Most people would have been satisfied with the money, but they insisted on counting it. They found it was four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king cursed, wondering where the missing money went. After searching in vain, the duke suggested the sick man had simply made a mistake and they should let it go. The king insisted he did not care about the loss, but he was worried about the count. He wanted to be completely transparent and count the money in front of everyone to avoid suspicion, but he was concerned about the discrepancy between their count and the amount the dead man claimed was there.

Poor Jack was later killed in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended, so in every way, it was a great success. It was, however, an extremely difficult costume to prepare, and it took him three full hours to get ready. Finally, he was satisfied with his appearance. The large leather riding boots were slightly too big, and he could only find one of his two pistols, but he was pleased. At a quarter past one, he slipped out of the wall and crept down the hall. Reaching the twins' room, known as the Blue Bed Chamber for its curtains, he found the door slightly open. Hoping for a dramatic entrance, he threw it wide, only for a heavy jug of water to fall on him, soaking him and narrowly missing his shoulder. He heard muffled laughter from the bed. The shock was so intense that he fled to his room, catching a severe cold the next day. He was only comforted by the fact that he had left his head behind; otherwise, the consequences could have been dire. He gave up hope of scaring the rude American family, settling for creeping through the halls in soft slippers, wearing a thick red scarf to avoid drafts, and carrying a small antique gun in case the twins attacked. The final blow came on September 19th. He went to the entrance hall, feeling safe, and amused himself by mocking the large photographs of the American Minister and his wife that had replaced the Canterville portraits. He was dressed simply in a shroud stained with graveyard dirt, his jaw tied up with yellow linen, and he carried a lantern and a shovel.

Although Perdita was never named, I felt certain her influence drove his indecision. Who better deserved the devotion of this self-important leader than my noble sister, a woman with the regal bearing of a queen? She loved him in return, even as his ambition warred with his feelings and her own disappointment dampened her ardor. We arrived at the House that evening. Raymond appeared lighthearted and indifferent, despite knowing his future would be determined by the coming debate. A deafening roar, like a massive swarm of bees, greeted us in the coffee-room. Groups of politicians gathered, their faces tense and their voices hushed or boisterous. The aristocratic faction, England’s wealthiest and most powerful men, seemed surprisingly calm, as the matter would be settled without their direct involvement. Near the hearth stood Ryland and his allies. Ryland, a man of humble origins who had amassed a fortune from his father’s manufacturing business, had long championed the popular reforms that followed the king’s abdication and the merger of the legislative houses. Initially, he had welcomed Lord Raymond’s schemes, as they siphoned support from his rivals, but the movement had grown excessive. The lesser nobility saw the potential return of monarchy as a path to reclaiming their vanished status. The dormant spirit of royalty was awakening; many citizens, like willing captives, seemed eager to submit to a crown. While some steadfast individuals remained, the term republic had lost its appeal to the masses, and many longed for the glitter of monarchy. Ryland, finally stirred to act, declared that he had tolerated this faction long enough and vowed to dismantle their influence entirely. As Raymond stepped into the room, his supporters cheered, crowding around him to tally their votes and discuss the new members who had yet to commit.

You have fostered an artificial spirit in him, ma'am, which is inappropriate for his station. As the board, who are practical philosophers, would tell you, what business do paupers have with soul or spirit? It is enough that we provide them with living bodies. If you had fed the boy only gruel, this would never have occurred. Dear me, Mrs. Sowerberry exclaimed, piously looking toward the ceiling, this is the result of being generous. Her generosity to Oliver had consisted of giving him the scraps no one else would eat, so there was a certain irony in her accepting Mr. Bumble’s harsh accusation, of which she was entirely innocent. Ah, Mr. Bumble said, once she looked down, the only solution now is to leave him in the cellar until he is sufficiently starved, then keep him on gruel throughout his apprenticeship. He comes from bad stock. His mother arrived here having endured hardships that would have killed any decent woman. Hearing his mother mentioned, Oliver began kicking with such violence that no other sound could be heard. Sowerberry returned, and after the ladies explained the offense with calculated exaggerations, he unlocked the cellar door and dragged his rebellious apprentice out by the collar. Oliver’s clothes were torn, his face bruised, and his hair disheveled, yet he scowled at Noah, entirely undismayed. You are a fine young man, aren't you? Sowerberry said, shaking him and boxing his ears. He insulted my mother, Oliver replied. What if he did, you ungrateful wretch? Mrs. Sowerberry said. She deserved it and worse. She did not, Oliver insisted. She did, she countered. It is a lie, Oliver shouted. Mrs. Sowerberry burst into tears. This left Mr. Sowerberry no choice. Had he hesitated to punish Oliver severely, he would have been branded a brute and a terrible husband, according to the established precedents of marital disputes.

When I finally caught Tom alone, I asked what his plan had been for Jim if the escape succeeded, especially since Jim was already free. He explained that he had intended for us to take Jim down the river on the raft, have adventures all the way to the mouth, and then reveal his freedom. We would have returned him home on a steamboat in style, paid him for his time, and organized a grand parade with torches and a brass band to make him a hero. I decided things turned out just as well as they were. We freed Jim from his chains quickly. Once Aunt Polly, Uncle Silas, and Aunt Sally learned how well Jim helped the doctor care for Tom, they treated him wonderfully, giving him plenty of food and rest. We visited him in the sickroom, where Tom gave Jim forty dollars for his patience. Jim was overjoyed and exclaimed that his earlier signs about becoming rich again had finally come true. Tom then suggested that the three of us sneak away soon to find supplies and head into the Territory for a few weeks of adventures among the Indians. I agreed, but mentioned I had no money for supplies and doubted I could get any from home, assuming my father had returned and spent it all. Tom assured me the money was still there, over six thousand dollars, and that my father had not been back.

It was Lady Windermere’s final gathering before Easter, and Bentinck House was packed beyond its usual capacity. Six Cabinet Ministers arrived from the Speaker’s Levée adorned in their ribbons and stars, the most attractive women displayed their finest gowns, and at the gallery’s edge, Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe—a stout, Tartar-featured woman with small dark eyes and magnificent emeralds—spoke broken French loudly, laughing excessively at every remark. It was a remarkable gathering. Splendid peeresses conversed kindly with radical agitators, famous clergymen mingled with noted doubters, a group of bishops trailed a stout opera singer, and Royal Academicians stood on the stairs, while the supper-room was reportedly filled with geniuses. It was truly a highlight for Lady Windermere, and the Princess remained until nearly eleven-thirty. Once she departed, Lady Windermere went back to the gallery, where a famous economist was gravely detailing the science of music to an annoyed Hungarian virtuoso, and she began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. She appeared stunning, with her ivory neck, large blue eyes, and thick golden hair. It was true gold, not the pale straw shade often called gold today, but the hue of sunbeams or ancient amber, lending her face the aura of a saint mixed with the allure of a sinner. She was a fascinating psychological subject. Early on, she realized that nothing mimics innocence quite like an indiscretion; through various bold, mostly harmless adventures, she earned the status of a unique personality. She had married three times, according to Debrett, yet because she kept the same lover, society had stopped gossiping about her. Now forty, childless, and possessing that insatiable thirst for pleasure that preserves youth, she suddenly scanned the room and asked in her clear contralto, Where is my palmist? Your what, Gladys? the Duchess asked, startled. My palmist, Duchess; I cannot do without him right now. Dear Gladys, you are always so unique, the Duchess whispered, struggling to recall if a palmist was the same as a foot doctor. He examines my hand twice every week, Lady Windermere added, and he is quite fascinating.

So, let me tell you how it happened. Miss Watson was always hard on me, but she promised she would never sell me down to New Orleans. Lately, I noticed a slave trader hanging around, which made me nervous. One night, I crept to the door and heard Miss Watson telling the widow that she was going to sell me for eight hundred dollars. She said it was too much money to turn down. I did not wait to hear the rest; I left immediately. I ran down the hill, hoping to steal a skiff along the shore, but there were still people around, so I hid in an old, broken-down barrel shop by the river. I stayed there all night. By morning, boats were passing by, and everyone was talking about how your father had come to town claiming you were killed. I felt terrible that you were dead, Huck, but I am glad to see you now. I stayed hidden under the wood shavings all day. I was hungry, but I was not afraid because I knew Miss Watson and the widow would be at a camp meeting all day. They assumed I was out with the cattle, so they would not miss me until dark. The other servants would be gone too, taking the day off. When it got dark, I walked two miles up the river road to where there were no houses. I had decided on a plan. If I kept running on foot, the dogs would track me. If I stole a boat to cross the river, they would notice it was missing and know exactly where to look for me on the other side.

Jupiter was overjoyed at the sight, but his master looked deeply disappointed. He urged us to keep digging, and I had barely started again when I tripped over a large iron ring buried in the dirt. We worked frantically for ten minutes, feeling more excited than ever. We uncovered a wooden chest, remarkably well-preserved and hard, likely treated with chemicals. It measured three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep, reinforced with riveted iron bands. Six iron rings on the sides suggested it was meant to be carried by six people. We could barely budge it, so we realized we could not move it. Fortunately, the lid was held only by two sliding bolts. We pulled them back, shaking with nerves. Suddenly, a priceless treasure sparkled before us. As our lantern light hit the pit, a dazzling pile of gold and jewels blinded us. I cannot describe my shock. Legrand was exhausted and silent. Jupiter looked pale with terror, completely stunned. He knelt in the pit and buried his arms deep into the gold, as if bathing in it. Finally, he sighed and muttered to himself, "And this is all because of the gold-bug! The pretty gold-bug! The poor little gold-bug I treated so badly! Aren't you ashamed of yourself?" Eventually, I had to remind them that we needed to move the treasure. It was getting late, and we had to get everything home before sunrise. We were so overwhelmed that we struggled to decide what to do next.

Well, Mr. Bumble, he finally said, there is no denying that since the new feeding system began, the coffins are narrower and shallower than before. Still, we must make a profit. Quality wood is expensive, and the iron handles are shipped by canal from Birmingham. Mr. Bumble agreed that every trade has its downsides and a fair profit is acceptable. Of course, the undertaker replied, if I lose money on one item, I make it up elsewhere. He chuckled. Mr. Bumble nodded. The undertaker continued, noting a major disadvantage: the stoutest people die the fastest. Those who were once better off and paid taxes are the first to fail when they enter the workhouse. A few extra inches beyond my estimate ruins my profit, especially with a family to support. Sowerberry spoke with the indignation of a wronged man. Sensing a slight against the parish, Mr. Bumble changed the subject to Oliver Twist. By the way, do you know anyone who needs a boy? A parish apprentice who is currently a burden? We offer generous terms. Bumble tapped his cane against the sign advertising five pounds. The undertaker grabbed Bumble’s lapel, saying that was exactly what he wanted to discuss. He then complimented Bumble’s elegant button. It is quite nice, the beadle said, looking at the brass buttons on his coat. The design matches the parish seal, showing the Good Samaritan helping the injured. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning. I remember wearing it for the first time at the inquest for that bankrupt tradesman who died in a doorway.

Yes, it is, and I could have had him if I were big enough; I saw him first. Who caught him? It was an old stranger who sold his claim for forty dollars because he had to head upriver and could not wait. Imagine that! I would have waited seven years. I agree, but perhaps his claim is not worth more if he sold it so cheaply. Maybe something is not right. It is perfectly legitimate. I saw the handbill myself. It describes him exactly, including the plantation he is from below New Orleans. There is no doubt about that deal. Give me a chew of tobacco, will you? I had none, so he left. I went to the raft and sat in the shelter to think, but I could not reach a conclusion. I thought until my head ached, but I saw no way out. After our long journey and all we did for those scoundrels, everything was ruined because they had the heart to betray Jim, making him a slave for life among strangers for forty dirty dollars. I briefly thought it would be better for Jim to be a slave back home with his family, so I considered writing to Tom Sawyer to tell Miss Watson where he was. I dismissed that idea for two reasons: she would be furious at his ingratitude and sell him down the river anyway, and everyone would despise him, making him feel disgraced. And then there was me. It would get out that Huck Finn helped a slave gain his freedom, and if I ever saw anyone from home again, I would be so ashamed I would have to grovel. That is how it goes; a person does something low and then wants to avoid the consequences, thinking that as long as it is hidden, it is not a disgrace. That was my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience gnawed at me, and the more wicked and low I felt.

I decided to get off as soon as we reached town to avoid him, and I succeeded. My small suitcase was under my feet; I simply unlatched it, dropped it, and climbed down, standing on the first paved street under a lamp. The convicts continued on the coach toward the river. In my mind, I pictured the boat waiting at the muddy stairs, heard the harsh command to row, and saw the dark, ominous vessel on the black water. I could not name my fear, but it was intense and vague. Walking to the hotel, I felt a dread far beyond the worry of being recognized, a sudden, shapeless return of childhood terror. The Blue Boar’s dining room was empty, and I was already eating before the waiter recognized me. After apologizing for his lapse in memory, he asked if he should fetch Mr. Pumblechook. I refused firmly. The waiter, who had served me during my apprenticeship, seemed surprised and quickly placed a stained local newspaper in front of me. I read a paragraph noting that the recent rise in fortune of a local blacksmith—a subject for the poet Tooby—was guided by a respected figure in the corn and seed trade located near the High Street. The article proudly claimed this man as the mentor to our young local success story.

She now wished the event had never occurred. Suspecting he had consumed too much of Mr. Weston’s wine, she anticipated foolish talk. To discourage him, she prepared to discuss the weather with composed gravity, but before she could begin, he seized her hand and began making passionate declarations. He spoke of his adoration, his fear of rejection, and his conviction that his intense devotion must surely be reciprocated, clearly intent on securing her immediate acceptance. Mr. Elton, Harriet’s supposed suitor, was now professing his love for her. Though she attempted to silence him, he persisted. Despite her anger, she resolved to remain restrained, attributing his behavior to intoxication. She responded with a blend of seriousness and levity, hoping to address his state: "I am astonished, Mr. Elton. You forget yourself; you mistake me for my friend. I shall gladly deliver any message to Miss Smith, but please, no more of this to me." He repeated her words with feigned bewilderment, prompting her to reply sharply, "This is extraordinary conduct. I can only assume you are not yourself, or you would not speak this way of Harriet or to me. Control yourself, and I will try to forget this." However, Mr. Elton was merely emboldened, not confused. He understood his own intentions perfectly. After dismissing her suspicions as insulting and briefly acknowledging his respect for Miss Smith—while expressing confusion as to why she was mentioned—he resumed his urgent pleas for a favorable response.

Well, Jupiter, what is the matter? How is your master? To tell the truth, sir, he is not as well as he could be. Not well? I am sorry to hear that. What is he complaining of? That is the problem. He never complains of anything, yet he is very sick. Very sick, Jupiter? Why didn't you say so? Is he in bed? No, he is not. That is exactly what worries me. I am very concerned about poor Master Will. Jupiter, I need to understand you. You say he is sick, but hasn't he told you what is wrong? Sir, don't get angry. Master Will says nothing is wrong, but he walks around with his head down, his shoulders hunched, and he is as pale as a ghost. He also keeps drawing symbols on a slate. He draws the strangest figures I have ever seen. I am getting scared. I have to watch him closely. The other day, he slipped away before sunrise and was gone all day. I had a big stick ready to give him a good beating when he returned, but I am such a fool that I didn't have the heart to do it. He looked so unwell. I think you should not be too harsh with him. Do not hit him, Jupiter; he cannot handle it. Do you have any idea what caused this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I last saw you? No, sir, nothing unpleasant has happened since then. I fear it happened before that, on the very day you were there. What do you mean? I mean the bug. The what? The bug. I am certain Master Will was bitten on the head by that gold bug. What makes you think that? It had plenty of claws and a mouth, sir. I have never seen such a bug. It kicked and bit everything near it. Master Will caught it first but had to let it go quickly. That must be when he was bitten. I didn't like the look of the bug's mouth, so I wouldn't touch it with my fingers. I caught it with a piece of paper instead.

During his brief visit, Emma had seen him rarely, yet enough to feel that their initial meeting was past and to conclude that his personality had not improved; he now carried an air of irritation and arrogance. She truly wondered how she had ever found him appealing. Seeing him was so linked to unpleasant memories that, unless viewed as a moral penance or a lesson in humility, she would have been relieved to never see him again. She wished him well, but his presence caused her distress, and she would be happiest knowing he was twenty miles away. His continued stay in Highbury would be easier to bear once he married. His wedding would resolve many awkward situations and allow their former intimacy to fade without comment, effectively resetting their social relationship. Emma gave little thought to the bride herself. She was likely suitable for Mr. Elton and Highbury, though she would probably look plain next to Harriet. Emma was unconcerned about the woman's social standing, convinced that despite Mr. Elton’s earlier disdain for Harriet, he had not married into a superior family. While her character remained a mystery, her background was clear: she brought no notable name or connections. Miss Hawkins was the daughter of a Bristol merchant, though his modest income suggested a similarly modest trade. She had spent winters in Bath, but her home was in Bristol, where she lived with an uncle who worked in the legal field—likely a low-level clerk. The family's only claim to prestige rested on an older sister who had married a man near Bristol wealthy enough to own two carriages. That was the extent of Miss Hawkins’s social glory.

Starve to death? Oh, Sir Simon, are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my bag. Would you like it? No, thank you, I do not eat anymore; but that is very kind of you. You are much nicer than the rest of your rude, vulgar, and dishonest family. Stop! Virginia cried, stamping her foot. You are the one who is rude and vulgar. As for dishonesty, you stole my paints to touch up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. You took all my reds, so I could not paint sunsets, then you took the green and yellow, leaving me only indigo and white for depressing moonlight scenes. I never told on you, even though I was annoyed. Besides, who has ever heard of emerald-green blood? Well, the ghost replied meekly, what was I to do? Real blood is hard to find, and since your brother started this with his detergent, I saw no reason not to use your paints. As for color, that is a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, but I know you Americans do not care for such things. You know nothing about it. You should move to America to improve your mind. My father would gladly pay for your passage. There is a tax on spirits, but the customs officers are Democrats, so there will be no trouble. You would be a huge success in New York. I know people who would pay a fortune to have a family ghost. I do not think I would like America. I suppose that is because we have no ruins or curiosities, Virginia said sarcastically. No ruins? No curiosities? the ghost replied. You have your navy and your manners. Good evening. I am going to ask my father to give the twins an extra week of holiday. Please do not go, Miss Virginia, he pleaded. I am so lonely and unhappy. I want to sleep, but I cannot. That is absurd. You just need to go to bed and blow out the candle.

Ten minutes later, the tea bell rang. When Virginia failed to appear, Mrs. Otis sent a servant to find her, but he returned saying she was nowhere to be found. Initially, Mrs. Otis was not worried, as Virginia often gathered flowers in the garden. However, by six o'clock, she grew truly anxious. She sent her sons to search while she and Mr. Otis checked every room. By half-past six, the boys returned empty-handed. In a panic, Mr. Otis remembered allowing a group of gypsies to camp in the park days earlier. He immediately set off for Blackfell Hollow with his eldest son and two farmhands. The young Duke of Cheshire begged to join them, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing a confrontation. Upon arrival, they found the camp abandoned; the fire still smoldered and plates remained on the grass, suggesting a hasty departure. After sending his son and the men to search the area, Mr. Otis rushed home to wire the local police about a kidnapped girl. He then ordered his horse, insisted his family eat dinner, and rode toward the Ascot Road with a groom. He had traveled only two miles when he heard hoofbeats. The young Duke was galloping after him on a pony, hatless and flushed. The boy gasped that he could not eat while Virginia was missing and pleaded to stay, suggesting that if they had been allowed to marry, this would not have happened. He refused to turn back. Mr. Otis, touched by the boy's devotion, smiled and agreed to let him join the search, provided they stopped in Ascot to find him a hat.

I want to see you settled in a good social position, so it is best to avoid unusual acquaintances. If you are still here when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with his sisters does not force you to know his wife, who will likely be an uneducated farmer’s daughter. Certainly. I do not think Mr. Martin would marry someone without an education, but I will not argue with you. I will not seek out his wife. I care for the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and would hate to lose them, as they are as well-educated as I am. But if he marries someone ignorant and vulgar, I will avoid her if I can. Emma watched her reaction and saw no signs of love. The young man had been interested first, but she hoped Harriet felt no deep attachment that would block her own plans. They met Mr. Martin the next day on the Donwell road. He was on foot and looked at Harriet with genuine joy. Emma walked ahead to observe him. He looked neat and sensible, but lacked any other distinction. She felt he would seem inferior when compared to true gentlemen. Harriet noticed his lack of polish, as she had previously admired her father’s refined manners. Mr. Martin seemed to have no manners at all. They spoke for only a few minutes so as not to delay Miss Woodhouse. Harriet returned with a smile and a flutter of excitement that Emma hoped to calm. Just think of meeting him! How strange! He said it was pure luck he did not take the other road. He did not think we walked this way, as he assumed we usually headed toward Randalls.

Is that all? That is not much. Many are in the Republic’s bad graces and must face the guillotine. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he? I am he. Naturally, as I am the last. Jarvis Lorry answers these questions while standing by the coach door, addressing a group of officials. They slowly inspect the carriage and its luggage, while local onlookers crowd around to stare. A mother holds her child’s arm out so the infant can touch the wife of an aristocrat destined for execution. Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, properly signed. May I leave, citizen? You may. Move on, postilions! Have a safe trip! I salute you, citizens. The first danger is behind us! Jarvis Lorry says this while clasping his hands and looking up. Inside the carriage, there is terror, weeping, and the heavy breathing of the unconscious passenger. Are we moving too slowly? Can they be made to go faster? Lucie asks, clinging to the old man. It would look like we are fleeing, my dear. I cannot push them too hard; it would raise suspicion. Look back and see if we are being followed! The road is clear, my dear. We are not being pursued yet. We pass scattered houses, farms, ruins, and leafless trees. The carriage rattles over hard, uneven pavement, flanked by deep mud. Sometimes we veer into the mud to avoid the jarring stones, or get stuck in ruts. Our impatience is agonizing; in our panic, we want to jump out and run, or hide, anything but stop. We pass more ruins, farms, and trees. Have they tricked us and brought us back the same way? Is this the same place? Thank God, no. A village. Look back to see if we are followed! Quiet! The posting-house. Our four horses are unhitched slowly. The coach sits in the street, motionless. New horses appear one by one, and new postilions follow, fiddling with their whips, while the old ones count their money, miscalculate, and grumble.

My companion carefully drove a stake into the earth exactly where the beetle had landed, then retrieved a tape measure from his coat. He secured one end to the tree trunk nearest the stake, extending the tape to the marker and continuing fifty feet further along the line formed by the tree and the first peg, while Jupiter hacked away the undergrowth with his scythe. A second stake was placed at this location, and a rough circle four feet wide was traced around it. Legrand handed us each a spade and insisted we begin excavating immediately. Honestly, I had little appetite for such labor, especially as evening approached and I was already exhausted, but I saw no way to refuse without upsetting my friend. I considered forcing the supposedly deranged man home, but I knew Jupiter would never help me oppose his master. I assumed Legrand had succumbed to local superstitions regarding buried treasure, likely fueled by the discovery of the beetle and Jupiter’s insistence that it was made of solid gold. Such notions easily sway a fragile mind, particularly when they align with existing obsessions, and I recalled his earlier claim that the insect would lead to his fortune. I felt frustrated but decided to comply, hoping that digging would quickly prove the folly of his beliefs. We lit our lanterns and began working with misplaced enthusiasm. As the light illuminated our group and tools, I reflected on how peculiar and suspicious our activities would seem to any unexpected witness. We labored diligently for two hours.

The studio smelled of roses, and as a summer breeze moved through the garden, the heavy scent of lilacs and the delicate fragrance of flowering thorn drifted through the open door. From his spot on the Persian divan, where he lay smoking his usual endless cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could see the honey-colored laburnum blossoms, their branches swaying under the weight of such vibrant beauty. Occasionally, the shadows of birds passed over the silk curtains covering the large window, creating a fleeting, artistic effect that reminded him of Japanese painters who capture motion through static art. The low hum of bees in the tall grass made the silence feel heavier, while the distant sound of London resembled the deep tone of an organ. In the center of the room, a full-length portrait of a remarkably handsome young man stood on an easel. Nearby sat the artist, Basil Hallward, whose mysterious disappearance years ago had once caused such public fascination. As Basil looked at the graceful figure he had captured, he smiled with satisfaction. Suddenly, he stood up and covered his eyes, as if trying to hold onto a dream he feared might vanish. It is your finest work, Basil, Lord Henry said lazily. You must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too crowded and common; I can never see the art for the people, or the people for the art. The Grosvenor is the only suitable choice. I do not think I will send it anywhere, Basil replied, tossing his head back in the peculiar way that used to amuse his friends at Oxford.

In English, the letter e appears most often, followed by a, o, i, d, h, n, r, s, t, u, y, c, f, g, l, m, w, b, k, p, q, x, and z. E is so dominant that it rarely fails to be the most common character in any lengthy sentence. This provides a solid foundation for analysis. While the frequency table is useful, we only need it partially here. Since 8 is the most frequent character, we will test it as e. To confirm, we check if 8 appears in pairs, as e frequently does in words like meet, fleet, or seen. In this short cipher, 8 is doubled five times. Assuming 8 is e, we look for the most common word, the, by searching for three-character sequences ending in 8. We find seven instances of ;48, suggesting ; is t, 4 is h, and 8 is e. This confirms our initial assumption. Having identified this word, we can determine the starts and ends of others. Looking at the penultimate ;48 sequence, we know the following ; starts a new word. With five of the six subsequent characters identified, we write t eeth. We can eliminate th as part of the first word, as no valid word fits the pattern. This leaves t ee, and testing the alphabet reveals tree as the only logical conclusion.

Mary never wrote to Bath herself; the burden of maintaining a sluggish and frustrating correspondence with Elizabeth fell entirely to Anne. Breakfast had barely concluded when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick arrived, as they had planned to take a final walk around Lyme. They were due to depart for Uppercross by one o'clock, intending to spend the interim outdoors together. Once they reached the street, Captain Benwick gravitated toward Anne. Their conversation the previous evening had encouraged him to seek her out again, and they walked for a while, debating the merits of Scott and Byron with the same inconclusive results as before, until the group shifted and Captain Harville took his place beside her. Miss Elliot, he said quietly, you have done a kindness by drawing that poor man out. I wish he had such company more often. It is unhealthy for him to remain so isolated, but we cannot leave him. No, Anne agreed, I can see that is impossible; but in time—we know what time does for grief, and you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend is still a recent mourner—only since last summer, I understand. True enough, he replied with a heavy sigh, only since June. And perhaps he did not learn of it until later. Not until the first week of August, when he returned from the Cape, having just been promoted on the Grappler. I was in Plymouth, dreading the news; he sent letters, but the Grappler was ordered to Portsmouth. The news had to reach him there, but who would break it? Not I. I would rather have been hanged. No one could do it but that good man, he said, gesturing toward Captain Wentworth. The Laconia had arrived in Plymouth the week before, safe from immediate deployment. Wentworth took the risk, requested leave, and without waiting for a reply, traveled day and night to Portsmouth. He rowed out to the Grappler immediately and stayed with him for a week. That is what he did; no one else could have saved poor James. You can imagine, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us. Anne considered this with absolute certainty and replied with as much warmth as her feelings allowed, or as he seemed able to bear, for he was too moved to continue the subject, and when he spoke again, it was of something entirely different.

Colonel Grangerford was a true gentleman, as was his entire family. He came from a distinguished background, a trait the Widow Douglas valued as highly in men as in horses, and even my father agreed, despite his own lack of refinement. The Colonel was tall and slender, with a pale, sallow complexion. He shaved his thin face daily, revealing sharp features: thin lips, narrow nostrils, a prominent nose, and heavy brows over deep-set, dark eyes that seemed to peer from caverns. His hair was straight, black, and shoulder-length. He wore pristine white linen daily, adding a blue tail-coat with brass buttons on Sundays, and carried a silver-headed mahogany cane. He was serious and soft-spoken, yet radiated a kindness that inspired immediate trust. While his rare smile was pleasant, his sudden, rigid anger was terrifying. He never needed to demand respect; his presence alone ensured good behavior. He brought a sense of warmth to any room, and his brief moments of displeasure were enough to keep everyone in line for days. When he and his wife entered the room each morning, the family stood until they were seated. Tom and Bob would prepare bitters for him, waiting to toast him with a formal, "Our duty to you, sir, and madam." The Colonel and his wife would acknowledge them with a slight bow, and after they drank, the sons would prepare a small mixture of water, sugar, and spirits for Buck and me to join in the toast.

Emma found no cause to revise her negative assessment of Mrs. Elton. Her initial judgment held firm; every subsequent encounter confirmed that the woman was arrogant, presumptuous, overly familiar, unrefined, and ignorant. Though possessing minor beauty and skills, Mrs. Elton lacked the sense to realize she was not the sophisticated social arbiter she imagined herself to be, nor was her previous status as Miss Hawkins as grand as she claimed. Mr. Elton appeared entirely aligned with his wife, seemingly proud to have introduced such a woman to Highbury, whom he clearly viewed as superior even to Miss Woodhouse. Most of the neighborhood, influenced by Miss Bates’s enthusiasm or a general tendency toward easy acceptance, praised the bride, while Emma maintained a polite, if hollow, facade by describing her as pleasant and well-dressed. Over time, Mrs. Elton’s attitude toward Emma soured, likely due to the lack of warmth her overtures received. This growing distance was welcome to Emma, though it only deepened her underlying resentment. Furthermore, the Eltons treated Harriet with blatant disdain and neglect. Emma hoped this would help Harriet move on, yet the malice behind their behavior lowered her opinion of them both. It was evident that Harriet’s past feelings had been shared as fodder for their private amusement, with Emma’s own role distorted to suit their narrative. Consequently, the couple made Emma a frequent target of their shared hostility, expressing their enmity through the mistreatment of her friend. Meanwhile, Mrs. Elton developed an immediate and intense fixation on Jane Fairfax. She was not content with mere admiration; she insisted on offering unsolicited patronage and support, a crusade she began detailing to Emma long before their own relationship had fully deteriorated.

It was early February, and after a month in Bath, Anne was anxious for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She had not heard from Mary in three weeks and wanted more detail. She knew Henrietta had returned home and Louisa was recovering in Lyme, but little else. One evening, she received a thick letter from Mary, accompanied by the compliments of Admiral and Mrs. Croft. The Crofts were in Bath, which immediately captured her interest. Sir Walter demanded to know why they had sent her a letter, and Anne explained it was from Uppercross. He remarked that he would have visited the Admiral regardless, as he knew his duties to a tenant. Anne ignored him, focused entirely on her letter, which began on February 1st. Mary wrote that she had not apologized for her silence, assuming Anne was too busy enjoying Bath to care about dull Uppercross. She complained about a boring Christmas, noting that the Musgroves had hosted no dinner parties. The holidays had finally ended, and the house was quiet, save for the Harville children, who had not yet gone home. Mary found this strange and disliked the children, noting that Mrs. Musgrove seemed to prefer them to her own grandchildren. She also complained about the terrible weather and the lack of visitors, save for Charles Hayter, whose frequent calls were unwelcome. She added that it was a shame Henrietta had not stayed in Lyme longer to avoid him.

We could certainly build a thrilling superstition around this. I suppose you will name the bug Scarabaeus caput hominis, or something similar—there are many such titles in natural history books. But where are the antennae you mentioned? The antennae! Legrand said, becoming strangely agitated. I am certain you must see them. I drew them as clearly as they appear on the actual insect, and I assume that is enough. Well, perhaps you did, I replied, but I still do not see them. I handed him the paper without further comment, not wanting to upset him. I was surprised by his reaction; his bad temper puzzled me. As for the drawing, there were definitely no antennae visible, and the whole thing looked remarkably like a standard illustration of a death’s-head moth. He took the paper peevishly and was about to crumple it to throw into the fire when a casual glance at the design suddenly caught his attention. His face turned bright red, then deathly pale. For several minutes, he scrutinized the drawing intently. Finally, he stood up, took a candle, and sat on a sea-chest in the corner to examine the paper again, turning it in every direction. He said nothing, which astonished me, but I thought it best not to provoke his moodiness. Eventually, he placed the paper in his wallet and locked it in his desk. He became calmer, but his earlier enthusiasm had vanished; he seemed less sulky than deeply distracted. As the evening progressed, he sank into a reverie I could not break. I had intended to stay the night, but seeing his state, I decided to leave. He did not ask me to stay, though he shook my hand with unusual warmth as I departed. About a month later, during which time I had not seen Legrand, his servant Jupiter visited me in Charleston. I had never seen the old man look so discouraged, and I feared some serious disaster had befallen my friend.

The insect’s heft was truly extraordinary, and I could scarcely fault Jupiter for his assessment; yet Legrand’s agreement with that view baffled me entirely. When I finished inspecting the beetle, he declared with grandiosity that he had summoned me to seek my advice and help in advancing the designs of Fate and the insect. I interrupted, insisting he was unwell and needed rest, suggesting I stay with him until he recovered from his apparent fever. He told me to check his pulse, which proved perfectly normal. Despite my insistence that he might be ill without fever and should retire, he maintained that his agitation was the only issue and that I could help by alleviating it. He explained that he and Jupiter were planning a trip into the mainland hills and required a trusted companion, insisting I was the only one. He claimed this would settle his nerves regardless of the outcome. When I asked if the beetle was linked to this excursion, he confirmed it was. I refused to participate in such a ridiculous endeavor, prompting him to say they would proceed alone. Concerned for his sanity, I asked how long they would be gone. He replied they would leave at once and return by sunrise. I made him promise that once this obsession was resolved, he would follow my medical advice. He agreed, and we departed. I joined him, Jupiter, and the dog with a heavy heart around four o’clock. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, seemingly more out of a desire to keep the tools away from his master than from any genuine industriousness.

These thoughts calmed me, and I fell into a deep sleep that afternoon, though my feverish blood denied me peaceful dreams. The horrors of the previous day played on a loop in my mind: the women fleeing and the enraged Felix dragging me from his father’s feet. I woke exhausted, and seeing it was night, I crept from my hiding place to find food. Once fed, I headed toward the familiar path to the cottage. Everything was quiet. I retreated to my hovel to wait for the family to rise. The hour passed and the sun climbed high, but they did not appear. I trembled, fearing some catastrophe. The cottage remained dark and silent; the agony of that suspense was indescribable. Soon, two countrymen stopped by the cottage and spoke with agitated gestures, but I could not understand their local dialect. Shortly after, Felix arrived with another man. I was surprised, as I knew he had not left earlier, and I listened intently to understand the situation. His companion asked, 'Do you realize you will owe three months' rent and lose your garden's harvest? I don't want to be unfair, so please take a few days to reconsider.' Felix replied, 'It is useless. We can never live here again. My father’s life is in grave danger because of what happened. My wife and sister will never recover from the shock. Please, do not argue. Take the property; I must leave.' Felix shook as he spoke. They entered the cottage for a few minutes, then left. I never saw the De Laceys again. I spent the rest of the day in my hovel, paralyzed by despair. My protectors were gone, severing the only link I had to the world. For the first time, hatred and a desire for revenge filled me. I made no effort to resist these feelings, letting them carry me toward thoughts of malice and destruction.

I passed several funerals, each with few mourners, viewed by onlookers as terrible omens. Some watched with intense curiosity, others fled in fear, and some wept openly. Adrian’s main goal, beyond helping the sick, was to hide the plague’s progress from Londoners. He knew fear and despair made people more vulnerable to infection. He kept shops open and maintained some activity to avoid a sense of panic. Still, to me, the city felt transformed. Carriages were gone, grass grew in the streets, houses looked abandoned, and people wore a haunted, frightened expression. My carriage drew attention as I traveled toward the Protectoral Palace, where the streets felt even more desolate. I found Adrian’s waiting room full. I watched the petitioners—mostly working-class people whose livelihoods had vanished with the collapse of trade. New arrivals looked anxious or terrified, while those leaving appeared calm and satisfied, a testament to Adrian’s influence. When the clock struck two, he stopped taking visitors. I then entered his office. I was struck by Adrian’s improved health. He no longer looked frail or exhausted; his eyes were bright, his expression composed, and he radiated a focused energy. He sat with secretaries organizing petitions. I admired his patience and fairness. He advised those who could afford to leave London to do so immediately, providing them with the necessary resources.

I bored a hole in the bottom of the keg and inserted a tapered wooden plug. After a few trials, I adjusted the plug so that water dripped into the pitcher below, filling it exactly in one hour. I determined this by checking how much water collected over a short period. My bed was positioned on the floor so my head rested directly beneath the pitcher. Once the pitcher filled, it would overflow from its spout, which sat lower than the rim. Falling from over four feet, the water would land on my face and wake me instantly, no matter how deeply I slept. By eleven o'clock, I finished these preparations and went to bed, confident in my device. It worked perfectly. Every hour, the water woke me, and I would empty the pitcher back into the keg before returning to sleep. These interruptions bothered me less than expected. When I finally woke for the day, it was seven o'clock, and the sun was high. On April 3rd, I found the balloon at a massive altitude, and the curve of the earth was clearly visible. Below, black specks in the ocean were surely islands. To the north, a thin, bright white line on the horizon appeared to be the ice of the Polar Sea. I was eager to travel further north, hoping to eventually fly directly over the Pole. However, I worried that my extreme height would prevent me from observing the area as clearly as I wanted.

The connection between body and soul remained a profound enigma. The soul possessed its own base instincts, just as the body experienced moments of spiritual elevation. Senses could be refined, while intellect might corrupt; the boundary between physical and psychical impulses remained impossible to define. The rigid classifications of psychologists seemed superficial, yet choosing between their conflicting theories was equally daunting. Whether the soul resided within a house of sin or the body existed within the soul, as Bruno suggested, the interplay between spirit and matter defied explanation. He pondered if psychology could ever become a precise science capable of uncovering every hidden motive. Currently, we remain strangers to ourselves and others. Experience holds no moral weight; it is simply a label for our past errors. While moralists claim experience shapes character by teaching us what to pursue or avoid, it lacks any true driving force. It merely proves that our future mirrors our past, and that sins once committed with disgust will eventually be repeated with pleasure. He concluded that the experimental method offered the only path to analyzing human passions, and Dorian Gray served as a perfect subject for such study. Dorian’s intense infatuation with Sibyl Vane was a fascinating psychological case. While curiosity and a thirst for novelty played a role, the emotion was far more intricate. The raw, youthful instincts had been reshaped by imagination into something Dorian perceived as transcendent, which only increased its peril. We are most enslaved by the passions we fail to understand, while our conscious motives remain our weakest. Often, in our attempts to experiment upon others, we are merely testing ourselves. As Lord Henry mused on these matters, his valet knocked to announce it was time to prepare for dinner.

He was dressed as Jonas the Graveless, the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn, a role that had famously sparked the Cantervilles' feud with Lord Rufford. It was past two in the morning, and the house seemed silent. As he headed toward the library to check for the bloodstain, two figures jumped from the shadows, waving their arms and screaming 'BOO!' in his ear. Terrified, he bolted for the stairs, only to find Washington Otis waiting with a garden syringe. Cornered, he dove into the unlit iron stove and escaped through the flues, reaching his room covered in soot and utterly defeated. He never attempted another midnight haunting. The twins tried to trap him, scattering nutshells in the halls, but he stayed hidden, his pride clearly wounded. Mr. Otis returned to his history of the Democratic Party, Mrs. Otis hosted a successful clam-bake, the boys played American games, and Virginia rode her pony with the visiting Duke of Cheshire. Everyone assumed the ghost had left, and Mr. Otis even wrote to Lord Canterville, who expressed his relief. The family was mistaken, however. The ghost remained, though weakened, and was eager to target the young Duke. His grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once bet he could play dice with the ghost, only to be found the next morning paralyzed and unable to speak anything but 'Double Sixes' for the rest of his life.

After I sent them in, I could not stay away, feeling they were less desperate when I was near. Driven by this restless anxiety, I wandered the evening streets, passing the offices where I had left the petitions. To this day, the cold, dusty streets of western London, with their stern, closed mansions and rows of lamps, remain melancholy to me because of those memories. My daily visits were now shortened, and he was more strictly guarded.
