Suspecting they thought I might bring him poison, I asked to be searched before sitting by his bed, telling the ever-present officer I would do anything to prove my intentions were pure. No one was cruel to us; they simply performed their duty. The officer and the other prisoners acting as nurses—criminals, yet capable of kindness—always told me he was worsening. As days passed, he lay staring at the ceiling, his face dull until my voice brightened it for a moment. When he could not speak, he squeezed my hand, and I learned to understand him. By the tenth day, I saw a significant change. His eyes lit up as I entered. "Dear boy," he said as I sat down, "I thought you were late, but I knew you couldn't be." "It is exactly the right time," I replied. "I waited at the gate." "You always wait at the gate, don't you?" "Yes, so I don't lose a moment." "Thank you, dear boy. God bless you! You never abandoned me." I squeezed his hand silently, haunted by the memory that I had once intended to desert him. "And the best part," he added, "is that you have been more comfortable with me since I have been under this dark cloud than when the sun was shining."

He had never oppressed or imprisoned anyone. Far from demanding his dues, he had voluntarily relinquished them, venturing into an indifferent world to secure his own livelihood. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the struggling estate under written orders to assist the tenants, providing them with whatever fuel and produce the creditors allowed. Gabelle had surely documented these efforts for his own protection, making them clear now. This supported the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would travel to Paris. Like the sailor in the legend, the currents had pulled him toward the Loadstone Rock, and he felt compelled to yield to its pull. Every thought pushed him closer to that fatal attraction. He had long been troubled that his homeland was being ruined by wicked men, and he felt guilty for not being there to advocate for mercy and prevent bloodshed. This internal conflict, combined with the contrast between his own inaction and the duty shown by others, was exacerbated by the stinging insults of Monseigneur and the coarse mockery of Stryver. Finally, Gabelle’s letter arrived—an innocent man’s plea for justice and honor. His choice was final; he had to go to Paris. The Loadstone Rock drew him onward toward an inevitable collision. He perceived little danger, believing his past intentions would be recognized and appreciated in France. He was captivated by the idealistic vision of tempering the violent Revolution, imagining he might exert some influence to guide its course.

He conveyed that Frank held her in high regard, finding her both beautiful and charming. Given his many positive qualities, she decided not to judge him too severely, echoing Mrs. Weston’s sentiment that young people are prone to occasional whims. However, not everyone in Surrey shared this leniency. While most residents of Donwell and Highbury were forgiving of a handsome young man with a pleasant smile and polite manners, Mr. Knightley remained unmoved. Upon hearing the news at Hartfield, he initially stayed quiet, only to mutter to himself while reading the paper, “Hum! Just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” Emma considered taking offense, but realizing he was merely venting his own thoughts rather than trying to provoke her, she chose to ignore it. Though the Westons brought mixed news, their visit proved timely, as Emma required their counsel on a matter, and their advice aligned perfectly with her own inclinations. The Coles, a friendly and unpretentious family of modest origins and trade backgrounds, had recently seen their fortunes rise significantly. With their newfound wealth, they expanded their home and lifestyle, now rivaling all but the most prominent families in the area. Their recent social gatherings for local bachelors signaled their intent to host larger dinner parties. Emma doubted they would dare invite the elite families of Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls, but she resolved that nothing would induce her to attend if they did, regretting only that her father’s predictable habits might obscure the significance of her refusal.

Lay down your weapons, brothers! Forgiveness, aid, and affection await your change of heart. You are precious to us, for you share our fragile human form; every one of you shall find a friend among these ranks. Why should man war against man, while the plague, our common enemy, looms above us, thriving on our slaughter, more merciless than the disease itself? Both armies hesitated. Our soldiers gripped their weapons tightly, eyeing the enemy with grim resolve. The opposing troops had not discarded their arms, driven more by fear than a desire to fight; they glanced at one another, seeking a lead that never came. Adrian dismounted and approached a fallen soldier. He was a man, he shouted, and now he is gone. Quickly, dress the wounds of the fallen; let no one perish. Do not let another soul depart through your cruel cuts to recount this fratricide before God. Bind their wounds and return them to their kin. Cast aside the savage hearts within you; discard those instruments of malice. In this moment of shared fate, let every man be a brother and protector to his neighbor. Abandon those bloodied weapons and hurry to tend these injuries. As he spoke, he knelt and lifted a man from whom life was rapidly draining. The poor soul gasped, and in the sudden silence of both armies, his moans were clearly audible. Every heart, recently set on total destruction, now beat with anxious hope for this single life. Adrian tore away his scarf to bind the wound, but it was futile. The man sighed deeply, his head slumped, and his body went limp. He is dead, Adrian declared, bowing his head in grief. The destiny of the world felt tied to this one death. On both sides, the soldiers dropped their weapons. Even the hardened veterans wept, and our men reached out to their former foes, a wave of profound affection washing over them. The two armies merged, unarmed and united, discussing only how to aid one another. Repenting for their past violence and cruelty, they followed the General’s command to march toward London.

Every normal boy eventually feels a strong urge to go dig for buried treasure. This desire suddenly struck Tom one day. He went to find Joe Harper but failed, and Ben Rogers was away fishing. Finally, he found Huck Finn, who was happy to join in. Huck was always ready for any adventure that was fun and cost nothing, as he had plenty of free time. Where should we dig, Huck asked. Oh, almost anywhere, Tom replied. Is it hidden everywhere, Huck wondered. No, Tom explained, it is hidden in specific spots like islands, under old dead trees where shadows fall at midnight, or under the floors of haunted houses. When Huck asked who hides it, Tom scoffed that it was obviously robbers, not Sunday-school leaders. Huck admitted he would rather spend the money than hide it, but Tom insisted robbers always leave it behind. They often forget where they put it or die, leaving the treasure to sit until someone finds a map covered in confusing symbols. When Huck asked if Tom had a map, Tom said no. He planned to search islands, haunted houses, and dead trees instead. When Huck pointed out that searching every tree would take all summer, Tom countered by asking how he would feel about finding a pot of gold or a chest of diamonds. Huck’s eyes lit up, and he agreed that finding even a hundred dollars would be wonderful.

Mr. Bennet stayed quiet during dinner, but once the servants left, he decided to engage his guest by mentioning how lucky he was to have such a patroness. Mr. Collins responded with great enthusiasm, praising Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s kindness and status. He spoke with solemn importance, claiming he had never seen such grace from someone of her rank. He noted that she had praised his sermons, invited him to dine at Rosings twice, and even included him in her card games. While some considered her proud, he insisted she was always friendly, treating him like any other gentleman. She encouraged him to marry wisely, allowed him to visit his relatives, and even visited his home to suggest improvements, such as adding shelves to his closets. Mrs. Bennet agreed that she sounded like a lovely woman and asked if she lived nearby. Mr. Collins explained that his home was just a lane away from her estate, Rosings Park. When Mrs. Bennet asked about her family, he mentioned she had one daughter who would inherit her vast fortune. Mrs. Bennet sighed, wondering if the girl was beautiful. Mr. Collins replied that she was charming, noting that Lady Catherine considered her superior to all other women because her features clearly displayed her noble birth.

She felt a sudden urge to check the front door to see if it was raining. Why question her own motives? Captain Wentworth had to be gone. She stood up, determined to go; she was tired of her mind constantly second-guessing itself. She would simply check the weather. However, she was immediately forced back by the arrival of Captain Wentworth himself, accompanied by a group of friends he must have met nearby. He seemed more visibly startled and flustered by her presence than she had ever seen him; his face flushed red. For the first time since they had reconnected, she felt she was handling the encounter with more composure than he was. She had the benefit of a few moments to prepare, and the initial, overwhelming shock had passed. Still, she felt a turbulent mix of agitation, pain, and pleasure. He spoke to her briefly before turning away, his manner clearly awkward. It was neither cold nor friendly; it was simply embarrassed. After a short while, he approached her again. They exchanged polite, meaningless pleasantries, though Anne noticed he was far less at ease than usual. While they had recently managed to speak with a veneer of indifference, he could not maintain it now. Whether due to time or Louisa, he was clearly unsettled. He looked healthy and spoke of the Musgroves and even Louisa with a fleeting hint of his old playfulness, yet he remained visibly uncomfortable and unable to hide it. It saddened, though did not surprise, Anne to see Elizabeth refuse to acknowledge him. She saw the mutual recognition between them and knew he was prepared to be greeted, yet she had to watch her sister turn away with icy indifference. Finally, the servant arrived to announce that Lady Dalrymple’s carriage had pulled up, much to Elizabeth’s relief.

He explained that his current location was a waste of time and that associates in London were urging his return to finalize their Indian business venture. Unable to postpone his departure any longer, and anticipating that his trip to London might soon lead to a much longer voyage, he begged me to spend as much time with him as possible. He asked me to abandon my isolated island and join him in Perth so we could travel south together. This request revived my spirits, and I resolved to leave the island in two days. Before leaving, however, I faced a daunting task: I had to pack my chemical equipment, which required entering the room where I had performed my repulsive work and touching the tools that now sickened me. At dawn the next day, I gathered my resolve and opened the laboratory. The remnants of the unfinished creature I had destroyed were strewn across the floor, and I felt as though I had mutilated a living person. After steadying myself, I entered the room. With shaking hands, I removed the instruments, realizing I could not leave the remains of my work to alarm the local villagers. I placed the scraps in a basket weighted with stones, intending to cast them into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the shore, cleaning and organizing my apparatus. My perspective had shifted entirely since the night the demon appeared. Previously, I had viewed my promise with hopeless despair, believing it had to be fulfilled regardless of the outcome. Now, it felt as if a veil had been lifted, allowing me to see clearly for the first time. The thought of resuming my work never crossed my mind; although the creature's threat weighed on me, I no longer believed my own actions could prevent it. I decided that creating another such monster would be an act of profound selfishness, and I dismissed any thought that might suggest otherwise.

I told him I needed the watermelon, but he argued that I did not need it to escape prison. He claimed it would only be acceptable if I were hiding a knife to help Jim kill the guard. I dropped the subject, though I found it annoying to debate such fine points whenever I just wanted a snack. That morning, we waited until the yard was empty. Tom took the sack into the shed while I kept watch. When he returned, we sat on the woodpile to talk. He said everything was ready except for the tools. I asked what tools he meant, and he explained we needed them to dig Jim out, since we could not just gnaw through the walls. I asked if the old, broken picks in the shed would work. Tom looked at me with pity and asked if I had ever heard of a prisoner using modern tools to escape. He argued that using shovels would ruin the heroics of the situation; they might as well just give him the key. He insisted we needed a couple of table knives instead. I told him it was foolish to try to dig out a cabin foundation with knives. Tom replied that it did not matter if it seemed foolish because it was the proper, traditional way. He claimed he had read all the books on the subject, and prisoners always used knives to dig through solid rock, a process that took weeks or even years. He asked me how long I thought a prisoner in the Castle of If had spent digging his way out. When I said I did not know, he told me to guess, and I suggested a month and a half.

I have not mentioned the most important point. What is that, Harry? asked the boy listlessly. The obvious comfort of taking someone else’s admirer when you lose your own. In high society, that always clears a woman’s reputation. But Dorian, Sibyl Vane was so different from the women we usually meet. There is something beautiful about her death. I am glad to live in an age where such wonders occur, as they make romance, passion, and love feel real. I was terribly cruel to her, you forget that. I suspect women appreciate cruelty above all else. They have primitive instincts; even though we have freed them, they remain slaves looking for masters. They love being dominated. I am sure you were magnificent. You told me something the other day that seemed fanciful then, but I now see it is the key to everything. What was that? You said Sibyl Vane represented all the heroines of romance to you—that she was Desdemona one night and Ophelia the next. She will never come to life again, the boy muttered, hiding his face in his hands. No, she has played her final part. Think of her lonely death in that cheap dressing room as a dark scene from a classic tragedy. She never truly lived, so she never truly died. To you, she was always a dream, a phantom that moved through Shakespeare’s plays. The moment she touched real life, she ruined it, and it ruined her. Mourn for Ophelia if you wish, or cry over Cordelia, but do not waste tears on Sibyl Vane. She was less real than they were. Silence filled the room as evening darkened. Shadows crept in from the garden, and the colors faded. After a while, Dorian Gray looked up.

I know she would! The Widow Douglas’ generous hospitality was a tempting offer. That, combined with Tom’s persuasion, won the argument. They decided to keep their plans for the night a secret. Tom then worried that Huck might show up tonight to give the signal, which dampened his excitement. Still, he could not bring himself to miss the fun at the Widow’s. He reasoned that since the signal had not come the night before, it was unlikely to happen tonight. The guaranteed fun outweighed the uncertain treasure, so he chose to follow his desire and stop thinking about the money. Three miles downstream, the ferry docked at a wooded hollow. The group swarmed ashore, their shouts and laughter echoing through the craggy hills. After exhausting themselves with games, they returned to camp with hearty appetites to feast. Following the meal, they rested and chatted under the oak trees until someone shouted, Who is ready for the cave? Everyone was. They grabbed bundles of candles and raced up the hill to the A-shaped entrance. The heavy oak door stood open. Inside, the chamber was as cold as an icehouse, with limestone walls slick with moisture. It felt romantic and mysterious to stand in the gloom looking out at the sunlit valley, but the novelty soon faded, and the play resumed. Whenever someone lit a candle, the others would rush them, leading to a struggle until the light was extinguished, followed by laughter and a new chase. Eventually, the group began filing down the main passage, their flickering lights revealing rock walls that rose sixty feet high. This main path was only eight to ten feet wide, with countless narrow, winding crevices branching off on either side, as McDougal’s cave was a vast, confusing labyrinth.

Stop the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the port! Come ahead on the starboard! Stop her! Let the outside turn over slowly! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Get that headline out! Lively now! Come on, get the spring-line out—what are you doing? Wrap the loop around that stump! Stand by the stage—let her go! Engines finished, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! Ssh! Ssh! Ssh! Tom kept whitewashing, ignoring the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment and said, Hey! You are in a tough spot, aren't you? Tom did not answer. He examined his last stroke with an artist's eye, brushed again, and inspected the result. Ben walked up beside him. Tom wanted the apple, but he kept working. Ben said, Hello, friend, you have to work, huh? Tom turned suddenly and said, Oh, it is you, Ben! I did not notice you. Say, I am going swimming. Do you not wish you could? But of course you would rather work, right? Naturally! Tom looked at the boy and asked, What do you call work? Why, is that not work? Tom resumed painting and replied casually, Well, maybe it is, and maybe it is not. All I know is that it suits Tom Sawyer. Oh come on, you do not mean to say you like it? The brush kept moving. Like it? Well, I do not see why I should not. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day? That changed things. Ben stopped eating his apple. Tom swept his brush back and forth, stepped back to check the effect, and added a few touches. Ben watched every move, becoming increasingly absorbed. Finally, he said, Say, Tom, let me whitewash a little. Tom considered it, then changed his mind. No, I do not think that would work, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence, since it faces the street. If it were the back fence, I would not mind, and neither would she. She is very strict about this one; it has to be done carefully. I doubt one boy in a thousand, maybe two thousand, can do it the right way. Is that so? Oh, come on, let me try. Just a little. I would let you if you were me, Tom. Ben, I would like to, honestly, but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she would not let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she would not let him either.

The line of gas lamps curved into the distance, and a lone hansom cab waited outside a small walled house with its driver asleep inside. He walked quickly toward Portland Place, glancing back occasionally as if afraid of being followed. At the corner of Rich Street, two men were reading a notice on a wooden fence. Driven by curiosity, he crossed the street. As he approached, the word 'Murder' in bold black letters caught his eye. He jumped, his face flushing. It was a reward notice for a man of medium height, aged thirty to forty, wearing a bowler hat, black coat, and plaid trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. He read it repeatedly, wondering if the man would be caught and how he had earned his scar. He feared that one day his own name might be posted on London walls, with a price on his head. The thought sickened him, and he hurried away into the night. He wandered aimlessly through a maze of grim streets, eventually reaching Piccadilly Circus at dawn. Walking toward Belgrave Square, he passed wagons heading to Covent Garden. The sunburnt carters in white smocks strode along, cracking whips and calling to one another. A chubby boy sat on a large grey horse, laughing while holding the mane, a bunch of primroses tucked into his hat. The piles of vegetables looked like jade against the pink morning sky. Lord Arthur felt strangely moved. The delicate beauty of the dawn seemed deeply sad, reminding him that days often begin in beauty and end in storms. He wondered what these simple, good-humored workers thought of the city. To them, London appeared as a pale, ghostly place, free from the night's sins and the day's smoke. He pondered whether they understood the city's hidden splendor and shame, its intense joys, its desperate hunger, and all it creates or destroys from morning until night.

Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to relieve you. But what scared you? What were you expecting us to find? Huck was in a tight spot. The man’s searching gaze was fixed on him, and he desperately needed a believable answer. Nothing came to mind, and as the man’s eyes bored into him, he blurted out a foolish reply: Sunday-school books, maybe. Huck was too anxious to smile, but the old man laughed heartily, shaking with mirth. He remarked that such a laugh was good for one’s health, then added, Poor boy, you look pale and exhausted. You aren’t well, which explains why you seem a bit rattled. Rest and sleep will set you right. Huck felt annoyed at himself for acting so suspicious. He had stopped believing the package from the tavern was the treasure after hearing the conversation at the widow’s gate, but he hadn't been certain. Now, he was relieved to know for sure that the bundle was not the treasure. Everything seemed to be falling into place; the gold must still be in room number two, the men would be arrested, and he and Tom could claim the loot that night without fear. Just as breakfast ended, a knock came at the door. Huck scrambled to hide, wanting no part in the recent events. The Welshman let in several guests, including the Widow Douglas, and saw crowds of people climbing the hill to look at the scene. The news had spread. The Welshman recounted the night’s events to the visitors. The widow expressed her deep gratitude for being saved. Don’t mention it, madam, the man replied. There is someone else you owe more to than me and my boys, but he won’t let me reveal his name. We wouldn’t have been there if not for him.

Meanwhile, gravitational force would steadily decrease following the inverse square law, causing my velocity to increase rapidly until I reached the regions where lunar attraction overcomes the earth's pull. Consequently, I deemed it unnecessary to carry more than forty days of provisions. Another concern troubled me slightly. It is well known that during high-altitude balloon flights, travelers suffer from respiratory distress, bodily discomfort, and nosebleeds, which worsen as they ascend. This was a daunting thought. Could these symptoms prove fatal? I ultimately concluded they would not. Their cause lies in the diminishing atmospheric pressure on the body, which distends superficial blood vessels, rather than any fundamental biological failure. Provided the blood is properly oxygenated, I saw no reason why life could not persist in a vacuum, as breathing is merely a muscular action. I believed that as my body adjusted to the lack of pressure, the pain would subside, and I trusted my robust constitution to endure the initial discomfort. Thus, your Excellencies, I have outlined some of the reasoning behind my lunar voyage. I shall now describe the outcome of this bold and unprecedented endeavor. Upon reaching an altitude of three and three-quarters miles, I released some feathers and observed that I continued to rise quickly, making it unnecessary to discard any ballast. I was pleased, as I intended to keep as much weight as possible for reasons I will explain later.

In reality, as you climb to higher altitudes, the amount of air you pass through does not decrease in direct proportion to the height gained; instead, the density drops at a constantly shrinking rate. It is clear that no matter how high we travel, we can never reach a point where the atmosphere ends entirely. I argued that it must continue to exist, even if it becomes infinitely thin. I knew that many people have argued for a definite limit to the atmosphere, beyond which there is no air at all. However, those who support this view have overlooked a detail that deserves serious study. When comparing the intervals between Encke’s comet returning to its closest point to the sun, and accounting for all gravitational pull from the planets, the orbital periods are clearly shrinking. The comet’s path is slowly but steadily shortening. This is exactly what would happen if the comet were meeting resistance from a very thin, invisible medium filling space. Such a medium would slow the comet down, weakening its outward force and allowing the sun’s gravity to pull it closer with every orbit. There is no other way to explain this change. Furthermore, the comet’s size shrinks rapidly as it nears the sun and expands as it moves away. Was I not right to assume, like M. Valz, that this change is caused by the compression of that same thin medium, which grows denser near the sun? The zodiacal light, a glowing phenomenon visible in the tropics, also caught my attention. It stretches upward from the horizon and follows the sun’s equator. It seemed to me to be a thin atmosphere extending from the sun, reaching at least past the orbit of Venus, and likely much further. I could not believe this medium was limited only to the comet’s path or the area immediately surrounding the sun.

He mounted the spirited horse that had carried him to victory in Greece, exhausting himself with intense exercise to drown his mental anguish in physical exertion. He slowly recovered, finally emerging from the haze of fever and passion like one recovering from poison, ready for calm reflection. He considered his next steps, struck by how long he had let madness dictate his actions. A month had passed since he last saw Evadne, and her influence over him had faded; he was no longer her slave or her lover. He resolved never to see her again, hoping to earn Perdita’s trust through his complete return. Yet, he could not help but picture the Greek girl’s miserable home, which she had refused to trade for luxury out of principle. He recalled her former splendor in Constantinople and contrasted it with her current poverty, her daily toil, and her gaunt, starving face. Compassion filled him; he decided to visit her one last time to arrange for her restoration to society before ending their connection permanently. He then reflected on how he had avoided Perdita for a month, fleeing from his own guilt. He felt cheerful as he resolved to fix this, planning to erase this lapse with future devotion. He remembered his promise to attend a festival that evening, October 19th, celebrating his election as Protector. He viewed it as a positive omen. He would briefly visit Evadne to explain his long absence, then return to Perdita, his public duties, and his position of power. Following the events described, Perdita had anticipated a total shift in Raymond’s behavior, hoping for open communication and a return to the affectionate intimacy that had once defined their life.

Yet, no joy existed in the small town that peaceful Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s household were draped in mourning, filled with profound sorrow and weeping. An uncommon stillness hung over the village, which was typically quiet enough as it was. The residents went about their business distractedly, speaking little but sighing frequently. The Saturday break felt like a weight to the children, who lost interest in their games and eventually abandoned them. In the afternoon, Becky Thatcher wandered the empty schoolyard, feeling deeply despondent. Finding no solace, she mused aloud, wishing she still possessed the brass andiron knob to remember him by, stifling a sob. She paused, reflecting on the past, and lamented that she would never see him again, which caused her to break down in tears. Soon, a group of Tom and Joe’s playmates gathered by the fence, speaking in hushed, reverent tones about the last things the boys had said or done, which now seemed prophetic. Each child pointed out where they had stood, recalling small gestures and the strange feelings they had experienced at the time. A debate arose over who had last seen the boys alive, with many claiming the grim honor and offering embellished proof. Once the final witnesses were identified, they assumed a solemn importance, envied by the others. One boy, lacking any other claim to fame, proudly noted that Tom Sawyer had once beaten him up, but this failed to impress, as most of the others could say the same. The group drifted away, continuing to share memories of the lost boys in hushed voices.

Ten minutes later, the tea bell rang. When Virginia failed to appear, Mrs. Otis sent a footman to find her, but he returned reporting she was nowhere to be found. Initially unconcerned, Mrs. Otis grew anxious by six o'clock. She sent her sons to search while she and Mr. Otis checked every room. By half-past six, the boys returned empty-handed. In a panic, Mr. Otis recalled granting a group of travelers permission to camp in the park days earlier. He immediately set out for Blackfell Hollow with his eldest son and two farmhands. The young Duke of Cheshire begged to join them, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing a confrontation. Upon arrival, they found the camp abandoned in haste, with the fire still smoldering and dishes left behind. After sending his son and the men to search the area, Mr. Otis returned home to wire police inspectors across the county regarding a suspected kidnapping. He then ordered his horse and, after insisting his family eat dinner, rode toward the Ascot Road with a groom. Two miles out, he heard galloping behind him and saw the Duke on his pony, hatless and flushed. The boy gasped that he could not eat while Virginia was missing and pleaded not to be sent back, suggesting their engagement would have prevented this crisis. Touched by the young man's devotion, Mr. Otis smiled, patted his shoulder, and agreed to let him join the search, provided they stopped in Ascot for a hat.

He shivered and returned, shutting the window. At the door, he turned the key and opened it, avoiding any look at the corpse. He felt the key to his survival was to ignore the reality of the situation. The friend who had painted the portrait that caused his misery was gone; that was enough. He then remembered the Moorish lamp, made of silver and steel with turquoise inlays. Fearing his servant might notice it missing, he hesitated, then returned to retrieve it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the body, which lay still with horribly white hands, resembling a grotesque wax figure. After locking the door, he crept downstairs. The floorboards creaked, sounding like cries of pain, but he paused and realized it was only his own footsteps. In the library, he found the bag and coat. He hid them in a secret wall compartment where he kept his disguises, planning to burn them later. Checking his watch, he saw it was twenty minutes to two. He sat to reflect. Men were often executed for such crimes, but what evidence existed against him? Basil Hallward had left at eleven, and no one had seen him return. Most servants were away, and his valet was asleep. Basil had intended to take the midnight train to Paris; his reserved nature meant it would be months before anyone grew suspicious. By then, all evidence would be gone. A sudden idea occurred to him. He put on his coat and hat and went to the hall. Hearing a policeman’s heavy footsteps and seeing a flashlight beam on the window, he held his breath. Moments later, he slipped out, closed the door quietly, and began ringing the bell.

Emma felt great satisfaction reflecting on her conversation with Mr. Knightley while walking on the lawn the next morning. She was pleased they agreed about the Eltons and felt gratified by his kind words regarding Harriet. The Eltons' rudeness, which had briefly threatened to spoil the ball, had ultimately led to a positive outcome: the end of Harriet’s crush on Mr. Elton. Based on Harriet’s comments, Emma believed her friend finally saw Mr. Elton for who he truly was. With Harriet acting rationally, Frank Churchill not overly infatuated, and Mr. Knightley on good terms with her, Emma anticipated a wonderful summer. She did not mind that Frank Churchill would not be visiting Hartfield that morning. Just as she prepared to return inside to attend to her young nephews and their grandfather, the gate opened. To her shock, Frank Churchill entered with Harriet leaning on his arm. Harriet looked pale and terrified, and Frank was attempting to comfort her. They quickly reached the house, where Harriet immediately fainted. After a few minutes of urgent care, Emma learned what had occurred. Harriet and a friend, Miss Bickerton, had gone for a walk on the Richmond road. While the path seemed safe, it eventually led them into a secluded, tree-lined area where they suddenly encountered a group of gypsies.

While occupied with my studies and Mr. Pocket, I received a letter that immediately agitated me. Although I had never seen the handwriting, I instinctively recognized the sender. It lacked a formal salutation and simply stated: I am arriving in London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I understand you are to meet me? Miss Havisham believes so, and I write accordingly. She sends her regards. Yours, Estella. Had time permitted, I would have purchased new attire, but I had to settle for what I owned. My appetite disappeared, and I found no tranquility until the day arrived. Even then, I was more restless than before, pacing the coach-office in Wood Street long before the coach could have departed from our town. Despite knowing the futility of my actions, I felt compelled to keep the office in view. I had been waiting for half an hour when Wemmick approached me. Hello, Mr. Pip, he remarked. How are you? I would not have expected to find you here. I explained I was meeting a passenger, then asked after his home and his father. Both are doing well, especially the Aged, who is in excellent spirits and turning eighty-two soon, Wemmick replied. I am considering firing my cannon eighty-two times, provided the neighbors do not object and the weapon holds up. But this is not business. Can you guess my destination? To the office? I asked. Nearly, he said. I am heading to Newgate. We are handling a case involving a banker's parcel, and after inspecting the scene, I must consult our client. Did he commit the robbery? I inquired. Good heavens, no, Wemmick answered dryly. But he is accused of it. Just as you or I might be.

Summer arrived, and under the sun’s intense heat, the plague unleashed its lethal reach across the world. Nations succumbed and perished. Abundant crops rotted in the fields, while the desperate parent, seeking food for their children, collapsed dead in the furrows. Majestic forests swayed above the dying, whose cries disrupted the peaceful woods. Birds flew and deer rested undisturbed, while livestock wandered from abandoned stables to graze in the wheat; death claimed only humanity. As summer deepened, so did our terror. My beloved Idris and I looked at each other and our children. I promised, “We will save them, Idris. Years from now, we will tell them of these fears, long since passed. Even if they are the only ones left, they will survive, their health and spirits intact.” Our eldest son sensed the surrounding tragedy and occasionally asked about the widespread ruin, yet his youthful joy soon eclipsed his worries. Evelyn, a cheerful, playful toddler, filled our halls with laughter, his innocence untouched by sorrow. Clara, our gentle, lovely daughter, was our comfort. She dedicated herself to nursing the sick, aiding the elderly, and cheering the young. She moved through our home like a celestial spirit, brightening our darkest moments. Though she was modest and playful, we marveled at the heroism and wisdom hidden within her grace. The summer dragged on, as we prayed winter would at least slow the disease. We dared not hope it would vanish entirely; to speak such a thought aloud was to invite a flood of tears, revealing how profound our fear had become and how fragile our hope remained.

These events deeply troubled Felix, making him the most unhappy of his family when I first met him. He could have handled poverty with pride, but the Turk’s betrayal and the loss of his beloved Safie were far more painful. Safie’s arrival, however, gave him new hope. When news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and status, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return home. Safie was outraged and tried to argue, but her father angrily repeated his demand. A few days later, the Turk told her he feared his location had been discovered and he would soon be turned over to the French government. He had hired a ship to Constantinople and planned to leave within hours, intending to have his daughter follow later with his remaining property. Alone, Safie decided what to do. She hated the idea of living in Turkey, as it went against her religion and personal beliefs. After finding her father’s papers, she learned where her lover was exiled. She eventually decided to leave. Taking her jewels and some money, she traveled to Germany with a servant from Leghorn who spoke Turkish. They reached a town near the De Lacey cottage, but the servant fell dangerously ill and died. Safie was left alone in a foreign land, unable to speak the language. Fortunately, she was helped by the woman at their boarding house, who ensured she safely reached her lover’s cottage.

Weeks passed, and I became increasingly obsessed with you. I had depicted you as Paris in delicate armor and as Adonis with a huntsman’s cloak. You sat on Adrian’s barge crowned with lotus blossoms, staring across the Nile, or leaned over a Greek woodland pool to admire your own reflection. It was all as art should be—idealized and distant. Then, on a day I now consider fateful, I decided to paint you as you truly are, in your own clothes and era. Whether it was the realism or the sheer intensity of your personality laid bare, I cannot say. But as I worked, every brushstroke seemed to expose my secret. I feared others would discover my devotion, feeling I had poured too much of myself into the canvas. I resolved never to exhibit it. You were annoyed, but you didn't understand what it meant to me. Harry laughed, but I didn't care. Once finished, I felt justified in my decision. Yet, once the painting left my studio and its overwhelming presence faded, I felt foolish for imagining it held anything beyond your beauty and my technical skill. I still believe the passion felt during creation isn't truly visible in the final work. Art is more abstract than we assume; form and color only speak of themselves. It often seems art hides the artist more than it reveals. When I received the offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the centerpiece of the exhibition, never dreaming you would refuse. I see now that you were right. The painting cannot be shown. Please don't be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have confessed.

He was a poet who published his first work at twenty-three, earning immediate and universal acclaim. His success was unprecedented, celebrated by both the public and the intellectual elite without a single critic. During this peak of fame, he met Elinor, a beautiful young heiress living with her guardian. They seemed perfectly matched. While Elinor lacked his poetic genius, she was noble, generous, and possessed a natural wisdom reflected in her deep blue eyes. They fell in love instantly, finding pure joy in their connection. Woodville, the son of a poor clergyman, was a celebrated figure, while Elinor was wealthy. Her guardian approved of their relationship, recognizing Woodville’s immense talent, but her father’s will prohibited her from marrying until she came of age. Though they had to wait until she turned twenty-one, they spent their time together in blissful anticipation, studying and planning their future. Woodville’s reputation continued to grow, and Elinor flourished under his guidance. With only two months left until her birthday, everything was ready for their wedding. Yet, such perfect happiness is rarely permitted in this world of sorrow. To allow a couple as ideal as they were to find complete fulfillment would have required a fundamental change in the nature of human existence.

Only after some time did I regain my composure enough to manage the balloon. Upon inspection, I was relieved to find it undamaged. My tools remained secure, and I had lost neither provisions nor ballast, as I had fastened them too firmly for such a mishap. Checking my watch, I noted it was six o’clock. I continued to climb, with my barometer indicating an altitude of three and three-quarter miles. Below, a small, dark, oblong object floated on the ocean, resembling a domino. Through my telescope, I identified it as a British ninety-four-gun vessel, sailing close-hauled and tossing in the waves, headed west-southwest. Beyond this ship, only the sea, the sky, and the risen sun were visible. It is time to clarify the purpose of my dangerous journey. You must understand that financial ruin in Rotterdam had driven me to contemplate suicide. I did not loathe life itself, but I was exhausted by the hardships of my condition. Seeking to live yet weary of existence, I found inspiration in a bookstall treatise. I decided to depart the world while remaining alive—in short, I resolved to attempt a voyage to the moon. To avoid appearing entirely insane, I will explain why I believed this difficult and perilous feat was possible for a bold spirit. First, I considered the moon’s distance. The average interval between the centers of the two bodies is about 237,000 miles. However, because the moon’s orbit is an ellipse with an eccentricity of 0.05484, if I could intercept the moon at its perigee, that distance would be significantly reduced.

They brought in a distinguished-looking older gentleman and a younger man with his arm in a sling. The crowd cheered and mocked them, but I saw no humor in it, and I doubted the duke and the king would either. I expected them to turn pale, but they didn't. The duke acted oblivious, looking as content as a jug pouring buttermilk, while the king gazed sorrowfully at the newcomers, as if the existence of such frauds pained him deeply. He played the part perfectly. Local leaders gathered around the king to show their support. The older man looked completely bewildered. Soon, he began to speak, and I immediately noticed he sounded like a genuine Englishman, unlike the king's decent imitation. He addressed the crowd: This is an unexpected surprise, and I admit I am ill-prepared to respond. My brother and I have faced misfortune; he has a broken arm, and our luggage was mistakenly left at a town upriver last night. I am Harvey Wilks, brother of Peter, and this is his brother William, who is deaf and mute and cannot easily communicate with only one hand. We are who we claim to be, and I will prove it once our luggage arrives. Until then, we will wait at the hotel. As he and his brother left, the king laughed and scoffed, calling the broken arm and lost luggage convenient excuses for a fraud who had not learned to sign. The crowd laughed along, except for a few, including the doctor, a sharp-looking lawyer named Levi Bell who had just arrived from Louisville, and a large, rugged man who had been listening intently to both sides.

If you want one for personal use, I can provide an excellent model and guarantee your satisfaction. May I ask who it is for? If it is for the police or anyone at Scotland Yard, I cannot help. English detectives are our best allies; their incompetence allows us to act freely, and I would hate to lose them. Lord Arthur replied that it had nothing to do with the police, as the clock was intended for the Dean of Chichester. Herr Winckelkopf remarked that he was surprised by Lord Arthur's religious devotion, which was rare for a young man. Lord Arthur blushed and admitted he knew nothing of theology. When the man asked if it was a private matter, Lord Arthur confirmed it was. Winckelkopf left and returned with a small cake of dynamite and a French clock topped with an ormolu figure of Liberty. Tom managed to scratch the cupboard with his tool and was planning to work on the bureau when he was called to get ready for Sunday school. Mary gave him a basin of water and soap. He set the basin on a bench outside, dipped the soap, poured the water out, and went inside to wipe his face on the towel. Mary took the towel away and scolded him for not actually washing. Tom felt embarrassed. He tried again, taking a deep breath and scrubbing his face. When he came back inside, he was dripping with soapy water, but his face was only clean up to his chin. Below that line, his skin remained dirty. Mary stepped in and scrubbed him until he was clean, then brushed his wet hair into neat curls. Tom secretly flattened the curls later, as he thought they looked girlish. Mary then brought out his Sunday clothes, which were the only other outfit he owned. She helped him dress, buttoning his jacket, adjusting his large collar, and putting on his straw hat. He looked much better but felt very stiff and miserable in his clean, restrictive clothes. He hoped she would forget his shoes, but she polished them with tallow and brought them out. Frustrated, Tom complained that he was always forced to do things he disliked.

It was Lady Windermere’s final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was packed. Six Cabinet Ministers arrived from the Speaker’s Levée in their formal regalia, while the most fashionable women wore their finest attire. At the end of the gallery, Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a stout woman with small black eyes and stunning emeralds, spoke loud, broken French and laughed boisterously. It was a remarkable mix of guests. Wealthy peeresses spoke to radical politicians, popular preachers mingled with famous skeptics, bishops trailed a prima donna, and artists stood on the staircase. It was one of Lady Windermere’s most successful evenings, and the Princess remained until nearly eleven-thirty. Once she left, Lady Windermere returned to the gallery, where a political economist lectured a frustrated Hungarian musician on the science of music, and she began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. Lady Windermere looked stunning, with her ivory throat, blue eyes, and heavy coils of golden hair. Her hair was a rich, deep gold—not the pale straw shade often called gold today, but a color like sunbeams or amber. It gave her the appearance of a saint, yet with the allure of a sinner. She was a fascinating study. Early on, she realized that nothing mimics innocence quite like an indiscretion, and through various reckless, mostly harmless escapades, she had earned the freedom of a unique reputation. She had married three times, but because she kept the same lover, society had stopped gossiping about her. Now forty and childless, she possessed the insatiable hunger for pleasure that keeps one young. Suddenly, she scanned the room and asked in a clear voice, “Where is my palm reader?” “Your what, Gladys?” the Duchess asked, startled. “My palm reader, Duchess; I cannot live without him right now.” “Dear Gladys, you are always so original,” the Duchess murmured, hoping a palm reader was not the same thing as a foot doctor. “He examines my hand twice a week,” Lady Windermere continued, “and he is absolutely fascinating.”

He was a man of slight stature yet stood remarkably straight, possessing the most melodic voice I had ever encountered. He opened his lecture by summarizing the history of chemistry and the advancements of various scholars, speaking the names of these notable pioneers with great passion. He then provided a brief overview of the field's current state and clarified several fundamental concepts. Following a few introductory demonstrations, he ended with a tribute to modern chemistry, the substance of which remains etched in my memory: The early practitioners of this discipline promised the impossible and achieved nothing. Modern experts promise little; they recognize that metal transmutation is impossible and the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these thinkers, whose hands appear suited only for filth and whose eyes are fixed upon microscopes or crucibles, have truly performed wonders. They delve into nature's secrets, revealing her hidden operations. They reach toward the heavens, having mapped the circulation of blood and the composition of the air. They have gained vast, nearly boundless capabilities; they can summon lightning, replicate earthquakes, and even imitate the unseen world with its own reflections. These were the professor's words—or rather, the words of fate—spoken to seal my doom. As he spoke, I felt as though my spirit were wrestling with a tangible foe; the various components of my character were being stirred one by one. My mind became consumed by a single, driving ambition. So much has been accomplished, the soul of Frankenstein cried out, yet I shall achieve far more. Following the established path, I will forge a new trail, investigate hidden forces, and reveal the profound mysteries of existence to the world. I did not sleep that night. My inner self was in a state of chaotic upheaval, and though I sensed that order might eventually emerge, I lacked the strength to bring it forth. Eventually, as dawn broke, slumber arrived. Upon waking, my thoughts from the previous night seemed like a dream. Only a firm resolve remained to return to my former studies and dedicate myself to a science for which I felt a natural aptitude. That same day, I visited M. Waldman. His private demeanor was even gentler and more engaging than his public persona, as the formal dignity he displayed during his lecture was replaced at home by immense warmth and kindness.

The charming lie seemed beautifully told to me, though I had only heard it once; it was surely more enjoyable when it was new. Sir Dinadan the Humorist woke first and stirred the others with a crude prank. He tied metal mugs to a dog's tail, sending the panicked animal racing through the room while other dogs chased it, creating a chaotic, deafening mess. The crowd laughed until they cried, some even rolling on the floor in delight. They acted just like children. Sir Dinadan was so proud that he repeated the story endlessly, laughing long after everyone else had stopped. He then decided to give a humorous speech, but it was just a collection of tired, ancient jokes. He was worse than any circus clown. It was depressing to sit there, thirteen hundred years before my own time, hearing the same stale jokes that had annoyed me as a boy in the future. It convinced me that no truly new joke exists. Everyone laughed at these antiques, as people always do. However, the boy did not laugh; he mocked everything. He claimed most of Dinadan's jokes were rotten and the rest were petrified. I agreed, noting that those jokes belonged in geologic periods. That comment went over the boy's head since geology had not been invented yet, but I made a note of it, planning to educate the public later. There is no point in wasting a good idea just because the time is not right. Then, Sir Kay stood up and began to mock me to entertain the crowd.

I recited the beautiful verses describing Dante’s arrival in the terrestrial Paradise, imagining how delightful it would be to walk those shores and witness the radiant chariot bringing my long-lost father back to me. I envisioned weaving a garland from the local blossoms to crown myself in celebration. I would sing my father’s preferred melody, sul margine d’un rio, letting my voice carry through the still air to signal my arrival at his resting place. The sorrow would vanish from my face, and I would gaze into his eyes, which always shone with pure, tender affection. Recalling that magical expression brought me to gentle tears, which I suppressed to keep from breaking the spell. I was so absorbed in this fantasy that I continued walking, only realizing I was on a barren, flowerless plain when I bent down to pick a bloom. The realization snapped me out of my reverie, leaving me disoriented. The sun had vanished, and the pink glow of twilight was fading. A breeze stirred, and I found myself in an unfamiliar landscape, unable to retrace my steps. As darkness deepened, every landmark disappeared. Eventually, night swallowed everything. Exhausted and knowing my servant was staying in a nearby village, I decided to remain where I was, feeling secure in the wilderness. My two years of solitary wandering had hardened me against the cold. I lay on the grass in absolute darkness. The night was perfectly still, with no insects or creatures to break the silence. This profound quiet calmed my body while stirring my spirit, allowing my mind to race through endless thoughts and visions.

Mr. Wickham felt entirely content with their discussion, ensuring he never again troubled himself or irritated his dear sister-in-law Elizabeth by revisiting the topic; she was relieved to see her words had successfully silenced him. When the time arrived for him and Lydia to depart, Mrs. Bennet had to accept the separation, which was expected to last at least a year since her husband refused to support her plan for the whole family to relocate to Newcastle. Oh, my dear Lydia, she lamented, when will we see each other again? Goodness, I have no idea. Perhaps not for two or three years, Lydia replied. Write to me frequently, my dear. I will write when I can, but you know married women have little time for correspondence. My sisters can write to me; they will have nothing else to occupy them. Mr. Wickham offered much warmer farewells than his wife, smiling handsomely while uttering many charming pleasantries. He is as fine a fellow as I have ever encountered, Mr. Bennet remarked once they had left, simpering and flirting with us all. I am immensely proud of him; I challenge even Sir William Lucas to present a more impressive son-in-law. Mrs. Bennet remained quite melancholy for several days following her daughter's departure. I often think there is nothing worse than parting with friends, she remarked, as one feels so abandoned without them. This is the result of marrying off a daughter, Elizabeth noted, which should make you more content that your other four remain single. That is not the case at all, Mrs. Bennet insisted. Lydia is not leaving because she is married, but because her husband's regiment is stationed so far away. Had it been closer, she would not have departed so soon. However, her despondency was soon lifted, and her spirits revived by news that began to circulate. The Netherfield housekeeper had been instructed to prepare for her master, who was arriving within a few days to shoot for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet became quite restless, alternating between smiling at Jane and shaking her head. Well, so Mr. Bingley is returning, she said to Mrs. Philips, who had delivered the news. That is all for the best. Not that I care, of course; he means nothing to us, and I certainly have no desire to see him again. Still, he is welcome to visit Netherfield if he chooses.

Despite these efforts, the boy grew increasingly somber, pale, and despondent. She introduced hot baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges, yet he remained as gloomy as a funeral carriage. She supplemented the water with a meager oatmeal diet and blister-plasters, measuring his intake like a vessel and dosing him with various patent medicines. Tom had grown numb to her ministrations, a change that deeply alarmed his aunt. Determined to shatter this apathy, she discovered Pain-killer and promptly acquired a supply. After tasting the fiery liquid, she abandoned her previous treatments in favor of this new remedy. She administered a teaspoonful to Tom, watching anxiously for a reaction. Her relief was immediate when the boy responded with a vigorous, frantic display of energy, as if he had been set ablaze. Sensing that his current situation lacked sufficient sentiment and offered too much chaotic variety, Tom decided to feign a fondness for the medicine. He requested it so frequently that he became a pest, eventually prompting his aunt to let him serve himself. While she would have trusted Sid, she secretly monitored the bottle with Tom. She noticed the level dropping, never suspecting he was using the liquid to mend a floorboard crack. One day, as Tom prepared to dose the floor, the aunt’s yellow cat approached, begging for a taste. Tom warned Peter that he should only partake if he truly desired it, but the cat insisted. After Tom cautioned him once more, he pried the cat’s jaws open and administered the dose. Peter leaped high into the air, let out a piercing cry, and raced around the room, colliding with furniture and overturning plants in a chaotic frenzy.

While reaching through the valve with a cup of water for the cat, my shirt sleeve caught on the basket's suspension loop, instantly detaching it. It vanished from sight as if it had dissolved into thin air; less than a tenth of a second passed between its release and its total disappearance. I wished them well, though I held no hope that the cat or her kittens could survive the fall. By six o'clock, a thick shadow began covering the earth to the east, and by five minutes to seven, the entire view was swallowed by darkness. Still, the setting sun continued to light the balloon for some time, which gave me great satisfaction. I realized that, at this altitude, I would see the sunrise hours before the people of Rotterdam, and each day I would enjoy longer periods of sunlight. I decided to keep a journal, tracking time in continuous twenty-four-hour cycles regardless of the darkness. At ten o'clock, feeling tired, I prepared to sleep, but suddenly faced a problem I had overlooked: how would the cabin air be refreshed while I slept? Breathing the same air for more than an hour or so would be impossible and potentially fatal. This dilemma deeply unsettled me; it is strange that after surviving so many dangers, I considered abandoning my mission entirely over this issue. However, my hesitation lasted only a moment.

These deputies traveled from Paris to Calais to meet Adrian, who had been chosen as the arbitrator. Throughout their journey through empty towns and desolate landscapes, they harbored intense hatred for one another, and they continued to argue their cases with fierce partisanship. By questioning the deputies separately, we discovered the true situation in Paris. Since parliament had named him Ryland’s deputy, all surviving English people had accepted Adrian as their leader, lawgiver, and protector. Originally, we had not planned for our group to be separated, and the Earl of Windsor was intended to hold supreme command. However, unforeseen events forced us to divide for nearly two months. Upon arriving in Paris in two separate groups, conflict broke out between them. They found Paris to be a ghost town. While we had once received regular news about the plague’s progress on the continent, communication eventually ceased as the death toll rose. Even within England, travel became rare. Few ships crossed the channel, and those who did often perished at sea or arrived already infected, dying before they could share news of France’s destruction. We had hoped to find many survivors abroad, but the plague had been even more devastating there. France was empty; we saw no one on the road from Calais to Paris. In the capital, only about a hundred people remained, wandering the streets and discussing the past with a surprising, lingering cheerfulness. The English took over the city, which was filled with lifeless, narrow streets. A few pale survivors gathered at the Tuileries, wondering why we had come to their doomed city. In their misery, they believed their own suffering was the worst, much like a person in pain who imagines that any other form of agony would be easier to bear.

I swear by the sun, the blue sky, and the love in my heart, that if you grant my request, you will never see me again as long as they live. Go home and begin your work. I will watch your progress with intense anxiety, and you need not fear; I will appear when you are ready. He left suddenly, perhaps afraid I might change my mind. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle, quickly vanishing into the icy landscape. His story had taken all day, and the sun was setting as he left. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before dark, but my heart was heavy and my pace slow. Navigating the mountain paths was difficult while I was distracted by the day's events. It was late when I reached the halfway point and sat by the fountain. The stars flickered through passing clouds, and the dark pines and fallen trees created a solemn, unsettling scene. I wept bitterly, clutching my hands in agony, and cried out to the stars, clouds, and winds to either end my suffering and memory or leave me in darkness. These were desperate thoughts, but the constant twinkling of the stars felt like a burden, and every gust of wind sounded like a destructive force coming to consume me. Morning arrived before I reached Chamounix. I did not rest, returning immediately to Geneva. I could not express my feelings; they weighed on me like a mountain, crushing my spirit. When I arrived home and saw my family, my wild, haggard appearance alarmed them, but I could not speak or answer their questions. I felt like an outcast, unworthy of their sympathy and unable to ever enjoy their company again.

The bewilderment I felt at this sudden shift in circumstances was perhaps the most inexplicable part of the experience. The reversal was not only logical and certain, but had been long foreseen as an inevitable consequence of reaching the point in my journey where the moon’s gravitational pull would overtake the earth’s. While I awoke from a deep sleep to a truly jarring sight, the event itself had been anticipated, if not at that precise instant. The transition must have occurred smoothly, and it is doubtful that even had I been awake, I would have noticed any physical sensation of the inversion or any disturbance to my equipment. Once I regained my composure and shook off the terror that had gripped me, I focused entirely on the moon’s physical landscape. It spread out below me like a map; though it remained quite distant, the surface features were remarkably sharp. The total lack of oceans, lakes, or any water was the most striking geological detail. Curiously, I observed vast, level alluvial plains, though most of the visible hemisphere was dominated by countless conical volcanic peaks that looked more artificial than natural. The tallest did not exceed three and three-quarter miles in height, yet a chart of the Campi Phlegraei would provide a better impression of the terrain than any description I could offer. Most were clearly erupting, demonstrating their immense power through the frequent, terrifying volleys of meteoric stones that whistled past my balloon with increasing intensity.

After I submitted the petitions, I could not stay away from the places where I had left them, feeling as though my presence offered some small comfort. Driven by this restless anxiety, I spent my evenings wandering the streets, passing the offices and homes where I had delivered my appeals. Even now, the cold, dusty streets of western London on a spring night, with their rows of stern, closed mansions and flickering lamps, fill me with sadness because of those memories. My daily visits were now shorter, and he was kept under stricter guard. Suspecting that I might be accused of trying to smuggle poison to him, I asked to be searched before sitting by his bed, telling the guard I would do anything to prove my intentions were honest. No one treated us cruelly; they were simply doing their duty. The guard and the other prisoners acting as nurses—criminals, yet capable of kindness—always told me he was growing weaker. As days passed, I noticed him lying quietly, staring at the ceiling with a dull expression that only brightened for a moment when I spoke. Often unable to talk, he would squeeze my hand, and I learned to understand him perfectly. By the tenth day, I saw a significant change. His eyes brightened as I entered, turning toward the door. Dear boy, he said as I sat down, I thought you were late, but I knew you couldn't be. It is exactly the right time, I replied. I waited at the gate. You always wait at the gate, don't you, dear boy? Yes, so I wouldn't lose a moment. Thank you, dear boy. God bless you. You have never abandoned me. I squeezed his hand in silence, unable to forget that I had once intended to leave him. And the best part of all, he added, is that you have been more comfortable with me since I have been in trouble than you were when things were going well.

We went to your home, the first man said, but we missed you. Hearing you were walking this way, we followed, hoping to catch you. Please, get into the carriage. Both men were demanding, and they moved to block my path to the carriage door. They were armed, and I was not. Gentlemen, I said, excuse me, but I usually ask who is requesting my help and what the situation is. The second man replied, Doctor, your clients are people of status. As for the case, we trust your skill to figure it out better than we could explain. That is enough. Get in. I had no choice but to obey and climbed in silently. They followed, the last one jumping in after closing the steps. The carriage turned and drove off quickly. I am repeating this conversation exactly as it happened, word for word. I am describing everything just as it occurred, keeping my focus steady. Where I leave gaps, I am stopping for now to hide my notes. The carriage left the city, passed the North Barrier, and reached the country road. About two miles later, it turned off the main path and stopped at a lonely house. We all got out and walked along a damp, overgrown garden path to the door. When the bell was rung, the door did not open right away, so one of my escorts struck the man who answered across the face with his heavy glove. I did not think much of it, as I had seen common people treated worse than dogs. However, the other man grew angry and struck the servant as well. Their expressions and movements were so identical that I realized then they were twin brothers. From the moment we arrived at the locked gate, I had heard cries coming from an upstairs room.

I would wake up eventually and look for the cause of a noise, perhaps seeing a steamboat chugging upstream so far away that I could only tell if it had a stern or side wheel. Then, for an hour, there would be nothing to see or hear, just pure solitude. Later, I might see a raft drifting in the distance with someone chopping wood. I would see the axe flash and fall, but hear nothing until the axe was raised again, when the sound finally reached us across the water. We spent our days lounging and listening to the silence. Once, a thick fog rolled in, and the passing rafts banged on tin pans to warn off steamboats. A boat passed so close we could hear the crew talking, swearing, and laughing, but we could see nothing. It felt eerie, like ghosts floating in the air. Jim thought they were spirits, but I told him spirits would not complain about the fog. When night fell, we pushed off, letting the current carry us while we smoked our pipes and dangled our legs in the water. We stayed naked day and night whenever the mosquitoes allowed, as I never cared much for clothes. Sometimes we had the river entirely to ourselves. We would watch the distant banks and islands, spotting a candle flickering in a cabin window or a light on a passing raft, sometimes hearing a fiddle or a song drift over the water. Life on a raft is lovely. We would lie on our backs, staring at the star-speckled sky, and argue about whether the stars were created or just happened to exist. Jim believed they were made, but I argued they just happened, as it would have taken too long to create so many.

He stayed inside the next day, mostly confined to his room, paralyzed by a frantic fear of death yet feeling detached from life. The sensation of being hunted and trapped consumed him. A fluttering curtain made him tremble, and dead leaves against the window felt like his own failed promises and regrets. Closing his eyes, he saw the sailor’s face in the glass again, and terror gripped him. Perhaps it was just his imagination conjuring vengeance. Reality was chaotic, but the mind was terrifyingly logical, using remorse to haunt sin and give every crime its consequences. In the real world, morality rarely dictated outcomes; the strong succeeded while the weak failed. Surely, if a stranger had been lurking, the staff would have noticed. He convinced himself it was just a hallucination; Sibyl Vane’s brother had likely perished at sea, and his youthful appearance had kept his identity hidden. Yet, if it were only an illusion, the power of his conscience to manifest such horrors was terrifying. What kind of existence would he have if his crimes haunted his every moment, mocking him from the shadows? The thought turned him pale, and the room felt suddenly freezing. He had been mad to kill his friend. The memory returned in vivid, gruesome detail, and his sin rose before him, stained in scarlet.

I must leave, unsure of what lies ahead, but I will return here or join your group as soon as I can. A single word or look will determine if I visit your father’s house tonight or never again. Recovering from such a letter was impossible. Ten minutes of reflection, constrained by her surroundings, only deepened her agitation. It was overwhelming joy. Before she could process her emotions, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta arrived. She struggled to maintain her composure, but soon found herself unable to follow their conversation. Pleading illness, she excused herself. They were shocked by her pale appearance and refused to leave her side. This was agonizing; she only wanted solitude. In desperation, she insisted on going home. Mrs. Musgrove urged her to go and rest for the evening, offering to call a sedan chair. Anne refused, fearing she would miss the chance to encounter Captain Wentworth on her walk. After Mrs. Musgrove confirmed Anne had not suffered a physical fall, she allowed her to leave. Desperate to ensure her message was clear, Anne added, Please, ma’am, ensure the other gentlemen know we expect your entire party tonight. I fear there was a misunderstanding; please tell Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth specifically that we hope to see them both. Oh, my dear, it is perfectly understood, I assure you.

“Tom!” No answer. “TOM!” No answer. “Where has that boy gone? You, Tom!” No answer. The old woman lowered her glasses to peer around the room, then pushed them up to look beneath them. She rarely looked through them for something as small as a boy; they were her formal pair, kept for style rather than utility—she could have seen just as well through stove lids. She looked confused for a moment, then said, not angrily but loudly enough for the furniture to hear: “Well, if I get my hands on you, I will—” She did not finish, as she was busy poking under the bed with a broom, needing her breath to punctuate the jabs. She pulled out nothing but the cat. “I have never seen the likes of that boy!” She went to the open door and scanned the tomato vines and weeds in the garden. No Tom. She raised her voice to carry and shouted: “Y-o-u-u TOM!” A slight noise behind her made her turn just in time to grab a small boy by his jacket and stop his escape. “There! I should have thought of that closet. What have you been doing in there?” “Nothing.” “Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that stuff?” “I don’t know, Aunt.” “Well, I know. It’s jam. I’ve told you forty times that if you didn’t leave that jam alone, I’d tan your hide. Hand me that switch.” The switch hovered in the air—the danger was immediate— “Oh! Look behind you, Aunt!” The old woman spun around, pulling her skirts out of the way. The boy fled instantly, scrambled up the high board fence, and vanished over it. His Aunt Polly stood surprised for a moment, then began to laugh softly. “Darn the boy, will I never learn? Hasn’t he played enough tricks like that for me to be ready for him by now? But old fools are the biggest fools of all. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks. But goodness, he never plays the same one twice, so how is a person to know what is coming? He seems to know exactly how long he can torment me before I lose my temper, and he knows that if he can distract me for a moment or make me laugh, my anger vanishes and I cannot bring myself to hit him.”

Elizabeth and I grew up together, less than a year apart in age. We never fought; harmony defined our bond, and our contrasting personalities only brought us closer. Elizabeth was calm and focused, while I was passionate, driven, and obsessed with learning. She loved the poetic beauty of our Swiss home, finding joy in the mountains, the changing seasons, and the quiet of winter. While she admired the world’s surface, I wanted to understand its inner workings. My earliest memories are of a deep curiosity and the thrill of discovering nature's hidden laws. When my younger brother was born seven years later, my parents settled permanently in Switzerland. We split our time between a house in Geneva and a country home on the shore of the lake, living a quiet, private life. I preferred a small circle of friends over crowds, so I ignored most of my classmates, except for Henry Clerval. Henry was the son of a local merchant, a boy of great imagination who loved adventure and danger. He was obsessed with stories of knights and chivalry, writing his own heroic songs and tales of magic. He often organized plays and masquerades based on legends like King Arthur or the crusaders. I had a perfectly happy childhood. My parents were incredibly kind and indulgent, acting not as strict rulers, but as the loving providers of all our joy.

Anne soon had enough opportunities to observe the group, though she kept her opinions to herself to avoid conflict at home. While Louisa seemed the favorite, Anne suspected Captain Wentworth was not in love with either sister. The women were infatuated with him, though it was merely a fleeting admiration that might eventually turn into genuine love. Charles Hayter appeared to feel ignored, yet Henrietta seemed torn between the two men. Anne wished she could warn them of the potential consequences, though she believed no one acted with malice. She was relieved that Captain Wentworth seemed unaware of the pain he caused; he showed no arrogance and likely remained ignorant of Charles Hayter’s feelings. He was simply wrong to accept the attentions of two women simultaneously. Eventually, Charles Hayter withdrew, staying away from Uppercross for three days and declining a dinner invitation. When Mr. Musgrove found him studying intensely, the family worried he was overworking himself. Mary hoped Henrietta had rejected him, while her husband expected his return. Anne simply thought Charles was acting wisely. One morning, while the men were out shooting, the Musgrove sisters visited the cottage. It was a beautiful November day, and they stopped by to announce they were going for a long walk, assuming Mary would not want to join. When Mary insisted on coming, clearly offended by the suggestion that she was not a good walker, Anne could tell the sisters did not want her company. She marveled at the family habit of forcing everyone to participate in every activity, regardless of whether it was convenient or desired.

Once my tears subsided, logic and recollection resumed, allowing me to contemplate my situation with composure. Though only hours had elapsed, my world had undergone a profound transformation; the weight of years seemed to have descended upon me since dawn. My father was effectively dead to me, and I felt as though I were mourning his actual passing. Yet he lived, though I, in my wretchedness, was forbidden from ever seeing or speaking to him again. I had to flee from him more urgently than from a foe, avoiding him in both city and wilderness. This realization left me gasping in agony, unable to organize my thoughts. I resolved to seek a life of bleak isolation, perhaps retreating to the Continent to live as a recluse, not out of religious devotion, but to remain forever severed from the world where I might weep undisturbed. Yet, what of my beloved, tormented father? Might he eventually conquer the fierce passion currently ruling him? Could he, years from now, once age had cooled his burning emotions, be a father to me again? This thought eased my brow, and a melancholy smile touched my lips. I dared to nurture hope; though years must pass, they would be buoyed by the prospect of reunion. Let him endure another sixteen years of lonely wandering, voicing his laments to distant forests and waterfalls, facing perils and hardships, his skin scorched by southern suns and his blood chilled by nocturnal rains. To this existence, miserable father, I consign you. Go, spend your days among savages and your nights beneath the open sky, until your body is weary, your heart frozen, and every trace of youth extinguished.

Emma felt great satisfaction from her conversation with Mr. Knightley. As she walked the lawn the next morning, she savored the memory of the ball. She was pleased they agreed on the Eltons and felt gratified by his praise of Harriet. The Eltons' rudeness, which had briefly threatened to spoil her evening, had instead led to these pleasant outcomes, and she hoped Harriet’s infatuation was finally cured. Harriet’s comments at the ball suggested she finally saw Mr. Elton for who he truly was. With Harriet becoming rational, Frank Churchill’s affections in check, and Mr. Knightley on good terms with her, Emma anticipated a wonderful summer. She did not mind that Frank Churchill would not visit that morning, as he had to return home. Having settled her thoughts, she prepared to return to her family duties when the gate opened. To her shock, Frank Churchill entered with Harriet leaning on his arm. Harriet looked pale and terrified, and Frank was attempting to comfort her. They quickly reached the hall, where Harriet promptly fainted. Emma soon learned the cause. Harriet and her friend Miss Bickerton had gone for a walk on the Richmond road. Though it seemed safe, the path became secluded and shaded by elms. A short distance past Highbury, they suddenly encountered a group of gypsies.
