When Tom woke up, he was momentarily confused about his surroundings. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and realized he was in the woods. It was a cool, gray dawn, and the forest felt peaceful and still. Not a leaf moved, and the silence was absolute. Dewdrops clung to the grass, and a thin trail of smoke rose from the campfire where Joe and Huck were still asleep. Soon, birds began to call, and a woodpecker started hammering. As the morning light brightened, the forest came to life. Tom watched in wonder as nature woke up. A small green worm crawled across a leaf, measuring the distance as it moved. When it finally climbed onto Tom’s leg, he was delighted, taking it as a sign that he would soon have a new suit of clothes—a pirate uniform. Nearby, a line of ants worked busily, one struggling to carry a dead spider up a tree. Tom recited a rhyme to a ladybug, and when it flew away, he felt satisfied, knowing he had tricked it as he often did. He poked a tumblebug, watching it curl up and play dead. By now, the birds were loud and active. A catbird sang from a branch above, mimicking other birds, while a bright blue jay landed nearby to inspect the boys with curiosity. A gray squirrel and a fox squirrel scurried past, pausing to chatter at the intruders, as these wild animals had likely never seen humans before and were unsure whether to be afraid.

So you will not, will you? You precious fool! It is wicked, is it not, Oliver? asked Charley Bates. He will end up hanged, will he not? I do not understand that term, Oliver answered. It means this, my friend, said Charley. He grabbed his neckerchief, held it high, let his head loll, and made a sharp noise with his teeth, demonstrating through pantomime that scragging meant hanging. That is what it means, Charley noted. Look at his expression, Jack! This boy is such excellent company; he will be the death of me. Charley laughed until he wept, then returned to his pipe. You have been raised poorly, the Dodger remarked, admiring his polished boots. Fagin will shape you, or you will be his first failure. You should start immediately, as you will join the trade sooner than you expect; you are wasting time, Oliver. Master Bates added his own moral advice, and then he and Mr. Dawkins described the joys of their lifestyle, urging Oliver to win Fagin’s favor quickly. Remember this, Nolly, the Dodger said as the Jew unlocked the door, if you do not steal handkerchiefs and watches— What is the point of that? Charley interrupted; he does not understand you. If you do not take them, the Dodger explained, someone else will, so the victims lose out, you lose out, and nobody gains anything except the thieves—and you have as much right to them as anyone. Certainly, certainly! said the Jew, who had entered unnoticed. It is simple, my dear; take the Dodger’s word for it. He knows his trade well. The old man rubbed his hands, delighted by his pupil’s logic. The discussion ended there, as the Jew arrived with Miss Betsy and a stranger named Tom Chitling, who had paused on the stairs to flirt with the lady before entering.

She was discovered deceased in her bed the following morning, seemingly having passed without suffering. Sir Mathew Reid was summoned immediately, yet nothing could be done, and her interment was scheduled for the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. Shortly before her passing, she had drafted a will bequeathing Lord Arthur her Curzon Street residence, along with her furnishings, belongings, and artwork, excluding her miniatures, which were left to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, intended for Sybil Merton. The estate held little worth, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, urged Lord Arthur to return promptly to settle numerous outstanding debts, as Lady Clementina had never maintained orderly records. Lord Arthur was deeply moved by her generosity and felt Mr. Podgers bore significant responsibility for the situation. Nevertheless, his devotion to Sybil eclipsed all other feelings, and the knowledge that he had fulfilled his obligation brought him solace. Upon reaching Charing Cross, he felt entirely content. The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil secured his promise that nothing would ever again separate them, and they set their wedding date for June 7th. Life appeared radiant once more, and his former joy returned. One day, while inspecting the Curzon Street house with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, they burned bundles of old letters and cleared out drawers of clutter. Suddenly, the young woman exclaimed in delight. "What have you discovered, Sybil?" Lord Arthur asked, smiling as he looked up from his task. "This charming little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. It is so quaint and Dutch. Please let me have it! I know amethysts won't suit me until I am over eighty." It was the container that had held the aconitine. Lord Arthur recoiled, a slight flush coloring his face. He had nearly forgotten his actions, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whom he had endured such profound distress, should be the one to bring it to mind. "Certainly, you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself." "Oh, thank you, Arthur; and may I keep the bonbon inside? I had no idea Lady Clementina enjoyed sweets. I assumed she was far too intellectual." Lord Arthur turned deathly pale as a terrifying thought struck him.

I am going, Master Will, I truly am, the man replied quickly, nearly at the tip now. At the tip? Legrand shouted, are you at the end of that branch? Almost there, master, oh my, Lord have mercy, what is this on the tree? Well, Legrand exclaimed, clearly pleased, what is it? It is just a skull, someone left their head in the tree and the crows have picked it clean. A skull? Very well, how is it attached to the limb? Look closely, master, it is a strange situation, there is a large nail pinning the skull to the wood. Jupiter, listen carefully, do you hear me? Yes, master. Pay attention, find the skull's left eye. Oh, that is difficult, there is no eye left at all. You fool, do you know your right from your left? Yes, I know that, it is my left hand I use to chop wood. Exactly, you are left-handed, and your left eye is on that same side. Now, can you find the left eye or where it used to be? After a long silence, the man asked, is the skull's left eye on the same side as its left hand? It has no hands, but never mind, I have found the left eye. What should I do? Drop the beetle through it as far as the string goes, but do not let go of the line. That is done, Master Will, it was easy to pass the bug through the hole, watch for it below. During this exchange, Jupiter remained hidden, but the beetle appeared at the end of the string, shining like polished gold in the final light of the setting sun. The scarab hung free of the branches and would have landed at our feet if released. Legrand used the scythe to clear a circular area several yards wide directly under the insect, then told Jupiter to release the string and descend.

Furthermore, this specific knot is rarely tied by anyone but a sailor, and it is characteristic of the Maltese. I discovered the ribbon beneath the lightning-rod; it could not have been owned by either victim. Even if my deduction that the Frenchman is a sailor from a Maltese ship is incorrect, my advertisement remains harmless. If I am mistaken, he will simply assume I was misled by circumstances he need not investigate. However, if I am correct, a significant advantage is achieved. Though innocent of the crime, the Frenchman will naturally be wary of answering the notice to reclaim his orangutan. He will think: I am innocent and poor, and this animal is a fortune. Why lose it to groundless fear? It was found far from the murder scene in the Bois de Boulogne. How could a beast be suspected of such violence? The police have no leads. Even if they find the animal, they cannot prove my involvement. Most importantly, I am known. The advertiser identifies me as the owner. I do not know how much he truly understands. If I fail to claim such valuable property, I only invite suspicion. It is safer to retrieve the creature and keep it hidden until the affair subsides. Just then, footsteps sounded on the stairs. Be prepared with your pistols, Dupin whispered, but do not draw or display them until I signal. The front door was unlocked, and the visitor had entered without ringing, pausing on the stairs before turning back. Then, he resumed his ascent, finally reaching our door and knocking firmly. Come in, Dupin called out cheerfully. A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—tall, robust, and muscular, with a bold, reckless expression that was not entirely unappealing.

I told him I needed the watermelon, but he argued that I did not need it to escape prison, which was the point of contention. He claimed it would have been acceptable if I intended to hide a knife inside to smuggle to Jim so he could kill the guard. I dropped the subject, though I found it frustrating to debate such fine, gold-leaf distinctions every time I saw a chance to grab a melon. As I was saying, we waited that morning until the yard was clear. Tom carried the sack into the shed while I kept watch. When he returned, we sat on the woodpile to talk. He said everything was ready except for tools, which would be easy to acquire. I asked what tools he meant, and he explained we needed them to dig. I asked if the old, broken picks in the shed were not sufficient. He looked at me with such pity it was almost heartbreaking. He asked if I had ever heard of a prisoner having modern tools to dig his way out. He argued that using such equipment would ruin the heroics of the situation; they might as well just hand him the key. He insisted that we needed a couple of case-knives instead. When I pointed out the absurdity of digging out a cabin foundation with knives, he insisted it was the proper, standard way. He claimed to have read all the books on the subject, noting that prisoners always use case-knives to tunnel through solid rock, a process that takes weeks or even years. He asked me to guess how long a prisoner in the Castle d'If took to dig his way out. I admitted I did not know, so he told me to guess. I guessed a month and a half.

The little man’s body was unusually broad, giving him a comical, round appearance. His feet were hidden, though a strange, hard substance occasionally poked through a hole in the bottom of his hat. His hands were massive. He had gray hair tied in a ponytail, a long, crooked, red nose, and sharp, bright eyes. His cheeks and chin were wrinkled but puffy, and he appeared to have no ears at all. He wore a loose sky-blue satin coat with matching tight breeches buckled at the knees, a bright yellow vest, and a white cap tilted jauntily. A large, blood-red silk handkerchief was tied in a fancy, oversized bow around his neck. Once he descended to about one hundred feet above the ground, the man grew nervous and seemed unwilling to land. He struggled to toss sand from a canvas bag, causing his craft to hover. Agitated, he pulled a large leather wallet from his pocket, weighed it with surprise, and opened it to retrieve a thick letter sealed with red wax and tied with red tape. He dropped it right at the feet of the mayor, Superbus Von Underduk. As the mayor bent to pick it up, the flustered traveler prepared to leave. To rise again, he dropped half a dozen bags of ballast. They landed directly on the mayor, rolling him over twenty-one times in front of everyone in Rotterdam. Naturally, the mayor did not intend to let this insult go unpunished.

Mrs. Otis, whose experience spending winters in Boston as a girl makes her quite an authority on art, informs me these jewels are highly valuable. Given this, Lord Canterville, I am sure you understand I cannot allow my family to keep them. Such ostentatious trinkets, while perhaps fitting for the British aristocracy, are entirely inappropriate for those raised on the strict, enduring principles of republican simplicity. Virginia, however, is very eager to keep the box as a memento of your unfortunate ancestor. Since it is quite old and damaged, I hope you might grant her request. I am surprised my daughter shows such sympathy for medievalism, though I suppose it stems from her being born in a London suburb shortly after her mother returned from Athens. Lord Canterville listened gravely, tugging his grey moustache to hide a smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he shook his hand warmly. My dear sir, your daughter did my ancestor, Sir Simon, a great service, and my family owes her a debt for her courage. The jewels are hers. If I were heartless enough to take them, I suspect the old ghost would rise from his grave within a fortnight to make my life miserable. They are not legal heirlooms, as their existence was unknown and they were never mentioned in any will. I have no more claim to them than your butler. When Virginia grows up, she will surely enjoy wearing them. Furthermore, you purchased the furniture and the ghost at a valuation; legally, anything belonging to the ghost became your property the moment you bought the estate.

Emma Woodhouse was beautiful, clever, and wealthy, living in a comfortable home with a cheerful personality. She seemed to possess the best of life's blessings and had spent nearly twenty-one years with very little to trouble her. As the younger of two daughters to a doting father, she had managed his household since her sister married. Her mother had passed away when Emma was very young, leaving her with only faint memories. Her place was filled by an excellent governess who loved Emma like a mother. Miss Taylor had been with the family for sixteen years, acting more as a friend than a teacher. She was especially close to Emma, and their relationship was like that of sisters. Because Miss Taylor was so gentle, she never truly exerted authority, and they lived as equals. Emma valued Miss Taylor's advice but ultimately followed her own path. The only real downsides to Emma's life were that she was used to getting her own way and tended to be a bit too confident. These flaws were not yet a problem for her. However, a gentle sorrow arrived when Miss Taylor married. On the wedding day, Emma felt a deep sense of loss. After the guests left, she and her father were left to dine alone, with no one else to brighten the long evening. Once her father fell asleep, Emma was left to reflect on her loneliness. Although the marriage was a happy one for her friend—as Mr. Weston was a kind, wealthy, and pleasant man—it was a difficult day for Emma. She knew she would miss Miss Taylor every hour. She thought back on sixteen years of kindness, remembering how Miss Taylor had taught her, played with her, and cared for her through every childhood illness.

But do not think I failed to see it as a problem. You can be sure they were perfectly comfortable. That does not make me like it any better. So many women and children have no right to be comfortable on a ship. My dear Frederick, you are being foolish. What would happen to us sailors' wives, who often need to travel to join our husbands, if everyone felt as you do? My feelings did not stop me from taking Mrs. Harville and her family to Plymouth. I dislike hearing you talk like a snob, as if women were delicate creatures rather than rational people. None of us expect a life without challenges. Ah, my dear, when he has a wife, he will change his tune. If we are lucky enough to see another war, he will act just as we have. He will be very grateful to anyone who brings his wife to him. Yes, he will. I am finished with this, Captain Wentworth said. When married people tell me I will think differently once I am married, I can only say I will not, and they insist I will, and that is the end of it. He stood up and walked away. You must have traveled a great deal, ma'am, Mrs. Musgrove said to Mrs. Croft. Quite a bit in my fifteen years of marriage, though many have done more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times and been to the East Indies once, along with time in Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. I never went past the Mediterranean or to the West Indies. We do not consider Bermuda or the Bahamas to be the West Indies, you know. Mrs. Musgrove had nothing to say, as she had never even thought about the matter. I assure you, ma'am, Mrs. Croft continued, that the accommodations on a large warship are excellent. On a frigate, you are more crowded, but any reasonable woman can be happy there. I can honestly say the happiest years of my life were spent on a ship. As long as we were together, there was nothing to fear.

When we reached the tree, he said, Jupiter, come here. Was the skull nailed to the branch facing out, or facing the wood? The face was out, master, so the crows could get at the eyes easily, Jupiter replied. Well, then, was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle? Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes. It was this eye, master—the left—just as you told me, Jupiter said, pointing to his own right eye. That will do, we must try again. I began to see a strange logic in my friend’s behavior. He moved the peg marking where the beetle fell three inches to the west. He measured fifty feet from the trunk in a straight line, marking a new spot several yards from where we had previously dug. We drew a larger circle around this new spot and began digging again. I was exhausted, yet I no longer minded the work. I felt strangely interested and even excited. Perhaps Legrand’s deliberate, thoughtful manner had affected me. I dug eagerly, finding myself actually expecting to find the treasure that had driven my friend mad. After about an hour and a half, the dog began howling violently again. This time, his distress was serious. When Jupiter tried to quiet him, the dog resisted, jumped into the hole, and frantically clawed at the dirt. Within seconds, he uncovered human bones, two complete skeletons mixed with metal buttons and rotted fabric. A few more spade strokes revealed a large Spanish knife, followed by several loose gold and silver coins.

I agree. It is for the best. Will you hold hands and swear that we— Oh no, that will not work for this. That is fine for trivial matters, especially with girls, because they always go back on their word if they get upset. For something this important, we need to write it down. And use blood. Tom loved the idea. It felt serious and dark, fitting the time and place perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle in the moonlight, took a piece of red chalk from his pocket, and carefully wrote, pressing his tongue between his teeth as he worked. Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about this, and they wish they may drop dead in their tracks if they ever tell and rot. Huckleberry admired Tom’s writing and his grand language. He pulled a pin from his lapel to prick his finger, but Tom stopped him. Wait, don't do that. The pin is brass and might have verdigris on it. What is verdigris? It is poison. Swallow some and you will see. Tom used a needle to prick their thumbs, squeezing out drops of blood. After some effort, Tom signed his initials using his finger, then showed Huckleberry how to write his. The oath was complete. They buried the shingle near the wall with solemn rituals, sealing their secret forever. A figure crept through the ruined building, but they did not notice. Tom, Huckleberry whispered, does this mean we can never tell, no matter what? Of course. It does not matter what happens; we must stay silent or we will drop dead. Do you understand? Yes, I suppose so. They whispered for a while until a dog let out a long, mournful howl just feet away. The boys grabbed each other in terror. Which one of us is he howling for? Huckleberry gasped. I do not know. Look through the crack. Quick! No, you look, Tom! I cannot, Huck!

Directly before him, illuminated by pale moonlight, stood a man of fearsome appearance. His eyes glowed like embers, long grey hair hung in tangled locks, and his archaic clothing was tattered and stained. Heavy, rusted shackles bound his wrists and ankles. Mr. Otis remarked that he must insist the chains be oiled, offering a bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for the task. He noted its effectiveness, citing testimonials from prominent clergymen, and placed the bottle on a marble table before retiring to his room. The Canterville ghost stood frozen in shock, then hurled the bottle to the floor and fled, groaning and glowing with a sickly green light. As he reached the oak staircase, two figures in white emerged and hurled a pillow at him. Realizing he was under attack, he vanished through the wall, leaving the house silent. Reaching a hidden room, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath, reflecting on his indignity. In three centuries of haunting, he had never been so insulted. He recalled the Duchess he had terrified, the hysterical housemaids, the rector he had traumatized, and Madame de Tremouillac, who had been bedridden for weeks after finding a skeleton reading her diary, eventually turning to the Church to escape her fright.

It hardly matters. She replied, I might as well ask why you chose to tell me you loved me against your will and better judgment, while clearly intending to insult me. Was that not reason enough for my rudeness? But I have other grievances. Even if I had been indifferent to you, do you think I would marry the man who ruined my beloved sister’s happiness? Darcy changed color, but he remained silent as she continued. I have every reason to think poorly of you. You cannot deny that you were the main cause of their separation, exposing them both to public judgment and deep misery. She paused, noticing with anger that he seemed entirely unrepentant, even wearing a look of skeptical amusement. Can you deny it? she asked. He replied calmly, I have no desire to deny that I did everything possible to separate my friend from your sister, and I am glad I succeeded. I acted out of kindness to him. Elizabeth ignored his comment, though it only deepened her resentment. My dislike is not based solely on that, she continued. Long before that, I had already formed my opinion of you through Mr. Wickham. What can you say to defend yourself regarding him? Darcy’s face flushed as he replied, You take a keen interest in that gentleman’s affairs. Who could hear of his misfortunes and not care? she asked. His misfortunes! Darcy repeated with contempt. Yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed. And you are the one who caused them, Elizabeth exclaimed. You have reduced him to poverty.

She abandoned everything, save for the memory that such events had transpired. Anne had not stepped foot in Kellynch since departing Lady Russell’s residence in September. It was never required, and she had managed to avoid the few opportunities that might have taken her to the Hall. Her return was marked by settling back into the refined rooms of the Lodge to delight its owner. Lady Russell felt a touch of worry alongside her happiness at the reunion, aware of Anne’s recent time at Uppercross. Fortunately, whether Anne had truly gained a healthier appearance or Lady Russell merely imagined it, the compliments she received amused her, as she linked them to her cousin’s quiet admiration and hoped for a renewed bloom of youth. As they spoke, Anne realized her own perspective had shifted. The matters that had consumed her thoughts when she left Kellynch, which she had felt ignored and forced to suppress while with the Musgroves, now seemed less significant. She had recently grown detached from her father, her sister, and Bath. Their affairs had been eclipsed by those at Uppercross. When Lady Russell returned to their previous concerns, expressing pleasure over the house in Camden Place and annoyance that Mrs. Clay remained, Anne felt guilty for how much more she dwelled on Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and her new acquaintances. The home and companionship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick felt far more compelling than her father’s residence or her sister’s bond with Mrs. Clay. She had to force herself to show an equal level of interest in topics that should have naturally held her primary attention. Their conversation hit a brief, awkward patch regarding the incident at Lyme. Lady Russell had heard the full story shortly after arriving, yet it required discussion; she had to inquire, express regret over the recklessness, lament the outcome, and both had to mention Captain Wentworth. Anne felt she handled this less skillfully than Lady Russell. She could not utter his name while meeting Lady Russell’s gaze until she resorted to briefly sharing her thoughts on the connection between him and Louisa.

I uncovered the embers, and a soft wind soon coaxed them into a blaze. I fashioned a fan from branches to revive the dying coals. By nightfall, I realized the fire provided both illumination and warmth, and it proved useful for my meals; I discovered that discarded scraps left by travelers tasted far better roasted than the raw berries I collected. I attempted to cook my own food on the embers, finding that while berries were ruined, roots and nuts were greatly enhanced. Food eventually grew scarce, and I spent entire days hunting for acorns to satisfy my hunger. I decided to abandon my home to find a place where my needs might be better met. I deeply regretted leaving behind the fire, as I had no idea how to rekindle it. After much fruitless contemplation, I wrapped myself in my cloak and headed west. After three days of wandering, I reached open country. A heavy snowfall had blanketed the fields in white, and the freezing, damp ground chilled my feet. Around seven in the morning, desperate for shelter and sustenance, I spotted a small shepherd's hut on a hill. Intrigued, I approached and entered the open door. An old man sat by the fire preparing breakfast; upon seeing me, he let out a sharp cry and fled across the fields with surprising agility. His strange appearance and sudden departure puzzled me, yet I was captivated by the hut. It offered a dry, sheltered refuge that seemed as divine to me as Pandemonium must have appeared to the demons escaping their fiery lake.

How would they live while Fate kept this grim outcome in the balance? The wedding had to be delayed at any price. He was certain of this. Despite his deep love for her—where even the brush of her hand sent thrills of joy through him—he saw his duty clearly. He knew he had no right to wed until he had carried out the murder. Once finished, he could approach the altar with Sybil Merton, offering his life to her without fear of sin. Then, he could hold her, certain she would never need to feel shame on his account. It had to be done, and the sooner, the better for them both. Many might have chosen an easier path, but Lord Arthur was too principled to prioritize pleasure. His love held more than passion; Sybil represented everything noble. Though he felt a brief, natural aversion to his task, it vanished. His heart framed it as a sacrifice, not a sin, and his reason confirmed there was no alternative. He had to choose between self-interest and the welfare of others, and he would not let selfishness conquer love. This choice faces everyone eventually, but it arrived early for Lord Arthur, before cynicism or vanity could corrupt him. He did not hesitate. He was no idle dreamer; he was practical. To him, life demanded action over contemplation, and he possessed the rare gift of common sense. The turbulent emotions of the night before had faded, and he looked back on his frantic wandering and agony with a sense of embarrassment. The very intensity of his past suffering now made it seem like a dream, and he wondered how he could have been so foolish as to struggle against the inevitable.

Should I ask them? Or perhaps Miss Bates? She is closer, and I suspect she understands everyone's preferences as well as anyone. We need more input. Shall I invite her to join us? If you like, Mrs. Weston said hesitantly, if you think she will be helpful. You will get nothing useful from Miss Bates, Emma replied. She will be full of joy and gratitude, but she will not listen to your questions or tell you anything. I see no point in consulting her. But she is so entertaining! I love hearing her talk, and I do not have to invite the whole family. Mr. Weston joined them then and approved of the plan. Yes, Frank, go get Miss Bates and settle this. She will enjoy the idea, and she is the perfect person to help us overcome obstacles. She is a living lesson in how to be happy. But bring them both. Both, sir? Can the older lady? The older lady? No, the younger one, of course. I will think you a fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece. Oh, I apologize, sir. I did not realize. I will certainly try to persuade them both. He ran off. Long before he returned with the brisk aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston had reconsidered the hallway and decided the issues were trivial. The remaining plans for furniture, lighting, music, and refreshments seemed to resolve themselves or could be handled later with Mrs. Stokes. Everyone invited would surely attend, and Frank had already written to Enscombe to extend his stay, which was certain to be approved. It was going to be a wonderful dance. When Miss Bates arrived, she enthusiastically agreed. She was not needed for advice, but her constant, warm approval was very welcome. For another half-hour, they walked between the rooms, suggesting ideas and enjoying the anticipation of the event.

I regretted Jim’s remark; it diminished him in my eyes. My conscience pricked me so severely that I finally promised it I would row to the bank at dawn and confess. Instantly, I felt relieved and buoyant, my burdens vanished. I scanned the darkness for a light, humming softly, until one appeared. Jim cried out, "We are safe, Huck! We are safe! Celebrate, for that is surely Cairo!" I replied, "I will take the canoe to verify; it might be a mistake." He eagerly prepared the boat, placing his coat for my comfort and handing me the paddle. As I departed, he added, "Soon I will shout for joy, knowing I am a free man because of you, Huck. You are my best and only friend; Jim will never forget this." I had been eager to betray him, but his words drained my resolve. I paddled slowly, uncertain of my intentions. When I was fifty yards away, Jim called out, "There you go, the only white gentleman who ever kept his word to old Jim." I felt nauseated, yet insisted to myself that I had to proceed. Just then, a skiff carrying two armed men approached. They stopped, and I followed suit. One asked, "What is that?" "A section of a raft," I answered. "Are you aboard it?" "Yes, sir." "Is there anyone else?" "Only one man." "Five slaves escaped tonight upstream. Is your companion white or black?" I hesitated, unable to force the words out. I lacked the courage to speak, and realizing my resolve was failing, I finally lied, "He is white." "We shall investigate ourselves," the man said. "I wish you would," I replied, "because my father is there, and perhaps you could assist me in towing the raft to the light."

Their arrival ignited a fervor in Saint Antoine, spreading quickly as they passed, with faces appearing at every door and window. Yet, no one followed, and silence fell as they entered the wine-shop, though every gaze fixed upon them. Good day, gentlemen, Monsieur Defarge said. This prompted a chorus of replies. It is bad weather, gentlemen, Defarge added, shaking his head. Everyone looked at their neighbor, then cast their eyes down in silence, save for one man who stood and left. My wife, Defarge announced to Madame Defarge, I have traveled with this road-mender, Jacques. I met him by chance outside Paris. He is a good man. Give him a drink! A second man stood and left. Madame Defarge served the road-mender, who tipped his cap and drank. He ate coarse bread from his blouse as he sat by the counter. A third man stood and left. Defarge drank some wine, then waited for the stranger to finish. He ignored the others, and they ignored him, even Madame Defarge, who was busy knitting. Have you finished, friend? he eventually asked. Yes, thank you. Come then! You shall see the room I mentioned. It will suit you perfectly. They left the shop, crossed a courtyard, climbed a steep staircase, and entered a garret—the same room where an old man once sat making shoes. The old man was gone, but the three men who had left the shop were waiting. They were linked to the old man by the memory of having once watched him through the wall. Defarge closed the door and whispered, Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness I, Jacques Four, have brought to meet you.

The following morning, the Otis family gathered for breakfast and spoke at length about the specter. The American Minister felt slightly vexed that his gift had been rejected. He stated that he had no desire to harm the spirit, yet he found it discourteous to pelt him with pillows, given his long tenure in the residence. This reasonable observation prompted the twins to erupt in laughter. He added that if the ghost refused the lubricant, they would be forced to confiscate his chains, as the racket outside their rooms made sleep impossible. The remainder of the week passed peacefully, save for the recurring bloodstain in the library. This was peculiar, as Mr. Otis kept the room locked and the windows secured each night. The stain’s shifting hues also drew notice, varying from dull red to vermilion, deep purple, and even a vibrant emerald-green during morning prayers. These transformations entertained the family, who placed bets on the color, though young Virginia remained troubled by the sight, nearly weeping when the stain turned green. The ghost reappeared on Sunday night. A loud crash in the hall startled the family from their beds. Downstairs, they discovered a suit of armor had toppled from its stand, and the Canterville ghost sat in a high-backed chair, nursing his knees in obvious pain. The twins immediately fired their pea-shooters with practiced precision, while the Minister leveled his revolver and ordered the spirit to raise his hands, per Californian custom. With a furious cry, the ghost vanished through them like mist, blowing out Washington’s candle and plunging the group into darkness.

He was certainly entertaining, but I felt let down. When I asked about the chainmail, he just laughed and claimed it was too cold for England. Oh, look, Mr. Podgers is here! Mr. Podgers, please read the Duchess of Paisley’s palm. Duchess, take off your glove—the right one, not the left. Dear Gladys, I’m not sure this is appropriate, the Duchess murmured, unbuttoning a stained kid glove. Nothing interesting ever is, Lady Windermere replied. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favorite palmist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley; if you claim her mount of the moon is larger than mine, I’ll never trust you again. I’m certain there’s nothing like that in my hand, the Duchess said seriously. Your Grace is correct, Mr. Podgers noted, observing her short, square fingers. The mount of the moon is undeveloped, but the life line is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines on the rascette! You will live to a great age and be very happy. Your ambition is moderate, your intellect is balanced, and your heart line— Do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers, Lady Windermere urged. I would love to, he replied with a bow, but I see only lasting affection and a strong sense of duty. Please continue, the Duchess said, looking pleased. Frugality is another of your virtues, Mr. Podgers added, causing Lady Windermere to burst into laughter. Frugality is a virtue, the Duchess remarked complacently. When I married Paisley, he owned eleven castles but not one livable house. And now he has twelve houses and not a single castle, Lady Windermere teased. Well, my dear, the Duchess began, I prefer— Comfort, Mr. Podgers interrupted, along with modern conveniences and hot water in every room. Your Grace is right; comfort is the only thing our civilization offers. You’ve read the Duchess perfectly, Mr. Podgers. Now, read Lady Flora’s. At a nod from the hostess, a tall girl with sandy hair and prominent shoulder blades stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa, offering a long, bony hand. Ah, a pianist, I see, Mr. Podgers observed. An excellent pianist, though perhaps not quite a musician.

I vow, he shouted, by the sun, the azure heavens, and the passion consuming my soul, that if you fulfill my request, you will never see me again as long as they live. Go home and begin your work; I will observe your progress with profound concern, and rest assured that I will return when you are prepared. With these words, he vanished, perhaps fearing I might change my mind. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle, soon disappearing into the icy expanse. His story had taken the entire day, and the sun was setting as he left. I knew I needed to hurry down to the valley before darkness fell, yet my spirit was burdened and my pace sluggish. Navigating the narrow mountain trails while lost in the day's intense emotions proved difficult. It was late when I reached the halfway point and sat by the fountain. Stars flickered between passing clouds, and the dark pines and fallen timber created a solemn, unsettling atmosphere. I wept in anguish, crying out to the stars, clouds, and winds to either end my consciousness and memory or leave me in total darkness. These were desperate, chaotic thoughts, yet I cannot convey how the constant starlight oppressed me or how every gust of wind felt like a scorching gale meant to destroy me. Dawn broke as I reached Chamounix, but I did not rest, traveling straight to Geneva. My internal turmoil was indescribable, pressing down with crushing weight. Upon returning home, my disheveled and frantic state alarmed my family, but I remained silent, unable to speak. I felt ostracized, as though I had forfeited my right to their comfort or any future connection with them.

Raymond paced the room in a fury. I waited to hear his accusations. Adrian, leaning against the wall, cried out, "This is utterly absurd; you are behaving like schoolboys." Raymond retorted, "You fail to grasp the situation. This is a calculated tyranny I refuse to endure. Must I be the empire's only slave simply because I am Protector? My privacy is violated, my conduct judged, and my friends slighted. I am finished with it all." He unpinned the star of his office and tossed it onto the table, declaring, "I resign my position and abdicate my authority—let someone else take it." Adrian countered, "Let whoever considers themselves your superior take it, though no man in England would dare. Recognize your own worth, Raymond, and your anger will fade. Recently, our prayers for the nation's success were inseparable from our prayers for your welfare. You dedicated your time to our prosperity, beautifying our cities and enriching our land. You protected the weak and humbled the unjust. It is no wonder we are devastated by this change. This mood will pass; resume your duties, and your supporters will rejoice while your enemies fall silent. Control yourself, and the world remains yours." Raymond replied gloomily, "That advice would be sound for someone else. You are the wise and just peer who could truly lead. I realize now, too late for England, that I am unfit for this role. I cannot govern my own impulses. Do not think this resignation is merely a temper tantrum. I swear by the living God that I will never reclaim that trinket or bear the burden of misery it represents again."

Listen! Monks replied. When his father fell ill in Rome, my mother, from whom he had long been separated, traveled from Paris with me to manage his affairs, though there was little affection between them. He was unconscious when we arrived and died the next day. Among his papers were two documents addressed to you, Mr. Brownlow, with instructions to deliver them only after his death. One was a letter to Agnes, and the other was a will. What of the letter? Mr. Brownlow asked. It was a long, desperate confession, Monks said. He had deceived Agnes, claiming a secret mystery prevented their marriage. She trusted him until it was too late. She was pregnant at the time. He wrote that if he died, she should not curse his memory or fear for their child, as the guilt was entirely his. He mentioned the locket and ring he had given her, begging her to keep them close, and his writing became frantic and incoherent, as if he had lost his mind. I believe he had. The will, Mr. Brownlow said as Oliver wept, was written in the same spirit. He spoke of the misery his wife had caused, and of your own malice and hatred, you being his only son. He left you and your mother each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. The rest of his estate he divided equally between Agnes Fleming and their child, provided the child lived to come of age.

However, in that harsh critique of Chantilly published in yesterday’s Musée, the writer made shameful remarks regarding the cobbler’s name change upon becoming an actor, citing a Latin verse we have discussed before: Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum. I had previously explained that this line concerns Orion, once spelled Urion, and I knew you would recall it. It was obvious you would connect Orion with Chantilly, and your smile confirmed you had done so. You were contemplating the cobbler’s tragic end. You had been walking with a stoop, but then you straightened up, and I knew you were considering Chantilly’s small stature. I interrupted your thoughts then to observe that, being such a tiny man, he would be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés. Shortly after, while reading the evening Gazette des Tribunaux, we noticed these paragraphs: Extraordinary Murders. At three this morning, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were awakened by terrifying screams from the fourth floor of a Rue Morgue residence occupied by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Camille. After failing to gain entry, neighbors forced the gate with a crowbar and entered with two gendarmes. The cries had stopped, but as they ascended the stairs, they heard two rough voices arguing above. By the second landing, silence had returned. The group searched the rooms, eventually forcing the locked door of a large back chamber on the fourth floor. The scene inside left everyone horrified and astonished. The room was in total chaos, with furniture smashed and scattered. The bed had been stripped and its mattress tossed into the center of the room. A blood-stained razor lay upon a chair.

Dorian, these rumors must concern you. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You surely do not want to be viewed as someone corrupt. While you have status and wealth, those things are not everything. I do not believe these stories, at least not when I look at you. Sin leaves a mark on a man’s face that cannot be hidden. There is no such thing as a secret vice; it reveals itself in the lines of the mouth, the eyelids, or even the hands. Last year, a man I will not name asked me to paint him. I refused, despite his high offer, because I despised the shape of his fingers. I later learned my instincts were correct; his life is truly wretched. But you, with your innocent face and youthful appearance, seem above reproach. Yet, I rarely see you, and when I hear the terrible things people whisper, I am at a loss. Why does the Duke of Berwick leave a club room when you arrive? Why do so many men in London avoid your company? Lord Staveley recently told me that while you have artistic taste, you are someone no decent woman should be near. He said this openly, and it was horrifying. Why is your friendship so destructive? Think of the young soldier who killed himself, or Sir Henry Ashton, who was forced to flee England in disgrace.

You are unfamiliar with me unless you have read The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, though that is irrelevant. Mr. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he mostly told the truth, despite some exaggerations. Everyone lies occasionally, except perhaps Aunt Polly, the widow, or Mary. Those individuals are featured in that largely truthful account. The story concludes with Tom and me discovering the robbers' hidden cave treasure, making us wealthy with six thousand dollars in gold each. Judge Thatcher invested it, providing us a daily dollar, which was more than we could spend. Widow Douglas adopted me, intending to civilize me, but her rigid, respectable lifestyle felt stifling. I eventually fled, returning to my old rags and sugar-hogshead for freedom. However, Tom Sawyer convinced me to return to the widow so I could join his planned band of robbers. The widow wept over me, calling me a lost lamb, and forced me back into uncomfortable new clothes. The routine resumed: I had to obey the dinner bell and wait for her to say grace over food that was perfectly fine, though I preferred the flavors of mixed leftovers. Afterward, she taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers. I was initially intrigued, but lost interest once I learned Moses had been dead for a long time, as I have no concern for the deceased.

You will be happy to hear that my journey has begun without the disasters you feared. I arrived yesterday, and my first priority is to assure my dear sister that I am well and increasingly confident in my success. I am already far north of London. As I walk the streets of St. Petersburg, a cold northern breeze brushes my cheeks, bracing my nerves and filling me with joy. Do you understand this feeling? This wind, blowing from the regions I am heading toward, gives me a taste of those icy lands. Inspired by this promising breeze, my daydreams grow more vivid. I cannot convince myself that the North Pole is merely a place of frost and desolation; I imagine it as a region of beauty and delight. There, Margaret, the sun is always visible, its broad disk skimming the horizon and casting perpetual light. Trusting the accounts of earlier explorers, I believe that snow and frost are banished there. Sailing over a calm sea, we may reach a land more wonderful and beautiful than any yet discovered. Its features may be unique, just as the stars appear different in those unexplored solitudes. What might we find in a land of eternal light? I may discover the mysterious force that attracts the compass needle and clarify celestial observations that currently seem inconsistent. I will satisfy my curiosity by seeing a part of the world never before visited and walking on land never touched by human feet. These goals are enough to overcome any fear of danger or death, making me start this difficult voyage with the joy of a child setting out on an adventure. Even if my theories are wrong, you cannot deny the immense benefit I will provide to all mankind by discovering a shortcut to distant countries or uncovering the secret of the magnet. These thoughts have calmed my initial nerves, and I feel an enthusiasm that lifts my spirits. Nothing settles the mind like a steady purpose upon which the soul can focus.

I mentioned he was a poet; at twenty-three, he released his debut poem, which the entire nation greeted with fervent acclaim. Fortune favored him constantly, establishing a reputation with unprecedented speed and universality. The public praised the very verses that captivated scholars in their studies, and not a single critic dissented. During this peak of fame, he met Elinor. She was a beautiful young heiress living with her guardian, and from their first meeting, they seemed destined for each other. While Elinor lacked Woodville’s genius, she possessed a noble, generous spirit, elevated by her youth and the universal affection she inspired to recognize only virtue. She was charming, with candid manners and deep blue eyes shining with the brilliance of combined sensibility and wisdom. They were perfect matches and quickly fell in love. Woodville experienced the joy of romance for the first time, while Elinor was thrilled to hold the heart of such a celebrated man. Could such a union produce anything but pure happiness? Woodville was a poet, courted by every social circle and the focus of every gaze, yet he was merely a clergyman’s son, while Elinor was a wealthy heiress. Her guardian did not object to their bond, as Woodville’s merit was too great to be dismissed for lack of fortune. However, her father’s will forbade her marriage until she reached her majority, a condition tied to her inheritance. Having just turned twenty, the couple had to accept this wait. They remained inseparable, living in near-paradise, studying together and crafting future plans, finding such delight in each other’s presence that they barely lamented the postponement of their wedding. Woodville’s fame continued to grow, and Elinor flourished in wisdom under his guidance. With only two months until Elinor turned twenty-one, all arrangements for their marriage were complete. How can I describe the ruin of such happiness? Yet the world would not be the place of sorrow it is if such angelic beings were permitted to remain together. One could search the globe and never find the perfect bliss their marriage promised; the established order of our miserable existence would have required a total upheaval to allow for such absolute joy.

If I cannot live on that, I will not ask for help. Is that satisfactory? A massive roar of applause followed, and the king’s voice rose above it, ordering his guards to release me. He declared that I was now his right hand, granted great power, and should be honored by everyone. He commanded that the darkness be lifted so the world could rejoice. I replied that while my own shame mattered little, it would dishonor the king if his minister remained naked. I asked for my clothes to be returned. The king insisted I be dressed like a prince instead. My plan was to delay until the eclipse was total, as I could not actually end the darkness. Requesting new clothes bought some time, but not enough, so I claimed the king might regret his impulsive decision. I insisted on waiting to see if he remained firm in his choice. Though no one was happy, I held my ground. As the sky grew pitch black, the crowd groaned in terror at the cold breeze and the appearance of stars. I was relieved when the eclipse finally became total, though everyone else was miserable. I announced that the king had kept his word, then raised my hands and solemnly commanded the enchantment to end. Silence filled the darkness for a moment. When the sun finally reappeared, the crowd erupted in cheers and rushed toward me, showering me with gratitude. Clarence was certainly among the first to reach me.

Lacking standard tools, the analyst adopts his opponent's perspective, merging with their mindset to instantly perceive the simple, often overlooked strategies that might lead them into mistakes or errors in judgment. Whist has long been recognized for challenging the calculating mind, attracting brilliant individuals who find chess trivial by comparison. No other pursuit tests analytical faculties quite like it. While a master chess player may excel only at that game, whist proficiency signals a talent for any intellectual conflict. True mastery involves grasping every potential advantage, many of which remain hidden from the average observer. While a sharp memory and adherence to Hoyle’s rules are often mistaken for the entirety of skilled play, the analyst’s true talent emerges beyond these basic guidelines. He silently gathers observations and deductions. While others may do the same, the analyst succeeds because he knows precisely what to observe. He does not limit his focus to the game itself, but draws conclusions from external details. He studies his partner’s face and those of his opponents, examines how they organize their hands, and tracks their glances at specific cards. He monitors every shift in expression—certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment—as the game unfolds. From the way a trick is collected, he determines if the player can win another in that suit. He identifies feints by the way cards are played. A stray word, a fumbled card, the way tricks are stacked, or signs of hesitation and anxiety all provide his intuitive mind with a clear picture of the situation.

“Basil, this is remarkable! I must meet Dorian Gray.” Hallward rose and paced the garden before returning. “Harry,” he stated, “Dorian Gray is merely an artistic inspiration to me. You might perceive nothing in him, yet I see everything. He influences my work even when his likeness is absent; he suggests a new style. I discover him in specific lines and subtle colors. That is all.” “Then why refuse to display his portrait?” Lord Henry inquired. “Because I have inadvertently infused it with a strange artistic devotion I have never mentioned to him. He remains unaware, and he shall stay that way. However, the public might discern it, and I refuse to expose my soul to their superficial scrutiny. My heart will not be examined under their lens. There is too much of myself in that work, Harry—far too much.” “Poets lack your hesitation. They understand that passion sells; a broken heart often leads to multiple editions.” “I despise them for it,” Hallward exclaimed. “An artist should produce beauty without injecting his own life into it. We live in an era where art is treated as autobiography, and we have abandoned the abstract sense of beauty. One day I will reveal its true nature, which is why the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.” “I believe you are mistaken, Basil, but I will not debate you. Only the intellectually adrift argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray fond of you?” The painter pondered briefly. “He likes me,” he replied eventually. “I flatter him excessively, finding a perverse pleasure in remarks I later regret. Generally, he is delightful, and we converse on countless topics in the studio. Occasionally, however, he is thoughtlessly cruel, seemingly enjoying my distress. At those moments, Harry, I feel I have surrendered my entire soul to someone who treats it like a mere flower for his lapel, a trinket to flatter his vanity, or a fleeting ornament for a summer day.”

Not everyone would have been so persistent as she was, refusing to accept Jane’s initial refusal. She insisted that Jane should not send a rejection letter yesterday, suggesting they wait instead. Sure enough, by last night, it was decided that Jane would take the position. It was a complete surprise to me; I had no idea. Jane pulled Mrs. Elton aside and explained that, after considering the benefits of Mrs. Smallridge’s offer, she had decided to accept it. I knew nothing about it until it was finalized. You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton? Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton insisted we come. It was arranged while we were walking on the hill with Mr. Knightley. She told us we all had to join them for the evening. Mr. Knightley was there too? No, he declined from the start. Even though Mrs. Elton said she would not let him off the hook, he did not come. My mother, Jane, and I went, and we had a pleasant evening. Kind friends are always agreeable, though everyone seemed tired after the morning outing. Even pleasure can be exhausting, and I cannot say the others seemed to enjoy it much. Still, I will always consider it a lovely party and am grateful to the friends who invited me. I suppose Miss Fairfax had been making up her mind throughout the day? I imagine so. Whenever she leaves, it will be difficult for her and her friends, but I hope her new position is as comfortable as possible, especially regarding the family's character. Thank you, Miss Woodhouse. Indeed, everything points to her being happy there. Aside from the Sucklings and Bragges, there is no nursery establishment as generous or elegant in all of Mrs. Elton’s circle. Mrs. Smallridge is a delightful woman, and their lifestyle is nearly as grand as Maple Grove. As for the children, they are the most elegant, sweet children anywhere, aside from the Sucklings and Bragges. Jane will be treated with such kindness; it will be a life of pure pleasure. And her salary! I really cannot bring myself to mention the amount to you, Miss Woodhouse.

Following supper, the entire group ventured out to search for turtle eggs along the sandbar. They probed the sand with sticks, and upon locating a soft patch, knelt to excavate with their hands. Occasionally, they retrieved fifty or sixty eggs from a single nest. These were perfectly spherical, white objects, slightly smaller than an English walnut. They enjoyed a grand feast of fried eggs that evening and again the following Friday morning. After breakfast, they dashed onto the bar, shouting and leaping, discarding their garments as they ran until they were entirely unclothed. They continued their play in the shallow water against the strong current, which frequently knocked them off balance, adding to their amusement. Periodically, they gathered to splash water at one another, approaching with heads turned to shield their faces from the spray, until they grappled and wrestled. The victor would dunk his companion, leaving them all submerged in a chaotic knot of limbs before they surfaced, sputtering and laughing for air. Once exhausted, they collapsed onto the sun-baked sand, burying themselves in it before eventually returning to the water to repeat the cycle. Eventually, realizing their bare skin resembled flesh-toned tights, they drew a ring in the sand and staged a circus, with three boys insisting on the role of clown. Next, they played marbles until the game lost its appeal. Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom declined, having realized he lost his string of rattlesnake rattles while undressing. Fearing the loss of his protective charm, he refused to enter the water until he recovered it. By then, the others were weary and sought rest. They drifted apart, feeling melancholy, and stared across the river toward the sleepy village. Tom began tracing the name BECKY in the sand with his toe, then angrily erased it, frustrated by his own sentimentality. Yet, he wrote it again, unable to resist, before finally smoothing it over and gathering the other boys to distract himself.

The ringmaster gave a short speech, asking for no more trouble and agreeing to let the man ride if he could stay on. The crowd laughed, and the man climbed on. Immediately, the horse began bucking and leaping. Two circus workers tried to hold the bridle while the drunk man clung to the horse's neck, his legs flying wildly. The audience stood and cheered until they were crying with laughter. Eventually, the horse broke free and galloped around the ring with the man flopping against its neck. I felt terrified for him, but soon he pulled himself upright, grabbed the reins, and stood tall on the horse's back. He looked perfectly steady, as if he had never been drunk. He began stripping off his clothes, tossing seventeen suits into the air. Underneath, he was slim, handsome, and wearing a brilliant costume. He whipped the horse to a faster pace before leaping off, bowing, and dancing away while the crowd roared with delight. The ringmaster realized he had been tricked by one of his own performers, who had planned the stunt in secret. The ringmaster looked miserable, and I felt foolish for being fooled, though I would not have traded places with him for anything. It was the best circus I had ever seen, and I would gladly pay to see it again.

As I reached through the valve with a cup of water for the cat, my shirt sleeve caught on the loop holding the basket, instantly detaching it from the bottom. The basket vanished from sight as if it had dissolved into thin air. Less than a second passed between the basket coming loose and its total disappearance along with its contents. I wished them well, though I held no hope that the cat or her kittens would survive the fall. By six o'clock, I saw a large shadow covering the earth to the east, which spread rapidly until the entire view was swallowed by night at five minutes before seven. The setting sun continued to light my balloon long after this, which, while expected, brought me great joy. It was clear that I would see the sunrise hours before the people of Rotterdam, despite their location to the east. As I climbed higher, I would enjoy sunlight for longer periods each day. I decided to keep a journal, counting days as continuous twenty-four-hour cycles regardless of the darkness. At ten o'clock, feeling tired, I planned to sleep, but a problem I had overlooked suddenly occurred to me. If I slept, how would the air in the cabin be refreshed? Breathing the same air for more than an hour or so would be impossible, and staying longer could be fatal. This dilemma worried me deeply. It may seem strange that after all I had endured, this issue made me consider giving up my mission and descending. However, my hesitation lasted only a moment.

He jumped up and grabbed her arm. "Show him to me. Which one is he? Point him out. I have to see him!" he demanded. Just then, the Duke of Berwick’s carriage blocked their view, and by the time it passed, the other vehicle had vanished. "He is gone," Sibyl murmured sadly. "I wish you had seen him." "I wish I had, because as surely as there is a God, if he ever hurts you, I will kill him." She stared at him in horror. He repeated the threat, his words sharp as a blade. Bystanders began to stare, and a woman nearby giggled. "Come away, Jim," she whispered. He followed her through the crowd, feeling satisfied with his warning. By the Achilles Statue, she turned to him. Her eyes held pity, though her lips curved into a smile. She shook her head. "You are foolish, Jim; just a bad-tempered boy. How can you say such horrible things? You are just jealous and unkind. I wish you would fall in love; it makes people good, and what you said was wicked." "I am sixteen," he replied, "and I know what I am doing. Mother is no help to you; she doesn't know how to look after you. I wish I weren't going to Australia. I would quit if my papers weren't already signed." "Don't be so serious," she said. "You sound like a hero from one of Mother’s silly melodramas. I won't fight with you. Seeing him is perfect happiness. You wouldn't harm anyone I love, would you?" "Not as long as you love him, I suppose," he muttered. "I will love him forever!" she cried. "And he?" "Forever, too!" "He had better." She pulled away, then laughed and touched his arm, dismissing him as just a boy. At Marble Arch, they caught a bus toward their shabby home on Euston Road. It was past five, and Sibyl needed to rest before her performance. Jim insisted on it, wanting to say goodbye without their mother present to cause a scene, which he detested.

We visited your home, the first man said, but missed you. Hearing you were walking this way, we followed, hoping to catch you. Please, get into the carriage. Their manner was commanding, and they positioned themselves to block my path to the door. They were armed; I was not. Gentlemen, I replied, forgive me, but I usually ask who is seeking my help and the nature of the case. The second man answered, Doctor, your clients are people of status. As for the case, we trust your skill to diagnose it better than we could describe it. That is enough. Get in. I had no choice but to comply, entering in silence. They followed, the last one jumping in after closing the steps. The carriage turned and sped off. I am recounting this conversation exactly as it happened, word for word. I am describing events precisely, keeping my mind focused. Where I leave gaps, I am pausing to hide my notes. The carriage left the city, passed the North Barrier, and reached the country road. About two miles later—a distance I measured later—it turned off the main road and stopped at a secluded house. We all got out and walked along a damp garden path past an overflowing, neglected fountain to the door. When the bell was answered, one of my escorts struck the man who opened it across the face with his heavy glove. I thought little of it, as I had seen commoners treated worse than dogs. However, the other man grew angry and struck him as well. Seeing their identical expressions and movements, I realized they were twin brothers. From the moment we entered the locked gate, I had heard cries coming from an upstairs room.

I was not worried about her. She was a capable woman who handled life well without my help. Honestly, she likely saw me as an idle boy, good for nothing but daydreaming, and was happy to see me go. It was a dark night when I said goodbye. I took the three creditors who had been bothering me along as helpers, and we carried the balloon and its gear to the station where the rest of my supplies were stored. Everything was untouched, so I got to work immediately. It was April first. The night was dark, starless, and a drizzling rain made us miserable. My main concern was the balloon; despite its varnish, it was getting heavy from the moisture, and the gunpowder was at risk. I kept my three creditors busy packing ice around the central cask and stirring the acid in the others. They constantly complained, asking what I was doing and grumbling about the hard labor. They could not understand why they should get soaked just to help with such strange tasks. I grew anxious and worked faster, fearing they might quit, as the fools clearly thought I was involved in some dark, supernatural business. I managed to calm them by promising to pay all my debts in full once I finished. They interpreted this to mean I would soon have plenty of cash, and as long as they were paid, they did not care what happened to me. After about four and a half hours, the balloon was inflated. I attached the basket and loaded my equipment, including the condensing device, plenty of water, and compact, nutritious food like pemmican.

Stop the starboard! Stop the larboard! Move ahead on the starboard! Stop her! Let the outside wheel turn slowly! Get that headline out! Quickly now! Get the spring-line out—what are you doing? Wrap it around that stump! Get the gangplank ready—let it go! Engines off! Tom kept whitewashing, ignoring the steamboat. Ben stared for a moment and said, "Hey! You are stuck, aren't you?" Tom did not answer. He studied his last stroke like an artist, brushed again, and checked the result. Ben walked up beside him. Tom wanted the apple, but he kept working. Ben said, "Hello, friend, you have to work, huh?" Tom turned suddenly. "Oh, it is you, Ben! I did not notice you." "I am going swimming. Don't you wish you could? But you would rather work, right? Of course you would!" Tom looked at him and asked, "What do you call work?" "Well, isn't that work?" Tom went back to painting, answering casually, "Maybe it is, maybe it isn't. All I know is that it suits Tom Sawyer." "Come on, you don't mean to say you like it?" The brush kept moving. "Like it? I don't see why I shouldn't. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?" That changed things. Ben stopped eating his apple. Tom brushed carefully, stepped back to check the effect, and added a few touches. Ben watched every move, becoming increasingly interested. Finally, he said, "Tom, let me whitewash a little." Tom thought about it, then shook his head. "No, I don't think that would work, Ben. Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence because it faces the street. If it were the back fence, I wouldn't mind, and neither would she. She is very strict; it has to be done perfectly. I don't think one boy in two thousand can do it right." "Is that so? Come on, let me try. Just a little. I would let you do it if I were you." "Ben, I would like to, honestly. But Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn't let him. Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn't let him either."

She was found dead in her bed the next morning, appearing to have passed away peacefully. Sir Mathew Reid was summoned immediately, but there was nothing to be done, and her funeral was scheduled for the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. She had written her will just days earlier, leaving Lord Arthur her Curzon Street house and all its contents, except for her miniature collection, which went to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which was left to Sybil Merton. The estate was modest, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, urged Lord Arthur to return quickly to settle numerous unpaid bills, as Lady Clementina had never managed her finances well. Lord Arthur was moved by her kindness and felt Mr. Podgers bore a heavy responsibility for the situation. Still, his love for Sybil outweighed everything else, and the knowledge that he had fulfilled his duty brought him peace. He felt truly happy upon arriving at Charing Cross. The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise that nothing would ever separate them again, and they set their wedding date for June 7th. Life felt bright and beautiful once more, and his former joy returned. One day, while he and Sybil were clearing out the Curzon Street house with the solicitor—burning old letters and sorting through drawers—Sybil suddenly cried out in delight. Lord Arthur looked up from his work and smiled, asking what she had found. She held up a charming silver candy box, asking if she could have it since amethysts would not suit her for years. It was the very box that had contained the poison. Lord Arthur started, his face flushing. He had nearly forgotten his actions, and it felt strange that Sybil, the reason for his terrible ordeal, was the one to remind him. He told her she could have it, noting he had given it to Lady Clementina himself. When she asked if she could also have the candy inside, noting she had no idea Lady Clementina enjoyed sweets, Lord Arthur turned deathly pale as a horrifying thought struck him.

The following day was set for the confrontation to ensure our honor remained intact. Drummle arrived with a polite note from Estella confirming she had danced with him several times. I had no choice but to apologize for my previous outburst and retract my earlier claims. Drummle and I sat there glaring at each other for an hour while the rest of the group argued, eventually declaring that our reconciliation was progressing remarkably well. I recount this casually, but it was deeply painful. It devastated me that Estella would show any interest in such a clumsy, dim-witted fool. I believe my reaction stemmed from a genuine, selfless love; I could not bear to see her lower herself to such a man. I would have been miserable regardless of her choice, but a more worthy suitor would have caused me a different kind of grief. I soon discovered that Drummle was pursuing her and she was permitting it. He followed her constantly, and we crossed paths daily. He persisted in his dull way, while Estella kept him on a string, alternating between encouragement and disdain, sometimes flattering him and other times acting as if he were a stranger. The Spider, as Jaggers called him, possessed the patience of his namesake. His arrogant reliance on his wealth and family status often served him as well as true focus. By doggedly watching Estella, he outlasted more impressive rivals, ready to strike at the perfect moment. At an assembly ball in Richmond, where Estella outshone everyone, Drummle hovered over her with her apparent consent. I decided to confront her about him at the first opportunity, which came while she sat alone among the flowers, waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home.

For years, Dorian Gray remained under the spell of that book, or rather, he made no effort to escape it. He acquired nine first-edition copies from Paris, binding them in various hues to match his shifting moods and the erratic impulses of a spirit he often struggled to govern. The protagonist, a remarkable youth who fused romantic and scientific sensibilities, served as a mirror for his own existence, as if his life had been chronicled before he lived it. Unlike the novel’s hero, Dorian never suffered the absurd fear of mirrors or reflective surfaces that plagued the Parisian after his beauty faded. He read the tragic conclusion with a sense of cruel delight, finding a dark satisfaction in the despair of a man who had forfeited the very beauty he prized above all else. His own exquisite appearance, which had captivated Basil Hallward and others, remained untouched by time. Despite the scandalous rumors circulating through London clubs, people found it impossible to believe ill of him upon seeing his face. His youthful purity silenced even the most vulgar men, reminding them of the innocence they had lost. They marveled that someone so graceful could remain untainted by a sordid, sensual era. Frequently, after returning from his long, mysterious excursions, he would retreat to his locked room. With his key in hand, he would stand before the portrait, comparing the decaying, wicked visage on the canvas with the radiant, laughing reflection staring back at him from the glass.

We eventually agreed to reside together for the duration of my city visit. Since my financial situation was slightly more stable than his, I took on the cost of leasing and decorating a decaying, eccentric mansion in a quiet, abandoned corner of the Faubourg St. Germain, a place long avoided due to local superstitions we chose not to investigate. If our daily habits had been public knowledge, we would have been labeled harmless lunatics. We lived in total isolation, receiving no guests. My former acquaintances were unaware of our location, and Dupin had long since vanished from Parisian society. We lived entirely within our own private world. My friend possessed a strange obsession with the night, a quirk I adopted with complete devotion. Since true darkness could not always be with us, we mimicked it. At dawn, we sealed the shutters of our home and lit scented candles that cast only faint, ghostly light. We spent our hours dreaming, reading, writing, or talking until the clock signaled the arrival of real night. We would then walk the streets together, discussing our thoughts or wandering the city to find the mental stimulation that comes from observing the shifting shadows of the crowd. During these walks, I often marveled at Dupin’s analytical prowess. He clearly relished exercising this skill and openly admitted his enjoyment. With a quiet chuckle, he claimed he could see into the hearts of others as if they had windows in their chests, often proving his deep insight into my own mind. At these times, his demeanor became cold and detached, his gaze unfocused, and his voice shifted from a rich tenor to a high, distinct treble that sounded almost petulant.

Certainly not, Duff replied. And, to explain the term yokel for the ladies, I assume you mean this attempt was not made by a countryman, Mr. Losberne said with a smile. That is it, sir, Blathers replied. This is all about the robbery, is it? All, the doctor confirmed. Now, what about this boy the servants are discussing? Blathers asked. Nothing at all, the doctor replied. A frightened servant assumed he was involved in the break-in, but it is pure nonsense. That is easily dismissed, Duff remarked. Blathers nodded, playing with his handcuffs. Who is the boy? What is his story? Where did he come from? He did not just fall from the sky, did he? Of course not, the doctor replied, glancing nervously at the ladies. I know his history, but we can discuss that later. You would like to see where the thieves made their attempt first, I assume? Certainly, Blathers agreed. We should inspect the premises before questioning the servants. That is standard procedure. Lights were brought, and the group went to the small room at the end of the hall to examine the window. They checked the lawn, inspected the shutter with a candle, traced footprints with a lantern, and poked the bushes with a pitchfork. Afterward, Giles and Brittles reenacted their roles in the previous night’s events six times, contradicting each other more frequently with each performance. Once finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room for a private, solemn consultation. Meanwhile, the doctor paced the next room anxiously while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched him. Upon my word, he said, stopping after many rapid turns, I hardly know what to do.

I cannot express the immense joy I felt returning from political turmoil and foreign hardships to the sanctuary of my own home, a place defined by goodness, love, and shared empathy. Had I never left Windsor, these feelings might be less profound, but my time in Greece was marked by fear and the tragic loss of two individuals who embodied greatness. Such misery could not touch the domestic life we cultivated in our secluded forest. While time inevitably left its mark on our expectations, life remained tranquil. Idris, a devoted wife and sister, was a deeply passionate mother. We had three children, but the loss of our second child while I was in Greece shattered her sense of security. Previously, she viewed our children as guaranteed, but now she lived in constant terror that death would claim the others. Any minor illness triggered panic, and she was miserable whenever separated from them, guarding her happiness like a treasure against a thief. Fortunately, her fears were largely unfounded. Alfred, now nine, was an upright, manly boy with a radiant expression and a gentle, independent spirit. Our youngest was still an infant, but he was healthy and his constant energy filled our home with laughter. Clara had outgrown the age that caused Idris such anxiety. She was cherished by everyone for her rare combination of intelligence, innocence, and grace; she was truly the jewel of our family. At the start of winter, nine-year-old Alfred began his studies at Eton. He viewed this as a significant step toward manhood and was appropriately excited. Engaging in shared studies and play further developed his character, highlighting his perseverance, generosity, and steady resolve.

Sydney Carton paused in the street, uncertain of his next move. "Tellson's bank at nine," he mused. "Should I make an appearance in the meantime? Yes, it is a wise precaution for these people to know I am here." He paced the darkening street, weighing the consequences of his decision. Convinced of his plan, he headed toward Saint Antoine. Defarge had mentioned running a wine shop in that district, and Carton found it easily without asking for directions. After locating the shop, he ate at a nearby cafe and fell into a deep sleep. For the first time in years, he had avoided strong spirits, having poured his brandy away the night before. He woke at seven, refreshed, and returned to the streets. Before reaching Saint Antoine, he stopped at a shop window to adjust his cravat, collar, and messy hair. He then entered Defarge's shop. Only Jacques Three was there, drinking at the counter with the Defarges and The Vengeance. Carton sat down and ordered a small wine in broken French. Madame Defarge glanced at him, then studied him more intently before approaching to confirm his order. He repeated it. "English?" she asked, raising her eyebrows. He looked at her as if struggling to process the language, then replied with a heavy foreign accent.

He remained silent on the subject until their guest departed for the evening, but once alone, he addressed his daughter: Jane, I offer my congratulations. You shall be a very happy woman.
