Jane immediately approached him, kissed his cheek, and expressed her gratitude for his kindness. You are a good girl, he answered, and it brings me great joy to imagine you so well established. I have no doubt you will thrive together. Your dispositions are quite similar. You are both so accommodating that you will never reach a decision, so easygoing that your servants will surely deceive you, and so generous that you will constantly overspend. I hope not, she replied. Such financial recklessness would be inexcusable in me. Overspend! My dear Mr. Bennet, his wife exclaimed, what are you saying? He possesses four or five thousand a year, if not more. Turning to her daughter, she continued, Oh, my dear Jane, I am overjoyed! I am certain I will not sleep a wink tonight. I knew this would happen. I always insisted it must eventually come to pass. I was certain your beauty could not be for nothing! I recall thinking, the moment I saw him arrive in Hertfordshire last year, how likely it was that you would unite. He is the most handsome young man ever seen! Wickham and Lydia were entirely forgotten. Jane was, without question, her favorite child, and for that moment, she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters soon began soliciting her for future favors. Mary requested access to the library at Netherfield, while Kitty pleaded for several balls there each winter. From that point on, Bingley became a daily visitor at Longbourn, arriving often before breakfast and staying until after supper, unless some detestable neighbor forced him to accept a dinner invitation. Elizabeth had little time to converse with her sister, as Jane focused entirely on him while he was present. However, she proved useful to them during their brief separations. When Jane was away, he sought Elizabeth out to speak of her, and when Bingley left, Jane consistently turned to her for the same comfort. He has made me so happy, she remarked one evening, by revealing that he was completely unaware of my presence in town last spring!

If you look at a star indirectly—using the outer edges of your retina, which are more sensitive to faint light—you see it more clearly. Its brightness actually fades if you stare directly at it. While more light hits your eye when looking straight on, the indirect view allows for better perception. Thinking too deeply can confuse and weaken the mind; even Venus can disappear from the sky if you study it with too much intensity. Regarding these murders, let us investigate for ourselves before forming an opinion. It will be an interesting exercise, and Le Bon once did me a favor I have not forgotten. We will visit the scene. I know the Prefect of Police and can easily get permission. We received authorization and went to the Rue Morgue, a dreary street between Rue Richelieu and Rue St. Roch. It was late afternoon when we arrived. The house was easy to find because a crowd was still gathered across the street, staring at the closed shutters. It was a typical Parisian building with a gateway and a small concierge booth. Before entering, we walked around the block and through an alley to examine the back of the house. Dupin studied the entire neighborhood and the building with a level of detail I found puzzling. We returned to the front, rang the bell, and were admitted by the police. We went upstairs to the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body was found and where the victims still lay. The room remained in its original state of disarray. I saw nothing that had not already been reported in the newspaper, but Dupin examined everything, including the bodies. Accompanied by a guard, we then inspected the other rooms and the yard.

My friend carefully drove a peg into the ground exactly where the beetle had landed, then pulled a tape measure from his pocket. He attached one end to the nearest point on the tree trunk, extended it to the peg, and continued fifty feet further in that same line while Jupiter cleared the brush with a scythe. At that spot, he drove a second peg and marked a rough four-foot circle around it. He handed spades to Jupiter and me, urging us to start digging immediately. Honestly, I had no desire for this task; I was exhausted, night was falling, and I wanted to decline. Yet, I saw no way out and feared upsetting my friend. I considered forcing him home, but I knew Jupiter would never help me oppose his master. I assumed Legrand had fallen victim to local superstitions about buried treasure, reinforced by the beetle and Jupiter’s insistence that it was made of solid gold. Such ideas easily sway a fragile mind, especially when they align with existing obsessions like his belief that the insect was his key to fortune. Frustrated and confused, I decided to make the best of it, hoping that digging would quickly prove his theory wrong. We lit our lanterns and began working with misplaced intensity. As the light illuminated our group and tools, I realized how strange and suspicious we must have looked to any accidental observer. We dug steadily for two hours.

He chose Friday, August 17th, for his appearance, spending the day reviewing his wardrobe before selecting a wide-brimmed hat with a red feather, a ruffled burial shroud, and a corroded dagger. As evening fell, a fierce rainstorm erupted, rattling the house’s doors and windows—the exact weather he preferred. His plan was to slip into Washington Otis’s room, gibber from the foot of the bed, and stab his own throat three times to the accompaniment of slow music. He held a grudge against Washington for repeatedly scrubbing away the Canterville bloodstain with detergent. After terrifying the youth, he intended to visit the Minister and his wife, placing a cold hand on her forehead while whispering graveyard secrets into her husband’s ear. He remained undecided about Virginia, who had been gentle and never insulted him; he thought a few hollow groans from her wardrobe or clawing at her bedsheets would suffice. He was resolved to punish the twins by sitting on their chests to induce nightmares, then standing between their beds as a frozen, green corpse before shedding his shroud to crawl about as the 'Suicide’s Skeleton,' a role he had perfected. At ten-thirty, he heard the family retiring. The twins’ laughter delayed him, but by eleven-fifteen, silence fell. As midnight struck, he emerged. An owl struck the glass, a raven croaked, and the wind moaned like a lost soul, yet the Otis family slept on, oblivious, while the Minister’s steady snoring rose above the storm.

There was something so striking about the growing intensity in Mr. Wopsle’s gaze, and he seemed so preoccupied and bewildered, that I could not understand it. I pondered it long after he had ascended into the clouds within a large watch-case, and I still could not make sense of it. I was still thinking about it an hour later when I left the theater and found him waiting for me by the door. How are you? I asked, shaking his hand as we walked down the street. I saw that you saw me. Saw you, Mr. Pip? he replied. Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there? Who else? It is the strangest thing, Mr. Wopsle said, drifting back into his vacant expression, and yet I could swear it was him. Growing alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain. Whether I would have noticed him initially if you had not been there, I cannot be certain, he continued in that same distant manner, yet I think I would have. Involuntarily, I looked around, as I usually did when heading home, for his mysterious words gave me a chill. Oh, he cannot be in sight, Mr. Wopsle said. He left before I went off stage. I saw him go. Given my reasons for suspicion, I even doubted this poor actor. I suspected a plot to trick me into an admission. Therefore, I watched him as we walked but said nothing. I had a ridiculous notion that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw you were completely unaware of him, sitting behind you like a ghost. My earlier chill returned, but I resolved to remain silent, as it was possible he was being used to make me link these references to Provis. Of course, I was certain Provis had not been there. I imagine you are puzzled by me, Mr. Pip; I can see that you are. But it is so strange! You will hardly believe what I am about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself if you told me. Indeed? I asked. Yes, indeed. Mr. Pip, do you remember that Christmas Day long ago, when you were a child and I dined at Gargery’s, and soldiers came to the door to have handcuffs mended? I remember it very well. And you remember the chase after two convicts, that we joined in, that Gargery carried you on his back, and that I took the lead while you kept up with me as best you could?

May I ask you two questions? You may ask, Monks replied with surprise, but whether I answer is another matter. That makes three, Mr. Bumble joked. Is that what you expected from me? the matron asked. It is, Monks replied. What is your other question? What do you plan to do with it? Can it be used against me? Never, Monks said. Nor against me. Look here, but do not step forward, or your life is forfeit. He shoved the table aside, pulled an iron ring, and opened a trapdoor at Mr. Bumble’s feet, causing him to scramble back. Look down, Monks said, lowering his lantern. Do not fear me. I could have dropped you in while you were sitting over it if I had wanted. The matron approached the edge, and Mr. Bumble followed, driven by curiosity. Below, the rain-swollen water rushed rapidly, its roar drowning out all other sounds as it churned against slimy wooden piles. Once a water-mill, the site now featured only rotting stakes and broken machinery that the river surged past. If you threw a body down there, where would it be by morning? Monks asked, swinging the lantern. Twelve miles downriver and shredded, Mr. Bumble replied, recoiling. Monks pulled the packet from his coat, tied it to a lead weight, and dropped it into the stream. It vanished into the water without a sound. The three looked at each other, breathing easier. There, Monks said, slamming the trapdoor shut. If the sea ever gives up its dead, it will keep its gold and silver, and that trash along with it. We are finished here. By all means, Mr. Bumble agreed quickly. You will keep your mouth shut, won't you? Monks asked with a threatening glare.

I rushed to her, held her close, and pleaded, "Speak to me, darling! What is wrong?" Her head slumped against my chest as she whispered, "Hello-Central!" I shouted to Clarence to summon the king's doctor immediately. Within moments, I was at the child's crib while Sandy sent servants racing through the palace. I recognized the illness instantly: croup. I leaned down and whispered, "Wake up, sweetheart." She opened her eyes slowly and murmured, "Papa." That gave me hope. I gathered sulfur and prepared the croup kettle myself; I never wait for doctors when my family is ill. I had plenty of experience nursing them, and I could often soothe this child when even her mother could not. Sir Launcelot soon strode past the hall, dressed in his finest armor on his way to the stock exchange. He served as president of the board, which was now comprised of the Knights of the Round Table conducting business. Despite his busy schedule and his aggressive financial dealings, he stopped when he saw his favorite child was sick. He tossed his helmet aside and immediately helped prepare the croup kettle. Sandy built a tent over the crib with blankets, and we were soon ready. Launcelot and I filled the kettle with lime, carbolic acid, and lactic acid, added water, and directed the steam under the canopy. Everything was set, and we sat on either side of the crib to begin our watch.

The Attorney-General told the jury that the young prisoner was a veteran in the treasonous activities that now threatened his life. He claimed this communication with the enemy was not recent, but that the prisoner had been traveling between France and England for years on secret, suspicious business. He argued that if treason could ever succeed, the man’s guilt might have remained hidden, but Providence had inspired a courageous patriot to uncover the schemes and report them to the government. This witness, he promised, would appear before them. He described this man as a noble figure who had once been the prisoner’s friend but, upon discovering his treachery, chose to sacrifice that friendship for the good of the country. While Britain did not erect statues to such heroes like the ancients did, he deserved one. The Attorney-General then spoke of the contagious nature of patriotism, noting that this witness’s example had inspired the prisoner’s own servant to search his master’s belongings and steal his private papers. He anticipated that the defense might criticize this servant, but he insisted he respected the man more than his own family and urged the jury to do the same. Finally, he stated that the testimony of these two men, along with the recovered documents, would prove the prisoner had been supplying the enemy with detailed information about British military forces and their readiness, leaving no doubt of his guilt.

Listen to me; I have mastered the language of despair. I am despair itself, a strange, triumphant force. Yet that is a lie, for the dark wave is not bitter. We close our eyes in a gentle sleep, and upon waking, we are free. Do not delay, you slow one! Look at this pleasant potion. I am a spirit of good, not a mere woman, inviting you to drink. As I spoke, I watched his face. His exquisite beauty and the heavenly compassion in his eyes softened my stern despair into gentle grief. I saw his own eyes grow moist as he took my hands and sat beside me. He said, This is a sad path you invite me to follow, and your pain must be deep to harbor such thoughts. You long for death, yet you fear it and want me to join you. I lack your courage; even with you, I dare not die. Listen to me before you try to convince me, even if your desperate eloquence makes death seem more inviting than heaven. I have also nurtured such thoughts and longed for death, but I have finally conquered that phantom. Just as you played the role of Despair, I will act as your guide to lead you safely from its dark cavern. Listen and let these words soften you. We do not understand this world or its mix of good and evil, yet we are placed here to live and hope. I do not know what we should hope for, but we must seek some greater good; that is our task. If misfortune strikes, we must fight it and continue our search. Whether this leads to another life or simply prepares the way for those who follow, I do not know.

The narrow alleys eventually opened into a wide, vacant area filled with animal pens and signs of a livestock market. Sikes slowed down, as the girl could no longer keep up with their frantic pace. He turned to Oliver and gruffly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand. When Oliver hesitated and glanced around, Sikes growled, "Do you hear me?" They stood in a dark corner, far from any passersby. Realizing resistance was useless, Oliver held out his hand, which Nancy gripped tightly. Sikes grabbed Oliver’s other hand and called, "Here, Bull’s-Eye!" The dog looked up and growled. Sikes pressed his hand against Oliver’s throat and warned, "Listen, boy! If he says a single word, grab him! Understand?" The dog growled again, licking his lips and staring at Oliver as if eager to tear out his throat. "He’s as ready as any person, I swear," Sikes said, looking at the dog with grim approval. "Now you know what to expect, so go ahead and shout if you want; the dog will put a stop to that quickly. Move on, kid!" Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail at the praise, let out one more warning growl at Oliver, and led the way. They were crossing Smithfield, though it could have been anywhere for all Oliver knew. The night was dark and foggy. Shop lights barely pierced the thick mist, which shrouded the streets in gloom and made the unfamiliar surroundings feel even more unsettling. They had walked only a short distance when a deep church bell began to toll. At the first sound, both his captors stopped and looked toward the noise. "It’s eight o’clock, Bill," Nancy said when the bell stopped. "What’s the point of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?" Sikes replied. "I wonder if they can hear it," Nancy mused. "Of course they can," Sikes answered. "It was fair time when I was arrested, and I could hear every penny trumpet squeaking. Once I was locked up for the night, the noise outside made the jail feel so silent that I could have smashed my head against the iron door."

Suddenly, Mr. Podgers dropped Lord Arthur’s right hand and grabbed his left, leaning down so far to inspect it that his glasses nearly touched the palm. For a second, his face turned pale with horror, but he quickly regained his composure. Looking up at Lady Windermere, he forced a smile and said, It is the hand of a charming young man. Of course it is, Lady Windermere replied, but will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know. All charming young men are, Mr. Podgers said. I do not think a husband should be too fascinating, Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully, it is dangerous. My dear, they are never too fascinating, Lady Windermere cried. But I want details. Details are the only things that matter. What will happen to Lord Arthur? Well, within the next few months, Lord Arthur will go on a voyage. Oh, his honeymoon, of course! And he will lose a relative. Not his sister, I hope? Lady Jedburgh asked sadly. Certainly not his sister, Mr. Podgers answered with a wave of his hand, just a distant relative. Well, I am disappointed, Lady Windermere said. I have nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives anymore. Still, she should probably have a black silk dress ready; it is always useful for church. Now, let us go to supper. They have likely eaten everything, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so distracted by politics lately that I am never sure about him. I wish General Boulanger would stay quiet. Duchess, you must be tired? Not at all, dear Gladys, the Duchess replied, waddling toward the door. I have enjoyed myself, and the palm reader is fascinating. Flora, where is my fan? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas. And my lace shawl? Thank you, Sir Thomas, you are very kind. The woman finally made it downstairs, dropping her perfume bottle only twice. Throughout this, Lord Arthur Savile stood by the fireplace, feeling a sense of dread and impending doom. He smiled sadly at his sister as she walked past on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking beautiful in pink silk and pearls. He barely heard Lady Windermere calling him to follow. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the fear that anything could separate them brought tears to his eyes.

I must warn you that I intend to tell Sybil everything. She is joining me for lunch tomorrow to discuss hats, and if Mr. Podgers discovers you have a bad temper, gout, or a secret wife in Bayswater, I will certainly inform her. Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. I am not afraid, he replied. Sybil knows me as well as I know her. I am sorry to hear that. A successful marriage is built on mutual misunderstanding. I am not being cynical, merely experienced, which is much the same. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile wants his palm read. Do not mention his engagement to one of London’s most beautiful women, as that was in the Morning Post a month ago. Dear Lady Windermere, the Marchioness of Jedburgh cried, let Mr. Podgers stay. He just told me I should be an actress, and I am fascinated. If he said that, I am taking him away. Come here, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand. Lady Jedburgh pouted as she rose. If I cannot be an actress, I must at least be in the audience. We all will be, Lady Windermere said. Now, Mr. Podgers, tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is a favorite of mine. When Mr. Podgers looked at Lord Arthur’s hand, he turned pale and fell silent. He shuddered, and his bushy eyebrows twitched in a strange, nervous way. Beads of sweat appeared on his yellow forehead, and his fat fingers turned cold and clammy. Lord Arthur noticed this agitation and felt fear for the first time. He wanted to run from the room but forced himself to stay. He preferred to know the worst rather than endure this terrible uncertainty. I am waiting, Mr. Podgers, he said. We are all waiting, Lady Windermere added impatiently, but the palmist remained silent. I suppose Arthur is going on the stage, Lady Jedburgh remarked, and Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him after your scolding.

Men marry out of exhaustion and women out of curiosity; both end up disappointed. I doubt I will marry, Harry. I am too much in love, which is one of your own sayings that I am now putting into practice. Who is she? Lord Henry asked. Dorian Gray blushed and said, An actress. Lord Henry shrugged. That is a common start. You would not say that if you saw her, Harry. Who is she? Her name is Sibyl Vane. I have never heard of her. No one has yet, but they will. She is a genius. My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are merely decorative. They have nothing to say, but they say it charmingly. They represent the triumph of matter over mind, just as men represent the triumph of mind over morals. Harry, how can you say that? It is true. I am studying women right now, so I should know. There are only two kinds: the plain and the colorful. The plain ones are useful for appearing respectable at dinner. The others are charming but make the mistake of using makeup to look young, whereas our grandmothers used it to appear witty. Now, women are satisfied just looking younger than their daughters. There are only five women in London worth talking to, and two of them are social outcasts. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her? Your views terrify me, Harry. Never mind that. How long? About three weeks. Where did you meet her? I will tell you, but do not be unkind. It never would have happened if I had not met you. You gave me a wild desire to understand life. For days, I felt a pulse in my veins. Walking through the park or down Piccadilly, I looked at everyone and wondered about their lives with a frantic curiosity. Some fascinated me, while others terrified me. The air felt poisoned, and I developed a passion for new sensations.

It took some time before I could focus on managing the balloon. When I finally checked it, I was relieved to find it undamaged. My tools were secure, and I had not lost any ballast or supplies, as I had packed them carefully enough to prevent such a loss. Checking my watch, I saw it was six o’clock. I was still climbing rapidly, and my barometer showed an altitude of three and three-quarter miles. Below me, a small, dark, oblong object floated in the ocean, looking much like a domino. Using my telescope, I identified it as a British ninety-four-gun ship, struggling against the waves and heading west-southwest. Beyond that ship, there was nothing but the sea, the sky, and the sun, which had risen long ago. It is time I explain to your Excellencies the purpose of my dangerous journey. You should know that financial ruin in Rotterdam had driven me to consider suicide. I did not hate life itself, but I could no longer endure the misery of my situation. While I wanted to live, I was exhausted by my circumstances, and a book I found at a stall sparked an idea. I decided to leave the world behind while still remaining alive. To put it simply, I resolved to travel to the moon. So that you do not think me entirely mad, I will explain why I believed this difficult and dangerous feat was possible for a bold spirit. First, I considered the moon’s distance from Earth. The average distance between the centers of the two bodies is about 237,000 miles. However, because the moon’s orbit is elliptical and the Earth sits at one focus, I realized that if I could meet the moon at its closest point, or perigee, that distance would be significantly reduced.

Do not assume I failed to see it as a misfortune in its own right. Rest assured, they were entirely at ease. Perhaps that does not improve my opinion of the situation. Such a crowd of women and children have no business being comfortable at sea. My dear Frederick, you speak foolishly. What would become of us sailors' wives, who frequently need transport to join our husbands, if everyone shared your sentiments? My sentiments did not stop me from transporting Mrs. Harville and her family to Plymouth. I dislike hearing you speak like a dandy, treating women as delicate creatures rather than rational beings. None of us expect calm seas forever. My dear, the Admiral remarked, once he has a wife, he will change his tune. If we survive to see another war, we shall see him act as we have, grateful to anyone who brings his wife to him. Indeed we shall. I am finished, Captain Wentworth declared. Once married people start telling me I will change my mind, I simply insist I will not, and the conversation ends there. He rose and departed. You must have traveled extensively, Mrs. Musgrove remarked to Mrs. Croft. Quite a bit during my fifteen years of marriage, though others have done more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times and made one trip to the East Indies, alongside various domestic ports like Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. I never ventured past the Straits or visited the West Indies; we do not consider Bermuda or the Bahamas part of the West Indies, you know. Mrs. Musgrove had no objection, having never labeled them as such in her life. I assure you, Mrs. Croft continued, that the accommodations on a man-of-war are excellent, particularly on larger vessels. On a frigate, space is limited, yet any sensible woman can be content; I can honestly say my happiest years were spent aboard ship. As long as we were together, there was nothing to fear.

April 7th. I woke early and was thrilled to finally see what I am certain is the North Pole. It lay directly beneath me, though I had climbed to such a height that I could not see it clearly. Based on my altitude readings between April 2nd and the time my barometer stopped, I estimate that by 4:00 A.M. on April 7th, I had reached at least 7,254 miles above sea level. This may seem extreme, but it is likely an underestimate. I could see the entire northern hemisphere spread out like a map, with the equator forming my horizon. While the unexplored Arctic regions were directly below, they were too small and distant to study in detail. Still, the view was fascinating. Beyond the known limits of human discovery, a vast sheet of ice stretches out. It starts flat, becomes a level plane, and eventually curves inward, ending at the Pole in a sharp, circular center. This dark spot, which looked blacker than anything else on the globe, measured about sixty-five seconds in diameter from my perspective. By noon, this circle had shrunk, and by 7:00 P.M., it vanished as my balloon drifted toward the equator. April 8th. The earth appears smaller today, and its color and overall appearance have noticeably changed.

I wish we had a donkey. Jane, Miss Bates, and I could ride them, with my dear husband walking alongside. I really must talk to him about buying one. In the country, I consider it a necessity. No matter how many hobbies a woman has, she cannot stay home forever, and long walks are difficult when it is dusty in summer or muddy in winter. You will find neither between Donwell and Highbury, as the lane is never dusty and is currently dry. Still, come by donkey if you prefer; you can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I want everything to be exactly to your liking. I am sure you do. I truly appreciate you, my friend. Despite your blunt manner, I know you have a warm heart. I tell Mr. Elton that you are quite a character. Believe me, Knightley, I am grateful for your thoughtfulness regarding this plan. You have suggested exactly what I wanted. Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse to join the party, knowing that sitting outdoors to eat would make the older man ill. He had to ensure Mr. Woodhouse was not tempted into discomfort under the guise of a pleasant morning drive. The invitation was made in good faith, and Mr. Woodhouse agreed. He had not visited Donwell in two years. He decided that he, Emma, and Harriet could go on a fine morning. He could sit with Mrs. Weston while the girls walked in the gardens, provided it was not damp. He wanted to see the old house again and meet the Eltons and his other neighbors. He saw no objection to the trip and thought it was kind and sensible of Mr. Knightley to invite them, as it was much better than dining out, which he disliked. Mr. Knightley was fortunate that everyone agreed so readily. The invitation was so well received that everyone felt it was a personal compliment. Emma and Harriet were excited, and Mr. Weston promised to bring Frank along if possible. Although Mr. Knightley would have preferred otherwise, he politely agreed that he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston promised to write immediately to convince him to come.

With their agreement settled, the contract was sealed with another cup of peppermint tea, which helped calm the lady’s nerves. As she drank, she informed Mr. Bumble that the old woman had passed away. Very good, he said, sipping his drink. I will stop by Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to collect the body tomorrow. Was that what upset you, my dear? It was nothing specific, she replied evasively. It must have been something, Mr. Bumble insisted. Won’t you tell your own B.? Not now, she said. One of these days, after we are married. After we are married! Mr. Bumble exclaimed. It wasn’t any insolence from those male paupers, was it? No, no, love, she quickly interrupted. If I thought any of them had dared to look at your lovely face with vulgar eyes, he continued. They wouldn’t have dared, she replied. They had better not, Mr. Bumble said, clenching his fist. Let any man, parishioner or otherwise, try it, and I promise he won’t do it a second time. Though his words were harsh, his aggressive gestures convinced the lady of his devotion, and she admiringly called him a dove. The dove then turned up his collar, donned his hat, and after an affectionate embrace, stepped back into the cold night. He paused briefly in the men’s ward to berate the paupers, confirming his ability to manage the workhouse with necessary severity. Satisfied, Mr. Bumble left with a light heart and visions of his future promotion, which occupied his thoughts until he reached the undertaker’s shop. Since Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry were out and Noah Claypole was too lazy to close the shop, the doors remained open despite the late hour. Mr. Bumble tapped his cane on the counter, but receiving no response, he noticed a light in the back parlor. He peeked inside and was quite surprised by what he saw.

April 7th. I woke early and was delighted to finally witness what I could only conclude was the North Pole. It lay directly below me, yet I had climbed to such a height that clear observation was impossible. Based on the barometric data recorded between April 2nd and the moment the instrument failed, I estimate that by four A.M. on April 7th, I had reached an altitude of at least 7,254 miles. While this seems vast, the calculation likely underestimates the true distance. I could see the entire major diameter of the globe; the northern hemisphere appeared as an orthographic map, with the equator marking my horizon. Your Excellencies can understand that the unexplored Arctic regions, while positioned directly beneath me and free from foreshortening, were too small and distant for precise study. Still, the view was remarkable. Beyond the known limits of human exploration, a nearly continuous sheet of ice stretches northward. It flattens initially, becomes a level plane, and eventually turns concave, ending at the Pole in a sharply defined circular center. This spot, which subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds, was darker than any other part of the hemisphere, occasionally appearing as an impenetrable black. By noon, this circle had shrunk, and by seven P.M., it vanished as the balloon drifted toward the western edge of the ice and moved rapidly toward the equator. April 8th. The earth’s apparent diameter has noticeably decreased, and its overall color and aspect have shifted significantly.

We finally lightened the box by removing two-thirds of its contents, allowing us to lift it from the hole with some effort. We hid the removed items in the brambles, leaving the dog to guard them with Jupiter’s strict orders not to move or bark until we returned. We hurried home with the chest, reaching the hut safely but exhausted at one in the morning. Too tired to continue, we rested until two, ate, and then headed back to the hills with three sturdy sacks we were lucky to find. Shortly before four, we reached the pit, divided the remaining loot as equally as possible, and returned to the hut with our golden burden just as dawn broke over the treetops. We were completely spent, yet the intense excitement kept us from sleeping. After a restless three or four hours, we rose by mutual agreement to examine our treasure. The chest had been filled to the brim, and we spent the entire day and most of the next night sorting through it. Everything had been tossed in without order. Once organized, we realized our wealth was even greater than expected. We estimated the gold coins to be worth over four hundred and fifty thousand dollars based on current exchange rates. There was no silver, only antique gold from France, Spain, Germany, and a few English guineas, along with some unfamiliar tokens. Several heavy, worn coins were impossible to identify, and there was no American currency. The jewels were harder to value. We found one hundred and ten large, fine diamonds, eighteen brilliant rubies, three hundred and ten beautiful emeralds, twenty-one sapphires, and an opal. These stones had been pried from their settings, which we found hammered flat, likely to prevent them from being identified.

This marriage is right. I doubted it at first, but I see it now. The gods created Sibyl Vane for you; without her, you would be incomplete. Thanks, Basil, Dorian Gray replied, pressing his hand. I knew you would understand. Harry is so cynical he scares me. But the orchestra is starting. It is terrible, but it only lasts five minutes. Then the curtain rises, and you will see the girl to whom I have dedicated my life and everything good in me. Fifteen minutes later, amidst loud applause, Sibyl Vane appeared on stage. She was lovely, one of the most beautiful creatures Lord Henry had ever seen. She possessed a shy, fawn-like grace, and her cheeks flushed as she looked at the enthusiastic crowd. Basil Hallward stood up to applaud, while Dorian Gray sat motionless, staring at her like a man in a dream. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, whispering that she was charming. The scene was the Capulet house, and Romeo had entered with his friends. As the music played, Sibyl moved through the group of poorly dressed actors like a creature from another world. She swayed like a plant in water, her throat curved like a lily, and her hands looked like cool ivory. Yet, she seemed strangely listless. She showed no joy when she looked at Romeo. The lines she spoke were delivered in a completely artificial way. Her voice was beautiful, but the tone was false, draining the life from the verse and making the passion feel unreal. Dorian Gray turned pale as he watched her, feeling puzzled and anxious. His friends remained silent, as she appeared completely incompetent to them.

How could I, a confused village boy, avoid the same contradictions that even the wisest men face daily? I told Biddy that while her warnings might be true, I still admired Estella deeply. I buried my face in my hands and pulled my hair, feeling like a fool for my misplaced feelings. I knew I deserved to be punished for my stupidity. Biddy, being wise, stopped arguing. She gently removed my hands from my hair and patted my shoulder. I cried into my sleeve, feeling sorry for myself, though I did not know who to blame. Biddy told me she was glad I trusted her and promised to keep my secrets. She hinted that if she were still my teacher, she would give me a difficult lesson, but she knew I had moved past her guidance. With a sigh, she stood up and asked if we should walk further or head home. I hugged her and promised to always tell her everything. She replied that I would only do so until I became a gentleman. I insisted I would never be one, so my promise would last forever. Biddy looked toward the ships and whispered softly before asking again if we should walk or go home. We chose to walk further as the summer afternoon faded into a beautiful evening.

There was a strange, enchanting quality to it all. It felt as if he had finally awakened from a long, dreamlike sleep, much like the legendary figures of old. Diana was gone, and his friends had either changed or passed away, leaving me as the only person he had left to love. The woods, mountains, and waters of Loch Lomond became infinitely more precious to me now that I had such a beloved companion for my walks. I explored every beautiful island, waterfall, and shaded path with my father. His conversation broadened my perspective, making me feel as though I had been reborn with a fresh sense of life. Before his arrival, my existence had been like a small, quiet stream destined to vanish unnoticed in its native fields. Now, it felt like a vibrant river winding through a beautiful landscape. I did not realize then that it would eventually reach a desolate desert, where jagged rocks would tear at its waters and reflect a distorted, hideous scene. Life was brilliant, and I began to learn how to hope, not realizing that nothing brings more bitter despair than hope destroyed. Is it not strange how quickly grief can follow such divine happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, only to find bitterness at the bottom of its sweetness. My heart was full of calm, deep affection, and I had no idea that love could lead to such misery. I was taught this lesson in a way few are forced to endure. I still mourn those few months of paradise; I broke no rules and ate no forbidden fruit, yet I was ruthlessly cast out. My companion was the one who faltered, and I was pulled down with him. But I digress; let sorrow come in its own time, for I can still speak of happiness at this point in my story. Three months of this delightful companionship passed before my aunt fell ill. I spent a month nursing her, but her condition was fatal. Her death left me inconsolable for a long time. Death is terrifying to the living; the bonds of habit are so powerful that even without deep affection, the heart suffers agony when they are broken.

He could not help it. It infuriated him to think that Becky Thatcher did not even realize he was alive. In truth, she saw him perfectly well; she knew she was winning her battle and felt satisfied to see him suffer just as she had. Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom made excuses about urgent tasks he had to finish, but the girl kept talking. He thought, "I wish she would leave me alone." Finally, he had to walk away, and she innocently mentioned she would be nearby when school ended. He hurried off, resenting her presence. "Any other boy!" Tom thought, grinding his teeth. "Anyone but that show-off from Saint Louis who thinks he is so fancy! I beat you once, and I will do it again. Just wait until I catch you!" He began shadowboxing, punching and kicking the air until he felt satisfied with the imaginary fight. Tom ran home at noon. He could not stand Amy’s happiness or his own jealousy any longer. Becky went back to looking at pictures with Alfred, but as time passed without Tom appearing to witness her triumph, she lost interest. She grew sad and distracted, listening for his footsteps, but he never came. Eventually, she felt miserable and regretted taking things so far. When Alfred kept trying to show her pictures, she snapped, "Leave me alone! I don't care about them!" and walked away crying. Alfred tried to follow and comfort her, but she shouted, "Go away! I hate you!" Alfred stopped, confused and hurt. He soon realized the truth: she had only used him to make Tom Sawyer jealous.

I recited the beautiful passage about Dante entering the terrestrial Paradise, imagining how wonderful it would be to walk those banks and see the chariot of light descend, bringing back my long-lost father. I pictured myself weaving a crown from the lovely flowers there, singing my father’s favorite song, 'sul margine d’un rio.' I imagined my voice drifting through the still air to tell him I had arrived. The sadness would vanish from my face, and I would look into his eyes, which always shone with innocent love. Thinking of his gaze made me weep, though I kept quiet to avoid breaking the spell. I was so lost in this daydream that I didn't notice where I was walking until I reached down to pick a flower on that barren plain, only to realize no flowers grew there. I woke from my reverie, completely disoriented. The sun had set, and the pink glow in the clouds was fading. A cold wind blew across the plain, and I could not recognize my surroundings. I tried to find my way, but the encroaching darkness hid every landmark. Eventually, the night became pitch black. Exhausted, and knowing my servant was staying in a nearby village so my absence would go unnoticed, I decided to sleep where I was. I was too tired to continue. The air was cold, but I was used to the elements after two years of wandering alone. I lay on the grass in total darkness. There was no sound; the insects were silent, and the barren land offered no shelter for any other creatures. A profound silence filled the air, calming my senses while stirring my soul, as my mind raced through endless thoughts.

His manner was intensely stubborn, and "that cursed bug" were the only words he spoke throughout our trek. I carried two dark lanterns, while Legrand held the scarab dangling from a piece of whip-cord, swinging it like a magician as he walked. Seeing this clear sign of his mental decline, I nearly wept. I decided to indulge his whim for now, hoping to intervene more effectively later. My attempts to learn the purpose of our journey failed; having convinced me to join him, he refused to discuss anything else, answering my inquiries only with "we shall see!" We crossed the island's creek in a skiff and climbed the mainland's high ground, heading northwest through a wild, desolate landscape devoid of human tracks. Legrand moved with purpose, pausing briefly only to check landmarks he had apparently set previously. After two hours, as the sun dipped low, we reached an even bleaker region. It was a plateau near the top of a steep, heavily forested hill, scattered with massive boulders that seemed held in place only by the trees they leaned against. Deep ravines added to the grim atmosphere. The platform we reached was choked with brambles, requiring a scythe to clear. Following Legrand's orders, Jupiter cut a path to the base of a towering tulip-tree. Standing among several oaks, it surpassed them all in the splendor of its leaves, the reach of its limbs, and its overall majestic stature.

Winters on Sullivan’s Island are rarely harsh, and fires are seldom needed in the autumn. However, in mid-October of that year, a day arrived with a sudden, biting chill. Just before sunset, I pushed through the evergreens to reach my friend’s hut. I had not visited in weeks, as I lived in Charleston nine miles away, and travel was much more difficult then than it is now. I knocked, but receiving no answer, I found the hidden key, unlocked the door, and entered. A fire blazed on the hearth—a welcome surprise. I removed my coat, sat in an armchair by the logs, and waited for my hosts. They arrived shortly after dark and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, grinning broadly, hurried to prepare marsh-hens for dinner. Legrand was in one of his typical states of intense excitement. He had discovered a new type of shellfish and, with Jupiter’s help, had captured a beetle he believed was a unique species. He wanted my opinion on it the next day. Why not tonight? I asked, warming my hands and wishing the beetle were elsewhere. Legrand explained that he had foolishly lent the bug to Lieutenant G from the fort earlier that day. He insisted I stay the night so Jupiter could retrieve it at sunrise. He described the creature as a brilliant, gold-colored beetle the size of a hickory nut, marked with three black spots. Jupiter interrupted, insisting that the bug was made of solid gold, noting how unusually heavy it felt.

Waking up eventually, I would check the cause of a disturbance, perhaps spotting a steamboat chugging upstream, so distant toward the far bank that I could only distinguish if it had a stern or side wheel. Then, for an hour, there would be nothing to see or hear—just pure solitude. Later, a raft would drift past in the distance, likely with a fellow chopping wood, as they often did; I would watch the axe flash downward, yet hear nothing until the blade rose again, when the dull thud finally reached us across the water. We spent our days idling, soaking in the quiet. Once, during a dense fog, passing rafts banged tin pans to warn off steamboats. A vessel drifted so near we could clearly hear the crew swearing and laughing, yet they remained invisible, which felt eerie, like ghosts haunting the air. Jim insisted they were spirits, but I countered that ghosts would not curse the fog. When night fell, we pushed off, letting the current carry us while we smoked and dangled our legs in the water. We remained naked whenever the mosquitoes allowed, as the clothes from Buck’s family felt too restrictive, and I never cared much for dressing up anyway. Occasionally, the river belonged entirely to us. We would watch the distant banks and islands, spotting a faint candle glow from a cabin window or the occasional light on a passing raft, sometimes accompanied by the sound of a fiddle or a song. Life on a raft is wonderful. We would lie on our backs beneath the star-speckled sky, debating whether the stars were created or simply happened. Jim believed they were made, but I argued they just happened, as creating so many would have taken far too long.

This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to retain at Lady Canterville’s request. She curtsied as they arrived and said, 'Welcome to Canterville Chase.' They followed her through the Tudor hall into a library paneled in black oak, featuring a large stained-glass window. Tea was prepared, and they sat to look around while Mrs. Umney served them. Suddenly, Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain by the fireplace. Unaware of its history, she remarked, 'I fear something has been spilled there.' The housekeeper replied quietly, 'Blood has been spilled on that spot.' 'How horrid,' Mrs. Otis exclaimed. 'I dislike bloodstains in a sitting room. It must be removed.' The old woman smiled mysteriously. 'It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, murdered there by her husband, Sir Simon, in 1575. Sir Simon vanished nine years later under strange circumstances. His body was never found, but his spirit haunts the house. The stain is famous and cannot be removed.' 'Nonsense,' Washington Otis declared. 'Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover will clean it instantly.' Before the terrified housekeeper could stop him, he knelt and scrubbed the floor with a cleaning stick. The stain vanished. 'I knew Pinkerton would work,' he said triumphantly. Immediately, a flash of lightning illuminated the room, a thunderclap made them jump, and Mrs. Umney fainted. 'What a monstrous climate!' the American Minister remarked, lighting a cigar. 'England is so crowded they lack decent weather. Emigration is the only solution.' 'My dear Hiram,' Mrs. Otis cried, 'what can we do with a woman who faints?' 'Charge it to her like breakages,' the Minister replied. 'She won’t faint again.' Shortly after, Mrs. Umney regained consciousness.

I encountered various funeral processions; they were sparsely followed by mourners and viewed by onlookers as signs of terrible misfortune. Some watched these corteges with frantic intensity, others retreated in fear, and some sobbed openly. Adrian’s primary goal, beyond providing immediate aid to the ill, was to conceal the plague’s symptoms and advancement from London’s citizens. He understood that terror and gloomy expectations greatly aided the sickness, as despair made the human body uniquely vulnerable to contagion. Consequently, no unsightly scenes were visible; shops generally remained open, and a level of pedestrian traffic was maintained. Yet, despite the avoidance of a typical plague-stricken city’s appearance, London seemed significantly altered to me, having not seen it since the outbreak began. Carriages were absent, tall grass grew in the thoroughfares, houses looked abandoned, most shutters were drawn, and the people I passed wore a ghastly, fearful expression, quite unlike the usual industrious manner of Londoners. My lone carriage drew attention as it clattered toward the Protectoral Palace, and the elite streets approaching it appeared even more desolate. I discovered Adrian’s antechamber packed, as it was his time for receiving visitors. Reluctant to interrupt his work, I waited, observing the flow of petitioners. They were mostly from the middle and lower classes, whose livelihoods had vanished with the halt of commerce and the nation’s typical obsession with profit. The newcomers displayed an air of anxiety or terror, which stood in sharp contrast to the resigned, even content, expressions of those who had already been seen. I recognized my friend’s influence in their brisk movements and brightened faces. When the clock struck two, no more were admitted; those turned away departed sullenly or in sorrow, while I proceeded into the audience chamber. I was impressed by the improvement in Adrian’s health. He no longer stooped like a fragile spring flower, which, having grown too rapidly, is burdened by its own blooms. His eyes were clear, his expression calm, and a sense of focused vigor radiated from him, a stark change from his previous lethargy. He sat at a desk with several secretaries organizing petitions or recording notes from the day’s sessions. A few petitioners remained. I marveled at his fairness and patience. He advised those with the means to live outside London to depart at once, providing them with the necessary resources to do so.

Do not assume I failed to see the inherent trouble in it. You can be certain they were perfectly comfortable. I might not like them more for that. So many women and children have no right to be comfortable on a ship. My dear Frederick, you are speaking nonsense. What would become of us sailors' wives, who often need to reach our husbands at different ports, if everyone shared your views? My views did not stop me from taking Mrs. Harville and her family to Plymouth. I hate hearing you talk like some posh gentleman, treating women as if they were delicate dolls rather than rational beings. None of us expect smooth sailing our entire lives. My dear, when he has a wife, he will change his tune. If we are lucky enough to see another war, we will see him act just as we have, grateful to anyone who brings his wife to him. Indeed we shall. I am finished, Captain Wentworth said. Once married people start telling me I will think differently when I am married, I can only say I will not, and they insist I will, and that is the end of it. He stood and walked away. You must have been a great traveler, ma'am, Mrs. Musgrove said to Mrs. Croft. Quite a bit in my fifteen years of marriage, though many have done more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times and been to the East Indies and back, along with time in Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. I never went past the Straits or to the West Indies. We do not consider Bermuda or the Bahamas to be the West Indies, you know. Mrs. Musgrove had no response, as she had never called them anything else in her life. I assure you, ma'am, Mrs. Croft continued, that nothing beats the accommodations on a warship, specifically the larger ones. On a frigate, you are more confined, but any reasonable woman can be perfectly happy there. I can safely say the happiest years of my life were spent on a ship. As long as we were together, there was nothing to fear.

It was Lady Windermere’s final party before Easter, and Bentinck House was packed. Six Cabinet Ministers arrived wearing their official honors, fashionable women displayed their finest gowns, and Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe stood in the picture gallery. She was a heavy-set woman with small black eyes and stunning emeralds, speaking loud, broken French and laughing at everything. The crowd was a strange mix. Wealthy noblewomen spoke with radical politicians, famous preachers mingled with skeptics, bishops followed a lead singer, and artists filled the rooms. It was a successful night, and the Princess stayed until nearly midnight. Once she left, Lady Windermere went to the gallery, where a political economist was lecturing a frustrated Hungarian musician on music theory, and she began speaking with the Duchess of Paisley. Lady Windermere looked beautiful, with her ivory skin, blue eyes, and thick golden hair. Her hair was a rich, deep gold that framed her face like a saint’s, yet held the charm of a sinner. She was a complex person. Early on, she learned that nothing appears as innocent as a minor scandal, and through various harmless adventures, she had earned a reputation that allowed her to do as she pleased. She had been married three times, but because she kept the same lover, society stopped gossiping about her. At forty, she remained childless and possessed a relentless desire for pleasure that kept her looking young. Suddenly, she scanned the room and asked in her clear voice, Where is my palm reader? Your what, Gladys? the Duchess asked, startled. My palm reader, Duchess; I cannot live without him right now. Dear Gladys, you are always so unique, the Duchess replied, trying to figure out what a palm reader was while hoping it was not a foot doctor. He examines my hand twice a week, Lady Windermere continued, and he is fascinating.

Mary avoided writing to Bath, leaving the burden of a tedious, unproductive correspondence with Elizabeth entirely to Anne. Shortly after breakfast, Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick arrived to join them for a final stroll through Lyme, as the group intended to depart for Uppercross by one o'clock and wished to spend their remaining time outdoors. Once they reached the street, Captain Benwick gravitated toward Anne. Their previous evening's discussion had encouraged him to seek her out again, and they walked for a while, debating the works of Scott and Byron with the same lack of consensus common to all readers. Eventually, the party shifted, and Captain Harville took Benwick's place at her side. Miss Elliot, he murmured, you have done a kindness by drawing that poor man into conversation. I wish he had such company more frequently. It is unhealthy for him to remain so isolated, yet we cannot bear to part. Anne agreed that separation seemed impossible, though she suggested that time might eventually ease his suffering, reminding him that his friend was still a recent mourner, having lost his partner only last summer. Indeed, he sighed, it was only June. And perhaps he did not learn of it immediately, she added. Not until August, when he returned from the Cape newly promoted to the Grappler, Harville explained. I was in Plymouth, dreading the task of informing him. He sent letters, but the Grappler was bound for Portsmouth. I could not bring myself to break the news; no one could have done it but that fine fellow, he said, gesturing toward Captain Wentworth. The Laconia had arrived in Plymouth, so he was free from immediate duty. He requested leave but, without waiting for a reply, traveled day and night to Portsmouth, rowed out to the Grappler, and stayed by his friend's side for a week. That is what he did; no one else could have saved poor James. You can imagine, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us. Anne reflected on this with absolute certainty and offered a reply that matched her own sentiments and his capacity to hear them, for he was too moved to continue the topic, and their subsequent conversation turned to entirely different matters.

A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired companion were riding through Brockley meadows when she snagged her riding habit on a hedge. Upon returning, she decided to use the back stairs to avoid being spotted. Passing the open door of the Tapestry Chamber, she thought she saw her mother’s maid and peered inside to request a repair. To her shock, she found the Canterville Ghost sitting by the window, gazing at the decaying autumn foliage. He appeared so dejected and disheveled that Virginia, initially inclined to flee, felt a surge of sympathy and resolved to console him. Her approach was so quiet and his sorrow so profound that he did not notice her until she spoke. I am sorry for you, she said, but my brothers return to Eton tomorrow, and if you act properly, no one will bother you. It is ridiculous to ask me to behave, he replied, turning in surprise toward the girl. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and wander at night; it is my sole purpose. That is no reason to exist, and you know you have been wicked, she countered. Mrs. Umney told us you murdered your wife. I admit it, the Ghost said peevishly, but that was a private family affair. Killing someone is wrong, Virginia insisted with a touch of Puritan solemnity. I despise such moralizing, he retorted. My wife was plain, failed to starch my ruffs, and was a poor cook. She even ruined a magnificent buck I had shot in Hogley Woods. Regardless, it is over now, though I still think it was unkind of her brothers to starve me to death in retaliation.

My father had been the center of my existence, and his memory remained the life of my life. While I could feel gratitude toward others, I could no longer love or hope as I once had; everything was suffering, and even my pleasures were merely endured rather than enjoyed. I felt like a lonely valley surrounded by steep, dark cliffs, where no warmth could reach and there was no path to brighter lands. Consequently, while friendship offered temporary comfort, it could not restore me. It arrived like a fleeting visit, and when it left, I barely noticed. The spark of life was extinguished within me, so do not be surprised that I neither welcomed the gift of a friend with joy nor mourned its departure with bitterness. My friend was named Woodville. I will briefly share his story so you may understand how cold my heart must have been to remain unmoved by his eloquence and sympathy, and how, as we were both deeply unhappy, we might have been a mutual comfort had I not been turned to stone by the misery I endured. Woodville’s misfortunes were not as profound as mine; his was a natural grief that served to purify rather than destroy, and he would eventually emerge brighter and happier once the shadow passed. Woodville was the son of a poor clergyman and had received a classical education. He was one of the rare few favored by fortune from birth, gifted with boundless intellect and charm, and protected from even the slightest imperfection or disappointment. His mind seemed crafted of pure excellence, and his understanding was beyond error. His genius was transcendent, rising like a bright star that drew everyone’s admiration. He was a poet, though that title is often degraded and fails to capture his true nature. He resembled the poets of antiquity, crowned by the muses at birth. Walking among men, he seemed surrounded by a heavenly aura that set him apart. His striking beauty, the intense fire in his eyes, and his captivating words left listeners in silent, ecstatic wonder, making everyone else seem merely like attendants to his superior excellence.

I summon you, spirits of the departed and agents of retribution, to assist and guide my mission. May that damned, infernal creature suffer profound torment; let him experience the hopelessness that now consumes me. I commenced this plea with gravity and a reverence that convinced me the ghosts of my slain companions witnessed and sanctioned my dedication, yet fury seized me by the end, stifling my voice. A harsh, demonic laugh broke the nocturnal silence. It echoed deeply, reverberating through the mountains until I felt surrounded by the mockery of hell. I might have succumbed to madness and ended my wretched life then, had I not known my oath was acknowledged and that I was destined for revenge. The laughter faded, replaced by a familiar, loathsome whisper near my ear: I am content, pathetic creature! You have chosen to survive, and that satisfies me. I lunged toward the sound, but the fiend slipped away. Suddenly, the moon emerged, illuminating his hideous, twisted form as he fled with supernatural velocity. I chased him, and this has been my occupation for many months. Following a faint trail, I tracked the Rhone to no avail. Upon reaching the Mediterranean, I chanced to see the monster board a ship destined for the Black Sea. I secured passage on the same vessel, yet he vanished once more. Across the wilderness of Tartary and Russia, I have relentlessly pursued his path. Occasionally, terrified peasants reported his movements; at other times, he left signs himself, fearing that losing his trail would drive me to despair. As snow fell, I traced his massive footprints across the frozen plains. To you, just beginning your journey and unacquainted with true suffering, how can I explain my agony? Hunger, cold, and exhaustion were minor trials; I carried my own internal hell. Yet, a benevolent force guided me, rescuing me from impossible situations whenever I faltered. When my body collapsed from starvation, I would miraculously find sustenance in the wasteland to restore my strength.

His sunburnt face was mostly obscured by a thick beard and mustache. He carried a heavy oak club but seemed to have no other weapons. He bowed awkwardly and greeted us in French, which, despite a regional accent, clearly marked him as a Parisian. Sit down, my friend, Dupin said. I assume you are here about the orangutan. I almost envy you for owning such a fine and valuable animal. How old do you think he is? The sailor sighed with relief and replied confidently, I cannot say for sure, but he is likely no more than four or five years old. Do you have him here? Oh no, we had no place to keep him. He is at a stable on Rue Dubourg nearby. You can collect him in the morning. I assume you are prepared to prove ownership? Certainly, sir. I will be sorry to lose him, Dupin remarked. I do not expect you to go to this trouble for nothing, the man said. I am happy to pay a reasonable reward for his recovery. Well, my friend replied, that is fair. Let me think. I will tell you what I want. My reward shall be all the information you can provide regarding the murders on Rue Morgue. Dupin spoke these last words quietly. He then walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. He calmly pulled a pistol from his coat and placed it on the table. The sailor turned red and struggled to breathe. He jumped up and grabbed his club, but immediately collapsed back into his chair, shaking and pale as death. He remained silent. I felt truly sorry for him. My friend, Dupin said kindly, you are worrying for no reason. We mean you no harm. I give you my word as a gentleman and a Frenchman that we intend no injury. I know you are innocent of the crimes on Rue Morgue, but you cannot deny that you are involved in some way.

Four days later, a funeral procession left Canterville Chase at eleven o’clock at night. A hearse pulled by eight black horses wearing ostrich plumes carried a leaden coffin draped in a purple cloth embroidered with the family crest. Servants walked alongside holding torches, creating a solemn scene. Lord Canterville, who traveled from Wales, served as chief mourner and rode in the first carriage with Virginia. The American Minister and his wife followed, then Washington and the boys, with Mrs. Umney in the final carriage, as she had earned the right to witness the ghost’s final rest after fifty years of fear. The Reverend Augustus Dampier conducted the service at a grave beneath an old yew tree. Once the ceremony concluded, the servants put out their torches. As the coffin was lowered, Virginia placed a cross of almond blossoms upon it. The moon emerged from the clouds, bathing the churchyard in silver light while a nightingale sang nearby. Remembering the ghost’s words about the Garden of Death, Virginia wept silently and remained quiet during the trip home. The following morning, Mr. Otis spoke with Lord Canterville about the jewels the ghost had given Virginia. They were magnificent, particularly a sixteenth-century ruby necklace, and Mr. Otis felt uneasy about his daughter keeping such valuable items. He told Lord Canterville that the jewels should rightfully belong to the family estate. He insisted that the peer take them back to London, noting that Virginia was still a child with no need for such expensive luxuries.

Count Rouvaloff stared at him in disbelief. Realizing he was serious, he wrote an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and handed it across the table. Scotland Yard would pay a fortune for this address, he remarked. Lord Arthur laughed and promised they would never get it. After shaking the Russian’s hand, he hurried downstairs, checked the address, and ordered his coachman to drive to Soho Square. He dismissed the carriage there and walked down Greek Street until he reached Bayle’s Court. Passing under the archway, he entered a dead-end alley filled with clotheslines and fluttering white laundry. He walked to the end and knocked on a small green house. After a delay, during which curious neighbors peered from every window, a rough-looking man opened the door and asked his business in broken English. Lord Arthur handed him the paper. The man bowed and led him into a shabby front room. Moments later, Herr Winckelkopf bustled in, wearing a wine-stained napkin around his neck and holding a fork. Lord Arthur bowed and introduced himself as Robert Smith, explaining he needed an explosive clock. The German laughed and said he was charmed to meet Lord Arthur, noting he had seen him at Lady Windermere’s. He invited Lord Arthur to join him for breakfast, offering him pâté and excellent Rhine wine. Surprised to be recognized, Lord Arthur sat in the back room, sipping wine from a fine glass and chatting with the famous conspirator. Explosive clocks are poor exports, Winckelkopf explained, because even if they clear customs, the unreliable train schedules usually cause them to detonate before reaching their destination.

Abruptly, Mr. Podgers released Lord Arthur’s right hand and grasped his left, stooping so close that his spectacles nearly brushed the skin. His expression briefly turned deathly pale, yet he quickly regained his composure. Looking toward Lady Windermere, he offered a strained smile and remarked that it was the hand of a delightful young man. Lady Windermere agreed, though she questioned whether he would make a delightful husband. Mr. Podgers insisted all such men do, while Lady Jedburgh mused that excessive fascination in a husband was perilous. Dismissing this, Lady Windermere demanded specific predictions regarding Lord Arthur’s future. Mr. Podgers foretold a voyage in the coming months, which Lady Windermere immediately identified as a honeymoon, followed by the loss of a relative. When Lady Jedburgh worried for his sister, Mr. Podgers clarified it was merely a distant relation. Lady Windermere expressed disappointment, noting that distant relatives were unfashionable and provided little gossip for Sybil. She suggested Sybil keep a black silk dress ready for church, then urged everyone to supper, fretting over the chef’s political distractions. The Duchess, declaring herself thoroughly entertained by the palmist, eventually made her way downstairs with Sir Thomas’s assistance, narrowly avoiding dropping her belongings. Meanwhile, Lord Arthur Savile stood by the hearth, gripped by a profound sense of impending doom. He watched his sister pass by in her finery, barely registering Lady Windermere’s summons. His thoughts remained fixed on Sybil Merton, and the fear of their separation filled his eyes with tears.

Reviewing his letter while drafting a reply softened Harriet so much that she needed firm reminders to stay resolute. She felt terrible about causing him pain and worried deeply about his family’s opinion, fearing they might think her ungrateful. Emma suspected that if the young man had appeared right then, Harriet would have accepted him. However, the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was secure. She remained subdued all evening, but Emma tolerated her gentle regrets, occasionally easing them by affirming their friendship or steering the conversation toward Mr. Elton. I will never be invited to Abbey-Mill again, Harriet said sadly. Even if you were, I could not bear to part with you, my dear Harriet. You are far too essential at Hartfield to be spared. And I am sure I would never want to go there; I am only happy at Hartfield. Later, she added, I think Mrs. Goddard would be shocked if she knew what happened. Miss Nash certainly would, as she considers her own sister well-married, even though he is just a linen-draper. One would hate to see more pride or refinement in a schoolteacher, Harriet. I suspect Miss Nash would envy your opportunity to marry. Even this conquest would seem valuable to her. As for anything better for you, she is surely unaware. The attentions of a certain person are likely not yet the subject of Highbury gossip. I believe you and I are the only ones who have noticed his behavior. Harriet blushed and smiled, wondering why people liked her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton was encouraging, yet she soon felt sympathetic toward the rejected Mr. Martin again. Now he has my letter, she whispered. I wonder what they are doing, if his sisters know, and if he is miserable. I hope he will not take it too hard. Let us focus on our absent friends who are more happily occupied, Emma urged. Perhaps Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his family right now, explaining how much more beautiful the original is, and after much pleading, finally revealing your name—your own dear name.

I do not have the nerves for this kind of thing. But could you really be comfortable spending the entire evening away from the poor boy? Yes, his father can do it, so why shouldn't I? Jemima is very careful and could send us updates every hour. I really think Charles should have told his father we would all come. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terrified yesterday, but today is different. Well, if you do not think it is too late to let them know, why not go with your husband? Leave little Charles in my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot object while I am here with him. Are you serious? Mary asked, her eyes lighting up. That is a wonderful idea. I might as well go, since I am of no use at home and it only stresses me out. You, lacking a mother's instincts, are the most suitable person to stay. You can make little Charles do anything; he always listens to you. It will be much better than leaving him with only Jemima. I will certainly go; I should, just as much as Charles, since they really want me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being alone. What an excellent thought, Anne. I will tell Charles and get ready immediately. You can send for us if anything happens, but I am sure there will be no cause for alarm. I would not go if I were not completely at ease about my dear child. A moment later, she was knocking on her husband's door. As Anne followed her upstairs, she overheard the entire conversation, which began with Mary saying triumphantly, I am going with you, Charles, because I am no more useful at home than you are. If I stayed locked up with the child forever, I could never convince him to do anything he disliked. Anne is staying; she offered to stay and look after him. It was her own idea, so I will go with you, which is much better, as I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday. That is very kind of Anne, her husband replied, and I would be glad to have you come, but it seems unfair that she should be left alone to nurse our sick child.

You might not know me unless you have read The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that does not matter. Mark Twain wrote that book, and he mostly told the truth, though he exaggerated a few things. Everyone lies occasionally, except perhaps Aunt Polly, the widow, or Mary. Those people are all featured in that book, which is largely accurate despite the embellishments. The story ends with Tom and me discovering the robbers' hidden treasure in the cave, which made us wealthy. We each received six thousand dollars in gold, a staggering amount. Judge Thatcher invested it for us, earning us a dollar a day each, which was more than we knew how to spend. The Widow Douglas adopted me and tried to civilize me, but living in her house was difficult because she was so incredibly rigid and proper. Eventually, I could not stand it anymore, so I ran away, put on my old rags, and returned to my sugar barrel, feeling free and content. However, Tom Sawyer found me and promised that if I returned to the widow and acted respectable, I could join his new band of robbers. So, I went back. The widow cried over me, calling me a poor lost lamb and other names, though she meant no harm. She forced me back into those new clothes, which made me sweat and feel restricted. The old routine resumed: she rang a bell for supper, and I had to be punctual. At the table, I had to wait for her to say grace over the food, even though there was nothing wrong with it, other than everything being cooked separately. I prefer when food is mixed together so the flavors blend. After dinner, she read to me about Moses and the bulrushes. I was interested at first, but when she mentioned that Moses had been dead for a long time, I lost interest, as I have no use for dead people.

Then, we constructed a wire barrier. A wire barrier? Indeed. You suggested it yourself a few years back. Ah, I recall—when the Church first challenged us and decided to delay for a better opportunity. How did you set it up? I ran twelve heavy, uninsulated wires from a cave dynamo, which lacks brushes save for a positive and negative one. Correct. The wires exit the cave to enclose a hundred-yard circle of flat land, forming twelve separate rings spaced ten feet apart, returning to the cave at their ends. Proceed. The wires are secured to sturdy oak posts spaced three feet apart, buried five feet deep. That is quite robust. Yes. The wires lack external ground connections. They emerge from the positive brush, while the negative brush provides the ground; the wire ends return to the cave and are grounded separately. No, that is inefficient. Why? It wastes power. You only need the ground connection via the negative brush. Each wire must return to the cave independently without grounding. Consider the savings: a cavalry charge hits the fence, yet you expend no power until the horses touch the wire, completing the circuit through the ground and falling instantly. Your energy remains stored like a loaded gun, costing nothing until triggered. Of course, I missed that. It is cheaper and more effective, as broken wires cause no issues. Especially with a cave monitor to disconnect damaged lines. Continue. The Gatlings? They are ready. I have mounted thirteen Gatling guns on a six-foot platform in the center, fully stocked with ammunition. Perfect. They cover every angle, and when the Church’s knights appear, it will be quite a spectacle. And the cliff above the cave? I have installed a wire fence and a Gatling gun there.

In my youth, dissatisfaction never troubled me, and whenever boredom struck, the beauty of nature or the brilliance of human achievement could always stir my heart and lift my spirits. Now, however, I am like a lightning-struck tree; the blow has pierced my soul. I realized then that I would endure only to display what I would soon no longer be: a wretched example of ruined humanity, pathetic to others and unbearable to myself. We spent significant time in Oxford, wandering its surroundings and trying to pinpoint locations linked to the most stirring periods of English history. Our explorations were frequently extended by the various sights we encountered. We saw the grave of the famous Hampden and the battlefield where that patriot died. For a fleeting moment, my spirit rose above its degrading fears to reflect on the noble concepts of liberty and sacrifice that these sites commemorated. I briefly dared to cast off my burdens and view the world with a liberated mind, but the scars ran too deep, and I collapsed once more into my trembling, hopeless state. We departed Oxford reluctantly and traveled to Matlock, our next stop. The landscape near this village somewhat mirrored the scenery of Switzerland, though on a smaller scale, lacking the distant, snow-capped peaks that grace the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We toured the remarkable cave and the small natural history displays, where the artifacts were arranged much like those in Servox and Chamounix. Hearing Henry speak the latter name made me shudder, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which had become linked to that horrific memory. Continuing north from Derby, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine I was back among the Swiss Alps. The patches of snow clinging to the northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all familiar and cherished sights. We also met acquaintances here who nearly tricked me into feeling happy. Clerval’s joy was even greater than mine; his intellect flourished among talented people, and he discovered within himself capabilities and strengths he had never realized while in the company of those less gifted.

Soon his voice called out, asking how much further he had to go. Legrand asked how high he was, and Jupiter replied that he was very high, able to see the sky through the treetops. Legrand told him to ignore the sky and count the limbs he had passed on his side of the trunk. Jupiter counted five. Legrand instructed him to climb one limb higher. Soon, Jupiter announced he had reached the seventh. Legrand, clearly excited, told him to crawl out as far as he could on that limb and report anything unusual. By now, I was convinced of my friend's insanity and worried about getting him home. Jupiter called down, saying he was afraid to venture far because the limb was mostly dead. Legrand asked in a trembling voice if it was truly dead, and Jupiter confirmed it was completely rotten. Legrand expressed great distress, so I intervened, urging him to come home and rest as he had promised. Ignoring me, Legrand asked Jupiter to test the wood with his knife.
