Jupiter replied that while it was rotten, it might hold his weight if he dropped the heavy bug first. Legrand, suddenly relieved, angrily threatened to break Jupiter's neck if he dropped the beetle. When Jupiter complained about being shouted at, Legrand promised him a silver dollar if he crawled out safely while keeping hold of the insect.

He crept out from the wall with a cruel smile. The moon hid behind a cloud as he passed the large window, where his family crest and that of his murdered wife were displayed in blue and gold. He glided forward like a dark shadow, as if the night itself rejected him. He paused when he heard a sound, but it was only a dog barking at the Red Farm. He continued on, muttering old curses and waving his rusty dagger. Finally, he reached the hallway leading to Washington’s room. He stopped, the wind blowing his grey hair and twisting his burial shroud into strange shapes. When the clock struck the quarter-hour, he knew it was time. He chuckled and turned the corner, but immediately recoiled with a cry of terror, hiding his pale face in his bony hands. Standing before him was a horrific ghost, still as a statue and monstrous as a nightmare. Its head was bald, its face round and white, and its features were frozen in a permanent, hideous grin. Red light streamed from its eyes, its mouth was like a pit of fire, and it wore a shroud similar to his own. On its chest was a sign with strange, ancient writing—a list of sins or a record of crimes—and it held a gleaming steel sword in its right hand. Having never seen a ghost before, he was terrified. After one quick look, he fled back to his room, tripping over his long shroud and dropping his dagger into the Minister’s boots, where the butler found it the next morning. Once inside his room, he threw himself onto his bed and hid under the covers. Eventually, his brave spirit returned, and he decided to speak to the other ghost at daybreak. As dawn touched the hills, he went back to where he had seen the phantom, thinking that two ghosts were better than one and that his new ally might help him deal with the twins.

Oh, I misunderstood. I thought you said anybody, and I assumed that meant everyone. It does, provided they are of noble birth, preferably royal. That seems reasonable, the abbot said, eager to keep the peace. It is unlikely such a gift would reveal the affairs of commoners. Our King Arthur— Would you like to know of him? the enchanter interrupted. Most gladly, the abbot replied. The crowd was immediately captivated again, those hopeless fools. They watched the magic intently, casting smug looks at me when the announcement came: The king is tired from the hunt and has been sleeping soundly in his palace for two hours. God bless him, the abbot said, crossing himself. May he find rest for body and soul. If he were actually sleeping, that might be true, I said, but the king is not sleeping; he is riding. Tension flared as the group struggled to choose who to believe, as I still held some credibility. The magician sneered, saying he had seen many prophets, but never one who could see the truth without performing a ritual. You have lived in the woods too long, I replied. I use rituals myself, as this brotherhood knows, but only when necessary. I knew how to hold my own in a war of words, and that barb made him squirm. When the abbot asked about the queen and the court, the magician claimed they were all overcome by fatigue and sleeping like the king. That is another lie, I said. Half of them are busy with their amusements, and the queen and the others are riding. Perhaps you can show off a bit more and tell us where they are headed? They are sleeping now, he insisted, but tomorrow they will ride toward the sea. And where will they be by sunset the day after? Far north of Camelot, with half their journey complete. That is another lie, off by a hundred and fifty miles.

He crept from the wall with a malicious smirk on his withered lips. The moon vanished behind a cloud as he slipped past the large bay window, which displayed his family crest and that of his murdered wife in blue and gold. He glided forward like a dark shadow, as if the night itself recoiled from his presence. He paused at a sound, but it was merely a dog barking at the Red Farm. Muttering archaic curses and waving his rusted dagger, he reached the hallway leading to Washington’s room. He stopped, the wind whipping his grey hair and twisting his burial shroud into grotesque shapes. As the clock struck the quarter-hour, he knew the moment had arrived. He chuckled and turned the corner, only to recoil with a cry of terror, shielding his pale face with bony hands. Before him stood a horrific specter, still as a statue and monstrous as a fever dream. Its head was bald and polished, its face round, fat, and white, twisted into a permanent, hideous grin. Scarlet light poured from its eyes, its mouth was a pit of fire, and a shroud like his own draped its massive frame. A placard on its chest bore strange, ancient writing—a record of sins and crimes. In its right hand, it held a gleaming steel sword. Having never encountered a ghost, he was terrified. After one glance, he fled down the corridor, tripping over his winding-sheet and dropping his dagger into the Minister’s boots, where the butler later found it. Safely in his room, he collapsed onto his bed and hid under the covers. Eventually, his courageous spirit returned, and he resolved to speak to the other ghost at daybreak. As dawn touched the hills, he returned to the spot, deciding that two ghosts were better than one and that his new ally might help him deal with the twins.

The thought that once sustained my early career now only drags me into the dirt. My ambitions and hopes are worthless; like the archangel who sought total power, I am bound in an endless hell. My imagination was sharp, matched by my analytical focus, and together these traits allowed me to conceive and create a man. I still recall with intense emotion the daydreams I had while the work was unfinished. I felt divine, exulting in my abilities and the potential impact of my discovery. I was raised with grand expectations, but how far I have fallen! My friend, if you had known me before, you would not recognize me in this ruined state. I rarely felt hopeless; a great destiny seemed to guide me, until I fell, never to rise again. Must I lose this remarkable man? I have long sought a friend who would sympathize with and love me. Here, on these desolate seas, I have found one, yet I fear I have only gained him to realize his worth before losing him. I want to convince him to live, but he rejects the idea. I thank you, Walton, he said, for your kindness toward such a miserable wretch. But when you speak of new bonds, do you think anyone can replace those I have lost? Can any man be to me what Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth? Even when feelings are not deeply stirred by exceptional character, childhood companions hold a power over our minds that later friends rarely achieve. They understand our early nature, which, though modified by time, is never erased; they can judge our actions with a clearer understanding of our true motives. A sibling can never suspect the other of deceit unless it was evident early on, whereas a new friend, no matter how devoted, may inevitably be viewed with suspicion. I enjoyed friends who were dear not just through habit, but for their own merits. Wherever I go, the gentle voice of my Elizabeth and the conversation of Clerval will echo in my ears. They are dead, and only one purpose could convince me to stay alive in this solitude. If I were committed to a noble goal of great benefit to humanity, I could live to see it through.

He let her know that Frank admired her greatly, finding her both beautiful and charming. Given his many positive qualities, she felt she could not judge him too severely. As Mrs. Weston noted, all young people have their quirks. However, one person in Surrey was not so forgiving. While most people in Donwell and Highbury were generous toward such a handsome, polite young man, Mr. Knightley remained unmoved by his charm. When he heard the news at Hartfield, he stayed silent at first, but Emma soon heard him mutter to himself while reading the paper, "Just the silly, trifling fellow I thought he was." She considered taking offense, but realized he was merely venting his own frustration rather than trying to provoke her, so she let it go. Although the Westons brought some disappointing news, their visit was timely. Emma needed advice on a matter, and they provided exactly the guidance she sought. The Coles, a friendly and unpretentious family, had lived in Highbury for years. Though they came from a modest background in trade, their recent business success had significantly increased their wealth. They expanded their home, hired more staff, and began living in a style second only to the Hartfield family. Their new dining room and social ambitions suggested they would soon start hosting dinner parties. Emma doubted they would dare invite the area's most prominent families, such as those from Donwell, Hartfield, or Randalls. She was determined not to attend if invited, though she worried her father’s predictable habits would make her refusal seem less significant than she intended.

He stood and left the room with my nurse, and my father entered immediately. Nothing could have pleased me more than his arrival. I reached out my hand and cried, "Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?" My father calmed me with assurances of their well-being, trying to lift my spirits by focusing on them, but he soon realized a prison cannot be a place of cheer. "What a place you are in, my son!" he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the room's wretched state. "You traveled to find happiness, but a curse seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—" The mention of my murdered friend was too much for my fragile state; I wept. "Alas, yes, Father," I replied. "Some horrible destiny hangs over me, and I must live to fulfill it, or I would have died on Henry's coffin." We were not allowed to talk long, as my health required constant rest. Mr. Kirwin arrived and insisted I not exhaust myself. Yet, my father's presence felt like a guardian angel, and I slowly recovered. As my sickness faded, I was consumed by a dark, unshakable melancholy. Clerval’s ghastly, murdered image was always before me. My agitation often made my friends fear a relapse. Why did they preserve such a miserable life? It must be to fulfill my destiny, which is now nearing its end. Soon, death will extinguish this anguish and grant me rest. Back then, death seemed distant, though I often sat for hours, motionless, wishing for some catastrophe to bury both me and my destroyer. The trial approached. I had been imprisoned for three months, and though still weak, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county town for court. Mr. Kirwin took charge of gathering witnesses and preparing my defense.

I would gladly share much more, but I must be brief to secure my reward. I long to return home. In exchange for the insights I can provide regarding physical and metaphysical science, I ask your honorable body to grant me a pardon for the deaths of my creditors when I left Rotterdam. This is the purpose of my letter. Its bearer, a lunar inhabitant I have instructed to act as my messenger, will wait for your decision and return with the pardon if it can be secured. I remain your humble servant, Hans Pfaall. Upon reading this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub reportedly dropped his pipe in shock. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk removed his spectacles, wiped them, and, forgetting his dignity, spun around three times in sheer amazement. They agreed the pardon must be granted. Rub-a-dub swore it, and Von Underduk concurred as they walked home to plan their next steps. At the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor noted that since the messenger had vanished—likely terrified by the locals—the pardon was useless, as no one else would travel such a distance. The burgomaster agreed, and the matter ended. Rumors, however, persisted. The published letter sparked endless gossip. Some skeptics made fools of themselves by dismissing the entire affair as a hoax, a term they use for anything beyond their understanding. I fail to see the basis for their accusations. Let us examine their claims.

The following day was set for the confrontation to ensure our honor remained intact. Drummle arrived with a polite note from Estella confirming she had danced with him several times. I had no choice but to apologize for my previous outburst and retract my earlier claims. Drummle and I sat there glaring at each other for an hour while the rest of the group argued, eventually declaring that our relationship had improved significantly. I recount this casually, but it was deeply painful. It hurt to see Estella show any interest in such a clumsy, sullen, and inferior man. I believe my love for her was so selfless that I could not bear to see her lower herself to such a person. While I would have been miserable regardless of whom she chose, a more worthy man would have caused me less distress. I soon discovered that Drummle was pursuing her and she was allowing it. He followed her constantly, and we crossed paths daily. He persisted in his dull way, while Estella kept him on a string, alternating between encouragement and disdain, sometimes flattering him and other times acting as if she barely knew him. The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers called him, had the patience of a predator. His arrogant confidence in his wealth and family status served him well, often acting as a substitute for true ambition. By doggedly watching Estella, he outlasted more impressive suitors, ready to strike at the perfect moment. At an assembly ball in Richmond where Estella outshone everyone, Drummle hovered around her with her apparent permission. I decided I had to speak to her about him. I found my chance when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home, sitting alone among the flowers.

“Indeed, Mr. Bumble,” he finally remarked, “it is true that under the current dietary regulations, coffins have become somewhat slimmer and shallower than before; yet we require a margin of gain, Mr. Bumble. Quality wood is costly, and the iron fittings arrive by canal from Birmingham.” “True,” Mr. Bumble agreed, “every business has its difficulties. A reasonable profit is certainly justified.” “Naturally,” the undertaker answered, “and if I miss a gain on one item, I recover it eventually—he! he! he!” “Quite so,” said Mr. Bumble. “Still,” the undertaker added, returning to his previous point, “I face a significant challenge: the stouter individuals perish the fastest. Those who were once prosperous and paid taxes are the first to succumb upon entering the workhouse; and let me assure you, Mr. Bumble, a few extra inches beyond my estimate significantly diminishes my earnings, especially with a family to support.” As Mr. Sowerberry spoke with the righteous frustration of an aggrieved man, and Mr. Bumble sensed a slight against the parish’s integrity, the latter decided to shift the conversation. Oliver Twist being on his mind, he introduced the subject. “By the way,” Mr. Bumble inquired, “do you know anyone in need of a boy? A parish apprentice who is currently a burden, a millstone around the parish’s neck? The terms are generous, Mr. Sowerberry.” As he spoke, Mr. Bumble tapped his cane against the sign above, striking the words “five pounds” printed in large Roman letters. “Goodness!” the undertaker exclaimed, grasping the gold-trimmed lapel of the beadle’s coat, “that is precisely what I wished to discuss. You know—my word, what a refined button this is, Mr. Bumble! I had not noticed it previously.” “Yes, I find it quite handsome,” the beadle replied, looking down with pride at the large brass buttons adorning his coat. “The design matches the parish seal—the Good Samaritan tending to the wounded man. The board gifted it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I recall wearing it for the first time to attend the inquest for that impoverished tradesman who passed away in a doorway at midnight.”

Next, we built a wire fence. A wire fence? Yes. You suggested it yourself a few years back. I remember now—back when the Church first challenged us and decided to wait for a better opportunity. How did you set it up? I ran twelve heavy, uninsulated wires from a dynamo in the cave. The wires extend from the cave to enclose a hundred-yard circle of flat ground, forming twelve independent, concentric rings spaced ten feet apart, with their ends returning to the cave. The wires are secured to sturdy oak posts, spaced three feet apart and buried five feet deep. That is strong. The wires have no external ground connection. They run from the positive brush, while the negative brush provides the ground. Each wire returns to the cave and is grounded separately. No, that is inefficient. You only need one ground connection at the negative brush. Bring the other ends back to the cave without grounding them. Think of the savings: a cavalry charge hits the fence, and you spend no energy until the horses touch the wire. At that moment, they complete the circuit through the ground and drop dead. The power is stored like a loaded gun, costing nothing until triggered. You are right; I missed that. It is cheaper and safer if the wires break. Especially if we monitor them from the cave. What about the Gatling guns? They are set. In the center of the inner circle, on a six-foot platform, I have mounted thirteen Gatling guns with plenty of ammunition. Perfect. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, we will be ready. And the cliff above the cave? I have a wire fence and a Gatling gun there as well.

Do not misunderstand; I was never truly insane. I remained aware of my condition even when frantic thoughts pushed me toward madness, keeping them hidden in quiet isolation. Those around me noticed nothing of this. They merely observed a spirit-broken girl who spoke softly and shed hidden tears beneath lowered lashes. They saw someone who avoided company, shunned attention, and never smiled—that was all. Eventually, I fled. I departed my guardian’s home and vanished; based on the letters I left, it was assumed I had taken my own life. Consequently, the search for me was half-hearted, and I was soon forgotten. I sailed from London on a small ship heading north. Having succeeded, I found peace in my solitude. As the vessel glided over calm waters, I sat on deck beneath the sky, feeling transformed. I was no longer the frantic, wretched Mathilda, but a young recluse committed to a quiet life, striving to keep my heart free from turmoil and despair. My simple, nun-like attire, the secret of my survival, and the prospect of permanent isolation fostered a sense of calm in my wounded spirit. The breeze refreshed me, and I watched the sunlit waves and birds skimming the water with serene eyes. I slept without dreams and awoke to enjoy my peaceful liberty. Four days later, we reached our destination. I left the coast immediately, heading inland to a location I had already chosen. I sought a lonely house on a vast plain, far from any neighbors, where I could view the entire horizon and wander undisturbed. I was not a misanthrope, yet I knew my emotional stability required solitude. I settled in a desolate expanse, a rocky heath covered in sparse grass, marked only by a few rushes near a small pond.

“Well, Jupiter,” I remarked, “what is the trouble? How is your master?” “To tell the truth, sir, he is not as well as he might be.” “I am sorry to hear that. What are his symptoms?” “That is the point; he never complains of anything, yet he is quite ill.” “Very ill, Jupiter? Why didn’t you say so? Is he bedridden?” “No, he is not confined at all, and that is exactly what worries me about poor Master Will.” “I don’t follow you. You claim he is sick, but has he not told you what is wrong?” “Sir, please don’t be angry. Master Will insists nothing is the matter, but he walks around with his head down, shoulders hunched, and looking as pale as a ghost. He keeps scribbling ciphers on his slate—the strangest figures I have ever seen. I am frightened and must keep a close watch on his movements. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and was gone all day. I had a heavy stick ready to give him a sound thrashing when he returned, but I am such a fool that I lacked the heart; he looked so wretched.” “Indeed? I think it is best you are not too harsh with him. Do not strike him, Jupiter; he is in no state for it. Can you guess what caused this change in behavior? Has anything unpleasant occurred since I last saw you?” “No, sir, nothing since then. I fear it happened before, on the very day you visited.” “What do you mean?” “I mean the bug, sir.” “The what?” “The bug. I am certain Master Will was bitten on the head by that gold-bug.” “What makes you think that?” “Claws and a mouth, sir. I never saw such a devilish insect; it kicked and bit everything near it. Master Will caught it first but had to drop it quickly, and that must be when he was bitten. I didn’t like the look of its mouth, so I refused to touch it with my fingers, catching it with a piece of paper instead.”

Because e is so common, it is rare to find a long sentence that does not feature it prominently. This gives us a solid starting point for breaking the code. While this frequency table is useful, we only need it slightly for this specific puzzle. Since the number 8 is the most frequent character, we will assume it represents e. To confirm this, we look for instances where 8 appears in pairs, as e is frequently doubled in English words like meet, fleet, or seen. In this short message, 8 appears as a double five times. Let us proceed with 8 as e. The word the is the most common in our language, so we should look for a three-character sequence ending in 8. We find the sequence ;48 repeated seven times. We can reasonably assume that ; is t, 4 is h, and 8 is e. This is a significant breakthrough. With this word identified, we can determine the starts and ends of other words. For instance, looking at one of the ;48 combinations near the end of the code, we can identify five of the six following characters. By substituting our known letters, we get t eeth. We can rule out th as part of the first word because no logical word fits that pattern. This leaves us with t ee. By testing the remaining letters of the alphabet, we quickly determine that the word must be tree.

He stood up and left the room with my nurse, and my father entered immediately. Seeing him brought me immense relief. I reached out my hand and asked, "Are you safe? And Elizabeth and Ernest?" My father comforted me by confirming they were well, trying to lift my spirits by talking about them, but he soon realized that a prison is no place for cheerfulness. "What a place you are living in, my son!" he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the miserable room. "You traveled to find happiness, but bad luck seems to follow you. And poor Clerval—" The mention of my murdered friend was too much for my fragile state, and I began to cry. "Yes, Father," I replied. "Some horrible destiny hangs over me. I must live to fulfill it, or I would have died on Henry's coffin." We were not allowed to talk for long, as my poor health required rest. Mr. Kirwin arrived and insisted I not exhaust myself. Still, my father's presence felt like a blessing, and I slowly began to recover. As my physical illness faded, I was consumed by a dark, heavy depression that nothing could lift. The image of Clerval's murdered body haunted me constantly. My friends worried that my distress would cause a relapse. Why did they keep me alive in such misery? It must be to fulfill my destiny, which is now nearing its end. Soon, death will silence this pain and relieve the crushing weight of my grief. At that time, death still felt distant, though I often sat for hours in silence, wishing for some catastrophe to destroy both me and my enemy. The court date approached. I had been in prison for three months, and although I was still weak, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the town where the trial would be held. Mr. Kirwin took charge of gathering witnesses and preparing my defense.
